Preface


This volume is a companion to the fifth edition of The Philosophy of Viability. The main book
develops a systematic metaphysics of identity and manifestation on the four-column framework of
cognition. It does not engage in dialogue with the philosophical traditions; it states its principles,
argues for them, and draws their consequences, and it leaves the comparison with the traditions
to a separate inquiry. The present volume is that inquiry.
   The comparison is offered as a comparison, not as a justification. No principle of the
main book is justified by its resemblance to a tradition, and no tradition is adjudicated by its
resemblance to the framework. The two are different undertakings, and the present volume holds
them apart even as it brings them into conversation. The reader who seeks a demonstration
that the framework is confirmed by the traditions will not find one here; the reader who seeks a
demonstration that the traditions are refuted by the framework will also not find one. What
the reader will find is a comparison of structures: where the framework and a tradition share a
structural feature, where they diverge, what each can say to the other, and what each costs the
other.


Why the Dialogues Are a Separate Volume
The fourth edition of the main book included, as Part IX, a series of dialogues with ten
philosophical traditions. Those dialogues remain, and they have been expanded. They now form
the present volume, which is published independently.
   The reason for the separation is a matter of philosophical principle, not of convenience. The
main book is written under the following commitment:

      The validity of no philosophical principle in this book depends on confirmation from
      any outside domain. Its concepts and principles are to be assessed through structural
      precision, internal coherence, and philosophical argument.

   This commitment does not forbid comparison with traditions. It forbids using comparison
as a ground of justification. A dialogue that says “Ibn Sina held a similar view, therefore the
framework’s view is plausible” would violate the commitment. A dialogue that says “Ibn Sina
held a different view, and here is where the framework’s view differs and why” is historical
and comparative, and is permitted—but it belongs to a different genre from the systematic
reconstruction the main book offers.
   The dialogues are works of comparative philosophy. They presuppose the framework and
compare it with other positions. The framework itself presupposes nothing outside philosophy,
and stands on its own arguments. Keeping the two genres together in one volume encouraged a
misreading: that the framework’s authority rested, in part, on the traditions it compared itself
with. The fifth edition removes that misreading by separation, and the present volume is the
result.

                                                xlix
l                                                                                             Preface


    The reader who has not read the main book can still follow the present volume. Each dialogue
states the framework’s position on the question at issue, in the terms the main book establishes,
before it turns to the tradition. The reader who wishes to see the framework’s arguments in full
is directed to the main book; the reader who wishes to see the framework in conversation with
the traditions is directed to the present volume.


The Method of the Dialogues
Each dialogue in this volume follows the same method, and the method is stated in Part I. The
method has three components.


First component: the autonomy of philosophical justification. No principle of the
framework is justified by its resemblance to a tradition, and no tradition is adjudicated by its
resemblance to the framework. The dialogue is a comparison of structures, not a derivation of
either side from the other. Where the framework and a tradition share a structural feature, the
sharing is noted, but it is not offered as evidence for the framework, and it is not offered as a
confirmation of the tradition.


Second component: resemblance, not equivalence. Where the framework and a tradition
use the same word, or develop a similar structure, the relation is one of resemblance or kinship,
not of equivalence. The framework’s terms have the sense the framework gives them, and the
tradition’s terms have the sense the tradition gives them; the two senses are not the same, and
the dialogue keeps them apart. Each dialogue ends with a statement of the kind of relation
(resemblance, not equivalence) and with a statement of what would refute the framework’s
reading of the tradition.


Third component: the ten criteria of depth. Each dialogue satisfies ten criteria, stated in
Part I. It states the tradition’s position with reference to primary texts; it identifies the internal
disputes within the tradition; it identifies the points of convergence and divergence; it presents
the tradition’s strongest objections to the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states
what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; it states what would refute the
framework’s reading; and it states the questions the dialogue leaves open. A dialogue that fails
any of the ten criteria is incomplete, and the volume states the criteria so that the reader can
assess each dialogue by them.


The Scope of the Volume
The volume covers fifteen parts and eighty-five chapters, of which eighty are dialogues. The parts
are organized by tradition and, within each tradition, by period.


Part I: The Method of Dialogue. States the method, the kind of relation, and the ten
criteria of depth.
Preface                                                                                         li


Parts II–V: The West. The ancient West (Parmenides and Heraclitus, Plato, Aristotle,
Stoicism, Plotinus, Proclus); the medieval West (Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus,
Ockham, Eckhart, Nicholas of Cusa); the modern West (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke
and Hume, Kant, Hegel, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche); the contemporary West (Husserl, Heidegger,
Merleau-Ponty and Sartre, Gadamer and Ricoeur, Whitehead, Peirce and the pragmatists,
Wittgenstein, Quine and Davidson, Kripke and Lewis, Foucault and Habermas, Derrida and
Deleuze).

Parts VI–VII: Islam. Classical Islamic philosophy (al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, al-Ghazali,
Ibn Rushd, the Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya, Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Mulla Sadra, Ibn Khaldun);
contemporary Islamic philosophy (Iqbal, Tabatabai, Motahhari, Shariati, al-Sadr, Nasr, Fazlur
Rahman, Arkoun, Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman, Soroush).

Parts VIII–IX: India and Buddhism. Indian philosophy (the Upanishads, Samkhya and
Yoga, Nyaya and Vaisheshika, Shankara, Ramanuja, Aurobindo); Buddhist and Jain philosophy
(Nagarjuna, Yogacara, Buddhist logic, Jainism).

Parts X–XI: East Asia. Chinese philosophy (Confucius and Mencius, Laozi and Zhuangzi,
Mozi and Han Feizi, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, Chinese Buddhism); Japanese philosophy
(Shinto, Dogen and Shinran, the Kyoto School).

Part XII: Jewish Philosophy. Philo and Saadia, Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi, Maimonides,
Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas.

Part XIII: African and Latin American Philosophy. Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub,
contemporary African philosophy, Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy.

Part XIV: Other Traditions. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism, Gnosticism and Hermeticism.

Part XV: Open Horizons. Traditions mentioned in passing, and the open questions of
dialogue.
   The scope is large, and it is not complete. The volume states what it covers and what it
does not, and it marks the traditions it mentions in passing as mentions, not as dialogues. The
reader who seeks a tradition that the volume does not cover is invited to propose it; the volume’s
method is stated so that the proposal can be assessed.


On the Sources and the Source Codes
Each dialogue cites the tradition’s primary texts, and where relevant, the secondary literature.
The citations are given in footnotes, with a code of the form [Dn-m], where n is the chapter
number and m is the source number within that chapter. The same source cited in more than
one chapter receives a distinct code in each chapter, so that the reader can locate every citation
in its chapter context.
lii                                                                                           Preface


      The codes used in the footnotes are of the same form as the codes used in the main book, with
one difference: the main book uses [Cn-m] (where C stands for Chapter), and the present volume
uses [Dn-m] (where D stands for Dialogue). The difference in letter marks the difference in
genre: the main book’s citations are to sources that bear on its arguments; the present volume’s
citations are to sources that bear on its comparisons. Neither set of citations is a premise of any
argument, and no principle of either book depends on them.
      The bibliography at the end of the volume lists the sources cited in the footnotes, organized
by chapter, with the same codes. The reader who wishes to see a source in its bibliographic
context is directed to the bibliography; the reader who wishes to see the passage cited is directed
to the footnote.


On the Use of Terms
The volume uses the framework’s technical terms with the senses the framework gives them, and
it uses the traditions’ technical terms with the senses the traditions give them. Where the two
uses coincide in vocabulary but not in sense—for example, the word “light” in the framework
and in Suhrawardi, or the word “substance” in the framework and in Aristotle—the volume
marks the difference explicitly, and it does not import one sense into the other. The reader who
reads a tradition’s term in the framework’s sense, or the framework’s term in a tradition’s sense,
has misread the dialogue; the volume’s method is designed to prevent the misreading, and each
dialogue states where the misreading would occur.
      No term in this volume carries normative or ethical weight. Every term is defined structurally
or historically, and its sense is fixed by the definition or the historical context. Where a tradition
uses a term with normative weight—“the Good” in Plato, “justice” in the Mu’tazila, “dharma” in
Indian philosophy—the volume reports the tradition’s use and does not adopt it; the framework’s
terms are structural, and the volume keeps them so.


Reading Paths
The volume can be read in four ways.

The systematic reader. Read from beginning to end, in the order of the chapters. Part I
states the method; Parts II–XIV apply it to the traditions; Part XV states the open horizon.
This is the intended path, and it is the path that shows the volume’s architecture.

The tradition-specific reader. Read the part or chapter that concerns the tradition you
wish to study, and follow the cross-references backward to Part I for the method. Each dialogue
is written to be read on its own; the reader who enters in the middle will find the framework’s
position stated at the start of the dialogue, and the method’s requirements stated where they
bear on the dialogue’s argument.

The concept-specific reader. Read the dialogues that concern the concept you wish to study,
using the Index of Concepts to locate them. The Index of Concepts lists the framework’s concepts
Preface                                                                                        liii


(light, identity, manifestation, mediation, unity and multiplicity, relation and order, viability,
time, death, self-awareness) and, for each, the dialogues in which the concept is discussed.

The comparative reader. Read the dialogues that compare the framework with two or more
traditions on the same question—for example, the dialogues on light (Plato, Plotinus, Dionysius,
Suhrawardi, Shankara) or the dialogues on identity (Aristotle, Ibn Sina, Scotus, Locke and
Hume, Kripke and Lewis). The comparative reader will find that the dialogues are written to be
compared, and that the comparisons across traditions are as important as the comparisons with
the framework.


A Note on the Limits of the Volume
The volume is large, but it is not complete. Three limits must be stated.

First limit: the traditions not covered. The volume does not cover every tradition. It
covers the traditions that have developed the framework’s central concepts with sufficient depth
to sustain a dialogue. The traditions that are not covered—the indigenous philosophies of
North America and Oceania, the lesser-known schools of the traditions that are covered, the
contemporary philosophers who are not yet part of a recognized tradition—are mentioned in
Part XV, and the volume marks them as open questions rather than as dialogues.

Second limit: the depth of each dialogue. Each dialogue satisfies the ten criteria of depth,
but the depth is relative to the space available. A dialogue of twenty pages cannot exhaust a
tradition that has developed over centuries; it can state the tradition’s position on the question
at issue, identify the internal disputes, present the objections and the reply, and state the kind
of relation. The reader who wishes to go deeper is directed to the primary texts and to the
secondary literature cited in the footnotes.

Third limit: the kind of comparison. The volume compares structures, not doctrines. It
does not adjudicate the truth of a tradition’s theological or metaphysical positions, and it does
not claim that the framework’s positions are true because a tradition held a similar view. The
comparison is historical and structural; it is not justificatory, and it is not adjudicative. The
reader who seeks a judgment on which tradition is right will not find one here; the reader who
seeks a comparison of structures will find one.


A Note on the Fifth Edition
The present volume is new. The fourth edition of the main book included a series of dialogues
with ten traditions; the present volume expands those dialogues to eighty-five chapters (eighty
of them dialogues) and fifteen parts, adds the method of dialogue as Part I, and separates the
whole from the main book. The expansion is substantial, but the principle is unchanged: the
dialogues are comparative, not justificatory; they are offered as a comparison of structures, not
as a confirmation of the framework.

Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map


Scope of This Book

This volume is a work of comparative philosophy. It compares the framework of The Philosophy of
Viability with the philosophical traditions of West, Islam, and East, and it does so by bringing the
framework into dialogue with each tradition on the questions the framework addresses. It makes
no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Its subject is the structure of the comparison, and the
structural relations among the framework and the traditions; it does not adjudicate the truth of
any tradition’s theological or metaphysical positions, and it does not claim that the framework is
confirmed by its resemblances to the traditions. The reader who seeks a demonstration that the
framework is true because a tradition held a similar view will not find one here; the reader who
seeks a demonstration that a tradition is wrong because the framework differs from it will also
not find one. The book is a comparison of structures, offered as a comparison, and its worth is
to be measured by the coherence, the discrimination, and the depth of the comparisons it makes.



The Problem

The main book develops a systematic metaphysics of identity and manifestation on the four-
column framework of cognition. It states its principles, argues for them, and draws their
consequences. It does not engage in dialogue with the philosophical traditions; it treats them, at
most, in footnotes, and it leaves the comparison to a separate inquiry. The present volume is
that inquiry.
    The problem the volume addresses is not the truth of the framework. The main book addresses
that problem, and the reader who wishes to assess the framework’s arguments is directed there.
The problem the volume addresses is the framework’s relation to the traditions: where the
framework and a tradition share a structural feature, where they diverge, what each can say to
the other, and what each costs the other. The problem is comparative, not justificatory, and the
volume states it as such.
    The problem has three parts, and the volume treats them in turn.


First part: the framework’s relation to the traditions. Does the framework stand in
a relation to the traditions, or is it a free-standing construction? The framework’s concepts—
identity, manifestation, light, realm, context, expression, cost—are not invented ex nihilo. They
have ancestors in the traditions, and the volume’s task is to identify the ancestors, to say where
the framework agrees and where it diverges, and to state the kind of relation between the
framework’s concepts and the traditions’ concepts. The relation is one of resemblance or kinship,
not of equivalence; the volume states it as such, and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading of the tradition.

                                                 lv
lvi                                                                                    Introduction


Second part: the traditions’ relation to the framework. The traditions have their own
accounts of the questions the framework addresses. What do they say that the framework does
not? What does the framework say that they do not? The volume’s task is to bring the two
into conversation, to present the traditions’ strongest objections to the framework, to present
the framework’s reply, and to state what each side costs the other. The conversation is not a
competition; it is a comparison of structures, in which each side is given its strongest formulation
and its strongest objection.

Third part: the kind of dialogue. What kind of dialogue is possible between the framework
and a tradition? Is it a dialogue of agreement, in which the two sides say the same thing in
different words? Is it a dialogue of disagreement, in which the two sides are incompatible? Or is
it a dialogue of resemblance, in which the two sides share a structural feature without sharing
the concept? The volume’s answer is that the dialogue is of the third kind: resemblance, not
equivalence, not agreement, not disagreement. The answer is stated in Part I, and it governs
every dialogue in the volume.


The Method
The method of the volume is comparative, and the comparison is governed by three principles
and ten criteria. The three principles are stated in Part I; the ten criteria are stated in the same
part. The method is not a novelty of the volume; it is the method that the volume inherits from
the comparative tradition in philosophy, adapted to the framework’s specific requirements.

First principle: the autonomy of philosophical justification. No principle of the frame-
work is justified by its resemblance to a tradition, and no tradition is adjudicated by its
resemblance to the framework. The dialogue is a comparison of structures, not a derivation of
either side from the other.

Second principle: resemblance, not equivalence. Where the framework and a tradition
use the same word, or develop a similar structure, the relation is one of resemblance or kinship,
not of equivalence. The framework’s terms have the sense the framework gives them, and the
tradition’s terms have the sense the tradition gives them; the two senses are not the same, and
the dialogue keeps them apart.

Third principle: depth over breadth. Each dialogue is governed by ten criteria of depth,
which are stated in Part I. A dialogue that fails any of the ten is incomplete; a dialogue that
satisfies all ten is a full dialogue, even if it is short. The volume prefers a small number of full
dialogues to a large number of shallow ones.
      The three principles are not independent of one another. The first governs the relation between
the framework and the traditions; the second governs the relation between the framework’s terms
and the traditions’ terms; the third governs the relation between the volume’s breadth and its
depth. Together, they yield the volume’s method: a comparative inquiry that is autonomous in
its justification, careful in its vocabulary, and deep in its treatment of each tradition.
Introduction                                                                                   lvii


The Map
The volume is organized into fifteen parts and eighty-five chapters. Eighty of the chapters are
dialogues, and the remaining five are the method, the statement of what the volume leaves aside,
and the open questions. The parts are organized by tradition and, within each tradition, by
period. The reader who follows the order of the chapters will find that each part presupposes
only what has come before; the reader who wishes to consult a particular tradition may begin
with the relevant chapter and follow the cross-references backward to Part I for the method.

Part I: The Method of Dialogue. States the three principles and the ten criteria of depth.
It is the shortest part, and it is the part that the reader who wishes to understand the volume’s
method should read first.

Parts II–V: The West. Six dialogues with the ancient West (Parmenides and Heraclitus,
Plato, Aristotle, Stoicism, Plotinus, Proclus); eight with the medieval West (Augustine, Dionysius,
Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus, Ockham, Eckhart, Nicholas of Cusa); eight with the modern West
(Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke and Hume, Kant, Hegel, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche); and eleven
with the contemporary West (Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Sartre, Gadamer and
Ricoeur, Whitehead, Peirce and the pragmatists, Wittgenstein, Quine and Davidson, Kripke and
Lewis, Foucault and Habermas, Derrida and Deleuze).

Parts VI–VII: Islam. Ten dialogues with classical Islamic philosophy (al-Kindi, al-Farabi,
Ibn Sina, al-Ghazali, Ibn Rushd, the Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya, Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi,
Mulla Sadra, Ibn Khaldun); and ten with contemporary Islamic philosophy (Iqbal, Tabatabai,
Motahhari, Shariati, al-Sadr, Nasr, Fazlur Rahman, Arkoun, Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman,
Soroush).

Parts VIII–IX: India and Buddhism. Six dialogues with Indian philosophy (the Upanishads,
Samkhya and Yoga, Nyaya and Vaisheshika, Shankara, Ramanuja, Aurobindo); and four with
Buddhist and Jain philosophy (Nagarjuna, Yogacara, Buddhist logic, Jainism).

Parts X–XI: East Asia. Five dialogues with Chinese philosophy (Confucius and Mencius,
Laozi and Zhuangzi, Mozi and Han Feizi, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, Chinese Buddhism); and
three with Japanese philosophy (Shinto, Dogen and Shinran, the Kyoto School).

Part XII: Jewish Philosophy. Four dialogues (Philo and Saadia, Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda
Halevi, Maimonides, Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas).

Part XIII: African and Latin American Philosophy. Three dialogues (Egyptian wisdom
and Zara Yaqub, contemporary African philosophy, Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin
American philosophy).

Part XIV: Other Traditions. Two dialogues (Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism, Gnosticism
and Hermeticism).

Part XV: Open Horizons. Two chapters that state the traditions mentioned in passing and
the open questions of dialogue. It is the part that states the volume’s limits, and it is the part
that invites the reader to continue the inquiry.
    The map is a guide to the volume’s architecture, not a summary of the volume’s content.
The reader who follows the map from beginning to end has followed the volume’s inquiry; the
reader who enters in the middle has entered one dialogue, and can follow the cross-references to
the volume’s method and to the dialogues that precede and follow.


A Note on the Two Genres
The main book and the present volume belong to two different genres, and the difference is worth
stating at the outset.
    The main book is a systematic reconstruction. It states its principles, argues for them, and
draws their consequences. It does not engage in dialogue with the traditions; it treats them, at
most, in footnotes, and it leaves the comparison to a separate inquiry. The main book is governed
by the principle of the autonomy of philosophical justification: its principles are justified by
philosophical argument, not by resemblance to a tradition.
    The present volume is a comparative inquiry. It presupposes the framework and compares it
with the traditions. It does not state the framework’s principles; the main book states them. It
does not argue for the framework’s principles; the main book argues for them. What the present
volume does is state where the framework and a tradition share a structural feature, where they
diverge, what each can say to the other, and what each costs the other. The present volume
is governed by the same principle of autonomy, applied to the comparison: no principle of the
framework is justified by the comparison, and no tradition is adjudicated by the comparison.
    The two genres are not in competition. They are two different undertakings, each answerable
to its own standards. The main book is answerable to coherence, argument, and the strength
of its own principles. The present volume is answerable to the depth of its comparisons, the
fairness of its representations, and the clarity of its statements of resemblance and divergence. A
reader who judges the present volume by the standards of the main book will find it unsatisfying;
a reader who judges it by the standards of comparative philosophy will find it what it is: a
comparative inquiry, offered as a comparison.


A Note on the Epistemic Status of Claims
Every major claim in this volume is tagged with one of five epistemic-status labels, or with the
label “resemblance” when the claim is a claim about the relation between the framework and a
tradition. The labels are the same as the main book’s, with one addition: the label “resemblance”
is specific to the present volume, and it names the claim that a structural feature is shared
between the framework and a tradition, without the claim that the two are equivalent.


(A) (A) Axiom / Foundational Commitment. A starting point that is adopted rather
than proved. Its justification is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness—not deduction.
Introduction                                                                                       lix


(T) (T) Argued. An argument is given in the text.


(E) (E) Estimate. A claim that is offered as approximate and subject to revision.


(Q) (Q) Open Philosophical Question. A philosophical question that has no final answer
yet, but can be examined within the system.


(S) (S) Speculation. A speculative extension, flagged for caution.


Resemblance. A claim that the framework and a tradition share a structural feature, without
the claim that the two are equivalent. The label is used in every dialogue, and it is the label
that marks the volume’s method.
   The reader is invited to assess each claim by the standard appropriate to its status. A
resemblance claim is not refuted by saying “the two are not the same”; the volume states that
they are not the same, and the claim is that they share a structural feature, not that they share
a concept. A resemblance claim is refuted by showing that the structural feature is not shared,
or that the framework’s reading of the tradition is wrong; the volume states, for each dialogue,
what would refute the reading, so that the reader knows where to press.



A Note on the Use of Terms

The volume uses two sets of technical terms, and the two sets are kept apart. The first set is
the framework’s terms: identity, manifestation, light, realm, context, expression, cost, viability,
and the other terms defined in the main book. These terms have the sense the main book gives
them, and they are used in the volume with that sense. The second set is the traditions’ terms:
substance, accident, process, relation, intellect, emanation, illumination, dharma, dao, and the
other terms that the traditions use. These terms have the sense the traditions give them, and
they are used in the volume with that sense.
   Where the two sets overlap in vocabulary but not in sense—for example, the word “light” in
the framework and in Suhrawardi, or the word “substance” in the framework and in Aristotle—the
volume marks the difference explicitly, and it does not import one sense into the other. The
reader who reads a tradition’s term in the framework’s sense, or the framework’s term in a
tradition’s sense, has misread the dialogue; the volume’s method is designed to prevent the
misreading, and each dialogue states where the misreading would occur.
   No term in this volume carries normative or ethical weight. Every term is defined structurally
or historically, and its sense is fixed by the definition or the historical context. Where a tradition
uses a term with normative weight—“the Good” in Plato, “justice” in the Mu’tazila, “dharma” in
Indian philosophy—the volume reports the tradition’s use and does not adopt it; the framework’s
terms are structural, and the volume keeps them so.
lx                                                                                       Introduction


A Note on the Structure of the Book
The book is divided into fifteen parts and eighty-five chapters. Eighty of the chapters are each a
dialogue with a tradition or a thinker, and each dialogue satisfies the ten criteria of depth stated
in Part I. The back matter contains four elements: a Bibliography, organized by chapter and
keyed to the source codes used in the footnotes; a Glossary of Traditions and Thinkers; an Index
of Dialogues; and an Index of Concepts.
     The Bibliography uses a code of the form [Dn-m], where n is the chapter number and m is
the source number within that chapter. The same source cited in more than one chapter receives
a distinct code in each chapter. The codes are used in the footnotes to identify a source by code,
name, and the passage cited.
     The Index of Dialogues lists the dialogues by tradition and chapter, with a cross-reference to
the part in which the dialogue appears. The Index of Concepts lists the framework’s concepts—
light, identity, manifestation, mediation, unity and multiplicity, relation and order, viability, time,
death, self-awareness—and, for each, the dialogues in which the concept is discussed. The reader
who wishes to follow a concept through the volume is directed to the Index of Concepts; the
reader who wishes to follow a tradition through the volume is directed to the Index of Dialogues.


A Note on Origins and Independence
The volume offers its comparisons on their own merits, and asks to be assessed in that way. No
principle of the framework is justified by reference to a tradition, and no tradition is adjudicated
by reference to the framework. The volume’s comparisons are historical and structural; they
carry no justificatory weight, and they are offered as comparisons, not as evidence.
     The framework’s architecture—the four-column framework, the seven realms, the distinction
between identity and manifestation, the structural account of light—is familiar in the history
of philosophy, and the reader who knows that history will see kinship. The volume’s task is to
identify the kinship, to state where the framework and a tradition share a structural feature,
where they diverge, and what each costs the other. The task is comparative, not justificatory; it
is offered as a comparison, and its worth is to be measured by the depth of the comparisons it
makes, not by the strength of the framework’s arguments, which the main book states.


Concluding Remark
This volume is offered as a proposal, not as a finished system. It invites objection, revision,
and refinement. The reader who finds a comparison unconvincing is invited to strengthen the
objection and continue the inquiry. The reader who finds a tradition under-represented is invited
to propose a fuller treatment. The reader who finds a structural feature shared that the volume
missed is invited to add it to the conversation.
     The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.

The Method of Dialogue




          1
Chapter 1

The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification


Scope. This chapter opens the part of the volume that states the method of dialogue. It states and
argues the first of the three principles of the method, the autonomy of philosophical justification,
as the principle applies to the comparative inquiry of this volume. It distinguishes three roles
that a reference to a tradition may play (motivation, coherence test, and legitimation) and a
fourth role, adjudication, which is the mirror of legitimation and runs from the framework to the
tradition. It argues that legitimation and adjudication are forbidden and that motivation and
coherence test are permitted under stated conditions. It then takes up the strongest objection to
the principle, the objection from the independent convergence of traditions, and states exactly
what the volume concedes to it. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “justification,” “legitimation,” “adjudication,” “motivation,” “coherence,” or
“autonomy,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
in the main book.


1.1       A Scene
Consider a mathematician who has proved a theorem. She presents the proof: definitions, lemmas,
the derivation, the conclusion. A colleague listens, and at the end says: This is the theorem that
Euclid proved, in a different notation. Your proof is confirmed by its resemblance to his.
    The mathematician is puzzled. The proof is not confirmed by its resemblance to Euclid’s; it is
confirmed by its own derivation. If the proof is valid, it is valid whether or not Euclid proved the
same theorem; if it is invalid, the resemblance does not save it. The resemblance is interesting.
It shows that the theorem has a history, that the mathematician works in a tradition, and that
the same structure can be reached by different routes. But it is a fact about the proof’s place in
history, not a fact about the proof’s validity.
    Now consider a philosopher who presents a metaphysical framework: a set of definitions, a
set of principles, a set of arguments. A reader listens, and at the end says: This is the framework
that Plotinus developed, in a different vocabulary. Your framework is confirmed by its resemblance
to his.
    The philosopher should be as puzzled as the mathematician, and for the same reason. The
framework is confirmed, if it is confirmed, by its own arguments. The resemblance to Plotinus
shows that the framework has ancestors; it does not show that the framework is sound.
    The scene has a second half, which is less often noticed. Suppose that the colleague had said
the opposite: Your proof differs from Euclid’s, and so it must be wrong. The mathematician
would be no less puzzled. A difference from an earlier proof is not an error in a later one. The
two halves of the scene are one lesson seen from two sides: resemblance does not transfer validity,
and difference does not remove it.

                                                  2
1.2. The Question                                                                                3


   The scene poses a question. What is the relation between a philosophical framework and
the traditions it resembles? Is the resemblance a ground of justification, or is it something else?
And if it is something else, what does it permit the comparative philosopher to say? The present
chapter answers these questions.




1.2     The Question

The main book is written under the principle of the autonomy of philosophical justification. The
principle was stated in its Introduction and has been observed throughout: no principle of the
framework is justified by confirmation from outside philosophy, and the framework’s concepts
are defined within the book. The main book’s references to the traditions are confined to its
notes, and they carry no justificatory weight.
   The present volume is a comparative inquiry, and it is written under the same principle. But
the principle has a wider application here than in the main book. In the main book it forbids
the use of a tradition as a ground of justification. In the volume it forbids that use and also
the converse use: it forbids the use of the framework as a ground for judging a tradition. The
volume’s task is comparison, neither justification nor adjudication, and the principle states what
comparison may and may not do.
   The question of the chapter is therefore: what does the principle permit, and what does it
forbid, in the comparative inquiry of this volume? The answer has three parts.




First part: the principle. The principle states that no principle of the framework is justified
by its resemblance to a tradition, and that no tradition is judged by its resemblance to, or its
difference from, the framework.




Second part: the roles and the argument. A reference to a tradition may play three roles:
motivation, coherence test, and legitimation. Its mirror in the other direction is adjudication.
The first two roles are permitted under stated conditions; the last two are forbidden. The chapter
argues for this division and answers the objection that the convergence of independent traditions
is itself evidence.




Third part: the consequence for the volume. The dialogues of the volume are comparisons
of structures. The chapter states what this requires of every dialogue, and it states the limits of
what the chapter establishes.
4                                      Chapter 1. The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification


1.3     The Principle

    Principle 1.1 (The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification in Comparative
    Inquiry)

    (A) The validity of no principle of the framework is established by its resemblance to a
    tradition, and the validity of no tradition is established or refuted by its resemblance to,
    or its difference from, the framework. The comparison of structures is a comparison, not a
    justification and not an adjudication.


    The principle is (A): it is adopted as a foundational commitment of the volume, and it is
the commitment that the main book adopts, applied to comparative inquiry. Its support is the
structure of philosophical justification: a principle is justified by argument, not by resemblance,
and a tradition stands or falls by its own arguments, not by its relation to another framework.
The principle would be put in question by a case in which a claim is justified by resemblance
alone, or a tradition judged by resemblance alone. The volume does not claim that no such case
can be described; it argues that none can be coherently described, given what justification is.
    The principle has two halves, and the reader should keep them distinct.




First half: no justification from resemblance. The framework’s principles are not justified
by their resemblance to a tradition’s principles. The framework’s arguments are given in the
main book, and the volume adds none. A comparison is not a substitute for an argument, and a
resemblance is not a substitute for a proof.




Second half: no adjudication from resemblance or difference. The traditions are not
judged by their relation to the framework. A tradition’s position is not refuted by diverging from
the framework and not confirmed by converging with it. The tradition’s arguments are its own,
addressed to its own premises, and the volume does not sit in judgment on them. A divergence
is not a refutation, and a convergence is not a verdict.
    Taken together, the halves state what comparison is and what it is not. The rest of the
chapter develops the consequences.




1.4     The Roles of a Reference to a Tradition

A reference to a tradition may play three roles in a philosophical work, and a fourth role runs in
the opposite direction. The roles are distinct, and they differ in whether they are permitted.
1.4. The Roles of a Reference to a Tradition                                                      5


 Role                Status          What it shows                      What it does not show

                     condition       lem with a history                 is correct

                     condition       dition can be compared

 Adjudication (the   forbidden       nothing about validity             —
 mirror)


1.4.1       First Role: Motivation

A reference to a tradition plays the role of motivation when it shows that the problem the
framework addresses is a real problem, one that has arisen in the history of thought and was
not invented by the framework. A framework that addressed a problem no one had ever posed
would be a curiosity; a framework that addresses a problem posed, in different terms, by several
traditions engages with the history of thought.
    The role is permitted on one condition: the reference must be marked as motivation and not
as reason. That a tradition posed the problem shows that the problem is worth posing; it does
not show that the framework’s answer is correct.

   Remark 1.1 (Motivation Is Not Justification)

   The distinction between motivation and justification is the distinction between showing
   that a question is worth asking and showing that an answer is correct. The first is a
   historical and structural claim; the second is a philosophical claim. The volume uses the
   first and does not use the second. A reader who takes a motivation for a justification has
   misread the volume.


1.4.2       Second Role: Coherence Test

A reference to a tradition plays the role of coherence test when it shows that the framework’s
principles do not contradict the tradition’s structural features, and that the two can therefore
enter into comparison. A framework that contradicted a tradition’s way of working in every
respect could not engage with it at all; a framework coherent with it in some respects can be set
beside it and compared.
    The role is permitted on one condition: the reference must be marked as a coherence test
and not as evidence. The coherence is a fact about the comparison, not about the framework’s
validity.

   Remark 1.2 (Coherence Test Is Not Confirmation)

   The distinction between coherence test and confirmation is the distinction between showing
   that two things can be compared and showing that one of them is true. The first is a
   structural claim; the second is a philosophical claim. The volume uses the first and does
   not use the second.
6                                       Chapter 1. The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification


1.4.3    Third Role: Legitimation

A reference to a tradition plays the role of legitimation when it derives the framework’s authority
from the tradition’s authority, treating the tradition’s having held a similar view as a reason
for holding the framework’s view. The role is forbidden. A tradition’s authority is its own and
does not transfer. The legitimation is a category mistake: it treats a tradition as a ground of
justification when the tradition is only a term of comparison.

    Remark 1.3 (Legitimation Is Forbidden)

    The prohibition on legitimation is the volume’s central methodological commitment. A
    dialogue that said “Ibn Sina held a similar view, therefore the framework’s view is plausible”
    would violate it. A dialogue that said “Ibn Sina held a different view; here is where the
    two differ, and why” is comparative and permitted. The dialogues of the volume are of
    the second kind.


1.4.4    The Mirror of Legitimation: Adjudication

The framework may also be used as a standard against which a tradition is measured: the
tradition is said to be right where it agrees with the framework and mistaken where it does not.
This is adjudication. It is forbidden for the same reason that legitimation is: the framework’s
having held a view is a fact about the framework. The framework’s reasons are given in the
main book and are addressed to its own premises. They are not thereby reasons addressed to a
tradition that does not share those premises.



1.5     The Argument

The argument for the principle proceeds from a definition and three observations.


Argument for the Autonomy of Philosophical Justification in Comparative Inquiry.            1. Definition.
      To justify a philosophical claim is to derive it from premises, by an argument that bears on
      the claim, where the premises are ones that the claim’s proponent accepts and can state.
      The premises may be commitments, and the argument may be a reductio, a transcendental
      argument, or an inference to the best explanation; but the justification is the derivation,
      not the resemblance of the claim to another view.

    2. First observation. That a tradition holds a view bears on the view’s truth only through
      the reasons the tradition has for it, or through the tradition’s reliability as a witness to it.
      The mere fact of holding is not a reason.

    3. Second observation. The traditions of the volume rest their views on premises of their
      own, among them revelation, cosmologies, and the authority of founding texts, which
      the framework does not assume and which the volume does not assess. Agreement in a
      conclusion reached from different premises is not agreement in reasons.
1.5. The Argument                                                                                   7


  4. Third observation. The framework’s reasons are the arguments of the main book, addressed
      to its own premises. They bear on a tradition’s view only if the tradition shares those
      premises, and the volume does not establish that it does.

  5. Conclusion. The resemblance between the framework and a tradition is neither a justification
      of the framework (by the first and second observations) nor an adjudication of the tradition
     (by the first and third). It is a fact about the two structures and about their comparison,
      and it is not a fact about validity.



   The force of the argument lies in the second and third observations. They say that a
resemblance of conclusions does not carry with it a resemblance of reasons, and that the reasons
of one side are not reasons addressed to the other. A reader who accepts the definition, and who
accepts that the premises of the traditions differ from the framework’s, is led to the principle.

   Remark 1.4 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the definition of philosophical justification, which is a commit-
   ment ((A)) of the main book and of the present volume, and on the observation that the
   premises of the traditions differ from those of the framework. A reader who rejects the
   definition has a reason to reject the principle, and the volume does not pretend otherwise.
   The value of the argument is not that it proves the principle from nothing, but that it
   makes the definition visible and shows exactly what follows from it.



1.5.1    The Strongest Objection: Independent Convergence

The strongest objection to the principle is not that resemblance is justification but that indepen-
dent convergence is evidence. If several traditions, working separately, with different methods
and sources, arrive at the same structure, the convergence is a kind of replication, and replication
is evidence in other fields. The volume should not refuse it.
   The volume concedes the objection in principle and denies that it applies to its dialogues. The
concession is this: if independent traditions reached the same structure by independent reasons,
the agreement could bear on the structure’s truth, in the way that the agreement of independent
witnesses bears on a fact. The denial rests on three conditions that such an argument would
have to meet, none of which the volume claims to have established.


Independence. The traditions must be historically independent. Many of those of the volume
are not: Neoplatonic doctrine passes into Islamic, Jewish, and Christian thought; Greek logic
and metaphysics enter the Arabic tradition by translation; Indian and Chinese Buddhism share
a source. Resemblance among such traditions may be inheritance and not convergence.


Independent reasons. The agreement must be in reasons and not merely in conclusions. As
the second observation notes, traditions reach their conclusions from premises of different kinds.
8                                       Chapter 1. The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification


No selection by the comparer. The resemblances must not be those the comparer has chosen
to see. A comparison made by someone who holds a framework tends to find that framework’s
structures, and a resemblance that is selected in this way confirms the comparer’s expectation
and nothing else.

    Remark 1.5 (Independent Convergence Is Left Open)

    The volume does not claim that independent convergence could never be evidence. It
    claims that the conditions for treating it as evidence are demanding, that the dialogues
    do not establish them, and that a claim of convergence in the volume is therefore never
    offered as support for the framework. Whether some convergence among some traditions
    meets the conditions is a question for a separate inquiry, and the volume leaves it open
    ((Q)).



1.6     The Consequence for the Volume
The volume’s dialogues are comparisons of structures. They are not justifications of the framework
and not adjudications of the traditions. Each dialogue states the tradition’s position, states the
disputes within the tradition, identifies the points of convergence and divergence, presents the
tradition’s strongest objections to the framework, presents the framework’s reply, states what
each side costs the other, and states the kind of relation (resemblance, not equivalence). The
dialogue does not say that the framework is true because the tradition agrees, and it does not say
that the tradition is false because the framework disagrees. It says what the two share, where
they differ, and what each costs the other.

    Remark 1.6 (The Consequence Is Not a Denial of the Traditions)

    The consequence is not a denial that the traditions have authority. They have the authority
    of their own arguments, and the volume respects it by presenting each position in its
    strongest form. What is denied is that this authority transfers to the framework. The
    distinction is between using a tradition as a ground of justification, which the volume does
    not do, and respecting a tradition as a philosophical interlocutor, which it does.

    Remark 1.7 (The Consequence Is Not a Denial of the Framework)

    The consequence is not a denial that the framework has arguments. They are given in
    the main book, and the volume adds none. What is denied is that those arguments are
    supported by the traditions’ agreement. The distinction is between resting the framework
    on the traditions, which the volume does not do, and resting it on its own arguments,
    which the main book does.


1.7     Scope and Vulnerability
The principle says that no principle of the framework is justified by its resemblance to a tradition,
and that no tradition is judged by its relation to the framework. It does not say that resemblance
1.8. Consequences                                                                                   9


is irrelevant. Resemblance is relevant for comparison, for motivation, and for coherence test. It
is not relevant for justification and not for adjudication.
   The principle rests on the definition of philosophical justification ((A)). Its force is no greater
than the force of the definition.
   The principle is not relativism. It does not say that every framework is as good as every other,
or that no framework is better than another. It says that comparing frameworks is not judging
them. The judgment is a separate question, answered by the arguments of each framework. The
volume compares; the main book argues. The two are different undertakings, and the principle
keeps them apart.
   The principle would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A case in which a principle of the framework is justified by its resemblance
to a tradition, and not by argument. If such a case could be given, the first half of the principle
would fail, and the volume’s comparison would be a justification in disguise. The volume does
not claim that no such case can be constructed. It claims that none has been constructed that
survives the distinction between motivation and justification, and it argues that none can be.


Second challenge. A case in which a tradition is judged by its relation to the framework, and
not by its own arguments. If such a case could be given, the second half would fail, and the
volume’s comparison would be an adjudication in disguise.

   Remark 1.8 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Comparison)

   The principle does not deny that comparison is possible; it denies that comparison is
   justification. Comparison is a structural relation between two frameworks, and justification
   is a relation between a claim and its ground. The two are different, and the principle
   keeps them apart.



1.8     Consequences
The principle has three consequences for the volume. They are stated here with their status.


First consequence: the dialogues are comparisons. Every dialogue is a comparison of
structures, with the form stated in the previous section. It does not say that the framework
is true because the tradition agrees, and it does not say that the tradition is false because the
framework disagrees. ((T))


Second consequence: the references are marked. Whenever a dialogue says that a
tradition holds something similar to the framework, it says in what respect, and it does not draw
from the similarity any conclusion about the validity of either side. Each reference to a tradition
is read as motivation, coherence test, or comparison, and none as justification or adjudication.
The marking is a discipline on the volume’s claims, and it lets the reader see what each reference
is doing. ((A))
10                                       Chapter 1. The Autonomy of Philosophical Justification


Third consequence: the volume’s worth is comparative. The worth of the volume is to
be measured by the depth of its comparisons, the fairness of its representations, and the clarity
of its statements of resemblance and divergence. It is not to be measured by the strength of the
framework’s arguments, which the main book states, or by the truth of the traditions’ positions,
which the volume does not judge. ((A))
      The three consequences are three aspects of one fact: the volume is a comparative inquiry,
and the principle keeps it so. The first concerns the dialogues, the second the references, the
third the worth.


1.9       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not settle whether a comparison of structures can, in some cases,
become a step toward a justification. It argues that the comparison is not a justification; it does
not rule out that a justification might be built on a comparison, and it does not rule out that
independent convergence, under the conditions stated above, might bear on a question of truth.
The chapter states the comparison itself and leaves what may be built on it to a separate inquiry.
      Second, the chapter does not give a full account of the coherence test. It distinguishes the
coherence test from confirmation and marks it as permitted on a condition, but it gives no
criterion for when a coherence test succeeds. The criterion is a matter for the dialogues that use
it.
      Third, the chapter does not claim that its method is the only method for comparative
philosophy. It states the method the volume uses and argues that this method is coherent with
the framework’s principles. Other methods are not thereby inferior; they are not the volume’s.
