A Question for Reflection
Consider a philosophical view you hold. Is it justified by its resemblance to a tradition, or by
its own arguments? If a tradition you respect held a different view, would that change your
justification, or would it change only the comparison? And if two traditions that had never met
held the same view, would you take that as a reason, and what would you need to know about
them before you did? What does your answer tell you about the relation between comparison
and justification?

The next chapter turns to the second principle of the method: resemblance, not equivalence
(Chapter 2). It argues that where the framework and a tradition use the same word, or develop a
similar structure, the relation is one of resemblance or kinship and not of equivalence, and it
states what the difference amounts to in the volume’s practice. The present chapter has stated
the principle of autonomy; the next chapter states the principle that governs the vocabulary of the
comparison.
Chapter 2

Resemblance, Not Equivalence


Scope. This chapter states and argues the second principle of the method of dialogue. It
distinguishes four relations that two philosophical positions may bear to one another (identity,
equivalence, agreement, and resemblance), and it distinguishes kinship, a resemblance that has
a historical source, from resemblance without one. It argues that the relation between the
framework and a tradition is to be taken as resemblance or kinship unless a test shows otherwise,
and it states the test: the substitution test, run in both directions. It states what the principle
requires of every dialogue. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “identity,” “equivalence,” “agreement,” “resemblance,” “kinship,” or “substitution,”
these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


2.1     A Scene
Consider two portraits of the same person. The first was painted by a court painter in the
seventeenth century: formal, composed, the face lit from one side, the hands resting on a book.
The second was painted three centuries later by a modern artist: informal, fragmentary, the face
broken into planes of color, the hands absent. Anyone who knew the person can see that, in
both, the person is present. But the two paintings are not the same painting, and neither can be
put in the other’s place without loss: a museum that hung the second where the first belonged
would not have made a small change of style; it would have changed what the wall says.
   The difference is not a difference in accuracy. The first may be more accurate in the structure
of the face, the second in the intensity of the gaze. The difference is that the two select different
features, arrange them differently, use different materials, and serve different purposes. They share
one thing, the person’s presence, and they do not share a material, a method, or a vocabulary.
   Now suppose a third painting, made in the style of the first by a painter who has studied it
and copied its technique. The third resembles the first in style, and it resembles the person in its
subject. But the third resembles the first in a way that the second does not: it has a source in it.
The first and the third are related by descent; the first and the second are related only by what
they portray. The two resemblances are different, and both are different from identity.
   The scene has one more turn. Suppose the same theorem is written down by two mathemati-
cians in two notations. Here, and almost only here, the two texts can be put in each other’s
place with no loss: every statement of the one translates into a statement of the other, with the
same consequences and no added content. The relation is not resemblance; it is equivalence. The
scene thus shows that the distinction is not a decoration, since there are cases on both sides of it,
and that the question is a question to be tested and not to be assumed.
   What, then, is the relation between two positions that resemble each other, and how is one
to tell whether the resemblance is the whole of the relation? The present chapter answers.

                                                 12
2.2. The Question                                                                                  13


2.2     The Question

The previous chapter stated the principle of the autonomy of philosophical justification: resem-
blance to a tradition does not justify the framework, and difference from the framework does not
refute a tradition. That principle tells us what resemblance cannot do. It does not yet tell us
what resemblance is, nor how it differs from the relations with which it is easily confused.
   The question is not idle. In comparative philosophy the temptation to take resemblance for
equivalence is strong. A reader who sees that the framework and Plotinus both speak of “light”
may be tempted to say that they mean the same thing. A reader who sees that the framework
and Ibn Arabi both speak of “manifestation” may be tempted to say that they hold the same
doctrine. The temptation is natural, and it is not always a mistake; it is a mistake when the two
uses share a structural role and not a concept, and the only way to tell is to test. The chapter’s
task is to state the difference between sharing a role and sharing a concept, to state how the
difference is tested, and to state who bears the burden when the test has not been run.
   The question has three parts.


First part: the four relations and kinship. What are identity, equivalence, agreement,
and resemblance, and what is kinship? The chapter defines them and distinguishes them.


Second part: the test. How is a resemblance distinguished from an equivalence? The chapter
states the substitution test, states how it is run, and applies it to two cases, one in which it fails
and one in which it succeeds.


Third part: the principle and its consequence. What follows for the volume? The chapter
states the principle as a default with a burden, and it states what every dialogue must do.


2.3     The Four Relations

Two philosophical positions may bear four relations to one another, and the four are distinct.

   Definition 2.1 (Identity)

   Two positions are identical when they are one position, stated in the same terms with the
   same sense. Identity is the limiting case: it holds only when there is no difference at all,
   not even a difference in formulation.

   Definition 2.2 (Equivalence)

   Two positions are equivalent when they are intertranslatable in the respects that matter:
   whatever can be said in the one can be said in the other, without loss of sense, without
   change of consequences, and without addition of content. Equivalent positions are two,
   but they are interchangeable.
14                                                          Chapter 2. Resemblance, Not Equivalence


     Definition 2.3 (Agreement)

     Two positions agree when they assert the same proposition, or the same set of propositions,
     with the same truth value. Agreement is compatible with difference of formulation, and
     it is compatible with difference of ground: two positions may assert one proposition for
     different reasons.

     Definition 2.4 (Resemblance)

     Two positions resemble one another when they share a structural feature: a pattern of
     relations, a form of argument, a way of distinguishing levels, a structure of dependence.
     Resemblance is compatible with difference of sense, of vocabulary, of consequence, and
     of purpose. It is the weakest of the four relations, and it is the relation with which the
     dialogues of the volume are concerned.

     Definition 2.5 (Kinship)

     Two positions are kin when they resemble one another and the resemblance has a historical
     source: one position descends from the other, or both descend from a third, by transmission,
     translation, or critical reply. Kinship is resemblance with a lineage. It is not a stronger
     relation of sense, and it is not evidence of one.

     The five definitions are structural, not evaluative. The following table sets them side by side
with the question that each asks.

     Relation             The question it asks                    What would show it

     Identity             Is it one position?                     No difference of any kind
     Equivalence          Can each be put in the other’s place?   The substitution test succeeds
     Agreement            Do both assert the same proposition?    The same proposition, same truth
                                                                  value
     Resemblance          Do both share a structural feature?     A shared pattern, form, or role
     Kinship              Does the resemblance have a lineage?    A historical line of transmission or re-
                                                                  ply

     Remark 2.1 (The Relations Are Not a Hierarchy of Value)

     The relations are not ranked by importance. Resemblance is not less valuable than
     equivalence; it is a different relation, and it is the one that the volume’s dialogues concern.
     A reader who takes identity to stand at the top and resemblance at the bottom as a scale
     of worth has misread the chapter. The order is an order of strength of the claim made,
     not of the worth of what is claimed.

     Remark 2.2 (Agreement Is Not Equivalence)

     Two positions may agree on a proposition and still not be equivalent: they may assert the
     same proposition on different grounds, with different consequences, in different frameworks.
     The distinction is between what is asserted and how it is grounded. The dialogues are
2.4. The Principle                                                                               15


   concerned with both, and they keep the two apart.


   Remark 2.3 (Resemblance Is Not Agreement)

   Two positions may resemble each other in structure and disagree in their propositions.
   The framework and Plotinus both speak of light, and they disagree about what light is:
   the framework treats light as a structural conveyor of effect, while Plotinus uses light as
   the principal image of the One’s giving of being and, on some readings, as more than an
   image. The resemblance is in the structural role; the disagreement is in the sense and the
   commitment. The two are distinct, and the volume keeps them apart.


   Remark 2.4 (Kinship Does Not Transfer Sense)

   That a position descends from another does not make the two positions equivalent, and it
   does not make them agree. Descent often changes sense: a doctrine received by a later
   tradition is received into new problems, and its terms are put to new work. Kinship is
   therefore a reason to look for resemblance, and it is no reason to presume equivalence.
   It also bears on the first principle: resemblance among kin is the resemblance least able
   to support an argument from independent convergence, since descent is the commonest
   explanation of agreement between positions that are not independent.



2.4     The Principle

   Principle 2.1 (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   (A) The relation between the framework and a tradition is to be taken as resemblance
   or kinship, and not as equivalence, agreement, or identity, unless the substitution test
   shows that it is equivalence. The burden of showing a stronger relation lies on the one
   who asserts it.

   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a foundational commitment of the volume, and it is
the second of the three principles of Part I. It is stated as a default with a burden, not as an
empirical claim that no tradition is ever equivalent to the framework. The reason for stating it so
is that the stronger relations are stronger claims. To say that two positions are equivalent is to
say that every statement of the one has a counterpart in the other with the same consequences,
and a claim of that strength needs a test. To say that they resemble is to say less, and it is safe
in the sense that it commits the comparer to no more than has been shown.
   The principle has two halves, and the reader should keep them distinct.


First half: resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s terms have the sense that the
framework gives them; a tradition’s terms have the sense that the tradition gives them. A shared
word, or a shared structural role, does not make the senses the same. The substitution test,
stated in the next section, is the criterion.
16                                                      Chapter 2. Resemblance, Not Equivalence


Second half: resemblance, not agreement. The framework and a tradition may share a
structural feature and differ in what they assert. The volume marks both the resemblance and
the difference, and it does not treat the first as the second.
     The principle is argued for in a later section. It is stated here so that the test can be stated
as the test of this principle.



2.5      The Test of Equivalence

The principle must be testable, and the test is stated in this section.

     Definition 2.6 (The Substitution Test)

     Let t be a term that the framework and a tradition share in vocabulary or in structural
     role, and let t′ be the counterpart term of the tradition. The relation with respect to t is
     equivalence only if, in the contexts in which t does its work, substituting t′ for t in the
     framework’s statements, and t for t′ in the tradition’s statements, preserves in each case
     (a) the truth of the statements, (b) their inferential consequences, and (c) their content,
     without addition. If the substitution fails on any of the three, in either direction, the
     relation with respect to t is resemblance, or kinship if it has a lineage.


     The test is structural, not interpretive. It does not ask whether the two positions feel alike;
it asks whether the one can be put in the place of the other without a change in what follows.
It is restricted to the contexts in which the term does its work, because no two systems are
intertranslatable in every context, and a test that demanded this would be failed by every pair,
including the notations of the scene. It is run in both directions, because a substitution that
preserves the framework’s statements may still alter the tradition’s.
     The test is run in three steps.



First step: identify the term and its contexts. The term to be tested is one that the
two positions share in vocabulary or in role, and the contexts are those in which it carries
consequences.



Second step: substitute, in both directions. Put the counterpart term in the place of the
term, in the framework’s statements, and then the framework’s term in the tradition’s statements,
and ask the three questions of the definition.



Third step: state the difference. If the substitution fails, state what is lost, changed, or
added, and in which direction. The difference is the difference between the framework’s sense
and the tradition’s sense, and it is what the dialogue must state.
2.6. The Argument                                                                                   17


   Remark 2.5 (A Case in Which the Test Fails: “Light” in the Framework and
   in Plotinus)

   The framework uses “light” for the conveyor of effect: an active structure with three
   properties (descending, ascending, reflective), distinct from what it conveys. Plotinus
   uses light as the principal image of the One’s giving of being to what comes after it, and
   the Enneads draw on it in describing intellect and soul. Put Plotinus’s light in the place
   of the framework’s, and the framework’s statements change: its light would then be a
   stage of divine being, and the properties that the framework ascribes to light as conveyor
   would have to be replaced by those of emanation. Put the framework’s light in the place
   of Plotinus’s, and the images of the ascent of the soul lose what they were used to say.
   The substitution fails in both directions. The relation is resemblance, and where the
   Plotinian line has descended into later traditions, kinship. The resemblance lies in the
   shared structural role (a mediator, that which makes relation possible); the difference
   lies in the sense (conveyor against emanation, structural against divine). The reading is
   vulnerable: it would be refuted by showing that the Plotinian image of light is used only
   as a conveyor and in no sense as a stage of being, and the dialogue with Plotinus states it
   as such.

   Remark 2.6 (A Case in Which the Test Succeeds: One Theorem, Two Nota-
   tions)

   The theorem of the opening scene, stated in the notation of Euclid and in a modern
   notation, passes the test. Every statement of the one has a counterpart in the other, the
   same consequences follow, and nothing is added. The relation is equivalence. The case
   matters because it shows that the test is not rigged: it is capable of returning “equivalent.”
   It matters also because it shows what the volume takes equivalence to be: a relation
   between positions that differ only in how they are written down.

   Remark 2.7 (The Test Is Not a Verdict)

   The test does not say that a tradition is wrong because its term is not substitutable for
   the framework’s. It says that the two terms are not the same and that the relation is
   resemblance. The tradition’s term has its own sense, consequences, and purpose, and so
   has the framework’s. The test states the difference and does not rank the two.


2.6     The Argument
The argument for the principle has two parts: an argument that resemblance is the right default,
and an argument that the burden lies where the principle puts it.

Argument for “Resemblance, Not Equivalence”.         1. The sense of a term depends on its system.
      A term in a philosophical position has its sense from its place in a system of definitions,
      arguments, and consequences. The framework’s “light” has its sense from the four-column
      framework and the principles that govern it; a tradition’s term has its sense from the
18                                                     Chapter 2. Resemblance, Not Equivalence


       tradition’s own system. Two terms that share a name or a role may therefore differ in sense
       without any difference of wording.

     2. Equivalence is a strong claim. To assert that two terms are equivalent is to assert that
       substituting one for the other, in the contexts in which each works, preserves truth,
       consequence, and content. That is a claim about a very large number of statements, and it
       cannot be made from a resemblance of wording or of role alone.

     3. Resemblance is the claim that has been shown. When two positions share a structural
       feature, what has been shown is that they share it. To assert more is to assert what has
       not been shown, and the one who asserts it must show it.

     4. Hence the default and the burden. The relation is to be taken as resemblance, or as kinship
       where there is a lineage, unless the test is run and succeeds; and the burden of running it
       lies on the one who asserts equivalence.


     The argument does not claim that every tradition fails the test. It claims that the test must
be run, and that until it is run the weaker claim is the one that has been established. The volume
runs the test in each dialogue and reports the result; where the test fails, as in the case of light
and Plotinus, it states what the failure shows.

     Remark 2.8 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

     The argument depends on the first premise, that the sense of a term depends on its system,
     and on the substitution test (Definition 2.6), which is a commitment ((A)) of the volume.
     A reader who rejects either has a reason to reject the principle, and the volume does not
     pretend otherwise. The value of the argument is not that it proves the principle from
     nothing; it is that it makes the premises and the test visible and shows what follows from
     them.

     Remark 2.9 (The Principle Is a Default, Not a Prediction)

     The principle does not predict that every dialogue will end in resemblance. It sets the
     starting point and assigns the burden. A dialogue that found equivalence for some term
     would report it, with the test run, and would depart from the default for that term alone.
     The volume’s practice is to expect that most terms will fail the test, since the systems
     differ, and to run the test nonetheless, since the expectation is not the result.



2.7       Scope and Vulnerability
The principle is valid for the comparative inquiry of the volume, and its scope must be stated
with precision.
     The principle says that the relation between the framework and a tradition is to be taken as
resemblance or kinship unless the test shows otherwise. It does not say that the traditions are
all different from one another; it concerns the relation between the framework and a tradition. It
2.8. Consequences                                                                                 19


does not say that the framework is superior to a tradition; it says that they are different positions
and that comparison is a comparison of structures.
   The principle rests on the first premise of the argument and on the substitution test ((A)).
Its force is no greater than theirs.
   The principle is not relativism. It does not say that every framework is as good as every
other. It says that comparing frameworks is not adjudicating them, which is the first principle,
and that comparing them requires a test of how far they are alike, which is the second. The
volume compares; the main book argues.
   The principle would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A case in which a framework term can be substituted for a tradition’s term,
in both directions, without loss, change, or addition, and in which the volume nonetheless asserts
only resemblance. If such a case were given, the principle’s default would have misled the dialogue
in that case, and the dialogue would have to be revised. The principle itself would stand, since it
allows that the test may succeed.


Second challenge. A case in which the framework and a tradition assert the same proposition
on the same grounds, and the volume treats them as merely resembling. If such a case were
given, the second half of the principle would have been misapplied, and the dialogue would again
be revised.

   Remark 2.10 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Resemblance)

   The principle does not deny that resemblance is important. It denies that resemblance is
   equivalence without a test. Resemblance is a structural relation between two positions,
   and equivalence is a relation of substitutability. The two are different, and the principle
   keeps them apart.



2.8     Consequences

The principle has four consequences for the volume, stated here with their status.


First consequence: every dialogue states the kind of relation. Every dialogue ends
with a statement of the kind of relation between the framework and the tradition: resemblance,
kinship, or, in the case in which the test succeeds, equivalence. The statement is structural and
not evaluative. ((A))


Second consequence: every dialogue runs the test and marks the difference in sense.
Wherever the framework and the tradition use the same word or the same role with different
senses, the dialogue runs the substitution test on the term, in both directions, and marks the
difference. The marking is a discipline on the dialogue’s claims, and it lets the reader see where
the resemblance ends and the difference begins. ((T))
20                                                     Chapter 2. Resemblance, Not Equivalence


Third consequence: every dialogue says whether the resemblance has a lineage.
Where a dialogue treats a tradition that descends from, or is the source of, another tradition in
the volume, it says so, so that kinship is not read as convergence. ((T))




Fourth consequence: every dialogue states what would refute the reading. Every
dialogue states what would refute the framework’s reading of the tradition. The statement is a
mark of the dialogue’s fallibility, and it lets the reader see where its claims are vulnerable. ((T))

     The four are four aspects of one fact: the volume is a comparative inquiry, and the principle
keeps the comparison at the strength that has been shown. The first names the relation; the
second names the difference; the third names the lineage; the fourth names the fallibility.


     Remark 2.11 (The Consequences Are Not a Denial of the Traditions)

     The consequences do not deny that the traditions have authority. They have the authority
     of their own arguments, and the volume respects it by presenting each position in its
     strongest form. What the consequences deny is that this authority is the framework’s.
     The distinction is between resemblance and equivalence, and the volume keeps it.




2.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

     First, the chapter does not settle whether a relation of resemblance can, in some cases, become
a relation of equivalence. It states the default and the test, and it allows that the test may
succeed for a term in some dialogue. It does not claim that no relation can be equivalence.

     Second, the chapter does not give a full account of what a “structural feature” is. It uses
the phrase and illustrates it (light as mediator, manifestation as appearance), but it gives no
general criterion for when a feature is shared. The criterion is stated in the dialogues that use
the phrase, and it is a matter for each dialogue.

     Third, the chapter does not claim that its four relations are the only useful distinction. It
states the distinction the volume uses, and it argues that this distinction suffices for the volume’s
task. Other distinctions are not thereby inferior; they are not the volume’s.

A Question for Reflection
Consider two views you hold, or two that you have met. Do they resemble each other, or could
one be put in the other’s place? Try the substitution, in both directions: what changes, and
what stays? And if one of the views came from the other, does the descent make them more
alike, or only make the resemblance easier to find? What does your answer tell you about the
difference between resemblance and equivalence?

The next chapter turns to the third principle of the method: the ten criteria of depth (Chapter 3).
It states the ten criteria by which a dialogue is assessed, and it argues that a dialogue that satisfies
all ten is a full dialogue even if it is short, while a dialogue that fails any of the ten is incomplete
even if it is long. The present chapter has stated the principle that governs the vocabulary of the
comparison; the next chapter states the criteria that govern the depth of each dialogue.
Chapter 3

The Ten Criteria of Depth


Scope. This chapter states and argues the third and final principle of the method of dialogue.
It states the ten criteria by which a dialogue in this volume is assessed, shows how the criteria
carry out the first two principles, and argues that the ten are jointly necessary for a dialogue to
be structurally complete. It distinguishes completeness, which the criteria measure, from fidelity
to the tradition, which they do not, and it states the rule of quotation by which the volume
protects fidelity. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks
of “depth,” “completeness,” “criterion,” or “failure,” these are structural terms; their sense is
fixed by the definitions in this chapter. “Depth” names a structural property of a dialogue, the
satisfaction of the ten criteria, and not a value.



3.1     A Scene

Consider two reviews of the same film. The first is a paragraph long: it summarizes the plot,
names the director, and says that the film is “powerful.” The second runs to several pages: it
states the film’s argument, places it among the director’s earlier work, presents the strongest
objections that critics have raised, replies to them, and says what the film costs the viewer and
what it offers. The first is short and shallow; the second is long and deep. But length is not the
difference. A third review, a single page long, could be deeper than the second if it answered the
same questions in fewer words.
   What separates the shallow review from the deep is the number of questions it asks and
answers. The shallow review asks what happens in the film. The deep review asks what the film
is arguing, how it continues or departs from what came before, what the strongest objections are,
how the film answers them, and what it costs and offers. Each of these is a criterion, and the
deep review meets them.
   The scene has a second lesson. Suppose a fourth review meets every one of these questions
and gets the plot wrong: it describes scenes that are not in the film. The review has the structure
of a deep review and it is nonetheless a bad one. The questions ensure that nothing essential is
left out; they do not ensure that what is said is true. A structure can be complete and unfaithful.
   Now consider a comparative dialogue between a philosophical framework and a tradition. It
can be shallow or deep in the same way, and it can be complete and unfaithful in the same way.
The present chapter states the criteria that measure the first, and the rule that guards against
the second.




                                                 22
3.2. The Question                                                                                23


3.2     The Question
The previous two chapters stated the first two principles of the method. The first, the autonomy
of philosophical justification, says that the dialogue is a comparison and not a justification or
an adjudication (Chapter 1). The second, resemblance, not equivalence, says that the relation
between the framework and a tradition is to be taken as resemblance or kinship unless the
substitution test shows otherwise (Chapter 2). The two tell us what the dialogue is not. They
do not yet tell us what a dialogue is in its full structure, and they do not say how to tell whether
a given dialogue has carried them out.
   The question is not idle. A comparative dialogue can be long and shallow, or short and deep.
The chapter’s task is to state the criteria so that the reader can assess each dialogue by them, to
say why these criteria and not others, and to say what they do not measure.
   The question has three parts.


First part: the ten criteria. What are they, and which failure does each exclude? The
chapter states each criterion in a definition and shows how the ten carry out the first two
principles.


Second part: the argument. Why are the ten jointly necessary for completeness, and in
what sense are they sufficient? The chapter argues for necessity from the failure each criterion
excludes, and it states exactly the limited sense in which the ten suffice.


Third part: the consequence for the volume. What follows for the assessment of each
dialogue, for the marking of incompleteness, and for the quotation of sources?


3.3     The Ten Criteria
The ten criteria are stated in ten definitions. Each states the criterion and the failure that it
excludes.

   Definition 3.1 (First Criterion: The Tradition’s Position, with Reference to
   Primary Texts)

   The dialogue states the tradition’s position on the question at issue, with reference to
   the tradition’s primary texts. The failure excluded is the summary of a tradition from
   secondary sources, without engagement with what the tradition itself says.


   Definition 3.2 (Second Criterion: The Internal Disputes Within the Tradition)

   The dialogue identifies the internal disputes within the tradition: the different positions
   that the tradition’s own thinkers have taken on the question, and the arguments given for
   them. The failure excluded is the treatment of the tradition as a monolith, as if all its
   thinkers said the same thing.
24                                                          Chapter 3. The Ten Criteria of Depth


     Definition 3.3 (Third Criterion: Points of Convergence)

     The dialogue identifies the points of convergence between the framework and the tradition:
     the structural features that the two share. The failure excluded is the treatment of the
     tradition as wholly other, with no point of contact.


     Definition 3.4 (Fourth Criterion: Points of Divergence)

     The dialogue identifies the points of divergence between the framework and the tradition:
     the structural features on which the two differ. The failure excluded is the treatment of
     the tradition as wholly the same as the framework, with no point of difference.


     Definition 3.5 (Fifth Criterion: The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework)

     The dialogue presents the tradition’s strongest objections to the framework: the objections
     that a thinker of the tradition would raise, on the tradition’s own premises, against the
     framework’s position on the question. The failure excluded is the presentation of a tradition
     without its critical force, as if it had nothing to say to the framework.


     Definition 3.6 (Sixth Criterion: The Framework’s Reply)

     The dialogue presents the framework’s reply to the tradition’s objections: the response
     that the framework can give on its own principles. The failure excluded is the presentation
     of objections without a reply, as if the framework had no resources to answer them.


     Definition 3.7 (Seventh Criterion: The Cost of Each Side)

     The dialogue states what the framework would cost the tradition, and what the tradition
     would cost the framework: the consequences that each side would have to accept if the
     other were correct. The failure excluded is the presentation of the two positions as if
     neither had a cost, as if the choice between them were free.


     Definition 3.8 (Eighth Criterion: The Kind of Relation)

     The dialogue states the kind of relation between the framework and the tradition (re-
     semblance, kinship, or, where the substitution test succeeds, equivalence), and states it
     with the precision that the second principle requires. The failure excluded is the vague
     statement that the two are “similar,” without specification of the kind of similarity.


     Definition 3.9 (Ninth Criterion: What Would Refute the Framework’s Reading
     of the Tradition)

     The dialogue states what would refute the framework’s reading of the tradition: the
     evidence, interpretation, or argument that, if produced, would show that the framework
     has misread the tradition. The failure excluded is the presentation of the reading as
     beyond challenge.
3.3. The Ten Criteria                                                                              25


   Definition 3.10 (Tenth Criterion: The Questions the Dialogue Leaves Open)

   The dialogue states the questions that it leaves open: the questions it does not settle and
   that a fuller treatment would have to address. The failure excluded is the presentation of
   the dialogue as if it had settled everything.

   The ten are not a checklist to be applied mechanically. They are the structure of a full
dialogue, and they fall into four groups. The first two concern the tradition. The third, fourth,
and eighth concern the relation between the tradition and the framework. The fifth, sixth, and
seventh concern the critical exchange. The ninth and tenth concern the dialogue’s own status,
its fallibility and its incompleteness.

3.3.1     How the Criteria Carry Out the Principles
The criteria are not a third, independent set of demands. They are the means by which the first
two principles are carried out, and the third principle is the demand that the means be used.
   The first principle, that a dialogue is neither a justification nor an adjudication, is carried out
by the fifth and sixth criteria, which give the tradition its own voice and the framework its own
reply, and by the seventh, which presents the cost of each side without a verdict. The second
principle, resemblance and not equivalence, is carried out by the third, fourth, and eighth criteria,
which require both what is shared and what differs, and the kind of relation. The ninth criterion
expresses the burden that the second principle puts on whoever asserts a stronger relation: to
say what would show the reading wrong.

    No.       Criterion                              Where it is carried out in a dialogue
                                                     chapter

    1         Position, from primary texts           The tradition’s position
    2         Internal disputes                      Internal Disputes
    3         Convergence                            Points of Convergence
    4         Divergence                             Points of Divergence
    5         Tradition’s objections                 The Tradition’s Objections
    6         Framework’s reply                      The Framework’s Reply
    7         Cost of each side                      The Cost of Each Side
    8         Kind of relation                       The Kind of Relation
    9         What would refute the reading          The Kind of Relation (closing statement)
    10        Open questions                         Open Questions

   Remark 3.1 (The Ten Criteria Are Not Independent)

   The criteria depend on one another. The fifth (the tradition’s objections) depends on the
   first and second: one cannot present a tradition’s objections without knowing its position
   and its disputes. The sixth depends on the framework’s principles, which are stated in
   the main book. The ninth depends on the eighth: one cannot say what would refute a
   reading without knowing what relation the reading asserts. The ten are a structure, and
   the structure is what a full dialogue is.
26                                                            Chapter 3. The Ten Criteria of Depth


     Remark 3.2 (The Ten Criteria Are Not a Ranking)

     No criterion is more important than another. Each is necessary, and the absence of any
     one is a failure of the dialogue. A dialogue that satisfies nine of the ten is not a nine-tenths
     dialogue; it is an incomplete one, and the incompleteness is structural.



3.4      The Principle

     Principle 3.1 (The Ten Criteria of Depth)

     (A) A dialogue in this volume is structurally complete if and only if it satisfies the ten
     criteria stated in Definitions 3.1 to 3.10. A dialogue that fails any of the ten is incomplete,
     however long; a dialogue that satisfies all ten is complete, however short. Completeness is
     not fidelity: a complete dialogue may misrepresent a tradition, and the volume guards
     against this by the rule of quotation stated below.


     The principle is (A): it is adopted as a foundational commitment of the volume and is the
third of the three principles of Part I. It is stated with two qualifications that the argument will
explain. It speaks of structural completeness, and it separates completeness from fidelity.
     The principle has two halves, which the reader should keep distinct.


First half: necessity. A dialogue that fails any of the ten is incomplete. Each criterion
excludes a specific failure, and the absence of any is the presence of its failure.


Second half: sufficiency of structure. A dialogue that satisfies all ten has the structure
of a full comparative dialogue. This is sufficiency for completeness of structure, and it is not
sufficiency for truth, accuracy, or persuasiveness.


3.5      The Argument
The argument has three steps. The first states the failures that the criteria exclude; the second
shows why the ten are jointly necessary; the third states in what sense, and only in what sense,
they suffice.


3.5.1     First Step: The Ten Failures

A comparative dialogue can fail structurally in ten specific ways. It can summarize the tradition
without engaging its primary texts. It can treat the tradition as a monolith. It can treat it as
wholly other, or as wholly the same. It can present it without its critical force. It can present
the objections without a reply. It can present the two positions as if neither had a cost. It can
state the relation vaguely. It can present its reading as beyond challenge. And it can present
itself as having settled everything. Each failure is excluded by one criterion, and each criterion
excludes one failure.
3.5. The Argument                                                                                 27


3.5.2   Second Step: Why the Ten Are Necessary
The necessity of each criterion is shown by what its absence does to the comparison. Without
the first, the dialogue compares the framework with a secondhand picture. Without the second,
it compares it with an average that no thinker held. Without the third and fourth, there is
nothing to compare or nothing that distinguishes. Without the fifth and sixth, the exchange is a
monologue, and under the first principle a monologue is an adjudication in disguise. Without
the seventh, the choice between the positions appears free, and the dialogue has hidden what
each side must give up. Without the eighth, the second principle is not carried out. Without the
ninth and tenth, the dialogue claims an authority that its own method denies it.

3.5.3   Third Step: In What Sense the Ten Suffice
The ten do not exhaust every way in which a dialogue can be bad. They exhaust the ways in
which a comparative dialogue can fail in structure: in the four groups of the previous section,
the tradition, the relation, the critical exchange, and the dialogue’s own status. A dialogue can
satisfy every criterion and still be inaccurate in what it says about the tradition, weak in its
argument, or poor in its prose. The criteria do not measure these, and the volume does not claim
that they do.

Argument for the Ten Criteria.      1. A comparative dialogue can fail structurally in the ten
     ways of the first step, and each is a failure to carry out one of the first two principles or to
     mark the dialogue’s own limits.

  2. Each criterion excludes exactly one of the ten failures, and the absence of the criterion is
     the presence of the failure (second step).

  3. Hence each criterion is necessary for structural completeness, and a dialogue that fails any
     one is incomplete.

  4. The ten cover the four aspects of a comparative dialogue: the tradition, the relation, the
     critical exchange, and the dialogue’s own status. A dialogue that satisfies all ten therefore
     has the full structure of a comparative dialogue.

  5. Hence a dialogue is structurally complete if and only if it satisfies the ten, and completeness
     of structure is distinct from the fidelity of the dialogue’s content.


   The argument’s force lies in step (4), the claim that the four aspects are the aspects of a
comparative dialogue. A reader who denies it must name an aspect that the ten do not cover,
and the volume will then have a criterion to add.

   Remark 3.3 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the claim that the four aspects exhaust the structure of a
   comparative dialogue, which is a commitment ((A)) of the volume, and on the first two
   principles, which it presupposes. A reader who rejects either has a reason to reject the
28                                                              Chapter 3. The Ten Criteria of Depth


     principle, and the volume does not pretend otherwise. The value of the argument is not
     that it proves the principle from nothing; it is that it makes the claim visible and shows
     what follows from it.


     Remark 3.4 (Completeness Is Not Fidelity)

     A dialogue can have every section and every move that the ten require, and still misrepresent
     the tradition: attribute to it a doctrine it did not hold, or give an interpretation that its
     texts do not bear. The ten criteria cannot detect this, because it concerns what is said
     and not the shape of what is said. The first criterion, which requires primary texts, and
     the ninth, which requires a statement of what would refute the reading, are the places
     at which the structure points outward to the check. The check itself is the work of the
     reader, the specialist, and the text.



3.6        The Test of Completeness

The principle must be testable, and the test is stated in this section.

     Definition 3.11 (The Test of Completeness)

     For any dialogue in the volume, check whether it satisfies each of the ten criteria. If it
     satisfies all ten, it is structurally complete. If it fails any, it is incomplete, and the criterion
     that it fails identifies the failure.

     The test is structural, not interpretive. It does not ask whether the dialogue feels complete;
it asks whether the ten are met. It is applied in three steps.


First step: identify the criteria. The ten are stated in the definitions of the section above.


Second step: check each. For each criterion, ask whether the dialogue meets it. Does the
dialogue state the tradition’s position with reference to primary texts? Does it identify the
internal disputes? And so on, through the tenth.


Third step: state the result. If all ten are met, the dialogue is complete; if any is not, it is
incomplete, and the unmet criterion is named. The result classifies the dialogue and does not
rank it.

     Remark 3.5 (The Test Is Not a Ranking)

     The test does not say that one dialogue is better than another; it says that a dialogue is
     complete or incomplete. Dialogues are classified, not ranked.
3.7. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                        29


   Remark 3.6 (The Test Is Not a Verdict on the Tradition)

   The test is a test of the dialogue and not of the tradition. A dialogue that fails a criterion
   is an incomplete dialogue, not a false one, and the tradition’s position may be correct
   whatever the state of the dialogue. The test leaves the tradition’s truth untouched.



3.7     Scope and Vulnerability
The principle is valid for the comparative inquiry of the volume, and its scope must be stated
with precision.
   The principle says that a dialogue is structurally complete if and only if it satisfies the ten
criteria. It does not say that every dialogue in the volume satisfies them. Some may not, and
the volume marks them as incomplete. The principle is a measure and not a guarantee.
   The principle rests on the claim that the four aspects exhaust the structure of a comparative
dialogue ((A)). Its force is no greater than the force of that claim.
   The principle is not relativism. It does not say that every dialogue is as good as every other.
It says that a dialogue is complete or incomplete in structure, that the two differ, and that the
question of accuracy is a further question.
   The principle would be put in question by two things.

First challenge. A dialogue that fails one of the ten and is nonetheless structurally complete,
in the sense that it carries out both the first and second principles and marks its own limits. If
such a case could be given, the criterion in question would not be necessary, and it would be
removed. The volume does not claim that no such case can be constructed; it claims that none
has been, and it argues, from the failure that each criterion excludes, that none can.

Second challenge. A dialogue that satisfies all ten and fails, in structure, to be a full
comparison. If such a case could be given, a criterion would have to be added. The volume invites
this challenge, since its claim of sufficiency is limited to structure and rests on the commitment
about the four aspects.

   Remark 3.7 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Depth)

   The principle does not deny that depth admits of degrees in other senses, such as the
   penetration of an analysis. It denies that depth, in the sense of the volume, is a matter
   of length. Depth in this sense is the satisfaction of the ten, and length is the number of
   words. The two are different, and the principle keeps them apart.



3.8     Consequences
The principle has four consequences for the volume, stated here with their status.

First consequence: every dialogue is assessed by the ten. Every dialogue is assessed by
the ten criteria, and its completeness is stated. The assessment classifies; it does not rank. ((A))
30                                                          Chapter 3. The Ten Criteria of Depth


Second consequence: incompleteness is marked. A dialogue that fails any criterion is
marked as incomplete and the criterion is named. The marking lets the reader see what remains
to be done. ((A))



Third consequence: the volume’s worth is not its length. The worth of the volume as a
comparative inquiry is measured by the number of its dialogues that satisfy the ten and by how
well the others are marked. It is not measured by length or by the number of dialogues. ((T))



Fourth consequence: the rule of quotation. The first criterion requires reference to
primary texts, and the volume holds the reference to a rule. A passage is set between quotation
marks, or in a box of quotation, only when it can be verified in a cited edition or translation, and
the citation names that edition. A passage that cannot be verified is given as a paraphrase and
is marked as one. No passage is attributed to a thinker in words that the thinker is not known
to have written. The rule protects fidelity, which the ten criteria cannot. ((A))
     The four are aspects of one fact: the volume’s dialogues are assessed by the ten, and the
volume’s worth is the completeness and the fidelity of its dialogues. The first names the assessment,
the second the marking, the third the measure, and the fourth the guard on what is said.

     Remark 3.8 (The Consequences Are Not a Denial of the Volume’s Worth)

     The consequences do not deny that the volume has worth. It has the worth of its
     complete dialogues, and of its incomplete dialogues as partial contributions; the marking
     of incompleteness is itself a contribution, because it shows what remains. What they deny
     is that the worth is measured by length or by the number of dialogues.




3.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
     First, the chapter does not settle whether the ten are the only possible criteria. It states the
ten that the volume uses and argues that they suffice for structural completeness. Other criteria
are not thereby inferior; they are not the volume’s.
     Second, the chapter does not state how the criteria are applied in each dialogue. The
application is a matter for each dialogue, and each states its own completeness. This chapter has
stated the criteria; the dialogues apply them.
     Third, the chapter does not claim that a complete dialogue is a good one. A dialogue can
be complete and wrong in its reading, complete and unpersuasive, or complete and dull. The
criteria measure structure, not value, and the volume uses them because they are a structural
measure.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a comparative discussion you have read, between two positions, two traditions, or a
theory and its critic. Which of the ten did it satisfy, and which did it fail? And was it faithful to
what each side actually held? What does your answer tell you about the difference between a
dialogue that is complete in structure and a dialogue that is true to its subjects?

Part I is now complete. The three principles of the method (the autonomy of philosophical
justification, resemblance not equivalence, and the ten criteria of depth) are in place. Part II
turns to the first dialogue: the dialogue with Parmenides and Heraclitus, on the question of unity,
change, and the structure of being. The method is stated; the dialogues are what the method
makes possible.

The Ancient West

Chapter 4

Parmenides and Heraclitus


Scope. This chapter opens Part II, the dialogues with the ancient West, with the two thinkers who
posed in its starkest form the problem that the framework’s metaphysics addresses: Parmenides
of Elea and Heraclitus of Ephesus. It states the positions of the two with reference to the
surviving fragments, cited by the numbers of Diels and Kranz (DK); it identifies the internal
disputes in the interpretation of each; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of identity as an invariance that is conserved through manifestation
and change is the nearest analogue to what the two thinkers dispute; it presents the objections
that each would raise; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other;
it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes
no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “being,” “becoming,”
“logos,” “flux,” or “unity,” these are the thinkers’ terms, and their sense is fixed by the fragments
and by the interpretive literature, not by the framework. The fragments are cited in paraphrase;
no passage is set in quotation marks, because the volume’s rule of quotation (Chapter 3) allows
a quotation only from a cited edition, and the chapter paraphrases.


4.1     A Scene
Consider a river. You step into it; the water around your feet is cold and clear. You step out,
and a moment later step back in. The water is still cold and clear, but it is not the same water:
what you stand in the second time was upstream a moment before. The river is the same river,
and the water is not the same water.
    Now look at the same river from above, in one glance. What you see is a pattern: a channel,
a flow, a shape that persists while the water passes through it. The pattern is not the water; it
is what the water does. It is also not the bank; it is what the bank contains. The pattern is
what makes the river one river across the changing water.
    A third standpoint is harder to occupy. Ask not what the river is doing, nor what shape
it has, but what it is. If you look for the river’s being, you find the flowing; if you look for
the flowing, you find the water; if you look for the water, you find the next water. There is no
moment at which the river simply is, without change. Its being seems to be its becoming.
    The scene poses the question that Parmenides and Heraclitus posed in different ways. What is
the relation of being and becoming, of the one and the many, of what persists and what changes?
Parmenides is read as holding that being is real and becoming an appearance; Heraclitus, as
holding that becoming is real and stability only apparent, or, on another reading, that stability
is an order within change. The framework answers that there is an invariance that is conserved
through change, and that manifestations and their changes are real. The chapter states the two
positions and the framework’s answer.

                                                 33
34                                                        Chapter 4. Parmenides and Heraclitus


4.2      The Question
The previous part stated the method of dialogue; the present part applies it to the traditions.
The first dialogue is with Parmenides and Heraclitus, because the two posed in its starkest
form the problem of the relation between unity and plurality, between permanence and change,
between being and becoming.
     The question is not whether Parmenides or Heraclitus was right. The question is what each
held, what each can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to each. The question
has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Parmenides hold, and what did Heraclitus hold? The
chapter states each position with reference to the fragments and identifies the internal disputes
in the interpretation of each.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and each thinker converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents
the objections that each would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and each
thinker? The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as
resemblance, not equivalence.


4.3      Parmenides’ Position
Parmenides of Elea (born c. 515 BCE) composed a hexameter poem in which a goddess instructs
the speaker in two ways: the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion. The Way of Truth survives
in large part, and it has shaped the history of metaphysics (DK 28 B1–B8).


4.3.1    The Two Roads

The goddess says that there are two roads of inquiry: that it is, and that it is not. The second
is impossible, because what is not can be neither thought nor spoken (DK 28 B2). The first is
the only road, and on it there are signs, set out in the eighth fragment: what is, is ungenerated
and imperishable, whole, of one kind, unmoved, and complete (DK 28 B8). It cannot have come
to be, for it would have to come from what is not; it cannot perish, for it would have to pass
into what is not; it is not divisible, for division would need a gap of what is not; and it does not
change, for change would be a passage between what is and what is not.


4.3.2    The Way of Opinion

The remainder of the poem describes the world of mortal belief, in which things come to be,
change, and are many. The goddess presents this account as plausible and as deceptive, and she
gives it no claim to truth. The consequence usually drawn is that becoming, plurality, and motion
4.4. Heraclitus’ Position                                                                           35


do not belong to what is in the strict sense. The world of change appears, and Parmenides does
not say that it is nothing, but it is not being.



4.4     Heraclitus’ Position

Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500 BCE) wrote a book of which only fragments survive, preserved in
the quotations of later authors (DK 22). The fragments are aphoristic and deliberately difficult,
and they present a cosmos ordered through change, tension, opposition, and transformation.


4.4.1    The Logos

The principle of the order is the logos, which holds always and is common to all, though most
people live as if they had an understanding of their own (DK 22 B1, B2, B50). The logos is not a
thing among things; it is the structure of the way things change. Fire serves as its image: always
consuming and renewing, it is one fire, kindled and quenched in measure (DK 22 B30).


4.4.2    Opposition and Order

Opposites are not merely exclusive. They are bound in a single order, and the tension between
them holds the order together, like that of the bow and the lyre (DK 22 B51; compare B53 on
strife, B60 on the road up and down). The famous sayings about rivers (DK 22 B12, B49a, B91)
are read as the claim that everything flows, or, on the reading that the chapter takes up in the
first dispute, as the claim that a river keeps its identity precisely through the change of its waters.
The unity of the world is the unity of a tension, not of a static substance.



4.5     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of both thinkers is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute on Parmenides: monism or not. One reading takes the poem to assert
that there is only one thing, strictly one. Another takes it to assert that whatever is must be
thus and so (ungenerated, whole, unchanging) while allowing a plurality of such things, a view
sometimes called a predicational monism. A third takes it as an argument about what can be
thought, rather than about what there is. The disagreement matters because the framework’s
plurality of identities can be set against a strict monism, and not against the weaker readings.


Second dispute on Parmenides: the status of the Way of Opinion. One reading takes
the Way of Opinion to be wholly false. Another takes it to be the best account that can be
given of appearances. A third takes it to be a dialectical demonstration of how mortals err.
The disagreement matters because the framework gives its manifestations a reality that the first
reading denies and the second partly allows.
36                                                         Chapter 4. Parmenides and Heraclitus


First dispute on Heraclitus: flux or order. The ancient tradition, beginning with Plato
and Aristotle, takes Heraclitus to teach that everything is in perpetual flux. A modern reading,
following Kirk and others, takes the river fragments to teach the identity of a river through change,
and takes the doctrine of the logos to be a doctrine of order within change. The disagreement is
not settled, and the chapter does not settle it.




Second dispute on Heraclitus: the unity of opposites. One reading takes Heraclitus
to hold that opposites are in some sense identical. Another takes him to hold that they are
interdependent and in a measured balance. The disagreement matters because the framework
states no doctrine of the unity of opposites, and the resemblance to it differs according to the
reading.




4.6     Points of Convergence
4.7. Points of Divergence                                                                          37


   Points of Convergence

   With Parmenides and Heraclitus. The framework shares six structural features with
   the two positions.

      1. The priority of invariance (Parmenides). Parmenides holds that what is, is not
         subject to coming to be and passing away. The framework holds that an identity is
         an invariance, conserved through its manifestations. Both give priority to what does
         not change over what does.

      2. The distinction between the invariant and its appearances (Parmenides). Parmenides
         distinguishes what is from the appearances of mortal opinion. The framework
         distinguishes an identity from its manifestations. Both hold that how a thing
         appears is not what it is.

      3. The rejection of generation from nothing (Parmenides). Parmenides argues that
         what is cannot come from what is not. The framework holds that an identity is
         enacted by a source and is not produced from nothing. Both reject generation ex
        nihilo.

      4. The reality of change (Heraclitus). Heraclitus holds that change is pervasive and real.
         The framework holds that manifestations arise, vary, and pass. Both treat change as
         something to be accounted for, and not as an illusion.

      5. The order within change (Heraclitus). Heraclitus holds that change is governed by
         a common order. The framework holds that manifestations are governed by the
         structure of the identity and its context. Both hold that change is orderly.

      6. The relational structure of reality (Heraclitus). Heraclitus holds that things are
         bound to their opposites in a tension. The framework holds that identities are
         expressed in realms and contexts and are not intelligible apart from them. Both
         hold that what is real is structured by relation.



4.7    Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Parmenides and Heraclitus. The framework diverges from the two positions in
   six respects.

      1. The reality of plurality. On a strict reading of Parmenides, there is one being and
         the many are not. The framework holds that there are many identities, each non-
         duplicable, enacted by one source. The framework does not collapse the many into
         the one.

      2. The reality of becoming. Parmenides denies becoming of what is. The framework
         holds that manifestations come to be and pass, and that this is not a defect of
38                                                          Chapter 4. Parmenides and Heraclitus


           knowledge.

       3. The status of the appearances. For Parmenides the appearances belong to opinion
           and have no claim to truth. For the framework manifestations are real and are what
           an identity is read through.

       4. The invariant. The framework’s invariance is conserved per identity and is non-
           duplicable. Heraclitus’s logos is a single common order, and Parmenides’s being is
           one. Neither is a plurality of conserved identities.

       5. The unity of opposites. The framework states no doctrine that opposites are one,
           nor that strife is the order of things.

       6. The status of stability. Heraclitus takes stability to be an order maintained within
           change. The framework takes the invariance to be conserved, a condition of the
           change being the change of one identity, and not merely a pattern in the change.



4.8      The Tradition’s Objections

     The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

     Parmenides’ objection. The framework asserts many identities and real change. But
     plurality requires difference, and difference requires that one thing is not another; what is
     not cannot be. A change requires that what was is not what is now, and again what is
     not cannot be. The framework’s plurality and its becoming each presuppose that what is
     not, is, and the road of “it is not” cannot be travelled.
     Heraclitus’ objection. The framework asserts an invariance that is conserved. But
     everything flows, and the thing that is said to stay the same is a thing that is always
     becoming other. An invariance that does not change is a static substance given the name
     of a structure, and the world does not contain it. The framework has turned the logos,
     which is the way of change, into a thing that stands apart from change.



4.9      The Framework’s Reply

     The Framework’s Reply

     Reply to Parmenides. The framework denies that difference requires non-being. To
     say that one identity is not another is to say that it is other, which is a way of being and
     not its absence; the argument depends on taking “is not” only in the sense of absolute
     non-existence. Plato’s Sophist, which descends from Parmenides’s problem, distinguishes
     the senses of “is not,” and the framework’s account of difference is of the kind that
     distinction allows. The framework’s change is likewise not a passage from non-being to
     being but a variation of manifestation within an identity that persists. This reply is open
4.10. The Cost of Each Side                                                                      39


   to the objection that it concedes more to Plato than to Parmenides, and the chapter marks
   it as a reply made from the standpoint of the framework.
   Reply to Heraclitus. The framework agrees that everything that manifests is subject
   to change, and it denies that the invariance is a thing that stands apart. The invariance
   is the condition under which a change is a change of one identity. Heraclitus’s own text
   requires something of this kind: on the reading of the river fragments that takes the river
   to be the same through the change of its waters, the sameness is what the saying is about,
   and the logos, which holds always and is common to all, is itself an invariant that governs
   the change. The framework gives the invariance a structural statement and does not claim
   that it is a substance.




4.10       The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Parmenides and Heraclitus’s cost. If Parmenides accepts the framework’s reply, he must
allow that “is not” has a sense in which it names difference and not absence, and that the world
of appearance contains something real. The cost is the loss of the strict identification of what is
with the one and the unchanging. If Heraclitus accepts the reply, he must allow that there is
something conserved through change, and that order within change presupposes an invariance.
The cost is the loss of the doctrine that change is the whole of the real.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Parmenides’s objection, it must give up
the plurality of identities or the reality of manifestation; it would collapse the many into the
one, or it would deny that change is real. If it accepts Heraclitus’s objection, it must give up the
conservation of identity, and it would have an order within change but no invariance of the kind
its principles assert. The cost is the loss of what the framework most distinctively holds.



The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what an account of the real must contain. The framework must take the
Parmenidean argument as a serious argument about what can be said to be, and the Heraclitean
saying as a serious claim about the pervasiveness of change. The two thinkers must take the
framework’s invariance as a claim about the condition of unity, and not as an evasion. The cost
of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between being and becoming as a choice between two
options.
40                                                         Chapter 4. Parmenides and Heraclitus


4.11       The Kind of Relation

     The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

     The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
     Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Parmenides’s
     term “what is” (to eon). If one substitutes “what is” for “identity” in the framework’s
     statements, the statements change: there would be one identity, indivisible and unmoved,
     and the plurality and the manifestations that the framework asserts would be lost. If one
     substitutes “identity” for “what is” in the poem, the poem changes: what is would be
     one among many conserved identities, and the argument from the impossibility of what
     is not would lose its target. The substitution fails in both directions, and the relation is
     resemblance, not equivalence.
     Substitution 2. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Par-
     menides’s “opinion” (doxa). If one substitutes “opinion” for “manifestation,” the statements
     change: manifestations are real and are the means by which an identity is read, while
     the opinions of mortals have no claim to truth. If one substitutes “manifestation” for
     “opinion,” the Way of Truth loses the contrast that gives it its point. The substitution
     fails in both directions.
     Substitution 3. The framework’s term “invariance” is not substitutable for Heraclitus’s
     “logos.” If one substitutes “logos” for “invariance,” the statements change: the logos is
     a common order, the same for all, while the invariance is conserved per identity and is
     non-duplicable. If one substitutes “invariance” for “logos,” the sayings lose their claim
     that the order is shared and that most people fail to grasp it. The substitution fails in
     both directions.
     The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Parmenides is resem-
     blance: both give priority to what does not change, distinguish it from appearances, and
     reject generation from nothing, and they differ on the reality of plurality and of becoming.
     The relation between the framework and Heraclitus is resemblance of a different kind:
     both treat change as real and orderly, and they differ on whether there is a conserved
     invariance. Neither relation is kinship in the volume’s sense, since the volume claims no
     line of transmission from either thinker to the framework; but the problem the two posed
     is the ancestor of the problems of the later chapters of Part II, in which Plato, Aristotle,
     Plotinus, and Proclus descend from it, and those chapters are kin to one another and to
     this one. Neither relation is equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading
     would be refuted by showing that Parmenides’s argument cannot be answered without
     giving up the plurality of identities that the framework asserts, or that Heraclitus’s logos,
     correctly read, excludes any invariance that persists through change.




4.12       Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
4.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                  41


First question. Does the reply to Parmenides succeed without the distinction that Plato later
drew? The chapter has argued that it does, but a reader who holds that the poem’s “is not”
allows only the sense of absolute non-existence has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Is Heraclitus’s river an image of flux or of persistence through flux? The
chapter has set out both readings and has not decided, and the force of the reply to Heraclitus
depends partly on the answer.

Third question. Can the framework’s invariance be stated without the notion of a source?
The chapter has taken the source as a premise of the main book, and a reader who holds that
the Eleatic argument excludes any source has a question the chapter leaves open.
