A Question for Reflection
Think of a person you have known for many years. What in them has changed beyond recognition,
and what, if anything, has stayed? When you say that they are the same person, what are you
pointing to? If you could not name it, would you retract the claim, or would you say that it
is present without being nameable? What does your answer tell you about whether being and
becoming must be set against each other?

The next chapter turns to Plato. It states the theory of Forms, the analogy of the sun, the divided
line, the cave, and the doctrine of the Good beyond being; it identifies the internal disputes in the
interpretation of Plato; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of light is the nearest ancient analogue to Plato’s sun. The present chapter has
stated the problem of being and becoming as the two earliest thinkers posed it; the next chapter
states the answer that Plato gave to it, and the framework’s dialogue with that answer.
Chapter 5

Plato


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Plato (428/427–348/347 BCE). It states the theory of
Forms, the analogy of the sun, the divided line, the image of the cave, and the doctrine of the
Good beyond being, with reference to the Republic (especially VI 507b–509c, 509d–511e, and VII
514a–520a), the Phaedo, the Timaeus, the Parmenides, and the Sophist, cited by the Stephanus
pagination. It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Plato; it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of light is the nearest ancient
analogue to Plato’s sun; it presents the objections that Plato would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind
of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “Form,” “the Good,” “participation,”
“recollection,” or “dialectic,” these are Plato’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the dialogues
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework. Passages are paraphrased, not quoted,
in accordance with the volume’s rule of quotation.


5.1     A Scene
Consider a person coming out of a dark room into the daylight. At first she is dazzled and sees
nothing; then objects take shape, and she sees colors, edges, the faces of those around her. It is
light that makes these visible, and yet she does not see the light as she sees the objects. She sees
by it. The light is neither one of the things seen nor the faculty that sees; it is what lets sight be
sight and objects be seen.
   Now consider a geometer drawing a circle in the sand. The circle is imperfect, and she knows
it is. Her proof is not about this circle; it is about the circle, which no drawing is. How does she
know the circle? She did not see it, since nothing in the sand is perfectly round. Yet she knows
it with a certainty that nothing in the sand could give.
   The two scenes are the two halves of one thought, which Plato develops through the analogy
of the sun. As light is to sight and to the visible, so the Good is to understanding and to the
intelligible. The scenes pose the question that the dialogue takes up: what is it that makes things
knowable and knowing possible, and how is it related both to what is known and to the knower?
The framework also has an account of light as the condition of manifestation and of reading. The
chapter asks how the two accounts stand to each other.


5.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated the problem of being and becoming as the earliest thinkers posed it.
Plato is the first of the ancient thinkers to give it a systematic answer in the form of a theory

                                                 42
5.3. Plato’s Position                                                                             43


of levels of being and of knowing, and the analogy of the sun is the image on which the later
tradition of the metaphysics of light is built.
   The question is not whether Plato was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Plato hold? The chapter states the theory of Forms, the
analogy of the sun, the divided line and the cave, and the Good beyond being, and it identifies
the internal disputes in the interpretation of the dialogues.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Plato converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Plato would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Plato?
The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as resemblance,
with a line of descent that bears on the first principle.


5.3     Plato’s Position
Plato does not give a systematic treatise; he writes dialogues, in which Socrates and other
speakers pursue questions by argument and by image. The position summarized here is the one
most commonly drawn from the middle dialogues, with the later dialogues taken up in the first
dispute.


5.3.1      The Forms

In the Phaedo and the Republic, Plato holds that beyond the many beautiful, just, and equal
things that we perceive there are the Beautiful itself, the Just itself, and the Equal itself: Forms,
which are unchanging, intelligible, and what the many things have a share in. The Forms are
objects of knowledge; the sensible things are objects of opinion, since they are always becoming
and never fully what they are (Phaedo 74a–75d, 78c–79a; Republic V 476a–480a).


5.3.2      The Sun, the Line, and the Cave

In the Republic Socrates says that the Good is to the intelligible realm what the sun is to the
visible (VI 507b–509c). The sun gives visible things their visibility and the eye its power of
seeing, and it also gives them their coming to be and growth, though it is not itself coming to
be. In the same way the Good gives the Forms their intelligibility and the mind its power of
knowing, and also their being, though the Good is not being but lies beyond being in dignity
and power (509b). The divided line sets out four levels of the visible and the intelligible, with
images, perceived things, mathematical objects reached by hypotheses, and Forms reached by
dialectic (509d–511e). The cave pictures the ascent from images to the sun and the descent to
those who remain (VII 514a–520a).
44                                                                                 Chapter 5. Plato


5.3.3     The Maker and the Receptacle
In the Timaeus Plato presents a likely account of the cosmos as the work of a craftsman who
looks to the Forms as a model and gives order to a receptacle (27d–29d, 47e–53c). The account
is offered as a likely story, and the interpretation of its status is part of the dispute about Plato’s
doctrine of the Forms.


5.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Plato is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the theory of Forms across the dialogues. One reading takes the Forms
of the middle dialogues to be separate entities, and takes the Parmenides (130a–135c, with the
argument of the third man at 132a–b) to be a serious criticism that Plato came to accept or to
answer. Another takes the Parmenides to be a test of the theory that leaves it standing. A third
takes Plato to have revised the doctrine in the later dialogues, in the Sophist and the Philebus.
The disagreement matters for the framework, because the objection from separation, which the
framework raises, is one that Plato raised against himself.

Second dispute: the status of the Good. One reading takes the Good to be the highest
Form. Another takes it to be beyond the Forms, a principle on which they depend, as the phrase
“beyond being” suggests. The disagreement matters because the framework’s one source is nearer
to the second reading than to the first.

Third dispute: the unwritten doctrines. Aristotle reports that Plato taught doctrines
in the Academy that are not in the dialogues, concerning the One and the indefinite Dyad as
principles (Metaphysics A 6, 987b). The Tübingen school (Krämer, Gaiser) takes these as the
key to the dialogues; Cherniss, Vlastos, and others reject or minimize them. The chapter does
not rely on the unwritten doctrines, and it records the dispute because the reading of the Good
depends partly on it.


5.5      Points of Convergence

     Points of Convergence

     With Plato. The framework shares four structural features with Plato’s position.

        1. Light as condition, not object. Plato says that the sun is not among the things seen
          but is what makes them seen. The framework says that light is not what it conveys
          but the conveyor. Both treat light as a condition of appearance and of knowing, and
          not as one of the things that appear.

        2. Light as the medium of both knowledge and being. In the analogy the sun gives
          both visibility and growth, and the Good gives both intelligibility and being. The
5.6. Points of Divergence                                                                           45


         framework holds that light conveys both effect and meaning. Both treat the medium
         as doing two kinds of work.

      3. The distinction between levels. Plato distinguishes the visible from the intelligible,
         and the four stages of the line. The framework distinguishes realms and holds that
         an identity manifests differently in each. Both hold that reality is differentiated into
         levels with different ways of being known.

      4. The hierarchy of levels. Plato holds that the levels are ordered, and that what is
         higher gives to what is lower. The framework holds that the descent of light is
         ordered across realms. Both hold that the order is not symmetrical.



5.6    Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Plato. The framework diverges from Plato’s position in four respects.

      1. The nature of light. For Plato the sun is the offspring of the Good and its image,
         and the analogy is an analogy. For the framework light is a conveyor with three
         properties, and it is a structure, not an image of a higher principle.

      2. The status of the Forms. Plato holds that the Forms are separate intelligible beings
         of which sensible things are images. The framework has no Forms separate from the
         identities that manifest.

      3. The status of the sensible world. For Plato the sensible world is a realm of becoming
         and opinion. For the framework manifestations are real and are what an identity is
         read through.

      4. The nature of knowledge. Plato holds that knowledge is of Forms, reached by dialectic
         and, in some dialogues, by recollection. The framework holds that knowledge of an
         identity is a reconstruction from its manifestations.



5.7    The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Plato’s first objection. The framework reads an identity from its manifestations. But
   manifestations are what the sensible world supplies, and the sensible world is always
   becoming and never fully what it is. A knowledge reconstructed from such material can
   be no better than opinion. Knowledge requires an object that stays what it is, and the
   framework has no such object apart from the manifestations.
46                                                                                 Chapter 5. Plato


     Plato’s second objection. The framework speaks of light as a conveyor, but it does
     not say why anything is intelligible at all. The Good is the answer to that question: it
     is what makes the Forms knowable. A philosophy that has a medium and no source of
     intelligibility has described how light travels and not why there is light.



5.8      The Framework’s Reply

     The Framework’s Reply

     Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that knowledge requires something
     that stays what it is, and it holds that the identity is such. The identity is conserved
     through its manifestations and is not itself one of them. The objection assumes that what
     stays what it is must be separate from what manifests it, and this is the assumption that
     Plato himself put to the test in the Parmenides, where the separation of the Forms from
     the things that share in them raises difficulties that the dialogue does not resolve. The
     framework keeps what knowledge requires and does not take on the separation.
     Reply to the second objection. The framework does have an account of why there
     is light and intelligibility: an identity is enacted by one source, and the conveyor of the
     source’s effect is light. The account is not the Good, and it does not claim that the source
     is beyond being in Plato’s sense. It states a structure and leaves the question of what the
     source is to a separate inquiry. The objection assumes that a source must be given the
     dignity that Plato gives the Good, and the framework does not make that assumption.



5.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Plato’s cost. If Plato accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that what is conserved and
knowable can be the identity of a thing that manifests, and that no separate intelligible realm is
required. The cost is the loss of the separation of the Forms and of the claim that the sensible
world can yield only opinion.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Plato’s objections, it must give up the
reconstruction of identity from manifestation as the form of knowledge, and it must admit a
realm of intelligible objects that stand apart from what manifests them. It must also give the
source the status of the Good. The cost is the loss of the immanence of the identity in its
manifestation.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim as
a claim about what knowledge requires. The framework must take the separation of the Forms as
an answer to a real difficulty, which is how what is known can be stable when what is perceived
5.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                          47


is not. Plato must take the conserved identity as an answer to the same difficulty. The cost of
the dialogue is the loss of the assumption that the only answer to the difficulty is separation.



5.10     The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for Plato’s “sun”
   in the analogy. If one substitutes “sun” for “light” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the sun is the offspring and image of the Good, and the framework’s
   light would then be a sensible image of a higher principle and not a conveyor with three
   properties. If one substitutes “light” for “sun” in the Republic, the analogy changes: the
   sun’s role as the source of growth, as well as of sight, is lost, and so is the relation of
   offspring to the Good. The substitution fails in both directions.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Plato’s “Form.”
   If one substitutes “Form” for “identity,” the statements change: Forms are separate, shared
   in by many sensible things, and the identities of the framework are non-duplicable and
   not shared. If one substitutes “identity” for “Form,” participation is lost, since an identity
   is not what many things share in. The substitution fails in both directions.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “one source” is not substitutable for Plato’s “the
   Good.” If one substitutes “the Good” for “one source,” the statements change: the Good
   is beyond being and is the cause of the intelligibility of the Forms, and the source of the
   framework is the enactor of an identity. If one substitutes “one source” for “the Good,”
   the superiority to being is lost. The substitution fails in both directions.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Plato is resemblance,
   with a line of descent that must be stated. The analogy of the sun is the ancestor of
   the light metaphors of later chapters of the volume: Plotinus, Augustine, Dionysius, and
   Suhrawardi, among others, draw on it or on its descendants, and those chapters are kin
   to this one and to one another. It follows that the recurrence of light imagery across
   these traditions is not an instance of independent convergence, and the volume does
   not offer it as evidence (Remark 1.5). The relation between the framework and Plato is
   neither kinship, since the volume claims no transmission from Plato to the framework, nor
   equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing
   that Plato’s sun is an image and nothing more, so that no structural role of light can be
   found in it, or that the Good beyond being excludes any account in which the source is
   the enactor of an identity.




5.11     Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
48                                                                              Chapter 5. Plato


First question. Is the Good beyond being a Form, or a principle of the Forms? The chapter
has noted both readings, and the resemblance to the framework’s one source is closer on the
second.

Second question. Does the objection from separation, which the Parmenides raises, defeat
the theory of Forms, or test it? The reply to Plato’s first objection depends partly on the answer.

Third question. Can an account of knowledge as reconstruction from manifestations avoid
the charge that it gives only opinion? The chapter has argued that it can, but a reader who
holds that only separate objects can ground knowledge has a question the chapter leaves open.

           sun

A Question for Reflection
When you understand something well, a proof, a person, a piece of music, is what you understand
the particular instance in front of you, or something that the instance gives you access to? If a
second instance appeared, what would you carry over to it? What does your answer tell you
about whether knowledge needs an object that is separate from its appearances?

The next chapter turns to Aristotle. It states the doctrine of substance, form and matter, the
four causes, the unmoved mover, and the critique of the separate Forms; it identifies the internal
disputes in the interpretation of Aristotle; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of identity is the nearest ancient analogue to Aristotle’s
substance. The present chapter has stated Plato’s answer, which separates the intelligible from
the sensible; the next chapter states the answer of Plato’s pupil, who denied the separation, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 6

Aristotle


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Aristotle (384–322 BCE). It states the doctrine of
substance (ousia), the analysis of substance into form and matter, the doctrine of potentiality
and actuality, the four causes, the unmoved mover, and the critique of the separate Forms,
with reference to the Categories, the Physics, the De Anima, and the Metaphysics (especially
books Z, H, Theta, and Lambda), cited by the pagination of Bekker. It identifies the internal
disputes in the interpretation of Aristotle; it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of identity is the nearest ancient analogue to Aristotle’s
substance; it presents the objections that Aristotle would raise against the framework; it presents
the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and
it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “substance,” “form,” “matter,” “essence,” “actuality,” or
“the unmoved mover,” these are Aristotle’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his texts and by
the interpretive tradition, not by the framework. Passages are paraphrased, not quoted, in
accordance with the volume’s rule of quotation.



6.1     A Scene

Consider a particular oak tree standing in a field. It was once an acorn, and it will one day be
timber and then rot. Through all of this we say that it is the same tree until it ceases to be one.
We can say what it is: an oak. We can say how it is: tall, green, damaged by last winter’s storm.
The how can change while the what remains, and when the what is lost, the tree is gone, though
the wood is still there.
   Consider next the question that a student asks of the tree: why is it as it is? There are four
answers. It is made of this wood and bark; it has the form of an oak; it came from this acorn;
and it grows toward being a full oak. None of these answers excludes the others, and a complete
account needs all four. The student has learned something about what a thing is and about
what it is for it to be, and neither lesson takes her out of the field to a realm of separate Forms.
   The scenes pose the question that Aristotle makes central: what is it for a particular thing
to be one thing, to persist through change, and to be knowable? Aristotle’s answer is that the
particular substance, composed of form and matter, is the primary being, and that the Forms
are not separate. The framework also takes the particular identity as the center of its account.
The chapter asks how the two answers stand to each other.




                                                49
50                                                                           Chapter 6. Aristotle


6.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Plato’s answer, in which the intelligible is separate from the sensible
and the sun is the image of the Good. Aristotle was Plato’s pupil and his critic, and his philosophy
begins from the denial that the Forms are separate. In this the dialogue with Aristotle is the
dialogue with the first thinker who took the particular, and not the separate universal, to be
what is primarily real.
     The question is not whether Aristotle was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Aristotle hold? The chapter states substance, form and
matter, potentiality and actuality, the four causes, and the unmoved mover, and it identifies the
internal disputes in the interpretation of the texts.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Aristotle converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Aristotle would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Aristotle?
The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as resemblance,
with the line of descent that bears on later chapters.


6.3      Aristotle’s Position
Aristotle’s works that survive are treatises, probably lecture notes, collected and arranged after
his death. The position summarized here is the one commonly drawn from the Categories, the
Physics, the De Anima, and the Metaphysics, with the disputes about their relation taken up
below.


6.3.1    Substance
In the Categories Aristotle distinguishes substance from the other categories, which are the
ways of being predicated of a substance: quantity, quality, relation, and the rest. The primary
substances are the individual things, this man, this horse; the species and genera are secondary
substances (Categories 5, 2a11–4b19). Everything else depends on substance, since accidents
exist only in substances. In the Metaphysics Aristotle asks what substance is, and in book Z he
considers three candidates, matter, form, and the composite of the two, and gives the first place
to form, which is what makes a thing the thing it is (Z 3, 7–9, 17). The form of a thing is not a
further part of it but the cause of its being one thing (Z 17, 1041b).


6.3.2    Potentiality, Actuality, and the Four Causes
A thing that changes is in potentiality what it will become, and the change is the actualization
of what it is potentially (Physics III 1–3; Metaphysics Theta). The soul is the form of a living
6.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             51


body, its first actuality (De Anima II 1). To explain a thing is to give its four causes: material,
formal, efficient, and final (Physics II 3, 7). For natural things the last of these, the end toward
which they develop, has an explanatory place that the modern sciences do not give it.

6.3.3     The Unmoved Mover and the Critique of the Forms
In Metaphysics Lambda Aristotle argues that the motion of the heavens requires a first mover
that is itself unmoved, pure actuality, and that it moves as an object of desire moves (Lambda
6–7). Its activity is thinking, and what it thinks is itself (Lambda 9). The Metaphysics also
contains Aristotle’s criticisms of the separate Forms: that they do not explain change, that they
double the things they are meant to explain, and that they cannot be the substance of the things
whose substance they are said to be (A 9, Z 14, M 4–5).


6.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Aristotle is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of form. One reading takes the form of a thing to be a universal,
the species it belongs to. Another takes forms to be particular, so that Socrates’s form and
Callias’s form are numerically two (Frede and Patzig on Metaphysics Z). The disagreement
matters for the framework, because the framework’s identities are non-duplicable, and the
resemblance to Aristotle is closer on the second reading than on the first.

Second dispute: the status of the unmoved mover. One reading takes Aristotle to hold
that there is one unmoved mover, which is God. Another takes him to hold that there are many,
one for each celestial sphere (Lambda 8, which speaks of forty-seven or fifty-five). A third takes
book Lambda as a separate and earlier work. The disagreement matters because the framework’s
one source can be compared to the first reading and not to the second.

Third dispute: the status of essence. Aristotle’s term for essence, the what it was to be
of a thing (to ti ēn einai), is used in several ways. One reading takes essence to be the form.
Another takes it to be the species. A third takes it to be a definition. The disagreement matters
because the question whether an essence can belong to an individual, and be known, is the
question on which the dialogue turns.


6.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Aristotle. The framework shares four structural features with Aristotle’s position.

        1. The priority of the particular. Aristotle holds that the individual thing is primary
          being. The framework holds that the identity is the center of its account and that an
          identity is of one particular. Both resist taking universals as the primary realities.
52                                                                           Chapter 6. Aristotle


       2. The reality of change. Aristotle holds that change is real and is the actualization of
          potentiality. The framework holds that manifestations arise and vary. Both treat
          change as a fact to be accounted for, and not as an appearance.

       3. The distinction between what a thing is and how it appears. Aristotle distinguishes
          substance from accident. The framework distinguishes an identity from its manifes-
          tations. Both hold that what a thing is does not vary with each of its features.

       4. The principle of unity. Aristotle holds that the form is the cause of a thing’s being
          one thing. The framework holds that an identity is the condition under which its
          manifestations are manifestations of one. Both treat the unity of a thing as requiring
          a principle.



6.6      Points of Divergence

     Points of Divergence

     With Aristotle. The framework diverges from Aristotle’s position in four respects.

       1. The nature of identity. On the standard reading, individuals of one species have one
          form and are numerically distinct by their matter. The framework holds that an
          identity is non-duplicable and is not shared by individuals. The framework has no
          principle of individuation by matter.

       2. The status of the final cause. Aristotle holds that natural things develop toward
          ends, and that this is part of their explanation. The framework states no teleology
          of nature.

       3. The status of the unmoved mover. The unmoved mover is an object of desire for the
          heavens, and it moves as such. The framework’s source enacts an identity and is not
          an end toward which things move.

       4. The status of the categories. Aristotle’s account is organized by the categories. The
          framework is organized by identity, manifestation, realm, and context, and it has no
          list of categories.



6.7      The Tradition’s Objections

     The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

     Aristotle’s first objection. The framework says that an identity is non-duplicable.
     But there is no knowledge of what is not shared: science concerns the universal, and the
     individual as such has no definition (Posterior Analytics I 31; Metaphysics Z 15). An
     identity that no other shares cannot be defined by genus and difference, and a thing that
6.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                          53


   cannot be defined cannot be known. The framework either gives up knowledge of identities
   or gives up their non-duplicability.
   Aristotle’s second objection. The framework gives an account of the source and its
   effect, and gives no account of why natural things are as they are. Nature does nothing
   without an end, and an explanation that omits the final cause omits half of what is to be
   explained (Physics II 8). The framework’s order is an order without a reason.



6.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that definition by genus and
   difference does not reach what is non-duplicable. It denies that definition is the only form
   of knowledge. The framework’s reconstruction reads an identity through its manifestations
   under a structure, and its knowledge is of the identity and not of a species. Aristotle’s own
   texts feel the difficulty: he says, in the Metaphysics, that the individual is not definable
   (Z 15) and that the sciences are of the universal (B 6, 999a–b), and he does not say
   that the individual is unknowable, since he takes perception and practical wisdom to
   grasp particulars. The framework adds a structural account of how an identity can be
   reconstructed, and it does not claim to define it.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework does not deny that nature is ordered,
   and it does not assert that the order is purposeless. It states the order in structural
   terms and leaves open whether the structure has an end. The objection assumes that an
   explanation is incomplete without a final cause, which is Aristotle’s premise and not the
   framework’s. The framework marks this as a divergence and a cost, and it does not claim
   to have refuted the premise.



6.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Aristotle’s cost. If Aristotle accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that there is a
knowledge of the particular that is not definition, and that the individual has a conserved identity
that is not its species. The cost is the loss of the thesis that science is of the universal alone, and
of individuation by matter.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Aristotle’s objections, it must give up the
non-duplicability of identities or the possibility of their being known, and it must give the order of
nature an end. The cost is the loss of the non-duplicable identity and of the structural neutrality
about ends.
54                                                                              Chapter 6. Aristotle


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what a particular is. The framework must take the problem of the knowability
of the individual as a real problem that Aristotle saw. Aristotle must take the non-duplicable
identity as an answer to it. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the assumption that what is
knowable is what is shared.



6.10       The Kind of Relation

     The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

     The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
     Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Aristotle’s
     “substance.” If one substitutes “substance” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the
     statements change: a substance is a composite of form and matter, with its individuation
     by matter, and an identity is non-duplicable without such a principle. If one substitutes
     “identity” for “substance” in the Metaphysics, the account of matter and individuation
     is lost. The substitution fails in both directions, and the relation is resemblance, not
     equivalence.
     Substitution 2. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Aristotle’s
     “accident.” If one substitutes “accident” for “manifestation,” the statements change: an
     accident inheres in a substance and has no being apart from it, while a manifestation is
     an appearance of an identity in a realm and is the means of reading it. If one substitutes
     “manifestation” for “accident,” the doctrine of the categories is lost. The substitution fails
     in both directions.
     Substitution 3. The framework’s term “one source” is not substitutable for Aristotle’s
     “unmoved mover.” If one substitutes “unmoved mover” for “one source,” the statements
     change: the mover moves as an object of desire and does not enact. If one substitutes
     “one source” for “unmoved mover,” the account of final causation is lost. The substitution
     fails in both directions.
     The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Aristotle is resemblance:
     both take the particular as primary, treat change as real, and distinguish what a thing
     is from how it appears, and they differ on the nature of identity, on the final cause, and
     on the source. The relation is also one of descent in the following sense, which bears on
     later chapters: Aristotle’s works are the source of much of the philosophy of the Islamic
     and Latin traditions, so that Ibn Sina, Ibn Rushd, Aquinas, and others stand in a line
     of descent from him, and their resemblances to the framework are not independent of
     one another (Remark 1.5). The relation between the framework and Aristotle is not
     equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing
     that Aristotle’s forms, read as particular, still do not support a non-duplicable identity,
     or that Aristotle’s account of knowledge of particulars excludes the reconstruction the
     framework describes.
6.11. Open Questions                                                                            55


6.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Are Aristotle’s forms universal or particular? The chapter has noted both
readings, and the resemblance to the framework’s identity is closer on the particular reading.

Second question. Is the individual knowable in Aristotle’s philosophy, and if so by what
faculty? The reply to Aristotle’s first objection rests on the claim that he allows some knowledge
of particulars, and a reader who holds that he does not has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Can the framework’s order of nature be stated without a final cause? The
chapter has not argued that it can, and it has marked the point as a cost.

A Question for Reflection
Take a particular thing you know well, a tool, a room, an animal. Can you define it, or only
the kind it belongs to? If a second thing of the same kind came along, what would you say was
different about it? What does your answer tell you about whether the individual can be known
as an individual, or only as an instance?

The next chapter turns to Stoicism. It states the doctrine of the logos, the physics of the pneuma,
the theory of fate and of freedom, and the cosmic cycle of conflagration and renewal; it identifies
the internal disputes in the interpretation of the Stoics; and it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of order and relation is the nearest ancient
analogue to the Stoic logos. The present chapter has stated Aristotle’s answer, which takes the
particular as primary; the next chapter states the answer of a school that took the cosmos as a
single ordered whole, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 7

Stoicism


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Stoicism, the school founded by Zeno of Citium (c. 334–
262 BCE) and developed by Cleanthes, Chrysippus (c. 280–207 BCE), Panaetius, Posidonius,
and, in the Roman period, by Seneca, Epictetus (c. 50–c. 135 CE), and Marcus Aurelius (121–180
CE). It states the doctrine of the logos, the physics of the pneuma, the theory of fate and of
freedom, the doctrine of the uniquely qualified individual, and the cosmic cycle of conflagration
and renewal. Because the writings of the early Stoics survive only in fragments and in reports,
the chapter relies on the collections of those fragments (Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, SVF,
and Long and Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers) and on the surviving works of the Roman
Stoics. It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of the school; it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of order and relation is the
nearest ancient analogue to the Stoic logos; it presents the objections that Stoicism would raise;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim, and the Stoic ethics is reported only as it bears on the metaphysical question.
Where the chapter speaks of “logos,” “pneuma,” “fate,” “assent,” or “conflagration,” these are
the Stoics’ terms, and their sense is fixed by the sources and by the interpretive literature, not
by the framework. Passages are paraphrased, not quoted, in accordance with the volume’s rule
of quotation.


7.1     A Scene
Consider a person on a ship in a storm. The wind, the waves, and the cargo are not in her power,
and she knows it. What is in her power is how she takes what happens: whether she gives her
assent to the thought that this is a disaster, or withholds it and attends to what can be done.
She does not make the storm. She does not control what comes. She governs the use she makes
of what comes.
   Consider the same ship from a wider view. The storm has causes in the weather, the weather
in the sea and sun, and these in the order of the whole. The ship, the sailor, and the storm
are parts of one system in which each affects every other. Nothing in the system is alone, and
nothing happens without a cause. The sailor’s assent is one of the causes in it.
   The scenes pose the question to which the Stoics gave their most distinctive answer: how is a
person to understand herself as a part of an ordered whole, and what remains up to her within
it? The Stoic answer is that the cosmos is a single living and rational being, pervaded by a logos,
that what happens happens in accordance with it, and that a person is free in the use of her own
judgment. The framework also gives an account of order and relation. The chapter asks how the
two accounts stand to each other.

                                                 56
7.2. The Question                                                                                57


7.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Aristotle’s answer, which takes the particular as primary and the
cosmos as ordered by form and end. The Stoics, who flourished in the generations after Aristotle,
took the cosmos as one ordered whole pervaded by a rational principle, and they placed the
human being within it.
   The question is not whether the Stoics were right. The question is what they held, what they
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question has three
parts.


First part: the position. What did the Stoics hold? The chapter states the logos and the
physics of the pneuma, fate and freedom, the uniquely qualified individual, and the cosmic cycle,
and it identifies the internal disputes.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Stoicism converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Stoicism would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Stoicism?
The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as resemblance,
with the lines of descent that bear on other chapters.


7.3      The Stoic Position
The Stoics divided philosophy into logic, physics, and ethics, and held that the three are parts of
one system. The position summarized here is the physics, which is the part that bears on the
dialogue, with a note on the ethics where the physics requires it.


7.3.1    Body, Logos, and Pneuma
The Stoics held that only bodies exist, in the strict sense, and that incorporeals such as void,
place, time, and what can be said (the lekton) subsist without being bodies. They distinguished
two principles in the cosmos: a passive principle, matter, and an active principle, which is the
logos, identified with god, reason, nature, and providence (Diogenes Laertius VII 134; LS 44).
The active principle is itself corporeal: it is the pneuma, a breath of fire and air, which pervades
matter and gives it its tension (tonos) and so its qualities. The cosmos is accordingly a single
living and rational body, in which everything is connected by sympathy (sympatheia), and in
which the logos works as a seed-principle (logos spermatikos) in each thing.


7.3.2    Fate, Assent, and Freedom
Every event has a cause, and the causes form a chain that the Stoics called fate (heimarmenē).
The early Stoics also held that human beings are responsible for their actions, since a person
assents or refuses to assent to the impressions that come to her. Chrysippus defended the
58                                                                          Chapter 7. Stoicism


compatibility of the two with the image of a cylinder and a cone: a push starts them moving,
but how each moves depends on its own shape, and in the same way an impression starts a
response whose character depends on the person (reported in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights VII 2).
The ancient critics, among them Alexander of Aphrodisias, denied that the position preserves
freedom, and the question is disputed to the present.

7.3.3     The Uniquely Qualified Individual and the Cycle of the Cosmos
The Stoics held that each individual has its own unique quality (idiōs poion), so that no two
things are exactly alike; Chrysippus is reported to have argued against the possibility of two
indiscernible individuals (Plutarch, On Common Conceptions 1077c–e; Cicero, Academica II 85).
The cosmos itself, they held, is periodically consumed by fire (ekpyrōsis) and reborn in the same
order (palingenesia), a doctrine whose details are among the most disputed in the school.


7.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Stoicism is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the logos. One reading takes the logos to be a divine body
that pervades the cosmos. Another takes it to be a rational structure that the physics describes
in corporeal terms because the Stoics had no other vocabulary. The disagreement matters for
the framework, since the framework’s order is a structure and not a body, and the resemblance
depends on which reading is taken.

Second dispute: the status of freedom. One reading takes Chrysippus to have defended
a compatibilism in which assent is up to us though fated. Another takes the doctrine to
be a determinism with a doctrine of responsibility that does not preserve alternatives. The
disagreement is relevant because the framework takes no position on determinism, and the Stoic
objection to the framework turns partly on it.

Third dispute: the status of the conflagration. Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus held
that the cosmos is periodically consumed by fire; Panaetius is reported to have doubted it;
Boethus of Sidon denied it. The disagreement matters because the cosmic cycle bears on the
permanence of the order, which is what the framework’s conservation of identity concerns, and
the chapter does not rely on the doctrine.


7.5      Points of Convergence

     Points of Convergence

     With Stoicism. The framework shares four structural features with the Stoic position.

        1. The primacy of order. The Stoics hold that the cosmos is ordered through and
          through by the logos. The framework holds that manifestations are governed by
7.6. Points of Divergence                                                                         59


        structure. Both treat order as basic, and not as something that disorder must first
        be overcome to reach.

      2. The immanence of order. The Stoic logos is in the cosmos and not outside it. The
        framework’s light is a conveyor within the realms. Both place the principle of order
        within what it orders.

      3. The unity of the cosmos. The Stoics hold that the parts of the cosmos are connected
        by sympathy. The framework holds that realms and identities are related through
        light. Both hold that the cosmos is a system of relations and not an aggregate.

      4. The unrepeatable individual. The Stoics hold that each individual has a unique
        quality, so that no two are exactly alike. The framework holds that an identity is
        non-duplicable. This is the closest convergence on the question of identity in Part II,
        and it is subject to the dispute over how much weight the Stoic doctrine bears, since
        it is known from reports.



7.6    Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Stoicism. The framework diverges from the Stoic position in four respects.

      1. The nature of order. The Stoic order is a corporeal pneuma holding matter in tension.
        The framework’s order is structural and is not a body.

      2. The status of teleology. The Stoics hold that the cosmos is providentially ordered
        toward the good of rational beings. The framework states no providence.

      3. The status of the human being. The Stoics hold that the human rational part is a
        portion of the divine logos. The framework treats a human being as an identity
        manifested in realms, and it does not hold that a human soul is a part of the source.

      4. The status of freedom. The Stoics defend a doctrine of assent as the seat of freedom
        within fate. The framework states no doctrine of freedom or of fate.


7.7    The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   The Stoic objection from unity. The framework holds that there are many non-
   duplicable identities, each enacted by one source. But the cosmos is one continuous body
   in which every part acts on every other, and a plurality of identities that are not shared
   breaks the continuity. The framework has to say what binds its identities, and if what
   binds them is the logos, it has the Stoic position under another name, and if it is not, the
60                                                                               Chapter 7. Stoicism


     cosmos falls apart.
     The Stoic objection from necessity. The framework speaks of manifestations and
     their conditions but does not say that everything has a cause. A cosmos in which some
     events lack causes is not ordered, and an order that tolerates exceptions is not an order.
     The framework either asserts universal causal order, and so fate, or it gives up order.



7.8      The Framework’s Reply

     The Framework’s Reply

     Reply to the objection from unity. The framework agrees that what binds the
     identities needs stating, and it states it: the identities are bound by their common source
     and by the light that conveys its effect, and they are related in realms and contexts. This
     is not the Stoic logos, since the binding is structural and not corporeal, and it is not a loss
     of unity, since unity of relation does not require unity of body. The Stoics themselves hold
     both the continuity of the cosmos and the uniqueness of each individual, and so their own
     position requires a unity that is compatible with a plurality of unrepeatable individuals.
     Reply to the objection from necessity. The framework does not assert that some
     events lack causes. It does not assert universal causal determination either, because
     its principles are about identity, manifestation, and context, and not about the causal
     structure of events. The objection assumes that order requires fate, which is the Stoic
     premise and not the framework’s. The framework marks the point as a divergence and a
     cost, and it does not claim to have refuted the premise.



7.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Stoicism’s cost. If the Stoics accept the framework’s reply, they must allow that the unity
of the cosmos is a unity of relation and not of one corporeal pneuma, and that order does not
by itself require a single chain of fate. The cost is the loss of the corporeal logos and of the
identification of order with fate.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the Stoic objections, it must give a fuller
account of what binds identities, and it must either assert universal causal order or admit that
its order is partial. The cost is the loss of the structural neutrality about causation.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what an ordered whole requires. The framework must take the Stoic claim that
order requires connection as a real constraint. The Stoics must take the framework’s unrepeatable
identities as an answer to a question their own doctrine of the individual raises. The cost of the
dialogue is the loss of the assumption that unity and plurality exclude each other.
7.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                           61


7.10     The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “structure of order” is not substitutable for the
   Stoic “logos.” If one substitutes “logos” for the framework’s term, the statements change:
   the logos is a corporeal pneuma that is also god and providence, and the framework’s
   structure is none of these. If one substitutes the framework’s term for “logos,” the physics
   of tension and the identification with providence are lost. The substitution fails in both
   directions, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the Stoic
  “uniquely qualified individual.” If one substitutes the Stoic term for “identity,” the
   statements change: the individual is a body with a unique quality, and the identity of the
   framework is enacted by a source and conserved through manifestation. If one substitutes
  “identity” for the Stoic term, the account of qualities as tensions of pneuma is lost. The
   substitution fails in both directions.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “context” is not substitutable for the Stoic “fate.”
   If one substitutes “fate” for “context,” the statements change: fate is a chain of causes,
   and context is a structural condition of validity and manifestation. If one substitutes
  “context” for “fate,” the doctrine of the necessity of events is lost. The substitution fails in
   both directions.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Stoicism is resemblance:
   both treat order as primary and immanent, the cosmos as a system of relations, and the
   individual as unrepeatable, and they differ on the nature of order, on providence, and on
   freedom. The relation is also one of descent in two lines that bear on other chapters. The
   Stoics took Heraclitus as a forerunner in their account of the logos and of fire, so that
   this chapter is kin to the chapter on Heraclitus; and the Stoic logos entered the thought
   of Philo and of the Christian tradition, so that later chapters are kin to this one. The
   resemblances among these chapters are therefore not independent (Remark 1.5). The
   relation is not equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be
   refuted by showing that the Stoic doctrine of the uniquely qualified individual is not a
   doctrine of unrepeatability, or that the Stoic logos, correctly read, is a structure and not a
   body so that the divergence on the nature of order disappears.



7.11     Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. How much weight can the Stoic doctrine of the uniquely qualified individual
bear, given that it is known from reports? The chapter has used it as the closest convergence,
and a reader who holds that the reports are too slight has a question the chapter leaves open.
62                                                                            Chapter 7. Stoicism


Second question. Is the Stoic logos a body or a structure? The chapter has taken both
readings and has not decided, and the force of the divergence on the nature of order depends on
the answer.

Third question. Can the framework state what binds identities without a doctrine of fate?
The chapter has argued that it can, and has marked the point as a cost.

A Question for Reflection
Think of an event that was not in your power, and of what you made of it. Which part of what
followed was the event, and which was your response? Could you have responded otherwise, and
in what sense? What does your answer tell you about whether order and freedom must be set
against each other?

Plotinus


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Plotinus (c. 204/205–270 CE). It states the doctrine of
the three principal realities, the One, Intellect, and Soul; the account of their derivation from
the One, called emanation in the later tradition; the doctrine of contemplation and of return;
the doctrine of the two activities; and the account of matter, with reference to the Enneads,
as arranged by Porphyry, and cited by treatise (for example V.1, V.4, VI.9) and chapter. It
identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Plotinus; it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of light and descent is the nearest ancient
analogue to Plotinus’s metaphysics of emanation; it presents the objections that Plotinus would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading.
It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the One,”
“Intellect,” “Soul,” “emanation,” “contemplation,” or “matter,” these are Plotinus’s terms, and
their sense is fixed by the Enneads and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.
Passages are paraphrased, not quoted, in accordance with the volume’s rule of quotation.



8.1     A Scene

Consider a lamp in a dark room. The lamp is a source, and the light fills the room. The room is
lit by the lamp and is not the lamp; the light at the far wall is fainter than at the lamp and is
the same light. The lamp has not been used up by shining. If the lamp were taken away, the
light would go, and the lamp would not be the lamp without a power to shine.
   Consider next a teacher whose pupil has understood. The teacher has given nothing away,
and what the pupil has is not a part of the teacher cut off. The understanding came from
the teacher and is the pupil’s own, and in having it the pupil is turned toward the teacher’s
knowledge, which she did not have before and has now in a lesser way.
   The two scenes pose the question that Plotinus makes central. How can there be a source of
what is, from which everything comes, without the source being diminished, divided, or changed
by giving? And how can what comes from the source be turned back toward it, and so be what
it is? Plotinus answers with an account of the One, Intellect, and Soul, in which each proceeds
from the one before it and is constituted by turning back to it. The framework also has an
account of light as conveyor of a source’s effect through realms. The chapter asks how the two
accounts stand to each other.




                                                  63
64                                                                             Chapter 8. Plotinus


8.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated the Stoic answer, in which the cosmos is one ordered body pervaded
by a corporeal logos. Plotinus is the thinker who most fully developed the metaphysics of light
and descent in the ancient West, and in doing so he drew on Plato, on Aristotle, and on the
Stoics, and he gave the later traditions much of their vocabulary.
     The question is not whether Plotinus was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Plotinus hold? The chapter states the One, Intellect,
and Soul, emanation and return, the two activities, and the account of matter, and it identifies
the internal disputes.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Plotinus converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Plotinus would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Plotinus?
The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as resemblance
and kinship, with the lines of descent that bear on many later chapters.


8.3      Plotinus’s Position
Plotinus taught in Rome, and his treatises were edited and arranged by his pupil Porphyry
into six groups of nine, the Enneads. The position summarized here is the one drawn from the
treatises on the three principal realities and on the soul, with the disputes taken up below.


8.3.1    The One, Intellect, and Soul

Plotinus holds that there are three principal realities, which he calls hypostases. The first is
the One, which is beyond being and beyond thought, the principle of all unity, and which can
be named only by negation and by analogy (V.1, V.4, VI.9). The second is Intellect, which
contains the Forms and is the unity of thinker and what is thought (V.9). The third is Soul,
which administers the sensible world and is both one and many (IV.3–5, IV.9). Below Soul lie
nature, the body, and matter.


8.3.2    Emanation and Return

The hypostases are derived from one another by a process that later writers called emanation.
The One produces Intellect, and Intellect produces Soul, without the One being diminished,
changed, or divided by the production, as a source of light is not diminished by shining (V.1.6,
V.4.1). The derivation is not temporal, and it is not an act of will in the ordinary sense; it is the
overflow of a perfect principle. What proceeds is incomplete until it turns back toward its source
8.4. Internal Disputes                                                                            65


and contemplates it, and in turning it is constituted as what it is (V.2.1, V.4.2). Each level thus
both proceeds and returns, and the return is what gives the lower level its form.



8.3.3    The Two Activities and the Account of Matter

Plotinus explains the derivation by the doctrine of two activities: each thing has an internal
activity, which is the thing itself in act, and an external activity, which proceeds from it and is a
likeness of it, as heat proceeds from fire and light from the sun (V.4.2). Matter, which stands
at the lower limit of the descent, is not a principle in the way the One is. It is the indefinite
substrate of form, which Plotinus treats as non-being, and in some treatises as the source or the
very nature of evil (I.8, II.4). The soul’s descent into the body and its ascent are the subject of
several treatises (IV.8, VI.9), in which the soul is said both to descend by a kind of necessity and
to descend by its own choice, and to remain in part undescended (IV.8.8).




8.4     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Plotinus is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the One. One reading takes the One to be beyond being and
wholly ineffable, so that every statement about it is only a pointer. Another takes the One to
have a kind of self-relation or self-awareness that is not thought. The disagreement matters
because the framework’s one source can be set against the One only on the first reading without
qualification.



Second dispute: emanation, necessity, and will. One reading takes emanation to be a
necessary overflow of the One, without will or choice. Another takes it to be compatible with a
kind of will of the One. A third holds that the word “emanation” misleads, since Plotinus’s own
image is of a derivation by activity, and not of a stream that leaves its source. The disagreement
matters because the framework’s account of the source’s effect is stated in terms that suit some
readings and not others.



Third dispute: the status of matter. Plotinus treats matter as the privation of form
in some treatises and as evil itself in others (I.8). One reading takes the two accounts to be
consistent. Another takes them to mark a development or a tension. The disagreement matters
because the framework has no doctrine of evil, and the divergence on matter differs according to
the reading.
66                                                                            Chapter 8. Plotinus


8.5      Points of Convergence




     Points of Convergence

     With Plotinus. The framework shares four structural features with Plotinus’s position.

       1. The hierarchy of levels. Plotinus holds that reality is ordered in levels, each derived
          from the one above. The framework holds that identities are expressed in ordered
          realms. Both hold that the order is not symmetrical.

       2. The priority of unity. Plotinus holds that the One is prior to all multiplicity. The
          framework holds that an identity is enacted by one source. Both give priority to
          unity over plurality.

       3. Light as the image of the derivation. Plotinus uses light, and the light of the sun in
          particular, as the image of the derivation of the lower from the higher. The framework
          uses light as the conveyor of the source’s effect. Both give light a structural role in
          the relation between a source and what comes from it.

       4. The non-diminishment of the source. Plotinus holds that the One is not diminished
          by what proceeds from it, and the doctrine of the two activities distinguishes the
          source in itself from its external activity. The framework holds that the source is
          not diminished by its effect. Both distinguish what a source is from what proceeds
          from it, and hold that the second does not use up the first.




8.6      Points of Divergence
8.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                    67


   Points of Divergence

  With Plotinus. The framework diverges from Plotinus’s position in four respects.

      1. The nature of emanation. For Plotinus the derivation produces the hypostases,
         which are levels of being, and Intellect and Soul are produced by the One. For the
         framework light conveys the effect of a source across realms, and the realms are not
         produced as levels of being by a derivation.

      2. The status of contemplation. For Plotinus a hypostasis is constituted by contemplating
         what is above it. The framework has no doctrine that contemplation constitutes
         what contemplates.

      3. The status of the ascent. Plotinus holds that the soul’s return ends in union with
         the One. The framework’s ascending light is a property of the conveyor and does
         not describe a union of the soul with the source.

      4. The status of matter. Plotinus treats matter as the lowest limit of the descent and
         as privation or evil. The framework has no doctrine of matter as privation and none
         of evil.



8.7    The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Plotinus’s first objection. The framework holds that identities are many and non-
   duplicable. But all souls are in a sense one soul, and what differentiates them is the
   body and the descent into it (IV.9). A philosophy that takes the plurality of identities as
   ultimate has taken the lower level for the highest, and it has no account of the unity from
   which the plurality comes.
   Plotinus’s second objection. The framework speaks of light as a conveyor distinct
   from the source and from what it conveys. But the light of the source is the source’s own
   activity, as heat is the activity of fire. A conveyor distinct from the source needs a source
   of its own, and the framework has set a regress in motion, or has made light a third thing
   that is neither the source nor its effect.



8.8    The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the plurality of identities
   needs an account of unity, and it gives one: the identities are enacted by one source and
   related by light. It denies that non-duplicability treats the many as ultimate. Plotinus
   himself asks, in the treatise on whether there are Ideas of particulars (V.7), whether
   the individual has its own form, and he inclines to say that individuals have their own
68                                                                               Chapter 8. Plotinus


     principles and are not mere instances of a species, so that the question of the unrepeatable
     individual is a question in his own philosophy. The framework gives the individual a
     conserved identity and places it under the source, and it does not make the many ultimate.
     Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the light of a source is
     the source’s activity, and it states this: light is the conveyor of the source’s effect, and it
     is not a separate source. It is not a third thing apart from the source, because it has no
     existence or work other than conveying. The distinction the framework draws between
     the conveyor and what it conveys is the distinction between an activity and its content,
     which is the distinction that Plotinus’s two activities draw between the internal act and
     the external act, and no regress follows.



8.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Plotinus’s cost. If Plotinus accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the unrepeatable
individual has an identity that is conserved and not merely a share in the One, and that the
structure of derivation can be stated without the doctrine that each level is constituted by
contemplating the one above. The cost is the loss of the thesis that individuality belongs only to
the lower levels, and of the constitutive role of contemplation.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Plotinus’s objections, it must say that the
plurality of identities is derivative of a prior unity, and that the light it speaks of is constituted
by return to its source. It must also admit a doctrine of the soul’s descent and ascent and give
an account of matter and evil. The cost is the loss of the structural neutrality about the soul
and about evil.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what a source and its effect require. The framework must take the doctrine of
the two activities as an answer to a real question about the relation of a source to what comes
from it. Plotinus must take the conserved identity of the individual as an answer to the question
that his own treatise on particulars raises. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the assumption
that the individual is either ultimate or derivative without remainder.


8.10       The Kind of Relation

     The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

     The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
     Substitution 1. The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for Plotinus’s “light”
     as the image of the derivation. If one substitutes the Plotinian image for the framework’s
     term, the statements change: the framework’s light would become a stage in the derivation
8.11. Open Questions                                                                                 69


   of levels of being, and its three properties would be replaced by descent and return. If one
   substitutes the framework’s term for the image in the Enneads, the image is stripped of
   what it was used to say about the constitution of the hypostases. The substitution fails in
   both directions, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “one source” is not substitutable for Plotinus’s
   “the One.” If one substitutes “the One” for “one source,” the statements change: the One
   is beyond being and thought, and the source of the framework enacts an identity. If one
   substitutes “one source” for “the One,” the claim that the One is beyond being, and that
   it can be named only by negation, is lost. The substitution fails in both directions.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “realm” is not substitutable for Plotinus’s
   “hypostasis.” If one substitutes “hypostasis” for “realm,” the statements change: a
   hypostasis is a level of being derived from the one above and constituted by its return,
   and a realm is a domain in which an identity manifests. If one substitutes “realm” for
   “hypostasis,” the doctrine that each level is constituted by contemplation is lost. The
   substitution fails in both directions.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Plotinus is resemblance
   and, in the line of descent that must be stated, kinship. It is resemblance in the structural
   role of light as the image of the relation of a source to what comes from it, and it is a
   difference in the nature of that relation. It is kinship in the following sense, which bears on
   many later chapters: Plotinus drew on Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics; his thought reached
   the Islamic tradition through Arabic paraphrases that were attributed to Aristotle (the
   so-called Theology of Aristotle) and through Proclus, and it reached the Latin tradition
   through Augustine and the Neoplatonists, so that the chapters on Augustine, Dionysius,
   Ibn Sina, Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Eckhart, and Cusa are kin to this chapter. The recurrence
   of the imagery of light and descent across these traditions is therefore not independent
   convergence, and the volume does not offer it as evidence (Remark 1.5). The relation
   between the framework and Plotinus is not equivalence, agreement, or identity. The
   framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Plotinus’s light is only a metaphor
   and that the doctrine of the two activities has no structural counterpart in the framework’s
   account of the conveyor, or that the framework’s conveyor cannot be distinguished from
   the source without the regress that Plotinus’s second objection describes.



8.11     Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the One beyond being in a sense that excludes every statement about it?
The chapter has taken both readings, and the resemblance to the framework’s source depends on
which is taken.


Second question. Is “emanation” the right word for Plotinus’s derivation? The chapter has
used it as the later tradition did, and a reader who holds that the word misleads has a question
70                                                                             Chapter 8. Plotinus


the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s distinction between the conveyor and its content do
the work of the doctrine of the two activities? The reply to the second objection says that it
does, and a reader who finds the correspondence forced has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Think of something that you gave to someone and that you did not lose by giving, a piece of
knowledge, a habit, a way of seeing. Where does it now live? Is it the same thing in the two of
you, or two things? What does your answer tell you about how a source can give without being
diminished?
