Chapter 9

Proclus


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Proclus (412–485 CE), the systematizer of Neoplatonism.
It states the triad of remaining, procession, and reversion; the doctrine of the henads; the
relation of the unparticipated to the participated; and the systematic and deductive form of
his metaphysics, with reference to the Elements of Theology (cited by proposition, as ET), the
Platonic Theology, and the commentaries on the Timaeus and the Parmenides. It identifies
the internal disputes in the interpretation of Proclus; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the three properties of light is the nearest
ancient analogue to Proclus’s triad; it presents the objections that Proclus would raise against
the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it
states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no
normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “remaining,” “procession,”
“reversion,” “henad,” or “participation,” these are Proclus’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his
texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework. Passages are paraphrased, not
quoted, in accordance with the volume’s rule of quotation.


9.1     A Scene

Consider a river with a source in the mountains. The spring remains where it is. From it the
water goes out down the valley, and as it goes it takes its shape from the land. Some of the water
returns, evaporated and fallen again on the high ground, and in returning it becomes spring once
more. The river has three moments, which are not three rivers: what stays at the source, what
goes out, and what comes back.
    Consider next a teacher, a lesson, and a pupil. The teacher remains what she is; the lesson
goes out from her to the pupil; and the pupil, in understanding it, turns back toward what the
teacher knows and is shaped by it. If any one of the three moments were missing, the teaching
would fail: without the teacher’s remaining there would be nothing to give, without the going
out nothing would reach the pupil, and without the return the pupil would have received nothing
that she could use.
    The scenes pose the question that Proclus answers with a single structure. How does a
principle give rise to what comes after it and remain itself, and how does what comes after it
come to be what it is? Proclus’s answer is that every effect remains in its cause, proceeds from
it, and reverts upon it, and that this triad is the form of every causal relation in the hierarchy of
being. The framework also states three properties of light. The chapter asks how the triad and
the three properties stand to each other.



                                                 71
72                                                                           Chapter 9. Proclus


9.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated Plotinus’s metaphysics of the One, Intellect, and Soul. Proclus took
the Plotinian inheritance, together with the later Neoplatonism of Iamblichus and the Athenian
school, and gave it a systematic and deductive form. The dialogue with Proclus is therefore the
dialogue with the most explicit of the ancient attempts to state the structure of procession in
general terms.
     The question is not whether Proclus was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Proclus hold? The chapter states the triad, the henads,
the unparticipated and the participated, and the systematic form, and it identifies the internal
disputes.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Proclus converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Proclus would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Proclus?
The chapter runs the substitution test in both directions and states the relation as resemblance
and kinship, with the lines of descent that bear on later chapters.


9.3     Proclus’s Position
Proclus headed the Platonic school at Athens for many years, and he wrote commentaries on
Plato and systematic treatises. The position summarized here is the one set out in the Elements
of Theology, a work of two hundred and eleven propositions, each with a demonstration, in the
manner of Euclid’s Elements.


9.3.1    The Triad of Remaining, Procession, and Reversion
Proclus holds that every effect, in being produced, remains in its cause, proceeds from it, and
reverts upon it (ET 30–35). The remaining is what the effect has in common with the cause; the
procession is its difference; and the reversion is the return by which it becomes what it is by
being directed to its cause. The triad is not one of several patterns; it is the structure of the
relation of every producer to what it produces, from the highest level to the lowest. Proclus also
holds that every cause is superior to its effect (ET 7), and that every manifold participates in
unity (ET 1).


9.3.2    The Unparticipated and the Participated
A principle that gives rise to many things is not itself shared among them; it stands above
them as an unparticipated monad, and what it produces is participated by the many (ET 23).
The soul, for instance, is the unparticipated source of the particular souls, and Intellect of the
9.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             73


particular intellects. Participation is thus not a relation between equals; it is the relation of what
receives to what gives without being shared.

9.3.3     The Henads and the Systematic Form
Above being, and below the One, Proclus places the henads, a plurality of unities, each of which
is a god and a principle of the order of being (ET 113–165). They are not parts of the One; each
is a unity of its own, and they are the source of the unity that beings have. The whole is set out
in a graded order, with each level exhibiting the triad and participating in the level above, and
the Elements presents it as a chain of demonstrations from first propositions.


9.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Proclus is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the henads. One reading takes the henads to be the gods of
traditional religion, reinterpreted as unities above being. Another takes them to be a technical
device for explaining how the plurality of beings can have its source in a single One without
being merely derivative of it. Dodds’s commentary on the Elements remains the standard point
of reference for the dispute. The disagreement matters because the resemblance of the henads to
the framework’s plurality of identities depends on the reading.

Second dispute: the originality of the triad. One reading attributes the triad of remaining,
procession, and reversion to Proclus. Another finds it already in Iamblichus and in Plotinus’s
account of the double activity and the turning back. The disagreement matters because a
reader who attributes the triad to the tradition will read the resemblance to the framework as a
resemblance to the Neoplatonic inheritance, and a reader who attributes it to Proclus will read
it as a resemblance to a particular thinker.

Third dispute: the status of the systematic form. One reading takes the deductive
form of the Elements to be a genuine demonstrative method. Another takes it to be a mode
of presentation that does not carry the force of demonstration, since the axioms are Platonic
doctrines. The disagreement matters because the framework’s own form, a set of principles with
arguments and epistemic statuses, can be set against the first reading and not the second.


9.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Proclus. The framework shares four structural features with Proclus’s position.

        1. The triadic structure. Proclus holds that every effect remains in its cause, proceeds
          from it, and reverts upon it. The framework holds that light has three properties,
          which on the reading taken here correspond in part to procession and reversion.
74                                                                              Chapter 9. Proclus


          Both state the relation of source and effect in three terms.

       2. The hierarchy of levels. Proclus holds that being is graded, each level exhibiting the
          triad and participating in the one above. The framework holds that identities are
          expressed in ordered realms. Both hold that the order is asymmetrical.

       3. The priority of unity. Proclus holds that every manifold participates in unity. The
          framework holds that an identity is enacted by one source. Both give priority to
          unity over plurality.

       4. The unparticipated and the participated. Proclus holds that the source of many
          things is not itself shared among them. The framework holds that the source is not
          diminished or divided by its effect. Both hold that a source can give without being
          given up.




9.6      Points of Divergence


     Points of Divergence

     With Proclus. The framework diverges from Proclus’s position in four respects.

       1. The nature of the triad. For Proclus the triad is the structure of every causal relation
          in the hierarchy of being. The framework states three properties of light, and it does
          not state them as a law of all being. The framework’s reflective property has no
          exact counterpart in the triad.

       2. The status of the henads. Proclus posits a plurality of unities above being, each a
          god. The framework posits one source and a plurality of identities, and it has no
          gods above being.

       3. The status of participation. For Proclus the many participate in the unparticipated
          monad that is above them. The framework’s identities are non-duplicable, and they
          are related to the source by light and not by participation.

       4. The status of the systematic form. Proclus presents his metaphysics as a deduction
          from first propositions that are Platonic doctrines. The framework presents its
          principles with epistemic statuses and distinguishes axioms from theorems.
9.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                     75


9.7    The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Proclus’s first objection. The framework states three properties of light, but it does
   not state that every effect remains in its cause, proceeds, and reverts. The triad is not a
   property of a medium; it is the law of every causal relation. A philosophy that confines
   it to light has taken a part for the whole, and it leaves the rest of reality without the
   structure that makes the relation of cause and effect intelligible.
   Proclus’s second objection. The framework holds that identities are non-duplicable
   and not shared. But every manifold participates in unity, and what is not shared has no
   relation to the one. If the identities are not participated in anything, they are unrelated
   to the source, and if they are related, they participate. The framework has abolished
   participation and has left itself no way to say how the many are related to the one.



9.8    The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the relation of a source to
   its effect has a general structure, and it states the properties of light as the structure of
   the conveyor, not as a law of all causal relations. It accepts that this is a narrower claim
   than Proclus’s, and it marks the narrowness as a difference. The framework’s conserved
   identity corresponds to the remaining, the descending property to the procession, and the
   ascending property to the reversion, and the reflective property has no counterpart; the
   correspondence is an interpretation and is marked as one. The objection assumes that the
   triad must be universal, which is Proclus’s premise, and the framework does not make it.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the identities must be
   related to the source, and it holds that they are related by the light that conveys the
   source’s effect. It denies that the relation must be participation in a shared form. Proclus’s
   own doctrine of the henads makes the point: each henad is a unity of its own and is not a
   part of the One or a shared instance of it, and yet the henads are related to the One and
   to the beings that depend on them. The framework’s identities stand to the source as the
   henads stand to the One on the reading of the henads that takes them to be unrepeatable
   unities, and the relation is one of dependence without participation.



9.9    The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Proclus’s cost. If Proclus accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the relation of
a source to its effect can be stated as a structure of a conveyor, without making the triad a
universal law, and that a plurality of unrepeatable unities need not be related to the source by
76                                                                               Chapter 9. Proclus


participation. The cost is the loss of the universality of the triad and of participation as the only
form of relation to the one.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Proclus’s objections, it must state the triad
as a law of all causal relation, and it must give a doctrine of participation that is compatible
with the non-duplicability of identities. The cost is the loss of the restriction of its structure to
the conveyor, and of the neutrality about participation.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim as
a claim about what a source-effect relation requires. The framework must take the triad as the
most developed statement in the ancient tradition of what the relation involves. Proclus must
take the conveyor as a way of stating a part of it without a claim to the whole. The cost of the
dialogue is the loss of the assumption that a structure of three terms must be either universal or
arbitrary.


9.10       The Kind of Relation

     The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

     The substitution test. The test is run on three terms, in both directions.
     Substitution 1. The framework’s term “the three properties of light” is not substitutable
     for Proclus’s “triad.” If one substitutes the triad for the three properties, the statements
     change: the triad is a law of every causal relation in the hierarchy of being, and the
     properties are those of a conveyor. If one substitutes the three properties for the triad in
     the Elements, the universality of the triad and the doctrine that reversion constitutes the
     effect are lost. The substitution fails in both directions, and the relation is resemblance,
     not equivalence.
     Substitution 2. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Proclus’s
     “henad.” If one substitutes “henad” for “identity,” the statements change: a henad is a
     god above being and a principle of the order of beings, and an identity is a conserved
     invariance expressed in realms. If one substitutes “identity” for “henad,” the divinity and
     the position above being are lost. The substitution fails in both directions.
     Substitution 3. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Proclus’s
     “the participated.” If one substitutes “the participated” for “manifestation,” the statements
     change: the participated is what many particulars share in, and a manifestation is an
     appearance of an identity that is not shared. If one substitutes “manifestation” for “the
     participated,” participation is lost. The substitution fails in both directions.
     The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Proclus is resemblance
     and, in the line of descent that must be stated, kinship. It is resemblance in the three-term
     structure of the relation of source and effect, and it is a difference in the scope and the
     content of that structure. It is kinship in the following sense, which bears on later chapters:
     Proclus received Plotinus and Iamblichus and passed on a vocabulary of procession and
9.11. Open Questions                                                                           77


   reversion to the Christian, Islamic, and Latin traditions, through Dionysius, through the
   Arabic Book of Causes that is largely drawn from the Elements, and through William of
   Moerbeke’s thirteenth-century Latin translation of the Elements; Aquinas, Eckhart, and
   Cusa belong to this line. The recurrence of triadic structures of procession and return
   across these traditions is therefore not independent convergence, and the volume does
   not offer it as evidence (Remark 1.5). The relation between the framework and Proclus
   is not equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by
   showing that the three properties of light cannot be correlated with the moments of the
   triad without distorting both, or that the framework’s conveyor, correctly read, is the
   universal law of causal relation that Proclus’s first objection takes it to omit.




9.11        Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Does the framework’s reflective property have a counterpart in Proclus? The
chapter has said that it does not, and a reader who finds a counterpart in the reversion or in the
remaining has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Do the henads resemble the framework’s plurality of identities, or only
name the problem of how plurality comes from unity? The chapter has treated the reading as
disputed.




Third question. Can a relation of dependence without participation be stated clearly? The
reply to the second objection says that it can, and a reader who holds that dependence without
participation is unintelligible has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Take a skill you have learned from someone. What stayed in them, what went out to you, and
what came back, in the form of something you now do in your own way? If you had to give up
one of the three, which would leave the skill in the worst state? What does your answer tell you
about whether a relation of source and effect needs all three moments?

Part II is now complete. The dialogues with the six figures and schools of the ancient West,
Parmenides and Heraclitus, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Plotinus, and Proclus, have been stated.
Part III turns to the medieval West. The first dialogue is with Augustine; the next is with
Dionysius the Areopagite; the next with Anselm; and so on through Aquinas, Scotus, Ockham,
Eckhart, and Cusa. The ancient tradition has asked what being is and how the many come from
the one; the medieval tradition will ask how this inheritance is to be thought within a creed.
     Part III

The Medieval West




        79
Chapter 10

Augustine


Scope. This chapter opens Part III, the dialogues with the medieval West, and it opens it with
Augustine of Hippo. It states Augustine’s account of time, memory, the inner light, the two cities,
and the relation between faith and reason, with reference to the Confessions, the City of God,
and the De Trinitate; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Augustine;
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of time
and inner light is the nearest patristic analogue to Augustine’s; it presents the objections that
Augustine would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what
each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “time,” “memory,” “the inner light,” “grace,” or “the two cities,” these are Augustine’s
terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the
framework.


10.1      A Scene
Consider a person remembering her childhood. She is in the present, recalling a past that is no
longer here. The past event is gone; the person who underwent it is gone; and yet, in the act of
memory, the past is present to her. She sees it, not with her eyes, but with her mind; she hears
it, not with her ears, but with her memory. The past is not here, and yet it is present; the past
is not now, and yet it is now in her memory.
   Now consider a second case, harder to state. Suppose she asks not what memory is, but what
time is. She knows what time is, she says, as long as no one asks her; but when she tries to
explain it, she does not know. The past is not, because it has passed; the future is not, because
it has not yet come; the present is not, because it has no duration. If none of the three is, what
is time? And yet time is real; we measure it; we speak of it; we live in it.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what time is, or what memory
is, but what makes her knowledge of either possible. She knows that she remembers; she knows
that she is the one who remembers; and she knows that her knowledge is not a matter of the
senses. The senses see the things of the world; the mind sees the truth of things. And the mind
sees the truth by a light that is not the light of the sun; it is an inner light, the light of the mind,
the light by which the mind knows what it knows.
   The scene is Augustine’s image, in the Confessions, of the structure of the inner life. The
past is in memory; the future is in expectation; the present is in attention. The three are not
three times; they are three aspects of one mind, stretched out (distentio animi) across the three.
And the mind, in its knowledge, is illuminated by a light that is not the light of the senses; it is
the light of the truth, the light of God, the light by which the mind sees what it sees.

                                                  80
10.2. The Question                                                                                 81


   The scene poses the question that Augustine was the first to pose in its full form. What is
time, if not a thing in the world? What is memory, if not a storehouse of the past? And what is
the inner light, if not the light of the sun? The present chapter states Augustine’s answer, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.


10.2      The Question
The previous part stated the positions of the ancient West: Parmenides and Heraclitus, Plato,
Aristotle, the Stoics, Plotinus, and Proclus. The ancient world posed the problem of change
and unity, and gave a series of systematic answers; each answer turned on a different principle:
Forms, substance, logos, emanation, triad. The present part turns to the medieval West, and its
first dialogue is with Augustine, in whom the ancient problem is transformed by the Christian
revelation.
   The question is not whether Augustine was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Augustine hold? The chapter states the account of time,
memory, the inner light, the two cities, and the relation between faith and reason, with reference
to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Augustine converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Augustine would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Augustine?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


10.3      The Position

10.3.1    Time

Augustine’s account of time is stated in the Confessions XI. The account begins with a question:
what is time? If no one asks, he knows; if he tries to explain, he does not know. The past is not,
because it has passed; the future is not, because it has not yet come; the present is not, because
it has no duration. And yet we measure time; we say that one period is longer than another; we
speak of the past, the present, and the future as if they were.
   Augustine’s answer is that time is a distension of the mind (distentio animi). The past is in
memory; the future is in expectation; the present is in attention. The three are not three times;
they are three aspects of one mind, stretched out across the three. Time is not a thing in the
world; it is the mind’s stretching out, the mind’s holding together the past, the present, and the
future in a single act of attention.
82                                                                          Chapter 10. Augustine


     The answer has three consequences. First, time is not a property of things; it is a property of
minds. Second, time is not a container; it is a distension. Third, time is not eternal; it is created,
and it begins with the world. The eternal is not time without end; it is the absence of time, the
simultaneity of the whole, the "today" that does not pass.

     From the Tradition

     “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one that asks, I
     know not. Yet I say boldly that I know nothing but a distension of the mind. For what is
     time but a distension of the mind?” (Augustine, Confessions XI.14.17 and XI.26.33, trans.
     after Pusey)


10.3.2      Memory
Augustine’s account of memory is stated in the Confessions X. The memory is a "great harbor,"
a "storehouse" of images, of knowledge, of affections. The memory contains the past, not as
the past, but as the present image of the past; it contains what we have learned, not as the
learning, but as the knowledge we have; it contains what we have felt, not as the feeling, but as
the memory of the feeling.
     The memory is also the place where the mind meets itself. In memory, the mind finds itself;
it finds what it has done, what it has suffered, what it has known. And in memory, the mind
finds God—not as an image, but as a presence; not as a thing remembered, but as the light by
which it remembers.
     The memory raises a question that Augustine does not fully answer: how can the mind
contain what it is? The memory contains the past, but the mind is not the past; the memory
contains the knowledge, but the mind is not the knowledge; the memory contains God, but the
mind is not God. The mind is present to itself in memory, and yet it is a mystery to itself; it
seeks itself, and does not find itself; it seeks God, and finds Him in memory, but not as it seeks
Him.

10.3.3      The Inner Light
Augustine’s account of the inner light is stated in the De Trinitate and in the Solidquies. The
mind knows the truth by a light that is not the light of the sun; it is the light of the truth itself,
the light of God, the light by which the mind sees what it sees. The light is not a thing among
the things the mind sees; it is the condition under which the mind sees. It is not a doctrine the
mind learns; it is the principle by which the mind learns any doctrine.
     The inner light is the light of the divine ideas, the eternal reasons, the Forms in the mind of
God. The mind sees the truth because it sees the eternal reasons; it sees the eternal reasons
because it is illuminated by the light of God. The light is not the mind; the light is not the truth;
the light is the condition under which the mind sees the truth.
     The inner light is also the light of faith. Faith is not a substitute for reason; faith is the
condition under which reason sees what it could not see without faith. "Unless you believe, you
will not understand"; the understanding is the reward of faith, and the faith is the light by which
the understanding sees.
10.4. Internal Disputes                                                                              83


   From the Tradition

   “The light of the mind is not the light of the eyes; it is the light of the truth, the light by
   which the mind sees what it sees. This light is not a thing among the things the mind
   sees; it is the condition under which the mind sees.” (Augustine, De Trinitate XII.15.24,
   trans. after McKenna)



10.3.4    The Two Cities

Augustine’s account of the two cities is stated in the City of God. The two cities are the city of
God and the city of man; the one is founded on the love of God, the other on the love of self.
The two cities are mingled in this world; they are distinguished only at the last judgment. But
the distinction is real, and it is the key to the understanding of history.
   The city of God is not a political entity; it is a spiritual community, the community of those
who love God. The city of man is not a political entity either; it is a spiritual community, the
community of those who love themselves. The two cities are not the church and the state; they
are the two orientations of the will, the two loves that govern human life.
   The two cities give Augustine a philosophy of history. History is not a cycle, as the ancient
world held; it is a line, with a beginning and an end. The beginning is the creation; the end is
the last judgment. The middle is the time of the two cities, the time of the pilgrimage of the city
of God through the city of man.


10.3.5    Faith and Reason

Augustine’s account of the relation between faith and reason is stated throughout his works, but
most clearly in the De Trinitate and in the Confessions. Faith and reason are not enemies; they
are complements. Faith is the condition of understanding; understanding is the reward of faith.
"Unless you believe, you will not understand"; the understanding is the reward of faith, and the
faith is the light by which the understanding sees.
   The relation is not a simple priority of faith over reason. Faith is not a substitute for reason;
it is a condition of reason. The mind that believes sees more than the mind that does not; the
mind that sees understands more than the mind that only believes. Faith and reason are two
moments of one act, the act of the mind that seeks God.
   Augustine’s account is also a critique of the ancient world. The ancient world held that
reason is autonomous; Augustine holds that reason is illuminated by faith. The ancient world
held that the philosopher is self-sufficient; Augustine holds that the philosopher needs grace. The
ancient world held that the goal of life is happiness; Augustine holds that the goal of life is God,
and that happiness is the enjoyment of God.



10.4     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Augustine is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
84                                                                        Chapter 10. Augustine


First dispute: the status of time. The traditional reading takes Augustine’s distentio animi
to be a psychological account: time is a feature of the mind, not of the world. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a metaphysical account: time is the distension of the mind, but the mind is
not the only thing that is distended; the world is also distended, and the distension of the mind
is a participation in the distension of the world. The two readings disagree on whether Augustine
is a subjectivist or a realist about time, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s time is a realm-relative succession, neither subjective nor
purely objective.

Second dispute: the status of the inner light. The traditional reading takes the inner light
to be the light of God, a divine illumination that is given to the mind by grace. A revisionary
reading takes it to be the light of reason, a natural capacity of the mind to see the truth. The
two readings disagree on whether Augustine is a supernaturalist or a naturalist about knowledge,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s light is
neither divine nor natural, but structural.

Third dispute: the status of the two cities. The traditional reading takes the two cities to
be two spiritual communities, one saved and one damned. A revisionary reading takes them to be
two orientations of the will, present in every person, not two groups of people. The two readings
disagree on whether Augustine is a dualist or a monist about humanity, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no two cities, and its ontology
has no saved and damned.
     The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Augustine is a subjectivist about time, the
framework’s dialogue with him is a dialogue between a psychological account and a structural
account. If Augustine is a realist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the
Confessions, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


10.5       Points of Convergence

     Points of Convergence

     With Augustine. The framework shares four structural features with Augustine’s
     position.

       1. Time as a structure of the mind’s relation to the world. Augustine holds that time is
          a distension of the mind, not a thing in the world. The framework holds that time is
          a realm-relative succession, not a container, and that its kind is fixed by the realm.
          Both hold that time is not a thing among things, and that it is a structural feature
          of the relation between mind and world.

       2. The distinction between the temporal and the eternal. Augustine distinguishes the
          distension of time from the simultaneity of eternity. The framework distinguishes the
10.6. Points of Divergence                                                                             85


          succession of the material realm from the atemporality of the First Determination
          and the eternity of the Structural Determination. Both hold that the temporal and
          the eternal are distinct, and that the eternal is not time without end.

       3. Light as the condition of knowledge. Augustine holds that the mind knows the truth
          by an inner light, which is the condition under which the mind sees. The framework
          holds that light is the condition of possibility of relation, and that it makes relation
          legible. Both hold that light is a condition, not an object, and that it is what makes
          knowledge possible.

       4. The limits of self-knowledge. Augustine holds that the mind is a mystery to itself;
          it seeks itself and does not find itself. The framework holds that self-knowledge
          is subject to the same structural limits as knowledge of any other identity; it is
          a reconstruction from manifestations, never the identity itself. Both hold that
          self-knowledge is partial and fallible.



10.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Augustine. The framework diverges from Augustine in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Augustine’s time, inner light, and two cities all turn on God; the
          distension of the mind is a participation in the eternity of God, the inner light is
          the light of God, and the two cities are the city of God and the city of man. The
          framework has no God; its time is a realm-relative succession, its light is a structural
          conveyor, and its ontology has no two cities. The framework is a metaphysics without
          God.

       2. The status of creation. Augustine holds that time begins with the creation; the
          world is created ex nihilo, and time is created with it. The framework holds that
          expression is a structural tendency, not a creation; the identity is not created, and
          the manifestation is not created ex nihilo. The framework’s ontology is an ontology
          of expression, not of creation.

       3. The status of grace. Augustine holds that grace is necessary for knowledge, for virtue,
          and for salvation; the mind cannot see the truth without grace, the will cannot do
          the good without grace, and the soul cannot be saved without grace. The framework
          has no grace; its knowledge is reconstruction, its virtue is left to a separate inquiry,
          and its salvation is not a category of the framework. The framework is a metaphysics
          without grace.

       4. The status of the two cities. Augustine holds that history is the story of the two cities,
          and that the end of history is the victory of the city of God. The framework has no
86                                                                         Chapter 10. Augustine


          history in this sense; its time is a realm-relative succession, and its expression has
          no end, no victory, no judgment. The framework’s ontology is without eschatology.



10.7       The Tradition’s Objections

     The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

     Augustine’s objection. The framework says that time is a realm-relative succession,
     and that the eternal is the atemporality of the First Determination and the eternity of
     the Structural Determination. But a time without God is a time without a ground; a
     succession without an eternal is a succession that has nothing to ground it. Augustine’s
     time is grounded in the eternity of God; the distension of the mind is a participation in
     the simultaneity of God. The framework’s time is a succession without a ground, and a
     succession without a ground is a succession without meaning. The framework’s cosmos
     is a cosmos without a Creator, and a cosmos without a Creator is a cosmos without a
     foundation.
     Augustine’s second objection. The framework says that light is a structural conveyor,
     and that knowledge is reconstruction from manifestations. But a light without God is a
     light without certainty; a reconstruction without an inner light is a reconstruction without
     a foundation. Augustine’s light is the light of God, and it gives the mind certainty; the
     framework’s light is a structural condition, and it gives no certainty. The framework’s
     knowledge is a hypothesis without a guarantee; it is a knowledge that can always be
     wrong, and a knowledge that can always be wrong is not knowledge. The framework’s
     epistemology is a scepticism in disguise.



10.8       The Framework’s Reply

     The Framework’s Reply

     Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a time without a ground
     is a time without a foundation, and it agrees that a succession without an eternal has
     nothing to ground it. But the framework denies that the ground must be God. The
     framework’s time is grounded in the structure of the realms: the succession of the material
     realm is grounded in the nature of the material realm, and the atemporality of the First
     Determination is grounded in the nature of the First Determination. The ground is
     structural, not divine; the succession is intelligible without a Creator, and the cosmos is
     founded without a God. The distinction is between a divine ground (Augustine’s) and a
     structural ground (the framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that
     the second is a ground, not an absence of ground.
     Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a light without a guarantee
     is a light without certainty, and it agrees that a reconstruction without a foundation
     is a reconstruction without a guarantee. But the framework denies that the guarantee
10.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                      87


   must be divine. The framework’s light is the condition of possibility of relation, and the
   knowledge it makes possible is a reconstruction from manifestations, which is fallible,
   partial, and revisable. The knowledge is not certain in Augustine’s sense; it is certain in
   the framework’s sense: it is a reconstruction at a certain degree of adequacy, and it is
   the best that a finite subject can achieve. The distinction is between a certain knowledge
   (Augustine’s) and a fallible knowledge (the framework’s); the framework holds the second,
   and it holds that the second is knowledge, not scepticism.



10.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Augustine’s cost. If Augustine accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
time, light, and history are grounded in God. He must accept that they are grounded in the
structure of the realms, and that the ground is structural, not divine. The cost is the loss of the
divine ground: the distension of the mind is no longer a participation in the eternity of God, the
inner light is no longer the light of God, and the two cities are no longer the city of God and the
city of man.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Augustine’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of grace, of divine illumination, of eschatology—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s time is the
succession of the realms, but not the participation in eternity, and the framework leaves the
second to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Augustine’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Augustine
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a scepticism; it is a structural condition that
Augustine’s God presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity
of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the other.


10.10        The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “time” is not substitutable for Augustine’s
   term “distentio animi.” If one substitutes “distentio animi” for “time” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s time is a realm-relative succession,
   and it is a feature of the realm, not only of the mind; Augustine’s distentio animi is
88                                                                            Chapter 10. Augustine


     a feature of the mind, and it is not a feature of the realm. The framework’s time is
     realm-relative; Augustine’s time is mind-relative. The substitution fails, and the relation
     is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for
     Augustine’s term “the inner light.” If one substitutes “the inner light” for “light” in the
     framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s light is a structural
     conveyor, and it is not divine; Augustine’s inner light is the light of God, and it is divine.
     The framework’s light is impersonal; Augustine’s inner light is personal. The substitution
     fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
     The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Augustine is resemblance:
     both hold that time is not a thing in the world, and they differ on whether it is mind-
     relative or realm-relative. Both hold that light is the condition of knowledge, and they
     differ on whether the light is divine or structural. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is
     agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Augustine would be refuted by
     showing that Augustine’s time or inner light cannot be formulated without the framework’s
     distinction between structure and ground—by showing, that is, that Augustine already
     distinguishes the structural condition from the divine ground, and that the framework’s
     distinction is a development of Augustine’s own.




10.11        Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s time a development of Augustine’s distentio animi, or is it
a departure from Augustine? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Augustine’s time is already realm-relative, not only
mind-relative, has a question the chapter leaves open.



Second question. Can the framework’s light be stated without the notion of a condition?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that light can be stated without a condition has a question the chapter leaves open.



Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Confessions do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the account of time, memory, and the inner light, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Confessions supports a different reading has a
question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you remembered something, or measured time, or knew something
with certainty. Was the time in your mind, or in the world, or in both? Was the light of your
knowledge your own, or given from outside? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Augustine’s distentio animi and the framework’s realm-relative succession?

The next chapter turns to Dionysius the Areopagite. It states the negative theology of the Divine
Names and the Mystical Theology, the hierarchy of light in the Celestial Hierarchy, and the
account of the divine darkness; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Dionysius; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of light and negation is the nearest patristic analogue to Dionysius’s apophaticism. The
present chapter has stated Augustine’s answer to the problem of time and the inner light; the
next chapter states Dionysius’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 11

Dionysius the Areopagite


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Dionysius the Areopagite (Pseudo-Dionysius). It states
Dionysius’s negative theology (apophatic theology), the divine names (cataphatic theology),
the hierarchy of light in the Celestial Hierarchy and the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, the divine
darkness of the Mystical Theology, and the triadic structure of hierarchy (purification, illumination,
perfection), with reference to the Corpus Dionysiacum; it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of Dionysius; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of light and negation is the nearest patristic analogue to Dionysius’s
apophaticism; it presents the objections that Dionysius would raise against the framework; it
presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “hierarchy,” “the divine darkness,” “the divine
names,” “procession,” or “return,” these are Dionysius’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the
Corpus and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


11.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is trying to see the sun. At dawn, she looks at the sky, and the sun is a
red disc on the horizon: bright, but not blinding, visible, but not overwhelming. At noon, she
looks at the sky, and the sun is too bright to look at; she must look away, or be blinded. At
night, she looks at the sky, and the sun is not there; but she knows that it is there, on the other
side of the earth, and that its light is what makes the moon visible.
   Three times of day, three relations to the sun. At dawn, the sun is visible; at noon, the sun
is too bright to be seen; at night, the sun is absent, but its light is present in what it illuminates.
The three relations are not three suns; they are three ways the one sun is present to the one who
looks.
   Now consider a person who is trying to speak of God. She can say that God is good, that
God is wise, that God is being, that God is light. These are the divine names; they are the ways
God is present to the mind, the ways the mind can speak of God. But she can also say that God
is not good, not wise, not being, not light—in the sense that God is beyond all these; the names
are not adequate to God, and the mind that speaks them knows that it has not said what God
is. This is the negative way, the apophatic way; it is the way of the divine darkness, in which
God is present, not as an object of knowledge, but as the absence of all objects.
   Now consider a third case, harder still. Suppose she asks not what God is, or how God
is present to the mind, but how the cosmos is ordered. She sees a hierarchy: the angels, the
archangels, the principalities, the powers, the dominions, the thrones, the cherubim, the seraphim;
and below them, the bishops, the priests, the deacons, the faithful. Each level is closer to God,

                                                  90
11.2. The Question                                                                                 91


or farther from God; each level receives the light from above, and passes it on to the level below.
The hierarchy is a hierarchy of light; it is the way the one light of God reaches the many levels
of the cosmos.
      The scene is Dionysius’s image, in the Corpus Dionysiacum, of the structure of reality. The
sun is God; the three times of day are the three ways God is present to the mind (cataphatic,
apophatic, and hierarchical); and the hierarchy is the way the one light of God reaches the many
levels of the cosmos. Each way is real; each way is necessary; and each way is a way of the one
light, not three lights.
      The scene poses the question that Dionysius was the first to pose in its full form. How can the
mind speak of God, if God is beyond all names? How can the mind know God, if God is beyond
all knowledge? And how is the cosmos ordered, if the one light of God reaches the many levels of
the cosmos? The present chapter states Dionysius’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with
it.


11.2        The Question
The previous chapter stated Augustine’s position: time, memory, the inner light, the two cities,
faith and reason. Augustine is the first great Latin father; Dionysius is the first great Greek
father of the mystical tradition, and his influence on the medieval West (through Eriugena,
Albert, Aquinas, and the author of the Cloud of Unknowing) is immense. The present chapter
states Dionysius’s position, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Dionysius was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Dionysius hold? The chapter states the negative theology,
the divine names, the hierarchy of light, the divine darkness, and the triadic structure of hierarchy,
with reference to the Corpus.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Dionysius converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Dionysius would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Dionysius?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


11.3        The Position

11.3.1      The Negative Theology

Dionysius’s Mystical Theology is the classic statement of negative theology (apophatic theology).
The way to God is not the way of affirmation, in which the mind says that God is good, wise,
being, light; it is the way of negation, in which the mind says that God is not good, not wise,
92                                                           Chapter 11. Dionysius the Areopagite


not being, not light. The affirmations are true, in a sense; but they are not adequate to God,
and the mind that stops at the affirmations has stopped short of God.
     The way of negation is not a denial of the affirmations; it is a transcendence of them. The
mind says that God is good, and then it says that God is beyond good; it says that God is being,
and then it says that God is beyond being. The two movements are not contradictory; they are
two moments of one movement, the movement of the mind toward God.
     The end of the way of negation is the divine darkness. The mind, having denied all names,
finds itself in a darkness that is not the absence of light but its excess; it is the darkness of the
divine light, which is too bright to be seen. In this darkness, the mind is united with God, not
by knowledge, but by presence; not by sight, but by touch.

     From the Tradition

     “The Cause of all things is neither soul nor intellect; nor has it imagination or opinion or
     reason or understanding; nor is it a word or a name; nor is it a number or a harmony; nor
     is it a body; nor is it without form; nor is it a figure; nor is it without figure; nor is it a
     place; nor is it a time; nor is it a substance; nor is it an accident; nor is it a thing that
     can be known; nor is it a thing that can be spoken.” (Dionysius, Mystical Theology 1048a,
     trans. after Rolt)



11.3.2      The Divine Names

Dionysius’s Divine Names is the classic statement of affirmative theology (cataphatic theology).
The names of God are the ways God is present to the mind; they are the ways the mind can speak
of God. The names are many: good, being, life, wisdom, power, justice, salvation, redemption,
light. Each name is a way the one God is present; each name is a way the one light shines.
     The names are not arbitrary; they are grounded in the processions of God, the ways God
goes out from God’s self into the cosmos. The processions are the divine activities: creation,
providence, justification, sanctification. Each procession is a name; each name is a procession.
The names are many because the processions are many; the processions are many because the
cosmos is many.
     The names are also hierarchical. Some names are closer to God than others; some names are
more adequate to God than others. The name "good" is more universal than the name "wise";
the name "being" is more universal than the name "life." The hierarchy of names is the hierarchy
of the processions, and the hierarchy of the processions is the hierarchy of the cosmos.


11.3.3      The Hierarchy of Light

Dionysius’s Celestial Hierarchy and Ecclesiastical Hierarchy state the hierarchy of light. The
cosmos is a hierarchy of levels; each level is closer to God, or farther from God; each level receives
the light of God, and passes it on to the level below.
     The celestial hierarchy has nine ranks, in three triads: the first triad (thrones, cherubim,
seraphim) is closest to God; the second triad (dominions, powers, principalities) is intermediate;
the third triad (archangels, angels) is closest to the world. The ecclesiastical hierarchy has its
11.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             93


own ranks: bishops, priests, deacons, and the faithful. Each rank is a level of light; each rank
receives the light and passes it on.
   The hierarchy is not a hierarchy of power; it is a hierarchy of light. The higher ranks are not
more powerful than the lower; they are more transparent to the light. The light passes through
them, and it reaches the lower ranks, not diminished, but accommodated to the capacity of each
rank. The hierarchy is the way the one light of God reaches the many levels of the cosmos.

   From the Tradition

   “The hierarchy is a sacred order, a state of understanding and an activity approximating
   as closely as possible to the divine. And it is in proportion to the enlightenment it receives
   from God that it is raised up to the imitation of God.” (Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy
   164d, trans. after Luibheid)


11.3.4     The Divine Darkness

Dionysius’s Mystical Theology culminates in the divine darkness. The darkness is not the absence
of light; it is the excess of light. The mind that has denied all names, that has gone beyond all
affirmations, finds itself in a darkness that is brighter than any light. In this darkness, God is
present, not as an object, but as the ground of all objects; not as a name, but as the source of all
names.
   The divine darkness is the goal of the mystical life. The mystical life is the ascent of the
mind to God; it is the purification, the illumination, and the perfection, the three moments of
the hierarchy. At the end of the ascent, the mind is united with God, not by knowledge, but by
presence; not by sight, but by touch; not by speech, but by silence.


11.3.5     The Triadic Structure of Hierarchy

Dionysius’s hierarchy has a triadic structure: purification (katharsis), illumination (photismos),
and perfection (teleiosis). Each rank of the hierarchy purifies the rank below, illuminates it,
and perfects it. The purification is the removal of what is not of God; the illumination is the
reception of the light of God; the perfection is the union with God.
   The triad is not three stages in time; it is three aspects of one activity. The purification is
the negative moment; the illumination is the affirmative moment; the perfection is the union of
the two. The three are inseparable: a rank that is purified but not illuminated is empty; a rank
that is illuminated but not perfected is incomplete; a rank that is perfected but not purified is
corrupt.
   The triad is also the structure of the mystical life. The mystic is purified by the denial of all
names; illuminated by the reception of the divine names; perfected by the union with God in the
divine darkness. The three are one movement, the movement of the mind toward God.


11.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Dionysius is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
94                                                         Chapter 11. Dionysius the Areopagite


First dispute: the identity of Dionysius. The traditional reading takes Dionysius to be the
Areopagite converted by Paul in Acts 17:34, the first bishop of Athens. A revisionary reading,
defended in modern scholarship, takes him to be a late fifth-century Syrian monk, writing under
the name of the Areopagite to give his works apostolic authority. The two readings disagree
on whether the Corpus is apostolic or pseudepigraphic, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the authority of the Corpus depends on its authorship.

Second dispute: the status of the hierarchy. The traditional reading takes the hierarchy
to be a real order of the cosmos, with real angels and real ecclesiastical ranks. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a symbolic order, a way of describing the relation between the mind and
God, without any real angelic or ecclesiastical hierarchy. The two readings disagree on whether
Dionysius is a realist or a symbolist about the hierarchy, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s seven realms are real levels, not symbols.

Third dispute: the status of the divine darkness. The traditional reading takes the divine
darkness to be a real state of the soul, a union with God that is beyond knowledge. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a limit-concept, a way of saying that God is beyond all knowledge, without
any real union. The two readings disagree on whether Dionysius is a mystic or a philosopher, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no mystical
union, and its light is structural, not mystical.
     The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Dionysius is the Areopagite, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an apostolic mysticism. If
Dionysius is a pseudepigraphic monk, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that
the framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the
Corpus, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


11.5       Points of Convergence

     Points of Convergence

     With Dionysius. The framework shares four structural features with Dionysius’s position.

       1. Light as condition, not object. Dionysius holds that the divine light is not one of
          the things it illuminates; it is the condition under which the things are illuminated.
          The framework holds that light is not one of the things related; it is the condition of
          possibility of relation. Both hold that light is a condition, not an object, and that
          the light is what makes knowledge possible.

       2. The hierarchy of levels. Dionysius holds that the cosmos is a hierarchy of levels, each
          receiving the light from above and passing it on to the level below. The framework
          holds that the seven realms are a hierarchy of levels, each related to the others by
          expression. Both hold that reality is stratified, and that the light passes through the
          levels.
11.6. Points of Divergence                                                                               95


       3. The negative moment. Dionysius holds that the mind must deny all names before it
          can be united with God. The framework holds that the mind must recognize the
          limits of its concepts before it can understand the framework’s principles. Both hold
          that the negative moment is necessary for understanding, and that the mind that
          stops at the affirmations has stopped short.

       4. The limits of language. Dionysius holds that God is beyond all names, and that the
          names are not adequate to God. The framework holds that its principles are stated
          at the strength their arguments support, and that the framework’s terms are not
          adequate to the reality they describe. Both hold that language has limits, and that
          the mind must recognize them.




11.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Dionysius. The framework diverges from Dionysius in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Dionysius’s light is the light of God; the hierarchy is the hierarchy
          of God; the divine darkness is the darkness of God. The framework has no God; its
          light is a structural conveyor, its hierarchy is a hierarchy of realms, and its darkness
          is the limit of its concepts. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the hierarchy. Dionysius’s hierarchy is a hierarchy of angels and
          ecclesiastical ranks; it is a real order of the cosmos, with real angelic and ecclesiastical
          beings. The framework’s seven realms are a hierarchy of ontological levels, not of
          angels or ecclesiastical ranks. The framework’s ontology is without angels and
          without church.

       3. The status of the divine darkness. Dionysius’s divine darkness is a real state of the
          soul, a union with God beyond knowledge. The framework has no mystical union;
          its negative moment is the recognition of the limits of its concepts, not a union with
          a divine beyond. The framework’s apophaticism is structural, not mystical.

       4. The status of the triadic structure. Dionysius’s triad (purification, illumination,
          perfection) is a real structure of the hierarchy, and it is the structure of the mystical
          life. The framework’s three properties of light (descending, ascending, reflective) are
          three directions of one conveyor, and they are not a triad of purification, illumination,
          and perfection. The framework’s triad is structural, not mystical.
96                                                           Chapter 11. Dionysius the Areopagite


11.7       The Tradition’s Objections

     The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

     Dionysius’s objection. The framework says that light is a structural conveyor, and that
     it is the condition of possibility of relation. But a structural conveyor is not a light; it
     is a mechanism. A mechanism does not illuminate; it does not reveal; it does not unite.
     Dionysius’s light is the light of God, and it is what reveals God to the mind and unites the
     mind with God. The framework’s light is a mechanism, and a mechanism is not a light.
     The framework’s cosmos is a cosmos without revelation, and a cosmos without revelation
     is a cosmos without God.
     Dionysius’s second objection. The framework says that the hierarchy is a hierarchy
     of realms, and that the realms are related by expression. But a hierarchy of realms is
     not a hierarchy of light; it is a hierarchy of being. A hierarchy of being does not purify,
     illuminate, or perfect; it does not raise the mind to God. Dionysius’s hierarchy is a
     hierarchy of light, and it is what raises the mind to God. The framework’s hierarchy is a
     hierarchy of being, and a hierarchy of being is not a hierarchy of light.



11.8       The Framework’s Reply

     The Framework’s Reply

     Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a structural conveyor is not a
     light in Dionysius’s sense, and it agrees that a mechanism is not a revelation. But the
     framework denies that its light is a mechanism. The framework’s light is the condition of
     possibility of relation; it is what makes relation legible; it is what makes the manifestation
     of an identity possible. The light is not a mechanism; it is a structural condition, and it is
     what makes knowledge possible. The distinction is between a revelatory light (Dionysius’s)
     and a structural light (the framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds
     that the second is a light, not a mechanism.
     Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a hierarchy of being is not
     a hierarchy of light in Dionysius’s sense, and it agrees that a hierarchy of being does not
     purify, illuminate, or perfect. But the framework denies that its hierarchy is a hierarchy
     of being without light. The framework’s hierarchy is a hierarchy of realms, and the realms
     are related by light; the light is what passes through the levels, and what makes the levels
     legible to one another. The hierarchy is a hierarchy of light, but the light is structural,
     not divine. The distinction is between a mystical hierarchy (Dionysius’s) and a structural
     hierarchy (the framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second
     is a hierarchy of light.



11.9       The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
11.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                         97


Dionysius’s cost. If Dionysius accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that light is the light of God. He must accept that light is a structural conveyor, and that the
hierarchy is a hierarchy of realms, not of angels. The cost is the loss of the divine light: the light
is no longer the light of God, and the hierarchy is no longer the hierarchy of angels.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Dionysius’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of revelation, of mystical union, of divine darkness—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s light is the
condition of relation, but not the light of God, and the framework leaves the second to a separate
inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Dionysius’s light is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s light does not capture. Dionysius must
accept that the framework’s light is not a mechanism; it is a structural condition that Dionysius’s
light presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


11.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for Dionysius’s
   term “the divine light.” If one substitutes “the divine light” for “light” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s light is a structural conveyor, and
   it is impersonal; Dionysius’s divine light is the light of God, and it is personal. The
   framework’s light is neutral between the sacred and the secular; Dionysius’s divine light
   is sacred. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The
   framework’s term “hierarchy” is not substitutable for Dionysius’s term “the hierarchy
   of light.” If one substitutes “the hierarchy of light” for “hierarchy” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s hierarchy is a hierarchy of realms,
   and it is not a hierarchy of angels; Dionysius’s hierarchy is a hierarchy of angels and
   ecclesiastical ranks, and it is a hierarchy of light. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Dionysius is resemblance:
   both hold that light is a condition, and they differ on whether the light is divine or
   structural. Both hold that reality is a hierarchy, and they differ on whether the hierarchy
   is angelic or ontological. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither
   is identity. The framework’s reading of Dionysius would be refuted by showing that
   Dionysius’s light cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between
98                                                        Chapter 11. Dionysius the Areopagite


     structure and revelation—by showing, that is, that Dionysius already distinguishes the
     structural condition from the divine revelation, and that the framework’s distinction is a
     development of Dionysius’s own.



11.11       Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s light a development of Dionysius’s light, or is it a departure
from Dionysius? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not
conclusive. A reader who holds that Dionysius’s light is already structural, not only divine, has
a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s hierarchy be stated without the notion of a level?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that hierarchy can be stated without levels has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Corpus do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the negative theology, the divine names, the hierarchy, and the divine darkness,
and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Corpus supports a
different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
