A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both revealed and hidden—a person, a tradition, a text. Is
the thing revealed by its appearances, or hidden behind them? Is the revelation a light, or a
darkness? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Dionysius’s divine light
and the framework’s structural light?

The next chapter turns to Anselm. It states the ontological argument of the Proslogion, the
account of faith seeking understanding, and the doctrine of the atonement; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Anselm; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of necessity and existence is the nearest medieval analogue to
Anselm’s argument. The present chapter has stated Dionysius’s answer to the problem of light
and hierarchy; the next chapter states Anselm’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 12

Anselm


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Anselm of Canterbury. It states Anselm’s ontological
argument in the Proslogion, the program of faith seeking understanding (fides quaerens intellec-
tum), the satisfaction theory of the atonement in Cur Deus Homo, and the account of God’s
necessary existence; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Anselm; it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of necessity
and existence is the nearest medieval analogue to Anselm’s argument; it presents the objections
that Anselm would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what
each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “that than which nothing greater can be conceived,” “faith seeking understanding,”
“satisfaction,” or “necessary existence,” these are Anselm’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the
treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.



12.1      A Scene

Consider a painter who is planning a painting. She has the painting in her mind before she paints
it: the composition, the colours, the figure, the light. The painting in her mind is real—it is a
plan, an intention, a conception—but it is not yet on the canvas. Then she paints it; the painting
on the canvas is real in a different way. It is not only in her mind; it is in the world, visible to
others, with weight and texture and presence. The painting in her mind and the painting on the
canvas are the same painting, in two modes of existence: one in the mind, one in the world.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose someone says: I can conceive of a painting greater than
any painting the painter could paint. A painting so beautiful, so perfect, so complete, that no
painting could be greater. Does this painting exist? The painter’s painting exists in her mind,
and then on the canvas. But the perfect painting exists only in the mind of the one who conceives
it; it has no canvas, no world, no presence. And yet, says the one who conceives it, a painting
that exists only in the mind is less great than a painting that exists in the world; so the perfect
painting must exist in the world, or it would not be perfect.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose the one who conceives says: I can conceive
of a being than which nothing greater can be conceived. Not a painting, not a person, not a
thing in the world, but a being beyond all beings, greater than any being that can be conceived.
Does this being exist? If it exists only in the mind, it is less great than a being that exists in the
world; so it must exist in the world, or it would not be that than which nothing greater can be
conceived. And so, says Anselm, the being than which nothing greater can be conceived exists,
not only in the mind, but in reality.

                                                 100
12.2. The Question                                                                               101


   The scene is Anselm’s argument, in the Proslogion, for the existence of God. It is the most
famous argument in the history of philosophy, and the most contested. It turns on the distinction
between existence in the mind (in intellectu) and existence in reality (in re), and on the claim
that a being that exists only in the mind is less great than a being that exists in reality.
   The scene poses the question that Anselm was the first to pose in its full form. Can the
existence of God be demonstrated from the concept of God? Is existence a perfection, such that
a being that lacks it is less great than a being that has it? And what is the relation between
faith and reason, between the God of the believer and the God of the philosopher? The present
chapter states Anselm’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


12.2      The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine and Dionysius. Augustine posed the
problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed the problem of light and hierarchy, and the
limits of language. Anselm is the third great figure of the medieval West, and he is the first to
attempt a purely rational demonstration of God’s existence, without appeal to revelation or to
authority. The present chapter states Anselm’s attempt, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Anselm was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Anselm hold? The chapter states the ontological
argument, the program of faith seeking understanding, the satisfaction theory of the atonement,
and the account of God’s necessary existence, with reference to the Proslogion, the Monologion,
and Cur Deus Homo.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Anselm converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Anselm would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Anselm?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


12.3      The Position

12.3.1    The Ontological Argument

Anselm’s Proslogion begins with a prayer, and then turns to an argument. The argument is
stated in chapters 2 and 3, and it has three steps.
   The first step is the definition: God is "that than which nothing greater can be conceived" (id
quo maius cogitari nequit). The definition is not a premise about God’s nature; it is a statement
of what the word "God" means. Whoever understands the word "God" understands that God is
that than which nothing greater can be conceived.
102                                                                           Chapter 12. Anselm


      The second step is the distinction: even the fool, who says in his heart that there is no God,
must have the concept of God in his mind; otherwise he could not deny it. So God exists at least
in the mind (in intellectu). But existence in the mind is less than existence in reality; a being
that exists only in the mind is less great than a being that exists in reality.
      The third step is the conclusion: if God existed only in the mind, then a being greater than
God could be conceived—namely, a being that exists both in the mind and in reality. But this
contradicts the definition of God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived. Therefore
God exists, not only in the mind, but in reality (in re).
      The argument’s form is a reductio: it supposes that God exists only in the mind, derives a
contradiction with the definition, and concludes that God exists in reality. Its force depends on
two premises: that existence is a perfection (so that a being that lacks it is less great), and that
the definition of God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived is coherent.

   From the Tradition

   “And so, Lord, you who give understanding to faith, grant me that I may understand, as
   much as you know it to be expedient, that you are as we believe, and that you are what
   we believe. And indeed we believe that you are a being than which nothing greater can be
   conceived. Or is there no such nature, since the fool has said in his heart, there is no God?
   But certainly that same fool, when he hears this very thing that I say—a being than which
   nothing greater can be conceived—understands what he hears; and what he understands
   is in his understanding, even if he does not understand that it exists.” (Anselm, Proslogion
   2, trans. after Deane)


12.3.2      Faith Seeking Understanding

Anselm’s program is stated in the title of the Proslogion: fides quaerens intellectum, faith seeking
understanding. The program is not a replacement of faith by reason, nor a replacement of reason
by faith; it is the use of reason in the service of faith. The believer believes; the believer also
seeks to understand what he believes. The understanding is not a substitute for the faith; it is
the faith’s own self-understanding.
      The program has three moments.


First moment: faith. The believer accepts the teachings of the faith on the authority of
revelation. Faith is not the conclusion of an argument; it is the starting point of the inquiry.
"Unless you believe, you will not understand."


Second moment: understanding. The believer seeks to understand what he believes. The
understanding is not the discovery of new content; it is the grasping of the content that faith
already contains. The understanding is the "reason" of the faith, the intelligible structure of
what is believed.


Third moment: the return to faith. The understanding returns to the faith, and the faith
is deepened by the understanding. The believer believes with understanding, not only with
12.3. The Position                                                                                103


authority; the faith is the same faith, but the believer’s grasp of it is transformed.
   The program is not the rationalism of the Enlightenment; it is the "rationalism" of the
medieval monastery. The reason is not autonomous; it is the reason of the believer, illuminated
by faith. The understanding is not the end of the inquiry; it is the deepening of the faith.

   From the Tradition

   “I do not seek to understand in order to believe; I believe in order to understand. For this
   also I believe: that unless I believe, I shall not understand.” (Anselm, Proslogion 1, trans.
   after Deane)


12.3.3    The Satisfaction Theory

Anselm’s Cur Deus Homo (Why the God-Man?) is the classic statement of the satisfaction
theory of the atonement. The question is: why did God become human? The answer turns on
the notion of satisfaction.
   The first premise: sin is an offense against God’s honour. The sinner takes from God what
belongs to God—obedience, worship, love—and offends God’s honour. The offense is infinite,
because God’s honour is infinite; and the offense cannot be compensated by a finite being.
   The second premise: satisfaction must be made, either by punishment or by compensation. If
the sinner is punished, the punishment must be infinite, because the offense is infinite; but a finite
being cannot bear an infinite punishment. If the sinner compensates, the compensation must be
infinite, because the offense is infinite; but a finite being cannot make an infinite compensation.
   The third premise: only a being who is both God and human can make the compensation.
As God, the being has the infinite value that is needed to compensate the infinite offense; as
human, the being belongs to the race that owes the compensation. Therefore the God-Man is
necessary; and therefore God became human.
   The satisfaction theory is not a commercial transaction; it is a structure of honour and justice.
The offense is against honour; the compensation is for honour; and the God-Man is the only
being who can restore the honour that the offense has taken.

   From the Tradition

   “For it is not fitting that God should leave the human race to perish; for it is not fitting
   that God’s purpose should be frustrated. And it is not fitting that God should compel
   the human being to enter into blessedness without the human being’s own free will; for
   that would be to compel, not to save. And so, since the human being cannot save himself,
   and God cannot save him without the human being’s own act, there must be a God-Man,
   who is both God and human.” (Anselm, Cur Deus Homo II.6, trans. after Deane)


12.3.4    Necessary Existence

Anselm’s argument in the Proslogion 3 is a further step in the argument. Suppose someone
conceives a being than which nothing greater can be conceived. Such a being cannot be conceived
not to exist; for if it could be conceived not to exist, a being that cannot be conceived not to
104                                                                          Chapter 12. Anselm


exist would be greater. Therefore the being than which nothing greater can be conceived exists
necessarily; its non-existence is impossible.
      The argument distinguishes two kinds of existence: existence that can be conceived not to be
(contingent existence), and existence that cannot be conceived not to be (necessary existence).
The being than which nothing greater can be conceived has the second kind; its existence is
necessary, and its non-existence is a contradiction.
      The doctrine of necessary existence is the key to Anselm’s argument. It is also the point on
which the argument has been most contested. Kant argued that existence is not a predicate,
and that the argument therefore fails. Others argued that the concept of necessary existence is
coherent, and that the argument succeeds. The debate continues.


12.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Anselm is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the argument. The traditional reading takes the ontological
argument to be a proof, in the strict sense: it demonstrates God’s existence from the concept
of God, without appeal to experience or to revelation. A revisionary reading takes it to be a
"prayerful meditation," a way of seeing what faith already contains; on this reading, the argument
is not a proof, but an illumination, and its conclusion is not new knowledge, but a deepened
understanding. The two readings disagree on whether Anselm is a rationalist or a mystic, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework is a rationalist
metaphysics, not a prayerful meditation.

Second dispute: the status of existence. The traditional reading takes existence to be a
perfection: a being that exists is greater than a being that does not exist. A revisionary reading
takes existence to be not a perfection, but a condition of having any perfections at all; on this
reading, the argument fails, because a being that exists only in the mind is not less great than a
being that exists in reality; it is simply a different case. The two readings disagree on whether
existence is a predicate, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s identity is not a predicate, and its existence is not a perfection.

Third dispute: the status of the satisfaction theory. The traditional reading takes the
satisfaction theory to be a real account of the atonement: the offense is real, the compensation is
real, and the God-Man is the real mediator. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor:
the offense and the compensation are ways of speaking about the relation between God and
humanity, without any real commercial or honour-based transaction. The two readings disagree
on whether Anselm is a realist or a symbolist about the atonement, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no atonement, and its ontology has no
honor-based transaction.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Anselm is a rationalist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between two rationalist metaphysics. If Anselm is a mystic,
the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct. The
12.5. Points of Convergence                                                                    105


framework holds that the second reading is closer to the Proslogion, but it does not rest its case
on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


12.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Anselm. The framework shares three structural features with Anselm’s position.

       1. The priority of structure over existence. Anselm argues from the concept of God
         to the existence of God; the concept is prior to the existence, and the existence is
         derived from the concept. The framework holds that the structure of identity is
         prior to the manifestation, and that the manifestation is derived from the identity.
         Both hold that structure is prior to existence, and that existence is the expression of
         structure.

       2. The distinction between the mind and the world. Anselm distinguishes existence in
         the mind (in intellectu) from existence in reality (in re); the two are distinct, and
         the second is greater than the first. The framework distinguishes manifestation from
         identity; the manifestation is not the identity, and it is real in its own realm. Both
         hold that the mind and the world are distinct, and that the world is not exhausted
         by the mind.

       3. The necessity of the necessary. Anselm holds that the being than which nothing
         greater can be conceived exists necessarily; its non-existence is impossible. The
         framework holds that the First Determination is invariant under all transformations;
         its change is impossible. Both hold that there is a level of reality that cannot not
         be, and that its necessity is structural, not contingent.



12.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Anselm. The framework diverges from Anselm in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Anselm’s argument is an argument for God; the being than
         which nothing greater can be conceived is God, the God of the Christian faith. The
         framework has no God; its First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a being
         than which nothing greater can be conceived. The framework is a metaphysics
         without God.

       2. The status of existence. Anselm holds that existence is a perfection; a being that
         exists is greater than a being that does not exist. The framework holds that existence
         is not a perfection; it is the enactment of an identity in a manifestation, and the
         enactment is neither greater nor lesser than the identity. The framework’s ontology
106                                                                         Chapter 12. Anselm


         is without the hierarchy of existence and non-existence.

       3. The status of faith. Anselm’s program is faith seeking understanding; the understand-
         ing is the deepening of the faith, and the faith is the condition of the understanding.
         The framework has no faith; its reason is autonomous, and its understanding is not
         the deepening of any faith. The framework is a philosophy without faith.

       4. The status of the atonement. Anselm’s satisfaction theory is an account of the
         atonement; the offense is real, the compensation is real, and the God-Man is the
         real mediator. The framework has no atonement; its ontology has no offense, no
         compensation, and no mediator. The framework is a metaphysics without salvation.



12.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Anselm’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that it is manifested in a realm. But a structural invariance is not a being; it is a pattern.
  A pattern does not exist; it is instantiated. Anselm’s God is a being, the highest being, the
  being than which nothing greater can be conceived; his existence is not the instantiation
  of a pattern, but the reality of a person. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a
  pattern is not a being. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of beings;
  it has no place for the God of Anselm.
  Anselm’s second objection. The framework says that reason is autonomous, and that
  understanding is not the deepening of faith. But a reason without faith is a reason without
  a goal; it does not seek understanding of what is believed, because it believes nothing.
  Anselm’s reason is the reason of the believer, illuminated by faith; it seeks to understand
  what it already believes. The framework’s reason is a reason without faith, and a reason
  without faith is a reason without an object. The framework’s philosophy is a philosophy
  without faith, and a philosophy without faith is a philosophy without the God of faith.



12.8      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a being
  in Anselm’s sense, and it agrees that Anselm’s God is a being, not a pattern. But the
  framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the
  invariance enacted by one source—a this, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment
  is the existence of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a person,
  and it is not a being among beings; it is the structural condition under which a thing
  is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls existence.
12.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     107


   The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a reality); the
   framework’s identity is the second, not the first. Anselm’s God is a being of a different
   kind: a person, the highest being, and the source of all beings. The framework’s identity
   is a source of a different kind: a structural condition, and the enactment of that condition
   in a manifestation. The two are different kinds of source, and the framework does not
   claim to be the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a reason without a goal
   is a reason without an object, and it agrees that Anselm’s reason is illuminated by faith.
   But the framework denies that a reason without faith is a reason without an object. The
   framework’s reason has an object: the structure of identity and manifestation. The reason
   seeks to understand the structure, and the understanding is the goal of the reason. The
   reason does not seek to understand what it believes, because it believes nothing; it seeks
   to understand what it investigates, and the investigation is its own goal. The distinction is
   between a reason illuminated by faith (Anselm’s) and a reason investigating structure (the
   framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is a reason
   with an object.



12.9       The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Anselm’s cost. If Anselm accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
existence is a perfection. He must accept that existence is the enactment of a structure, not a
perfection added to a being; and he must accept that the being than which nothing greater can
be conceived is not greater by existing, but is greater by being what it is. The cost is the loss of
the ontological argument: the argument turns on existence as a perfection, and if existence is
not a perfection, the argument fails.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Anselm’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of personhood, of faith, of the God of faith—that its ontology does not capture. The
cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not a person, and the framework leaves the person to a separate
inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Anselm’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Anselm
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural source that Anselm’s
God presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.
108                                                                           Chapter 12. Anselm


12.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Anselm’s
   term “that than which nothing greater can be conceived.” If one substitutes the Anselmian
   definition for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s identity is an invariance under a class of allowable transformations, and it is
   manifested in a realm; the Anselmian being is beyond all transformations, and it is not
   manifested, because it is not one of the things manifested. The framework’s identity is
   multiple (there are many identities); the Anselmian being is one, and there is nothing
   greater than it. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The
   framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Anselm’s term “satisfaction.” If one
   substitutes “satisfaction” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, enacted by an identity in a
   realm; Anselm’s satisfaction is a compensation for an offense, and it is not a tendency, but
   a transaction. The framework’s expression is non-transactional; Anselm’s satisfaction is
   transactional. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Anselm is resemblance:
   both hold that structure is prior to existence, and they differ on whether existence is
   a perfection or the enactment of a structure. Both hold that there is a level of reality
   that cannot not be, and they differ on whether that level is a person or a realm. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Anselm would be refuted by showing that Anselm’s argument cannot be formulated
   without the framework’s distinction between structure and existence—by showing, that is,
   that Anselm already distinguishes the structural condition from the existence that fulfils
   it, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Anselm’s own.



12.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Anselm’s being, or is it a
departure from Anselm? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Anselm’s being is already a structural condition, not a
person, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Proslogion do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the ontological argument, the program of faith seeking understanding, and the
12.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              109


satisfaction theory, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the
Proslogion supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that exists both in your mind and in the world—a person, a place,
a work of art. Is the thing greater because it exists in the world? Is the thing in your mind
the same thing as the thing in the world? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Anselm’s ontological argument and the framework’s distinction between identity and
manifestation?

The next chapter turns to Thomas Aquinas. It states the five ways, the distinction between essence
and existence, the analogy of being, and the relation between faith and reason; it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Aquinas; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of essence and existence is the nearest medieval
analogue to Aquinas’s. The present chapter has stated Anselm’s answer to the problem of God’s
existence; the next chapter states Aquinas’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 13

Thomas Aquinas


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Thomas Aquinas. It states the Five Ways (Quinque
Viae) for the existence of God, the real distinction between essence and existence (esse and
essentia), the analogy of being (analogia entis), the doctrine of participation, and the harmony
of faith and reason, with reference to the Summa Theologiae, the Summa Contra Gentiles, and
the De Ente et Essentia; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Aquinas;
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of essence
and existence is the nearest medieval analogue to Aquinas’s; it presents the objections that
Aquinas would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “esse,”
“essentia,” “analogy,” “participation,” or “natural law,” these are Aquinas’s terms, and their
sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


13.1      A Scene
Consider a flame. It is hot; it heats what is near it; it moves upward; it flickers and dances. The
flame is one thing, but it has many properties, and the properties are not the flame. The heat is
not the flame; the light is not the flame; the motion is not the flame. And yet the flame is hot,
luminous, moving. The flame has its properties, and it is not its properties.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose you ask not what the flame has, but what the flame is.
The flame is a process of combustion; it is the oxidation of a fuel, with the release of heat and
light. The what-it-is of the flame is the process; the properties of the flame are what the process
produces. The what-it-is is the essence; the properties are the accidents.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose you ask not what the flame is, or what it
has, but whether it is. The flame exists; but its existence is not its essence. The flame’s essence
is combustion; its existence is the fact that the combustion is occurring. The existence is not the
essence; the existence is the act by which the essence is. If the flame goes out, its essence is still
conceivable (combustion is still a kind of process), but its existence has ceased. The existence is
distinct from the essence.
   The scene is Aquinas’s image, in the De Ente et Essentia, of the structure of creatures. Every
creature is a compound of essence and existence: the essence is what the creature is; the existence
is the act by which the creature is. In God alone are essence and existence identical: God’s
essence is to exist. In every creature, the two are really distinct; the essence does not include
existence, and the existence is received from God.
   The scene poses the question that Aquinas was the first to pose in its full form. What is the
relation between what a thing is and that it is? Is existence a property of things, or is it the act

                                                 110
13.2. The Question                                                                                111


by which things are? And how does the existence of creatures relate to the existence of God?
The present chapter states Aquinas’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


13.2      The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine, Dionysius, and Anselm. Augustine
posed the problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed the problem of light and hierarchy,
and the limits of language; Anselm posed the problem of God’s existence, and attempted a purely
rational demonstration. Aquinas is the fourth great figure of the medieval West, and he is the
great synthesizer: he synthesizes Aristotle and Christianity, reason and faith, philosophy and
theology. The present chapter states Aquinas’s synthesis, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Aquinas was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the position. What did Aquinas hold? The chapter states the Five Ways, the
essence/existence distinction, the analogy of being, the doctrine of participation, and the harmony
of faith and reason, with reference to the treatises.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Aquinas converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Aquinas would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Aquinas?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


13.3      The Position

13.3.1    The Five Ways
Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae I, q.2, a.3, gives five arguments for the existence of God, known as
the Five Ways (Quinque Viae). Each argument proceeds from a feature of the world to a first
cause, and each concludes that the first cause is what we call God.

First Way: motion. We observe that things are in motion. Whatever is in motion is moved
by another. If the mover is itself in motion, it must be moved by another, and so on. This chain
cannot be infinite, because an infinite chain would have no first mover, and without a first mover
there would be no motion at all. Therefore there must be a first mover, itself unmoved, and this
is what we call God.

Second Way: efficient causation. We observe that things have efficient causes. Nothing
can be the efficient cause of itself, because it would then be prior to itself. The chain of efficient
causes cannot be infinite, for the same reason as in the First Way. Therefore there must be a
first efficient cause, and this is what we call God.
112                                                                Chapter 13. Thomas Aquinas


Third Way: contingency. We observe that things come to be and pass away; they are
contingent, not necessary. If everything were contingent, there would be a time when nothing
existed; and if there were a time when nothing existed, nothing could have come to be, because
nothing comes from nothing. Therefore there must be a necessary being, and this is what we call
God.


Fourth Way: degrees of perfection. We observe that things are more or less good, more or
less true, more or less noble. The more and the less are predicated of things according as they
approach a maximum. Therefore there must be a maximum of goodness, truth, and nobility,
and this is what we call God.


Fifth Way: governance. We observe that natural bodies act for an end: the acorn grows
into the oak, the eye sees, the arrow flies to the target. Things that lack intelligence do not act
for an end unless they are directed by an intelligent being. Therefore there must be an intelligent
being who directs all natural things to their end, and this is what we call God.
      The Five Ways are not five independent proofs; they are five articulations of one movement,
the movement from the world to its ground. Each Way is a via, a way; each Way arrives at the
same conclusion, but by a different route.

   From the Tradition

   “The first and more manifest way is the argument from motion. It is certain, and evident
   to our senses, that in the world some things are in motion. Now whatever is in motion is
   put in motion by another. For it is clear that whatever is in motion must be in a state of
   potentiality towards that towards which it is in motion. But nothing can be reduced from
   potentiality to act except by something in a state of act.” (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I,
   q.2, a.3, trans. after the Fathers of the English Dominican Province)



13.3.2      Essence and Existence

Aquinas’s De Ente et Essentia is the classic statement of the real distinction between essence
and existence. The essence (essentia) is what a thing is; it is the whatness of the thing, the
definition, the nature. The existence (esse) is the act by which the thing is; it is not a property
added to the essence, but the act that makes the essence to be.
      The distinction is real, not merely conceptual. In a creature, the essence does not include
existence; the essence is possible, and the existence is actual. The essence of a human being
is rational animal; the existence of a human being is the act by which this rational animal is.
The essence does not make itself to be; it must receive existence from another. In God alone
are essence and existence identical: God’s essence is to exist; God is existence itself (ipsum esse
subsistens).
      The distinction is the key to Aquinas’s metaphysics. It explains why creatures are creatures:
they do not have existence in themselves; they receive it from God. It explains why God is God:
God’s existence is not received; it is God’s essence. And it explains why the created order is an
13.3. The Position                                                                               113


order of dependence: every creature depends on God for its existence, not only for its beginning
but for its continuation.

   From the Tradition

   “Being itself (ipsum esse) is that which is most perfect in all things; for it is the actuality
   of all things, and therefore the perfection of all perfections. But in God alone is being
   identical with his essence; in every creature, being is received from another, and is distinct
   from the essence that receives it.” (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.3, a.4 and De Ente et
   Essentia 4, trans. after Maurer)



13.3.3    The Analogy of Being

Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae I, q.13, states the analogy of being. When we say that God is good,
and that creatures are good, we do not use the word "good" univocally, as if God and creatures
were good in the same sense; nor do we use it equivocally, as if the word had no relation between
its two uses. We use it analogically: the goodness of creatures is a likeness of the goodness of
God, and the goodness of God is the source of the goodness of creatures.
   The analogy has three moments: the analogy of attribution, the analogy of proportion, and
the analogy of proportionality. In the analogy of attribution, the term is predicated primarily of
God, and secondarily of creatures, because creatures are related to God as to their source. In the
analogy of proportion, the term is predicated of God and creatures according to the proportion
that each has to its own being. In the analogy of proportionality, the term is predicated of God
and creatures according to a proportion between proportions: as God’s goodness is to God’s
being, so the creature’s goodness is to the creature’s being.
   The analogy of being is what makes theological language possible. Without the analogy, our
words for God would be either too small (univocal) or too empty (equivocal). With the analogy,
our words are neither: they reach God through the creatures, and they reach God as the source
of the creatures.


13.3.4    Participation

Aquinas’s doctrine of participation is the account of how creatures relate to God. Creatures are
not God; they are not parts of God; they are not emanations of God in Plotinus’s sense. They
are creatures: they are made by God, and they participate in God’s being. To participate is to
have a share in something that is not one’s own; to participate in being is to have a share in the
being that God is.
   The doctrine of participation unites the Five Ways with the essence/existence distinction.
The Five Ways arrive at a first cause; the essence/existence distinction shows that the first cause
is the source of existence; the doctrine of participation shows how creatures relate to the first
cause: they are not the first cause, but they participate in its being.
114                                                                  Chapter 13. Thomas Aquinas


13.3.5      Faith and Reason

Aquinas’s account of faith and reason is the classic statement of their harmony. Faith and reason
are not enemies; they are two ways of knowing the same truth. Reason knows the truth of the
natural order; faith knows the truth of the supernatural order. The two orders are distinct, but
they are not opposed: the supernatural order presupposes the natural order, and the natural
order is fulfilled in the supernatural.
      The harmony has three moments. First, reason can demonstrate the preambles of faith: the
existence of God, the unity of God, the immortality of the soul. Second, faith can illuminate
reason: faith gives reason the truths that reason cannot reach (the Trinity, the Incarnation, the
resurrection), and reason can reflect on these truths without comprehending them. Third, reason
and faith can never contradict each other: the truth is one, and the two are two ways of knowing
it. If a philosophical argument contradicts a truth of faith, the argument is defective, not the
faith.
      The harmony is not the subordination of reason to faith, nor the subordination of faith to
reason. It is the recognition that the two are two ways of knowing one truth. "Grace does not
destroy nature, but perfects it" (gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit). Reason is not destroyed
by faith; it is perfected by faith.

   From the Tradition

   “The gifts of grace are added to nature in such a way that they do not destroy it, but
   perfect it. And so it is that the light of faith, which is given by grace, does not destroy the
   light of reason, which is given by nature; rather, it perfects it, and adds to it.” (Aquinas,
   Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8, trans. after the Fathers of the English Dominican Province)



13.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Aquinas is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Five Ways. The traditional reading takes the Five
Ways to be demonstrations, in the strict sense: they prove the existence of God from premises
that are evident to reason. A revisionary reading takes them to be "ways," not proofs: they
are articulations of a movement from the world to its ground, and they are persuasive, not
demonstrative. The two readings disagree on whether Aquinas is a rationalist or a fideist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework is a rationalist
metaphysics, not a fideist meditation.


Second dispute: the status of the essence/existence distinction. The traditional reading
takes the distinction to be a real distinction, in the thing itself: the essence and the existence are
really distinct in the creature. A revisionary reading takes it to be a conceptual distinction, in
the mind: the essence and the existence are distinct in our way of thinking, not in the thing. The
two readings disagree on whether Aquinas is a realist or a conceptualist about the distinction,
13.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      115


and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is
not a real essence distinct from a real existence; it is the invariance enacted by one source.




Third dispute: the status of the analogy of being. The traditional reading takes the
analogy to be the key to Aquinas’s theology: without the analogy, our words for God would
be either too small or too empty. A revisionary reading takes it to be a linguistic device, a
way of speaking about God that is useful but not essential. The two readings disagree on
whether Aquinas is a realist or a nominalist about analogy, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s language is structural, not analogical.



   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Aquinas is a rationalist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between two rationalist metaphysics. If Aquinas is a fideist,
the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct. The
framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Summa Theologiae, but it does not rest its
case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.




13.5     Points of Convergence
116                                                                Chapter 13. Thomas Aquinas


  Points of Convergence

  With Aquinas. The framework shares four structural features with Aquinas’s position.

       1. The priority of act. Aquinas holds that existence is the act of acts (actus actuum),
         the actuality of every actuality; the essence is the potency that existence actualizes.
         The framework holds that manifestation is the act of acts in its own register: it is
         the enactment of the identity, the actuality of the invariance. Both hold that act is
         prior to potency, and that existence is the actuality of what is.

       2. The distinction between essence and existence. Aquinas holds that in every creature,
         essence and existence are really distinct; in God alone, they are identical. The
         framework holds that identity and manifestation are distinct: the identity is the
         invariance; the manifestation is the appearance. Both hold that what a thing is
         and that it is are distinct, and that the distinction is the key to understanding the
         creature.

       3. The hierarchy of being. Aquinas holds that creatures are arranged in a hierarchy,
         from the lowest material beings to the highest angels, according to their degree of
         participation in being. The framework holds that the seven realms are arranged in
         a hierarchy, from the most unified to the most multiple. Both hold that reality is
         stratified, and that the strata are ordered by their degree of unity.

       4. The harmony of faith and reason. Aquinas holds that faith and reason are two ways
         of knowing one truth; they cannot contradict each other. The framework holds that
         its principles are autonomous, and that they are compatible with the truths of any
         inquiry that does not contradict them. Both hold that truth is one, and that the
         different ways of knowing it must be in harmony.



13.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Aquinas. The framework diverges from Aquinas in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Aquinas’s metaphysics is a metaphysics of God; the Five Ways,
         the essence/existence distinction, the analogy of being, and the participation of
         creatures all turn on God. The framework has no God; its First Determination is
         a realm of pure unity, not a being whose essence is to exist. The framework is a
         metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of creation. Aquinas holds that the world is created by God, and that
         the relation between God and the world is the relation between the Creator and the
         creature. The framework holds that the manifestation is expressed by the identity,
         and that the relation between identity and manifestation is the relation between the
         source and its expression. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of expression,
13.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                               117


         not of creation.

       3. The status of analogy. Aquinas holds that theological language is analogical; the
         words we use for God are neither univocal nor equivocal, but analogical. The
         framework holds that its language is structural; its terms are defined within the
         framework, and they are neither univocal nor equivocal nor analogical with respect
         to any other framework. The framework’s language is structural, not analogical.

       4. The status of natural law. Aquinas holds that there is a natural law, a participation
         of the eternal law in the rational creature, and that the natural law is the ground of
         morality. The framework has no natural law; its ontology is a description of structure,
         and it leaves morality to a separate inquiry. The framework is a metaphysics without
         natural law.


13.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Aquinas’s objection. The framework says that identity is an invariance, and that it
   is manifested in a realm. But an invariance is a form, and a form without existence is
   a mere potency. Aquinas’s metaphysics is a metaphysics of act: the form is real only
   when it is actualized by existence; the essence is real only when it is. The framework’s
   identity is a form without existence; it is a pure potency, and a pure potency is not real.
   The framework’s ontology is an ontology of potencies, not of acts; it has no place for the
   actuality that makes a thing to be.
   Aquinas’s second objection. The framework says that language is structural, and
   that its terms are defined within the framework. But a language without analogy is a
   language without God; our words for God must be analogical, because God is beyond
   all our categories. The framework’s language is a language without God, and a language
   without God is a language without the highest truth. The framework’s philosophy is
   a philosophy without God, and a philosophy without God is a philosophy without the
   ground of all things.



13.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a form without existence
   is a potency, and it agrees that act is prior to potency. But the framework denies that
   its identity is a pure potency. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
   source—a this, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the actuality of the identity
   in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pure form; it is the enactment of a form,
   and the enactment is what makes the identity to be. The distinction is between a form
118                                                                Chapter 13. Thomas Aquinas


   without existence (Aquinas’s potency) and an enactment (the framework’s actuality); the
   framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a language without analogy
   is a language that cannot speak of God, and it agrees that our words for God must be
   analogical. But the framework denies that its language is a language without God. The
   framework’s language is structural; its terms are defined within the framework, and they
   are adequate to the structure they describe. The framework does not claim to speak
   of God; it claims to speak of the structure of identity and manifestation, and it leaves
   the question of God to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a language that
   speaks of God (Aquinas’s) and a language that speaks of structure (the framework’s); the
   framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is a language, not a silence.




13.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Aquinas’s cost. If Aquinas accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
world is created by God. He must accept that the manifestation is expressed by the identity,
and that the relation between them is expression, not creation. The cost is the loss of the
Creator-creature distinction: the world is no longer a creature, and God is no longer the Creator.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Aquinas’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of act, of existence as the actuality of essence, of God as ipsum esse subsistens—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted, but not the act of existence, and the framework
leaves the second to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Aquinas’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Aquinas
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pure potency; it is a structural enactment
that Aquinas’s act presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.
13.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                  119


13.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Aquinas’s
   term “essence.” If one substitutes “essence” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is an invariance under a class of allowable
   transformations, and it is enacted in a manifestation; Aquinas’s essence is a whatness, and
   it is actualized by existence, not by manifestation. The framework’s identity is enacted;
   Aquinas’s essence is actualized. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Aquinas’s
   term “existence.” If one substitutes “existence” for “manifestation” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation is the appearance of
   the identity in a realm, and it is distinct from the identity; Aquinas’s existence is the
   act by which the essence is, and it is not an appearance. The framework’s manifestation
   is appearance; Aquinas’s existence is act. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Aquinas is resemblance:
   both hold that act is prior to potency, and they differ on whether act is existence or
   manifestation. Both hold that reality is a hierarchy, and they differ on whether the
   hierarchy is of being or of realms. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Aquinas would be refuted by showing that
   Aquinas’s essence/existence distinction cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between identity and manifestation—by showing, that is, that Aquinas already
   distinguishes the structural condition from the actuality that fulfils it, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of Aquinas’s own.



13.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Aquinas’s essence, or is it a
departure from Aquinas? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Aquinas’s essence is already an invariance, not a
whatness, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s manifestation be stated without the notion of enact-
ment? The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who
holds that manifestation can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves
open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Summa Theologiae do justice to the
text? The chapter has used the Five Ways, the essence/existence distinction, the analogy of
120                                                                   Chapter 13. Thomas Aquinas


being, and the participation of creatures, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A
reader who holds that the Summa Theologiae supports a different reading has a question the
chapter leaves open.
