A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both what it is and that it is—a person, a work of art, a
community. Is the whatness distinct from the thatness? Is the thatness a property added to
the whatness, or the act by which the whatness is? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between Aquinas’s essence/existence distinction and the framework’s distinction between
identity and manifestation?

The next chapter turns to Duns Scotus. It states the formal distinction, the doctrine of thisness
( haecceitas), the univocity of being, and the account of the will; it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of Scotus; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of thisness is the nearest medieval analogue to Scotus’s haecceitas.
The present chapter has stated Aquinas’s answer to the problem of essence and existence; the
next chapter states Scotus’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 14

Duns Scotus


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with John Duns Scotus. It states the doctrine of thisness
(haecceitas), the formal distinction, the univocity of being, the primacy of the will, and the
account of radical contingency, with reference to the Ordinatio, the Quaestiones Subtillissimae
super Libros Metaphysicorum, and the Reportatio; it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of Scotus; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of primitive thisness is the nearest medieval analogue to Scotus’s haecceitas; it
presents the objections that Scotus would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s
reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what
would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where
the chapter speaks of “thisness,” “the formal distinction,” “univocity,” or “contingency,” these
are Scotus’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not
by the framework.


14.1      A Scene
Consider two drops of water, exactly alike. Same size, same shape, same chemical composition,
same temperature, same position relative to the glass. If you look at them under a microscope,
you cannot tell them apart; every qualitative feature of the one is a qualitative feature of the
other. And yet they are two drops, not one. There is a fact about the one that distinguishes it
from the other, even though no qualitative feature distinguishes it.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose you ask what makes the one drop *this* drop, and not
the other. It is not the size, because the other has the same size. It is not the shape, because
the other has the same shape. It is not the position, because if you swapped them, the same
question would arise. The fact that makes the one drop this drop is not a qualitative feature at
all; it is the bare fact that it is *this* one, and not the other. Scotus calls this fact the haecceitas,
the "thisness" of the thing.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose you ask whether the thisness is something
in the thing, or something added to the thing by the mind. If it is added by the mind, then the
two drops are not really two; they are one drop seen twice, or one drop plus a mental fiction. If it
is in the thing, then the thisness is a real feature of the thing, and the thing is really two because
of it. Scotus holds the second: the thisness is a positive entity in the thing, not a negation, not a
relation, not a mental fiction. It is what makes the thing be *this* thing, and without it, the
thing would be only an instance of a kind, not a this.
   The scene is Scotus’s image, in the Ordinatio, of the structure of individuation. Every
individual thing has two principles: a common nature, which makes it be of this kind (a human
being, a drop of water, a horse), and a thisness, which makes it be *this* individual of the kind.

                                                  121
122                                                                       Chapter 14. Duns Scotus


The common nature is not individuated by itself; it is individuated by the thisness. The two
principles are formally distinct but really identical: they are not two things, but two aspects of
one thing, distinguished by a distinction that is more than conceptual but less than real.
      The scene poses the question that Scotus was the first to pose in its full form. What makes
an individual be an individual? Is the individuating principle a common nature, a matter, a
bundle of properties, or a thisness? And what is the relation between the common nature and
the thisness? The present chapter states Scotus’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


14.2        The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, and Aquinas.
Augustine posed the problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed the problem of light
and hierarchy; Anselm posed the problem of God’s existence; Aquinas posed the problem of
essence and existence. Scotus is the fifth great figure of the medieval West, and he is the great
critic of Aquinas: he criticizes Aquinas’s account of individuation, his account of analogy, and his
account of the relation between intellect and will. The present chapter states Scotus’s critique,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Scotus was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Scotus hold? The chapter states the doctrine of thisness,
the formal distinction, the univocity of being, the primacy of the will, and the account of radical
contingency, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Scotus converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Scotus would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Scotus?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


14.3        The Position

14.3.1      Thisness (Haecceitas)

Scotus’s doctrine of thisness is stated in the Ordinatio II, d.3, and in the Quaestiones Subtillissimae
VII. The doctrine is a response to the question: what makes an individual be an individual?
      Aquinas had held that the principle of individuation is matter (materia signata): the individual
is the form in this matter, and the matter is what distinguishes one individual of a kind from
another. Scotus rejects this. Matter cannot individuate, because matter is itself common; if
individuation were by matter, there would be no individual matter, and the regress would follow.
What individuates must be a positive entity, not a negation, not a relation, not a privation.
14.3. The Position                                                                               123


   Scotus’s answer is the haecceitas: the thisness of the thing. The thisness is a positive entity
that makes the thing be *this* thing and not another; it is the ultimate determination of the
individual, the principle by which the common nature becomes this individual. The thisness is
not a qualitative feature; it is not a what, but a *which*; it does not add a new property to the
thing, but it makes the thing be the individual it is.
   The thisness is formally distinct from the common nature, but really identical with it. The
two are not two things; they are one thing, with two principles that the mind can distinguish,
and that are really distinct in a formal sense. The formal distinction is the key to Scotus’s
account: it is more than a conceptual distinction (it is grounded in the thing), and less than a
real distinction (it does not divide the thing into two things).

   From the Tradition

   “The individuating principle is not matter, nor quantity, nor any accident; it is a positive
   entity, by which the individual is this individual. This entity is the thisness (haecceitas),
   and it is formally distinct from the common nature, though really identical with it.”
   (Scotus, Ordinatio II, d.3, q.1, trans. after Wolter)


14.3.2    The Formal Distinction
Scotus’s formal distinction is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in the Ordinatio I,
d.2, and in the Quaestiones Subtillissimae VII. The distinction is between the common nature
and the thisness; between the divine attributes (wisdom, goodness, power); between the essence
and the persons of the Trinity.
   The formal distinction is not a conceptual distinction: the two terms of the distinction are
not merely two ways of thinking about one thing; they are two aspects of one thing, and the
aspects are grounded in the thing itself. The formal distinction is not a real distinction: the two
terms are not two things; they are one thing, and the distinction does not divide the thing into
two.
   The formal distinction is the key to Scotus’s metaphysics. It allows Scotus to say that the
common nature and the thisness are one thing, and yet to say that they are formally distinct; it
allows him to say that the divine attributes are one God, and yet to say that wisdom is formally
distinct from goodness; it allows him to say that the essence and the persons of the Trinity are
one God, and yet to say that they are formally distinct. The distinction is the tool by which
Scotus preserves both the unity and the plurality of the divine and the creaturely.

14.3.3    The Univocity of Being
Scotus’s doctrine of the univocity of being is stated in the Ordinatio I, d.3, and in the Quaestiones
Subtillissimae IV. The doctrine is a response to Aquinas’s analogy of being.
   Aquinas had held that being is said analogically of God and creatures: the being of God and
the being of creatures are not the same, and yet they are not unrelated. The analogy preserves
both the transcendence of God and the intelligibility of creaturely being.
   Scotus rejects the analogy. If being is said analogically, our concept of being is not a single
concept; it is a family of related concepts, and none of them is adequate to both God and
124                                                                        Chapter 14. Duns Scotus


creatures. If our concept of being is not a single concept, we cannot reason from creatures to
God, because the middle term of the argument would be ambiguous. To preserve the possibility
of natural theology, Scotus holds that being is said univocally of God and creatures: the concept
of being is one, and it applies to God and to creatures in the same sense.
      The univocity of being is not a denial of the transcendence of God. Scotus holds that God is
infinite being, and that creatures are finite being; the univocity is in the concept of being, not in
the mode of being. The concept of being is one; the modes of being are different. God is infinite
being; creatures are finite being; the two are the same in being, and different in mode.

    From the Tradition

   “Being is said univocally of God and creatures. For if being were said analogically, our
    concept of being would not be one, and there would be no middle term by which we could
    demonstrate anything of God from creatures. Therefore being must be one concept, and
    it must apply to God and to creatures in the same sense.” (Scotus, Ordinatio I, d.3, q.1,
    trans. after Wolter)


14.3.4      The Primacy of the Will
Scotus’s doctrine of the primacy of the will is stated in the Ordinatio II, d.6, and in the Reportatio
IV, d.49. The doctrine is a response to Aquinas’s account of the relation between intellect and
will.
      Aquinas had held that the intellect is prior to the will: the intellect presents the good to the
will, and the will chooses it. The will is free, but its freedom is determined by the good that the
intellect presents; the will cannot choose what the intellect does not present as good.
      Scotus rejects this. If the will were determined by the intellect, it would not be free; it would
be a natural appetite, moved by its object, as the stone is moved by gravity. The will must be
free, not only from external coercion, but from internal necessity; it must be able to choose what
the intellect does not present as good, and it must be able to choose what the intellect presents
as good, but not necessarily.
      The primacy of the will is the foundation of Scotus’s ethics. The good is not what the intellect
presents; the good is what the will chooses. The will is not determined by the good; it determines
what is good. The freedom of the will is the freedom to choose, and the choice is not determined
by the intellect.

14.3.5      Radical Contingency
Scotus’s doctrine of radical contingency is stated in the Ordinatio I, d.39. The doctrine is a
response to the necessity of the created order in Aquinas and in the Arabic Aristotelians.
      Aquinas had held that the created order is contingent, but that it is not arbitrary: God
creates the world freely, but God’s freedom is compatible with the necessity of the created order,
because the created order is the expression of God’s wisdom. Scotus rejects this. If the created
order were necessary, God would not be free; if God is free, the created order is contingent, and
its contingency is not merely the contingency of our knowledge, but the contingency of the thing
itself.
14.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         125


   The radical contingency is the foundation of Scotus’s account of freedom. The world is not
necessary; it is contingent; it could have been otherwise. The freedom of God is the freedom to
create, and the created order is the expression of this freedom. The contingency of the world is
not a defect; it is the mark of its dependence on the free will of God.

   From the Tradition

   “The created order is contingent, not necessary. It could have been otherwise, and it would
   have been otherwise if God had willed it so. The contingency is not in our knowledge,
   but in the thing itself; the thing is contingent because it is the expression of a free will.”
   (Scotus, Ordinatio I, d.39, q.1, trans. after Wolter)



14.4     Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Scotus is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the thisness. The traditional reading takes the thisness to be
a positive entity, a real feature of the thing, distinct from the common nature. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a limit-concept, a way of saying that the individual is irreducible to the
common nature, without any positive entity. The two readings disagree on whether Scotus is
a realist or a conceptualist about thisness, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s primitive thisness is a real feature, not a limit-concept.


Second dispute: the status of the formal distinction. The traditional reading takes the
formal distinction to be a real distinction in the thing, more than conceptual and less than real.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a semantic distinction, a way of speaking about one thing
under two descriptions, without any real distinction in the thing. The two readings disagree on
whether Scotus is a realist or a semanticist about the formal distinction, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s distinction between identity and
manifestation is a real distinction, not a semantic one.


Third dispute: the status of the will. The traditional reading takes the primacy of the will
to be a real feature of the human person: the will is free, and its freedom is not determined by
the intellect. A revisionary reading takes it to be a phenomenological description: the will seems
free, but its freedom is compatible with a deeper determinism. The two readings disagree on
whether Scotus is a libertarian or a compatibilist about the will, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no doctrine of the will, and its freedom
is not the Scotist freedom.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Scotus is a realist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between two realist metaphysics. If Scotus is a conceptualist, the dialogue
is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct. The framework holds
that the first reading is closer to the Ordinatio, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it
states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
126                                                                      Chapter 14. Duns Scotus


14.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Scotus. The framework shares four structural features with Scotus’s position.

       1. Primitive thisness. Scotus’s haecceitas is a positive entity that makes a thing be
         *this* thing, not another of the same kind. The framework’s primitive thisness is an
          individuating feature that is not qualitative, and that distinguishes one thing from an
          exact qualitative duplicate. The two are not the same (Scotus’s thisness is a principle
          of individuation; the framework’s is the invariance as enacted by one source), but
          the structural analogy is exact. The framework’s account of non-duplicability and
          its verdicts on cloning, teleportation, and fission are the direct heirs of the Scotist
          tradition.

       2. The irreducibility of the individual. Scotus holds that the individual is not reducible
          to the common nature; the individual is *this* individual, and its thisness is not
          a common property. The framework holds that the identity is not reducible to its
          manifestations; the identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and its unity
          is not the unity of a pattern. Both hold that the individual is irreducible to the
          universal.

       3. The distinction between the thing and its appearances. Scotus’s formal distinction
          distinguishes the common nature from the thisness; the two are one thing, but they
          are formally distinct. The framework’s distinction between identity and manifestation
          distinguishes the invariance from the appearance; the two are one thing, but they
          are structurally distinct. Both hold that what a thing is and how it appears are
          distinct, without being two things.

       4. The contingency of the world. Scotus holds that the world is radically contingent; it
          could have been otherwise. The framework holds that the expression of an identity
          is a structural tendency, not a necessity; the identity could have been expressed
          differently, or not at all, depending on the receiving realm. Both hold that the world
          is not necessary, and that its contingency is a real feature of it.



14.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Scotus. The framework diverges from Scotus in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Scotus’s metaphysics is a metaphysics of God; the thisness, the
          formal distinction, the univocity of being, and the primacy of the will all turn on
          God. The framework has no God; its First Determination is a realm of pure unity,
          not a being whose essence is to exist. The framework is a metaphysics without God.
14.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  127


       2. The status of univocity. Scotus holds that being is said univocally of God and
          creatures; the concept of being is one, and it applies to God and to creatures in the
          same sense. The framework holds that its terms are defined within the framework,
          and that they are not univocal with respect to any other framework. The framework’s
          language is structural, not univocal with respect to God.

       3. The status of the will. Scotus holds that the will is superior to the intellect, and that
          its freedom is not determined by the good that the intellect presents. The framework
          has no doctrine of the will; its expression is a structural tendency, not a free choice,
          and its freedom is not the Scotist freedom. The framework is a metaphysics without
          a doctrine of the will.

       4. The status of radical contingency. Scotus holds that the world is radically contingent,
          because it is the expression of a free will; the contingency is not a defect, but a
          mark of dependence. The framework holds that the expression of an identity is a
          structural tendency, not a free choice; the world is not contingent in Scotus’s sense,
          because there is no free will to make it contingent. The framework’s contingency is
          structural, not voluntarist.




14.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Scotus’s objection. The framework says that identity is an invariance, and that its
   individuation is the enactment of the invariance by one source. But an invariance is a
   universal, and a universal is not an individual. If the framework’s identity is a universal,
   it is not a *this*; it is a what, not a which. The framework’s primitive thisness is a thin
   substitute for the Scotist haecceitas; it gives the individual a name, but not a principle.
   Scotus’s haecceitas is a positive entity that makes the individual be *this* individual; the
   framework’s primitive thisness is a negation, a bare fact that the individual is not another,
   without any positive content. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of bare facts, not
   of positive entities.
   Scotus’s second objection. The framework says that expression is a structural tendency,
   not a free choice. But a tendency without a will is a tendency without freedom; and
   a world without freedom is a world without contingency. Scotus’s world is contingent
   because it is the expression of a free will; the framework’s world is necessary because it is
   the expression of a structural tendency. If the framework’s world is necessary, there is
   no room for the contingency that Scotus’s haecceitas presupposes; and a world without
   contingency is a world without individuality. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
   necessities, not of individuals.
128                                                                     Chapter 14. Duns Scotus


14.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an invariance is a universal,
   and it agrees that a universal is not an individual. But the framework denies that its
   identity is a universal. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
   *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is what makes the identity be *this*
   identity, not another. The framework’s primitive thisness is not a negation; it is the
   positive fact that the invariance is enacted by one source, and not by another. The
   distinction is between a universal (a what) and an enactment (a which); the framework’s
   identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a tendency without a will is
   a tendency without freedom, and it agrees that a world without freedom is a world without
   contingency. But the framework denies that its world is necessary. The framework’s
   expression is a structural tendency, not a necessity; the identity could have been expressed
   differently, or not at all, depending on the receiving realm. The contingency is structural,
   not voluntarist; it is not the contingency of a free will, but the contingency of a structural
   tendency. The distinction is between a voluntarist contingency (Scotus’s) and a structural
   contingency (the framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the
   second is a contingency, not a necessity.



14.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Scotus’s cost. If Scotus accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
thisness is a positive entity. He must accept that the thisness is the enactment of an invariance
by one source, and that the enactment is not a positive entity added to the common nature.
The cost is the loss of the Scotist haecceitas: the thisness is no longer a positive entity, and the
individual is no longer individuated by a positive principle.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Scotus’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of positive individuation, of the haecceitas—that its ontology does not capture. The
cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of an invariance, but not the positive entity of the thisness, and the framework leaves
the second to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Scotus’s haecceitas is not
a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s enactment does not capture. Scotus
must accept that the framework’s enactment is not a negation; it is a positive fact that Scotus’s
14.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                       129


haecceitas presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of
the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


14.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “primitive thisness” is not substitutable
   for Scotus’s term “haecceitas.” If one substitutes “haecceitas” for “primitive thisness” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s primitive thisness is
   the positive fact that an invariance is enacted by one source, and it is not a positive entity
   added to a common nature; Scotus’s haecceitas is a positive entity, and it is added to the
   common nature to individuate it. The framework’s thisness is an enactment; Scotus’s
   thisness is an entity. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Scotus’s term “the free act of
   the will.” If one substitutes “the free act of the will” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency,
   and it is not free; Scotus’s free act is a choice, and it is not a tendency. The framework’s
   expression is structural; Scotus’s act is voluntarist. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Scotus is resemblance:
   both hold that the individual is irreducible to the universal, and they differ on whether the
   individuating principle is a positive entity or an enactment. Both hold that the world is
   contingent, and they differ on whether the contingency is voluntarist or structural. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Scotus would be refuted by showing that Scotus’s haecceitas cannot be formulated
   without the framework’s distinction between enactment and entity—by showing, that is,
   that Scotus already distinguishes the enactment from the positive entity, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of Scotus’s own.



14.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s primitive thisness a development of Scotus’s haecceitas,
or is it a departure from Scotus? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Scotus’s haecceitas is already an enactment,
not a positive entity, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s contingency be stated without the notion of a tendency?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that contingency can be stated without a tendency has a question the chapter leaves open.
130                                                                      Chapter 14. Duns Scotus


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Ordinatio do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the haecceitas, the formal distinction, the univocity of being, and the primacy of
the will, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Ordinatio
supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an instance of a kind and an individual—a person, a
work of art, a place. Is the individuality something added to the kind, or something that the
kind itself requires? Is the individuality a positive feature, or a bare fact that the thing is *this*
one? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Scotus’s haecceitas and the
framework’s primitive thisness?

The next chapter turns to William of Ockham. It states the nominalist critique of universals, the
razor (Ockham’s razor), the account of intuitive cognition, and the primacy of the individual;
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ockham; and it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose nominalism about universals and its
account of the individual are the nearest medieval analogues to Ockham’s. The present chapter
has stated Scotus’s answer to the problem of individuation; the next chapter states Ockham’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 15

William of Ockham


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with William of Ockham. It states Ockham’s nominalism
(the rejection of real universals), the razor (pluralitas non est ponenda sine necessitate), intuitive
and abstractive cognition, the primacy of the individual, and the critique of Scotus’s formal
distinction, with reference to the Summa Logicae, the Ordinatio, and the Quodlibeta Septem;
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ockham; it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose structural realism is the nearest modern
analogue to Ockham’s nominalism; it presents the objections that Ockham would raise against
the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it
states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no
normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “universal,” “nominalism,”
“intuitive cognition,” “the razor,” or “individual,” these are Ockham’s terms, and their sense is
fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


15.1        A Scene
Consider a person who has seen many horses. She has seen a black horse, a white horse, a brown
horse, a young horse, an old horse. From these perceptions, she has formed a concept: the
concept of horse. The concept is one, and it applies to many horses; the many horses are many,
and none of them is the concept. If she asks whether the concept is a thing, she may be tempted
to say that it is: there is a horse in the mind, a universal horse, in which all the individual horses
participate. Ockham rejects the temptation: the universal is not a thing; it is a concept, a sign
in the mind, a way of grouping the individuals. The universal does not exist outside the mind;
only the individuals exist.
    Now consider a second case, harder to state. Suppose she asks not what a universal is, but
how many things are needed to explain the world. She can posit universals, essences, formal
distinctions, real relations, species, genera, powers, faculties, and a long list of other entities. Or
she can posit only individuals and their relations. Ockham’s razor says: do not multiply entities
beyond necessity. The universals, the essences, the formal distinctions, and the other entities
are not necessary; the individuals and their relations are sufficient. The razor does not say that
the world is simple; it says that our explanations should not be more complex than the world
requires.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what a universal is, or how
many things are needed, but what knowledge is. Ockham distinguishes intuitive cognition from
abstractive cognition. Intuitive cognition is the direct, evident knowledge of an individual thing:
I see this horse, and I know that it exists. Abstractive cognition is the knowledge of an essence,
a universal, or an absent thing: I know what a horse is, whether or not any horse is present.

                                                 131
132                                                               Chapter 15. William of Ockham


The two are distinct, and intuitive cognition is prior: the knowledge of the individual is the
foundation of the knowledge of the universal.
      The scene is Ockham’s image, in the Summa Logicae and the Ordinatio, of the structure
of knowledge and reality. Only individuals exist; universals are concepts; the razor cuts away
the unnecessary entities; intuitive cognition is the foundation of knowledge. The scene poses
the question that Ockham was the first to pose in its full form. What is a universal? Is it a
thing, a concept, or a name? How many entities are needed to explain the world? And what is
the relation between the knowledge of the individual and the knowledge of the universal? The
present chapter states Ockham’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


15.2        The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, and Scotus.
Augustine posed the problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed the problem of light
and hierarchy; Anselm posed the problem of God’s existence; Aquinas posed the problem of
essence and existence; Scotus posed the problem of individuation and thisness. Ockham is
the sixth great figure of the medieval West, and he is the great critic of the realist tradition:
he criticizes the real universals of Plato and of the realist interpreters of Aristotle, the formal
distinction of Scotus, and the essence/existence distinction of Aquinas. The present chapter
states Ockham’s critique, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Ockham was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ockham hold? The chapter states the nominalism, the
razor, intuitive and abstractive cognition, the primacy of the individual, and the critique of
Scotus’s formal distinction, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ockham converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Ockham would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ockham?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


15.3        The Position

15.3.1      Nominalism

Ockham’s nominalism is stated in the Summa Logicae I, cc. 14–17, and in the Ordinatio I, d.2,
qq. 4–8. The doctrine is a response to the question: what is a universal?
      The realist tradition, from Plato through the realist interpreters of Aristotle, had held that
universals are real things: the Form of Horse, the species Horse, the essence of horse, existing
15.3. The Position                                                                               133


in a separate realm or in the individuals themselves. The universal is one, and the individuals
participate in it; the universal is the reality, and the individuals are its instances.
   Ockham rejects the realist tradition. A universal, he holds, is not a thing; it is a sign. There
are two kinds of signs: natural signs (concepts in the mind) and conventional signs (words in a
language). The concept of horse is a natural sign that signifies many horses; the word "horse" is
a conventional sign that signifies the same many horses. Neither the concept nor the word is a
thing in the world; both are signs by which the mind or the language groups the individuals.
   The nominalism has three consequences. First, only individuals exist; the world is a world of
individuals, not of universals. Second, science is about individuals, not about universals; the
object of scientific knowledge is the individual thing, known through intuitive cognition. Third,
the universals are fictions of the mind or conventions of language; they are useful, but they are
not real.

   From the Tradition

   “No universal is a substance, or a real thing outside the soul. Every universal is either a
   concept in the mind or a word in a language. The individual alone is real; the universal is
   a sign of the individual, not a thing alongside it.” (Ockham, Summa Logicae I, c.15, trans.
   after Boehner)



15.3.2      The Razor

Ockham’s razor is stated in the Quodlibeta Septem and in the Ordinatio. The formula is: pluralitas
non est ponenda sine necessitate (a plurality is not to be posited without necessity), or, in another
formulation, entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem (entities are not to be multiplied
beyond necessity).
   The razor is not a metaphysical principle; it is a methodological one. It does not say that the
world is simple; it says that our explanations should not posit more entities than are needed.
If a phenomenon can be explained by individuals and their relations, there is no need to posit
universals, essences, or formal distinctions. If a phenomenon can be explained by intuitive
cognition, there is no need to posit abstractive species.
   The razor has been applied by Ockham to a long list of entities: universals, essences, formal
distinctions, real relations, active powers, sensible species, intelligible species, and the will’s
freedom. In each case, Ockham holds that the entity is not necessary; the individual and its
relations are sufficient.


15.3.3      Intuitive and Abstractive Cognition

Ockham’s account of cognition is stated in the Ordinatio I, prologue, q.1, and in the Reportatio
II, qq. 12–13. The account distinguishes intuitive cognition from abstractive cognition.
   Intuitive cognition is the direct, evident knowledge of an individual thing. When I see this
horse, I have intuitive cognition of it; I know that it exists, and I know it as this individual.
Intuitive cognition is the foundation of all knowledge of the world; without it, there would be no
knowledge of individuals.
134                                                              Chapter 15. William of Ockham


      Abstractive cognition is the knowledge of an essence, a universal, or an absent thing. When
I know what a horse is, whether or not any horse is present, I have abstractive cognition of
the essence of horse. Abstractive cognition is derived from intuitive cognition; it is the mind’s
abstraction from the individual to the concept.
      The distinction has three consequences. First, intuitive cognition is prior to abstractive
cognition; the knowledge of the individual is the foundation of the knowledge of the universal.
Second, intuitive cognition is evident; it gives certainty about the existence of the individual.
Third, abstractive cognition is not evident about existence; it gives knowledge of the essence, not
of the existence.

   From the Tradition

   “Intuitive cognition is the cognition by which I know that this thing exists, and that it is
   present to me. Abstractive cognition is the cognition by which I know what the thing is,
   whether or not it is present. The first is the foundation of the second; without intuitive
   cognition, there would be no abstractive cognition.” (Ockham, Ordinatio I, prologue, q.1,
   trans. after Boehner)



15.3.4      The Primacy of the Individual

Ockham’s primacy of the individual is the metaphysical counterpart of his nominalism. If only
individuals exist, then the individual is the primary reality; the universal is secondary, a sign of
the individual. The individual is not individuated by a thisness, as Scotus held; it is individuated
by itself, by the fact that it is this individual and not another. The thisness is not a positive
entity; it is the individual itself, considered as not-other.
      The primacy of the individual has three consequences. First, the individual is the object of
intuitive cognition; it is what we know directly. Second, the individual is the object of scientific
knowledge; science is about individuals, not about universals. Third, the individual is the object
of God’s knowledge and love; God knows and loves the individual, not the universal.


15.3.5      The Critique of Scotus’s Formal Distinction

Ockham’s critique of Scotus’s formal distinction is stated in the Ordinatio I, d.2, qq. 1–3. The
critique is an application of the razor.
      Scotus had held that the formal distinction is more than conceptual and less than real:
the common nature and the thisness are one thing, but they are formally distinct; the divine
attributes are one God, but they are formally distinct. The formal distinction allows Scotus to
preserve both the unity and the plurality of the divine and the creaturely.
      Ockham rejects the formal distinction. If the two terms are one thing, then the distinction
is conceptual; if the two terms are two things, then the distinction is real. There is no middle
ground. The formal distinction is an unnecessary entity; the razor cuts it away. The world is a
world of individuals, not of things with formal distinctions; the divine attributes are one God,
not one God with formal distinctions.
15.4. Internal Disputes                                                                        135


   From the Tradition

   “A distinction is either real or conceptual; there is no middle ground. If the two terms are
   one thing, the distinction is conceptual; if the two terms are two things, the distinction is
   real. The formal distinction is an unnecessary entity; it is to be cut away by the razor.”
   (Ockham, Ordinatio I, d.2, q.1, trans. after Boehner)



15.4     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Ockham is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of nominalism. The traditional reading takes Ockham’s nom-
inalism to be a metaphysical doctrine: only individuals exist, and universals are fictions. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a semantic doctrine: the universal is a sign, and the question
of its reality is a question of language, not of metaphysics. The two readings disagree on whether
Ockham is a metaphysical or a semantic nominalist, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structural realism is a metaphysical doctrine, not
a semantic one.


Second dispute: the status of the razor. The traditional reading takes the razor to be a
metaphysical principle: the world is simple, and the razor reflects its simplicity. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a methodological principle: our explanations should not be more complex
than necessary, but the world may be as complex as it is. The two readings disagree on whether
Ockham is a metaphysical or a methodological simplifier, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework uses the razor as a methodological principle, not a
metaphysical one.


Third dispute: the status of intuitive cognition. The traditional reading takes intuitive
cognition to be the foundation of knowledge: without it, there would be no knowledge of
individuals. A revisionary reading takes it to be a species of cognition, not the foundation;
on this reading, intuitive and abstractive cognition are two species of cognition, and neither
is more fundamental. The two readings disagree on whether Ockham is a foundationalist or a
coherentist about knowledge, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because
the framework’s knowledge is neither foundationalist nor coherentist, but structural.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ockham is a metaphysical nominalist, the
framework’s dialogue with him is a dialogue between two metaphysics that reject real universals.
If Ockham is a semantic nominalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Summa
Logicae, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.
136                                                              Chapter 15. William of Ockham


15.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Ockham. The framework shares four structural features with Ockham’s position.

       1. The rejection of real universals. Ockham holds that universals are not real things;
          only individuals exist. The framework holds that identity is not a universal; it is
          the invariance enacted by one source, and there are many identities, each one a
         *this*. Both reject the realist tradition that posits universals as separate entities or
          as common natures in the individuals.

       2. The primacy of the individual. Ockham holds that the individual is the primary
          reality, and that the universal is a sign of the individual. The framework holds that
          identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and that the source is a *this*, not
          a what. Both hold that the individual is primary, and that the universal is derived.

       3. The razor as a methodological principle. Ockham’s razor says: do not multiply
          entities beyond necessity. The framework’s principle of parsimony says: do not posit
          more structure than the phenomena require. Both hold that explanation should be
          as simple as the phenomena allow, and that unnecessary entities are to be cut away.

       4. The distinction between the individual and the universal. Ockham distinguishes
          intuitive cognition (of the individual) from abstractive cognition (of the universal);
          the two are distinct, and the first is prior. The framework distinguishes manifestation
         (of the individual) from reconstruction (of the pattern); the two are distinct, and
          the first is the source of the second. Both hold that the knowledge of the individual
          is prior to the knowledge of the universal.



15.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Ockham. The framework diverges from Ockham in four respects.

       1. The status of the invariant. Ockham holds that universals are fictions of the mind or
          conventions of language; only individuals exist. The framework holds that identity
          is invariant under a class of allowable transformations, and that the invariance is
          real: it is neither a fiction nor a convention. The framework’s structural realism is
          neither Ockham’s nominalism nor Plato’s realism; it is a third position, in which
          the invariant is real but not a separate entity. Ockham would say that this third
          position is a fiction; the framework says that it is the structure that the individual
          exhibits.

       2. The status of the formal distinction. Ockham rejects Scotus’s formal distinction as an
15.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  137


         unnecessary entity; there is no middle ground between real and conceptual distinction.
         The framework holds that the distinction between identity and manifestation is
         real, but not real as two things: it is the distinction between the invariant and
         its appearance, which are one thing but structurally distinct. Ockham would
         say that this is a formal distinction in disguise; the framework says that it is a
         structural distinction, different from both Ockham’s real distinction and Scotus’s
         formal distinction.

       3. The status of cognition. Ockham holds that intuitive cognition is the direct, evident
         knowledge of the individual thing; it is the foundation of all knowledge. The
         framework holds that knowledge is reconstruction from manifestations; it is never
         direct or evident, but always fallible and partial. The framework’s account of
         knowledge is neither intuitive nor evident; it is structural and reconstructive.

       4. The status of the individual. Ockham holds that the individual is individuated by
         itself, by the fact that it is this individual and not another. The framework holds
         that the individual is individuated by the enactment of the invariance by one source;
         the source is a *this*, but its thisness is not a bare fact, it is the positive fact that
         the invariance is enacted by this source. The framework’s individuation is neither
         Ockham’s bare fact nor Scotus’s positive entity; it is the enactment of the structural
         invariance.




15.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ockham’s objection. The framework says that identity is an invariance, and that the
   invariance is real. But an invariance is a universal; the invariant is what is common to
   many manifestations. If the invariance is real, then the universal is real; and if the universal
   is real, the razor is violated. The framework’s identity is a universal in disguise; it is the
   common nature of the many manifestations, and the framework’s structural realism is a
   realism of universals. The framework’s claim to have rejected real universals is a verbal
   manoeuvre; in fact, the framework posits a real universal, and it calls it by another name.
   Ockham’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction
   from manifestations, and that it is fallible and partial. But a reconstruction without
   intuitive cognition is a reconstruction without a foundation; it is a house built on sand.
   Ockham’s intuitive cognition is the direct, evident knowledge of the individual; it is the
   foundation of all knowledge. The framework’s reconstruction has no foundation; it floats
   without anchor, and a knowledge without anchor is not knowledge. The framework’s
   epistemology is a scepticism in disguise.
138                                                              Chapter 15. William of Ockham


15.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an invariance is a universal, in
   one sense of the word: it is what is common to many manifestations. But the framework
   denies that this makes its identity a real universal in the sense Ockham rejects. The
   framework’s identity is not a common nature, not a separate entity, not a form that the
   individuals participate in; it is the invariance enacted by one source, and the enactment is
   not a universal, it is a *this*. The distinction is between the universal as a common nature
   (which Ockham rejects) and the invariant as the enacted pattern (which the framework
   affirms). The framework’s invariant is real, but not a thing; it is the structure that the
   manifestations exhibit, and its reality is the reality of the structure, not of a separate
   entity.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that knowledge needs a founda-
   tion, and it agrees that a reconstruction without intuitive cognition is a reconstruction
   without an anchor. But the framework denies that its reconstruction is without anchor.
   The framework’s reconstruction is anchored in the manifestations themselves; the manifes-
   tations are given, and the reconstruction is the mind’s reading of them. The manifestations
   are the foundation; the reconstruction is the structure that the mind builds on them.
   The distinction is between intuitive cognition (which sees the individual directly) and
   structural cognition (which reads the invariant from the manifestations). The framework
   holds that the second is a kind of knowledge, not a scepticism.



15.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Ockham’s cost. If Ockham accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
universals are only fictions or conventions. He must accept that the invariant is real, in the sense
the framework gives to "real": not a separate entity, but the structure that the manifestations
exhibit. The cost is the loss of the razor’s full force: the razor no longer cuts away the invariant,
because the invariant is not an unnecessary entity, it is the structure itself.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ockham’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its identity is not a universal. It must accept that the invariant is a universal in
Ockham’s sense, and that the framework is a realism of universals. The cost is the loss of the
framework’s nominalist credentials: the framework is no longer a structural realism that rejects
universals; it is a realism that posits them.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ockham’s razor is not
a mistake; it is a necessary discipline on our explanations. Ockham must accept that the
15.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     139


framework’s invariant is not a fiction; it is a structural condition that the individuals exhibit.
The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals,
they are complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


15.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ock-
   ham’s term “the individual.” If one substitutes “the individual” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invari-
   ance enacted by one source, and it is not identical with the individual that enacts it;
   Ockham’s individual is the primary reality, and it is not an invariance. The framework’s
   identity is the structure; Ockham’s individual is the thing. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is
   not substitutable for Ockham’s term “intuitive cognition.” If one substitutes “intuitive
   cognition” for “manifestation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm, and it is not a
   cognition; Ockham’s intuitive cognition is the direct knowledge of the individual, and it is
   a cognition. The framework’s manifestation is ontological; Ockham’s intuitive cognition is
   epistemological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ockham is resemblance:
   both reject real universals, and they differ on whether the invariant is real. Both use the
   razor, and they differ on whether the razor cuts away the invariant. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Ockham
   would be refuted by showing that Ockham’s nominalism cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and entity—by showing, that is, that Ockham
   already distinguishes the structural condition from the entity that exhibits it, and that
   the framework’s distinction is a development of Ockham’s own.



15.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ockham’s nominalism, or is it a
departure from Ockham? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ockham’s individual is already a structural condition,
not a bare fact, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s invariant be stated without the notion of a structure?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that the invariant can be stated without a structure has a question the chapter leaves open.
140                                                               Chapter 15. William of Ockham


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Summa Logicae do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the nominalism, the razor, and the intuitive cognition, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Summa Logicae supports a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
