A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an individual and an instance of a kind—a person, a work
of art, a place. Is the individuality prior to the kind, or is the kind prior to the individuality? Is
the kind a real thing, or a concept, or a convention? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between Ockham’s nominalism and the framework’s structural realism?

The next chapter turns to Meister Eckhart. It states the account of the ground of the soul, the
detachment ( abgeschiedenheit), the birth of God in the soul, and the distinction between God and
the Godhead; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Eckhart; and it states
the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the inner ground
is the nearest medieval analogue to Eckhart’s. The present chapter has stated Ockham’s answer to
the problem of universals; the next chapter states Eckhart’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
Chapter 16

Meister Eckhart


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Meister Eckhart. It states the account of the ground of the
soul (Seelengrund), detachment (Abgeschiedenheit), the birth of God in the soul (Gottesgeburt),
the distinction between God (Gott) and the Godhead (Gottheit), and the "living without why"
(leben sunder warumbe), with reference to the German Sermons, the Latin Opus Tripartitum, and
the Book of Divine Consolation; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Eckhart; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of the enacted ground is the nearest medieval analogue to Eckhart’s Seelengrund; it presents the
objections that Eckhart would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “the ground,” “detachment,” “the Godhead,” “the birth of God,” or “living
without why,” these are Eckhart’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the sermons and by the
interpretive tradition, not by the framework.



16.1     A Scene

Consider a person who is trying to hear a sound. She is in a noisy room; there are voices,
footsteps, the hum of a machine. She closes her eyes; she stops her ears; she tries to silence the
noise. But the noise does not stop. She can close her eyes, but she cannot close her ears; the
noise continues, and her attention is scattered among the many sounds.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she does not try to stop the noise, but tries to become
empty of the noise. She does not close her ears; she lets the noise be, but she does not cling to
it. She does not say "this noise is good" or "this noise is bad"; she does not prefer one sound
to another. She is detached from the noise, and in her detachment, the noise is no longer a
distraction. She hears the noise, but the noise does not hold her.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not how to hear the sound, or
how to become empty of the noise, but where the hearing itself comes from. The hearing is not
the ear; the ear is the organ, but the hearing is the act. The hearing comes from a ground that
is deeper than the ear, deeper than the mind, deeper than any faculty. This ground is what
Eckhart calls the ground of the soul (Seelengrund); it is the point in the soul where the soul is
one with God, and where God is born in the soul.
   The scene is Eckhart’s image, in the German Sermons, of the structure of the inner life. The
noise is the world; the detachment is the Abgeschiedenheit; the ground is the Seelengrund. The
soul that is detached from the world is empty; the soul that is empty is open to the birth of God;
the soul that is open to the birth of God is united with God in the ground.

                                                141
142                                                                   Chapter 16. Meister Eckhart


      The scene poses the question that Eckhart was the first to pose in its full form. What is
the ground of the soul? Is it a faculty, a substance, or a point of union? What is detachment?
Is it a state, an activity, or a way of being? And what is the birth of God in the soul? Is it
a metaphor, a doctrine, or a reality? The present chapter states Eckhart’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


16.2        The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus,
and Ockham. Augustine posed the problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed the
problem of light and hierarchy; Anselm posed the problem of God’s existence; Aquinas posed the
problem of essence and existence; Scotus posed the problem of individuation; Ockham posed the
problem of universals. Eckhart is the seventh great figure of the medieval West, and he is the
great mystic of the tradition: he turns from the scholastic distinctions to the inner experience of
union with God. The present chapter states Eckhart’s turn, and the framework’s dialogue with
it.
      The question is not whether Eckhart was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Eckhart hold? The chapter states the ground of the soul,
detachment, the birth of God in the soul, the distinction between God and the Godhead, and
the "living without why," with reference to the sermons and the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Eckhart converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Eckhart would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Eckhart?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


16.3        The Position

16.3.1      The Ground of the Soul

Eckhart’s account of the ground of the soul is stated in the German Sermons, especially in
the sermon Intravit Iesus in quoddam castellum and in the sermon Beati pauperes spiritu. The
ground is not a faculty; it is not the intellect, the will, or the memory. It is deeper than any
faculty; it is the point in the soul where the soul is one with God.
      The ground is not a thing; it is not a substance; it is not a part of the soul. It is the soul’s
own being, considered at the point where it is not yet distinguished from God. The soul, in its
ground, is not the soul as distinct from God; it is the soul as one with God, before the distinction
between the soul and God has been made.
16.3. The Position                                                                                143


   The ground is also called the "little spark" (vünkelîn) or the "castle" of the soul. It is the
point that is always open to God, the point that no sin can close, the point that is the image of
God in the soul. The ground is what makes the soul capable of union with God; it is the point
of contact between the soul and God.

   From the Tradition

   “There is something in the soul that is above the soul, and that is uncreated and uncreatable.
   It is the ground of the soul, and it is the point where the soul is one with God. In this
   ground, the soul is not the soul; it is God.” (Eckhart, Sermon 2, Intravit Iesus in quoddam
   castellum, trans. after Walshe)


16.3.2    Detachment (Abgeschiedenheit)

Eckhart’s account of detachment is stated in the treatise On Detachment (Von Abgeschiedenheit)
and in the sermons. Detachment is not a state; it is an activity; it is the soul’s activity of letting
go of all things, including itself, in order to be open to God.
   The detachment is not a withdrawal from the world; it is a transformation of the soul’s
relation to the world. The detached soul does not flee the world; it lives in the world without
being attached to it. The detached soul does not prefer one thing to another; it does not cling to
the good or avoid the bad; it is empty of all preference, and in its emptiness, it is open to God.
   The detachment has three moments: the detachment from things, the detachment from self,
and the detachment from God. The first is the letting go of external attachments; the second
is the letting go of the self’s own will and images; the third is the letting go of every image of
God, every concept, every name. In the third detachment, the soul is united with God in the
Godhead, beyond all distinction.

   From the Tradition

   “Perfect detachment is the highest virtue, and it is the ground of all the virtues. It is the
   soul’s letting go of all things, of itself, and of every image of God, so that the soul may be
   open to God in the Godhead, beyond all distinction.” (Eckhart, Von Abgeschiedenheit,
   trans. after Colledge-McGinn)


16.3.3    The Birth of God in the Soul

Eckhart’s account of the birth of God in the soul is stated in the sermon Intravit Iesus in quoddam
castellum and in many other sermons. The birth is not a metaphor; it is a reality; it is the eternal
birth of the Son in the ground of the soul.
   The birth has three moments: the birth of the Son in the soul, the birth of the soul in the
Son, and the birth of the soul in the Godhead. In the first, the Son is born in the ground of the
soul; the soul receives the Son, and the Son is the image of the Father. In the second, the soul is
born in the Son; the soul becomes the Son, and the Son is the soul’s own being. In the third, the
soul is born in the Godhead; the soul is united with God in the Godhead, beyond the Son and
beyond the soul.
144                                                                 Chapter 16. Meister Eckhart


      The birth is eternal; it is not a moment in time. The birth is always happening; it is the
eternal birth of the Son in the soul, and the eternal birth of the soul in the Godhead. The soul
that is detached is open to the birth; the soul that is attached is closed to it. The birth is not a
reward for detachment; it is what detachment makes possible.

   From the Tradition

   “The Father gives birth to his Son in the soul, and the soul is born in the Son, and the soul
   is born in the Godhead. This birth is eternal; it is always happening; it is the eternal life
   of the soul in God.” (Eckhart, Sermon 6, Iusti vivent in aeternum, trans. after Walshe)


16.3.4      God and the Godhead

Eckhart’s distinction between God (Gott) and the Godhead (Gottheit) is stated in the sermon
Beati pauperes spiritu and in many other sermons. The distinction is not a division; it is a
distinction between two ways of considering the one divine reality.
      God is God as he is manifested: God as creator, as revealer, as redeemer; God as he is named
by the names of the tradition; God as he is present in the Trinity. The Godhead is God as he is
in himself: God beyond all names, beyond all manifestations, beyond the Trinity; God as the
ground of the soul, the uncreated and uncreatable.
      The distinction is the key to Eckhart’s mysticism. The soul that is detached from all images
of God is united with God in the Godhead, beyond the God of the names and the images. The
soul that clings to the images of God is united with God as God, but not with God as the
Godhead. The Godhead is what the soul seeks when it seeks God beyond all images.

   From the Tradition

   “Some people want to see God with their eyes, as they see a cow; and they want to love
   God as they love a cow. So they love God for the sake of their own profit. But the soul
   that is detached loves God without why, and in its love, it is united with God in the
   Godhead, beyond all images of God.” (Eckhart, Sermon 16, Quasi stella matutina, trans.
   after Walshe)


16.3.5      Living Without Why

Eckhart’s account of "living without why" (leben sunder warumbe) is stated in the sermon Beati
pauperes spiritu and in the treatise On Detachment. The phrase is not a slogan; it is a description
of the soul’s life in God.
      The soul that lives without why does not act for the sake of a reason; it does not love God
for the sake of a reward; it does not seek God for the sake of a benefit. It loves God because
it loves God; it seeks God because it seeks God; it lives because it lives. The soul that lives
without why is free from all calculation; it is free from the means-end structure of ordinary life.
      The phrase is not a denial of reason; it is a denial of the means-end reasoning that makes
the soul a merchant in its relation to God. The soul that lives without why is not irrational;
it is beyond the rationality that calculates and exchanges. It is the rationality of love, not the
16.4. Internal Disputes                                                                          145


rationality of commerce.

   From the Tradition

   “The poor in spirit are those who have no will of their own, who do not know why they
   act, who live without why. They are free from all calculation, and in their freedom, they
   are united with God.” (Eckhart, Sermon 52, Beati pauperes spiritu, trans. after Walshe)




16.4     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Eckhart is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Godhead. The traditional reading takes the distinction
between God and the Godhead to be a real distinction: the Godhead is beyond God, and the
soul’s union with the Godhead is beyond its union with God. A revisionary reading takes it to
be a conceptual distinction: the Godhead and God are one reality, seen under two aspects; the
distinction is a way of speaking about the ineffable, not a division in God. The two readings
disagree on whether Eckhart is a monist or a trinitarian, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s First Determination is neither a God beyond
God nor a trinitarian God, but a realm of pure unity.


Second dispute: the status of detachment. The traditional reading takes detachment to
be an activity of the soul: the soul lets go of all things, and in its letting go, it is united with
God. A revisionary reading takes it to be a state: the soul is detached when it is empty of all
images, and its emptiness is its union with God. The two readings disagree on whether Eckhart
is an activist or a quietist about detachment, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s expression is an activity, not a state.


Third dispute: the status of the birth. The traditional reading takes the birth of God in
the soul to be a real event: the Son is really born in the ground of the soul, and the soul is really
united with God. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor: the birth is a way of speaking
about the soul’s union with God, not a real birth. The two readings disagree on whether Eckhart
is a mystic or a poet, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s expression is a structural reality, not a metaphor.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Eckhart is a mystic, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a mystical monism. If Eckhart is a poet,
the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct. The
framework holds that the first reading is closer to the German Sermons, but it does not rest its
case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
146                                                                Chapter 16. Meister Eckhart


16.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Eckhart. The framework shares four structural features with Eckhart’s position.

       1. The priority of the ground. Eckhart holds that the ground of the soul is deeper than
         any faculty, and that the soul is united with God in the ground. The framework holds
         that the identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and that the source is not
         any of its manifestations. Both hold that the source is deeper than its appearances,
         and that the appearances are not the source.

       2. Detachment as the recognition of limits. Eckhart holds that detachment is the soul’s
         letting go of all images of God, so that the soul may be open to God beyond all
         images. The framework holds that the recognition of the limits of its concepts is the
         condition of understanding its principles. Both hold that the recognition of limits
         is the condition of union, and that the soul that clings to images is closed to the
         source.

       3. The non-attachment of the source. Eckhart holds that the Godhead is beyond
         all images, all names, all manifestations. The framework holds that the First
         Determination is pure unity, and that it is not any of the manifestations of the lower
         realms. Both hold that the source is not exhausted by its appearances, and that the
         appearances do not capture the source.

       4. Living without why. Eckhart holds that the soul that lives without why is free from
         the means-end structure of ordinary life. The framework holds that expression is
         a structural tendency, not a teleological purpose, and that the identity expresses
         itself without aiming at an end. Both hold that the source is beyond the means-end
         structure, and that its activity is not a means to an end.



16.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Eckhart. The framework diverges from Eckhart in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Eckhart’s ground of the soul is the point of union with God; the
         Godhead is beyond God, and the soul is united with the Godhead in the ground.
         The framework has no God; its First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a
         being with whom the soul is united. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of union. Eckhart holds that the soul is united with God in the ground;
         the union is the goal of the soul’s life, and it is a real union, not a metaphor. The
         framework has no union; its returning light is a structural feature of the relation
16.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                147


         between identity and manifestation, not a mystical union. The framework’s return
         is structural, not mystical.

       3. The status of the birth. Eckhart holds that the Son is really born in the ground of
         the soul; the birth is eternal, and it is the life of the soul in God. The framework has
         no birth of God; its recursive manifestation is the structure by which a manifestation
         is the occasion for further manifestations of the same identity, and it is not a birth
         of God in the soul. The framework’s recursion is structural, not mystical.

       4. The status of the soul. Eckhart holds that the soul is united with God in the ground,
         and that the soul’s union with God is its own being. The framework holds that
         the identity is not a soul, and that its expression in the Material Manifestation is
         a manifestation, not a union. The framework is a metaphysics without a soul in
         Eckhart’s sense.


16.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Eckhart’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its expression is a structural tendency. But a structural invariance is not a ground; it
   is a pattern. A pattern does not give birth; it does not unite; it does not live. Eckhart’s
   ground of the soul is a living ground, a point of union with God, a birth of the Son. The
   framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not a ground. The framework’s ontology
   is an ontology of patterns, not of grounds; it has no place for the birth of God in the soul.
   Eckhart’s second objection. The framework says that expression is a structural
   tendency, not a purpose, and that the identity expresses itself without a why. But a
   tendency without a why is a tendency without a ground; it is a blind drift. Eckhart’s
  "living without why" is not a blind drift; it is the life of the soul in God, and its ground is
   the Godhead. The framework’s "without why" is a "without ground"; it is a life without a
   source. The framework’s ontology is a groundless tendency, not a life in God.



16.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a ground, and
   it agrees that a ground must be living, not merely structural. But the framework denies
   that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source—a this, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the life of the identity
   in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is the life of the thing.
   The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a reality); the
148                                                                 Chapter 16. Meister Eckhart


   framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a tendency without a
   ground is a blind drift, and it agrees that a "living without why" requires a ground. But
   the framework denies that its "without why" is without ground. The framework’s "without
   why" is grounded in the structure of identity: the identity expresses itself because it is
   its nature to express itself, not because it seeks an end. The ground is the identity itself,
   and the expression is the identity’s own act. The distinction is between a groundless drift
   (which the framework rejects) and a grounded tendency (which the framework affirms).
   The framework’s "without why" is grounded, not groundless.




16.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.




Eckhart’s cost. If Eckhart accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
ground of the soul is a union with God. He must accept that the ground is a structural condition,
not a point of union, and that the soul’s life in God is a metaphor, not a reality. The cost is the
loss of the mystical union: the soul is no longer united with God, and the birth of God in the
soul is no longer a birth.




The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Eckhart’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—
the dimension of mystical union, of the birth of God, of the Godhead beyond God—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a union with God, and the
framework leaves the second to a separate inquiry.




The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Eckhart’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Eckhart
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural ground that
Eckhart’s Godhead presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.
16.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      149


16.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Eckhart’s
   term “the ground of the soul.” If one substitutes “the ground of the soul” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Eckhart’s ground is the
   point of union with God, and it is not manifested, because it is the point where the soul
   is one with God. The framework’s identity is multiple (there are many identities); the
   ground of the soul is one, and it is the same in every soul. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not
   substitutable for Eckhart’s term “the birth of God in the soul.” If one substitutes “the
   birth of God in the soul” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, enacted by an identity in
   a realm; Eckhart’s birth is the eternal birth of the Son in the ground of the soul. The
   framework’s expression is non-mystical; Eckhart’s birth is mystical. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Eckhart is resemblance:
   both hold that the source is deeper than its appearances, and they differ on whether the
   source is a union with God or a structural enactment. Both hold that detachment is the
   recognition of limits, and they differ on whether detachment is a letting go of all images or
   a recognition of the limits of concepts. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Eckhart would be refuted by showing that
   Eckhart’s ground of the soul cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and union—by showing, that is, that Eckhart already distinguishes the
   structural condition from the mystical union, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of Eckhart’s own.



16.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Eckhart’s ground of the soul,
or is it a departure from Eckhart? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Eckhart’s ground is already a structural
condition, not a mystical union, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s "without why" be stated without the notion of a
ground? The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader
who holds that "without why" can be stated without a ground has a question the chapter leaves
open.
150                                                               Chapter 16. Meister Eckhart


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the German Sermons do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the ground of the soul, detachment, the birth of God, the Godhead, and
"living without why," and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that
the sermons support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a ground and an appearance—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the ground deeper than the appearance, or is the ground the appearance itself? Is
the ground a union with something beyond, or is it the structure of the thing? What does your
answer tell you about the relation between Eckhart’s ground of the soul and the framework’s
identity?

The next chapter turns to Nicholas of Cusa. It states the coincidence of opposites ( coincidentia
oppositorum), the learned ignorance ( docta ignorantia), the infinite line, and the conception of
God as the infinite circle whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere; it identifies
the internal disputes within the interpretation of Cusa; and it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of the infinite and the finite is the nearest
Renaissance analogue to Cusa’s. The present chapter has stated Eckhart’s answer to the problem
of the ground; the next chapter states Cusa’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 17

Nicholas of Cusa


Scope. This chapter closes Part III, the dialogues with the medieval West, and it closes it with
Nicholas of Cusa (Nicolaus Cusanus). It states the learned ignorance (docta ignorantia), the
coincidence of opposites (coincidentia oppositorum), the infinite line and the infinite circle, the
conception of God as the infinite circle whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere,
and the account of the finite as the explication of the infinite, with reference to De Docta
Ignorantia, De Coniecturis, and De Visione Dei; it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of Cusa; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of the infinite and the finite is the nearest Renaissance analogue to Cusa’s; it
presents the objections that Cusa would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s
reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what
would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where
the chapter speaks of “learned ignorance,” “the coincidence of opposites,” “the infinite,” “the
finite,” or “the explication,” these are Cusa’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and
by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


17.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is trying to measure a circle with a straight ruler. The ruler is straight;
the circle is curved. The ruler can measure the diameter, the chord, the tangent; but it cannot
measure the curve itself. The more sides the ruler’s polygon has, the closer it comes to the
circle; but the polygon is always a polygon, and the circle is always a circle. The straight can
approximate the curved, but it cannot become the curved.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not how to measure the circle, but what the
circle is. The circle is the figure whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere;
the infinite circle is the figure in which center and circumference coincide. The finite circle has a
center that is not the circumference; the infinite circle has no distinction between center and
circumference. The finite circle is a figure; the infinite circle is the coincidence of all figures.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the circle is, but what
God is. God is the infinite circle; God is the coincidence of all opposites; God is the infinite line
in which all finite lines coincide; God is the maximum in which the minimum coincides. The
finite mind cannot grasp the infinite God; the finite mind can only know its own ignorance, and
in its knowledge of its ignorance, it is united with God.
   The scene is Cusa’s image, in De Docta Ignorantia, of the structure of the relation between the
finite and the infinite. The finite is the explication of the infinite; the infinite is the complication
of the finite. The finite mind cannot comprehend the infinite; it can only approach it through
the coincidence of opposites, and through the learned ignorance that recognizes its own limits.

                                                  151
152                                                                   Chapter 17. Nicholas of Cusa


      The scene poses the question that Cusa was the first to pose in its full form. What is the
relation between the finite and the infinite? Is the infinite a larger finite, or is it the coincidence
of all finites? And how can the finite mind know the infinite, if the infinite is beyond all finite
concepts? The present chapter states Cusa’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


17.2       The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus,
Ockham, and Eckhart. Augustine posed the problem of time and the inner light; Dionysius posed
the problem of light and hierarchy; Anselm posed the problem of God’s existence; Aquinas posed
the problem of essence and existence; Scotus posed the problem of individuation; Ockham posed
the problem of universals; Eckhart posed the problem of the ground of the soul. Cusa is the last
great figure of the medieval West, and he is the transitional figure to the Renaissance: he turns
from the scholastic distinctions to the mathematical image of the infinite, and from the mystical
union to the learned ignorance. The present chapter states Cusa’s turn, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Cusa was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Cusa hold? The chapter states the learned ignorance, the
coincidence of opposites, the infinite line and circle, the conception of God as the infinite circle,
and the account of the finite as the explication of the infinite, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Cusa converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Cusa would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Cusa? The
chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


17.3       The Position

17.3.1      Learned Ignorance (Docta Ignorantia)

Cusa’s De Docta Ignorantia (1440) opens with the claim that the highest wisdom is the knowledge
of one’s own ignorance. The claim is not a confession of ignorance; it is a doctrine: the finite mind,
because it is finite, cannot comprehend the infinite; it can only know that it cannot comprehend
it. The knowledge of one’s inability to know is the learned ignorance (docta ignorantia).
      The learned ignorance has three moments. First, the recognition of the limits of the finite
mind: the mind cannot grasp the infinite by concepts, because the concepts are finite, and the
infinite exceeds them. Second, the recognition of the proportion between the finite and the
infinite: the finite is to the infinite as the polygon is to the circle; the polygon can approach the
17.3. The Position                                                                                 153


circle, but it can never become the circle. Third, the recognition of the coincidence of opposites:
the infinite is the coincidence of all the opposites that the finite mind cannot reconcile; the
infinite is beyond the distinctions that the finite mind makes.
   The learned ignorance is not a skepticism; it is a way of knowing. The mind that knows
its own ignorance is the mind that is open to the infinite; the mind that thinks it knows is the
mind that is closed. The learned ignorance is the highest form of knowledge, because it is the
knowledge that opens the mind to what exceeds it.

   From the Tradition

   “The highest wisdom is the knowledge of one’s own ignorance. The finite mind cannot
   comprehend the infinite; it can only know that it cannot comprehend it. And in this
   knowledge, it is united with the infinite.” (Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia I.1, trans. after
   Heron)



17.3.2    The Coincidence of Opposites (Coincidentia Oppositorum)

Cusa’s doctrine of the coincidence of opposites is stated throughout De Docta Ignorantia, but
most clearly in I.22 and II.1. The doctrine is a response to the question: how can the finite mind
speak of the infinite, if the infinite is beyond all the distinctions the finite mind makes?
   The answer is that the infinite is the coincidence of all opposites. In the finite order, the
opposites are distinct: the maximum is not the minimum, the straight is not the curved, the
one is not the many. In the infinite, the opposites coincide: the maximum is the minimum, the
straight is the curved, the one is the many. The infinite is not a larger finite; it is the coincidence
of all finites, and in its coincidence, the distinctions that the finite mind makes are transcended.
   The coincidence has three moments. First, the coincidence of the maximum and the minimum:
the infinite is the maximum, and it is also the minimum, because it is beyond all measure. Second,
the coincidence of the one and the many: the infinite is one, and it is also many, because it
contains all things in its simplicity. Third, the coincidence of being and non-being: the infinite is
being, and it is also non-being, because it is beyond both.
   The coincidence is not a contradiction; it is a transcendence. The finite mind cannot reconcile
the opposites, because it is finite; the infinite is the reconciliation of the opposites, because it is
infinite. The coincidence is the way the infinite is present to the finite mind: not as an object,
but as the limit of all objects.

   From the Tradition

   “The infinite is the coincidence of all opposites. In the infinite, the maximum is the
   minimum, the straight is the curved, the one is the many. For the infinite is beyond all
   measure, beyond all distinction, beyond all opposition.” (Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia I.22,
   trans. after Heron)
154                                                                  Chapter 17. Nicholas of Cusa


17.3.3       The Infinite Line and the Infinite Circle

Cusa’s mathematical images are stated in De Docta Ignorantia I.13–15 and in De Coniecturis.
The images are not proofs; they are ways of seeing what the concepts cannot say.
      The infinite line is the line in which all finite lines coincide: the straight, the curved, the
triangle, the circle. The infinite line is the maximum line, and in its maximum, the distinctions
that the finite mind makes are transcended. The infinite line is the coincidence of all figures.
      The infinite circle is the circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is
nowhere. The finite circle has a center that is not the circumference; the infinite circle has no
distinction between center and circumference. The infinite circle is the coincidence of center and
circumference, and in its coincidence, the finite mind sees the coincidence of the finite and the
infinite.
      The infinite triangle is the triangle whose three angles are one angle, and whose three sides
are one side. The finite triangle has three angles that are distinct; the infinite triangle has three
angles that coincide. The infinite triangle is the image of the Trinity: three persons, one God;
three angles, one angle.
      The images are not proofs; they are the mind’s way of approaching the infinite through the
finite. The finite mind can see the coincidence of opposites in the mathematical image, and
through the image, it can approach the coincidence of opposites in God.

   From the Tradition

   “The infinite circle is the circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is
   nowhere. In the infinite circle, center and circumference coincide; and in this coincidence,
   the mind sees the coincidence of the finite and the infinite.” (Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia
   I.21, trans. after Heron)



17.3.4       God as the Infinite Circle

Cusa’s conception of God is the infinite circle: God is the center that is everywhere and the
circumference that is nowhere. God is not a being among beings; God is the coincidence of
being and non-being, the coincidence of the maximum and the minimum, the coincidence of all
opposites.
      The conception has three consequences. First, God is not a larger finite; God is the infinite
in which all finites coincide. Second, God is not a being among beings; God is being itself, and in
being itself, all beings coincide. Third, God is not knowable by the finite mind; God is knowable
only through the learned ignorance, which recognizes that God exceeds all concepts.
      The conception is not a pantheism; it is a panentheism. God is not the world; God is in the
world, and the world is in God. The world is the explication of God; God is the complication of
the world. The two are distinct, but they are not separate; the world is the finite expression of
the infinite, and God is the infinite ground of the finite.
17.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             155


17.3.5     The Finite as the Explication of the Infinite

Cusa’s account of the relation between the finite and the infinite is stated in De Docta Igno-
rantia II.3 and in De Coniecturis. The account turns on the distinction between complication
(complicatio) and explication (explicatio).
   Complication is the way the infinite contains all things in its simplicity: the infinite is the
complication of all finites; it contains them without distinction, in its unity. Explication is the
way the finite unfolds the infinite: the finite is the explication of the infinite; it unfolds the
infinite in the multiplicity of finite things.
   The relation is not a creation; it is an unfolding. The infinite does not make the finite out of
nothing; it unfolds itself in the finite, and the finite is the unfolded infinite. The relation is not a
pantheism; the finite is not the infinite; it is the unfolded infinite, distinct from the infinite, but
not separate from it.
   The account is the key to Cusa’s metaphysics. It explains why the finite is real: it is the
explication of the infinite, and the infinite is real in its explication. It explains why the finite
is limited: it is the explication of the infinite, and the explication is always partial. And it
explains why the finite can know the infinite: the finite is the explication of the infinite, and in
its explication, it can read the infinite.

   From the Tradition

   “God is the complication of all things; the world is the explication of God. God contains
   all things in his simplicity; the world unfolds all things in its multiplicity. The two are
   distinct, but they are not separate.” (Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia II.3, trans. after Heron)



17.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Cusa is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the coincidence. The traditional reading takes the coincidence
of opposites to be a real feature of the infinite: in God, the opposites really coincide, and the
finite mind cannot grasp the coincidence because it is finite. A revisionary reading takes it to be
a regulative idea: the coincidence is a way of saying that the finite mind cannot comprehend the
infinite, not a description of the infinite itself. The two readings disagree on whether Cusa is a
mystic or a Kantian before Kant, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s First Determination is a real realm, not a regulative idea.


Second dispute: the status of the explication. The traditional reading takes the explication
to be a real relation: the world is really the explication of God, and God is really the complication
of the world. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor: the world is not literally
the explication of God; it is a way of speaking about the relation between the finite and the
infinite. The two readings disagree on whether Cusa is a panentheist or a metaphorist, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s expression is a real
relation, not a metaphor.
156                                                                     Chapter 17. Nicholas of Cusa


Third dispute: the status of the learned ignorance. The traditional reading takes the
learned ignorance to be a mystical doctrine: the mind that knows its own ignorance is united
with God in the learned ignorance. A revisionary reading takes it to be an epistemological
doctrine: the learned ignorance is the recognition of the limits of knowledge, not a mystical
union. The two readings disagree on whether Cusa is a mystic or an epistemologist, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s recognition of limits
is epistemological, not mystical.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Cusa is a mystic, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a mystical panentheism. If Cusa is an
epistemologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to De Docta Ignorantia, but it does
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


17.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Cusa. The framework shares four structural features with Cusa’s position.

        1. The recognition of limits. Cusa’s learned ignorance is the recognition of the limits
           of the finite mind: the mind cannot comprehend the infinite, and it can only know
           its own inability to comprehend. The framework’s principle of the impossibility
           of super-identity is the recognition of the limits of the finite subject: the subject
           cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. Both hold that the
           recognition of limits is the condition of knowledge, and that the mind that thinks it
           knows everything is closed to what exceeds it.

        2. The coincidence of opposites. Cusa’s coincidence of opposites is the way the infinite
           is present to the finite mind: not as an object, but as the limit of all objects. The
           framework’s category-relative predication is the way the framework’s principles are
           present to the finite mind: not as absolute truths, but as relative to a realm and
           a respect. Both hold that the finite mind cannot grasp the infinite, and that the
           infinite is present as the limit of what the finite mind can grasp.

        3. The explication of the infinite in the finite. Cusa holds that the world is the explication
           of God; the infinite unfolds itself in the finite, and the finite is the unfolded infinite.
           The framework holds that manifestation is the expression of identity; the invariant
           unfolds itself in the manifestation, and the manifestation is the expressed invariant.
           Both hold that the finite is the expression of the infinite, and that the finite is real
           in its expression.

        4. The non-separability of the finite and the infinite. Cusa holds that the finite and the
           infinite are distinct, but not separate; the world is in God, and God is in the world.
17.6. Points of Divergence                                                                       157


         The framework holds that identity and manifestation are distinct, but not separate;
         the identity is in the manifestation, and the manifestation is in the identity, as its
         expression. Both hold that the finite and the infinite are inseparable, and that their
         distinction is a distinction of aspects, not of things.




17.6      Points of Divergence


   Points of Divergence

   With Cusa. The framework diverges from Cusa in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Cusa’s metaphysics is a metaphysics of God; the learned ignorance,
         the coincidence of opposites, the infinite circle, and the explication all turn on God.
         The framework has no God; its First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not
         a being whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. The
         framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the infinite. Cusa’s infinite is the infinite God, the maximum in which
         the minimum coincides, the coincidence of all opposites. The framework’s infinite is
         the infinite of contexts and manifestations, not the infinite of God; it is a structural
         infinite, not a divine infinite. The framework’s infinity is the infinity of contexts and
         manifestations, not the infinity of God.

       3. The status of the explication. Cusa holds that the world is the explication of God;
         the infinite unfolds itself in the finite, and the finite is the unfolded infinite. The
         framework holds that the manifestation is the expression of identity; the invariant
         unfolds itself in the manifestation, and the manifestation is the expressed invariant.
         But the framework’s expression is structural, not divine; the framework’s identity is
         not God, and its manifestation is not the world. The framework’s expression is a
         structural relation, not a divine unfolding.

       4. The status of the learned ignorance. Cusa holds that the learned ignorance is a union
         with God: the mind that knows its own ignorance is united with God in the learned
         ignorance. The framework holds that the recognition of limits is a structural feature
         of knowledge: the mind that knows its own limits is a mind that knows what it
         can and cannot know. The framework’s learned ignorance is epistemological, not
         mystical; it is the recognition of the limits of reconstruction, not a union with God.
158                                                                  Chapter 17. Nicholas of Cusa


17.7    The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Cusa’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
  its manifestation is a structural expression. But a structural invariance is not an infinite;
  it is a finite pattern. A finite pattern does not contain all things in its simplicity; it is one
  pattern among many, and it cannot be the complication of the world. Cusa’s God is the
  infinite complication of all things; the framework’s identity is a finite pattern, and a finite
  pattern is not a complication of the world. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
  finite patterns, not of the infinite; it has no place for the coincidence of opposites.
  Cusa’s second objection. The framework says that the finite mind can reconstruct
  the invariant from its manifestations, and that the reconstruction is fallible and partial.
  But a reconstruction without learned ignorance is a reconstruction without a limit; it
  is a reconstruction that does not know its own limits. Cusa’s learned ignorance is the
  recognition of the limits of knowledge; the framework’s reconstruction is a knowledge
  without the recognition of its limits. The framework’s epistemology is a knowledge without
  learned ignorance, and a knowledge without learned ignorance is a knowledge without
  humility.



17.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a structural invariance is
  not an infinite, and it agrees that a finite pattern is not a complication of the world. But
  the framework denies that its identity is a finite pattern. The framework’s identity is the
  invariance enacted by one source, and the enactment is the structural condition under
  which a thing is one thing. The identity is not a pattern among patterns; it is the structure
  of the pattern, and the structure is not a finite thing among finite things. The distinction
  is between a pattern (a finite content) and a structure (the principle of the pattern); the
  framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a reconstruction without
  learned ignorance is a reconstruction without a limit, and it agrees that a knowledge
  without the recognition of its limits is a knowledge without humility. But the framework
  denies that its reconstruction is without learned ignorance. The framework’s principle of
  the impossibility of super-identity is precisely the learned ignorance of the framework: the
  recognition that the subject cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts,
  and that every reconstruction is a pseudo-identity, partial and fallible. The framework’s
  reconstruction is a reconstruction with learned ignorance; it is a knowledge that knows its
  own limits, and in its knowledge of its limits, it is a knowledge with humility.
17.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     159


17.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Cusa’s cost. If Cusa accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
coincidence of opposites is a real feature of God. He must accept that the coincidence is a
structural feature of the relation between the finite and the infinite, not a divine attribute. The
cost is the loss of the divine infinite: the infinite is no longer God, and the coincidence is no
longer a divine mystery.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Cusa’s objections, it must give up the claim
that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the dimension
of the divine infinite, of the coincidence of opposites, of the explication of God in the world—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the complication of the world,
and the framework leaves the second to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Cusa’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Cusa must
accept that the framework’s structure is not a finite pattern; it is a structural condition that
Cusa’s infinite presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity
of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the other.


17.10        The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Cusa’s
   term “God.” If one substitutes “God” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it
   is manifested in a realm; Cusa’s God is the infinite circle, the coincidence of opposites, the
   complication of the world. The framework’s identity is multiple; Cusa’s God is one. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term
   “manifestation” is not substitutable for Cusa’s term “the explication.” If one substitutes
   “the explication” for “manifestation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change:
   the framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm, and it is one
   expression of the identity; Cusa’s explication is the unfolding of the infinite in the finite,
   and it is the unfolding of the whole world. The framework’s manifestation is structural;
   Cusa’s explication is divine. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
160                                                               Chapter 17. Nicholas of Cusa


   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Cusa is resemblance:
   both recognize the limits of the finite mind, and they differ on whether the recognition
   is mystical or epistemological. Both hold that the finite is the expression of the infinite,
   and they differ on whether the expression is divine or structural. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Cusa
   would be refuted by showing that Cusa’s learned ignorance cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structural limits and divine mystery—by showing,
   that is, that Cusa already distinguishes the structural condition from the divine mystery,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Cusa’s own.




17.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s learned ignorance a development of Cusa’s docta ignorantia,
or is it a departure from Cusa? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Cusa’s learned ignorance is already epistemological,
not mystical, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s infinite be stated without the notion of a limit? The
chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that
the infinite can be stated without a limit has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of De Docta Ignorantia do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the learned ignorance, the coincidence of opposites, the infinite circle, and
the explication, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that De
Docta Ignorantia supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both finite and open to the infinite—a person, a tradition,
a work of art. Is the finite a limitation, or is it the condition of the infinite’s presence? Is the
infinite a larger finite, or the coincidence of all finites? What does your answer tell you about
the relation between Cusa’s infinite and the framework’s infinite?

Part III is now complete. The dialogues with the seven great figures of the medieval West—
Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus, Ockham, Eckhart, and Cusa—have been stated.
Part IV turns to the modern West. The first dialogue is with Descartes, on the cogito, doubt,
and the foundation of knowledge; the next with Spinoza, on substance, necessity, and freedom;
the next with Leibniz, on monads, harmony, and the best of all possible worlds; the next with
Locke and Hume, on empiricism, personal identity, and causation; the next with Kant, on the
Copernican revolution, the categories, and the limits of reason; the next with Hegel, on dialectic,
spirit, and history; the next with Kierkegaard, on existence, subjectivity, and faith; and the last
with Nietzsche, on the will to power, the eternal return, and nihilism. The medieval West has
transformed the ancient problem; the modern West will question the medieval synthesis.
