Chapter 18

Descartes


Scope. This chapter opens Part IV, the dialogues with the modern West, and it opens it with
René Descartes. It states Descartes’s method of doubt, the cogito ergo sum, the criterion of clear
and distinct ideas, the proofs for the existence of God, the mind-body dualism (res cogitans and
res extensa), and the wax argument, with reference to the Meditationes de Prima Philosophia,
the Discours de la Méthode, and the Principia Philosophiae; it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of Descartes; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of the cogito and the wax is the nearest modern analogue to
Descartes’s; it presents the objections that Descartes would raise against the framework; it
presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “doubt,” “the cogito,” “clear and distinct ideas,”
“substance,” or “the evil demon,” these are Descartes’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the
treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


18.1     A Scene
Consider a person who has been taught many things, and who now discovers that many of them
are false. She was taught that the earth is the centre of the universe, and now she learns that it
is not; she was taught that the stars are fixed in a sphere, and now she learns that they are suns
like our own; she was taught that the senses are reliable, and now she sees that they deceive
her—the stick in water looks bent, the tower in the distance looks round, the sun looks small. If
so much that she was taught is false, what can she trust? She resolves to doubt everything that
can be doubted, until she finds something that cannot be doubted.
   Now consider a harder case. She doubts the senses; she doubts the world; she doubts her
own body. She can imagine that she has no body, that there is no world, that an evil demon
is deceiving her about everything. But she cannot doubt that she is doubting. Even the evil
demon, if it is deceiving her, must be deceiving *someone*; even the doubt, if it is doubt, must
be *her* doubt. In the very act of doubting, she discovers something that cannot be doubted:
she exists. Cogito ergo sum: I think, therefore I am.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what she is, but how she
knows that she is. She knows that she is, because she thinks; and she knows that she thinks,
because she is immediately aware of her thinking. The knowledge of her existence is not a
deduction; it is an intuition; it is the direct, evident, clear and distinct perception of her own
existence in the act of thinking. The cogito is not an inference; it is a foundation.
   The scene is Descartes’s image, in the Meditationes, of the structure of knowledge. The doubt
clears away the uncertain; the cogito provides the certain; the clear and distinct perception is the

                                                163
164                                                                         Chapter 18. Descartes


criterion of the certain; and from the cogito, Descartes rebuilds the edifice of knowledge, through
the existence of God and the existence of the world.
      The scene poses the question that Descartes was the first to pose in its full form. What can
be known with certainty? Is knowledge founded on the senses, on reason, or on the immediate
awareness of the self? And what is the relation between the mind and the body, between the
thinking substance and the extended substance? The present chapter states Descartes’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.


18.2       The Question
The previous parts stated the positions of the ancient and medieval West. Parmenides and
Heraclitus posed the problem of change; Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Plotinus, and Proclus gave
systematic answers; Augustine, Dionysius, Anselm, Aquinas, Scotus, Ockham, Eckhart, and Cusa
transformed the ancient problem in the light of Christian revelation. Descartes is the founder
of modern philosophy, and he is the first to attempt a complete reconstruction of knowledge
on a new foundation: the cogito. The present chapter states Descartes’s foundation, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Descartes was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Descartes hold? The chapter states the method of doubt,
the cogito, the criterion of clear and distinct ideas, the proofs for the existence of God, the
mind-body dualism, and the wax argument, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Descartes converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Descartes would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Descartes?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


18.3       The Position

18.3.1      The Method of Doubt

Descartes’s method of doubt is stated in the Meditationes I and in the Discours de la Méthode
IV. The method is not a skepticism; it is a way of clearing away the uncertain in order to find
the certain. The doubt is methodological, not metaphysical; it is a means, not an end.
      The doubt has three stages.


First stage: the doubt of the senses. The senses sometimes deceive us; the stick in water
looks bent; the tower in the distance looks round. If the senses deceive us sometimes, they may
18.3. The Position                                                                                165


deceive us always; we cannot trust them without a criterion that distinguishes the true from the
false.


Second stage: the dream argument. We cannot distinguish waking from dreaming by any
certain sign; what seems real in a dream seems real while we dream it. If we cannot distinguish
waking from dreaming, we cannot be certain that the world we perceive is real.


Third stage: the evil demon. Suppose an evil demon, as powerful as it is cunning, employs
all its energies in deceiving us. It deceives us about the world, about our bodies, about the truths
of mathematics. Nothing is certain; everything can be doubted.
    The doubt reaches its limit in the cogito. Even the evil demon cannot deceive us about our
own existence; even the doubt, if it is doubt, must be *our* doubt. The doubt that doubts
everything discovers that it cannot doubt itself.

   From the Tradition

   “I have persuaded myself that there is nothing in the world: no heaven, no earth, no
   minds, no bodies. Is it not then true that I do not exist? But certainly I existed, if I
   persuaded myself of something. But there is a deceiver, supremely powerful and cunning,
   who employs all his energies in deceiving me. Then certainly I exist, if he deceives me;
   and let him deceive me as much as he can, he will never bring it about that I am nothing,
   so long as I think that I am something.” (Descartes, Meditatio II, AT VII 25, trans. after
   Cottingham)


18.3.2    The Cogito

The cogito ergo sum is stated in the Meditatio II and in the Discours IV. The formula is not a
syllogism; it is an intuition. The ergo is not the ergo of a deduction; it is the ergo of an immediate
evidence: in the very act of thinking, I am immediately aware that I exist.
    The cogito has three features.


First feature: immediacy. The cogito is not inferred from a premise; it is seen in the act.
The mind that thinks sees its own existence in the thinking, as the eye sees the light in the seeing.


Second feature: certainty. The cogito is certain; it cannot be doubted; even the evil demon
cannot make it doubtful. It is the first principle of the new philosophy, the Archimedean point
from which the world can be moved.


Third feature: subjectivity. The cogito is the thinking subject; it is the “I” that thinks.
The cogito is not a proposition about thinking in general; it is the self-awareness of the particular
thinker, in the particular act of thinking.
    The cogito is the foundation of modern philosophy. It turns philosophy from the object to
the subject; from the world to the thinker; from being to consciousness. The cogito is the first
principle of the modern age.
166                                                                          Chapter 18. Descartes


18.3.3      Clear and Distinct Ideas
Descartes’s criterion of truth is stated in the Meditatio III and in the Principia I.43. The
criterion is clear and distinct perception: whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly is true.

Clarity. A perception is clear when it is present and manifest to the attentive mind, as a
visible object is present and manifest to the eye. The clear perception is not obscured by other
perceptions; it stands out, as the sun stands out in a clear sky.

Distinctness. A perception is distinct when it is clear and when it is separated from all other
perceptions, as a distinct object is separated from its background. The distinct perception is not
confused with other perceptions; it is precisely what it is, and not another.
      The criterion is not a guarantee of truth; it is a criterion. The mind that perceives clearly
and distinctly perceives what is true, because God, who is not a deceiver, has made the mind
such that clear and distinct perception is true. The criterion is grounded in the veracity of God.

   From the Tradition

   “I now seem to be able to lay it down as a general rule that whatever I perceive very clearly
   and distinctly is true.” (Descartes, Meditatio III, AT VII 35, trans. after Cottingham)


18.3.4      The Proofs for the Existence of God
Descartes’s proofs for the existence of God are stated in the Meditatio III and in the Meditatio
V. There are two proofs, and they are distinct.

First proof: the causal proof. I have an idea of God, the idea of an infinite, perfect,
omnipotent being. The idea has more objective reality than any other idea; it represents more
perfection than any other idea. But the cause of an idea must have at least as much reality as
the idea has objective reality. Therefore the cause of my idea of God must be a being with at
least as much reality as the idea; and such a being is God. Therefore God exists.

Second proof: the ontological proof. I have the idea of God, the idea of a being than
which nothing greater can be conceived. Existence is a perfection; a being that exists is greater
than a being that does not exist. Therefore God, the being than which nothing greater can be
conceived, must exist; for if God did not exist, a greater being could be conceived, namely, a
God who exists. Therefore God exists.
      The two proofs have different structures. The first is a causal proof; it proceeds from the idea
to its cause. The second is an ontological proof; it proceeds from the concept to the existence.
The first is distinctively Cartesian; the second is derived from Anselm, and Descartes gives it a
distinctively Cartesian form.

18.3.5      Mind-Body Dualism
Descartes’s dualism is stated in the Meditatio VI and in the Principia I. The dualism is between
two substances: the thinking substance (res cogitans) and the extended substance (res extensa).
18.3. The Position                                                                               167


The thinking substance. The thinking substance is the mind; its essence is thought; it is not
extended, not divisible, not localized. The mind is a substance, in the Cartesian sense: it is a
thing that exists in itself, and does not need any other thing in order to exist.

The extended substance. The extended substance is the body; its essence is extension; it is
extended, divisible, localized. The body is a substance, in the Cartesian sense: it is a thing that
exists in itself, and does not need any other thing in order to exist.
   The two substances are really distinct: the mind can exist without the body, and the body
can exist without the mind. The union of the two is not a substantial union; it is a union of
interaction, in which the mind and the body act on each other. The interaction is the mystery of
Cartesianism; how two substances so different can act on each other is a question Descartes does
not fully answer.

   From the Tradition

   “I am a thinking thing, that is, a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills,
   refuses, imagines, and senses. And I am distinct from my body, and can exist without it.”
   (Descartes, Meditatio VI, AT VII 78, trans. after Cottingham)


18.3.6    The Wax Argument
Descartes’s wax argument is stated in the Meditatio II. The argument is a test of the criterion of
clear and distinct ideas.
   Take a piece of wax, fresh from the honeycomb. It has a certain smell, a certain colour, a
certain shape, a certain size. It is hard, cold, and makes a sound when struck. But bring it near
the fire: the smell evaporates, the colour changes, the shape melts, the size increases, it becomes
soft, hot, and makes no sound. What remains of the wax? None of the sensory qualities remain.
And yet we say that the wax remains; it is the same wax, in a different form.
   What is it that remains? It is not the sensory qualities; they have all changed. It is not the
imagination; the imagination cannot grasp the infinite variety of forms the wax can take. It is
the intellect; the intellect grasps the essence of the wax, which is extension, and the extension is
what remains through all the changes. The wax is known by the intellect, not by the senses; it is
grasped by a clear and distinct perception, not by a confused sensory perception.
   The wax argument is the key to Descartes’s epistemology. It shows that the senses are not
the foundation of knowledge; the intellect is. It shows that the essence of a thing is not a sensory
quality; it is an intelligible structure. And it shows that the mind is better known than the body;
for the mind knows the wax by its own act, and in that act, it knows itself.

   From the Tradition

   “Let us consider the wax: it has just been taken from the honeycomb; it has not yet lost the
   sweetness of the honey; it retains some of the scent of the flowers; its colour, shape, and
   size are manifest; it is hard, cold, and easily handled; and it makes a sound when struck.
   But while I am speaking, it is brought near the fire: the remaining taste is removed, the
   scent evaporates, the colour changes, the shape is lost, the size increases, it becomes liquid,
168                                                                         Chapter 18. Descartes


   hot, and makes no sound. Does the same wax remain after these changes?” (Descartes,
   Meditatio II, AT VII 30, trans. after Cottingham)




18.4        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Descartes is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the cogito. The traditional reading takes the cogito to be a
foundation: it is the first principle, certain and indubitable, from which the rest of knowledge is
derived. A revisionary reading takes it to be a performance: it is not a proposition, but an act;
the cogito is the mind’s act of seeing its own existence, and it cannot be stated as a proposition
without losing its performative character. The two readings disagree on whether Descartes is a
foundationalist or a performativist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s foundation is structural, not subjective.



Second dispute: the status of the criterion. The traditional reading takes clear and distinct
perception to be the criterion of truth, grounded in the veracity of God. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a psychological criterion, a mark of the mind’s assent, without any metaphysical
grounding. The two readings disagree on whether Descartes is a rationalist or a naturalist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s criterion is
structural, not psychological.



Third dispute: the status of dualism. The traditional reading takes dualism to be a
metaphysical doctrine: mind and body are two really distinct substances. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a methodological distinction: the mind and the body are two ways of describing
the same thing, without any real distinction. The two readings disagree on whether Descartes is
a dualist or a monist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework has no dualism of substances.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Descartes is a foundationalist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a subjectivist foundationalism. If
Descartes is a performativist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Meditationes, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.
18.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      169


18.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Descartes. The framework shares four structural features with Descartes’s position.

       1. The distinction between the thing and its appearances. Descartes’s wax argument
          distinguishes the wax from its sensory qualities; the wax is known by the intellect,
          not by the senses. The framework distinguishes identity from manifestation; the
          identity is known by reconstruction, not by direct perception. Both hold that what
          a thing is is not the same as how it appears, and that the essence is grasped by the
          intellect, not by the senses.

       2. The priority of the intelligible over the sensible. Descartes holds that the essence of
          the wax is extension, an intelligible structure, and that the senses give only confused
          perceptions. The framework holds that the identity is the invariance under a class
          of allowable transformations, an intelligible structure, and that the manifestations
          give only partial perceptions. Both hold that the intelligible is prior to the sensible,
          and that the sensory is not the foundation of knowledge.

       3. The criterion of clarity and distinctness. Descartes’s criterion of truth is clear and
          distinct perception; the mind that perceives clearly and distinctly perceives what is
          true. The framework’s criterion of a valid context is cross-checkability, minimality,
          and consistency; the context that satisfies the criteria is a valid context. Both hold
          that there is a criterion of truth, and that the criterion is structural, not arbitrary.

       4. The doubt as a method. Descartes’s doubt is a method: it clears away the uncertain
          in order to find the certain. The framework’s principle of the impossibility of super-
          identity is a method: it clears away the claim to complete knowledge in order to
          find what a finite subject can achieve. Both hold that the recognition of limits is
          the condition of knowledge, and that the mind that thinks it knows everything is a
          mind that does not know its own limits.



18.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Descartes. The framework diverges from Descartes in four respects.

       1. The status of the subject. Descartes’s cogito is the foundation of knowledge; the
          thinking subject is the first certainty, and the world is known through the subject. The
          framework has no cogito; its foundation is the structure of identity and manifestation,
          not the self-awareness of the subject. The framework is a metaphysics of structure,
          not a metaphysics of subjectivity.
170                                                                          Chapter 18. Descartes


       2. The status of dualism. Descartes’s dualism is a dualism of substances: the mind and
         the body are two really distinct substances, with different essences. The framework
         has no dualism; its realms are levels of one structure, and its identity is the invariance
         enacted by one source, not a substance. The framework is a structural monism, not
         a substance dualism.

       3. The status of God. Descartes’s proofs for the existence of God are the ground of the
         criterion of truth: the clear and distinct perception is true because God is not a
         deceiver. The framework has no God; its criterion is structural, not theological. The
         framework is a metaphysics without God.

       4. The status of innate ideas. Descartes holds that some ideas are innate: the idea of
         God, the idea of the self, the idea of extension. The framework has no innate ideas;
         its concepts are defined within the framework, and they are not innate in the mind.
         The framework is a metaphysics of structure, not of innate ideas.



18.7        The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Descartes’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  not a subject; it is a pattern. A pattern does not think; it does not doubt; it does not
  know itself. Descartes’s cogito is the thinking subject, the self that knows itself in the
  act of thinking; the framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not a self. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of subjects; it has no place for the
  cogito.
  Descartes’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction
  from manifestations, and that it is fallible and partial. But a reconstruction without a
  clear and distinct perception is a reconstruction without a criterion; it is a knowledge
  without a foundation. Descartes’s criterion is clear and distinct perception, grounded in
  the veracity of God; the framework’s reconstruction has no such criterion, and a knowledge
  without a criterion is not knowledge. The framework’s epistemology is a skepticism in
  disguise.



18.8        The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a subject,
  and it agrees that a self is not a pattern. But the framework denies that its identity is a
  pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in
18.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     171


   the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
   framework’s identity is not a pattern among patterns; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (an
   act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework does not claim
   that its identity is a subject; it claims that its identity is a structure, and it leaves the
   subject to a separate inquiry.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a reconstruction without a
   criterion is a reconstruction without a foundation, and it agrees that knowledge needs a
   criterion. But the framework denies that its reconstruction is without a criterion. The
   framework’s criterion is structural: a reconstruction is valid when it is cross-checkable,
   minimal, and consistent; a context is valid when it satisfies the criteria. The framework’s
   criterion is not clear and distinct perception, grounded in God; it is cross-checkability,
   minimality, and consistency, grounded in the structure of the realms. The distinction is
   between a theological criterion (Descartes’s) and a structural criterion (the framework’s);
   the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is a criterion, not a skepticism.



18.9       The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Descartes’s cost. If Descartes accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the cogito is the foundation of knowledge. He must accept that the foundation is the structure
of identity and manifestation, not the self-awareness of the subject. The cost is the loss of the
subject as foundation: the cogito is no longer the first principle, and the world is no longer known
through the subject.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Descartes’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of subjectivity, of the cogito, of the self—that its ontology does not capture. The
cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not a subject, and the framework leaves the subject to a separate
inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Descartes’s cogito is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Descartes
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
cogito presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.
172                                                                         Chapter 18. Descartes


18.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Descartes’s term “the cogito.” If one substitutes “the cogito” for “identity” in the frame-
   work’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Descartes’s cogito is the thinking
   subject, and it is not manifested, because it is the subject that knows itself in the act of
   thinking. The framework’s identity is multiple (there are many identities); the cogito is
   one, and it is the same in every act of thinking. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable
   for Descartes’s term “the clear and distinct idea.” If one substitutes “the clear and distinct
   idea” for “manifestation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm, and it is not a
   perception; Descartes’s clear and distinct idea is a perception of the mind, and it is not an
   appearance in a realm. The framework’s manifestation is ontological; Descartes’s idea is
   epistemological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Descartes is resemblance:
   both distinguish the thing from its appearances, and they differ on whether the essence is
   a sensory quality or an intelligible structure. Both hold that the intelligible is prior to the
   sensible, and they differ on whether the foundation is the subject or the structure. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Descartes would be refuted by showing that the cogito cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structure and subject—by showing, that is, that
   Descartes already distinguishes the structural condition from the subjective awareness,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Descartes’s own.



18.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Descartes’s cogito, or is it a
departure from Descartes? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Descartes’s cogito is already a structural condition, not
a subject, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s criterion be stated without the notion of a subject?
The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that
the criterion requires a subject has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Meditationes do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the doubt, the cogito, the criterion, the proofs for the existence of God, the
18.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                173


dualism, and the wax argument, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the Meditationes supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a subject and an object—a person, a work of art, a
text. Is the subject prior to the object, or is the object prior to the subject? Is the subject the
foundation of knowledge, or is the structure the foundation? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Descartes’s cogito and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Spinoza. It states the account of substance, the Deus sive Natura,
the attributes and modes, the conatus, and the intellectual love of God; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Spinoza; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of the one and the many is the nearest modern analogue to
Spinoza’s. The present chapter has stated Descartes’s answer to the problem of the foundation;
the next chapter states Spinoza’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 19

Spinoza


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Baruch (Benedict) Spinoza. It states the account
of substance, the Deus sive Natura, the attributes and modes, the parallelism of thought and
extension, the conatus, the determinism, the intellectual love of God (amor Dei intellectualis),
and the account of freedom as the understanding of necessity, with reference to the Ethica ordine
geometrico demonstrata and the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus; it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of Spinoza; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of the one and the many is the nearest modern analogue to
Spinoza’s; it presents the objections that Spinoza would raise against the framework; it presents
the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and
it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “substance,” “attribute,” “mode,” “conatus,” “Deus sive
Natura,” or “the intellectual love of God,” these are Spinoza’s terms, and their sense is fixed by
the Ethica and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


19.1      A Scene
Consider a single wave on the ocean. The wave rises, crests, falls, and disappears. It seems to be
a thing in its own right: it has a shape, a motion, a history; it comes into being and passes away.
But if you look more carefully, you see that the wave is not a thing separate from the ocean; it is
the ocean itself, in a particular configuration. The wave is a mode of the ocean; the ocean is the
substance of which the wave is a mode. The wave rises and falls, but the ocean remains; the
wave is transient, but the ocean is eternal.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose you ask what the ocean is. The ocean is not just water;
it is also the movement of the water, the salt in the water, the temperature of the water, the
light on the water. The ocean can be described in many ways: as a body of water, as a system
of currents, as a chemical solution, as a physical system. Each description is true, and each is a
description of the same ocean under a different attribute. The ocean has many attributes, and
each attribute is a way of describing the same substance.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose you ask not what the ocean is, or how it is
described, but what makes it be. The ocean is not caused by anything outside itself; it is the
totality of things, and there is nothing outside it. The ocean is the cause of itself (causa sui); its
existence is not contingent, but necessary; it could not not be. What we call "the ocean" is what
Spinoza calls "God or Nature" (Deus sive Natura): the one substance, infinite, eternal, necessary,
of which all particular things are modes.
   The scene is Spinoza’s image, in the Ethica, of the structure of reality. There is one substance,
God or Nature; it has infinitely many attributes, of which we know two, thought and extension;

                                                 174
19.2. The Question                                                                               175


and it has infinitely many modes, which are the particular things that exist in the attributes.
The wave is a mode of extension; the idea of the wave is a mode of thought; both are modes of
the one substance, and both are governed by the same necessity.
   The scene poses the question that Spinoza was the first to pose in its full form. Is there one
substance, or many? Are mind and body two substances, or two attributes of one substance? Is
the world necessary, or contingent? And what is freedom, if everything is determined by the
necessity of the divine nature? The present chapter states Spinoza’s answer, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.


19.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Descartes’s position: the method of doubt, the cogito, clear and
distinct ideas, the proofs for the existence of God, mind-body dualism, and the wax argument.
Descartes is the founder of modern philosophy, and Spinoza is his greatest successor and his
greatest critic. Spinoza accepts Descartes’s geometrical method and his rationalism, but he
rejects his dualism, his voluntarism, and his account of freedom. The present chapter states
Spinoza’s critique, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Spinoza was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Spinoza hold? The chapter states the account of substance,
the attributes and modes, the parallelism, the conatus, the determinism, the intellectual love of
God, and the account of freedom, with reference to the Ethica.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Spinoza converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Spinoza would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Spinoza?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


19.3      The Position

19.3.1    Substance: Deus sive Natura

Spinoza’s account of substance is stated in the Ethica I, especially in the definitions and the first
fifteen propositions. The account has three features.


First feature: one substance. There is only one substance, and it is God or Nature (Deus
sive Natura). A substance is what exists in itself and is conceived through itself; it does not need
any other thing in order to exist or to be conceived. If there were two substances, they would
have to be distinguished by their attributes; but attributes are what the intellect perceives as
176                                                                         Chapter 19. Spinoza


constituting the essence of substance, and two substances with the same attribute would not be
two. Therefore there is only one substance.


Second feature: the substance is causa sui. The one substance is the cause of itself (causa
sui); its essence involves its existence; it cannot not be. The existence of the substance is not
contingent, but necessary; it follows from the essence of the substance, as the properties of a
triangle follow from the essence of the triangle.


Third feature: the substance is infinite. The one substance is infinite; it has infinitely
many attributes, each of which expresses its essence in a different way. We know two of these
attributes, thought and extension; the others we do not know, but they are real, and they express
the same infinite essence.
      The substance is not a personal God; it is not a creator who chooses to create the world;
it is not a judge who rewards and punishes. It is the necessary order of things, the totality of
what is, considered under the aspect of its unity. "God or Nature" is the formula that unites the
theological and the naturalistic aspects of Spinoza’s thought: God is not beyond Nature; God is
Nature, considered as the one substance of which all things are modes.

   From the Tradition

   “By substance I understand what is in itself and is conceived through itself, that is, that
   whose concept does not require the concept of another thing, from which it must be formed.
   By God I understand a being absolutely infinite, that is, a substance consisting of infinite
   attributes, each of which expresses eternal and infinite essence.” (Spinoza, Ethica I, def. 3
   and def. 6, trans. after Curley)



19.3.2      Attributes and Modes

Spinoza’s account of attributes and modes is stated in the Ethica I, def. 4 and def. 5, and in the
propositions that follow. The account has two parts.


Attributes. An attribute is what the intellect perceives as constituting the essence of a
substance. The one substance has infinitely many attributes; we know two of them, thought
(cogitatio) and extension (extensio). Thought is the attribute under which the substance is
conceived as thinking; extension is the attribute under which the substance is conceived as
extended. The two attributes are distinct, but they are attributes of the same substance; they
are not two substances, but two ways of conceiving one substance.


Modes. A mode is a modification of a substance; it is what is in another thing, and is conceived
through that other thing. The modes of extension are bodies; the modes of thought are ideas.
Every body is a mode of extension; every idea is a mode of thought; and every body has a
corresponding idea, and every idea has a corresponding body, because both are modes of the
same substance.
19.3. The Position                                                                               177


   The relation between attributes and modes is the relation between the substance and its
modifications. The substance is the whole; the modes are the parts; but the parts are not
separate from the whole, because they are modes of the whole. The wave is a mode of the ocean;
the ocean is the substance of which the wave is a mode.


19.3.3    Parallelism

Spinoza’s parallelism is stated in the Ethica II, prop. 7: "The order and connection of ideas is
the same as the order and connection of things" (ordo et connexio idearum idem est ac ordo
et connexio rerum). The formula states the relation between thought and extension: the two
attributes are parallel, and the order in one is the same as the order in the other.
   The parallelism has three consequences.


First consequence: no interaction. The mind and the body do not interact; the mind does
not cause the body, and the body does not cause the mind. They are parallel expressions of the
same substance; what happens in the mind is the idea of what happens in the body, and what
happens in the body is the object of what happens in the mind. The apparent interaction is an
illusion of the imagination; in reality, the two are two aspects of one process.


Second consequence: no dualism. The mind and the body are not two substances; they
are two attributes of one substance. Descartes’s dualism is a mistake; it treats the two attributes
as two substances, and it posits an interaction between them that is unintelligible. Spinoza’s
monism resolves the problem: the mind and the body are two ways of describing the same thing,
and their apparent interaction is the parallelism of the two descriptions.


Third consequence: the identity of the order. The order of ideas and the order of things
are the same order; the same necessity governs both. What is true of the one is true of the other,
under the appropriate attribute. The order of nature is the order of thought; the necessity of
nature is the necessity of thought.

   From the Tradition

   “The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things.”
   (Spinoza, Ethica II, prop. 7, trans. after Curley)



19.3.4    The Conatus

Spinoza’s account of the conatus is stated in the Ethica III, prop. 6: "Each thing, as far as it can
by its own power, strives to persevere in its being" (unaquaeque res, quantum in se est, in suo
esse perseverare conatur). The conatus is the striving of each thing to persevere in its being; it is
the essence of the thing, its power of acting, its tendency to preserve itself.
   The conatus has three features.
178                                                                            Chapter 19. Spinoza


First feature: it is the essence of the thing. The conatus is not a property added to the
essence; it is the essence itself, considered as a striving. The thing strives to persevere in its
being because it is its nature to strive; the striving is what the thing is.


Second feature: it is the power of the thing. The conatus is the power of the thing to
act and to be acted upon; it is the degree of reality of the thing, its participation in the infinite
power of the substance. The more power a thing has, the more it can persevere in its being; the
less power it has, the less it can.


Third feature: it is the ground of the affects. The conatus is the ground of the affects:
joy is the increase of the conatus, sadness is its decrease, desire is the conatus itself, considered
as conscious. The affects are not irrational movements; they are the modifications of the conatus,
and they are intelligible through the conatus.


19.3.5       Determinism

Spinoza’s determinism is stated in the Ethica I, prop. 29 and prop. 32. The doctrine is a
consequence of the necessity of the substance: if the substance is necessary, and if all things are
modes of the substance, then all things are necessary; there is no contingency, no free will, no
arbitrary choice.
      The determinism has three features.


First feature: no contingency. Nothing is contingent; every thing follows from the necessity
of the divine nature, as the properties of a triangle follow from its essence. What we call
"contingent" is what we do not yet understand; it is the ignorance of the causes, not the absence
of causes.


Second feature: no free will. The will is not a faculty of choice; it is a mode of thought,
like any other; it is determined by the causes that determine it, as the body is determined by the
causes that determine it. The freedom of the will is an illusion of the imagination; the will is not
free, but determined.


Third feature: no purpose. Nature has no purpose; it does not act for an end; it does not
aim at a good. The purposes we attribute to nature are projections of our own desires; we think
that nature acts for an end because we act for an end, but nature is beyond the means-end
structure.


19.3.6       The Intellectual Love of God

Spinoza’s account of the intellectual love of God (amor Dei intellectualis) is stated in the Ethica
V, prop. 32–37. The account is the culmination of the Ethica: it is the highest form of knowledge,
the highest form of freedom, the highest form of blessedness.
      The intellectual love of God has three features.
19.3. The Position                                                                                179


First feature: it is knowledge. The intellectual love of God is not an emotion; it is a form
of knowledge, the third kind of knowledge, the intuitive knowledge of things under the aspect of
eternity (sub specie aeternitatis). The mind that knows things under the aspect of eternity knows
them as they are in God; it knows them as necessary, as eternal, as modes of the one substance.

Second feature: it is love. The intellectual love of God is not a cold knowledge; it is a love,
the joy that accompanies the knowledge of God. The mind that knows God loves God; it loves
God because it knows God; it knows God because it loves God. The knowledge and the love are
one act.

Third feature: it is eternal. The intellectual love of God is eternal; it is not a state that
comes and goes; it is the eternal act of the mind that knows God. The mind that knows God
under the aspect of eternity participates in the eternity of God; its love is the love of God for
himself, the love by which God loves himself.

   From the Tradition

   “The intellectual love of God, which arises from the third kind of knowledge, is eternal.
   For God is the cause of this love, insofar as he is eternal, and it is the very nature of
   God to be eternal. Therefore the intellectual love of God is eternal.” (Spinoza, Ethica V,
   prop. 33–34, trans. after Curley)


19.3.7     Freedom as the Understanding of Necessity
Spinoza’s account of freedom is stated in the Ethica IV, prop. 67 –73, and in the Ethica V,
prop. 42. The account is a rejection of the ordinary notion of freedom: freedom is not the absence
of causes; it is the understanding of necessity.
   The account has three features.

First feature: freedom is not the absence of causes. The free man is not the man who
has no causes; there is no such man. The free man is the man who acts from his own nature,
not from external causes; he acts from the necessity of his own nature, not from the necessity of
external things. The free man is the man who understands the necessity of his actions.

Second feature: freedom is the understanding of necessity. The free man is the man
who knows that his actions are necessary, and who acts with the knowledge of that necessity.
The knowledge of necessity is not a burden; it is a liberation. The man who knows that his
actions are necessary is no longer a slave of the passions; he is a master of himself, because he
understands himself.

Third feature: freedom is the life of reason. The free man is the man who lives according
to reason; he is the man who knows the causes of his actions, and who acts from the knowledge
of those causes. The life of reason is the life of freedom; the life of passion is the life of slavery.
Freedom is not the absence of causes; it is the knowledge of causes.
180                                                                           Chapter 19. Spinoza


   From the Tradition

   “Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself; nor do we enjoy it because we
   restrain our lusts; on the contrary, because we enjoy it, we are able to restrain our lusts.”
   (Spinoza, Ethica V, prop. 42, trans. after Curley)




19.4        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Spinoza is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of substance. The traditional reading takes the one substance to
be God, in a pantheistic or panentheistic sense: God is the totality of things, and the things are
modes of God. A revisionary reading takes the one substance to be Nature, in a naturalistic
sense: the substance is the totality of things, and the word "God" is a name for the totality. The
two readings disagree on whether Spinoza is a pantheist or an atheist, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework is a structural realism, neither
pantheistic nor atheistic in Spinoza’s sense.



Second dispute: the status of the attributes. The traditional reading takes the attributes
to be real features of the substance: thought and extension are real aspects of the one substance.
A revisionary reading takes them to be ways of conceiving the substance: thought and extension
are ways the mind conceives the substance, not real aspects of the substance. The two readings
disagree on whether Spinoza is a realist or a conceptualist about the attributes, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are real
levels, not ways of conceiving.



Third dispute: the status of the intellectual love of God. The traditional reading takes
the intellectual love of God to be a mystical union with God: the mind is united with God in
the third kind of knowledge. A revisionary reading takes it to be a form of self-knowledge: the
mind knows itself in God, and the joy that accompanies this knowledge is the intellectual love.
The two readings disagree on whether Spinoza is a mystic or a rationalist, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no mystical union.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Spinoza is a pantheist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a pantheistic monism. If Spinoza is an
atheist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct.
The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Ethica, but it does not rest its case on
this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
19.5. Points of Convergence                                                                     181


19.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Spinoza. The framework shares four structural features with Spinoza’s position.

       1. The priority of the one over the many. Spinoza’s one substance is the reality of
         which the modes are the appearances; the modes are real, but they are modes of the
          one substance, not separate things. The framework’s identity is the invariance of
         which the manifestations are the appearances; the manifestations are real, but they
          are expressions of the identity, not separate things. Both hold that the one is prior
          to the many, and that the many is real in the one.

       2. The rejection of the means-end structure. Spinoza’s nature has no purpose; it does
          not act for an end; it is the necessary order of things. The framework’s expression
          has no purpose; it is a structural tendency, not a teleological movement. Both hold
          that reality is beyond the means-end structure, and that the ends we attribute to
          nature are projections of our own desires.

       3. The distinction between the appearance and the reality. Spinoza distinguishes the
          imagination from the intellect; the imagination sees the world as contingent and
          purposive; the intellect sees the world as necessary and lawful. The framework
          distinguishes the manifestation from the identity; the manifestation is the appearance
          of the identity in a realm; the identity is the invariance that the manifestation
          exhibits. Both hold that the appearance is not the reality, and that the intellect (or
          the reconstruction) is the way to the reality.

       4. The union of freedom and necessity. Spinoza holds that freedom is not the absence
          of causes; it is the understanding of necessity. The framework holds that expression
          is not a free choice; it is a structural tendency, and the identity expresses itself
          necessarily. Both hold that freedom and necessity are not opposites, and that the
          free life is the life that understands its own necessity.



19.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Spinoza. The framework diverges from Spinoza in four respects.

       1. The status of substance. Spinoza’s one substance is God or Nature; it is infinite, nec-
          essary, eternal, and it is the totality of things. The framework’s First Determination
          is not a totality; it is a realm of pure unity, one of the seven realms; and it is not
          the substance of which the other realms are modes. The framework’s ontology is a
          hierarchy of realms, not a monism of substance.
182                                                                           Chapter 19. Spinoza


       2. The status of the attributes. Spinoza’s attributes are infinite; we know two, thought
         and extension. The framework’s realms are seven; they are not attributes of one
         substance, but distinct levels of one architecture. The framework’s plurality of realms
         is not the plurality of attributes; it is the plurality of levels, each with its own mode
         of existence.

       3. The status of the modes. Spinoza’s modes are modifications of the substance; they are
         what the substance is in a particular configuration. The framework’s manifestations
         are expressions of the identity; they are what the identity is in a particular realm.
         The framework’s manifestation is not a modification of a single substance; it is the
         appearance of an identity in a realm, and there are many identities, each with its
         own manifestations.

       4. The status of the intellectual love of God. Spinoza’s intellectual love of God is the
         highest form of knowledge and freedom; it is the mind’s union with God under the
         aspect of eternity. The framework has no intellectual love of God; its highest form
         of knowledge is the structural reconstruction of identity from its manifestations, and
         its freedom is not the understanding of necessity in Spinoza’s sense. The framework
         is a metaphysics without the intellectual love of God.




19.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Spinoza’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are real in their own realms. But a structural invariance is not a
  substance; it is a pattern. A pattern does not exist in itself; it is conceived through the
  things that exhibit it. Spinoza’s substance exists in itself and is conceived through itself;
  it is the one reality of which all things are modes. The framework’s identity is a pattern,
  and a pattern is not a substance. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns,
  not of substance; it has no place for the one substance.
  Spinoza’s second objection. The framework says that there are many identities, each
  with its own manifestations. But if there are many identities, there are many substances;
  and if there are many substances, there is no one substance. The framework’s plurality of
  identities is a plurality of substances in disguise; it is a return to the Cartesian dualism,
  with many substances instead of two. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of plurality,
  not of unity; it has no place for the one substance of which all things are modes.
19.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                   183


19.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a substance,
   and it agrees that a substance exists in itself and is conceived through itself. But the
   framework denies that its identity is a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act*
   of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern among patterns; it
   is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that
   condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an
   abstraction) and an enactment (an act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the
   first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that many identities would be
   many substances if the identities were substances in Spinoza’s sense. But the framework
   denies that its identities are substances in Spinoza’s sense. The framework’s identities are
   not substances that exist in themselves and are conceived through themselves; they are
   invariances enacted by one source, and they are manifested in a realm. The framework’s
   identities are not substances; they are *this*-structures, and their plurality is not a
   plurality of substances. The distinction is between a substance (which exists in itself) and
   a *this*-structure (which is enacted in a realm); the framework’s identity is the second,
   not the first.



19.9        The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Spinoza’s cost. If Spinoza accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that there
is only one substance. He must accept that there are many identities, and that their plurality is
not a plurality of modes of one substance, but a plurality of *this*-structures enacted in realms.
The cost is the loss of the one substance: the world is no longer one substance with many modes,
but many identities with many manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Spinoza’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the one substance, of the necessity of the divine nature, of the intellectual love
of God—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the
structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a mode of
one substance, and the framework leaves the second to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Spinoza’s one substance
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s *this*-structures do not
184                                                                          Chapter 19. Spinoza


capture. Spinoza must accept that the framework’s *this*-structures are not substances; they
are structural conditions that Spinoza’s one substance presupposes as its condition. The cost
of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are
complements, and each is incomplete without the other.



19.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Spinoza’s
   term “substance.” If one substitutes “substance” for “identity” in the framework’s state-
   ments, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Spinoza’s substance is what exists in itself
   and is conceived through itself, and it is not enacted, because it is the one reality. The
   framework’s identity is multiple; Spinoza’s substance is one. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not
   substitutable for Spinoza’s term “mode.” If one substitutes “mode” for “manifestation”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation
   is the appearance of the identity in a realm, and it is one expression of the identity;
   Spinoza’s mode is a modification of the one substance, and it is not an expression, but a
   modification. The framework’s manifestation is expression; Spinoza’s mode is modification.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Spinoza is resemblance:
   both hold that the one is prior to the many, and they differ on whether the one is a substance
   or a *this*-structure. Both hold that reality is beyond the means-end structure, and they
   differ on whether the beyond is the necessity of the divine nature or the structurality
   of expression. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity.
   The framework’s reading of Spinoza would be refuted by showing that Spinoza’s one
   substance cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between substance
   and *this*-structure—by showing, that is, that Spinoza already distinguishes the structural
   condition from the one substance, and that the framework’s distinction is a development
   of Spinoza’s own.



19.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Spinoza’s substance, or is it a
departure from Spinoza? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Spinoza’s substance is already a structural condition,
not a substance, has a question the chapter leaves open.
19.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                  185


Second question. Can the framework’s plurality of identities be stated without the notion of
substance? The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader
who holds that plurality requires substance has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Ethica do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the substance, the attributes and modes, the parallelism, the conatus, the
determinism, the intellectual love of God, and the freedom, and it has stated what would refute
its reading. A reader who holds that the Ethica supports a different reading has a question the
chapter leaves open.
