A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a whole and a part—a person, a society, a work of art.
Is the whole prior to the parts, or are the parts prior to the whole? Is the whole a substance, or
a structure, or a pattern? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Spinoza’s
one substance and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Leibniz. It states the account of monads, the pre-established harmony,
the principle of sufficient reason, the best of all possible worlds, and the distinction between truths
of reason and truths of fact; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Leibniz;
and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of
the many within the one is the nearest modern analogue to Leibniz’s. The present chapter has
stated Spinoza’s answer to the problem of the one and the many; the next chapter states Leibniz’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 20

Leibniz


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. It states the account of
monads, the pre-established harmony, the principle of sufficient reason, the principle of identity
of indiscernibles, the best of all possible worlds, the distinction between truths of reason and
truths of fact, and the universal characteristic, with reference to the Monadologie, the Discours de
métaphysique, the Essais de Théodicée, and the Principes de la nature et de la grâce; it identifies
the internal disputes within the interpretation of Leibniz; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the many within the one is the nearest modern
analogue to Leibniz’s; it presents the objections that Leibniz would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind
of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “monad,” “pre-established harmony,”
“sufficient reason,” “compossibility,” or “the best of all possible worlds,” these are Leibniz’s terms,
and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.



20.1      A Scene

Consider two clocks that keep exactly the same time. They have no connection to each other; no
wire runs from one to the other; no signal passes between them. And yet, when one strikes twelve,
the other strikes twelve; when one shows three, the other shows three. How is this possible?
There are three answers. First, the clocks influence each other; but this is excluded by hypothesis.
Second, a clockmaker adjusts them continually; this is the way of occasionalism. Third, the
clockmaker has made them so perfectly that they agree from the beginning, without any further
adjustment; this is the way of pre-established harmony.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose you ask not how the two clocks agree, but what each
clock is. Each clock is a machine: a system of wheels, springs, and gears; it is a compound, made
of parts. But suppose you ask what the simplest thing is, the thing that has no parts. The
simplest thing is not a machine; it is a simple substance, a monad. The monad has no parts, no
extension, no shape; it is a point of force, a centre of perception, a windowless unity that mirrors
the whole universe from its own perspective.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose you ask not what the monad is, or how
the monads agree, but why there is anything at all. Everything that is has a sufficient reason;
nothing is without a reason why it is rather than not. The sufficient reason for the world cannot
be found in any particular thing; it must be found in a being whose reason is in itself, a necessary
being, God. And God, being good, has chosen the best of all possible worlds; the world we
inhabit is the best that could be, because God’s goodness and wisdom required it.

                                                 186
20.2. The Question                                                                               187


   The scene is Leibniz’s image, in the Monadologie and the Théodicée, of the structure of reality.
The monads are the simple substances; the pre-established harmony is their agreement without
interaction; the principle of sufficient reason is the ground of their being; and the best of all
possible worlds is the choice of God. The monads are many, and each is one; the harmony is one,
and it is the harmony of the many; and God is the one who grounds both the many and the
harmony.
   The scene poses the question that Leibniz was the first to pose in its full form. What is the
simple substance? How do simple substances relate to one another, if they do not interact? And
why is there a world at all, rather than nothing? The present chapter states Leibniz’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.



20.2       The Question

The previous chapters stated the positions of Descartes and Spinoza. Descartes posed the problem
of the foundation and the dualism; Spinoza posed the problem of the one substance and its
modes. Leibniz is the third great figure of the modern West, and he is the great synthesizer:
he synthesizes the new science with the old metaphysics, the mechanical philosophy with the
doctrine of substantial forms, the plurality of substances with the unity of the world. The present
chapter states Leibniz’s synthesis, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Leibniz was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Leibniz hold? The chapter states the account of monads,
the pre-established harmony, the principle of sufficient reason, the identity of indiscernibles, the
best of all possible worlds, the truths of reason and fact, and the universal characteristic, with
reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Leibniz converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Leibniz would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Leibniz?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.



20.3       The Position

20.3.1     The Monads

Leibniz’s account of monads is stated in the Monadologie (1714) and in the Principes de la nature
et de la grâce (1714). The account has three features.
188                                                                          Chapter 20. Leibniz


First feature: the monad is simple. A monad is a simple substance; it has no parts; it is
indivisible. The things we see are compounds; they are made of parts, and the parts are made
of parts, and so on. But the regress cannot be infinite; there must be simple substances, the
ultimate constituents of things. These are the monads.


Second feature: the monad is windowless. A monad has no windows; nothing enters it
from outside; nothing leaves it to outside. The monad is a self-contained unity, a centre of force,
whose states unfold from its own internal principle. The monad does not interact with other
monads; its apparent interaction is the pre-established harmony.


Third feature: the monad is a mirror of the universe. Each monad perceives the whole
universe from its own perspective; it expresses the whole in its own way. The monad is a living
mirror (miroir vivant) of the universe; it contains the whole in its perceptions, though it does
so confusedly. The monad’s perceptions are its expressions of the whole; its appetitions are its
tendencies to pass from one perception to another.
      The monad is not a physical point; it is a metaphysical point, a point of force, a centre of
perception and appetition. The physical point is divisible; the metaphysical point is not. The
physical point is in space; the metaphysical point is not. The monad is a simple substance, and
its simplicity is the ground of its individuality.

   From the Tradition

   “The monad, of which we shall speak here, is nothing but a simple substance which
   enters into compounds; simple, that is to say, without parts. And there must be simple
   substances, since there are compounds; for a compound is nothing but a collection or
   aggregate of simple things. Now where there are no parts, there can be neither extension
   nor figure, nor divisibility. These monads are the true atoms of nature, and, in a word,
   the elements of things.” (Leibniz, Monadologie §1–3, trans. after Latta)



20.3.2      The Pre-Established Harmony

Leibniz’s account of the pre-established harmony is stated in the Monadologie §78–81 and in the
Discours de métaphysique §14. The doctrine is a response to the question: how do monads relate
to one another, if they do not interact?
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: no interaction. The monads do not interact; they have no windows; nothing
passes between them. The apparent interaction of body and mind, of one body and another, is
not a real interaction; it is an appearance, produced by the harmony that God has established
among the monads.


Second feature: the harmony. The harmony is pre-established: God, in creating the monads,
has chosen them such that their internal unfoldings agree with one another. The harmony is like
20.3. The Position                                                                              189


the harmony of two clocks that keep the same time without being connected; the clockmaker has
made them so that they agree.


Third feature: the agreement. The agreement is real; it is not an illusion. When I will
to raise my arm, and my arm rises, the two events are in harmony; the will is a monadic state
of the mind, the rising is a monadic state of the body, and God has made the two agree. The
agreement is not a causal interaction; it is a pre-established correspondence.
   The pre-established harmony is the key to Leibniz’s metaphysics. It explains how the monads
can be many and yet form a single world; it explains how the mind and the body can agree
without interacting; and it explains how the world can be a cosmos, an ordered whole, without
any real causal connections among its parts.

   From the Tradition

   “The soul follows its own laws, and the body follows its own, and they meet in virtue of
   the pre-established harmony among all substances, since they are all representations of
   one and the same universe.” (Leibniz, Monadologie §78, trans. after Latta)



20.3.3    The Principle of Sufficient Reason

Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason is stated in the Monadologie §31–32 and in the Théodicée
§44. The principle has three features.


First feature: nothing is without a reason. Nothing happens without a reason why it
is so and not otherwise. The principle applies to all things: to events, to existences, to truths.
Every event has a cause; every existence has a reason; every truth has a proof.


Second feature: the reason must be sufficient. The reason must be sufficient to account
for the thing; a partial reason is not sufficient. The principle demands the whole reason, the
reason that leaves nothing unexplained. A reason that leaves something unexplained is not a
sufficient reason.


Third feature: the reason may be in the thing or outside it. For contingent things,
the reason is outside the thing; the reason for the world is God, whose reason is in himself. For
necessary things, the reason is in the thing; the reason for a mathematical truth is the essence
of the thing, which contains the truth. The principle thus distinguishes the necessary from the
contingent: the necessary has its reason in itself; the contingent has its reason in another.
   The principle of sufficient reason is the foundation of Leibniz’s theism. From the principle,
Leibniz argues that the world must have a sufficient reason; that the sufficient reason cannot
be any particular thing; and that the sufficient reason must be a necessary being, God. The
principle is also the foundation of Leibniz’s optimism: since God is good and wise, and since
God has a sufficient reason for what he creates, the world he creates must be the best possible.
190                                                                            Chapter 20. Leibniz


20.3.4    The Identity of Indiscernibles
Leibniz’s principle of the identity of indiscernibles is stated in the Discours de métaphysique §9
and in the correspondence with Clarke. The principle has three features.

First feature: no two things are exactly alike. There are no two indistinguishable things
in nature. If two things were exactly alike in all their properties, they would not be two things;
they would be one thing under two names. The principle is not a contingent fact; it is a necessary
truth, grounded in the nature of things.

Second feature: the principle grounds individuality. What makes a thing individual is
not its matter, nor its position, nor its relations; it is the whole of its properties, the complete
concept that God has of it. Every monad is individuated by its complete concept; no two monads
have the same complete concept.

Third feature: the principle excludes indiscernible duplicates. If two things had all
the same properties, they would be one thing; the principle excludes the possibility of exact
duplicates. The principle is the basis of Leibniz’s account of identity: the identity of a thing is
its complete concept, and the complete concept is unique to the thing.

   From the Tradition

   “There are no two individual things in nature which are exactly alike. For if there were,
   God and nature would act without reason, and there would be no sufficient reason why
   one should be in one place rather than the other.” (Leibniz, Discours de métaphysique §9,
   trans. after Lucas-Donaldson)


20.3.5    The Best of All Possible Worlds
Leibniz’s account of the best of all possible worlds is stated in the Théodicée (1710) and in the
Monadologie §53–55. The account has three features.

First feature: God chooses among possible worlds. Before creating, God surveys the
infinite possibilities of worlds; each possible world is a set of compossible things, things that can
exist together. God chooses the world that is the best: the world with the greatest variety, the
greatest order, the greatest perfection.

Second feature: the actual world is the best. The actual world is the best of all possible
worlds; it is the world that God, in his wisdom and goodness, has chosen. The world is not
perfect, in the sense of having no evil; it is the best possible, in the sense that no better world is
compossible.

Third feature: evil is compatible with the best world. Evil exists, but it is not a defect
of the world; it is a condition of the world’s perfection. The world’s perfection requires variety,
contrast, and hierarchy; evil is the shadow that makes the light visible. The world is the best
20.3. The Position                                                                              191


possible, not because it has no evil, but because the evil it has is the condition of the greater
good.
   The doctrine is the foundation of Leibniz’s theodicy: the justification of God’s goodness in
the face of evil. The doctrine has been criticized from Voltaire onward; but it is a serious attempt
to reconcile the goodness of God with the reality of evil.

   From the Tradition

   “God, in creating the world, has chosen the best of all possible worlds; and since the best
   is not the one with the least evil, but the one with the greatest good, the world we inhabit
   is the best that God could have created.” (Leibniz, Théodicée §8, trans. after Huggard)


20.3.6    Truths of Reason and Truths of Fact

Leibniz’s distinction between truths of reason and truths of fact is stated in the Monadologie
§33–37. The distinction has three features.


First feature: truths of reason are necessary. Truths of reason are necessary; their
negation is impossible; they are grounded in the principle of non-contradiction. Mathematical
truths, logical truths, and metaphysical truths are truths of reason; they are true in all possible
worlds.


Second feature: truths of fact are contingent. Truths of fact are contingent; their negation
is possible; they are grounded in the principle of sufficient reason. Empirical truths, historical
truths, and truths about particular things are truths of fact; they are true in this world, but not
in all possible worlds.


Third feature: the two are distinct, but related. The two kinds of truth are distinct, but
they are related: God knows all truths, both of reason and of fact; the human mind knows the
truths of reason with certainty, and the truths of fact with probability. The distinction is the key
to Leibniz’s epistemology: the truths of reason are the foundation of science; the truths of fact
are the foundation of history.


20.3.7    The Universal Characteristic

Leibniz’s project of the universal characteristic (characteristica universalis) is stated in many
places, notably in the Discours de métaphysique and in the letters. The project has three features.


First feature: a universal language. The universal characteristic is a universal language, in
which all concepts can be expressed and all truths can be demonstrated. The language is not a
natural language; it is an artificial language, constructed on logical principles.


Second feature: a calculus of reasoning. The universal characteristic is a calculus, a
calculus ratiocinator, in which reasoning is reduced to calculation. When two philosophers
192                                                                           Chapter 20. Leibniz


disagree, they can sit down and calculate; the calculation will resolve the dispute, as arithmetic
resolves a dispute about numbers.


Third feature: the unity of knowledge. The universal characteristic is the foundation
of the unity of knowledge; it is the instrument by which all the sciences can be unified. The
characteristic is the dream of the mathesis universalis, the universal mathematics, the science of
all sciences.
      The project is a dream, but it is a productive dream. It is the source of modern symbolic
logic; it is the source of the project of artificial intelligence; it is the source of the ideal of a
unified science.


20.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Leibniz is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of monads. The traditional reading takes monads to be real
substances, simple unities that exist in themselves. A revisionary reading takes them to be
limit-concepts, ways of describing the world as a system of simple unities, without any real simple
substances. The two readings disagree on whether Leibniz is a realist or a conceptualist about
monads, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
identities are real invariances, not limit-concepts.


Second dispute: the status of the pre-established harmony. The traditional reading
takes the pre-established harmony to be a real relation, established by God, among the monads.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor, a way of describing the systematic agreement of
things, without any divine establishment. The two readings disagree on whether Leibniz is a
theist or a naturalist about harmony, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s expression is structural, not harmonious in Leibniz’s sense.


Third dispute: the status of the best of all possible worlds. The traditional reading
takes the best of all possible worlds to be a real fact: God has chosen the best world, and the
world we inhabit is the best. A revisionary reading takes it to be a regulative idea: the best
world is a way of speaking about the world’s perfection, not a fact about God’s choice. The
two readings disagree on whether Leibniz is an optimist or a Kantian before Kant, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no doctrine of
the best world.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Leibniz is a realist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a monadological realism. If Leibniz is
a conceptualist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Monadologie, but it does
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.
20.5. Points of Convergence                                                                    193


20.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Leibniz. The framework shares four structural features with Leibniz’s position.

       1. The plurality of simple substances. Leibniz holds that there are many monads, each
         a simple substance. The framework holds that there are many identities, each the
         invariance enacted by one source. Both hold that reality is constituted by a plurality
         of simple unities, not by one substance (as Spinoza held) or by two substances (as
         Descartes held).

       2. The expression of the whole from a perspective. Leibniz holds that each monad
         perceives the whole universe from its own perspective; it expresses the whole in its
         own way. The framework holds that each identity is manifested in many realms, and
         that each manifestation expresses the identity in the mode of the receiving realm.
         Both hold that the many are perspectives on the one, and that each perspective is
         real in its own way.

       3. The identity of indiscernibles. Leibniz holds that no two things are exactly alike;
         if they were, they would be one. The framework holds that no two identities are
         exactly alike; if they were, they would be one. Both hold that identity is individuated
         by a complete determination, and that exact duplication is impossible.

       4. The principle of sufficient reason. Leibniz holds that nothing is without a reason.
         The framework holds that every principle is stated with its status and its dependency;
         nothing is asserted without a reason. Both hold that reason is the ground of things,
         and that a thing without a reason is unintelligible.



20.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Leibniz. The framework diverges from Leibniz in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Leibniz’s monadology is a theistic metaphysics; the monads are
         created by God, the harmony is established by God, and the best world is chosen by
         God. The framework has no God; its identities are not created, and its expression is
         not established by any divine will. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the pre-established harmony. Leibniz holds that the monads agree
         because God has pre-established their harmony; the agreement is a divine arrange-
         ment, not a structural feature. The framework holds that the manifestations of an
         identity agree because they are manifestations of the same identity; the agreement
         is structural, not divine. The framework’s expression is a structural correspondence,
194                                                                         Chapter 20. Leibniz


         not a pre-established harmony.

       3. The status of the best of all possible worlds. Leibniz holds that the actual world is
         the best of all possible worlds, because God has chosen it. The framework has no
         doctrine of the best world; it holds that expression is a structural tendency, and
         that the world is what it is, not a choice among possibilities. The framework is a
         metaphysics without optimism or pessimism.

       4. The status of the universal characteristic. Leibniz holds that there is a universal
         characteristic, a calculus of reasoning, in which all truths can be demonstrated.
         The framework has no universal characteristic; its formalization is sparse, and its
         arguments are philosophical, not calculative. The framework’s method is structural,
         not calculative.


20.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Leibniz’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are real in their own realms. But a structural invariance is a
  pattern, and a pattern is not a monad. The monad is a simple substance, a centre of
  force, a windowless unity that mirrors the whole universe. The framework’s identity is a
  pattern, and a pattern is not a simple substance. The framework’s ontology is an ontology
  of patterns, not of monads; it has no place for the simple substances that are the true
  atoms of nature.
  Leibniz’s second objection. The framework says that expression is a structural tendency,
  and that the manifestations of an identity agree because they are manifestations of the
  same identity. But an agreement without a sufficient reason is a coincidence; and a
  coincidence is not an agreement. Leibniz’s pre-established harmony is the sufficient reason
  of the agreement; it is God who has established the harmony. The framework’s structural
  agreement is a coincidence in disguise; it has no sufficient reason. The framework’s ontology
  is an ontology of coincidences, not of harmonies.



20.8      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a monad, and
  it agrees that a monad is a simple substance. But the framework denies that its identity
  is a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*,
  in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
  framework’s identity is not a pattern among patterns; it is the structural condition under
  which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
20.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                   195


   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (an
   act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework does not claim
   that its identity is a monad; it claims that its identity is a structure, and it leaves the
   simple substance to a separate inquiry.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that an agreement without a
   sufficient reason is a coincidence, and it agrees that a coincidence is not an agreement.
   But the framework denies that its structural agreement is a coincidence. The framework’s
   structural agreement has a sufficient reason: the identity that is manifested in both
   manifestations. The identity is the reason why the manifestations agree; the agreement
   is not a coincidence, but a consequence of the identity. The distinction is between a
   divine pre-established harmony (Leibniz’s) and a structural consequence of identity (the
   framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is a sufficient
   reason.



20.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Leibniz’s cost. If Leibniz accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
monads are simple substances. He must accept that the identities are structural conditions, not
substances, and that their agreement is structural, not pre-established by God. The cost is the
loss of the monadology: the monads are no longer simple substances, and the harmony is no
longer a divine arrangement.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Leibniz’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of simple substances, of windowless unities, of the pre-established harmony—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a monad, and the framework
leaves the monad to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Leibniz’s monads are not
a mistake; they are a dimension of the real that the framework’s *this*-structures do not capture.
Leibniz must accept that the framework’s *this*-structures are not patterns; they are structural
conditions that the monads presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss
of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is
incomplete without the other.
196                                                                           Chapter 20. Leibniz


20.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Leibniz’s
   term “monad.” If one substitutes “monad” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; the Leibnizian monad is a simple substance, and it is
   windowless, because it does not interact with other monads. The framework’s identity is
   manifested in a realm; the Leibnizian monad is not manifested, because it is the reality
   itself, not an appearance. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Leibniz’s
   term “perception.” If one substitutes “perception” for “manifestation” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the
   identity in a realm, and it is not a perception; the Leibnizian perception is a monadic state,
   and it is not an appearance in a realm. The framework’s manifestation is ontological; the
   Leibnizian perception is monadic. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Leibniz is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is constituted by a plurality of simple unities, and they differ on
   whether the unities are monads or *this*-structures. Both hold that the many agree,
   and they differ on whether the agreement is a pre-established harmony or a structural
   consequence of identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is
   identity. The framework’s reading of Leibniz would be refuted by showing that Leibniz’s
   monadology cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure
   and monad—by showing, that is, that Leibniz already distinguishes the structural condition
   from the simple substance, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of
   Leibniz’s own.



20.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Leibniz’s monad, or is it a
departure from Leibniz? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Leibniz’s monad is already a structural condition, not a
simple substance, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of harmony?
The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that
expression requires harmony has a question the chapter leaves open.
20.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               197


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Monadologie do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the monads, the pre-established harmony, the sufficient reason, the identity of
indiscernibles, the best of all possible worlds, and the universal characteristic, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Monadologie supports a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a simple unity and a mirror of the whole—a person, a
culture, a text. Is the unity prior to the whole, or is the whole prior to the unity? Is the unity
a monad, or a perspective, or a structure? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Leibniz’s monad and the framework’s identity?

knowledge and personal identity is the nearest modern analogue to theirs. The present chapter

Locke’s and Hume’s answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
Chapter 21

Locke and Hume


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with John Locke and David Hume, the two great figures
of British empiricism. It states Locke’s empiricism, the tabula rasa, the distinction between
primary and secondary qualities, the account of personal identity through memory, and the
account of substance as the unknown support of qualities; it states Hume’s empiricism, the
account of causation as constant conjunction, the problem of induction, the bundle theory of the
self, the critique of substance, and the is/ought gap; it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of Locke and Hume; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of empirical knowledge and personal identity is the nearest modern
analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that Locke and Hume would raise against the
framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the
kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “impression,” “idea,” “association,”
“bundle,” or “constant conjunction,” these are Locke’s and Hume’s terms, and their sense is fixed
by the Essay Concerning Human Understanding and the Treatise of Human Nature, and by the
interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


21.1     A Scene
Consider a newborn child. She has eyes, ears, hands, a brain; she has the organs of perception,
but she has no ideas. She does not know what red is; she does not know what sweet is; she does
not know what a table is. Then she opens her eyes; she sees the light; she hears a voice; she
touches a hand. From these perceptions, she begins to form ideas: the idea of red, the idea of
sweet, the idea of a table, the idea of a person. Where do these ideas come from? Locke’s answer:
from experience. The mind is a tabula rasa, a blank slate, on which experience writes.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not where her ideas come from, but what a
thing is. She sees a red apple; she touches it; she tastes it; she smells it. She has the ideas of
red, round, sweet, fragrant. But what is the apple itself? Is it the collection of these ideas, or
is it something that supports them, something behind them? Locke’s answer: the apple is a
substance, an unknown support of the qualities we perceive. The substance is not the qualities; it
is what the qualities are in. But we have no idea of the substance itself; we only infer it, because
we cannot conceive how qualities could exist without a support.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not where her ideas come from,
or what a thing is, but what she herself is. She has a continuous stream of perceptions; she
remembers her past; she anticipates her future. But is there a self behind the perceptions, a
substance that persists through them? Locke’s answer: the self is the continuity of consciousness,
the memory that connects the present perception to the past one. Hume’s answer, more radical:

                                                198
21.2. The Question                                                                                199


there is no self behind the perceptions; the self is nothing but the bundle of perceptions, the
collection of impressions and ideas that succeed one another with remarkable rapidity.
   The scene is the empiricist image, in Locke’s Essay and Hume’s Treatise, of the structure of
knowledge and the self. The mind is a blank slate; the ideas come from experience; the self is
the continuity of consciousness (Locke) or the bundle of perceptions (Hume); and the substance
is the unknown support of qualities (Locke) or an illusion of the imagination (Hume). The
empiricist turn is a turn from the innate to the acquired, from the rational to the sensory, from
the substance to the appearance.
   The scene poses the question that Locke and Hume were the first to pose in its full form.
Where do our ideas come from? Is the mind a blank slate, or does it have innate ideas? What is
a substance, and do we have any idea of it? And what is the self, if it is not a substance? The
present chapter states Locke’s and Hume’s answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


21.2      The Question

The previous chapters stated the positions of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz. Descartes posed
the problem of the foundation and the dualism; Spinoza posed the problem of the one substance
and its modes; Leibniz posed the problem of the many monads and their harmony. Locke and
Hume are the great critics of the rationalist tradition: they reject the innate ideas, the substantial
forms, and the pre-established harmony; they turn from reason to experience, from substance to
appearance, from the metaphysical to the empirical. The present chapter states their critique,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Locke and Hume were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Locke and Hume hold? The chapter states Locke’s
empiricism, the tabula rasa, the primary/secondary qualities, the memory criterion of personal
identity, and the account of substance; and Hume’s empiricism, the account of causation, the
problem of induction, the bundle theory of the self, and the is/ought gap.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two empiricists converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Locke and Hume would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Locke
and Hume? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


21.3      Locke’s Position
200                                                                 Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


21.3.1      The Tabula Rasa

Locke’s empiricism is stated in the Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), especially in
Book I and Book II. The doctrine is a rejection of innate ideas: there are no ideas that the mind
has by nature, before experience; the mind is a tabula rasa, a blank slate, on which experience
writes.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: no innate ideas. There are no ideas that are present in the mind from
birth; the alleged innate ideas—the idea of God, the idea of substance, the principle of non-
contradiction—are not innate. The child does not have them; the savage does not have them; if
they were innate, everyone would have them, and they do not.


Second feature: all ideas come from experience. All ideas come from experience, and
experience is of two kinds: sensation and reflection. Sensation is the perception of external things;
reflection is the perception of the operations of our own minds. From sensation and reflection,
the mind receives simple ideas; from simple ideas, it compounds complex ideas.


Third feature: the mind is active in compounding. The mind is not entirely passive; it
is active in compounding, comparing, and abstracting. From the simple ideas of red and round,
it compounds the complex idea of a red ball; from the ideas of particular triangles, it abstracts
the general idea of a triangle. But the activity of the mind is always on materials given by
experience; it does not create new simple ideas.

   From the Tradition

   “Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without
   any ideas: How comes it to be furnished? To this I answer, in one word, from experience.
   In that all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself.” (Locke,
   Essay II.1.2, ed. Nidditch)


21.3.2      Primary and Secondary Qualities

Locke’s distinction between primary and secondary qualities is stated in the Essay II.8. The
distinction has three features.


First feature: primary qualities. Primary qualities are qualities that are really in the things
themselves, whether or not we perceive them: solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, number.
These qualities are inseparable from the body; they are the qualities that the body has in itself.


Second feature: secondary qualities. Secondary qualities are qualities that are not in the
things themselves, but are powers in the things to produce ideas in us: colour, sound, taste,
smell. These qualities are not in the things; they are in the relation between the things and our
senses; they are the effects of the primary qualities on our organs.
21.3. Locke’s Position                                                                           201


Third feature: the distinction is real. The distinction is not a distinction of ideas; it is
a distinction in the things themselves. The primary qualities are in the things; the secondary
qualities are in the perceiver. The red of the apple is not in the apple; it is in the eye that sees
it; the extension of the apple is in the apple, whether or not any eye sees it.
   The distinction is the foundation of Locke’s realism about the external world. The world has
primary qualities, which are real and independent of the perceiver; the secondary qualities are
the effects of the primary qualities on the perceiver; and the primary qualities are the ground of
the similarity between the ideas of different perceivers.


21.3.3    Substance

Locke’s account of substance is stated in the Essay II.23. The account has three features.


First feature: substance is the support of qualities. A substance is the unknown support
of the qualities we perceive. We perceive the qualities of a thing—its colour, its shape, its weight;
we do not perceive the substance that supports them. The substance is what the qualities are in;
it is the substratum, the underlying subject.


Second feature: we have no idea of substance. We have no clear idea of substance; we
have only a confused idea of it, as the unknown support of the qualities. The word “substance”
does not stand for an idea; it stands for a supposition, a posit, which we make because we cannot
conceive how qualities could exist without a support.


Third feature: the two kinds of substance. There are two kinds of substance: the thinking
substance (the mind) and the extended substance (the body). We know the two kinds by their
qualities; we do not know the substances themselves. The substance is the unknown ground of
the known qualities.

   From the Tradition

   “The idea then we have, to which we give the general name substance, being nothing but
   the supposed, but unknown, support of those qualities we find existing, which we imagine
   cannot subsist without something to support them, we call that support substantia.”
   (Locke, Essay II.23.2, ed. Nidditch)



21.3.4    Personal Identity

Locke’s account of personal identity is stated in the Essay II.27. The account has three features.


First feature: personal identity is continuity of consciousness. Personal identity is not
the identity of substance, whether material or immaterial; it is the identity of consciousness. A
person is the same person as long as her consciousness extends backward to her past actions; she
is the same person as the one who did those actions, because she remembers them as hers.
202                                                               Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


Second feature: memory is the criterion. Memory is the criterion of personal identity;
the person is the same as the one who remembers the past action. If she remembers the action,
she is the same person; if she does not, she is not. The memory is not just a psychological fact;
it is the constitutive relation of the person to her past.

Third feature: the person is a forensic concept. The person is a forensic concept, a
concept of accountability; the person is the one who can be held responsible for her actions,
because she remembers them as hers. The person is not the substance; the person is the
consciousness, and the consciousness is what the law and morality address.
      The account has been criticized, notably by Butler and Reid, for its circularity: memory
presupposes personal identity, because to remember is to remember one’s own past; and the
account cannot handle the transitivity problem (the brave officer case). Locke’s account is a
pioneering attempt to ground personal identity in consciousness rather than in substance, and it
is the ancestor of the psychological continuity accounts of Parfit and others.


21.4       Hume’s Position

21.4.1      Empiricism and the Copy Principle
Hume’s empiricism is stated in the Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40) and in the Enquiry
Concerning Human Understanding (1748). The doctrine has three features.

First feature: impressions and ideas. All the perceptions of the mind are of two kinds:
impressions and ideas. Impressions are the perceptions that are most vivid and forceful; they
are the perceptions we have when we see, hear, feel, love, hate. Ideas are the faint copies of
impressions; they are the perceptions we have when we think, remember, imagine. The distinction
is a distinction of vivacity, not of content.

Second feature: the copy principle. Every simple idea is a copy of a simple impression.
This is Hume’s “copy principle,” the first principle of his science of human nature. If an idea
cannot be traced to an impression, it is not a genuine idea; it is a word without meaning, a
fiction of the mind.

Third feature: the empirical criterion of meaning. From the copy principle follows an
empirical criterion of meaning: when we suspect that a philosophical term has no meaning, we
ask from what impression it is derived; if no impression can be found, the term is meaningless.
This criterion is the instrument by which Hume criticizes the metaphysical notions of substance,
causation, and the self.

   From the Tradition

   “All the perceptions of the human mind resolve themselves into two distinct kinds, which I
   shall call impressions and ideas. The difference betwixt these consists in the degrees of
   force and liveliness with which they strike upon the mind.” (Hume, Treatise I.1.1.1, ed.
21.4. Hume’s Position                                                                            203


   Norton-Norton)



21.4.2    Causation as Constant Conjunction

Hume’s account of causation is stated in the Treatise I.3 and in the Enquiry IV–V. The account
has three features.


First feature: the idea of causation. The idea of causation is the idea of a necessary
connection between two events: the cause produces the effect, and the effect follows necessarily
from the cause. But from what impression is this idea derived? Not from the events themselves;
we see one event follow another, but we do not see a necessary connection between them. Not
from reason; reason can discover relations of ideas, but not matters of fact. The idea of necessary
connection must come from somewhere else.


Second feature: constant conjunction. The idea of necessary connection comes from
custom or habit. We observe that one event constantly follows another (fire is constantly followed
by smoke; bread is constantly followed by nourishment); we come to expect the second event
when we see the first; and from this expectation, we form the idea of a necessary connection.
The necessity is not in the things; it is in our minds.


Third feature: the problem of induction. The problem of induction follows: how can we
justify the inference from the observed to the unobserved, from the past to the future? The
inference is not deductive; the conclusion does not follow necessarily from the premises. And the
inference is not inductive, if by induction we mean a justified inference; the justification would
be circular, because it would presuppose the principle of induction. The inference is a matter of
custom, not of reason; it is a psychological fact, not a logical justification.
   Hume’s account of causation is one of the most important contributions to philosophy. It has
been criticized, notably by Kant, who argued that causation is a category of the understanding,
not a custom of the mind; but it has never been refuted, and it is the starting point of all modern
discussions of causation.

   From the Tradition

   “After a repetition of similar instances, the mind is carried by habit, upon the appearance
   of one event, to expect its usual attendant, and to believe that it will exist. This connexion,
   therefore, which we feel in the mind, this customary transition of the imagination from
   one object to its usual attendant, is the sentiment or impression from which we form the
   idea of power or necessary connexion.” (Hume, Enquiry VII.2, ed. Selby-Bigge)



21.4.3    The Bundle Theory of the Self

Hume’s account of the self is stated in the Treatise I.4.6. The account has three features.
204                                                                  Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


First feature: no impression of the self. When I look inward, I find only particular
perceptions—a perception of heat, a perception of light, a perception of love, a perception of
anger. I never find a perception of a self, a substance that persists through the perceptions. The
self is not an impression; it is a fiction.


Second feature: the bundle theory. The self is nothing but the bundle of perceptions, the
collection of impressions and ideas that succeed one another with remarkable rapidity. The self
is not a substance; it is a bundle, a collection, a series. The unity of the self is the unity of a
bundle, not the unity of a substance.


Third feature: the fiction of the self. The belief in a self, in a substantial soul that persists
through the perceptions, is a fiction of the imagination. The imagination, seeing the similarity
among the perceptions, mistakes the similarity for identity; it supposes a substance behind the
perceptions, though no such substance is given.
      The bundle theory is one of the most radical results of Hume’s empiricism. It has been
criticized, notably by Reid, who argued that the theory is inconsistent with the facts of memory
and personal identity; but it has been influential, and it is the ancestor of the no-self doctrines of
Buddhist philosophy and of the bundle theories of contemporary analytic philosophy.

   From the Tradition

   “For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on
   some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain
   or pleasure. I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can
   observe any thing but the perception.” (Hume, Treatise I.4.6.3, ed. Norton-Norton)


21.4.4      The Is/Ought Gap

Hume’s account of the is/ought gap is stated in the Treatise III.1.1. The account has three
features.


First feature: the gap. There is a gap between descriptions (what is) and prescriptions
(what ought to be). From premises about what is, no conclusion about what ought to be follows
without a further premise. The gap is logical, not psychological; it is a matter of what follows
from what.


Second feature: the critique of moral rationalism. The gap is the ground of Hume’s
critique of moral rationalism. The rationalists held that morality is a matter of reason, that reason
can discover the moral truths, and that the moral truths are as objective as the mathematical
truths. Hume denies this: reason is the slave of the passions; it can discover means to ends, but it
cannot determine the ends. The moral distinctions are derived from sentiment, not from reason.


Third feature: the moral sentiment. The moral distinctions are derived from the moral
sentiment, the feeling of approval or disapproval that we have when we contemplate an action or
21.5. Internal Disputes                                                                         205


a character. The sentiment is not arbitrary; it is grounded in the human nature, in the sympathy
that we have for our fellow human beings. But the sentiment is not a discovery of reason; it is a
fact of the heart.
   The is/ought gap is one of the most important contributions to moral philosophy. It has been
criticized, notably by the moral realists, who argue that moral facts are real and that reason can
discover them; but it has never been refuted, and it is the starting point of all modern discussions
of the relation between facts and values.

   From the Tradition

   “In every system of morality, which I have hitherto met with, I have always remark’d, that
   the author proceeds for some time in the ordinary way of reasoning, and establishes the
   being of a God, or makes observations concerning human affairs; when of a sudden I am
   surpriz’d to find, that instead of the usual copulations of propositions, is, and is not, I
   meet with no proposition that is not connected with an ought, or an ought not.” (Hume,
   Treatise III.1.1.27, ed. Norton-Norton)



21.5      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Locke and Hume is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute (Locke): the status of substance. The traditional reading takes Locke’s
substance to be a real, though unknown, support of qualities. A revisionary reading takes it to
be a placeholder, a word without an idea, which Locke uses because he cannot do without it.
The two readings disagree on whether Locke is a realist or a sceptic about substance, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is a real
invariance, not a placeholder.

Second dispute (Hume): the status of causation. The traditional reading takes Hume’s
account of causation to be a scepticism: causation is not a real relation, but a custom of the
mind. A revisionary reading takes it to be a naturalism: causation is a real feature of the world,
but our idea of it is derived from custom, not from a perception of necessity. The two readings
disagree on whether Hume is a sceptic or a naturalist, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s expression is a real structural relation, not a
custom.

Third dispute (Hume): the status of the self. The traditional reading takes the bundle
theory to be a scepticism: there is no self, only a bundle of perceptions. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a naturalism: the self is a real, though constructed, unity, a fiction that the
imagination projects on the bundle of perceptions. The two readings disagree on whether Hume
is a sceptic or a naturalist about the self, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s identity is a real invariance, not a fiction.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Locke and Hume are sceptics, the framework’s
dialogue with them is a dialogue between a structural realism and a scepticism. If they are
206                                                                Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


naturalists, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct.
The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does not rest its case
on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


21.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Locke. The framework shares three structural features with Locke’s position.

       1. The empirical origin of knowledge. Locke holds that all ideas come from experience;
         there are no innate ideas. The framework holds that all knowledge comes from
         manifestations; there is no direct access to the identity apart from its manifestations.
         Both hold that knowledge is empirical, in the sense that it begins with what is given.

       2. The distinction between primary and secondary qualities. Locke holds that primary
         qualities are in the things, secondary qualities are in the perceiver. The framework
         holds that the identity is in the source, the manifestation is in the receiving realm;
         the identity is the invariant, the manifestation is the appearance. Both hold that
         there is a distinction between what is in the thing and what is in the perceiver, and
         that the distinction is real.

       3. The continuity of consciousness. Locke holds that personal identity is the continuity
         of consciousness; the person is the same as long as her memory extends. The
         framework holds that identity is the invariance under a class of transformations,
         and that the reconstruction of a pseudo-identity is the way the subject knows the
         invariance. Both hold that identity is not the substance, and that the knowledge of
         identity is the reconstruction of a continuity.

   With Hume. The framework shares three structural features with Hume’s position.

       1. The empirical criterion of meaning. Hume holds that every idea must be traceable
         to an impression; otherwise the idea is meaningless. The framework holds that every
         concept must be definable within the framework; otherwise the concept is empty.
         Both hold that meaning is grounded in what is given, and that a concept without a
         ground is a fiction.

       2. The critique of substance. Hume holds that there is no impression of substance; the
         belief in substance is a fiction of the imagination. The framework holds that identity
         is not a substance; it is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is not a thing
         among things. Both hold that substance is not the ground of identity, and that the
         appeal to substance is a mistake.

       3. The bundle theory of the self. Hume holds that the self is nothing but the bundle
         of perceptions; there is no self behind the perceptions. The framework holds that
21.7. Points of Divergence                                                                 207


        identity is the invariance enacted by one source; there is no substance of the self,
        but there is a structure. Both hold that the self is not a substance, and that the
        unity of the self is not the unity of a substance.




21.7     Points of Divergence
208                                                                 Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


  Points of Divergence

  With Locke. The framework diverges from Locke in three respects.

      1. The status of substance. Locke holds that substance is the unknown support of
         qualities; we have no idea of it, but we posit it because we cannot conceive how
         qualities could exist without it. The framework holds that identity is the invariance
         under a class of transformations; it is not an unknown support, but a knowable
         structure. The framework’s identity is not a substratum; it is the pattern that the
         manifestations exhibit.

      2. The status of the memory criterion. Locke holds that personal identity is the
         continuity of consciousness, and that memory is the criterion. The framework holds
         that identity is the invariance, and that memory is one of its manifestations, not its
         criterion. The framework’s identity is not the memory; it is the invariance that the
         memory expresses.

      3. The status of the primary qualities. Locke holds that primary qualities are in the
         things, secondary qualities are in the perceiver. The framework holds that the
         identity is in the source, the manifestation is in the receiving realm; the two are
         not primary and secondary qualities, but the invariant and the appearance. The
         framework’s distinction is structural, not qualitative.

  With Hume. The framework diverges from Hume in three respects.

      1. The status of causation. Hume holds that causation is constant conjunction plus
         custom; the necessity is in the mind, not in the things. The framework holds that
         expression is a structural relation; the necessity is in the structure, not in the mind.
         The framework’s expression is not a custom; it is a structural condition.

      2. The status of the self. Hume holds that the self is a bundle of perceptions; there is no
         self behind the bundle. The framework holds that identity is the invariance enacted
         by one source; there is a structure behind the bundle, though not a substance. The
         framework’s identity is not a bundle; it is the invariant that the bundle expresses.

      3. The status of the is/ought gap. Hume holds that there is a gap between facts and
         values; the moral distinctions are derived from sentiment, not from reason. The
         framework holds that its subject is structure, not value; it makes no claim about the
         good or the right. The framework’s silence on ethics is not a gap; it is a boundary.
21.8. The Tradition’s Objections                                                              209


21.8     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Locke’s objection. The framework says that identity is an invariance under a class
   of transformations. But an invariance is an abstract pattern, and an abstract pattern
   is not a substance. The substance is the concrete thing that supports the qualities; the
   invariance is the abstract form that the thing exhibits. The framework has replaced the
   concrete substance with an abstract pattern, and an abstract pattern is not a thing. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of abstractions, not of substances.
   Hume’s objection. The framework says that expression is a structural tendency, and
   that identity is a real invariance. But a structural tendency is a metaphysical posit, and a
   metaphysical posit is not an impression. Hume’s criterion of meaning is the copy principle:
   every idea must be traceable to an impression; otherwise it is a fiction. The framework’s
   identity, its expression, its structure—none of these is traceable to an impression. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of fictions, not of impressions.
   Hume’s second objection. The framework says that the identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source. But the source is not an impression; it is a posit. And the
   enactment is not an impression; it is a posit. The framework’s source and enactment are
   the modern equivalents of the scholastic substance and the scholastic form; they are the
   same fictions under new names. The framework’s ontology is a scholasticism in disguise.



21.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Locke’s objection. The framework agrees that an abstract pattern is not a
   substance, and it agrees that the concrete thing is not an abstraction. But the framework
   denies that its identity is an abstract pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act*
   of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not an abstract pattern; it is the
   structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition
   is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between an abstraction (a pattern)
   and an enactment (an act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Hume’s first objection. The framework agrees that every idea must be
   traceable to something given, and it agrees that a metaphysical posit without a ground is
   a fiction. But the framework denies that its identity is a posit without a ground. The
   framework’s identity is grounded in the manifestations: the manifestations are given,
   and the identity is the invariance that the manifestations exhibit. The identity is not an
   impression; it is the structure of the impressions. The distinction is between an impression
  (a particular perception) and a structure (the invariant of the perceptions); the framework’s
   identity is the second, not the first.
210                                                               Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


   Reply to Hume’s second objection. The framework agrees that the scholastic
   substance and the scholastic form are fictions, and it agrees that a fiction under a new
   name is still a fiction. But the framework denies that its source and its enactment are
   fictions. The framework’s source is the invariance enacted by one source; the enactment
   is the act of the identity in its realm. The two are not substances; they are structural
   conditions. The distinction is between a substance (an unknown support) and a structure
   (a knowable pattern); the framework’s source and enactment are the second, not the first.




21.10      The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Locke’s cost. If Locke accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that substance
is an unknown support. He must accept that identity is a knowable structure, not a substratum,
and that the identity of a thing is its invariance, not its substance. The cost is the loss of the
substratum: the thing is no longer a support of qualities, but an invariance of manifestations.


Hume’s cost. If Hume accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
identity is a fiction. He must accept that the identity is a real structure, grounded in the
manifestations, though not an impression. The cost is the loss of the radical empiricism: not
every idea is traceable to an impression; some ideas are structures of impressions.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Locke and Hume, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the concrete substance, of the vivid impression, of the sentiment—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the invariance of the manifestations, but not the concrete substance,
and the framework leaves the second to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the concrete substance
and the vivid impression are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structures do not capture. Locke and Hume must accept that the framework’s structures are
not fictions; they are structural conditions that the concrete substance and the vivid impression
presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.
21.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                     211


21.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Locke). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Locke’s term “substance.” If one substitutes “substance” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance under a
   class of transformations; Locke’s substance is the unknown support of qualities. The
   framework’s identity is knowable; Locke’s substance is unknown. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is
   not substitutable for Locke’s term “quality.” If one substitutes “quality” for “manifestation”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation is the
   appearance of the identity in a realm; Locke’s quality is a feature of the substance, which
   we perceive. The framework’s manifestation is ontological; Locke’s quality is perceptual.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Hume). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Hume’s term “bundle.” If one substitutes “bundle” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
   by one source; Hume’s bundle is a collection of perceptions. The framework’s identity
   is one; Hume’s bundle is many. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Hume’s term
  “custom.” If one substitutes “custom” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation; Hume’s custom is
   a habit of the mind. The framework’s expression is in the things; Hume’s custom is in the
   mind. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Locke is resemblance:
   both hold that knowledge begins with experience, and they differ on whether the ground
   of knowledge is a substance or a structure. The relation between the framework and
   Hume is resemblance: both reject the substance and the self-as-substance, and they differ
   on whether the rejection leaves a structure or a bundle. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Locke and Hume
   would be refuted by showing that their empiricism cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and substance—by showing, that is, that Locke
   and Hume already distinguish the structural condition from the substance, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of their own.



21.12      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Locke’s substance or Hume’s
bundle, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Locke’s substance is already a structural
212                                                                 Chapter 21. Locke and Hume


condition, or that Hume’s bundle is already a structural unity, has a question the chapter leaves
open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of structure?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without a structure has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Essay and the Treatise do justice to the
texts? The chapter has used the tabula rasa, the primary/secondary qualities, the substance, the
personal identity, the causation, the bundle, and the is/ought gap, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a substance and a bundle—a person, a tradition, a text.
Is the thing the substance that supports its properties, or the bundle of its properties? Is the
self a continuity of consciousness, or a bundle of perceptions? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Locke’s substance and Hume’s bundle, and between both and the
framework’s identity?

knowledge; the next chapter states Kant’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.

Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Immanuel Kant. It states the Copernican revolution,
the synthetic a priori, the transcendental aesthetic (space and time as forms of intuition), the
transcendental analytic (the categories of the understanding and the transcendental deduction),
the distinction between phenomena and noumena, the paralogisms and antinomies of pure reason,
