“transcendental,” “category,” “phenomenon,” “noumenon,” or “the categorical imperative,” these
are Kant’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the Kritiken and by the interpretive tradition, not
by the framework.


22.1        A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a rainbow. She sees the colours: red, orange, yellow, green,
blue, indigo, violet. She knows that the rainbow is produced by the refraction of light in raindrops;
she knows that the colours are not in the raindrops, but in the light as it is bent by the drops.
And yet she sees the colours; they are real to her; they are the way the light appears to her.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the rainbow is, but what makes
the rainbow possible as an experience. The rainbow is possible because she has eyes that see
colours; because she has a mind that orders the colours into a band; because she has a spatial
and temporal framework in which the band appears. The eyes, the mind, the framework—these
are not the rainbow; they are the conditions under which the rainbow appears. The rainbow is
the phenomenon; the conditions are the transcendental structures that make the phenomenon
possible.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what makes the rainbow
possible, but what the rainbow is in itself, apart from the conditions under which it appears.
She cannot answer; she cannot know the rainbow in itself; she can know it only as it appears to
her, under the forms of space and time, under the categories of the understanding. The rainbow
in itself is the thing-in-itself, the noumenon; it is thinkable, but not knowable.
    The scene is Kant’s image, in the Kritik der reinen Vernunft, of the structure of experience.
The rainbow is the phenomenon; the forms of intuition and the categories of the understanding

                                                214
22.2. The Question                                                                            215


are the transcendental conditions of the phenomenon; the thing-in-itself is the noumenon, the
limit of knowledge. The Copernican revolution is the shift from the object to the subject: instead
of asking how our knowledge conforms to the object, we ask how the object conforms to the
conditions of our knowledge.
   The scene poses the question that Kant was the first to pose in its full form. What are
the conditions of possible experience? Are they in the object, or in the subject? And what
can we know, and what can we not know? The present chapter states Kant’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


22.2     The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, and Hume.
Descartes posed the problem of the foundation; Spinoza posed the problem of the one substance;
Leibniz posed the problem of the many monads; Locke and Hume posed the problem of empirical
knowledge. Kant is the great synthesizer of the modern West, and he is the philosopher who
responds to Hume: he accepts Hume’s critique of the rationalist metaphysics, but he rejects
Hume’s scepticism about causation and the self; he turns from the object to the subject, and he
asks what the subject contributes to experience. The present chapter states Kant’s synthesis,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Kant was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Kant hold? The chapter states the Copernican revolution,
the synthetic a priori, the forms of intuition, the categories, the transcendental deduction, the
phenomena/noumena distinction, the antinomies, the categorical imperative, and the limits of
reason, with reference to the Kritiken.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Kant converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Kant would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Kant? The
chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


22.3     The Position

22.3.1    The Copernican Revolution

Kant’s Copernican revolution is stated in the Kritik der reinen Vernunft (1781/1787), in the
Preface to the second edition and in the Introduction. The revolution is a shift in the method of
philosophy: instead of assuming that our knowledge must conform to the object, we assume that
the object must conform to the conditions of our knowledge.
216                                                                           Chapter 22. Kant


      The revolution has three features.


First feature: the priority of the subject. The subject is not a passive receiver of
impressions; it is an active constructor of experience. The subject contributes the forms of
intuition (space and time) and the categories of the understanding (causality, substance, unity,
etc.) to the raw material of sensation. Without these contributions, there would be no experience,
only a chaos of sensations.


Second feature: the conditions of possible experience. The forms of intuition and the
categories are the conditions of possible experience. They are not derived from experience; they
are a priori, and they make experience possible. The subject that did not have these forms and
categories could not have experience; it would be a consciousness without a world.


Third feature: the limits of knowledge. The Copernican revolution has a consequence: we
can know only what appears under the forms and categories; we cannot know the thing-in-itself,
the noumenon. Knowledge is limited to the phenomenal world; the noumenal world is thinkable,
but not knowable.

   From the Tradition

   “Hitherto it has been assumed that all our knowledge must conform to objects. But all
   attempts to extend our knowledge of objects by establishing something in regard to them
   a priori, by means of concepts, have, on this assumption, ended in failure. We must
   therefore make trial whether we may not have more success in the tasks of metaphysics,
   if we suppose that objects must conform to our knowledge.” (Kant, Kritik der reinen
   Vernunft B xvi, trans. after Norman Kemp Smith)



22.3.2      The Synthetic A Priori

Kant’s distinction between analytic and synthetic judgments, and between a priori and a posteriori
judgments, is stated in the Kritik der reinen Vernunft, Introduction. The distinction has three
features.


First feature: analytic and synthetic. An analytic judgment is one in which the predicate
is contained in the subject; its truth is grounded in the principle of non-contradiction. “All
bachelors are unmarried” is analytic. A synthetic judgment is one in which the predicate is not
contained in the subject; its truth requires something beyond the principle of non-contradiction.
“All bodies are heavy” is synthetic.


Second feature: a priori and a posteriori. An a priori judgment is one that is known
independently of experience; its truth is necessary and universal. “7 + 5 = 12” is a priori.
An a posteriori judgment is one that is known through experience; its truth is contingent and
particular. “The sun is warm” is a posteriori.
22.3. The Position                                                                               217


Third feature: the synthetic a priori. The synthetic a priori is the combination of the two
distinctions: a judgment that is synthetic (its predicate is not contained in its subject) and a
priori (its truth is necessary and universal). “7 + 5 = 12” is synthetic a priori; so is “every event
has a cause.” The synthetic a priori is the central question of the Kritik: how are synthetic a
priori judgments possible?
   Kant’s answer is the Copernican revolution: the synthetic a priori is possible because the
subject contributes the forms and categories that make the synthesis possible. The forms of
intuition (space and time) make synthetic a priori judgments about mathematics possible; the
categories of the understanding (causality, substance, etc.) make synthetic a priori judgments
about natural science possible.


22.3.3    The Forms of Intuition

Kant’s account of the forms of intuition is stated in the Transcendental Aesthetic, the first part
of the Kritik der reinen Vernunft. The account has three features.


First feature: space is the form of outer intuition. Space is not an empirical concept
derived from experience; it is the a priori form of outer intuition. We cannot represent anything
as outside us without presupposing space; space is the condition under which outer things appear
to us.


Second feature: time is the form of inner intuition. Time is not an empirical concept
derived from experience; it is the a priori form of inner intuition. We cannot represent anything
as in us without presupposing time; time is the condition under which inner states appear to us.


Third feature: space and time are forms, not things. Space and time are not things in
themselves, nor are they relations among things in themselves; they are forms of our intuition.
They are subjective conditions of experience, not objective features of reality.
   The forms of intuition are the foundation of Kant’s account of mathematics. Mathematics is
synthetic a priori because it concerns the forms of intuition; geometry concerns space, arithmetic
concerns time. The forms of intuition make mathematics possible; without them, there would be
no mathematical knowledge.


22.3.4    The Categories and the Transcendental Deduction

Kant’s account of the categories is stated in the Transcendental Analytic, the second part of the
Kritik der reinen Vernunft. The account has three features.


First feature: the categories are pure concepts of the understanding. The categories
are the a priori concepts by which the understanding synthesizes the manifold of intuition.
There are twelve categories, in four groups: quantity (unity, plurality, totality); quality (reality,
negation, limitation); relation (substance, causality, community); modality (possibility, existence,
necessity).
218                                                                             Chapter 22. Kant


Second feature: the categories are the conditions of experience. The categories are not
derived from experience; they are the a priori conditions under which the manifold of intuition is
synthesized into experience. Without the categories, there would be no experience; there would
be only a chaos of sensations.


Third feature: the transcendental deduction. The transcendental deduction is the
argument that the categories are necessary conditions of experience. The argument proceeds
from the unity of consciousness: for experience to be possible, the manifold of intuition must be
unified in a single consciousness; and for the manifold to be unified, it must be synthesized by
the categories. Therefore the categories are necessary conditions of experience.
      The categories are the key to Kant’s account of natural science. Natural science is synthetic
a priori because it concerns the categories; the laws of nature are the laws of the categories. The
categories make natural science possible; without them, there would be no scientific knowledge.

   From the Tradition

   “The categories are the pure concepts of the understanding, which synthesize the manifold
   of intuition into the unity of experience. Without them, there would be no experience;
   there would be only a chaos of sensations.” (Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft A 79/B 105,
   trans. after Norman Kemp Smith)


22.3.5      Phenomena and Noumena

Kant’s distinction between phenomena and noumena is stated in the Kritik der reinen Vernunft,
in the chapter on phenomena and noumena and in the Transcendental Dialectic. The distinction
has three features.


First feature: phenomena are appearances. Phenomena are the things as they appear to
us, under the forms of intuition and the categories of the understanding. Phenomena are the
objects of possible experience; they are what we can know.


Second feature: noumena are things in themselves. Noumena are the things as they
are in themselves, apart from the forms of intuition and the categories of the understanding.
Noumena are not the objects of possible experience; they are what we can think, but not know.


Third feature: the limit of knowledge. The distinction is the limit of knowledge: we can
know phenomena, but not noumena. The thing-in-itself is the limit of knowledge; it is thinkable,
but not knowable. The distinction is not a division of reality; it is a division of the ways we can
relate to reality.
      The distinction is the foundation of Kant’s critique of the rationalist metaphysics. The
rationalists claimed to know the thing-in-itself—God, the soul, the world as a whole; Kant
denies that such knowledge is possible. The rationalist arguments (the ontological proof, the
cosmological proof, the physico-theological proof) are all fallacious; they apply the categories
beyond the limits of possible experience.
22.3. The Position                                                                           219


22.3.6    The Antinomies of Pure Reason
Kant’s account of the antinomies is stated in the Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter
II. The antinomies are the contradictions into which reason falls when it applies the categories
beyond the limits of possible experience.
   There are four antinomies.

First antinomy. Thesis: the world has a beginning in time and is limited in space. Antithesis:
the world has no beginning in time and no limits in space; it is infinite.

Second antinomy. Thesis: every composite substance is made of simple parts. Antithesis: no
composite substance is made of simple parts.

Third antinomy. Thesis: there is freedom, a causality through freedom, besides the causality
of nature. Antithesis: there is no freedom; everything happens according to the laws of nature.

Fourth antinomy. Thesis: there is a necessary being, either as part of the world or as its
cause. Antithesis: there is no necessary being, either in the world or outside it.
   Kant’s solution to the antinomies is the transcendental idealism: the antinomies arise because
reason treats phenomena as if they were noumena. The thesis and the antithesis are both
true, but in different respects: the thesis is true of the noumenal world, the antithesis of the
phenomenal world. The antinomies are not contradictions in reality; they are contradictions in
reason’s attempt to go beyond the limits of possible experience.


22.3.7    The Categorical Imperative
Kant’s ethics is stated in the Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten (1785) and in the Kritik
der praktischen Vernunft (1788). The central concept is the categorical imperative, the moral
law that commands unconditionally, without reference to any end or desire.
   The categorical imperative has three formulations.

First formulation: the formula of universal law. “Act only according to that maxim
whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” The moral law is
the law that can be universalized; an action is moral if its maxim can be willed as a universal
law.

Second formulation: the formula of humanity. “Act in such a way that you treat humanity,
whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never merely as a means to an end,
but always at the same time as an end.” The moral law requires that we treat persons as ends in
themselves, not merely as means.

Third formulation: the formula of autonomy. “So act that your will can regard itself at
the same time as making universal law through its maxim.” The moral law is the law that the
will gives to itself; autonomy is the ground of morality.
220                                                                               Chapter 22. Kant


      The categorical imperative is the foundation of Kant’s ethics. The moral law is not derived
from experience; it is a priori, and it is binding on all rational beings. The moral law is the law
of freedom; it is what the will commands when it acts autonomously, apart from the inclinations
of sensibility.

   From the Tradition

   “Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should
   become a universal law.” (Kant, Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten AA 4:421, trans.
   after Paton)


22.3.8      The Limits of Reason
Kant’s account of the limits of reason is stated throughout the Kritik der reinen Vernunft. The
account has three features.

First feature: reason seeks the unconditioned. Reason is not content with the conditioned;
it seeks the unconditioned, the absolute, the ultimate ground of things. Reason seeks the soul,
the world as a whole, God.

Second feature: reason oversteps its limits. When reason seeks the unconditioned, it
oversteps the limits of possible experience. It applies the categories beyond the phenomenal
world, and it falls into illusion. The illusion is not a mistake of the individual; it is a natural
tendency of reason.

Third feature: the critique of reason. The critique of reason is the discipline that keeps
reason within its limits. The critique is not a scepticism; it is a self-knowledge of reason. Reason
that knows its limits is reason that is free from illusion; it is reason that can be used legitimately,
within the bounds of possible experience.
      The critique of reason is the foundation of Kant’s philosophy. The critique distinguishes the
legitimate use of reason (in science and morality) from the illegitimate use (in the rationalist
metaphysics). The critique is the Copernican revolution applied to reason itself: reason turns
from the object to its own conditions, and it discovers its own limits.

   From the Tradition

   “I had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.” (Kant, Kritik der reinen
   Vernunft B xxx, trans. after Norman Kemp Smith)



22.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Kant is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the thing-in-itself. The traditional reading takes the thing-in-
itself to be a real, though unknowable, entity: there is a noumenal world, and we cannot know it.
22.5. Points of Convergence                                                                     221


A revisionary reading takes the thing-in-itself to be a limit-concept: the thing-in-itself is not an
entity, but the limit of our knowledge; the concept marks the boundary, not a beyond. The two
readings disagree on whether Kant is a realist or a phenomenalist about the noumenon, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no noumenal
realm.

Second dispute: the status of the categories. The traditional reading takes the categories
to be the a priori concepts of the understanding, necessary conditions of experience. A revisionary
reading takes them to be the conceptual framework of a particular form of life, historically
contingent. The two readings disagree on whether Kant is a transcendental philosopher or
a proto-pragmatist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s four columns are analytical roles, not transcendental conditions.

Third dispute: the status of the categorical imperative. The traditional reading
takes the categorical imperative to be a universal moral law, binding on all rational beings.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a formal principle that underdetermines moral content,
requiring a substantive ethics to be applied. The two readings disagree on whether Kant is a
moral universalist or a formalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework has no ethics.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Kant is a transcendental philosopher, the
framework’s dialogue with him is a dialogue between two transcendental structures. If Kant is a
proto-pragmatist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Kritik der reinen Vernunft,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.


22.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Kant. The framework shares four structural features with Kant’s position.

       1. The structural conditions of experience. Kant holds that experience is possible only
         under the forms of intuition and the categories of the understanding; these are the a
         priori conditions of possible experience. The framework holds that explanation is
         complete only under the four columns; these are the analytical conditions of complete
         explanation. Both hold that there are structural conditions that make a certain kind
         of cognition possible, and that these conditions are not derived from the cognition
         itself.

       2. The limits of knowledge. Kant holds that we can know phenomena, but not noumena;
         the thing-in-itself is thinkable, but not knowable. The framework holds that we can
         reconstruct a pseudo-identity from the manifestations, but not the identity itself; the
         identity is the source, not the object of reconstruction. Both hold that knowledge
222                                                                                Chapter 22. Kant


          has limits, and that the limits are structural, not contingent.

       3. The active role of the subject. Kant holds that the subject is not a passive receiver;
          it contributes the forms and categories to experience. The framework holds that
          the subject is not a passive receiver; it reconstructs a pseudo-identity from the
          manifestations, and the reconstruction is active. Both hold that knowledge is an
          activity, not a reception.

       4. The critique of the rationalist metaphysics. Kant holds that the rationalist proofs
         (the ontological, cosmological, and physico-theological proofs) are fallacious; they
          apply the categories beyond the limits of possible experience. The framework holds
          that the claim to complete knowledge (super-identity) is impossible; it presupposes
          that the subject can stand outside the contexts it surveys. Both hold that the
          pretension to absolute knowledge is a mistake.



22.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Kant. The framework diverges from Kant in four respects.

       1. The status of the categories. Kant’s categories are the a priori concepts of the
          understanding, necessary conditions of possible experience; they are twelve, in four
          groups. The framework’s four columns are analytical roles, not a priori concepts; they
          are four, not twelve, and they are not conditions of possible experience, but conditions
          of complete explanation. The framework’s columns are not Kant’s categories.

       2. The status of the noumenon. Kant holds that there is a noumenal world, a thing-in-
          itself, which is thinkable but not knowable. The framework has no noumenal world;
          its identity is not a thing-in-itself, but the invariance that the manifestations exhibit;
          it is knowable through reconstruction, though always partially. The framework’s
          identity is not a noumenon.

       3. The status of the subject. Kant’s subject is the transcendental unity of apperception,
          the "I think" that accompanies all my representations. The framework has no
          transcendental subject; its identity is not a subject, and its reconstruction is not an
          act of a transcendental ego. The framework is a metaphysics of structure, not of
          subjectivity.

       4. The status of ethics. Kant’s ethics turns on the categorical imperative, the moral
          law that commands unconditionally. The framework has no ethics; its subject is the
          structure of identity and manifestation, and it leaves the moral law to a separate
          inquiry. The framework is a metaphysics without ethics.
22.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 223


22.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Kant’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that its
   manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not a category;
   it is a pattern. Kant’s categories are the a priori concepts that make experience possible;
   the framework’s four columns are the analytical roles that make explanation complete.
   The two are not the same; the framework has confused the conditions of experience with
   the conditions of explanation. The framework’s columns are not transcendental; they are
   analytical, and analytical roles do not make experience possible.
   Kant’s second objection. The framework says that identity is knowable through
   reconstruction, though always partially. But if identity is knowable, even partially, it is
   not a noumenon; it is a phenomenon. And if identity is a phenomenon, it is not the source
   of the manifestations; it is one of the manifestations. The framework’s identity is either a
   noumenon (and then unknowable) or a phenomenon (and then not the source). It cannot
   be both; the framework’s distinction between identity and manifestation is incoherent.
   Kant’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not value.
   But a metaphysics without ethics is an incomplete metaphysics; the human being is not
   only a knower, but also an agent; the moral law is as fundamental as the categories. The
   framework’s silence on ethics is not a boundary; it is a gap.



22.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a structural invariance is
   not a category, and it agrees that Kant’s categories are conditions of possible experience.
   But the framework denies that its four columns are conditions of possible experience;
   they are conditions of complete explanation. The two are different kinds of condition; the
   framework’s columns are analytical, Kant’s categories are transcendental. The distinction
   is not a confusion; it is a distinction between two kinds of structural condition, each valid
   in its own domain.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that an identity cannot be
   both a noumenon and a phenomenon, and it agrees that if identity is a phenomenon, it
   is not the source. But the framework denies that its identity is either a noumenon or a
   phenomenon. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not a
   thing-in-itself, and it is not an appearance; it is the structure that the appearance exhibits.
   The distinction is between a noumenon (a thing apart from all conditions) and a structure
  (the invariant of the appearances); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without ethics
   is incomplete, and it agrees that the human being is not only a knower, but also an agent.
224                                                                           Chapter 22. Kant


   But the framework denies that its silence on ethics is a gap. The framework is a work
   of metaphysics, not of ethics; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation,
   not the moral law. The framework states the structural condition of reality; it leaves the
   moral law to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics and an ethics;
   the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it is not a gap but a boundary.



22.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Kant’s cost. If Kant accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
categories are the a priori conditions of possible experience. He must accept that the four
columns are the analytical roles of complete explanation, and that the two are different. The cost
is the loss of the transcendental deduction: the categories are no longer the necessary conditions
of experience; they are one set of structural conditions among others.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Kant’s objections, it must give up the claim
that its four columns are the complete conditions of explanation. It must accept that there is a
dimension of reality—the dimension of the transcendental conditions of experience, of the forms
of intuition, of the categorical imperative— that its columns do not capture. The cost is the loss
of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s columns are the analytical roles,
but not the transcendental conditions, and the framework leaves the second to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Kant’s transcendental
conditions are not a mistake; they are a dimension of the real that the framework’s columns
do not capture. Kant must accept that the framework’s columns are not a confusion; they are
analytical roles that the transcendental conditions presuppose as their condition. The cost of
the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are
complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


22.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “four columns” is not substitutable
   for Kant’s term “categories.” If one substitutes “categories” for “four columns” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s four columns are fixed
   elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context; Kant’s categories are quantity,
   quality, relation, and modality. The framework’s columns are four, Kant’s categories are
   twelve. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The
   framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Kant’s term “the thing-in-itself.” If
22.11. Open Questions                                                                           225


   one substitutes “the thing-in-itself” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and
   it is manifested in a realm; Kant’s thing-in-itself is the thing apart from all conditions
   of possible experience, and it is not manifested. The framework’s identity is knowable;
   Kant’s thing-in-itself is not. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Kant is resemblance:
   both hold that there are structural conditions of cognition, and they differ on whether the
   conditions are transcendental or analytical. Both hold that knowledge has limits, and they
   differ on whether the limits are the noumena or the identity. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Kant would be refuted
   by showing that Kant’s transcendental conditions cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between the analytical and the transcendental—by showing, that
   is, that Kant already distinguishes the analytical roles from the transcendental conditions,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Kant’s own.




22.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Kant’s thing-in-itself, or is it a
departure from Kant? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not
conclusive. A reader who holds that Kant’s thing-in-itself is already a structural condition, not a
noumenal entity, has a question the chapter leaves open.



Second question. Can the framework’s four columns be stated without the notion of explana-
tion? The chapter has argued that they cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader
who holds that the columns can be stated without an explanation has a question the chapter
leaves open.



Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Kritik der reinen Vernunft do justice to
the text? The chapter has used the Copernican revolution, the synthetic a priori, the forms of
intuition, the categories, the transcendental deduction, the phenomena/noumena distinction, the
antinomies, the categorical imperative, and the limits of reason, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Kritik supports a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a phenomenon and a structure—a person, a work of
art, a text. Is the thing the appearance under the forms of intuition, or the structure behind
the appearance, or both? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Kant’s
phenomena and noumena, and between both and the framework’s identity and manifestation?

The next chapter turns to Hegel. It states the dialectic, the Aufhebung, the master-slave dialectic,
the Geist, the end of history, and the critique of Kant’s thing-in-itself; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Hegel; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of expression and self-manifestation is the nearest modern
analogue to Hegel’s. The present chapter has stated Kant’s answer to the problem of the conditions
of experience; the next chapter states Hegel’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 23

Hegel


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. It states the dialectic,
the Aufhebung, the master-slave dialectic, the Geist (spirit), the Phänomenologie des Geistes, the
logic, the philosophy of history, the critique of Kant’s thing-in-itself, and the end of history, with
reference to the Phänomenologie des Geistes, the Wissenschaft der Logik, and the Vorlesungen
über die Philosophie der Geschichte; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of Hegel; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of expression and self-manifestation is the nearest modern analogue to Hegel’s; it presents the
objections that Hegel would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where
the chapter speaks of “dialectic,” “Aufhebung,” “Geist,” “absolute knowledge,” or “the end of
history,” these are Hegel’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


23.1      A Scene
Consider a seed. The seed is a unity; it is one thing, with a single form, a single purpose. Then
it sprouts: it becomes a stem, a leaf, a bud. The unity is broken; the seed is negated; the plant
is many things, not one. Then it flowers: the flower is the synthesis, the unity that contains the
many, the form that includes the stem, the leaf, the bud. The flower is not the seed; it is the
seed fulfilled, the seed raised to a higher level. The seed is preserved in the flower, but it is also
cancelled; the flower is the truth of the seed.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose you ask not what the plant is, but what the process is.
The process is not a linear sequence; it is a movement in which each stage negates the previous
one, and in negating it, preserves it, and in preserving it, raises it to a higher level. This is
the dialectic: the movement of the concept through its contradictions, to a higher unity. The
dialectic is not a method imposed on reality; it is the movement of reality itself, the way the real
develops through its contradictions.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose you ask not what the process is, or how
the dialectic works, but what the whole is. The whole is not a collection of parts; it is the unity
that contains the parts, the totality that is present in each stage. The whole is the Geist: the
spirit that develops through history, that is present in each individual consciousness, and that is
realized in the state, in art, in religion, in philosophy. The whole is the absolute; it is the totality
of reality, the unity of subject and object, the identity of thinking and being.
   The scene is Hegel’s image, in the Phänomenologie des Geistes, of the structure of reality.
The seed is the immediate unity; the plant is the mediation; the flower is the mediated unity.

                                                  227
228                                                                               Chapter 23. Hegel


The dialectic is the movement from the first to the third, through the second. The Geist is the
whole that is realized in the movement; the absolute is the totality that contains the movement.
The real is not a static substance; it is a living process, a self-manifesting whole.
      The scene poses the question that Hegel was the first to pose in its full form. What is the
structure of reality? Is it a static order, or a living process? Is it a collection of substances, or a
self-manifesting whole? And what is the place of contradiction in reality—is it a defect, or the
motor of development? The present chapter states Hegel’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.



23.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated Kant’s position: the Copernican revolution, the synthetic a priori,
the forms of intuition, the categories, the phenomena/noumena distinction, the antinomies, the
categorical imperative, and the limits of reason. Kant is the great synthesizer of the modern West,
and Hegel is his greatest successor and his greatest critic. Hegel accepts Kant’s transcendental
turn, but he rejects Kant’s dualism of phenomenon and noumenon, his formalism in ethics, and
his limitation of knowledge to the phenomenal world. The present chapter states Hegel’s critique,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Hegel was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Hegel hold? The chapter states the dialectic, the
Aufhebung, the master-slave dialectic, the Geist, the logic, the philosophy of history, the critique
of Kant, and the end of history, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Hegel converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Hegel would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Hegel? The
chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.



23.3       The Position

23.3.1      The Dialectic

Hegel’s dialectic is stated in the Phänomenologie des Geistes (1807) and in the Wissenschaft der
Logik (1812–16). The dialectic is the movement of the concept through its contradictions, to a
higher unity. The movement has three moments.
23.3. The Position                                                                                229


First moment: the immediate. The immediate is the starting point, the abstract unity that
has not yet been mediated. It is the seed, the bare concept, the "in itself." The immediate is
one-sided; it does not yet contain its other; it is abstract, not concrete.


Second moment: the mediation. The mediation is the negation of the immediate, the
moment of difference, the "for itself." The immediate is negated; the unity is broken; the many
appear. The mediation is the moment of contradiction, in which the concept encounters its other,
and in encountering it, is transformed.


Third moment: the mediated unity. The mediated unity is the synthesis, the "in and for
itself," the concrete unity that contains the many. The immediate is preserved in the mediated
unity, but it is also cancelled; the contradiction is resolved, but it is also preserved. The mediated
unity is the truth of the immediate; it is the immediate raised to a higher level.
   The dialectic is not a method imposed on reality; it is the movement of reality itself. The
real is not a static substance; it is a living process, a self-manifesting whole. The dialectic is the
way the real develops; it is the logic of reality.

   From the Tradition

   “The dialectic is not an external activity of subjective thought, but the very soul of the
   content, which organically develops its branches and fruits. It is the movement of the
   concept itself, the movement through which the content becomes what it is.” (Hegel,
   Wissenschaft der Logik, trans. after Miller)



23.3.2    The Aufhebung

Hegel’s Aufhebung is the key concept of the dialectic. The word has a double meaning: it means
both "to cancel" and "to preserve," and also "to raise" (as in "to raise to a higher level"). The
Aufhebung is the movement in which a moment is cancelled, preserved, and raised.
   The Aufhebung has three features.


First feature: cancellation. The moment is cancelled; it is negated; it is shown to be
one-sided, abstract, inadequate. The immediate is cancelled by the mediation; the abstract unity
is cancelled by the difference.


Second feature: preservation. The moment is preserved; it is not destroyed; it is taken up
into the higher unity. The immediate is preserved in the mediated unity; the seed is preserved in
the flower; the child is preserved in the adult.


Third feature: elevation. The moment is raised to a higher level; it is not merely preserved,
but transformed. The immediate is raised to the mediated unity; the seed is raised to the flower;
the child is raised to the adult. The Aufhebung is the movement from the lower to the higher,
from the abstract to the concrete, from the one-sided to the whole.
230                                                                              Chapter 23. Hegel


      The Aufhebung is the logic of reality. Everything that is real is subject to the Aufhebung;
everything that is real is in process, in development, in self-manifestation. The real is not what
it is immediately; it is what it becomes through its Aufhebung.


23.3.3      The Master-Slave Dialectic

Hegel’s master-slave dialectic is stated in the Phänomenologie des Geistes, Chapter IV, Section
A. The dialectic is a parable of the development of self-consciousness.
      The dialectic has three moments.


First moment: the struggle for recognition. Two self-consciousnesses encounter each
other; each seeks recognition from the other; each wants the other to acknowledge its superiority.
The struggle is a life-and-death struggle; each is willing to risk its life for recognition.


Second moment: master and slave. One wins the struggle; the other submits. The winner
becomes the master; the loser becomes the slave. The master enjoys the recognition; the slave
works for the master. The master seems to have won; the slave seems to have lost.


Third moment: the reversal. But the relation is reversed. The master depends on the
slave for recognition; the slave’s recognition is not freely given, so it is not true recognition. The
slave, on the other hand, works on the world; through work, the slave transforms the world and
transforms himself; through work, the slave achieves self-consciousness. The master, who does
not work, remains dependent; the slave, who works, becomes free.
      The master-slave dialectic is one of the most famous passages in Hegel’s work. It has been
read as a parable of the struggle for recognition, as a parable of the development of labor, and as
a parable of the master-slave relation in history. Its influence extends from Marx to Kojève to
Sartre to Fanon.

   From the Tradition

   “The master is the consciousness that exists for itself; the slave is the consciousness
   that exists for another. The master has achieved recognition, but the recognition is
   one-sided; the slave has not achieved recognition, but through work, the slave achieves
   self-consciousness.” (Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes IV.A, trans. after Miller)



23.3.4      The Geist (Spirit)

Hegel’s Geist is the central concept of his philosophy. The Geist is spirit: the collective
consciousness of humanity, the self-manifesting whole that develops through history. The Geist
is not a substance; it is a subject; it is the "I that is We, and the We that is I" (Ich, das Wir,
und Wir, das Ich ist).
      The Geist has three features.
23.3. The Position                                                                              231


First feature: the Geist is collective. The Geist is not the individual consciousness; it
is the collective consciousness of a people, a culture, an age. The individual consciousness is a
moment of the Geist; it is the Geist become aware of itself in an individual.


Second feature: the Geist develops. The Geist develops through history; it moves from
one form to another; it realizes itself in art, in religion, in philosophy. The development is not a
linear progress; it is a dialectical movement, in which each form is aufgehoben in the next.


Third feature: the Geist is free. The Geist is free; its freedom is its essence; its development
is the development of freedom. The end of history is the realization of freedom, the self-
consciousness of the Geist in its freedom.
   The Geist is the absolute; it is the totality of reality; it is the unity of subject and object,
of thinking and being, of the individual and the collective. The Geist is what reality is, when
reality is understood as a self-manifesting whole.


23.3.5       The Phänomenologie des Geistes

Hegel’s Phänomenologie des Geistes (1807) is the phenomenology of spirit: the science of the
experience of consciousness. The book traces the development of consciousness from the simplest
form (sense-certainty) to the highest form (absolute knowledge). It is the Bildungsroman of
consciousness, the story of its education.
   The book has three parts.


First part: consciousness. Consciousness is the awareness of an object; it is the simplest
form of experience. The first part traces the development of consciousness from sense-certainty
(the immediate awareness of a particular) to perception (the awareness of a thing with properties)
to understanding (the awareness of a world of laws).


Second part: self-consciousness. Self-consciousness is the awareness of oneself as a subject;
it is the second form of experience. The second part traces the development of self-consciousness
from desire (the immediate striving for satisfaction) to the master-slave dialectic (the struggle
for recognition) to the unhappy consciousness (the awareness of one’s own division).


Third part: reason, spirit, religion, absolute knowledge. The third part traces the
development from reason (the awareness of oneself as the truth of the world) to spirit (the
awareness of oneself as a moment of a collective whole) to religion (the awareness of the absolute
in image and representation) to absolute knowledge (the awareness of the absolute in concept).
   The Phänomenologie is the story of the education of consciousness; it is the story of how
consciousness comes to know itself as the absolute. The end of the story is absolute knowledge;
the beginning is the simplest experience. The movement from the beginning to the end is the
dialectic.
232                                                                              Chapter 23. Hegel


23.3.6      The Logic

Hegel’s Wissenschaft der Logik (1812–16) is the science of the pure concept. The logic is not the
logic of formal inference; it is the logic of reality; it is the movement of the concept through its
determinations.
      The logic has three parts.


First part: the logic of being. The logic of being is the logic of the immediate; it is the
logic of quality, quantity, and measure. Being is the simplest determination; it is the bare "is"; it
is the immediate unity that has not yet been mediated.


Second part: the logic of essence. The logic of essence is the logic of the mediated; it is
the logic of reflection, appearance, and actuality. Essence is the ground of being; it is the inner
determination that appears in the outer.


Third part: the logic of the concept. The logic of the concept is the logic of the mediated
unity; it is the logic of the subjective concept, the object, and the idea. The concept is the unity
of being and essence; it is the self-manifesting whole, the absolute.
      The logic is the foundation of Hegel’s philosophy. It is the science of the concept; it is the
science of what is; it is the science of the absolute. The logic is the movement of the concept; it
is the dialectic in its pure form.


23.3.7      The Philosophy of History

Hegel’s philosophy of history is stated in the Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Geschichte
(1822–31). The philosophy of history is the study of the Geist in its development; it is the study
of the realization of freedom in history.
      The philosophy of history has three features.


First feature: reason in history. Reason governs history; the Geist develops according to
reason; the movement of history is the movement of the concept. The "cunning of reason" (List
der Vernunft) is the way reason uses the passions of individuals to achieve its ends.


Second feature: the development of freedom. The development of history is the develop-
ment of freedom. The ancient world knew that some are free (the masters); the modern world
knows that all are free (the citizens); the end of history is the realization of universal freedom.


Third feature: the end of history. The end of history is the realization of freedom, the
self-consciousness of the Geist in its freedom. The end is not a chronological end; it is the
realization of the concept; it is the moment when the Geist knows itself as free.
      The philosophy of history is the application of the dialectic to history. History is not a
collection of contingent events; it is the development of the Geist; it is the realization of freedom.
The end of history is the realization of the absolute.
23.3. The Position                                                                                 233


   From the Tradition

   “The history of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of freedom.”
   (Hegel, Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Geschichte, trans. after Sibree)


23.3.8    The Critique of Kant
Hegel’s critique of Kant is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in the Glauben und
Wissen (1802) and in the Enzyklopädie der philosophischen Wissenschaften (1817). The critique
has three features.

First feature: the critique of the thing-in-itself. Kant’s thing-in-itself is an abstraction;
it is the empty beyond, the limit of knowledge that cannot be known. The thing-in-itself is not a
thing; it is a concept; it is the concept of the limit. And the limit, when it is known as a limit, is
already transcended; the thing-in-itself is not beyond knowledge; it is a moment of knowledge.

Second feature: the critique of the categories. Kant’s categories are the a priori forms of
the understanding; they are the conditions of possible experience. But the categories are not
fixed; they develop; they are moments of the dialectic. The categories are not the static forms of
the understanding; they are the living moments of the concept.

Third feature: the critique of the categorical imperative. Kant’s categorical imperative
is a formal principle; it is the form of the moral law, without content. But a formal principle is
empty; it cannot determine what is right; it can only test what is universalizable. The moral law
must have content; it must be realized in the ethical life, in the family, in the civil society, in the
state.
   Hegel’s critique is not a rejection of Kant; it is a Aufhebung of Kant. Hegel preserves Kant’s
transcendental turn, his critique of the rationalist metaphysics, his ethics of autonomy; but he
raises them to a higher level. The thing-in-itself is aufgehoben in the absolute; the categories are
aufgehoben in the concept; the categorical imperative is aufgehoben in the ethical life.

23.3.9    The End of History
Hegel’s end of history is stated in the Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Geschichte and
in the Phänomenologie des Geistes. The end of history is the realization of freedom, the
self-consciousness of the Geist in its freedom.
   The end of history has three features.

First feature: the realization of the concept. The end of history is not a chronological
end; it is the realization of the concept. The concept of freedom, which was implicit at the
beginning of history, becomes explicit at the end; the Geist knows itself as free.

Second feature: the end is present. The end of history is not a future state; it is present
in the modern state, in the modern art, in the modern philosophy. The modern world is the
realization of freedom; it is the end of history.
234                                                                               Chapter 23. Hegel


Third feature: the end is not a cessation. The end of history is not a cessation of events;
it is the realization of the concept. History continues; but the fundamental question of history—
the question of freedom—has been answered.
      The end of history is the culmination of Hegel’s philosophy. It is the realization of the
absolute; it is the self-consciousness of the Geist in its freedom. It is the goal of the dialectic; it
is the truth of the whole.



23.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Hegel is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the dialectic. The traditional reading takes the dialectic to
be a metaphysical principle: reality itself is dialectical; the dialectic is the logic of the real. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a method: the dialectic is a way of thinking about reality,
not a feature of reality itself. The two readings disagree on whether Hegel is a metaphysician
or a methodologist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s structure is real, not methodological.



Second dispute: the status of the Geist. The traditional reading takes the Geist to be
a collective subject: the Geist is a real, collective consciousness, developing through history.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor: the Geist is a way of speaking about the
collective life of a culture, not a real subject. The two readings disagree on whether Hegel is
a metaphysician of spirit or a philosopher of culture, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no collective subject.



Third dispute: the status of the end of history. The traditional reading takes the end
of history to be a real event: history has reached its goal in the modern state. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a regulative idea: the end of history is a way of speaking about the goal of
history, not a real state. The two readings disagree on whether Hegel is an optimist or a Kantian
before Kant, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework
has no end of history.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Hegel is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an absolute idealism. If Hegel
is a methodologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Phänomenologie, but it does
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.
23.5. Points of Convergence                                                                        235


23.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Hegel. The framework shares four structural features with Hegel’s position.

       1. The priority of process over substance. Hegel holds that reality is not a static
          substance; it is a living process, a self-manifesting whole. The framework holds
          that reality is not a collection of static substances; it is a structure of expression, in
         which identities are enacted in manifestations. Both hold that reality is dynamic,
          not static, and that the dynamic is the truth of the static.

       2. The self-manifestation of the whole. Hegel holds that the Geist manifests itself in
          history, in art, in religion, in philosophy; the whole is present in each moment. The
          framework holds that the identity manifests itself in its manifestations; the whole is
          present in each manifestation. Both hold that the whole manifests itself in the parts,
          and that the parts are the manifestation of the whole.

       3. The Aufhebung of the moments. Hegel holds that each moment is cancelled, preserved,
          and raised to a higher level; nothing is lost, but everything is transformed. The
          framework holds that each manifestation is a real expression of the identity, and
          that the manifestations are related by recursive manifestation; each manifestation
          is preserved, but transformed, in the next. Both hold that the movement is not a
          destruction, but a transformation, and that nothing is lost in the movement.

       4. The critique of abstraction. Hegel holds that the abstractions of the understanding
         (the thing-in-itself, the formal moral law) are one-sided; the truth is the concrete,
          the whole. The framework holds that the abstractions of the understanding (the
          isolated identity, the isolated manifestation) are one-sided; the truth is the relation,
          the structure. Both hold that abstraction is not the truth, and that the truth is the
          concrete whole.



23.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Hegel. The framework diverges from Hegel in four respects.

       1. The status of the dialectic. Hegel’s dialectic is a triadic movement (immediate, medi-
          ation, mediated unity); it is the movement of the concept through its contradictions.
         The framework’s structure is not triadic; it is a structure of expression, in which
          identities are enacted in manifestations. The framework has no dialectical movement;
          it has a structural relation. The distinction is between a dialectical process (Hegel’s)
          and a structural relation (the framework’s).
236                                                                                 Chapter 23. Hegel


       2. The status of the Geist. Hegel’s Geist is a collective subject; it is the spirit of
          a people, a culture, an age; it develops through history. The framework has no
          collective subject; its identities are enacted by one source, not by a collective spirit;
          its expression is a structural relation, not a historical development. The framework
          is a metaphysics without a collective subject.

       3. The status of the end of history. Hegel’s end of history is the realization of freedom,
          the self-consciousness of the Geist in its freedom. The framework has no end of
          history; its expression is never completed (the non-completion of expression); the
          movement of expression is not a movement toward an end. The framework is a
          metaphysics without an end of history.

       4. The status of the absolute. Hegel’s absolute is the totality of reality, the unity of
          subject and object, the identity of thinking and being. The framework has no
          absolute; its structure is not a totality, but a relation; its identity is not the absolute,
          but the invariance enacted by one source. The framework is a metaphysics without
          the absolute.




23.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Hegel’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
  its manifestations are related by expression. But a structural invariance is an abstraction;
  it is the one-sided unity that has not yet been mediated. The truth of the identity is not its
  invariance, but its development; the identity is not a static structure, but a living process.
  The framework’s identity is an abstraction; it is the seed without the plant, the immediate
  without the mediation. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of abstractions, not of
  the concrete whole.
  Hegel’s second objection. The framework says that expression is a structural tendency,
  not a dialectical movement. But a tendency without contradiction is a tendency without
  development; it is a movement without a motor. Hegel’s dialectic is the motor of develop-
  ment; contradiction is the ground of movement. The framework’s expression is a movement
  without contradiction; it is a movement that does not develop. The framework’s ontology
  is an ontology of static structures, not of living processes.
  Hegel’s third objection. The framework says that identity is the invariance enacted by
  one source, and that the source is a *this*-structure. But a *this*-structure is not the
  Geist; it is not the collective subject that develops through history. Without the Geist,
  there is no history; without history, there is no freedom. The framework’s ontology is an
  ontology without history, and an ontology without history is an ontology without freedom.
23.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      237


23.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an abstraction is one-sided, and
   it agrees that the truth is the concrete whole. But the framework denies that its identity
   is an abstraction. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
   *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its
   realm. The framework’s identity is not an abstraction; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls
   *act*. The distinction is between an abstraction (a one-sided unity) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a movement without
   contradiction is a movement without development, and it agrees that contradiction is the
   motor of movement. But the framework denies that its expression is a movement without
   contradiction. The framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the contradiction is
   between the identity and the receiving realm, between the invariant and the manifestation.
   The contradiction is structural, not dialectical; it is the tension between the source and its
   expression, not the self-contradiction of the concept. The distinction is between a dialectical
   contradiction (Hegel’s) and a structural tension (the framework’s); the framework holds
   the second, and it holds that the second is a kind of contradiction.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a *this*-structure is not the
   Geist, and it agrees that without the Geist there is no history in Hegel’s sense. But the
   framework denies that its ontology is without history. The framework’s ontology has a
   history: the history of the manifestations, the history of the realms, the history of the
   expression. The history is not the history of the Geist; it is the history of the identities
   and their manifestations. The distinction is between a history of spirit (Hegel’s) and a
   history of structure (the framework’s); the framework holds the second, and it holds that
   the second is a kind of history.



23.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Hegel’s cost. If Hegel accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
dialectic is the logic of reality. He must accept that the structure of expression is not dialectical,
and that contradiction is structural, not dialectical. The cost is the loss of the dialectical
movement: the real is no longer a self-developing process, but a structure of expression.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Hegel’s objections, it must give up the claim
that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the dimension
of dialectical development, of the Geist, of the end of history— that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
238                                                                             Chapter 23. Hegel


enactment of a structure, but not a moment of a dialectical process, and the framework leaves
the second to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Hegel’s dialectic is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Hegel
must accept that the framework’s structure is not an abstraction; it is a structural condition that
the dialectic presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of
the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


23.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Hegel’s
   term “the concept.” If one substitutes “the concept” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
   by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Hegel’s concept is the self-developing
   whole, and it is not manifested, because it is the whole. The framework’s identity is
   multiple; Hegel’s concept is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Hegel’s term “the
   dialectic.” If one substitutes “the dialectic” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation, and it is not a
   movement; Hegel’s dialectic is a movement, and it is not a structure. The framework’s
   expression is static; Hegel’s dialectic is dynamic. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Hegel is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is process, and they differ on whether the process is dialectical
   or structural. Both hold that the whole manifests itself in the parts, and they differ on
   whether the whole is the Geist or the structure. Neither relation is equivalence; neither
   is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Hegel would be refuted by
   showing that Hegel’s dialectic cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and process—by showing, that is, that Hegel already distinguishes the
   structural condition from the dialectical movement, and that the framework’s distinction
   is a development of Hegel’s own.



23.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Hegel’s concept, or is it a
departure from Hegel? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
23.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 239


not conclusive. A reader who holds that Hegel’s concept is already a structural condition, not a
dialectical movement, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of tension?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without a tension has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Phänomenologie do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the dialectic, the Aufhebung, the master-slave dialectic, the Geist, the
logic, the philosophy of history, the critique of Kant, and the end of history, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the Phänomenologie supports a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a unity and a process—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the unity that develops, or the process that unifies? Is the movement dialectical,
structural, or both? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Hegel’s dialectic
and the framework’s expression?

identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Kierkegaard; and it states the points of
240                                                                           Chapter 23. Hegel


convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the individual and the existential
is the nearest modern analogue to Kierkegaard’s. The present chapter has stated Hegel’s answer
to the problem of the whole; the next chapter states Kierkegaard’s answer, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.
