Kierkegaard


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Søren Kierkegaard. It states the three stages of existence
(the aesthetic, the ethical, the religious), the subjectivity of truth, the leap of faith, the absurd,
the critique of Hegel’s system, the analysis of despair and anxiety, the single individual, the
repetition, and the knight of faith, with reference to Enten–Eller (Either/Or), the Frygt og Bæven
(Fear and Trembling), the Sygdommen til Døden (The Sickness unto Death), the Afsluttende
uvidenskabelig Efterskrift (Concluding Unscientific Postscript), and the Begrebet Angest (The
Concept of Anxiety); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Kierkegaard;
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the
individual and the existential is the nearest modern analogue to Kierkegaard’s; it presents the
objections that Kierkegaard would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply;
it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “existence,” “the leap,” “the absurd,” “the single individual,” or “the stages,”
these are Kierkegaard’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


24.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is trying to decide how to live. She has read the philosophers; she has
read Hegel; she has understood the system. She knows that history is the development of the
Spirit; she knows that her life is a moment in that development; she knows that the system
explains everything. But she does not know how to live. The system explains everything, but it
does not tell her what to do; it is a Wissenschaft, a science, but her life is not a science.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she does not try to understand the system, but tries to
understand herself. She looks inward; she finds despair. She is not at peace with herself; she is
divided; she is a self that is not at one with itself. The despair is not a passing mood; it is a
structural condition; it is the sickness unto death, the sickness of the self that will not be itself,
or will not be the self that it is.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she does not try to understand herself,
but tries to decide. She stands at the edge of a decision; she must choose; but she does not know
what to choose; she cannot reason her way to the choice; the reasons are balanced; the choice
is a leap. The leap is not irrational; it is the act of the individual who chooses in the face of
uncertainty, who commits without guarantee, who becomes herself by choosing.
    The scene is Kierkegaard’s image, in Enten–Eller, in Frygt og Bæven, and in the Afsluttende
uvidenskabelig Efterskrift, of the structure of existence. The system is the Hegelian system; the
despair is the sickness of the self; the leap is the leap of faith. The individual is not a moment in

                                                 241
242                                                                      Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


the system; she is the single individual, the existing thinker, the one who must choose. The truth
is not the system; it is the subjective truth, the truth that is true for the existing individual.
      The scene poses the question that Kierkegaard was the first to pose in its full form. What
is existence? Is it a moment in the system, or the reality that the system cannot capture?
What is truth? Is it the objective truth of the system, or the subjective truth of the existing
individual? And what is faith? Is it the conclusion of an argument, or the leap of the individual
who commits without guarantee? The present chapter states Kierkegaard’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


24.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Hegel’s position: the dialectic, the Aufhebung, the master-slave
dialectic, the Geist, the logic, the philosophy of history, the critique of Kant, and the end of
history. Hegel is the great systematizer of the modern West, and Kierkegaard is his greatest
critic and his greatest antithesis. Kierkegaard accepts Hegel’s critique of Kant’s formalism, but
he rejects Hegel’s system, his absolute knowledge, and his absorption of the individual into the
collective. The present chapter states Kierkegaard’s critique, and the framework’s dialogue with
it.
      The question is not whether Kierkegaard was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Kierkegaard hold? The chapter states the three stages
of existence, the subjectivity of truth, the leap of faith, the absurd, the critique of Hegel, the
analysis of despair and anxiety, the single individual, the repetition, and the knight of faith, with
reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Kierkegaard converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Kierkegaard would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and
Kierkegaard? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


24.3       The Position

24.3.1      The Three Stages of Existence

Kierkegaard’s three stages of existence are stated in Enten–Eller (1843) and in the Afsluttende
uvidenskabelig Efterskrift (1846). The stages are not chronological stages; they are existential
possibilities; they are ways of existing, not periods of life.
24.3. The Position                                                                                243


First stage: the aesthetic. The aesthetic stage is the stage of the senses, of pleasure, of
the moment. The aesthete lives for the moment; she seeks the interesting, the pleasurable, the
beautiful; she avoids commitment, boredom, and repetition. The aesthete’s life is a series of
moments, each unrelated to the next; it is a life without continuity, without a self, without a
center. The aesthete’s representative is Don Juan, the seducer who lives for the pleasure of the
moment.


Second stage: the ethical. The ethical stage is the stage of commitment, of duty, of the
universal. The ethical person chooses herself; she commits to a vocation, to a marriage, to a
duty; she accepts the universal law, the law of reason, the law of morality. The ethical person’s
representative is Socrates, the one who chose the ethical life and died for it. The ethical stage is
higher than the aesthetic; it has continuity, selfhood, center. But it is not the highest stage; it is
still within the realm of the universal; it has not yet reached the religious.


Third stage: the religious. The religious stage is the stage of faith, of the absurd, of the
single individual before God. The religious person is not the universal; she is the single individual;
she stands before God alone; she is related to the absolute, not to the universal. The religious
person’s representative is Abraham, the knight of faith, the one who was willing to sacrifice Isaac,
the one whose faith is absurd, the one who is justified by faith, not by morality. The religious
stage is the highest; it is the stage of the leap of faith.
   The three stages are not a dialectical progression; they are not aufgehoben in the Hegelian
sense. They are existential possibilities; each is a way of existing; each has its own truth and its
own despair. The transition from one stage to the next is not a logical deduction; it is a leap.

   From the Tradition

   “There are three existence-spheres: the aesthetic, the ethical, the religious. The aesthetic
   is the sphere of immediacy; the ethical is the sphere of requirement; the religious is the
   sphere of fulfillment.” (Kierkegaard, Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift, trans. after
   Swenson-Lowrie)


24.3.2    The Subjectivity of Truth

Kierkegaard’s subjectivity of truth is stated in the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift. The
doctrine is a rejection of the objective truth of the Hegelian system: the truth is not the system;
the truth is the subjective truth, the truth that is true for the existing individual.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: objective truth is not existential truth. Objective truth is the truth of
propositions, of systems, of mathematics; it is the truth that can be stated, proved, and taught.
Existential truth is the truth of the individual’s relation to the truth; it is the truth that the
individual lives; it is the truth that is true for her. The two are different; objective truth does
not entail existential truth; the philosopher who knows the system does not thereby exist in the
truth.
244                                                                       Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


Second feature: subjectivity is truth. Subjectivity is truth; the truth is the individual’s
relation to the truth; the truth is the appropriation of the truth by the existing individual. The
subjectivity is not a defect of truth; it is the truth itself, in its existential dimension. The truth
is not a thing to be known; it is a relation to be lived.


Third feature: the paradox. The truth is a paradox; it is the truth that the eternal has
entered time, that God has become man; it is the truth that cannot be grasped by reason, that
can only be believed. The paradox is not a contradiction; it is the limit of reason; it is what
reason cannot master, and what faith can accept.
      The subjectivity of truth is the foundation of Kierkegaard’s existentialism. The truth is not
the system; the truth is the individual’s relation to the truth; the truth is the appropriation
of the truth by the existing individual. The truth is subjective; it is the truth of the single
individual before God.

   From the Tradition

   “The objective uncertainty held fast in an appropriation-process of the most passionate in-
   wardness is the truth, the highest truth attainable for an existing individual.” (Kierkegaard,
   Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift, trans. after Swenson-Lowrie)



24.3.3      The Leap of Faith

Kierkegaard’s leap of faith is stated in Frygt og Bæven (1843) and in the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig
Efterskrift. The leap is the act of the individual who commits to the truth without guarantee,
who chooses the truth without proof, who lives the truth without certainty.
      The leap has three features.


First feature: the leap is not irrational. The leap is not a denial of reason; it is the
recognition of the limits of reason. Reason can take us to the edge; it cannot take us across; the
leap is the act that takes us across. The leap is not against reason; it is beyond reason; it is the
act of the individual who has reached the limit of reason, and who chooses to believe.


Second feature: the leap is the act of the individual. The leap is not the act of the
crowd, of the community, of the system; it is the act of the single individual. The individual
stands alone before the choice; she cannot delegate the choice; she cannot hide in the crowd; she
must choose, and the choice is hers.


Third feature: the leap is the leap of faith. The leap is the leap of faith; it is the act
of believing what cannot be proved; it is the act of trusting what cannot be guaranteed. The
leap is the act of Abraham, who was willing to sacrifice Isaac; it is the act of the Christian, who
believes that God became man; it is the act of the individual, who chooses to live in the truth.
      The leap of faith is the core of Kierkegaard’s religious stage. The leap is not a proof; it is
not a conclusion; it is not a deduction; it is the act of the individual who chooses to believe.
24.3. The Position                                                                                  245


The leap is the highest act of existence; it is what makes the individual an individual; it is what
makes her a self.

   From the Tradition

   “Faith is precisely the paradox that the single individual as the particular is higher than
   the universal, is justified before it, not as inferior to it but as superior to it.” (Kierkegaard,
   Frygt og Bæven, trans. after Swenson)



24.3.4    The Absurd

Kierkegaard’s absurd is stated in Frygt og Bæven and in the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift.
The absurd is the object of faith; it is the truth that cannot be grasped by reason; it is the truth
that is beyond the limits of reason.
   The absurd has three features.


First feature: the absurd is not the contradictory. The absurd is not a logical contra-
diction; it is not the violation of the law of non-contradiction. The absurd is the truth that is
beyond reason; it is the truth that reason cannot master; it is the truth that is not against reason
but beyond reason.


Second feature: the absurd is the object of faith. The absurd is what faith believes; it is
the content of faith; it is the truth that the individual accepts in the leap of faith. The absurd is
not the absence of truth; it is the truth that transcends reason.


Third feature: the absurd is the absolute paradox. The absolute paradox is the paradox
that God became man; it is the paradox that the eternal entered time; it is the paradox that
cannot be resolved by reason, and that must be accepted by faith. The absolute paradox is the
content of Christian faith; it is the truth that the Christian believes.
   The absurd is the limit of reason. The absurd is what reason cannot reach; it is what reason
cannot master; it is what reason cannot explain. The absurd is the truth that is beyond reason;
it is the truth that is known by faith; it is the truth that is lived by the existing individual.


24.3.5    The Critique of Hegel

Kierkegaard’s critique of Hegel is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in the Afsluttende
uvidenskabelig Efterskrift and in the Sygdommen til Døden. The critique has three features.


First feature: the critique of the system. Hegel’s system is a system of absolute knowledge;
it claims to know everything; it claims to explain everything; it claims to absorb the individual
into the whole. But the system is not existence; it is a description of existence; it is a map, not
the territory. The existing individual cannot live in the system; she can only live in existence;
the system is not a home, but a museum.
246                                                                        Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


Second feature: the critique of the collective. Hegel’s Geist is a collective subject; it
is the spirit of a people, a culture, an age; it absorbs the individual into the whole. But the
individual is not a moment of the Geist; she is the single individual; she is the one who must
choose; she is the one who stands before God. The collective is not the truth; the individual is
the truth; the single individual is the truth of the truth.

Third feature: the critique of the mediator. Hegel’s philosophy is a philosophy of
mediation; everything is mediated; the immediate is aufgehoben in the mediated. But there is no
mediator between the individual and God; the individual stands alone before God; the relation is
direct, not mediated; the relation is existential, not systemic. The single individual before God
is the truth of existence.
      Kierkegaard’s critique is not a refutation of Hegel; it is a correction. Kierkegaard does not
deny the truth of the system; he denies that the system is the truth of existence. The system
may be true, but the truth of existence is subjective, not objective; it is the truth of the single
individual, not the truth of the whole.


24.3.6      The Analysis of Despair and Anxiety
Kierkegaard’s analysis of despair and anxiety is stated in Sygdommen til Døden (1849) and in
the Begrebet Angest (1844). The analysis has three features.

First feature: despair is the sickness of the self. Despair is the sickness of the self; it is
the sickness of the self that will not be itself, or will not be the self that it is. The despair is not
a passing mood; it is a structural condition; it is the condition of the self that is not at one with
itself.

Second feature: despair is universal. Despair is universal; every human being is in despair;
the despair may be hidden, may be unconscious, may be disguised as contentment; but it is
there; it is the condition of the self that is not grounded in God.

Third feature: anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom;
it is the dizziness that the individual feels when she stands at the edge of the choice; it is the
dizziness that the individual feels when she realizes that she is free, and that the choice is hers.
The anxiety is not a defect; it is the condition of freedom; it is what makes the choice possible.
      The analysis of despair and anxiety is the foundation of Kierkegaard’s psychology. The self is
not a substance; it is a relation; it is the relation that the self has to itself; and the self is not
at one with itself unless it is grounded in God. The despair is the sign of the self’s not being
grounded; the anxiety is the sign of the self’s freedom.

    From the Tradition

   “Despair is a sickness of the spirit, of the self, and accordingly can take three forms: in
    despair not to be conscious of having a self (not despair in the strict sense); in despair not
    to will to be oneself; in despair to will to be oneself.” (Kierkegaard, Sygdommen til Døden,
24.3. The Position                                                                                247


   trans. after Hong-Hong)


24.3.7    The Single Individual
Kierkegaard’s single individual (den Enkelte) is the central concept of his philosophy. The single
individual is not the individual as opposed to the collective; she is the individual as the one who
exists, who chooses, who stands before God.
   The single individual has three features.

First feature: the single individual is the existing thinker. The single individual is the
existing thinker; she is not the abstract thinker of the system; she is the thinker who exists, who
thinks in existence, who thinks about existence. The existing thinker is not the pure thinker; she
is the passionate thinker; she is the thinker whose thought is rooted in her existence.

Second feature: the single individual is the one who chooses. The single individual is
the one who chooses; she is the one who stands at the edge of the choice; she is the one who must
decide. The choice is not a deduction; it is a leap; it is the act of the individual who chooses in
the face of uncertainty.

Third feature: the single individual is the one before God. The single individual is the
one before God; she is the one who stands alone before God; she is the one whose relation to God
is direct, not mediated; she is the one whose existence is defined by her relation to the absolute.
   The single individual is the truth of Kierkegaard’s philosophy. The system is not the truth;
the collective is not the truth; the single individual is the truth; she is the one who exists, who
chooses, who stands before God. The single individual is the category through which the truth
of existence must be understood.

   From the Tradition

   “The crowd is untruth. The single individual is the truth. The single individual is
   the category through which the truth of existence must be understood.” (Kierkegaard,
   Synspunktet for min Forfatter-Virksomhed, trans. after Hong-Hong)


24.3.8    Repetition
Kierkegaard’s repetition (Gjentagelsen) is stated in Gjentagelsen (1843) and in the Afsluttende
uvidenskabelig Efterskrift. The repetition is the category of the ethical and the religious; it is the
category of the individual who chooses herself, who becomes herself, who repeats herself.
   The repetition has three features.

First feature: repetition is not recollection. Recollection is the Platonic category; it is
the recovery of what was lost; it is the return to the past. Repetition is the Christian category;
it is the recovery of what was lost, but in a new form; it is the return to the past, but as a new
future. Repetition is not the repetition of the same; it is the repetition of the self in a new form.
248                                                                          Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


Second feature: repetition is the movement of the self. Repetition is the movement
of the self; it is the self’s becoming itself; it is the self’s recovery of itself, in a new form, in a
new relation. The self that repeats itself is the self that has chosen itself, that has committed to
itself, that has become itself.

Third feature: repetition is the category of freedom. Repetition is the category of
freedom; it is the category of the self that is free, that chooses, that becomes. The self that
repeats itself is the self that is free; the self that does not repeat itself is the self that is enslaved
to the past, to the moment, to the aesthetic.
      The repetition is the foundation of Kierkegaard’s ethics. The ethical life is the life of
repetition; it is the life of the self that chooses itself, that commits to itself, that becomes itself.
The repetition is the movement of the self; it is the self’s becoming what it is.


24.3.9      The Knight of Faith
Kierkegaard’s knight of faith is stated in Frygt og Bæven. The knight of faith is the individual
who has made the leap of faith; she is the one who has accepted the absurd; she is the one who
has given up everything, and has received everything back.
      The knight of faith has three features.

First feature: the knight of faith is the knight of infinite resignation. The knight of
faith has first made the movement of infinite resignation; she has given up everything; she has
renounced the world; she has accepted the loss. The infinite resignation is the condition of faith;
it is what makes faith possible.

Second feature: the knight of faith makes the movement of faith. The knight of faith
then makes the movement of faith; she believes that she will receive everything back; she believes
that the loss will be restored; she believes that the absurd is true. The movement of faith is the
movement of Abraham, who was willing to sacrifice Isaac, and who believed that Isaac would be
restored.

Third feature: the knight of faith is the single individual. The knight of faith is the
single individual; she is the one who stands alone before God; she is the one whose faith is not
mediated by the universal, but is direct, immediate, existential. The knight of faith is the one
who is justified by faith, not by morality; she is the one who is higher than the universal.
      The knight of faith is the highest form of existence. She is the individual who has made the
leap, who has accepted the absurd, who has given up everything and received everything back.
She is the one who lives in the truth; she is the one who is the truth; she is the one who is the
single individual before God.

   From the Tradition

   “The knight of faith is the one who has made the movement of infinite resignation, and
   then, by virtue of the absurd, has received everything back.” (Kierkegaard, Frygt og Bæven,
24.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         249


   trans. after Swenson)




24.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Kierkegaard is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the stages. The traditional reading takes the three stages
to be a hierarchy: the aesthetic is the lowest, the ethical is higher, the religious is highest. A
revisionary reading takes them to be existential possibilities: each stage is a way of existing, and
none is simply "higher" than the others; the choice of stage is the choice of existence. The two
readings disagree on whether Kierkegaard is a hierarchical thinker or a pluralist about existence,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are
hierarchical, not pluralist.



Second dispute: the status of the leap. The traditional reading takes the leap to be an
irrational act: the leap is the sacrifice of reason, the acceptance of the absurd, the surrender
of the intellect. A revisionary reading takes it to be a rational act: the leap is the recognition
of the limits of reason, and the choice to go beyond them; it is not against reason but beyond
reason. The two readings disagree on whether Kierkegaard is a fideist or a rationalist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework is a rationalist
metaphysics, not a fideist one.



Third dispute: the status of the single individual. The traditional reading takes the
single individual to be the isolated individual, the one who stands alone, who rejects the crowd,
who rejects the community. A revisionary reading takes her to be the individual who is most
fully herself, and who is therefore most fully related to others; the single individual is not the
isolated individual, but the individual who is free from the crowd, and who is therefore free
for the community. The two readings disagree on whether Kierkegaard is an individualist or
a relational thinker, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s identity is relational, not isolated.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Kierkegaard is a fideist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a rationalist metaphysics and a fideist existentialism. If
Kierkegaard is a rationalist about the limits of reason, the dialogue is a dialogue between two
positions that the framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is
closer to the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift, but it does not rest its case on this reading;
it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
250                                                                      Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


24.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Kierkegaard. The framework shares four structural features with Kierkegaard’s
  position.

       1. The limits of the system. Kierkegaard holds that the system cannot capture existence;
         the existing individual is not a moment of the system; the system is a description, not
         the reality. The framework holds that no finite subject can know all manifestations
         of an identity in all contexts; the systematic knowledge is impossible; what remains
         is a pseudo-identity, partial and fallible. Both hold that the system has limits, and
         that the limits are structural, not contingent.

       2. The subjective truth. Kierkegaard holds that the truth is subjective; it is the
         individual’s relation to the truth; it is the appropriation of the truth by the existing
         individual. The framework holds that knowledge is reconstruction; it is the subject’s
         reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations; the reconstruction is not the
         truth itself, but the subject’s relation to the truth. Both hold that knowledge is
         situated, and that it is the subject’s relation to what is known.

       3. The individual. Kierkegaard holds that the individual is the truth; the single
         individual before God is the truth of existence; the collective is not the truth. The
         framework holds that identity is enacted by one source; the individual identity is the
         *this*, not a moment of the collective; the manifestations are many, but the identity
         is one. Both hold that the individual is irreducible to the collective, and that the
         individual is the site of the truth.

       4. The limits of reason. Kierkegaard holds that reason has limits; the absurd is beyond
         reason; the leap of faith is beyond reason. The framework holds that reason has
         limits; the impossibility of super-identity is a limit of reason; the recognition of the
         limit is the condition of knowledge. Both hold that reason has limits, and that the
         recognition of the limits is the condition of wisdom.



24.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Kierkegaard. The framework diverges from Kierkegaard in four respects.

       1. The status of faith. Kierkegaard holds that faith is the leap; it is the acceptance
         of the absurd; it is the highest form of existence. The framework has no faith; its
         knowledge is reconstruction, not belief; its relation to the truth is structural, not
         existential. The framework is a metaphysics without faith.
24.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  251


       2. The status of God. Kierkegaard’s existentialism is a Christian existentialism; the
          single individual stands before God; the leap of faith is the leap toward God. The
          framework has no God; its single individual is the source of the identity, not the one
         who stands before God. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       3. The status of the absurd. Kierkegaard holds that the absurd is the object of faith; it
          is the truth that reason cannot master. The framework has no absurd; its truths
          are structural, not absurd; they are what reason can reconstruct, though never
          completely. The framework is a metaphysics without the absurd.

       4. The status of the stages. Kierkegaard holds that there are three stages of existence
         (aesthetic, ethical, religious), and that the transition between them is a leap. The
          framework has no stages of existence; its realms are ontological levels, not existential
          stages; its structure is not a progression, but a hierarchy of expression. The framework
          is a metaphysics without existential stages.




24.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Kierkegaard’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   an abstraction; it is not an existence. Existence is not a structure; it is a task; it is what
   the individual must become; it is what the individual is in the process of becoming. The
   framework’s identity is an abstraction; it is not an existence; it is not a task; it is not what
   the individual must become. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of abstractions, not
   of existences.
   Kierkegaard’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction
   is not existence; it is not the individual’s relation to the truth; it is not the appropriation
   of the truth by the existing individual. The framework’s knowledge is objective; it is the
   knowledge of the structure; it is not the subjective truth, the truth that is true for the
   existing individual. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of objectivity, not
   of subjectivity.
   Kierkegaard’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure,
   not existence. But a metaphysics without existence is an incomplete metaphysics; the
   individual is not only a knower, but also an exister; the task of existence is as fundamental
   as the knowledge of structure. The framework’s silence on existence is not a boundary; it
   is a gap.
252                                                                      Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


24.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an abstraction is not an
   existence, and it agrees that existence is a task. But the framework denies that its identity
   is an abstraction. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
   *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its
   realm. The framework’s identity is not an abstraction; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls
   *act*. The distinction is between an abstraction (a one-sided unity) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction is not
   existence, and it agrees that the subjective truth is not the objective truth. But the
   framework denies that its epistemology is an epistemology of objectivity. The framework’s
   knowledge is reconstruction; it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the
   manifestations; the reconstruction is the subject’s relation to the truth; it is not the truth
   itself, but the subject’s appropriation of the truth. The distinction is between an objective
   knowledge (a description of the structure) and a reconstructive knowledge (the subject’s
   relation to the structure); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is
   a kind of knowledge.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without
   existence is incomplete, and it agrees that the individual is not only a knower but also an
   exister. But the framework denies that its silence on existence is a gap. The framework
   is a work of metaphysics, not of ethics or of existential philosophy; its subject is the
   structure of identity and manifestation, not the task of existence. The framework states
   the structural condition of reality; it leaves the task of existence to a separate inquiry.
   The distinction is between a metaphysics and an ethics or an existential philosophy; the
   framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it is not a gap but a boundary.



24.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Kierkegaard’s cost. If Kierkegaard accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that existence is not a structure. He must accept that existence is enacted in a structure, and
that the structure is not an abstraction but an enactment. The cost is the loss of the radical
existentialism: existence is no longer simply the task of the individual, but the enactment of a
structure.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Kierkegaard’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of existence, of the task, of the leap of faith—that its ontology does not capture. The
24.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      253


cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not the task of existence, and the framework leaves the second to
a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Kierkegaard’s existence
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Kierkegaard must accept that the framework’s structure is not an abstraction; it is a structural
condition that existence presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


24.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Kierkegaard’s term “the single individual.” If one substitutes “the single individual”
   for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s iden-
   tity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Kierkegaard’s
   single individual is the existing thinker, the one who chooses, the one who stands be-
   fore God. The framework’s identity is multiple; Kierkegaard’s single individual is the
   one who exists, not one of many identities. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable
   for Kierkegaard’s term “the leap.” If one substitutes “the leap” for “expression” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural
   relation; Kierkegaard’s leap is an existential act. The framework’s expression is structural;
   Kierkegaard’s leap is existential. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Kierkegaard is resem-
   blance: both hold that the system has limits, and they differ on whether the limits are
   structural or existential. Both hold that the individual is irreducible, and they differ on
   whether the individual is a structure or an existence. Neither relation is equivalence; neither
   is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Kierkegaard would be refuted
   by showing that Kierkegaard’s existence cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and existence—by showing, that is, that Kierkegaard already
   distinguishes the structural condition from the existential task, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of Kierkegaard’s own.



24.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
254                                                                     Chapter 24. Kierkegaard


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Kierkegaard’s single individual,
or is it a departure from Kierkegaard? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Kierkegaard’s single individual is already a
structural condition, not an existence, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift do
justice to the text? The chapter has used the stages, the subjectivity of truth, the leap of faith,
the absurd, the critique of Hegel, the analysis of despair and anxiety, the single individual, the
repetition, and the knight of faith, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift supports a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection

Consider a thing you know that is both a system and an existence—a person, a tradition, a
text. Is the thing the system that explains it, or the existence that exceeds the system? Is the
truth the objective truth of the system, or the subjective truth of the existing individual? What
24.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                255


does your answer tell you about the relation between Kierkegaard’s single individual and the
framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Nietzsche. It states the will to power, the eternal return, the Übermensch,
the death of God, the master and slave morality, and the amor fati; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Nietzsche; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of power and creation is the nearest modern
analogue to Nietzsche’s. The present chapter has stated Kierkegaard’s answer to the problem of
existence; the next chapter states Nietzsche’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 25

Nietzsche


Scope. This chapter closes Part IV, the dialogues with the modern West, and it closes it with
Friedrich Nietzsche. It states the will to power (Wille zur Macht), the eternal recurrence (ewige
Wiederkunft), the Übermensch, the death of God, the master and slave morality, ressentiment,
nihilism, perspectivism, amor fati, and the revaluation of all values, with reference to Also sprach
Zarathustra, Jenseits von Gut und Böse, Zur Genealogie der Moral, Die fröhliche Wissenschaft,
and Ecce Homo; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Nietzsche; it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of power and
creation is the nearest modern analogue to Nietzsche’s; it presents the objections that Nietzsche
would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side
costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “will
to power,” “eternal recurrence,” “Übermensch,” “nihilism,” “ressentiment,” or “amor fati,” these
are Nietzsche’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive tradition, not
by the framework.



25.1     A Scene

Consider a person who has lost her faith. She was raised in a tradition; she believed its teachings;
she ordered her life by its commandments. Then she loses the faith. The teachings seem to her
to be fables; the commandments seem to her to be chains; the order seems to her to be a cage.
And with the faith, she loses the ground of her values. If God is dead, she asks, what is the
ground of good and evil? If the tradition is a fable, what is the ground of truth? She stands at
the edge of an abyss; the ground has given way; she does not know where to stand.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she does not fall into the abyss, but asks what lies on
the other side. If God is dead, she says, then the human being is free; free to create values, free
to create herself, free to become what she is. The death of God is not a catastrophe; it is an
opportunity; it is the opening of a space in which the human being can become the creator of
her own values. This is the Übermensch: the one who has passed beyond the old values, who
creates new values, who lives without the comfort of the metaphysical ground.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what lies on the other side,
but what the whole is. The whole is not a system; it is not a moral order; it is not a purpose.
The whole is the will to power: the striving of every living thing to expand, to dominate, to
overcome. The whole is the eternal recurrence: the possibility that everything that has happened
will happen again, eternally, without end. And the whole is amor fati: the love of fate, the
affirmation of what is, the acceptance of the eternal recurrence.

                                                256
25.2. The Question                                                                               257


   The scene is Nietzsche’s image, in Also sprach Zarathustra and in Die fröhliche Wissenschaft,
of the structure of reality after the death of God. The old values have collapsed; the abyss
has opened; the Übermensch has appeared; the will to power has been affirmed; the eternal
recurrence has been embraced. The scene poses the question that Nietzsche was the first to pose
in its full form. What is the ground of value, after the death of God? What is the human being,
if not the image of God? And what is reality, if not a moral order? The present chapter states
Nietzsche’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


25.2      The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Hume, Kant,
Hegel, and Kierkegaard. Descartes posed the problem of the foundation; Spinoza posed the
problem of the one substance; Leibniz posed the problem of the many monads; Locke and
Hume posed the problem of empirical knowledge; Kant posed the problem of the conditions of
experience; Hegel posed the problem of the dialectical whole; Kierkegaard posed the problem
of the existing individual. Nietzsche is the last great figure of the modern West, and he is the
great diagnostician of the crisis of modernity: he announces the death of God, the collapse of the
metaphysical ground, the advent of nihilism. The present chapter states Nietzsche’s diagnosis,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Nietzsche was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Nietzsche hold? The chapter states the will to power, the
eternal recurrence, the Übermensch, the death of God, the master and slave morality, ressentiment,
nihilism, perspectivism, and amor fati, with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Nietzsche converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Nietzsche would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Nietzsche?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


25.3      The Position

25.3.1    The Death of God

Nietzsche’s announcement of the death of God is stated in Die fröhliche Wissenschaft (1882),
§125, in the parable of the madman, and in Also sprach Zarathustra. The announcement is not a
theological claim; it is a cultural diagnosis: the belief in God has collapsed; the metaphysical
ground of the old values has given way; the human being stands without a ground.
   The death of God has three features.
258                                                                         Chapter 25. Nietzsche


First feature: the collapse of the metaphysical ground. The belief in God was the
ground of the old values; the good was good because God commanded it; the true was true
because God guaranteed it; the beautiful was beautiful because God created it. With the death
of God, the ground has collapsed; the old values have lost their foundation.


Second feature: the advent of nihilism. The collapse of the ground produces nihilism:
the sense that nothing has value, nothing has meaning, nothing has ground. Nihilism is not the
denial of God; it is the condition that follows the death of God; it is the condition of the human
being who has lost the ground of value.


Third feature: the opportunity of the Übermensch. The death of God is not only a
catastrophe; it is also an opportunity. The human being who has passed beyond the old values can
create new values; she can become the creator of her own values; she can become the Übermensch.
The death of God is the opening of a space in which the human being can become what she is.

   From the Tradition

   “God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him! How shall we console ourselves,
   the murderers of all murderers? The holiest and the mightiest of all that the world has yet
   possessed has bled to death under our knives; who will wipe this blood off us?” (Nietzsche,
   Die fröhliche Wissenschaft §125, trans. after Kaufmann)



25.3.2      The Will to Power

Nietzsche’s will to power (Wille zur Macht) is stated throughout his works, but most clearly
in Jenseits von Gut und Böse (1886) and in the posthumous notes collected as Der Wille zur
Macht. The will to power is the fundamental drive of all living things: the drive to expand, to
dominate, to overcome.
      The will to power has three features.


First feature: it is the essence of life. The will to power is not a psychological drive, like
the will to pleasure or the will to self-preservation; it is the essence of life itself. Every living
thing strives to expand its power; every living thing seeks to overcome resistance; every living
thing seeks to grow. The will to power is the inner dynamic of life.


Second feature: it is not the will to domination. The will to power is not the crude will
to dominate others; it is the drive to overcome oneself, to surpass oneself, to become more than
one is. The will to power is the drive to self-overcoming; it is what makes life creative; it is what
makes life grow.


Third feature: it is the ground of value. The will to power is the ground of value: the
good is what enhances the will to power; the bad is what diminishes it. The value is not in the
object; it is in the relation between the object and the will to power; it is the enhancement of life.
25.3. The Position                                                                              259


   The will to power is the foundation of Nietzsche’s philosophy. It is what remains after the
death of God; it is the ground of the new values; it is the creative principle of the world.

   From the Tradition

   “This world is the will to power—and nothing besides! And you yourselves are also this
   will to power—and nothing besides!” (Nietzsche, Der Wille zur Macht §1067, trans. after
   Kaufmann)


25.3.3       The Eternal Recurrence
Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence (ewige Wiederkunft) is stated in Die fröhliche Wissenschaft §341
and in Also sprach Zarathustra. The eternal recurrence is the thought that everything that has
happened will happen again, eternally, without end; that every moment, every joy, every sorrow,
every thought will return, in exactly the same way, forever.
   The eternal recurrence has three features.

First feature: it is a test. The eternal recurrence is a test of the individual’s affirmation of
life: if she can affirm that everything will return, exactly as it was, then she has affirmed life
completely; if she cannot, she has not affirmed life. The eternal recurrence is the test of the
amor fati.

Second feature: it is a cosmology. The eternal recurrence is not only a test; it is also a
cosmology. The world has no beginning and no end; it is a finite quantity of force, in an infinite
time; and therefore every configuration of force must return, infinitely often. The cosmology is
speculative, but it is the cosmological expression of the affirmation of life.

Third feature: it is the ground of amor fati. The eternal recurrence is the ground of
amor fati: the love of fate, the affirmation of what is, the acceptance of everything, including the
suffering, the loss, the death. The one who loves fate loves the eternal recurrence; the one who
loves the eternal recurrence loves fate.
   The eternal recurrence is the highest thought of Nietzsche’s philosophy. It is the thought
that tests the individual; it is the thought that affirms life; it is the thought that makes the
Übermensch possible.


25.3.4       The Übermensch
Nietzsche’s Übermensch is stated in Also sprach Zarathustra (1883–85), in the prologue and in
the speeches of Zarathustra. The Übermensch is the overman, the one who has passed beyond the
old values, who creates new values, who lives without the comfort of the metaphysical ground.
   The Übermensch has three features.

First feature: the Übermensch is the creator of values. The Übermensch is not the one
who obeys the old values; she is the one who creates new values. She does not find the values
ready-made; she makes them; she is the source of the values. The Übermensch is the creator.
260                                                                         Chapter 25. Nietzsche


Second feature: the Übermensch is the one who has overcome herself. The Übermensch
is not the one who has conquered others; she is the one who has conquered herself. She has
overcome the old values in herself; she has overcome the ressentiment in herself; she has overcome
the temptation to escape into the beyond. She is the one who has become what she is.


Third feature: the Übermensch is the meaning of the earth. The Übermensch is not
the one who hopes for another world; she is the one who affirms this world. She is the meaning
of the earth; she is the one who gives meaning to the earth; she is the one who lives without the
consolation of the beyond. "Remain faithful to the earth, my brothers, and do not believe those
who speak to you of superterrestrial hopes!"
      The Übermensch is the highest form of the human being, in Nietzsche’s philosophy. She is
the one who has passed beyond the human being; she is the one who has become what she is;
she is the one who has created the new values.

   From the Tradition

   “I teach you the Übermensch. Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you
   done to overcome him? All beings so far have created something beyond themselves; and
   do you want to be the ebb of this great flood, and even go back to the beasts rather than
   overcome man?” (Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra, Prologue §3, trans. after Kaufmann)


25.3.5      Master and Slave Morality

Nietzsche’s distinction between master and slave morality is stated in Zur Genealogie der Moral
(1887), in the First Essay. The distinction is a genealogy of morality: it shows the origin of the
moral values in the will to power.
      The distinction has three features.


First feature: master morality. Master morality is the morality of the strong, the noble, the
powerful. It evaluates by the standard of the good: the good is what is strong, noble, powerful;
the bad is what is weak, base, slavish. Master morality says "yes" to life; it affirms the world; it
creates its own values.


Second feature: slave morality. Slave morality is the morality of the weak, the oppressed,
the powerless. It evaluates by the standard of the good: the good is what is weak, humble,
patient; the evil is what is strong, noble, powerful. Slave morality says "no" to life; it denies the
world; it resents the strong.


Third feature: ressentiment. The slave morality is born from ressentiment: the resentment
of the weak against the strong, the envy of the powerless against the powerful, the hatred of the
base against the noble. The slave morality is the revenge of the weak; it is the inversion of the
master values; it is the triumph of the weak.
      The master-slave distinction is the key to Nietzsche’s genealogy of morality. It shows that
morality is not a given; it is a creation; it is the expression of the will to power. The master
25.3. The Position                                                                               261


morality is the expression of the strong; the slave morality is the expression of the weak. The
two are not the same; the two are not equally valid; the master morality is higher, because it is
the expression of life.

   From the Tradition

   “The slave revolt in morality begins when ressentiment itself becomes creative and gives
   birth to values: the ressentiment of those beings who, being denied the proper response of
   action, compensate for it only with imaginary revenge.” (Nietzsche, Zur Genealogie der
   Moral I.10, trans. after Kaufmann)



25.3.6       Nihilism

Nietzsche’s diagnosis of nihilism is stated in Der Wille zur Macht and in Jenseits von Gut und
Böse. Nihilism is the condition that follows the death of God: the condition of the human being
who has lost the ground of value, who has lost the meaning of life, who has lost the purpose of
existence.
   Nihilism has three features.


First feature: passive nihilism. Passive nihilism is the nihilism of the weak; it is the
recognition that there is no ground, but it is the recognition without the strength to create a
new ground. Passive nihilism is the despair that follows the death of God; it is the paralysis of
the will.


Second feature: active nihilism. Active nihilism is the nihilism of the strong; it is the
recognition that there is no ground, and it is the recognition with the strength to create a new
ground. Active nihilism is the destruction of the old values; it is the clearing of the ground for
the new values.


Third feature: the overcoming of nihilism. The overcoming of nihilism is the creation of
new values; it is the work of the Übermensch; it is the affirmation of life. Nihilism is not the end;
it is the passage; it is the night before the dawn.
   Nihilism is the diagnosis of the modern condition. It is not a philosophy; it is a condition; it
is the condition of the human being who has lost the ground. The overcoming of nihilism is the
task of the new philosophy; it is the task of the Übermensch.


25.3.7       Perspectivism

Nietzsche’s perspectivism is stated in Jenseits von Gut und Böse and in Zur Genealogie der Moral.
Perspectivism is the doctrine that there is no view from nowhere; there are only perspectives;
each perspective is a way of seeing; each perspective is valid in its own way.
   Perspectivism has three features.
262                                                                              Chapter 25. Nietzsche


First feature: no facts, only interpretations. There are no facts; there are only interpre-
tations. What we call a fact is an interpretation that has become stable; what we call truth is a
perspective that has become dominant. The world is not a given; it is an interpretation; it is a
construction.


Second feature: the plurality of perspectives. There are many perspectives; each is a
way of seeing; each is valid in its own way. The perspectives are not reducible to one; they are
not all saying the same thing; they are many; they are irreducible.


Third feature: the will to power in interpretation. The interpretation is not neutral;
it is the expression of the will to power. The one who interprets is the one who imposes her
perspective; the one who knows is the one who dominates. Knowledge is a form of power; truth
is a form of will.
      Perspectivism is the epistemological expression of the will to power. It is not a relativism;
it is not the view that all perspectives are equally valid; it is the view that all perspectives are
expressions of the will to power, and that the strong perspective is the one that imposes itself.

   From the Tradition

   “There are no facts, only interpretations.” (Nietzsche, Der Wille zur Macht §481, trans.
   after Kaufmann)


25.3.8      Amor Fati

Nietzsche’s amor fati is stated in Die fröhliche Wissenschaft and in Ecce Homo. Amor fati is the
love of fate: the affirmation of what is; the acceptance of everything, including the suffering, the
loss, the death; the love of the eternal recurrence.
      Amor fati has three features.


First feature: the affirmation of life. Amor fati is the affirmation of life; it is the "yes" to
everything that is; it is the acceptance of the joy and the sorrow, the pleasure and the pain, the
life and the death. It is not the resignation to fate; it is the love of fate.


Second feature: the greatness of the soul. Amor fati is the sign of the greatness of the
soul; the one who loves fate has a great soul; she can embrace the whole; she can affirm the whole.
The small soul cannot love fate; she can only resent it; she can only wish it were otherwise.


Third feature: the eternal recurrence. Amor fati is the love of the eternal recurrence; the
one who loves fate loves the return of everything; she loves the eternal return of the same. The
one who loves the eternal recurrence has passed the test; she has affirmed life completely.
      Amor fati is the highest virtue of Nietzsche’s philosophy. It is the virtue of the Übermensch;
it is the virtue of the one who has overcome nihilism; it is the virtue of the one who has become
what she is.
25.4. Internal Disputes                                                                           263


   From the Tradition

   “My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be
   different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity. Not merely bear what is necessary,
   still less conceal it—but love it.” (Nietzsche, Ecce Homo, trans. after Kaufmann)


25.3.9    The Revaluation of All Values
Nietzsche’s revaluation of all values (Umwertung aller Werte) is stated in Der Wille zur Macht
and in Ecce Homo. The revaluation is the creation of new values, after the death of God; it is
the work of the Übermensch; it is the overcoming of nihilism.
   The revaluation has three features.

First feature: the critique of the old values. The revaluation begins with the critique of
the old values; it shows that the old values are expressions of the slave morality; it shows that
the old values are the product of ressentiment; it shows that the old values deny life.

Second feature: the creation of the new values. The revaluation continues with the
creation of the new values; it creates the values that affirm life; it creates the values that enhance
the will to power; it creates the values that are the expression of the strong.

Third feature: the revaluation is a task. The revaluation is not a doctrine; it is a task; it
is the task of the Übermensch; it is the task of the new philosophy. The revaluation is not yet
accomplished; it is the work that remains to be done.
   The revaluation is the goal of Nietzsche’s philosophy. It is the creation of the new values;
it is the overcoming of nihilism; it is the affirmation of life. The revaluation is the task of the
Übermensch; it is the task of the philosophy of the future.


25.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Nietzsche is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the will to power. The traditional reading takes the will to
power to be a metaphysical principle: all reality is will to power; everything is the expression of
the will to power. A revisionary reading takes it to be a psychological hypothesis: the will to
power is the fundamental drive of living things, not a metaphysical principle; it is a description
of life, not of reality. The two readings disagree on whether Nietzsche is a metaphysician or a
naturalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
expression is a structural relation, not a drive.

Second dispute: the status of the eternal recurrence. The traditional reading takes
the eternal recurrence to be a cosmology: the world really does return, eternally; the eternal
recurrence is a factual claim about the structure of time. A revisionary reading takes it to be
a test: the eternal recurrence is a thought-experiment, a test of the individual’s affirmation of
264                                                                         Chapter 25. Nietzsche


life; it is not a factual claim, but an existential test. The two readings disagree on whether
Nietzsche is a cosmologist or an existentialist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework has no eternal recurrence, but it has a structural recurrence
(the non-completion of expression).

Third dispute: the status of the Übermensch. The traditional reading takes the Übermen-
sch to be a future species: the Übermensch is the next stage of human evolution, the being who
will come after the human being. A revisionary reading takes the Übermensch to be an ideal: the
Übermensch is a symbol of the human being who has overcome herself, not a biological species; it
is a possibility, not a destiny. The two readings disagree on whether Nietzsche is a biological
evolutionist or an existential idealist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework has no species, but it has the individual who enacts her identity.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Nietzsche is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of will to power.
If Nietzsche is a naturalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


25.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Nietzsche. The framework shares four structural features with Nietzsche’s position.

        1. The rejection of the metaphysical ground. Nietzsche holds that there is no meta-
           physical ground; the death of God is the collapse of the ground; the world has no
           foundation in a beyond. The framework holds that there is no absolute ground;
           the structure of identity and manifestation is not grounded in a beyond; it is the
           structure itself. Both hold that the ground is not in a beyond, and that the world is
           not founded on a metaphysical absolute.

        2. The priority of process over substance. Nietzsche holds that reality is will to power,
           a process of overcoming, not a static substance. The framework holds that reality is
           expression, a process of enactment, not a static substance. Both hold that reality is
           dynamic, not static, and that the dynamic is the truth of the static.

        3. The plurality of perspectives. Nietzsche holds that there is no view from nowhere;
           there are only perspectives; each is valid in its own way. The framework holds that
           knowledge is reconstruction; it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from
           the manifestations; there is no complete knowledge of the identity; there are only
           pseudo-identities, partial and fallible. Both hold that knowledge is situated, and
           that no perspective is complete.

        4. The affirmation of life. Nietzsche holds that amor fati is the highest virtue; the
25.6. Points of Divergence                                                                       265


         affirmation of life is the affirmation of the whole, including the suffering. The
         framework holds that the expression of the identity is a structural tendency; the
         identity expresses itself necessarily, and the manifestation is the expression of the
         identity. Both hold that the world is to be affirmed, not denied, and that the
         affirmation is the truth of existence.




25.6      Points of Divergence


   Points of Divergence

   With Nietzsche. The framework diverges from Nietzsche in four respects.

       1. The status of the will to power. Nietzsche holds that the will to power is the
         fundamental drive of all living things; it is the essence of life; it is the creative
         principle of the world. The framework has no will to power; its identities are not
         drives; their expression is a structural tendency, not a will. The framework is a
         metaphysics without the will to power.

       2. The status of the eternal recurrence. Nietzsche holds that the eternal recurrence is
         the highest thought; it is the test of the affirmation of life; it is the cosmology of
         the will to power. The framework has no eternal recurrence; its expression is never
         completed (the non-completion of expression); the return is not the return of the
         same, but the ongoing expression of the identity. The framework is a metaphysics
         without the eternal recurrence.

       3. The status of the Übermensch. Nietzsche holds that the Übermensch is the meaning
         of the earth; she is the creator of values; she is the one who has overcome herself.
         The framework has no Übermensch; its individual is the source of the identity, not
         the creator of values; her task is not to create values, but to reconstruct the identity
         from the manifestations. The framework is a metaphysics without the Übermensch.

       4. The status of nihilism. Nietzsche holds that nihilism is the condition of modernity;
         it is the collapse of the metaphysical ground; it is the task of the Übermensch to
         overcome it. The framework has no nihilism; its structure is not grounded in a
         beyond, but it is also not in crisis; the structure is what it is, and the reconstruction
         is possible within the structure. The framework is a metaphysics without nihilism.
266                                                                      Chapter 25. Nietzsche


25.7    The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Nietzsche’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  a fiction; it is the invention of the weak; it is the slave morality in epistemological form.
  The strong do not need the invariance; they create their own values; they affirm the flux;
  they live without the comfort of the structure. The framework’s identity is a fiction; it is
  the ressentiment of the weak against the flux. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
  fictions, not of the will to power.
  Nietzsche’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction
  is a form of domination; it is the will to power in epistemological form. The one who
  reconstructs is the one who imposes her perspective; the one who knows is the one who
  dominates. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of domination; it is the slave
  morality in epistemological form.
  Nietzsche’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not
  value. But a metaphysics without value is an incomplete metaphysics; the question of
  value is the fundamental question; the question of the meaning of existence is the question
  of philosophy. The framework’s silence on value is not a boundary; it is a flight; it is
  the flight from the task of the Übermensch. The framework’s philosophy is a philosophy
  without value, and a philosophy without value is a philosophy without life.



25.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an invention is a fiction, and
  it agrees that the weak may invent fictions to console themselves. But the framework
  denies that its identity is a fiction. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
  by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of
  the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a fiction; it is the structural
  condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what
  the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a fiction (an invention) and an
  enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The
  framework’s identity is not the ressentiment of the weak; it is the structure of the strong.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction can be a
  form of domination, and it agrees that the strong impose their perspective on the weak.
  But the framework denies that its reconstruction is a form of domination. The framework’s
  reconstruction is a structural relation; it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity
  from the manifestations; it is not the imposition of a perspective, but the reading of a
25.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                      267


   structure. The distinction is between a domination (the imposition of a perspective) and a
   reconstruction (the reading of a structure); the framework holds the second, and it holds
   that the second is a kind of knowledge, not a kind of domination.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without value
   is an incomplete metaphysics, and it agrees that the question of value is a fundamental
   question. But the framework denies that its silence on value is a flight. The framework
   is a work of metaphysics, not of ethics or of value theory; its subject is the structure of
   identity and manifestation, not the value of existence. The framework states the structural
   condition of reality; it leaves the question of value to a separate inquiry. The distinction is
   between a metaphysics and an ethics; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it
   is not a flight, but a boundary.




25.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Nietzsche’s cost. If Nietzsche accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
identity is a fiction. He must accept that identity is a structural condition, enacted by one source,
and that the structure is not the ressentiment of the weak. The cost is the loss of the radical
perspectivism: identity is no longer a fiction, but a structure; the structure is not a perspective,
but a condition.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Nietzsche’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the will to power, of the Übermensch, of the eternal recurrence—that its ontology
does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the
framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a will to power, and the framework
leaves the second to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Nietzsche’s will to power
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Nietzsche must accept that the framework’s structure is not a fiction; it is a structural condition
that the will to power presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.
268                                                                       Chapter 25. Nietzsche


25.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ni-
   etzsche’s term “the will to power.” If one substitutes “the will to power” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Nietzsche’s will to
   power is the fundamental drive of all living things, and it is not enacted in a realm,
   because it is the essence of life. The framework’s identity is multiple; Nietzsche’s will
   to power is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Nietzsche’s term “the eternal
   recurrence.” If one substitutes “the eternal recurrence” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation,
   and it is never completed; Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence is the return of the same, and it
   is completed, because it is eternal. The framework’s expression is incomplete; Nietzsche’s
   eternal recurrence is complete. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Nietzsche is resemblance:
   both reject the metaphysical ground, and they differ on whether the ground is replaced
   by the structure or by the will to power. Both hold that reality is dynamic, and they
   differ on whether the dynamic is the structure or the will. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Nietzsche would
   be refuted by showing that Nietzsche’s will to power cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and drive—by showing, that is, that Nietzsche
   already distinguishes the structural condition from the drive, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of Nietzsche’s own.



25.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Nietzsche’s will to power, or is it
a departure from Nietzsche? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Nietzsche’s will to power is already a structural
condition, not a drive, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Also sprach Zarathustra do justice to the
text? The chapter has used the death of God, the will to power, the eternal recurrence, the
25.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                             269


Übermensch, the master and slave morality, nihilism, perspectivism, amor fati, and the revaluation
of all values, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the text
supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a structure and a will—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the structure that persists, or the will that overcomes? Is the truth the
structure that is reconstructed, or the perspective that is imposed? What does your answer tell
you about the relation between Nietzsche’s will to power and the framework’s identity?

Part IV is now complete. The dialogues with the eight great figures of the modern West—Descartes,
Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke and Hume, Kant, Hegel, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche—have been stated.
Part V turns to the contemporary West. The first dialogue is with Husserl, on phenomenology and
the life-world; the next with Heidegger, on being, time, and technology; the next with Whitehead,
on process and reality; the next with Wittgenstein, on language and forms of life; the next with
Quine and Davidson, on naturalism and interpretation; the next with Kripke and Lewis, on
modality and possible worlds; and the last with Derrida and Deleuze, on deconstruction and
difference. The modern West has questioned the ground; the contemporary West will question the
question itself.

The Contemporary West
