Husserl


Scope. This chapter opens Part V, the dialogues with the contemporary West, and it opens it
with Edmund Husserl. It states the phenomenological method, the intentionality of consciousness,
the epoché and the reductions, the life-world (Lebenswelt), the crisis of the European sciences,
intersubjectivity, and the time-consciousness, with reference to the Logische Untersuchungen,
the Ideen zu einer reinen Phänomenologie und phänomenologischen Philosophie, the Cartesian-
ische Meditationen, and the Krisis der europäischen Wissenschaften und die transzendentale
Phänomenologie; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Husserl; it states
the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the structural
conditions of cognition is the nearest modern analogue to Husserl’s transcendental phenomenol-
ogy; it presents the objections that Husserl would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “intentionality,” “epoché,” “reduction,” “life-world,” “noema,”
or “noesis,” these are Husserl’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


26.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a tree. She sees the trunk, the branches, the leaves, the
green of the leaves, the shadow of the trunk on the grass. She sees the tree from one side, then
from another; she walks around it, and the tree presents itself from many angles; each angle is
different, and yet each is an angle of the same tree. The tree is one; the appearances are many;
and the appearances are not the tree, but they are the tree’s way of appearing.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she does not look at the tree, but at her looking at
the tree. She does not see the tree; she sees her seeing; she does not see the green; she sees her
perceiving the green. The seeing has a structure: it is a seeing of something; it is intentional;
it is directed toward an object. The tree is the object of her seeing; her seeing is the act; and
between them, there is the relation of intentionality.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what she is seeing, or what
her seeing is, but what the world is that makes her seeing possible. The world is not just the
sum of the things she sees; it is the horizon in which the things appear; it is the background
against which the things stand out; it is the Lebenswelt, the life-world, the world as it is lived,
before it is theorized, before it is mathematized, before it is objectified. The life-world is the
foundation of the sciences; the sciences presuppose it, and cannot replace it.
   The scene is Husserl’s image, in the Ideen and in the Krisis, of the structure of experience.
The tree is the intentional object; the seeing is the intentional act; the life-world is the horizon in

                                                 271
272                                                                            Chapter 26. Husserl


which both appear. The phenomenological method is the way to describe this structure: the
epoché suspends the natural attitude; the reduction leads back to the transcendental subjectivity;
and the description reveals the essential structures of experience.
      The scene poses the question that Husserl was the first to pose in its full form. What is the
structure of consciousness? Is consciousness a thing, a substance, or an intentional act? What is
the world that consciousness inhabits? Is it the objectified world of the sciences, or the lived
world of everyday experience? And what is the method by which we can describe the structure
of experience without presupposing it? The present chapter states Husserl’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


26.2       The Question
The previous part stated the positions of the modern West: Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke
and Hume, Kant, Hegel, Kierkegaard, and Nietzsche. Descartes posed the problem of the
foundation; Kant posed the problem of the conditions of experience; Hegel posed the problem of
the dialectical whole; Nietzsche posed the problem of value after the death of God. Husserl is
the founder of phenomenology, and he is the philosopher who attempts to renew philosophy as a
rigorous science: he turns from the metaphysical systems to the things themselves; he suspends
the natural attitude; he describes the essential structures of experience. The present chapter
states Husserl’s renewal, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Husserl was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Husserl hold? The chapter states the phenomenological
method, the intentionality, the epoché and the reductions, the life-world, the crisis of the sciences,
intersubjectivity, and the time-consciousness, with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Husserl converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Husserl would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Husserl?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


26.3       The Position

26.3.1      The Phenomenological Method

Husserl’s phenomenological method is stated in the Ideen (1913) and in the Cartesianische
Meditationen (1931). The method is not a doctrine; it is a way of doing philosophy; it is the
description of the essential structures of experience, without presupposing any theory about
them.
26.3. The Position                                                                              273


   The method has three features.


First feature: the return to the things themselves. The method returns to the things
themselves (zu den Sachen selbst); it does not begin with theories about the things; it begins
with the things as they are given in experience. The things themselves are not the things of
the sciences, nor the things of the metaphysical systems; they are the things as they appear in
experience, in their essential structures.


Second feature: the description, not the explanation. The method describes, it does not
explain. It describes the essential structures of experience; it does not explain them by causes,
by functions, or by mechanisms. The description is not a description of particular experiences; it
is a description of the essences that are given in the particular experiences.


Third feature: the eidetic intuition. The method uses the eidetic intuition (Wesensschau);
it grasps the essence of the thing, not the particular thing. The eidetic intuition is the seeing of
the essence; it is the intuition of the invariant structure that is present in the variations of the
particular.
   The method is the foundation of phenomenology. It is the way to describe the structure
of experience; it is the way to grasp the essences; it is the way to do philosophy as a rigorous
science.

   From the Tradition

   “We must go back to the things themselves. We must not be diverted by prejudices, by
   traditions, by systems; we must look at the things as they are given, and describe them as
   they are given.” (Husserl, Logische Untersuchungen, Prolegomena, trans. after Moran)



26.3.2     Intentionality

Husserl’s intentionality is stated in the Logische Untersuchungen (1900–01) and in the Ideen.
Intentionality is the fundamental structure of consciousness: consciousness is always consciousness
of something; every act of consciousness is directed toward an object.
   The intentionality has three features.


First feature: the intentional object. Every act of consciousness has an intentional object;
every act is directed toward something. The intentional object is not a thing in the world; it is
the object as it is intended, the object as it appears in the act. The intentional object is the
noema; the act is the noesis.


Second feature: the intentional act. The intentional act is the act of consciousness; it is
the act of perceiving, imagining, remembering, judging, loving, hating. The act is not the object;
it is the act that intends the object. The act has its own structure; it has its own essence; it can
be described.
274                                                                             Chapter 26. Husserl


Third feature: the correlation. The intentional object and the intentional act are correlated;
they are not two separate things; they are two poles of one structure. The object is the object
of the act; the act is the act of the object; the two are inseparable. The correlation is the
fundamental structure of intentionality; it is what phenomenology describes.
      The intentionality is the key to Husserl’s philosophy. It is what distinguishes consciousness
from things; it is what makes consciousness a relation, not a substance. The intentionality is the
foundation of the phenomenological method; it is what the method describes.

26.3.3      The Epoché and the Reductions
Husserl’s epoché and reductions are stated in the Ideen and in the Cartesianische Meditationen.
The epoché is the suspension of the natural attitude; the reductions are the steps that lead from
the natural attitude to the transcendental subjectivity.
      The epoché and the reductions have three features.

First feature: the epoché. The epoché is the suspension of the natural attitude. The natural
attitude is the attitude of everyday life, in which we take the world for granted, in which we
believe that the world exists, in which we are absorbed in the things of the world. The epoché
suspends this attitude; it puts the world in brackets; it does not deny the world, but it suspends
the belief in the world.

Second feature: the eidetic reduction. The eidetic reduction is the step from the particular
to the essence. The reduction takes the particular experience and varies it in the imagination; it
sees what remains invariant across the variations; it grasps the essence. The eidetic reduction is
the way to the essential structures of experience.

Third feature: the transcendental reduction. The transcendental reduction is the step
from the world to the transcendental subjectivity. The reduction leads back to the consciousness
that constitutes the world; it reveals the transcendental ego, the "I" that is the source of all
meaning. The transcendental reduction is the way to the transcendental subjectivity.
      The epoché and the reductions are the method of phenomenology. They are the way to the
things themselves; they are the way to the essences; they are the way to the transcendental
subjectivity. They are not a denial of the world; they are a suspension of the belief in the world,
in order to see the world as it is constituted.

   From the Tradition

   “The epoché is the suspension of the natural attitude; it is the putting in brackets of the
   world, in order to see the world as it is constituted by consciousness.” (Husserl, Ideen
   §31–32, trans. after Kersten)


26.3.4      The Life-World (Lebenswelt)
Husserl’s life-world is stated in the Krisis (1936). The life-world is the world as it is lived, before
it is theorized, before it is mathematized, before it is objectified. It is the world of everyday
26.3. The Position                                                                                  275


experience, the world of the natural attitude, the world that is presupposed by all the sciences.
   The life-world has three features.


First feature: the life-world is the foundation of the sciences. The life-world is the
foundation of the sciences; the sciences presuppose it; the sciences cannot replace it. The sciences
are abstractions from the life-world; they are built on the life-world; they are not the life-world
itself. The crisis of the sciences is the crisis of forgetting the life-world.


Second feature: the life-world is intersubjective. The life-world is intersubjective; it is
the world that we share with others; it is the world that is constituted by the community of
subjects. The life-world is not the private world of an individual; it is the common world of a
community.


Third feature: the life-world is historical. The life-world is historical; it is the world that
is handed down from generation to generation; it is the world that is shaped by the traditions of
a culture. The life-world is not a static structure; it is a historical process; it is the world that is
lived in a particular time and place.
   The life-world is the key to Husserl’s later philosophy. It is the world that the sciences have
forgotten; it is the world that phenomenology recovers; it is the world that is the foundation of
all meaning.

   From the Tradition

   “The life-world is the world as it is lived, before it is theorized; it is the world that is
   presupposed by all the sciences, and that the sciences have forgotten.” (Husserl, Krisis
   §33–34, trans. after Carr)



26.3.5     The Crisis of the European Sciences

Husserl’s account of the crisis is stated in the Krisis (1936). The crisis is the crisis of the
European sciences; it is the crisis of the sciences that have forgotten the life-world; it is the crisis
of a culture that has lost its meaning.
   The crisis has three features.


First feature: the objectivism of the sciences. The sciences are objectivist; they treat the
world as a collection of objects; they mathematize the world; they reduce the world to quantities.
The objectivism of the sciences is the source of the crisis; it is the forgetting of the life-world.


Second feature: the loss of meaning. The objectivism of the sciences produces a loss
of meaning; the world that the sciences describe is a world without meaning; it is a world of
quantities, not of qualities; it is a world of facts, not of values. The loss of meaning is the crisis
of the European sciences.
276                                                                              Chapter 26. Husserl


Third feature: the task of phenomenology. The task of phenomenology is to recover the
life-world; to show that the sciences presuppose the life-world; to show that the meaning of the
sciences is grounded in the life-world. The task of phenomenology is the response to the crisis.
      The crisis is the diagnosis of the modern condition. It is not a critique of the sciences; it is a
critique of the forgetfulness of the sciences; it is a call to remember the life-world. The crisis is
the occasion for phenomenology; it is the occasion for the recovery of meaning.


26.3.6      Intersubjectivity

Husserl’s account of intersubjectivity is stated in the Cartesianische Meditationen, the Fifth
Meditation. The account is the response to the question: how can the transcendental ego
constitute the other ego?
      The intersubjectivity has three features.


First feature: the problem of the other. The other is not given to me in the same way as
the things of the world; the other is not an object; the other is a subject. The other is given to
me through empathy (Einfühlung); I recognize the other as a subject because I recognize her
body as analogous to my body.


Second feature: the constitution of the other. The other is constituted by the transcen-
dental ego; the other is an alter ego, an other I. The other is not a thing; the other is a subject;
the other is constituted by the same structures that constitute my own subjectivity.


Third feature: the intersubjective world. The intersubjective world is the world that
is constituted by the community of subjects; it is the world that we share with others; it is
the life-world. The intersubjective world is the foundation of objectivity; it is what makes the
sciences possible.
      The intersubjectivity is the key to Husserl’s social philosophy. It is the way from the
transcendental ego to the community; it is the way from the private world to the common world;
it is the way from solipsism to objectivity.


26.3.7      Time-Consciousness

Husserl’s account of time-consciousness is stated in the Vorlesungen zur Phänomenologie des
inneren Zeitbewusstseins (1905–10). The account is the description of how time is constituted by
consciousness.
      The time-consciousness has three features.


First feature: the retention. The retention is the consciousness of the just-past; it is the
holding onto the moment that has just passed. The retention is not memory; it is the immediate
consciousness of the past that is still present in the present.
26.4. Internal Disputes                                                                          277


Second feature: the protention. The protention is the consciousness of the about-to-come;
it is the anticipation of the moment that is about to arrive. The protention is not expectation; it
is the immediate consciousness of the future that is already present in the present.


Third feature: the living present. The living present is the unity of retention, primal
impression, and protention. The living present is not a point; it is a flow; it is the flow
of consciousness that constitutes time. The living present is the foundation of all temporal
experience.
   The time-consciousness is the deepest level of Husserl’s phenomenology. It is the level at
which time is constituted; it is the level at which the flow of consciousness is described; it is the
level at which the transcendental ego is revealed as temporal.


26.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Husserl is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the transcendental ego. The traditional reading takes the
transcendental ego to be a real subject: the transcendental ego is the source of all meaning, the
"I" that constitutes the world. A revisionary reading takes it to be a structural principle: the
transcendental ego is not a subject, but a structure; it is the structure of consciousness, not a
thing. The two readings disagree on whether Husserl is a transcendental idealist or a structuralist,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is
not a subject.


Second dispute: the status of the life-world. The traditional reading takes the life-world
to be a cultural formation: the life-world is the world of a particular culture, a particular time, a
particular tradition. A revisionary reading takes it to be a universal structure: the life-world is
the universal horizon of all experience, the structure that is presupposed by all cultures. The
two readings disagree on whether Husserl is a historicist or a universalist, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are universal structures,
not cultural formations.


Third dispute: the status of intersubjectivity. The traditional reading takes intersubjec-
tivity to be a problem: the problem of how the transcendental ego constitutes the other ego. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a given: the life-world is always already intersubjective; the
problem is not how the other is constituted, but how the other is recognized. The two readings
disagree on whether Husserl is a solipsist or a relational thinker, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is relational, not solipsistic.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Husserl is a transcendental idealist, the
framework’s dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a transcendental
idealism. If Husserl is a structuralist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the Krisis,
278                                                                             Chapter 26. Husserl


but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.




26.5      Points of Convergence


   Points of Convergence

   With Husserl. The framework shares four structural features with Husserl’s position.

       1. The intentional structure of consciousness. Husserl holds that consciousness is always
          consciousness of something; every act is directed toward an object; the act and the
          object are correlated. The framework holds that cognition is always cognition of
          something; every explanation is directed toward an object; the four columns are the
          structure of the relation. Both hold that cognition is intentional, and that the act
          and the object are correlated.

       2. The structural conditions of experience. Husserl holds that experience has essential
          structures; the essences are the invariant structures that are given in the variations of
          the particular. The framework holds that explanation has structural conditions; the
          four columns are the invariant roles that are given in the variations of the particular
          explanation. Both hold that there are structural conditions of cognition, and that
          these conditions can be described.

       3. The life-world as horizon. Husserl holds that the life-world is the horizon in which
          all experience appears; it is the foundation of the sciences; it is the world that is
          presupposed by all meaning. The framework holds that the context is the horizon
          in which all explanation appears; it is the foundation of the four columns; it is the
          frame that is presupposed by all cognition. Both hold that there is a horizon that is
          presupposed by all cognition, and that the horizon is not itself an object of cognition.

       4. The critique of objectivism. Husserl holds that the objectivism of the sciences is
          the source of the crisis; it is the forgetting of the life-world; it is the reduction of
          the world to quantities. The framework holds that the reduction of cognition to
          computation is a mistake; it is the forgetting of the structure; it is the reduction of
          the world to data. Both hold that objectivism is a mistake, and that the recovery of
          meaning requires the recovery of the structure.
26.6. Points of Divergence                                                                         279


26.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Husserl. The framework diverges from Husserl in four respects.

       1. The status of the transcendental ego. Husserl holds that the transcendental ego is
          the source of all meaning; the ego constitutes the world; the world is the correlate of
          the ego. The framework has no transcendental ego; its structure is not a subject; its
          identity is not an ego; its manifestation is not a constitution. The framework is a
          metaphysics without a transcendental ego.

       2. The status of the epoché. Husserl holds that the epoché is the suspension of the
          natural attitude; it is the putting in brackets of the world; it is the way to the
          transcendental subjectivity. The framework has no epoché; it does not suspend the
          world; it describes the structure of the world; it does not put the world in brackets.
          The framework is a metaphysics without an epoché.

       3. The status of the essence. Husserl holds that the essence is the invariant structure
          that is grasped by the eidetic intuition; the essence is the what of the thing; it is the
          universal that is present in the particular. The framework holds that identity is the
          invariance under a class of transformations; it is not an essence; it is not a what; it
          is the structure of the particular. The framework is a metaphysics without essences.

       4. The status of the life-world. Husserl holds that the life-world is the cultural horizon of
          experience; it is the world of a particular time and place; it is the world that is handed
          down by tradition. The framework holds that the context is the structural horizon of
          explanation; it is not a cultural formation; it is the frame that is presupposed by all
          cognition. The framework is a metaphysics without a life-world in Husserl’s sense.



26.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Husserl’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is an
   abstraction; it is not a phenomenon; it is not given in experience. The phenomenon is the
   thing as it appears; the phenomenon is the given; the structural invariance is a construction,
   not a given. The framework’s identity is an abstraction; it is not a phenomenon; it is
   not the thing itself. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of abstractions, not of
   phenomena.
   Husserl’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
   the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction is
   not description; it is not the description of the given; it is the construction of a model. The
280                                                                            Chapter 26. Husserl


   phenomenological method describes the given; it does not construct a model; it does not
   reconstruct the identity. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of construction,
   not of description.
   Husserl’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not the
   life-world. But a metaphysics without the life-world is an incomplete metaphysics; the
   life-world is the foundation of all meaning; the sciences presuppose it; the philosophy
   must recover it. The framework’s silence on the life-world is not a boundary; it is a
   forgetfulness. The framework’s philosophy is a philosophy without the life-world, and a
   philosophy without the life-world is a philosophy without meaning.



26.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an abstraction is not a
   phenomenon, and it agrees that the phenomenon is the given. But the framework denies
   that its identity is an abstraction. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the
   identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not an abstraction; it is the structural
   condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what
   the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between an abstraction (a construction) and
   an enactment (a given); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction is not
   description, and it agrees that the phenomenological method describes the given. But
   the framework denies that its epistemology is an epistemology of construction. The
   framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the given; it is the subject’s reading of the
   manifestations; it is not the construction of a model, but the reading of a structure. The
   distinction is between a construction (the imposition of a model) and a reading (the
   interpretation of the given); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second
   is a kind of description.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without
   the life-world is incomplete, and it agrees that the life-world is the foundation of all
   meaning. But the framework denies that its silence on the life-world is a forgetfulness. The
   framework is a work of metaphysics, not of phenomenology; its subject is the structure
   of identity and manifestation, not the life-world. The framework states the structural
   condition of reality; it leaves the life-world to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between
   a metaphysics and a phenomenology; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it
   is not a forgetfulness, but a boundary.



26.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
26.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     281


Husserl’s cost. If Husserl accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
transcendental ego is the source of all meaning. He must accept that the structure is not a subject,
and that the meaning is not constituted by an ego. The cost is the loss of the transcendental
ego: the world is no longer the correlate of the ego, but the structure of the identity and the
manifestation.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Husserl’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the phenomenon, of the given, of the life-world—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not a phenomenon, and the framework leaves the phenomenon to
a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Husserl’s phenomenon
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Husserl must accept that the framework’s structure is not an abstraction; it is a structural
condition that the phenomenon presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss
of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is
incomplete without the other.


26.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Husserl’s
   term “the essence.” If one substitutes “the essence” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Husserl’s essence is the invariant structure
   that is grasped by the eidetic intuition, and it is not manifested, because it is the what
   of the thing. The framework’s identity is multiple; Husserl’s essence is universal. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s
   term “expression” is not substitutable for Husserl’s term “constitution.” If one substitutes
   “constitution” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s expression is a structural relation; Husserl’s constitution is an act of the
   transcendental ego. The framework’s expression is not an act; Husserl’s constitution is an
   act. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Husserl is resemblance:
   both hold that cognition is intentional, and they differ on whether the intention is an act of
   consciousness or a structure of explanation. Both hold that there are structural conditions
   of cognition, and they differ on whether the conditions are transcendental or analytical.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
282                                                                         Chapter 26. Husserl


   reading of Husserl would be refuted by showing that Husserl’s transcendental phenomenol-
   ogy cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and
   act—by showing, that is, that Husserl already distinguishes the structural condition from
   the act of consciousness, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Husserl’s
   own.




26.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Husserl’s essence, or is it a
departure from Husserl? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Husserl’s essence is already a structural condition, not a
universal, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Ideen and the Krisis do justice to the
texts? The chapter has used the method, the intentionality, the epoché, the life-world, the crisis,
the intersubjectivity, and the time-consciousness, and it has stated what would refute its reading.
A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a phenomenon and a structure—a person, a work of art,
a text. Is the thing the phenomenon that is given, or the structure that is reconstructed? Is the
meaning constituted by the ego, or enacted by the identity? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Husserl’s essence and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Heidegger. It states the question of being, the Dasein, being-in-the-world,
being-toward-death, the Gestell, and the critique of the metaphysical tradition; it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Heidegger; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of being and expression is the nearest contemporary
analogue to Heidegger’s. The present chapter has stated Husserl’s answer to the problem of
consciousness; the next chapter states Heidegger’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 27

Heidegger


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Martin Heidegger. It states the question of being
(Seinsfrage), the ontological difference between being and beings, the analysis of Dasein (being-
in-the-world, being-with, being-toward-death, temporality), the they (das Man), authenticity
and inauthenticity, the clearing (Lichtung), the critique of the metaphysical tradition, the turn
(Kehre), enframing (Gestell) and technology, and language as the house of being, with reference
to Sein und Zeit, the Brief über den Humanismus, the Vorträge und Aufsätze, and the Beiträge
zur Philosophie; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Heidegger; it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of being
and expression is the nearest contemporary analogue to Heidegger’s; it presents the objections
that Heidegger would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states
what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “being,” “Dasein,” “the clearing,” “the fourfold,” “enframing,” or “the turn,” these are
Heidegger’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive tradition, not by
the framework.


27.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is hammering a nail. She does not think about the hammer; she uses it;
the hammer is ready-to-hand (zuhanden); it disappears into the task; the nail, the board, the
wall, the room, the project of building a house—all are present in the act of hammering, but
none is an object of explicit awareness. The hammer is not an object; it is a tool; it is what it is
in its use. And when the hammer breaks, then it becomes an object; then it is present-at-hand
(vorhanden); then it stands out, as a thing, from the network of equipment.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the hammer is, or how she uses it,
but what makes the hammer possible as a hammer. The hammer is possible because there is a
world: a network of equipment, of projects, of practices, of meanings; a world in which nails are
for building, boards are for walls, walls are for houses, houses are for dwelling. The hammer is
what it is because it belongs to a world; the world is the horizon in which the hammer appears;
and the world is not the sum of the things in it, but the structure of the relations among them.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the world is, or how the
hammer appears, but what being is. Being is not a being; being is not a thing among things;
being is not the sum of the beings. Being is the very event of appearing, the very event of
unconcealment, the very event in which beings come to be what they are. Being is the clearing
(Lichtung) in which beings stand; being is the light in which beings are visible; being is what
makes beings be.

                                                284
27.2. The Question                                                                                285


   The scene is Heidegger’s image, in Sein und Zeit and in the later essays, of the structure of
being. The hammer is the ready-to-hand; the world is the horizon of equipment; the clearing
is the event of unconcealment; being is not a being, but the event of beings. The ontological
difference is the difference between being and beings; the forgetting of being is the forgetting of
this difference; and the question of being is the question that the tradition has forgotten.
   The scene poses the question that Heidegger was the first to pose in its full form. What
is being? Why is there something rather than nothing? What is the difference between being
and beings? And how has the tradition forgotten this difference? The present chapter states
Heidegger’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.



27.2      The Question

The previous chapter stated Husserl’s position: the phenomenological method, intentionality, the
epoché, the life-world, the crisis of the sciences, intersubjectivity, and time-consciousness. Husserl
is the founder of phenomenology, and Heidegger is his greatest student and his greatest critic.
Heidegger accepts Husserl’s method, but he rejects Husserl’s transcendental ego, his essentialism,
and his neglect of the question of being. The present chapter states Heidegger’s critique, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Heidegger was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Heidegger hold? The chapter states the question of
being, the ontological difference, the analysis of Dasein, the they, authenticity, the clearing, the
critique of metaphysics, the turn, enframing, and language, with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Heidegger converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Heidegger would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Heidegger?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.



27.3      The Position

27.3.1    The Question of Being

Heidegger’s question of being (Seinsfrage) is stated in Sein und Zeit (1927), in the Introduction,
and in the later essays. The question is the oldest question of philosophy, and it is the question
that the tradition has forgotten.
   The question has three features.
286                                                                         Chapter 27. Heidegger


First feature: the question is forgotten. The question of being is forgotten; the tradition
has asked about beings—about their essences, their causes, their properties—but it has not
asked about being itself. The forgetting of being (Seinsvergessenheit) is the hidden history of
philosophy; it is the history of the oblivion of the difference.


Second feature: the question is the question of the meaning of being. The question is
not what beings are; it is what being means; it is the meaning of being (Sinn von Sein). The
question is asked by a being who already understands being—by Dasein; it is the question that
Dasein asks about its own being.


Third feature: the question requires a new method. The question cannot be answered
by the methods of the sciences; it requires a new method; it requires the phenomenological
method, applied to Dasein; it requires the analysis of existence (Existenzialanalyse).
       The question of being is the foundation of Heidegger’s philosophy. It is what distinguishes
his philosophy from the tradition; it is what makes his philosophy a new beginning; it is what
makes his philosophy a repetition (Wiederholung) of the question that the Greeks first asked.

       From the Tradition

       “The question of being has today been forgotten. It is the question that the tradition has
       posed, and that the tradition has forgotten; it is the question that we must pose again.”
       (Heidegger, Sein und Zeit, §1, trans. after Macquarrie-Robinson)



27.3.2        The Ontological Difference

Heidegger’s ontological difference is stated in Sein und Zeit and in the later essays. The ontological
difference is the difference between being (Sein) and beings (Seiende); it is the difference between
the event of appearing and the things that appear; it is the difference between the light and the
lit.
       The ontological difference has three features.


First feature: being is not a being. Being is not a being; being is not a thing among things;
being is not the highest being; being is not God. Being is the event of appearing, the event of
unconcealment, the event in which beings come to be what they are.


Second feature: being is the being of beings. Being is the being of beings; being is what
makes beings be; being is the condition of possibility of beings. Being is not separate from beings;
being is not a beyond; being is the very event of beings.


Third feature: the difference is the forgotten difference. The difference is forgotten;
the tradition has collapsed the difference; it has treated being as a being; it has treated the event
of appearing as one of the things that appear. The forgetting of the difference is the source of
the crisis of the tradition.
27.3. The Position                                                                             287


    The ontological difference is the key to Heidegger’s critique of the tradition. The tradition
has forgotten the difference; it has reduced being to a being; it has reduced the event to a thing.
The task of philosophy is to remember the difference; to recover the question of being; to think
being as the event of appearing.


27.3.3         The Analysis of Dasein

Heidegger’s analysis of Dasein is stated in Sein und Zeit, Division I. Dasein is the being who
asks the question of being; it is the human being, considered not as a substance, not as a subject,
but as the being whose being is an issue for it.
    The analysis has three features.


First feature: being-in-the-world. Dasein is being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein); it is
not a subject separated from an object; it is not a consciousness separated from a world; it is a
being whose being is to be in a world. The world is not the sum of the things; it is the horizon
of meaning; it is the structure of the relations in which Dasein lives.


Second feature: being-with. Dasein is being-with (Mitsein); it is not an isolated individual;
it is a being whose being is to be with others. The others are not objects; they are co-Dasein;
they are the ones with whom Dasein shares the world. The being-with is the structure of the
social life.


Third feature: being-toward-death. Dasein is being-toward-death (Sein-zum-Tode); it is
not a being that lives forever; it is a being whose being is finite; it is a being that is oriented
toward its own death. The being-toward-death is the structure of existence; it is what makes
existence authentic; it is what makes existence a whole.
    The analysis of Dasein is the foundation of Heidegger’s fundamental ontology. It is the
analysis of the being who asks the question of being; it is the analysis of the being whose being
is an issue for it; it is the analysis of the being who exists.

   From the Tradition

   “The essence of Dasein lies in its existence. The being of Dasein is being-in-the-world; the
   being of Dasein is being-with; the being of Dasein is being-toward-death.” (Heidegger,
   Sein und Zeit, §9, trans. after Macquarrie-Robinson)



27.3.4         The They (das Man)

Heidegger’s analysis of the they is stated in Sein und Zeit, Division I, Chapter IV. The they (das
Man) is the anonymous collective; it is the "one" of everyday life; it is the "they say," the "one
does," the "one thinks."
    The they has three features.
288                                                                            Chapter 27. Heidegger


First feature: the they is anonymous. The they is anonymous; it is no one in particular;
it is everyone and no one; it is the "one" who does what one does. The they is not a group; it is
a structure of everyday life; it is the way in which Dasein loses itself in the crowd.


Second feature: the they levels down. The they levels down; it reduces everything to
the average; it makes everything mediocre; it suppresses the exceptional; it makes everything
"interesting" in the same way. The they is the structure of inauthenticity; it is the structure of
the fall (Verfallen).


Third feature: the they is the structure of everyday life. The they is not a defect; it is
a structure; it is the way in which Dasein lives in its everyday life. The they is the condition of
the possibility of the average; it is the condition of the possibility of communication; it is the
condition of the possibility of the common world.
      The analysis of the they is the diagnosis of the modern condition. It is the diagnosis of the
loss of the self in the crowd; it is the diagnosis of the leveling of the exceptional; it is the diagnosis
of the inauthenticity of everyday life. The task of philosophy is to recover the self; to recover the
authenticity; to recover the singularity of Dasein.


27.3.5       Authenticity and Inauthenticity

Heidegger’s analysis of authenticity and inauthenticity is stated in Sein und Zeit, Division I,
Chapter IV, and Division II, Chapter I. The analysis is the distinction between the two modes of
existence.
      The analysis has three features.


First feature: inauthenticity. Inauthenticity (Uneigentlichkeit) is the mode of existence in
which Dasein loses itself in the they; it is the mode in which Dasein does what one does; it is the
mode in which Dasein is absorbed in the world. Inauthenticity is not a defect; it is a structure;
it is the structure of everyday life.


Second feature: authenticity. Authenticity (Eigentlichkeit) is the mode of existence in
which Dasein owns itself; it is the mode in which Dasein chooses itself; it is the mode in which
Dasein becomes what it is. Authenticity is not a state; it is a task; it is the task of existence.


Third feature: the call of conscience. The call of conscience (Gewissensruf ) is the call
that summons Dasein from the they to itself; it is the call that summons Dasein to its ownmost
possibility; it is the call that summons Dasein to its own death. The call is not a voice; it is a
silence; it is the silence in which Dasein hears itself.
      The authenticity and inauthenticity are the two modes of existence. They are not two kinds
of human being; they are two ways of existing; they are two ways of being Dasein. The task of
philosophy is to think both; to think the they; to think the self; to think the call.
27.3. The Position                                                                                289


27.3.6     Temporality
Heidegger’s analysis of temporality is stated in Sein und Zeit, Division II. Temporality (Zeitlichkeit)
is the meaning of the being of Dasein; it is the horizon in which Dasein understands being; it is
the structure of existence.
   The temporality has three features.

First feature: the three ecstases. Temporality has three ecstases: the future (Zukunft), the
past (Gewesenheit), and the present (Gegenwart). The three are not three parts of time; they
are three dimensions of temporality; they are three ways in which Dasein is outside itself.

Second feature: the primacy of the future. The future is primary; temporality is fun-
damentally futural; Dasein is always ahead of itself; Dasein is always projecting itself into its
possibilities. The primacy of the future is what makes Dasein a being of possibility, not a being
of actuality.

Third feature: the temporalization. Temporality temporalizes itself (zeitigt sich); it is not
a thing; it is an event; it is the event in which Dasein is. The temporalization is the structure of
existence; it is what makes existence possible; it is what makes existence a whole.
   The temporality is the key to Heidegger’s fundamental ontology. It is the meaning of being;
it is the horizon of the question of being; it is what makes the question possible.

27.3.7     The Clearing (Lichtung)
Heidegger’s clearing is stated in the later essays, notably in "Vom Wesen der Wahrheit" (1930)
and in "Der Ursprung des Kunstwerkes" (1935). The clearing is the event of unconcealment; it is
the opening in which beings appear; it is the light in which beings are visible.
   The clearing has three features.

First feature: the clearing is not a thing. The clearing is not a thing; it is not a space; it
is not a field; it is the event in which beings appear. The clearing is what makes beings be; it is
not one of the beings; it is the condition of the beings.

Second feature: the clearing is the truth of being. The clearing is the truth of being; it
is the unconcealment (Unverborgenheit) of beings; it is what the Greeks called aletheia. The
truth is not the correctness of a proposition; it is the unconcealment of beings; it is the event of
appearing.

Third feature: the clearing is historical. The clearing is historical; it is not the same in
every age; it is not the same in every culture. The clearing is the epoch of being; it is the way in
which being reveals itself in a particular time.
   The clearing is the central concept of Heidegger’s later philosophy. It is what replaces the
transcendental ego; it is what replaces the subject; it is what replaces the metaphysical ground.
The clearing is the event of being; it is the light in which beings appear.
290                                                                         Chapter 27. Heidegger


   From the Tradition

   “The clearing is the open region in which beings can appear, in which they can be what
   they are. The clearing is not a being; it is the event of unconcealment; it is the truth of
   being.” (Heidegger, "Vom Wesen der Wahrheit," trans. after Krell)



27.3.8      The Critique of Metaphysics

Heidegger’s critique of metaphysics is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in the later
essays. The critique is the diagnosis of the forgetting of being; it is the diagnosis of the collapse
of the ontological difference.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the tradition has forgotten being. The tradition has forgotten being; it
has asked about beings; it has asked about their essences, their causes, their properties; it has
not asked about being itself. The forgetting of being is the hidden history of philosophy; it is the
history of the oblivion of the difference.


Second feature: the tradition has reduced being to a being. The tradition has reduced
being to a being; it has treated being as the highest being; it has treated being as God; it has
treated being as the substance. The reduction of being to a being is the source of the crisis of
the tradition.


Third feature: the tradition has reached its end. The tradition has reached its end; it
has exhausted its possibilities; it has become a technique; it has become a calculation. The end
of philosophy is the beginning of the new thinking; it is the beginning of the thought of being.
      The critique of metaphysics is the task of the new thinking. It is not a refutation of the
tradition; it is a recovery of what the tradition has forgotten. The new thinking is the thought
of being; it is the thought that thinks being as being; it is the thought that remembers the
difference.


27.3.9      The Turn (Kehre)

Heidegger’s turn is stated in the Brief über den Humanismus (1947) and in the later essays. The
turn (Kehre) is the turn from the fundamental ontology to the thought of being; it is the turn
from Dasein to being; it is the turn from the analysis of existence to the history of being.
      The turn has three features.


First feature: the turn is not a change of position. The turn is not a change of position;
it is a deepening of the same question; it is the discovery that the question of being cannot be
asked by Dasein alone; it must be asked by being itself. The turn is the realization that being is
not the being of Dasein, but the event in which Dasein and beings appear.
27.3. The Position                                                                                291


Second feature: the turn is the turn to language. The turn is the turn to language; it
is the discovery that language is the house of being (Haus des Seins); it is the discovery that
language is not a tool, but the event in which being reveals itself. The turn is the turn from the
analysis of existence to the analysis of language.


Third feature: the turn is the turn to poetry. The turn is the turn to poetry; it is the
discovery that poetry is the thinking of being; it is the discovery that the poet (Hölderlin, Trakl,
Rilke) is the one who hears the call of being. The turn is the turn from philosophy to poetry; it
is the turn from the concept to the image.
   The turn is the key to Heidegger’s later philosophy. It is what distinguishes his later work
from his earlier work; it is what makes his later work a new beginning; it is what makes his later
work a thinking of being.


27.3.10     Enframing (Gestell) and Technology

Heidegger’s analysis of technology is stated in "Die Frage nach der Technik" (1954). The analysis
is the diagnosis of the modern condition; it is the diagnosis of the essence of technology.
   The analysis has three features.


First feature: technology is not a tool. Technology is not a tool; it is not a means to an
end; it is not a neutral instrument. Technology is a way of revealing; it is a way in which being
reveals itself; it is a way in which beings appear.


Second feature: enframing (Gestell). Enframing is the essence of modern technology; it
is the way in which beings are revealed as standing-reserve (Bestand); it is the way in which
everything is reduced to a resource, to be calculated, to be used, to be stored. Enframing is the
supreme danger; it is the danger that the human being is reduced to a resource; it is the danger
that the world is reduced to a stockpile.


Third feature: the saving power. The saving power (das Rettende) is the possibility of the
overcoming of enframing; it is the possibility of the turn; it is the possibility of the new revealing.
The saving power is not a human achievement; it is the gift of being; it is the event of the turn.
   The analysis of technology is the diagnosis of the modern condition. It is not a rejection of
technology; it is a thinking of the essence of technology. The task of philosophy is to think the
essence of technology; to think enframing; to think the saving power.

   From the Tradition

   “The essence of technology is by no means anything technological. The essence of technology
   is enframing; it is the way in which beings are revealed as standing-reserve.” (Heidegger,
   "Die Frage nach der Technik," trans. after Lovitt)
292                                                                            Chapter 27. Heidegger


27.3.11       Language as the House of Being
Heidegger’s analysis of language is stated in the later essays, notably in "Brief über den Humanis-
mus" and in "Die Sprache" (1950). Language is the house of being; it is the event in which being
reveals itself.
      The analysis has three features.

First feature: language is not a tool. Language is not a tool; it is not a means of
communication; it is not an instrument of expression. Language is the event in which being
reveals itself; language is the house of being; language is what makes beings be.

Second feature: language speaks. Language speaks (die Sprache spricht); it is not the
human being who speaks; it is language that speaks through the human being. The human being
is the one who listens to language; the human being is the one who responds to the call of being.

Third feature: the poetic language. The poetic language (Dichtung) is the language that
hears the call of being; it is the language that reveals being; it is the language that thinks. Poetry
is not a decoration; it is the thinking of being; it is the saying of being.
      The analysis of language is the culmination of Heidegger’s later philosophy. It is the thinking
of being; it is the saying of being; it is the response to the call of being.


27.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Heidegger is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the turn. The traditional reading takes the turn to be a break:
the early Heidegger (the fundamental ontology) is different from the later Heidegger (the thought
of being); there are two Heideggers. A revisionary reading takes the turn to be a deepening: the
same question is asked from a different angle; there is one Heidegger, with one question. The two
readings disagree on whether the turn is a break or a deepening, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is not a subject, and its history
is not a history of being.

Second dispute: the status of being. The traditional reading takes being to be a real event:
being is the event of appearing; it is the light in which beings are visible. A revisionary reading
takes being to be a grammatical construction: being is not an event; it is a way of speaking
about the difference between the subject and the object. The two readings disagree on whether
Heidegger is a realist or a linguistic idealist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a real structure, not a grammatical construction.

Third dispute: the status of the clearing. The traditional reading takes the clearing to be
a metaphysical principle: the clearing is the event of being; it is the truth of being; it is what
makes beings be. A revisionary reading takes the clearing to be a phenomenological description:
the clearing is a way of describing the way in which things appear, without any claim about
27.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      293


a metaphysical event. The two readings disagree on whether Heidegger is a metaphysician or
a phenomenologist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s structure is a phenomenological description, not a metaphysical posit.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Heidegger is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a thinking of being. If Heidegger
is a phenomenologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats
as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does not
rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.



27.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Heidegger. The framework shares four structural features with Heidegger’s
   position.

       1. The critique of the metaphysical tradition. Heidegger holds that the tradition has
         forgotten being; it has reduced being to a being; it has collapsed the ontological
         difference. The framework holds that the tradition has conflated identity with
         manifestation; it has reduced the identity to its manifestations; it has collapsed the
         structural difference. Both hold that the tradition has made a mistake, and that the
         mistake is the collapse of a distinction.

       2. The priority of the event over the substance. Heidegger holds that being is an event,
         not a substance; being is the event of appearing, not a thing. The framework holds
         that expression is a structural tendency, not a substance; expression is the event of
         enactment, not a thing. Both hold that reality is an event, not a substance; both
         hold that the event is the truth of the substance.

       3. The structure of the world. Heidegger holds that Dasein is being-in-the-world; the
         world is the horizon of meaning; it is not the sum of the things. The framework holds
         that explanation is always in a context; the context is the horizon of the explanation;
         it is not the sum of the elements. Both hold that the world is a structure, not a
         collection; both hold that the world is presupposed by the things in it.

       4. The clearing as the condition of appearance. Heidegger holds that the clearing is the
         condition of appearance; it is the light in which beings are visible; it is the event
         of unconcealment. The framework holds that light is the condition of possibility of
         relation; it is what makes the manifestation legible; it is the conveyor of effect. Both
         hold that there is a condition of appearance, and that the condition is not itself an
         object of appearance.
294                                                                        Chapter 27. Heidegger


27.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Heidegger. The framework diverges from Heidegger in four respects.

       1. The status of being. Heidegger holds that being is the event of appearing; being is
         not a being; being is the light in which beings are visible. The framework has no
         being in Heidegger’s sense; its structure is not an event of appearing; its identity is
         not the light in which beings are visible. The framework is a metaphysics without a
         question of being.

       2. The status of Dasein. Heidegger holds that Dasein is the being who asks the
         question of being; Dasein is being-in-the-world, being-with, being-toward-death. The
         framework has no Dasein; its subject is not the being who asks the question of being;
         its identity is not an existence. The framework is a metaphysics without Dasein.

       3. The status of the clearing. Heidegger holds that the clearing is the event of uncon-
         cealment; it is the light in which beings are visible; it is the truth of being. The
         framework holds that light is a structural conveyor; it is the condition of possibility
         of relation; it is not an event of unconcealment. The framework’s light is structural;
         Heidegger’s clearing is ontological.

       4. The status of language. Heidegger holds that language is the house of being; language
         speaks; the human being is the one who listens to language. The framework holds
         that language is a structural system; it is a set of signs; it is not the house of being.
         The framework’s language is structural; Heidegger’s language is ontological.



27.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Heidegger’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  a being; it is a thing among things; it is not being. The framework has collapsed the
  ontological difference; it has treated being as a being; it has forgotten the question of
  being. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of beings, not of being; it has no place for
  the question of being.
  Heidegger’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction
  is a technique; it is a calculation; it is the enframing of the world as standing-reserve.
  The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of enframing; it reduces the world to
  a resource; it reduces knowledge to a calculation. The framework’s epistemology is the
  supreme danger.
27.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                    295


   Heidegger’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not
   being. But a metaphysics without being is an incomplete metaphysics; the question of
   being is the fundamental question; the forgetting of being is the crisis of the tradition.
   The framework’s silence on being is not a boundary; it is a forgetfulness. The framework’s
   philosophy is a philosophy without being, and a philosophy without being is a philosophy
   without ground.



27.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a structural invariance is a
   being, and it agrees that being is not a being. But the framework denies that its identity is
   only a being. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*,
   in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm.
   The framework’s identity is not a thing among things; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a being (a thing) and an enactment (a structure);
   the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework does not claim to
   answer the question of being; it claims to describe the structure of beings, and it leaves
   the question of being to a separate inquiry.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction can be a
   technique, and it agrees that enframing is the supreme danger. But the framework denies
   that its reconstruction is enframing. The framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; it is not a reduction of the world to a resource; it is a recognition of the
   structure of the world. The distinction is between a technique (the reduction of the world
   to standing-reserve) and a reading (the recognition of the structure of the world); the
   framework holds the second, and it holds that the second is a kind of knowledge, not a
   kind of enframing.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without being
   is incomplete, and it agrees that the question of being is fundamental. But the framework
   denies that its silence on being is a forgetfulness. The framework is a work of metaphysics,
   not of fundamental ontology; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation, not
   the question of being. The framework states the structural condition of beings; it leaves
   the question of being to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics of
   beings and a fundamental ontology of being; the framework keeps it, and it holds that
   keeping it is not a forgetfulness, but a boundary.



27.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
296                                                                        Chapter 27. Heidegger


Heidegger’s cost. If Heidegger accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the framework has forgotten being. He must accept that the framework is a metaphysics of
beings, and that the question of being is left to a separate inquiry. The cost is the loss of the
radical critique: the framework is no longer a forgetfulness of being, but a discipline that keeps
the question open.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Heidegger’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of being, of the ontological difference, of the clearing—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the event of being, and the framework leaves
the event of being to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Heidegger’s being is
not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Heidegger must accept that the framework’s structure is not a being; it is a structural condition
that the question of being presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


27.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Heideg-
   ger’s term “being.” If one substitutes “being” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; Heidegger’s being is the event of appearing, and it is not
   enacted, because it is the event. The framework’s identity is multiple; Heidegger’s being is
   one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The frame-
   work’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Heidegger’s term “the clearing.” If one
   substitutes “the clearing” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation; Heidegger’s clearing is the
   event of unconcealment. The framework’s expression is structural; Heidegger’s clearing is
   ontological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Heidegger is resemblance:
   both critique the metaphysical tradition, and they differ on whether the critique is of the
   collapse of the identity or of the collapse of being. Both hold that reality is an event,
   and they differ on whether the event is the expression or the clearing. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Heidegger
   would be refuted by showing that Heidegger’s question of being cannot be formulated
27.11. Open Questions                                                                       297


   without the framework’s distinction between structure and event—by showing, that is,
   that Heidegger already distinguishes the structural condition from the event of being, and
   that the framework’s distinction is a development of Heidegger’s own.




27.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Heidegger’s being, or is it a
departure from Heidegger? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Heidegger’s being is already a structural condition,
not an event, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Sein und Zeit do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the question of being, the ontological difference, the analysis of Dasein, the
they, authenticity, temporality, the clearing, the critique of metaphysics, the turn, enframing,
and language, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that Sein
und Zeit supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
