A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a being and an event—a person, a work of art, a text. Is
the thing the being that stands in the clearing, or the event of its appearing? Is the truth the
correctness of a proposition, or the unconcealment of being? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Heidegger’s clearing and the framework’s light?

The next chapter turns to Merleau-Ponty and Sartre. It states the lived body, motor intentionality,
and the flesh in the one, and the in-itself, the for-itself, nothingness, and bad faith in the other; it
identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of both; and it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of expression and of the manifestation of an
identity in a realm is the nearest phenomenological analogue to the philosophy of the body. The
present chapter has stated Heidegger’s answer to the question of being; the next chapter states the
answer of the phenomenology of the body and of freedom, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 28

Merleau-Ponty and Sartre


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961 CE) and Jean-Paul
Sartre (1905–1980 CE), the two French philosophers who carried Husserl’s and Heidegger’s
phenomenology into the philosophy of the body, of freedom, and of the other. It states Merleau-
Ponty’s account of perception, of the lived body (le corps propre), of motor intentionality, and
of the flesh (la chair), with reference to The Structure of Behavior (1942), Phenomenology of
Perception (1945), and the posthumous The Visible and the Invisible (1964); it states Sartre’s
distinction between being-in-itself (l’en-soi) and being-for-itself (le pour-soi), his doctrine of
nothingness, freedom, and bad faith, and his later turn toward the practico-inert, with reference to
The Transcendence of the Ego (1936), Being and Nothingness (1943), and Critique of Dialectical
Reason (1960). It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of both thinkers; it states
the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of expression
and of the manifestation of an identity in a realm is the nearest phenomenological analogue to
Merleau-Ponty’s account of the body; it presents the objections that each would raise against
the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it
states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes
no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the lived body,” “the
flesh,” “nothingness,” “bad faith,” or “facticity,” these are the terms of the two thinkers, and
their sense is fixed by their works and by the interpretive literature, not by the framework.


28.1      A Scene
Consider a person reaching for a cup on a table. She does not first compute the distance, form a
representation of the cup, and then command her arm. Her hand opens as it travels, shaped
by the cup it has not yet touched. If someone moves the cup an inch, her hand corrects itself
before she has noticed the change. The reaching is neither a thought about space nor a mere
mechanical motion; it is a way of being in space that already understands space.
   Now consider a second person, a waiter in a café, whom Sartre describes with a certain irony.
His movements are a little too quick, a little too exact; he bends forward with a studied eagerness.
He is playing at being a waiter. He is not wrong that he is a waiter, and yet to be a waiter is not,
for him, to be what a table is, a thing that simply is what it is. The waiter must make himself a
waiter at each moment, and he can also refuse to. His being is, as Sartre puts it, a being that is
not what it is and is what it is not.
   The two scenes belong to different philosophical temperaments, and they pose one question
from opposite sides. In the first, the subject is so thoroughly incarnate that perception and
action cannot be separated from the body that performs them. In the second, the subject is so
thoroughly free that no description of what it is can close upon what it does. The question for

                                                299
300                                                         Chapter 28. Merleau-Ponty and Sartre


the framework is whether an identity that is an invariance, enacted by one source and manifested
in a realm, can be stated in a world where the manifesting subject is either wholly a body or
wholly a freedom.


28.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Heidegger’s position: the question of being, being-in-the-world, the
ontological difference, and the critique of metaphysics as onto-theology. Merleau-Ponty and
Sartre receive Heidegger and Husserl at once, and they turn the phenomenological inheritance
toward the concrete: the body that perceives, the freedom that chooses, and the other who looks.
      The question is not whether Merleau-Ponty or Sartre was right. The question is what each
held, what each can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to each. The two
are treated in one chapter because they stand in a relation of disagreement within a common
method, and because the framework’s relation to the one is clearer when set beside its relation
to the other. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Merleau-Ponty and Sartre hold? The chapter states
the lived body, motor intentionality, and the flesh in the one, and the in-itself, the for-itself,
nothingness, and bad faith in the other.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and
presents the objections that each thinker would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and each
thinker? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


28.3       Merleau-Ponty’s Position
Merleau-Ponty begins from a refusal of two inherited pictures of the perceiving subject: the
empiricist picture, in which perception is the passive reception of sensations, and the intellectualist
picture, in which perception is the judgment of a constituting consciousness. In Phenomenology
of Perception he argues that both pictures presuppose what they claim to explain, namely a
perceived world already organized for a perceiver. Perception is the primordial contact with that
world, and it is carried out by the body.


28.3.1      The Lived Body

The body in question is not the body of the anatomist, an object among objects. It is the
corps propre, the body as lived from within, the body through which there is a world at all.
Merleau-Ponty draws on the clinical case of Schneider, a patient with a brain injury who could
perform a familiar movement on command only when it was embedded in a concrete situation,
28.4. Sartre’s Position                                                                          301


to show that normal movement is not the execution of a represented plan. It is a practical
understanding that the body has of its surroundings. He calls this motor intentionality: the
body is directed toward the world in its capacities, before it is directed toward it in thought.


28.3.2      The Flesh

In his last, unfinished work Merleau-Ponty tries to go beyond the vocabulary of subject and
object. The flesh is not matter, nor mind, nor substance; it is the element in which the seer and
the seen, the toucher and the touched, belong to one another. The chiasm, the crossing of the
two, is the structure of this belonging: when one hand touches the other, each is both touching
and touched, and the roles reverse without ever coinciding. Perception is thus a reversibility of
the sensible, and expression is the way in which this reversibility is taken up in speech and in
painting.



28.4        Sartre’s Position

Sartre’s Being and Nothingness divides being into two regions. Being-in-itself is the being of
things: it is what it is, opaque, complete, without relation to itself. Being-for-itself is the being
of consciousness: it is not what it is and is what it is not, because consciousness is always a
relation to what it is not, an opening that distances itself from every content. The for-itself is,
in Sartre’s phrase, a lack, and the nothingness that it carries is the condition of questioning, of
negation, of imagination, and of freedom.


28.4.1      Freedom and Bad Faith

Because consciousness is not a thing, it has no nature that determines its choices. Existence
precedes essence: a human being first exists and then makes of itself what it is. This freedom
is not optional; one is condemned to it. Bad faith (mauvaise foi) is the attempt to flee this
condition by treating oneself as a thing, as the waiter does when he identifies wholly with his
role, or, in the opposite direction, by treating oneself as a pure transcendence that no facts about
one’s situation can touch. Sartre insists that facticity, the givenness of one’s body, past, and
place, and transcendence, the surpassing of the given, are two aspects of one condition that
cannot be fused.


28.4.2      The Other and the Practico-Inert

The other enters Sartre’s account as the one whose look transforms me into an object in a world
that is not mine. Being-for-others is a dimension of being that I cannot constitute alone. In the
Critique of Dialectical Reason Sartre revisits the relation between freedom and the world: the
results of past human action congeal into the practico-inert, a field of scarcity, institutions, and
things that turn back on the agents who made them. Freedom is not abolished, but it is now
situated in a history that no single for-itself can master.
302                                                      Chapter 28. Merleau-Ponty and Sartre


28.5      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of both thinkers is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: Merleau-Ponty’s relation to Husserl. One reading takes Merleau-Ponty to
complete Husserl’s project by carrying the phenomenological reduction into the body. Another
takes him to abandon transcendental phenomenology for an ontology of the flesh that no reduction
can reach. The disagreement matters for the framework because the framework’s relation to a
phenomenological method depends on whether the method still asks for conditions of possibility
or has become a description of an elemental being.

Second dispute: the unity of Sartre’s work. One reading holds that the early Sartre of
freedom and the later Sartre of the practico-inert are one thinker developing a single insight.
Another holds that the later work revises the early doctrine of absolute freedom so deeply that
the two cannot be read together. The disagreement matters because the framework’s objections
to a philosophy of freedom differ according to whether freedom is absolute or situated.

Third dispute: the quarrel between the two. Merleau-Ponty and Sartre were allies, then
opponents. Merleau-Ponty held that Sartre’s for-itself leaves too little to the density of the
world and of the body, and that Sartre’s dualism of in-itself and for-itself is a residue of the
philosophy of consciousness. Sartre held that Merleau-Ponty’s ambiguity softens the radical
difference between consciousness and things. The disagreement matters because the framework
must say, for each, which side of the quarrel its own structure favors.


28.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Merleau-Ponty and Sartre. The framework shares four structural features with
   the two positions.

       1. The rejection of the representational picture. Merleau-Ponty holds that perception is
         not the construction of a representation, and Sartre holds that consciousness is not
         a container of contents. The framework holds that the subject does not possess an
         identity as an object in view; it reads an identity through its manifestations. Both
         reject the view that the relation to what is known is the inspection of an inner copy.

       2. The primacy of the situated relation. Merleau-Ponty places the subject in a world
         through the body; Sartre places the for-itself in a situation. The framework places
         every manifestation in a realm and in a context. Both hold that no account of a
         subject or a thing is complete when it is detached from the situation in which it
         appears.

       3. The role of expression. For Merleau-Ponty the body expresses, and speech and
         painting extend that expression. For Sartre the choice of oneself is expressed in
28.7. Points of Divergence                                                                      303


          each act. The framework holds that identity is expressed in manifestation and that
          expression has a structure and a cost. Both treat expression as constitutive, not as
          the outward sign of an inner fact already complete.

       4. The refusal of a fixed substance. Neither thinker holds that the subject is a substance
         with a determinate nature given in advance. The framework holds that an identity
          is not a substance but an invariance enacted by one source. Both resist the picture
          of a self that is simply there, apart from its relations and its acts.



28.7      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Merleau-Ponty and Sartre. The framework diverges from the two positions in
   four respects.

       1. Identity as invariance. The framework holds that an identity is an invariance,
          conserved and non-duplicable. Sartre denies that the for-itself has any invariant
          nature, and Merleau-Ponty holds that the body’s unity is a unity of style, not of a
          fixed core. The framework’s conservation of identity has no counterpart in either.

       2. The status of the source. The framework holds that an identity is enacted by one
          source. Neither thinker admits such a source: for Merleau-Ponty the flesh has no
          author, and for Sartre the for-itself is its own foundation without ground. The
          framework’s account of enactment is a departure from both.

       3. The status of structure. The framework states its principles as structural claims
          about identities, realms, and light. Merleau-Ponty distrusts any structure that is
          not found in lived experience, and Sartre distrusts any structure that would limit
          freedom. The framework’s structural register is not theirs.

       4. The method. The two thinkers describe; the framework argues from premises and
          marks each claim with an epistemic status. The difference is one of method, and it
          bears on how each tradition would assess a claim that is neither a description nor a
          deduction in its own sense.



28.8      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Merleau-Ponty’s objection. The framework speaks of an identity that is manifested in
   a realm and read by reconstruction. But the subject is not outside the world, reading it.
   The subject is the body, and the body is of the world’s flesh. A reconstruction presupposes
   a standpoint from which the manifestations can be surveyed, and no such standpoint
304                                                       Chapter 28. Merleau-Ponty and Sartre


   exists. The framework’s epistemology keeps the distance between knower and known that
   perception has already overcome.
   Sartre’s first objection. The framework says that an identity is an invariance, conserved
   and non-duplicable. But a free subject is not what it is. To assign it an invariant identity
   is to treat it as a thing, and this is precisely bad faith. The framework’s identity is the
   in-itself disguised as a structure.
   Sartre’s second objection. The framework says that manifestations are read to
   reconstruct the identity. But the other’s look is not a reading; it is the transformation of
   me into an object that I cannot control. The framework’s account of knowledge among
   subjects has no place for this violence, and in leaving it out it makes knowledge too gentle.



28.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Merleau-Ponty. The framework agrees that the subject is not outside the
   world, and it agrees that the body is the site of a primordial contact. But the framework
   denies that reconstruction requires a standpoint outside the world. Reconstruction is a
   reading carried out from within a context, by a subject that is itself a manifestation in
   a realm. The distance it presupposes is not a spatial or a spectatorial distance; it is the
   structural distance between an identity and its manifestations, which Merleau-Ponty’s
   own reversibility of the sensible already contains, since the touching hand never coincides
   with the touched.
   Reply to Sartre’s first objection. The framework agrees that a subject is not a thing
   and that to treat it as a thing is a failure. But it denies that an invariance is a thing.
   The framework’s identity is not a set of properties fixed in advance; it is the condition
   under which acts and manifestations can be the acts and manifestations of the same one.
   Sartre’s own text requires some such condition, for the unity of a life of choices is what
   makes a single act of self-choice intelligible. The framework states that condition and does
   not claim that it determines what is chosen.
   Reply to Sartre’s second objection. The framework accepts that the other’s look is not
   a reading, and it accepts that being-for-others is a dimension that cannot be constituted
   from a single standpoint. The framework’s account of reconstruction is an account of one
   relation among manifestations, not of every relation among subjects. It leaves the relation
   of the look to a separate treatment and does not claim that reconstruction exhausts it.



28.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Merleau-Ponty and Sartre’s cost. If Merleau-Ponty and Sartre accept the framework’s
reply, they must allow that a structural condition, an invariance, underlies the unity of the body’s
28.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                    305


style and of a life of choices. Merleau-Ponty must grant that the flesh has a structure that can
be stated apart from its being lived. Sartre must grant that freedom has a condition that is not
itself chosen. The cost is the loss of the claim that the lived is self-sufficient.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its structural account is the first word about the subject. It must accept that there is
a dimension of the subject, the lived body and the free act, that is prior to the framework’s
categories and that the framework presupposes. The cost is the loss of the independence of the
structural register from the lived.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
seriously. The framework must take the primacy of the lived and the freedom of the act as claims
about the very possibility of manifestation, not as psychological colorings. The two thinkers
must take the framework’s invariance as a claim about the condition of unity, not as a reduction
of the subject to a thing. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simple opposition between
structure and lived experience.


28.11       The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Merleau-Ponty and Sartre.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Merleau-
   Ponty’s term “expression.” If one substitutes “expression” for “manifestation” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation is the
   appearance of an identity in a realm, and it presupposes the identity; Merleau-Ponty’s
   expression has no prior signified, since the meaning arises in the act of expressing. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Sartre’s term
   “essence.” If one substitutes “essence” for “identity,” the statements change: Sartre’s
   essence is what a being makes of itself after it exists, while the framework’s identity is
   conserved and is the condition of the manifestations. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for either
   thinker’s term “perception.” If one substitutes “perception” for “reconstruction,” the state-
   ments change: perception is the immediate contact with the world, while reconstruction is
   a reading of manifestations. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Merleau-Ponty is
   resemblance: both hold that the subject is situated and that expression is constitutive, and
   they differ on whether there is an identity behind the expression. The relation between
306                                                       Chapter 28. Merleau-Ponty and Sartre


   the framework and Sartre is resemblance of a different kind: both hold that a subject is
   not a mere thing, and they differ on whether a subject has an invariant condition. Neither
   relation is equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted
   by showing that Merleau-Ponty’s style or Sartre’s original choice cannot be stated without
   an invariance of the kind the framework asserts, or, in the other direction, by showing
   that the framework’s invariance can be stated without any presupposition of the lived
   body or the free act.



28.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s invariance compatible with Sartre’s absolute freedom, or
only with the situated freedom of the later work? The chapter has argued for the second, but
the argument is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that the early Sartre cannot be so read
has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s reconstruction be stated without a standpoint? The
chapter has argued that it can, but a reader who holds that every reading presupposes a standpoint
that the flesh dissolves has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to the late Merleau-Ponty? The
chapter has used the flesh and the chiasm as they appear in the working notes and the unfinished
text, and a reader who holds that these resist any systematic reading has a question the chapter
leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider an act you perform without thinking, such as walking through a familiar room, and an
act you choose against resistance, such as refusing a demand. In the first, is there something that
persists across the movements that you could name as what you are? In the second, does the
choice reveal what you already were, or make it? What does your answer tell you about whether
an identity can be both invariant and free?

The next chapter turns to Gadamer and Ricoeur. It states philosophical hermeneutics, the fusion
of horizons, the effective-historical consciousness, the hermeneutics of suspicion and of faith,
and the theory of narrative identity; it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of
both; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of reconstruction and of identity is the nearest hermeneutical analogue to their accounts of
understanding and of the self. The present chapter has stated the answer of the phenomenology
of the body and of freedom; the next chapter states the answer of the philosophy of interpretation,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 29

Gadamer and Ricoeur


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Hans-Georg Gadamer (1900–2002 CE) and Paul Ricoeur
(1913–2005 CE), the two principal figures of twentieth-century philosophical hermeneutics.
It states Gadamer’s account of understanding as an event of tradition, the rehabilitation of
prejudice (Vorurteil), effective-historical consciousness (Wirkungsgeschichtliches Bewußtsein),
and the fusion of horizons (Horizontverschmelzung), with reference to Truth and Method (1960);
it states Ricoeur’s hermeneutics of the symbol, the conflict of interpretations, the distinction
between the hermeneutics of suspicion and of faith, the theory of the text and of metaphor, and
the theory of narrative identity and of the capable human being, with reference to The Symbolism
of Evil (1960), The Conflict of Interpretations (1969), Time and Narrative (1983–85), Oneself
as Another (1990), and The Course of Recognition (2004). It identifies the internal disputes in
the interpretation of both thinkers; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of reconstruction and of identity is the nearest hermeneutical analogue
to their accounts of understanding and of the self; it presents the objections that each would
raise; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the
kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “prejudice,” “horizon,” “distanciation,”
“narrative identity,” or “attestation,” these are the terms of the two thinkers, and their sense is
fixed by their works, not by the framework.


29.1      A Scene
Consider a reader who takes up a very old text, a treatise or a poem, written in a language and
for a world that are no longer hers. She does not read it as a blank. She brings to it questions,
expectations, and a vocabulary that her own time has given her, and the text answers some
of these questions and refuses others. After a long reading the text and the reader have both
changed: she can no longer read it as she did on the first page, and the text has become a thing
that speaks in her time as well as in its own.
    Consider next a person asked to say who she is. She does not offer a list of properties. She
tells a story: where she was born, what she did, what she lost and what she kept. The story has
a plot, and the plot makes her the same person across years in which nearly everything about
her changed. Yet the story could have been told otherwise, and others tell it differently of her.
She is not quite the author of her story, nor merely its subject.
    The two scenes pose a single question: what is it to understand something that is not present
as an object and not available as a fact, a text or a life, and how does the understanding relate
to what is understood? Gadamer answers by describing understanding as an event in which
tradition and interpreter belong to one another. Ricoeur answers by describing understanding as

                                                 308
29.2. The Question                                                                               309


a long detour through signs, texts, and stories toward a self that is only reached by that detour.
The framework answers with a theory of reconstruction. The chapter asks how the three answers
stand to one another.


29.2        The Question
The previous chapter stated the phenomenology of the body and of freedom in Merleau-Ponty
and Sartre. Gadamer and Ricoeur take up the other half of the phenomenological inheritance,
the one that runs from Heidegger’s account of understanding as a mode of being. For them the
primary situation of the human being is that of an interpreter, and philosophy is a reflection on
interpretation.
   The question is not whether Gadamer or Ricoeur was right. The question is what each held,
what each can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to each. The two are
treated together because Ricoeur’s work is both a development of and a criticism of Gadamer’s,
and the framework’s relation to hermeneutics is clearer when the two are set side by side. The
question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Gadamer and Ricoeur hold? The chapter states tradition,
prejudice, and the fusion of horizons in the one, and the conflict of interpretations, distanciation,
and narrative identity in the other.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and
presents the objections that each would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and hermeneu-
tics? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


29.3        Gadamer’s Position
Gadamer’s Truth and Method argues that the model of method, inherited from the natural
sciences and applied to the human sciences, misdescribes understanding. Understanding is not
the application of a procedure by a subject who stands outside what is understood. It is a way
of being of the interpreter, who is always already within a tradition that makes understanding
possible.


29.3.1      Prejudice and Tradition

The Enlightenment condemned prejudice as the enemy of reason. Gadamer holds that the
condemnation is itself a prejudice. Prejudices, in the literal sense of pre-judgments, are the
conditions under which anything can be understood at all. The task is not to eliminate them
but to distinguish the legitimate from the illegitimate, and this can only be done in the course of
310                                                            Chapter 29. Gadamer and Ricoeur


understanding itself. Tradition is not an inert past; it is what transmits and addresses, and an
interpreter who stands in it is addressed by it.


29.3.2    The Fusion of Horizons
An interpreter has a horizon, the range of what can be seen from where she stands, and a text or
a tradition has its own. Understanding is neither the interpreter’s leaving her horizon to enter
the past, nor the projection of her horizon onto it, but a fusion in which a wider horizon arises
that includes both. Effective-historical consciousness is the awareness that the interpreter is
shaped by the history of what she interprets, and that this history is part of what is understood.
Gadamer’s model of this is the dialogue, in which a question and an answer reach beyond what
either partner brought.


29.4     Ricoeur’s Position
Ricoeur accepts the hermeneutical turn and resists Gadamer’s apparent opposition of truth and
method. Understanding requires explanation as its necessary detour: one cannot reach the self
or the text except through structural analysis, symbols, and the critique of ideology. Philosophy
is a reflection that proceeds by interpreting signs.


29.4.1    Symbol, Suspicion, and Faith
In The Symbolism of Evil and The Conflict of Interpretations Ricoeur treats the symbol as
the primary datum of reflection: a double meaning in which a first, literal sense points to a
second that is not otherwise accessible. He distinguishes two attitudes toward symbols. The
hermeneutics of suspicion, which he finds in Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, unmasks the illusions of
consciousness. The hermeneutics of faith or of recollection listens for a meaning offered. Ricoeur
holds that both are necessary and that no single interpretation can claim the whole.


29.4.2    Distanciation and the Text
A written text is detached from its author, its first audience, and its situation. Ricoeur treats
this detachment, distanciation, not as a loss but as a condition of meaning: the text opens a
world in front of itself, a way of being that a reader may appropriate. Explanation, in the form of
structural analysis, belongs to the text’s detachment; understanding belongs to its appropriation;
and the two form an arc.


29.4.3    Narrative Identity and the Capable Human Being
In Time and Narrative and Oneself as Another Ricoeur distinguishes two senses of identity: idem-
identity, sameness over time, and ipse-identity, selfhood, the keeping of one’s word. Narrative
mediates between them: a life is told as a plot in which a character remains the same by the
coherence of a story, even as it changes. In his later work the self is described as capable of
speaking, acting, narrating, and being held responsible, and the self’s certainty of itself is not an
intuition but an attestation, a trust in the testimony of one’s acts.
29.5. Internal Disputes                                                                         311


29.5      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of both thinkers is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the relation of truth and method. One reading takes Gadamer to reject
method as such. Another takes him to reject only the claim that method alone gives truth. The
disagreement matters for the framework because the framework states its claims by a method
of argument and of epistemic marking, and its relation to hermeneutics depends on whether
hermeneutics rejects methods or only their monopoly.


Second dispute: the Gadamer–Habermas quarrel. Habermas argued that Gadamer’s
emphasis on tradition leaves no place for a critique of tradition that stands outside it, and
Gadamer replied that such a standpoint is itself a tradition. Ricoeur tried to mediate. The
disagreement matters because the framework’s own claim to autonomy from every tradition is a
claim of the kind that the quarrel concerns.


Third dispute: the status of narrative identity. One reading takes narrative identity to be
a philosophical account of what a self is. Another takes it to be a mode of self-interpretation that
leaves open what the self is. The disagreement matters for the framework because the framework’s
identity is an invariance, and whether narrative identity competes with or complements it depends
on how this dispute is resolved.


29.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Gadamer and Ricoeur. The framework shares four structural features with the
   two positions.

       1. The rejection of the view from nowhere. Gadamer and Ricoeur hold that understand-
         ing is always carried out from a situation. The framework holds that every reading
         is carried out within a context and that no context is the context of all contexts.
         Both deny that there is an understanding from outside every standpoint.

       2. The mediation of knowledge. Ricoeur holds that the self is known only through the
         detour of signs, texts, and works. The framework holds that an identity is known
         only through its manifestations. Both hold that the access to what is known is
         mediated and that the mediation is not a defect.

       3. The primacy of the relation of question and answer. Gadamer’s logic of question
         and answer holds that a text is understood only as an answer to a question. The
         framework holds that a manifestation is read only as a manifestation of an identity
         under a structure. Both hold that the object of understanding is intelligible only
         within a relation.
312                                                            Chapter 29. Gadamer and Ricoeur


       4. The plurality of readings. Ricoeur’s conflict of interpretations and Gadamer’s openness
          of tradition hold that no single reading is final. The framework holds that contexts
          are infinite and that a reconstruction is always revisable. Both hold that the plurality
          of readings is not a scandal.




29.7      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Gadamer and Ricoeur. The framework diverges from the two positions in four
  respects.

       1. The status of the object. For the hermeneutical thinkers the object of understanding
          is a text, a tradition, or a life, a meaning that is already linguistic. The framework’s
          object is an identity, a structural condition that is not a text. The framework does
          not hold that being is language.

       2. The priority of tradition. Gadamer holds that understanding belongs to tradition.
          The framework holds that its structure is autonomous and that it does not depend
          on any tradition. The framework’s autonomy is not Gadamer’s belonging.

       3. The account of the self. Ricoeur’s self is constituted by narrative and attestation. The
          framework’s identity is conserved and non-duplicable, and it is not constituted by
          the story that is told of it. The framework separates the identity from its narration.

       4. The role of suspicion. Ricoeur holds that interpretation must include a critique of
          the illusions of consciousness. The framework does not make the critique of ideology
          a part of its structure, and it states no hermeneutics of suspicion.




29.8      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Gadamer’s objection. The framework claims autonomy from every tradition. But there
  is no standpoint outside tradition, and the claim to autonomy is the oldest prejudice of
  the Enlightenment. The framework speaks within a tradition of systematic metaphysics
  and conceals its own belonging by calling it structure.
  Ricoeur’s first objection. The framework says that an identity is an invariance and
  that it is read through manifestations. But the self is not reached by a reconstruction
  that a subject performs on an object. The self is reached only through the detour of signs
  and stories, and it keeps its word through time without being the same in the way an
  invariance is the same. The framework confuses idem with ipse.
29.9. The Framework’s Reply                                                                     313


   Ricoeur’s second objection. The framework presents its claims with an epistemic
   status but without a critique of the interests that shape them. A philosophy that does
   not ask what its own system of concepts conceals is open to the hermeneutics of suspicion.
   The framework’s neutrality is itself an interpretation, not an escape from interpretation.



29.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Gadamer. The framework agrees that no one speaks from outside every
   tradition, and it does not claim to. Its autonomy is the autonomy of justification, not
   of origin: a claim’s truth is assessed by its premises and its arguments, whatever the
   tradition from which it arose. Gadamer’s own account distinguishes legitimate from
   illegitimate prejudices by their fruit in understanding, and this distinction has the form
   of a justification that is not simply a belonging. The framework’s autonomy is the claim
   that such a distinction can be drawn.
   Reply to Ricoeur’s first objection. The framework agrees that idem and ipse must
   be distinguished, and it agrees that narrative mediates between them. But it denies that
   the framework’s identity is idem. The framework’s invariance is not the sameness of a set
   of properties; it is the structural condition under which a story can be the story of one.
   Ricoeur’s own account of attestation presupposes a self that is not exhausted by its story,
   and the framework gives that condition a structural statement without claiming that the
   story is dispensable.
   Reply to Ricoeur’s second objection. The framework accepts that its neutrality is
   not an escape from interpretation, and it marks its claims by status for that reason: an
   axiom is labeled an axiom so that its interest can be seen. A critique of the interests that
   shape the framework is welcome and is not excluded by the structure. The framework
   does not make such critique a part of its principles, because its principles state conditions,
   not diagnoses.



29.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Gadamer and Ricoeur’s cost. If Gadamer and Ricoeur accept the framework’s reply, they
must allow that understanding has a structural condition that is not itself an event of tradition
or an act of attestation. Gadamer must grant that there is a justification that is not merely a
belonging. Ricoeur must grant that selfhood has an invariant condition that narrative presupposes.
The cost is the loss of the claim that the interpretive situation is the last word.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its autonomy is complete. It must accept that its statements are made in a language and a
314                                                             Chapter 29. Gadamer and Ricoeur


tradition, and that the reconstruction it describes is itself an interpretation that has a history.
The cost is the loss of the innocence of the structural register.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about the possibility of understanding. The framework must take the situatedness
of the interpreter as a condition of its own statements. The hermeneutical thinkers must take
structure as a way of stating what interpretation presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the
loss of the opposition between structure and interpretation.


29.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Gadamer and Ricoeur.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Gadamer’s
   term “understanding.” If one substitutes “understanding” for “reconstruction,” the state-
   ments change: reconstruction is a reading of manifestations by a subject, while Gadamer’s
   understanding is an event in which the interpreter is addressed by tradition. The substitu-
   tion fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ricoeur’s term
   “narrative identity.” If one substitutes “narrative identity” for “identity,” the statements
   change: the framework’s identity is conserved and enacted by one source, while narrative
   identity is the coherence of a told life. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “context” is not substitutable for Gadamer’s term
   “horizon.” If one substitutes “horizon” for “context,” the statements change: a context is a
   structural condition of validity, while a horizon is the range of what can be seen from a
   standpoint. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Gadamer is resemblance:
   both hold that understanding is situated and mediated, and they differ on whether the
   situation is tradition or context. The relation between the framework and Ricoeur is
   resemblance of a closer kind: both hold that the self is reached through mediation and that
   the mediation does not abolish the self, and they differ on whether the self’s invariance
   is attested or structural. Neither relation is equivalence, agreement, or identity. The
   framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Ricoeur’s attestation cannot be
   stated without an invariance of the framework’s kind, or that Gadamer’s belonging excludes
   every claim to a justification that is not a belonging.



29.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
29.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                             315


First question. Is the framework’s reconstruction a species of interpretation, or something
prior to it? The chapter has argued that it is a reading carried out within a context and so a
species of interpretation in a wide sense, but the argument is not conclusive.

Second question. Can the framework state the relation between its invariance and a told life
without making the story dispensable? The chapter has argued that it can, but a reader who
holds that narrative is the only access to the self has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Truth and Method do justice to Gadamer’s
claim that method does not give truth? The chapter has stated that the framework uses method
as a mode of justification, and a reader who holds that Gadamer’s claim excludes this has a
question the chapter leaves open.
