A Question for Reflection
Think of a text that changed its meaning for you over the years, a poem, a letter, a founding
document. Was it the text that changed, or you, or the relation between you? If you try to say
what stays the same across your readings, what do you refer to? What does your answer tell you
about whether understanding needs something invariant to understand?

The next chapter turns to Whitehead. It states the philosophy of organism, the actual occasion,
concrescence, the prehension, the eternal objects, and the dipolar God; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Whitehead; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of process and expression is the nearest contemporary
analogue to Whitehead’s. The present chapter has stated the answer of the philosophy of
interpretation; the next chapter states Whitehead’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 30

Whitehead


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Alfred North Whitehead. It states the philosophy
of organism, the actual occasion, concrescence, prehension, the eternal objects, creativity, the
dipolar God, the fallacy of misplaced concreteness, and the critique of the bifurcation of nature,
with reference to Process and Reality, Science and the Modern World, Adventures of Ideas, and
Religion in the Making; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Whitehead;
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of process
and expression is the nearest contemporary analogue to Whitehead’s; it presents the objections
that Whitehead would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states
what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “actual occasion,” “concrescence,” “prehension,” “eternal object,” “creativity,” or “the
dipolar God,” these are Whitehead’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the
interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


30.1     A Scene
Consider a flash of lightning. It is one event: a sudden brightness, a crack of thunder, a moment
of illumination. It has a beginning, a middle, an end; it arises from the meeting of clouds, and it
passes into the night. It is not a substance; it is not a thing; it is an event; it is what Whitehead
calls an actual occasion.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the flash is, but what makes the flash
be. The flash is not made of parts; it is a unity; it is a "growing together" of many elements: the
electrical charge, the atmospheric conditions, the observer’s perception, the past events that led
to it, the future events it will affect. The flash is a concrescence: a "growing together" of many
into one; it is the process by which the many become one, and are increased by one.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the flash is, or how it
grows together, but what the whole is. The whole is not a collection of substances; it is a process;
it is the creative advance of the universe; it is the ongoing concrescence of actual occasions, each
of which grows together from the past and contributes to the future. The whole is creativity:
the ultimate category, the principle of novelty, the source of all that is.
   The scene is Whitehead’s image, in Process and Reality, of the structure of reality. The flash
is the actual occasion; the growing together is the concrescence; the whole is the creative advance.
The actual occasion is not a substance; it is an event; it is a process; it is what reality is made
of. The eternal objects are the forms that the occasions can take; the prehensions are the ways
the occasions grasp one another; and God is the principle of order and novelty that makes the
creative advance possible.

                                                316
30.2. The Question                                                                               317


   The scene poses the question that Whitehead was the first to pose in its full form. What is
reality made of? Is it made of substances, or of events? Is it static, or is it process? And what is
the relation between the many and the one? The present chapter states Whitehead’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.


30.2      The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Husserl and Heidegger. Husserl posed the problem
of consciousness and the life-world; Heidegger posed the problem of being and the ontological
difference. Whitehead is the third great figure of the contemporary West, and he is the philosopher
who attempts a complete cosmology: a systematic account of reality as process, as organism,
as creative advance. The present chapter states Whitehead’s cosmology, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Whitehead was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Whitehead hold? The chapter states the philosophy
of organism, the actual occasion, concrescence, prehension, the eternal objects, creativity, the
dipolar God, the fallacy of misplaced concreteness, and the critique of the bifurcation of nature,
with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Whitehead converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Whitehead would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Whitehead?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


30.3      The Position

30.3.1    The Philosophy of Organism

Whitehead’s philosophy of organism is stated in Process and Reality (1929). The philosophy of
organism is a cosmology: a systematic account of reality as process, as organism, as creative
advance. It is not a philosophy of substance; it is a philosophy of events; it is not a philosophy of
being; it is a philosophy of becoming.
   The philosophy of organism has three features.


First feature: reality is process. Reality is not made of static substances; it is made of
processes, of events, of occasions. The actual occasion is the fundamental unit of reality; it is not
a thing, but an event; it is not a substance, but a process; it is not a being, but a becoming.
318                                                                        Chapter 30. Whitehead


Second feature: reality is organism. Reality is not a collection of separate things; it is an
organism; it is a whole in which each part is related to every other part. The actual occasions
are not separate atoms; they are interconnected; they prehend one another; they grow together;
they form a single, interconnected process.

Third feature: reality is creative advance. Reality is not a static order; it is a creative
advance; it is the ongoing production of novelty; it is the process by which the many become
one, and are increased by one. The creative advance is the fundamental character of reality; it is
what makes reality a process, not a substance.
      The philosophy of organism is the foundation of Whitehead’s cosmology. It is the systematic
account of reality as process; it is the alternative to the philosophy of substance; it is the new
beginning of metaphysics.

   From the Tradition

   “The philosophy of organism is the effort to frame a coherent, logical, necessary system
   of general ideas in terms of which every element of our experience can be interpreted.”
   (Whitehead, Process and Reality, p. 3, corrected edition)


30.3.2      The Actual Occasion
Whitehead’s account of the actual occasion is stated in Process and Reality, Part I and Part II.
The actual occasion is the fundamental unit of reality; it is the "final real things of which the
world is made."
      The actual occasion has three features.

First feature: the actual occasion is an event. The actual occasion is not a substance;
it is an event; it is a process. It has a beginning, a middle, and an end; it arises, it grows, it
perishes. It is not a thing that persists; it is an event that occurs.

Second feature: the actual occasion is a unity. The actual occasion is a unity; it is a
"growing together" of many elements into one. It is not a collection of parts; it is a whole; it is a
single event, with a single subjective form, a single aim, a single satisfaction.

Third feature: the actual occasion is a perspective. The actual occasion is a perspective
on the whole universe; it prehends the whole from its own standpoint; it grasps the whole in its
own way. Each actual occasion is a unique perspective; no two occasions prehend the same; no
two occasions are identical.
      The actual occasion is the key to Whitehead’s cosmology. It is what reality is made of; it is
the unit of process; it is the unit of creativity; it is the unit of the creative advance.


30.3.3      Concrescence
Whitehead’s account of concrescence is stated in Process and Reality, Part II. Concrescence is
the "growing together" of many elements into one actual occasion; it is the process by which the
30.3. The Position                                                                               319


many become one.
    The concrescence has three features.


First feature: the initial phase. The initial phase is the phase of prehension; the actual
occasion prehends the past actual world; it grasps the many elements that will constitute it. The
prehensions are of two kinds: positive prehensions (feelings) and negative prehensions (exclusions).
The positive prehensions are the elements that enter into the occasion; the negative prehensions
are the elements that are excluded.


Second feature: the middle phase. The middle phase is the phase of subjective form;
the actual occasion integrates the prehensions into a unity; it gives them a subjective form, an
emotional tone, an aim. The subjective form is what makes the occasion an occasion; it is what
makes it a unity, not a collection.


Third feature: the final phase. The final phase is the phase of satisfaction; the actual
occasion achieves its satisfaction; it becomes what it is; it perishes. The satisfaction is the
completion of the occasion; it is the moment at which the occasion becomes a "superject," an
object for future occasions.
    The concrescence is the process by which the many become one. It is the process of creativity;
it is the process of the creative advance; it is the process of reality.

   From the Tradition

   “The many become one, and are increased by one.” (Whitehead, Process and Reality, p. 21,
   corrected edition)


30.3.4    Prehension

Whitehead’s account of prehension is stated in Process and Reality, Part II. Prehension is the
way in which an actual occasion grasps another actual occasion; it is the way in which the past
enters into the present; it is the way in which the many become one.
    The prehension has three features.


First feature: the subject. The subject is the actual occasion that prehends; it is the "I" of
the prehension; it is the occasion that grasps the other. The subject is not a substance; it is an
event; it is a process; it is what becomes.


Second feature: the object. The object is the actual occasion that is prehended; it is the
"it" of the prehension; it is the occasion that is grasped. The object is not a thing; it is an event;
it is a past occasion; it is what has perished.


Third feature: the subjective form. The subjective form is the way in which the subject
grasps the object; it is the emotional tone, the aim, the perspective of the prehension. The
320                                                                         Chapter 30. Whitehead


subjective form is what makes the prehension a prehension; it is what makes it a feeling, not a
mere relation.
      The prehension is the key to Whitehead’s cosmology. It is the way in which the past enters
into the present; it is the way in which the many become one; it is the way in which reality is a
process, not a substance.


30.3.5      The Eternal Objects
Whitehead’s account of the eternal objects is stated in Process and Reality, Part I. The eternal
objects are the pure forms; they are the possibilities that the actual occasions can realize; they
are what Plato called the Forms.
      The eternal objects have three features.

First feature: the eternal objects are pure potentials. The eternal objects are pure
potentials; they are not actual; they are not realized; they are the possibilities that the actual
occasions can realize. The eternal objects are not things; they are forms; they are what the
actual occasions can become.

Second feature: the eternal objects are eternal. The eternal objects are eternal; they are
not in time; they are not temporal; they are the forms that are beyond time. The eternal objects
are what they are, regardless of what is actual; they are the pure possibilities, the pure forms.

Third feature: the eternal objects are ingressing. The eternal objects ingress into the
actual occasions; they enter into the actual occasions; they become the forms of the actual
occasions. The ingression is the way in which the eternal objects become actual; it is the way in
which the possible becomes real.
      The eternal objects are the forms of reality. They are what the actual occasions realize; they
are what makes the actual occasions be what they are; they are the possibilities that the creative
advance actualizes.


30.3.6      Creativity
Whitehead’s account of creativity is stated in Process and Reality, Part I. Creativity is the
ultimate category; it is the principle of novelty; it is the source of all that is.
      The creativity has three features.

First feature: creativity is the ultimate. Creativity is the ultimate; it is the most general
category; it is what all things have in common. Creativity is not a thing; it is not a being; it is
the principle of novelty; it is the source of all that is.

Second feature: creativity is the many becoming one. Creativity is the many becoming
one; it is the process by which the many become one, and are increased by one. Creativity is
the principle of concrescence; it is the principle of the actual occasion; it is the principle of the
creative advance.
30.3. The Position                                                                               321


Third feature: creativity is dipolar. Creativity is dipolar; it has two poles: the pole of
the many and the pole of the one; the pole of the past and the pole of the future; the pole of
actuality and the pole of possibility. The two poles are not separate; they are two aspects of one
process; they are two aspects of one creativity.
   The creativity is the key to Whitehead’s cosmology. It is the ultimate category; it is the
principle of novelty; it is the source of all that is. The creativity is what makes reality a process;
it is what makes reality an organism; it is what makes reality a creative advance.

30.3.7    The Dipolar God
Whitehead’s account of God is stated in Process and Reality, Part V. God is dipolar; God has
two natures: the primordial nature and the consequent nature.
   The dipolar God has three features.

First feature: the primordial nature. The primordial nature is the nature of God as the
principle of order; it is the nature of God as the home of the eternal objects; it is the nature of
God as the ground of possibility. The primordial nature is not conscious; it is not temporal; it is
the eternal order of the possible.

Second feature: the consequent nature. The consequent nature is the nature of God as
the principle of novelty; it is the nature of God as the receiver of the world; it is the nature of
God as the ground of the actual. The consequent nature is conscious; it is temporal; it is the
ongoing reception of the world into the divine life.

Third feature: the dipolar unity. The two natures are not two gods; they are two aspects
of one God. The primordial nature is the ground of possibility; the consequent nature is the
ground of actuality; the two are united in the one God, who is the principle of order and novelty,
the ground of possibility and actuality.
   The dipolar God is the key to Whitehead’s theology. God is not the creator of the world; God
is not the omnipotent ruler; God is the principle of order and novelty; God is the fellow-sufferer
who understands. The dipolar God is the God of the philosophy of organism; it is the God of
the creative advance.

   From the Tradition

   “God is not to be treated as an exception to all metaphysical principles, invoked to save
   their collapse. He is their chief exemplification.” (Whitehead, Process and Reality, p. 343,
   corrected edition)


30.3.8    The Fallacy of Misplaced Concreteness
Whitehead’s fallacy of misplaced concreteness is stated in Science and the Modern World (1925).
The fallacy is the mistake of treating an abstraction as if it were concrete; it is the mistake of
treating a model as if it were reality.
   The fallacy has three features.
322                                                                         Chapter 30. Whitehead


First feature: the abstraction. The abstraction is a model, a simplification, a selection
of features; it is not the concrete reality; it is a way of describing the concrete reality. The
abstraction is useful; it is necessary; but it is not the reality.

Second feature: the misplaced concreteness. The misplaced concreteness is the mistake
of treating the abstraction as if it were the reality; it is the mistake of treating the model as if it
were the thing; it is the mistake of treating the simplification as if it were the whole.

Third feature: the correction. The correction is the recognition that the abstraction is
an abstraction; it is the recognition that the model is a model; it is the recognition that the
simplification is a simplification. The correction is the return to the concrete; it is the return to
the whole; it is the return to the process.
      The fallacy of misplaced concreteness is the diagnosis of the modern condition. It is the
diagnosis of the scientist who treats the model as if it were the reality; it is the diagnosis of the
philosopher who treats the concept as if it were the thing; it is the diagnosis of the culture that
treats the abstraction as if it were the concrete.

30.3.9      The Critique of the Bifurcation of Nature
Whitehead’s critique of the bifurcation of nature is stated in The Concept of Nature (1920) and
in Science and the Modern World. The bifurcation of nature is the split between the nature that
is perceived and the nature that is described by science; it is the split between the colours and
the sounds and the quantities and the laws.
      The critique has three features.

First feature: the bifurcation. The bifurcation is the split between the apparent world and
the real world; it is the split between the world of the senses and the world of the sciences; it is
the split between the qualities and the quantities. The bifurcation is the source of the crisis of
the modern world.

Second feature: the critique. The critique is the recognition that the bifurcation is a
mistake; it is the recognition that the apparent world and the real world are one world; it is the
recognition that the qualities and the quantities are aspects of one reality. The critique is the
return to the concrete; it is the return to the whole; it is the return to the process.

Third feature: the alternative. The alternative is the philosophy of organism; it is the
cosmology of process; it is the account of reality as one, as interconnected, as creative. The
alternative is the new beginning; it is the new metaphysics; it is the new cosmology.
      The critique of the bifurcation is the foundation of Whitehead’s cosmology. It is the diagnosis
of the modern condition; it is the response to the crisis; it is the new beginning of philosophy.


30.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Whitehead is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
30.5. Points of Convergence                                                                    323


First dispute: the status of God. The traditional reading takes God to be a real entity: God
is the principle of order and novelty; God is the fellow-sufferer who understands. A revisionary
reading takes God to be a symbol: God is not a being; God is a way of speaking about the
principle of order and novelty; God is a personification of the creativity. The two readings
disagree on whether Whitehead is a theist or a naturalist, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no God.

Second dispute: the status of the eternal objects. The traditional reading takes the
eternal objects to be real forms: the eternal objects are the pure potentials; they are what the
actual occasions realize. A revisionary reading takes them to be conceptual constructs: the
eternal objects are abstractions; they are ways of describing the forms that the actual occasions
take. The two readings disagree on whether Whitehead is a Platonist or a conceptualist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no separate
forms.

Third dispute: the status of creativity. The traditional reading takes creativity to be
a metaphysical principle: creativity is the ultimate category; it is the source of all that is. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a description: creativity is a way of describing the process
of the actual occasions; it is not a principle, but a description. The two readings disagree on
whether Whitehead is a metaphysician or a phenomenologist, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a description, not a principle.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Whitehead is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a process metaphysics. If
Whitehead is a descriptive philosopher, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to Process
and Reality, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


30.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Whitehead. The framework shares four structural features with Whitehead’s
   position.

       1. The priority of process over substance. Whitehead holds that reality is process, not
         substance; the actual occasion is an event, not a thing; the creative advance is the
         fundamental character of reality. The framework holds that reality is expression,
         not substance; the identity is enacted in the manifestation; the expression is the
         fundamental character of reality. Both hold that reality is dynamic, not static, and
         that the dynamic is the truth of the static.

       2. The critique of misplaced concreteness. Whitehead holds that the fallacy of misplaced
         concreteness is the mistake of treating an abstraction as if it were concrete. The
324                                                                        Chapter 30. Whitehead


         framework holds that the fallacy of super-identity is the mistake of treating an
         aggregate of manifestations as if it were the identity. Both hold that abstraction is a
         mistake, and that the return to the concrete is the task of philosophy.

       3. The relationality of reality. Whitehead holds that the actual occasions are inter-
         connected; they prehend one another; they form a single, interconnected process.
         The framework holds that the identities are related through light; they manifest
         themselves in the realms; they form a single, interconnected structure. Both hold
         that reality is relational, not atomistic, and that the relations are constitutive of the
         things related.

       4. The creative advance. Whitehead holds that reality is a creative advance; it is the
         ongoing production of novelty; it is the process by which the many become one, and
         are increased by one. The framework holds that expression is a structural tendency;
         it is the ongoing enactment of the identity; it is the process by which the identity
         is manifested. Both hold that reality is creative, not static, and that the creative
         advance is the fundamental character of reality.



30.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Whitehead. The framework diverges from Whitehead in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Whitehead’s cosmology is a theistic cosmology; God is the
         principle of order and novelty; God is the fellow-sufferer who understands. The
         framework has no God; its structure is not a divine principle; its creativity is not a
         divine act. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the eternal objects. Whitehead holds that the eternal objects are real
         forms; they are the pure potentials; they are what the actual occasions realize. The
         framework holds that the identity is the invariance under a class of transformations;
         it is not a form; it is not a potential; it is the structure of the actual. The framework
         is a metaphysics without eternal objects.

       3. The status of creativity. Whitehead holds that creativity is the ultimate category;
         it is the source of all that is; it is the principle of novelty. The framework holds
         that expression is a structural tendency; it is not the ultimate category; it is not the
         source of all that is; it is the structure of the actual. The framework is a metaphysics
         without creativity.

       4. The status of the actual occasion. Whitehead holds that the actual occasion is the
         fundamental unit of reality; it is an event; it is a process; it is what reality is made
         of. The framework holds that the identity is the fundamental unit of reality; it is
30.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  325


            an invariance; it is a structure; it is what reality is made of. The framework is a
            metaphysics without actual occasions.



30.7        The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Whitehead’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is an
   abstraction; it is the fallacy of misplaced concreteness; it treats the model as if it were
   the reality. The concrete reality is the actual occasion; it is the event; it is the process.
   The framework’s identity is an abstraction; it is not the concrete; it is not the actual. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of abstractions, not of actual occasions.
   Whitehead’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction
   is a static relation; it is not a process; it is not a creative advance. The concrete reality
   is the process; it is the creative advance; it is the ongoing production of novelty. The
   framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of static relations, not of creative processes.
   Whitehead’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not
   process. But a metaphysics without process is an incomplete metaphysics; the concrete
   reality is the process; it is the creative advance; it is the ongoing production of novelty. The
   framework’s silence on process is not a boundary; it is a fallacy. The framework’s philosophy
   is a philosophy without process, and a philosophy without process is a philosophy without
   reality.



30.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that an abstraction is not a
   concrete reality, and it agrees that the fallacy of misplaced concreteness is a mistake. But
   the framework denies that its identity is an abstraction. The framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment
   is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not an abstraction; it
   is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that
   condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between an abstraction (a
   model) and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the
   first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction is not a
   process, and it agrees that the concrete reality is the process. But the framework denies
   that its epistemology is an epistemology of static relations. The framework’s reconstruction
   is a reading of the manifestations; it is the subject’s reading of the process; it is not a
326                                                                       Chapter 30. Whitehead


   static relation, but a dynamic reading. The distinction is between a static relation (a
   model) and a dynamic reading (an interpretation); the framework holds the second, and it
   holds that the second is a kind of knowledge, not a kind of static relation.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without
   process is incomplete, and it agrees that the concrete reality is the process. But the
   framework denies that its silence on process is a fallacy. The framework is a work of
   metaphysics, not of cosmology; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation,
   not the process of the actual occasions. The framework states the structural condition of
   reality; it leaves the process to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics
   of structure and a cosmology of process; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping
   it is not a fallacy, but a boundary.




30.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Whitehead’s cost. If Whitehead accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the concrete reality is the actual occasion. He must accept that the concrete reality is the
enactment of a structure, and that the actual occasion is a moment of the enactment. The cost
is the loss of the radical process metaphysics: the actual occasion is no longer the fundamental
unit of reality, but a moment of the structural enactment.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Whitehead’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of process, of the actual occasion, of the creative advance—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a process, and the framework leaves the process
to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Whitehead’s process is
not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Whitehead must accept that the framework’s structure is not an abstraction; it is a structural
condition that the process presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.
30.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                       327


30.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for White-
   head’s term “the actual occasion.” If one substitutes “the actual occasion” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Whitehead’s actual
   occasion is the fundamental unit of reality, and it is not manifested, because it is the
   reality. The framework’s identity is multiple; Whitehead’s actual occasion is the unit
   of reality. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The
   framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Whitehead’s term “concrescence.”
   If one substitutes “concrescence” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation; Whitehead’s
   concrescence is the growing together of many into one. The framework’s expression is
   structural; Whitehead’s concrescence is processual. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Whitehead is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is process, and they differ on whether the process is the actual
   occasion or the expression. Both hold that reality is relational, and they differ on whether
   the relation is prehension or expression. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Whitehead would be refuted by showing
   that Whitehead’s process metaphysics cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and process—by showing, that is, that Whitehead already
   distinguishes the structural condition from the process, and that the framework’s distinction
   is a development of Whitehead’s own.



30.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Whitehead’s actual occasion, or
is it a departure from Whitehead? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Whitehead’s actual occasion is already a
structural condition, not a process, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Process and Reality do justice to the text?
The chapter has used the philosophy of organism, the actual occasion, concrescence, prehension,
the eternal objects, creativity, the dipolar God, the fallacy of misplaced concreteness, and the
328                                                                      Chapter 30. Whitehead


critique of the bifurcation of nature, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader
who holds that the text supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a process and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the process that becomes, or the structure that persists? Is the truth the
actual occasion that perishes, or the identity that is enacted? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Whitehead’s actual occasion and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Peirce and the pragmatists. It states the pragmatic maxim, the
categories, the theory of signs, and the community of inquiry in Peirce, the pragmatic theory of
truth and radical empiricism in James, and instrumentalism in Dewey; it identifies the internal
disputes in the interpretation of the three; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of context and of the revision of reconstruction is the nearest
pragmatist analogue to their account of inquiry. The present chapter has stated Whitehead’s
answer; the next chapter states the answer of the pragmatists, and the framework’s dialogue with
it.
Chapter 31

Peirce and the Pragmatists


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914 CE), William
James (1842–1910 CE), and John Dewey (1859–1952 CE), the founders and principal developers
of American pragmatism. It states Peirce’s pragmatic maxim, his three categories (firstness,
secondness, thirdness), his theory of signs, his account of abduction, deduction, and induction,
his fallibilism, and his synechism, with reference to the papers “The Fixation of Belief” (1877)
and “How to Make Our Ideas Clear” (1878) and to the posthumous Collected Papers; it states
James’s pragmatism and radical empiricism, with reference to The Principles of Psychology
(1890), The Will to Believe (1897), Pragmatism (1907), and Essays in Radical Empiricism (1912);
and it states Dewey’s instrumentalism and his theory of inquiry, with reference to Experience and
Nature (1925) and Logic: The Theory of Inquiry (1938). It identifies the internal disputes in the
interpretation of the three; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of context and of the revision of reconstruction is the nearest pragmatist analogue
to the pragmatists’ account of inquiry; it presents the objections that the pragmatists would
raise; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the
kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the pragmatic maxim,” “thirdness,”
“abduction,” “radical empiricism,” or “inquiry,” these are the terms of the pragmatists, and their
sense is fixed by their works and by the interpretive literature, not by the framework.



31.1     A Scene

Consider a chemist who has a substance in a flask and wishes to know whether it is an acid. She
does not consult a definition and then decide. She asks what would follow if it were an acid:
that it would turn blue litmus red, that it would react with a carbonate, that it would taste sour
to those who risk the taste. She tries these, and she revises her belief by what she finds. The
belief is not a picture of the flask; it is a habit of expecting, and its meaning is the whole range
of conduct and experience that it would govern.
   Consider next a community of such chemists. No one of them has the final word, and a
conclusion that one reached may be overturned by another. Yet the community, taken over a
long time, converges on beliefs that resist doubt and that the world does not contradict. The
truth is not what any member now holds, nor what all now hold, but what inquiry would settle
on if it were pursued far enough.
   The two scenes pose a question the framework also poses: how is a claim about what is real
to be tested, revised, and stated with its own degree of certainty? The pragmatists answer by
tying the meaning of a claim to its conceivable effects and by tying its truth to the long career

                                                329
330                                                     Chapter 31. Peirce and the Pragmatists


of inquiry. The framework answers with a structural account of contexts and a status for each
claim. The chapter asks how the two answers stand to each other.


31.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Gadamer’s and Ricoeur’s hermeneutics. The pragmatists belong
to another line of the contemporary West, one that begins not from the phenomenology of
the interpreter but from the logic of inquiry. Peirce, James, and Dewey differ widely among
themselves, but they share the conviction that thought is to be understood by what it does in
the course of a life.
      The question is not whether the pragmatists were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The three are
treated together because they stand within a common tradition and because the disputes among
them, especially over truth and over realism, are central to the dialogue. The question has three
parts.


First part: the position. What did Peirce, James, and Dewey hold? The chapter states
the pragmatic maxim, the categories, and the community of inquiry in Peirce, the pragmatic
theory of truth and radical empiricism in James, and instrumentalism and the theory of inquiry
in Dewey.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the pragmatists converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents
the objections that the pragmatists would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and pragma-
tism? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


31.3       Peirce’s Position
Peirce’s pragmatism begins as a rule for clarifying meaning. In “How to Make Our Ideas Clear”
he proposes that one grasps the meaning of a concept by considering what practical effects the
object of the concept might conceivably have; the whole of the concept is the whole of these
effects. Pragmatism, for Peirce, is a method of clarification and not a theory of truth. He later
renamed his own doctrine “pragmaticism” to distinguish it from what others made of it.


31.3.1      The Categories and the Theory of Signs

Peirce holds that there are three irreducible categories of phenomena. Firstness is quality, the
mere possibility of what is felt. Secondness is brute reaction, the encounter with what resists.
Thirdness is mediation, law, habit, and the relation of sign to object and interpretant. The theory
of signs builds on the third: a sign stands for an object to an interpretant, and the interpretant
31.4. James’s Position                                                                           331


is itself a further sign, so that signification is an unending process. Reality, for Peirce, is what
would be the object of the final opinion of an unlimited community of inquirers.


31.3.2    Inquiry and Fallibilism

Doubt, Peirce says, is the irritation that sets inquiry going, and belief is the settlement that ends
it. Inquiry proceeds by three kinds of inference: abduction, the adoption of a hypothesis that
would explain a surprising fact; deduction, the drawing of its consequences; and induction, the
testing of those consequences. No belief is exempt from revision. Fallibilism, the doctrine that
any belief may be mistaken, is joined to synechism, the doctrine that continuity is the principle
of the real, and to a cosmology in which law itself is a habit that has grown.


31.4     James’s Position

James takes the pragmatic method and gives it a broader and more personal reading. In
Pragmatism he holds that a true idea is one that can be assimilated, validated, corroborated,
and verified, and that truth is something that happens to an idea in the course of experience. He
is read, and sometimes reads himself, as holding that truth is what works, though he qualifies
this by the requirement that what works must work in the whole of experience.


31.4.1    Radical Empiricism and the Will to Believe

In the essays collected as Essays in Radical Empiricism James holds that experience contains
relations as well as terms and that no entity of a different kind, neither a transcendental ego nor
a material substance, is needed to bind them. In The Will to Believe he argues that in matters
in which the evidence cannot decide and the choice is forced, living, and momentous, one may
rightfully adopt a belief on the strength of one’s passional nature.


31.5     Dewey’s Position

Dewey treats thinking as a mode of the interaction of an organism with its environment. In
Experience and Nature he holds that experience is not a veil between the subject and nature but
a mode of nature’s own transactions. In Logic: The Theory of Inquiry he defines inquiry as the
controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate one, and he replaces
the notion of truth by that of warranted assertibility: a proposition is warranted when it is the
outcome of competent inquiry.


31.5.1    Instrumentalism

Ideas, theories, and concepts are instruments for dealing with problematic situations. They are
tested by how well they resolve the situations that called them forth. Dewey does not claim
that the instrument is therefore unreal or arbitrary; he holds that the distinction between an
instrument and a copy of reality is a mistaken legacy of a spectator theory of knowledge.
332                                                     Chapter 31. Peirce and the Pragmatists


31.6      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of the pragmatists is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: Peirce’s realism. One reading takes Peirce to be a scholastic realist, holding
that generals are real. Another takes him to be an idealist of the limit of inquiry, holding that
reality is constituted by the final opinion. The disagreement matters for the framework because
the framework’s account of the real as that which an identity enacts differs from each, and the
difference differs according to the reading.

Second dispute: what James meant by truth. One reading takes James to hold that
a belief is true because it is useful. Another takes him to hold that usefulness is a mark of
the truth that a belief has through its fit with reality. The disagreement matters because the
framework’s treatment of viability as a descriptive and not a normative condition must be
carefully distinguished from any equation of truth with success.

Third dispute: the unity of pragmatism. Peirce disowned James’s pragmatism, and
Dewey’s differs from both. One reading holds that pragmatism is a single movement with a
common core. Another holds that the name covers three distinct philosophies. The disagreement
matters because the framework’s relation to the one may differ widely from its relation to the
others.


31.7      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the pragmatists. The framework shares four structural features with the three
   positions.

       1. Fallibilism. Peirce holds that no belief is exempt from revision. The framework holds
          that reconstruction is always revisable and marks its own claims with an epistemic
          status. Both hold that the openness to revision is a structural feature of knowledge,
          not a weakness.

       2. The relation of a claim to its conditions. The pragmatic maxim holds that the
          meaning of a concept lies in its conceivable consequences. The framework holds that
          a claim is intelligible only under a context and a structure. Both hold that a claim
          has no sense apart from the conditions under which it is made and tested.

       3. The rejection of the spectator theory. Dewey rejects the view that the knower is
          a spectator copying a given reality, and James holds that experience has no gap
          between its terms. The framework holds that a subject is itself a manifestation in a
          realm. Both hold that the subject stands within what it knows.

       4. The community of inquiry. Peirce holds that reality is what an unlimited community
31.8. Points of Divergence                                                                      333


         would settle upon. The framework holds that contexts are infinite and that no single
          context validates a claim finally. Both hold that no individual inquirer is the measure
          of the real.



31.8      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With the pragmatists. The framework diverges from the three positions in four respects.

       1. The theory of truth. Peirce defines the real by the limit of inquiry, James by what
          proves itself in experience, and Dewey by warranted assertibility. The framework
          does not define reality or truth by inquiry or by success; it states identity as a
          condition prior to any inquiry into it.

       2. The role of consequences. The pragmatists tie the meaning of a claim to its conceivable
          effects. The framework holds that the meaning of a structural claim lies in its place
          in a structure and in the arguments for it, and it does not reduce this to practical
          consequences.

       3. The status of viability. The framework’s viability is a descriptive condition on the
          relation between an identity and its manifestations. The pragmatists’ success is a
          criterion of belief. The framework attaches no value or end to viability and does not
          treat it as a test of truth.

       4. The treatment of the source. The framework holds that an identity is enacted by one
          source. The pragmatists, especially Peirce in his evolutionary cosmology and Dewey
          in his naturalism, hold that law and structure emerge from processes of habit and
          interaction. The framework’s source is not an emergent.



31.9      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Peirce’s objection. The framework holds that an identity is real independently of any
   inquiry into it. But a reality that could in principle never be known is a reality of which
   the word has no meaning. The framework’s identity is, by the pragmatic maxim, either
   an idle notion or a name for what inquiry would reach in the end.
   James’s objection. The framework claims that its principles are argued and that
   some are axioms. But the choice among rival metaphysical systems cannot be settled by
   argument alone, and a person who adopts one does so partly out of temperament and
   partly for what it lets her live. The framework conceals its passional commitments by
   calling them axioms.
334                                                       Chapter 31. Peirce and the Pragmatists


   Dewey’s objection. The framework separates a structural register from the situations in
   which problems arise. But philosophy is a reconstruction of problematic situations, and a
   metaphysics that does not begin from them and return to them is a flight from experience.
   The framework’s neutrality is a refusal to be tested by the difference it makes.



31.10          The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Peirce. The framework agrees that a notion with no conceivable bearing on
   experience is idle, and it denies that the identity is such a notion. An identity is manifested,
   and its manifestations are exactly what inquiry reads. The framework does not deny that
   the identity is what inquiry would reach; it denies that this is what the identity is. Peirce’s
   own scholastic realism holds that a general is real whether or not it is ever known, and
   the framework’s identity is real in that sense.
   Reply to James. The framework agrees that temperament enters the choice among
   systems, and it marks that entry by labeling the commitments that cannot be argued for
   as axioms, so that they can be seen. This is not concealment but the opposite. James’s
   own defense of the will to believe is restricted to cases where evidence cannot decide, and
   the framework does not claim that the evidence decides the cases it labels as axioms.
   Reply to Dewey. The framework agrees that philosophy arises from problematic
   situations, and it holds that the problem it addresses, the relation between an identity
   and its manifestations, is such a situation. It denies that a structural statement is a flight
   from experience. A structure that states what experience presupposes is tested by whether
   the experience can be intelligibly described without it, and this test is a pragmatic one in
   Dewey’s own sense.



31.11          The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Peirce and the pragmatists’s cost. If the pragmatists accept the framework’s reply, they
must allow that reality is not exhausted by the limit of inquiry or by warranted assertibility, and
that an identity has a structural condition that precedes any inquiry. Peirce must grant that
the real is not constituted by the final opinion. James must grant that some commitments are
axioms and not passional wagers. Dewey must grant that a structural register can be stated
apart from a problematic situation. The cost is the loss of the claim that inquiry is the measure
of the real.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its identity is intelligible apart from any possible inquiry, and it must accept that the choice
31.12. The Kind of Relation                                                                     335


among systems is not wholly a matter of argument. The cost is the loss of the independence of
the structural register from the practice of inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim as
a claim about the possibility of knowledge. The framework must take fallibilism as a structural
feature of its own claims. The pragmatists must take structure as a way of stating what inquiry
presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between structure and inquiry.


31.12      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   the pragmatists.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Peirce’s term
   “the real.” If one substitutes “the real” for “identity,” the statements change: the real is
   what the final opinion would represent, while the identity is the invariance enacted by one
   source. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “viability” is not substitutable for James’s term
   “what works.” If one substitutes “what works” for “viability,” the statements change:
   viability is a descriptive condition without value, while what works is a criterion of belief.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Dewey’s
   term “inquiry.” If one substitutes “inquiry” for “reconstruction,” the statements change:
   reconstruction is a reading of manifestations, while inquiry is the controlled transformation
   of an indeterminate situation. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Peirce is resemblance of
   a close kind: both hold that the real is more than what is now known, that claims are
   revisable, and that structure is mediation, and they differ on whether reality is defined by
   the limit of inquiry. The relation between the framework and James and Dewey is a more
   distant resemblance: both hold that the knower stands within what is known, and they
   differ on whether truth is tied to success. Neither relation is equivalence, agreement, or
   identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Peirce’s thirdness
   cannot be stated without a source of the kind the framework asserts is excluded, or that
   the pragmatic maxim, correctly applied, shows the framework’s identity to be idle.



31.13      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity different from Peirce’s real as what the final
opinion would represent? The chapter has argued that it is, but the argument is not conclusive,
336                                                      Chapter 31. Peirce and the Pragmatists


and a reader who holds that the two are the same in everything but name has a question the
chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s axioms be distinguished from James’s passional
commitments? The chapter has argued that they can by being labeled and open to criticism, but
a reader who holds that the label does not change the nature of the commitment has a question
the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s structural register pass the pragmatic test in Dewey’s
sense? The chapter has argued that it does, by describing what experience presupposes, and a
reader who holds that only a consequence in conduct passes the test has a question the chapter
leaves open.
