A Question for Reflection
Take a belief you hold firmly and ask what you would expect to see if it were false. If you can
name nothing, what is the belief about? If you can name something, what would you do on
finding it? What does your answer tell you about whether the meaning of a claim lies in what
could be found, or in what the claim is a claim about?

The next chapter turns to Wittgenstein. It states the picture theory of language, the Tractatus,
the later philosophy of language games, the forms of life, and the critique of metaphysics; it
identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Wittgenstein; and it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of language and structure is
the nearest contemporary analogue to Wittgenstein’s. The present chapter has stated the answer
of the pragmatists; the next chapter states Wittgenstein’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
Chapter 32

Wittgenstein


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Ludwig Wittgenstein. It states the picture theory
of language, the saying/showing distinction, the limits of language, the ladder metaphor, and
the silence of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus; the later philosophy of language games,
forms of life, family resemblance, meaning as use, the rule-following consideration, the private
language argument, and the critique of the Augustinian picture of language, with reference to the
Philosophische Untersuchungen; the notion of aspect-seeing and the duck-rabbit; and the critique
of metaphysics in both periods; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Wittgenstein; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of language and structure is the nearest contemporary analogue to Wittgenstein’s; it
presents the objections that Wittgenstein would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “language game,” “form of life,” “family resemblance,”
“rule-following,” or “aspect,” these are Wittgenstein’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.



32.1      A Scene

Consider a person who is learning a language. She learns the word "apple": she points to an
apple, and someone says "apple"; she points to another apple, and someone says "apple"; she
points to an orange, and someone says "not apple." She learns the word by its use; she learns
what the word does; she learns the game in which the word is played.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not how she learns the word, but what the
word means. The word "apple" means what it does; it means the role it plays in the language
game; it means the practice in which it is used. There is no entity "the meaning of apple" behind
the word; there is only the use, the practice, the game. The meaning is the use; the use is the
practice; the practice is the form of life.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the word means, or
how it is used, but what the limits of language are. There are things that can be said; there are
things that cannot be said; there are things that can only be shown. The limits of language are
the limits of the world; what lies beyond the limits cannot be spoken; it can only be shown, or
passed over in silence. "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."
    The scene is Wittgenstein’s image, in the Tractatus and in the Philosophical Investigations,
of the structure of language. The word is the game; the game is the practice; the practice is the
form of life. The limits of language are the limits of the world; the silence is the space beyond

                                                337
338                                                                     Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


the limits. The early Wittgenstein draws the limits from the side of logic; the later Wittgenstein
draws the limits from the side of practice.
      The scene poses the question that Wittgenstein was the first to pose in its full form. What is
the meaning of a word? Is it an entity, a picture, or a use? What are the limits of language? Are
they logical, practical, or both? And what lies beyond the limits—nothing, or the unsayable?
The present chapter states Wittgenstein’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


32.2        The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Husserl, Heidegger, and Whitehead. Husserl posed
the problem of consciousness and the life-world; Heidegger posed the problem of being; Whitehead
posed the problem of process. Wittgenstein is the fourth great figure of the contemporary West,
and he is the philosopher who turns from consciousness, being, and process to language: he asks
what language is, how it works, and what its limits are. The present chapter states Wittgenstein’s
turn, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Wittgenstein was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Wittgenstein hold? The chapter states the early
philosophy (the picture theory, the saying/showing distinction, the limits, the silence) and the
later philosophy (language games, forms of life, family resemblance, meaning as use, rule-following,
private language, aspect-seeing), with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Wittgenstein converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Wittgenstein would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Wittgen-
stein? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


32.3        The Position

32.3.1      The Picture Theory of Language

Wittgenstein’s picture theory is stated in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921). The theory
is the early Wittgenstein’s account of how language represents reality.
      The picture theory has three features.


First feature: the proposition is a picture. A proposition is a picture of a possible state
of affairs; it represents the world by sharing its logical form with the world. The proposition and
32.3. The Position                                                                               339


the state of affairs have the same logical structure; the proposition is true if the structure of the
world matches the structure of the proposition.


Second feature: the elementary proposition. The elementary proposition (Elementarsatz)
is the simplest proposition; it consists of names in a logical arrangement; it pictures an atomic
state of affairs. Complex propositions are truth-functions of elementary propositions.


Third feature: the limits of representation. The picture theory has a limit: the picture
cannot picture its own pictorial relation to the world; it cannot picture its own logical form. The
logical form can only be shown, not said. This is the origin of the saying/showing distinction.
   The picture theory is the foundation of the early Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is the account
of how language hooks onto the world; it is the account of the logical structure of representation;
it is the account that leads to the saying/showing distinction.

   From the Tradition

   “The proposition is a picture of reality. The proposition is a model of reality as we imagine
   it.” (Wittgenstein, Tractatus 4.01, trans. after Ogden-Ramsey)



32.3.2    The Saying/Showing Distinction

Wittgenstein’s saying/showing distinction is stated in the Tractatus, especially in propositions
4.121–4.1212. The distinction is between what language can say and what language can only
show.
   The distinction has three features.


First feature: what can be said. What can be said is what can be pictured; what can be
represented by a proposition; what has a logical form that matches the world. The sayable is the
domain of factual propositions; it is the domain of the sciences; it is the domain of what can be
stated truly or falsely.


Second feature: what can only be shown. What can only be shown is what cannot be
pictured; what cannot be represented by a proposition; what has no logical form that matches
the world. The showable is the domain of logic, of ethics, of aesthetics, of religion; it is the
domain of what makes saying possible; it is the domain of the unsayable.


Third feature: the limits of saying. The limits of saying are the limits of the world; what
lies beyond the limits cannot be said; it can only be shown, or passed over in silence. The
distinction is the foundation of the early Wittgenstein’s critique of metaphysics: the metaphysical
propositions are attempts to say what can only be shown; they are nonsense.
   The saying/showing distinction is the key to the Tractatus. It is what makes the book a
critique of metaphysics; it is what makes the book end in silence; it is what makes the book a
ladder that must be thrown away.
340                                                                     Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


32.3.3      The Limits of Language and the Silence

Wittgenstein’s account of the limits of language and the silence is stated in the Tractatus,
especially in propositions 6.4–7. The limits of language are the limits of the world; the silence is
the space beyond the limits.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the limits of language. The limits of language are the limits of what can be
said; the limits of what can be pictured; the limits of what has a logical form. The limits are
drawn from within language; they are the limits of sense; they are what distinguishes sense from
nonsense.


Second feature: the silence. The silence is the space beyond the limits; it is the space of
what cannot be said; it is the space of what can only be shown. The silence is not a failure of
language; it is the recognition of the limits of language; it is the respect for what lies beyond.


Third feature: the ladder. The Tractatus is a ladder; its propositions are rungs; whoever
climbs the ladder must throw it away; whoever understands the book must recognize that its
propositions are nonsense. The ladder is the instrument; the silence is the destination.

    From the Tradition

    “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.” (Wittgenstein, Tractatus 7, trans.
    after Ogden-Ramsey)


32.3.4      The Later Philosophy: Language Games

Wittgenstein’s later philosophy is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen (1953). The later
philosophy is a rejection of the picture theory; it is a new account of language; it is the account
of language games.
      The language games have three features.


First feature: language is a game. Language is a game; it is a practice; it is an activity
governed by rules. The game is not a system of propositions; it is a form of life; it is a way of
acting; it is a way of being with others.


Second feature: the plurality of games. There are many games; there are many ways of
using language; there is no single essence of language. The games are not all the same; they are
not all instances of a single form; they are many; they are irreducible.


Third feature: the rules of the game. The game is governed by rules; the rules are not
explicit; they are implicit in the practice; they are learned by training; they are followed without
being formulated. The rules are the practice; the practice is the game; the game is the form of
life.
32.3. The Position                                                                               341


   The language games are the foundation of the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. They are the
new account of language; they are the rejection of the picture theory; they are the new method
of philosophy.

   From the Tradition

   “The term ’language game’ is meant to bring into prominence the fact that the speaking
   of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life.” (Wittgenstein, Philosophische
   Untersuchungen §23, trans. after Anscombe)


32.3.5    Forms of Life
Wittgenstein’s account of forms of life is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen, especially
in §19, §23, §241. The forms of life are the practices, the customs, the institutions in which
language is embedded; they are what makes language possible.
   The forms of life have three features.

First feature: language is embedded in life. Language is not a separate system; it is
embedded in life; it is part of the practices, the customs, the institutions of a community. The
meaning of a word is its role in the form of life; the form of life is the background against which
the word has meaning.

Second feature: the plurality of forms of life. There are many forms of life; there are
many communities, many practices, many customs. The forms of life are not all the same; they
are not all instances of a single form; they are many; they are irreducible.

Third feature: agreement in forms of life. The agreement that makes language possible
is not agreement in opinions; it is agreement in forms of life. "If language is to be a means of
communication there must be agreement not only in definitions but also (queer as this may
sound) in judgments."
   The forms of life are the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. They are what grounds
language; they are what makes meaning possible; they are what makes the language game a
game.

   From the Tradition

   “So you are saying that human agreement decides what is true and what is false?—It is
   what human beings say that is true and false; and they agree in the language they use.
   That is not agreement in opinions but in form of life.” (Wittgenstein, Philosophische
   Untersuchungen §241, trans. after Anscombe)


32.3.6    Family Resemblance
Wittgenstein’s account of family resemblance is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen,
especially in §65–67. The family resemblance is the alternative to the essence; it is the alternative
to the definition; it is the alternative to the picture theory.
342                                                                     Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


      The family resemblance has three features.


First feature: no common essence. There is no common essence; there is no single feature
that all games share; there is no definition that captures what a game is. The games are related
by a network of similarities; the similarities overlap; they crisscross; they form a family.


Second feature: the network of similarities. The similarities are not a single feature; they
are a network; they overlap; they crisscross; they form a family. The family resemblance is the
network; the network is the family; the family is the concept.


Third feature: the open concept. The concept is open; it is not bounded by a definition;
it is extended by the practice; it is applied by the community; it is learned by training. The
concept is not a fixed essence; it is a living practice.
      The family resemblance is the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is what replaces
the essence; it is what replaces the definition; it is what replaces the picture theory.


32.3.7      Meaning as Use

Wittgenstein’s account of meaning as use is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen,
especially in §43. The meaning of a word is its use in the language; the meaning is not an entity;
it is not a picture; it is not a mental state; it is the use.
      The meaning as use has three features.


First feature: the meaning is the use. The meaning of a word is its use; the use is the role
it plays in the game; the role is the practice; the practice is the form of life. The meaning is not
behind the use; the meaning is the use.


Second feature: no mental entity. The meaning is not a mental entity; it is not an image;
it is not a feeling; it is not an intention. The meaning is the use; the use is public; the use is
observable; the use is teachable.


Third feature: the context of use. The meaning is context-dependent; the meaning is
determined by the use; the use is determined by the game; the game is determined by the form
of life. The meaning is not fixed; it is fluid; it is the practice.
      The meaning as use is the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is what replaces the
picture theory; it is what replaces the reference; it is what replaces the essence.


32.3.8      The Rule-Following Consideration

Wittgenstein’s rule-following consideration is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen,
especially in §138–242. The consideration is the problem of how a rule determines its application;
it is the problem of how a rule can be followed; it is the problem of what makes a rule a rule.
      The rule-following consideration has three features.
32.3. The Position                                                                                 343


First feature: the regress. The regress is the problem of how a rule determines its application;
every application requires a rule; every rule requires an interpretation; every interpretation requires
a rule; the regress is infinite. The regress is the problem of the picture theory: the picture cannot
determine its application.


Second feature: the practice. The practice is the solution; the rule is followed in the practice;
the practice is the background against which the rule has meaning; the practice is the custom;
the custom is the institution; the institution is the form of life.


Third feature: the community. The community is the ground of the practice; the community
agrees in the practice; the agreement is not in opinions; the agreement is in forms of life. The
community is what makes the rule a rule; the community is what makes the practice a practice.
   The rule-following consideration is the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is what
grounds the practice; it is what grounds the community; it is what grounds the form of life.

   From the Tradition

   “This was our paradox: no course of action could be determined by a rule, because every
   course of action can be made out to accord with the rule. The answer was: if everything
   can be made out to accord with the rule, then it can also be made out to conflict with it.
   And so there would be neither accord nor conflict here.” (Wittgenstein, Philosophische
   Untersuchungen §201, trans. after Anscombe)


32.3.9    The Private Language Argument

Wittgenstein’s private language argument is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen,
especially in §243–315. The argument is the rejection of the private language; it is the rejection
of the language that only the speaker can understand; it is the rejection of the language that
refers to private sensations.
   The private language argument has three features.


First feature: the private language. The private language is the language that only the
speaker can understand; the words refer to private sensations; the meanings are private; the rules
are private. The private language is the language of the isolated self; it is the language of the
Cartesian ego.


Second feature: the impossibility. The private language is impossible; the words have no
meaning; the rules have no application; the sensations have no criterion. The private language is
not a language; it is a noise; it is a confusion.


Third feature: the public criterion. The public criterion is the condition of language; the
words have meaning because they are used in the public practice; the practice is the game; the
game is the form of life. The public criterion is what makes the language a language; the public
criterion is what makes the meaning a meaning.
344                                                                        Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


      The private language argument is the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is what
rejects the Cartesian ego; it is what rejects the private sensation; it is what grounds the public
practice.


32.3.10       Aspect-Seeing and the Duck-Rabbit
Wittgenstein’s account of aspect-seeing is stated in the Philosophische Untersuchungen, Part II,
§11. The aspect-seeing is the seeing of an aspect; it is the seeing of something as something; it is
the seeing that is not just the seeing of a sensation.
      The aspect-seeing has three features.


First feature: the duck-rabbit. The duck-rabbit is the image that can be seen as a duck or
as a rabbit; the image is the same; the seeing is different. The aspect-seeing is the seeing of the
image as a duck; the aspect-seeing is the seeing of the image as a rabbit; the two seeings are not
two sensations; they are two aspects.


Second feature: the aspect. The aspect is not a property of the image; the aspect is the
way the image is seen; the aspect is the organization of the image; the aspect is the seeing-as.
The aspect is not in the image; the aspect is in the seeing; the aspect is the practice.


Third feature: the change of aspect. The change of aspect is the change of the seeing; it is
the change of the organization; it is the change of the practice. The change is not a change of
sensation; it is a change of aspect; it is a change of the form of life.
      The aspect-seeing is the key to the later Wittgenstein’s philosophy of perception. It is what
shows that perception is not just sensation; it is what shows that perception is a practice; it is
what shows that perception is embedded in the form of life.


32.3.11       The Critique of Metaphysics
Wittgenstein’s critique of metaphysics is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in
the Tractatus and in the Philosophische Untersuchungen. The critique is the diagnosis of the
metaphysical confusion; it is the therapy of the metaphysical question; it is the dissolution of the
metaphysical problem.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the metaphysical proposition. The metaphysical proposition is an attempt
to say what can only be shown; it is an attempt to go beyond the limits of language; it is an
attempt to say the unsayable. The metaphysical proposition is nonsense; it is not false; it is
meaningless.


Second feature: the metaphysical confusion. The metaphysical confusion is the confusion
of grammar with reality; it is the confusion of the form of language with the form of the world;
it is the confusion of the practice with the essence. The metaphysical confusion is the source of
the metaphysical problem.
32.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         345


Third feature: the therapy. The therapy is the dissolution of the metaphysical problem; it
is the showing that the problem is a confusion; it is the return to the practice; it is the return
to the form of life. The therapy is not a doctrine; it is a method; it is the method of the later
Wittgenstein.
   The critique of metaphysics is the key to Wittgenstein’s philosophy. It is what makes the
Tractatus end in silence; it is what makes the Investigations a therapy; it is what makes the
philosophy a practice, not a doctrine.


32.4     Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Wittgenstein is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the continuity between the early and the later Wittgenstein. The
traditional reading takes the early and the later Wittgenstein to be discontinuous: the Tractatus
and the Investigations are two different philosophies; there are two Wittgensteins. A revisionary
reading takes them to be continuous: the same question—the limits of language—is asked from
a different angle; there is one Wittgenstein, with one question. The two readings disagree on
whether the early and the later philosophy are continuous, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is not a language game, and its limits
are not the limits of language.

Second dispute: the status of the rule-following consideration. The traditional reading
takes the rule-following consideration to be a skeptical paradox: the rule cannot determine its
application; the practice is the solution; the community is the ground. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a grammatical investigation: the rule-following consideration shows that the rule is
a practice, not a mental entity; it is not a paradox, but a clarification. The two readings disagree
on whether Wittgenstein is a skeptic or a grammarian, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a practice, not a mental entity.

Third dispute: the status of the private language argument. The traditional reading
takes the private language argument to be a refutation of the Cartesian ego: the private sensation
has no criterion; the private language is impossible. A revisionary reading takes it to be a
grammatical investigation: the private language argument shows that the language of the private
sensation is a confusion; it is not a refutation, but a clarification. The two readings disagree
on whether Wittgenstein is a refuter or a grammarian, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is not a Cartesian ego, but a structural
condition.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Wittgenstein is a skeptic, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a skeptical practice. If
Wittgenstein is a grammarian, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the Investigations,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.
346                                                                      Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


32.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Wittgenstein. The framework shares four structural features with Wittgenstein’s
  position.

       1. The critique of metaphysics. Wittgenstein holds that the metaphysical proposition
          is an attempt to say what can only be shown; it is nonsense; it is a confusion. The
          framework holds that the claim to complete knowledge is impossible; it is a confusion
          of the identity with its manifestations. Both hold that the metaphysical pretension
          is a mistake, and that the mistake is a confusion of the limits.

       2. The critique of the private. Wittgenstein holds that the private language is impossible;
          the meaning is public; the practice is the ground. The framework holds that the
          identity is not a private sensation; it is a structural condition; the manifestation is
          public; the reconstruction is public. Both hold that the private is a confusion, and
          that the public is the ground.

       3. The priority of practice over theory. Wittgenstein holds that language is a practice;
          the practice is the ground; the theory is the description. The framework holds that
          explanation is a practice; the practice is the ground; the theory is the description.
          Both hold that the practice is prior to the theory, and that the theory is the
          description of the practice.

       4. The plurality of forms. Wittgenstein holds that there are many language games;
          there are many forms of life; there is no single essence. The framework holds that
          there are many contexts; there are many apparatuses; there is no single explanation.
          Both hold that the plurality is irreducible, and that the unity is not the essence.



32.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Wittgenstein. The framework diverges from Wittgenstein in four respects.

       1. The status of the structure. Wittgenstein holds that language is a practice; it has
          no essence; it has no structure. The framework holds that there is a structure of
          identity and manifestation; the structure is not an essence; it is not a practice; it is
          a structural condition. The framework is a metaphysics of structure, not of practice.

       2. The status of the limits. Wittgenstein holds that the limits of language are the limits
          of the world; the silence is the space beyond the limits. The framework holds that the
          limits of knowledge are the limits of the reconstruction; the identity is not exhausted
          by the manifestations; the silence is the space of the identity. The framework’s limits
32.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                347


         are structural, not linguistic.

       3. The status of the unsayable. Wittgenstein holds that the unsayable can only be
         shown; it cannot be said; it must be passed over in silence. The framework holds
         that the identity can be indicated; it can be estimated; it can be reconstructed; it is
         not unsayable; it is not ineffable. The framework’s identity is not the unsayable; it
         is the structural condition.

       4. The status of the community. Wittgenstein holds that the community is the ground
         of the practice; the community agrees in the form of life; the form of life is the
         ground. The framework holds that the structure is the ground of the practice; the
         structure is not the community; the structure is the condition of the practice. The
         framework is a metaphysics of structure, not of community.



32.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Wittgenstein’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is a
   metaphysical proposition; it is an attempt to say what can only be shown; it is nonsense.
   The framework’s identity is a metaphysical entity; it is not a practice; it is not a game; it
   is not a form of life. The framework’s ontology is a metaphysics of the unsayable, not a
   description of the practice.
   Wittgenstein’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the subject’s reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. But reconstruction
   is a theory; it is not a practice; it is not a game. The meaning is the use; the use is the
   practice; the practice is the form of life. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology
   of theory, not of practice; it misunderstands the nature of knowledge.
   Wittgenstein’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not
   practice. But a metaphysics without practice is an incomplete metaphysics; the practice
   is the ground; the form of life is the ground. The framework’s silence on practice is not a
   boundary; it is a confusion. The framework’s philosophy is a philosophy without practice,
   and a philosophy without practice is a philosophy without meaning.



32.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysical proposition
   can be a confusion, and it agrees that the identity is not a thing among things. But the
   framework denies that its identity is a metaphysical entity. The framework’s identity
348                                                                     Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


   is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the
   enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a
   metaphysical entity; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and
   the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is
   between a metaphysical entity (an unsayable thing) and a structural condition (a sayable
   structure); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction can be a
   theory, and it agrees that the practice is the ground of meaning. But the framework denies
   that its reconstruction is only a theory. The framework’s reconstruction is a practice; it
   is the subject’s practice of reading the manifestations; it is not a theory imposed on the
   practice; it is the reading of the practice. The distinction is between a theory (a doctrine)
   and a practice (a reading); the framework holds the second, and it holds that the second
   is a kind of knowledge, not a kind of theory.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without
   practice is incomplete, and it agrees that the practice is the ground. But the framework
   denies that its silence on practice is a confusion. The framework is a work of metaphysics,
   not of philosophy of language; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation, not
   the practice of the language game. The framework states the structural condition of reality;
   it leaves the practice to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics of
   structure and a philosophy of practice; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping
   it is not a confusion, but a boundary.



32.9       The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Wittgenstein’s cost. If Wittgenstein accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the structure is a metaphysical entity. He must accept that the structure is a structural
condition, and that the practice is the reading of the structure. The cost is the loss of the radical
practice: the practice is no longer the ground; the structure is the ground; the practice is the
reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Wittgenstein’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the practice, of the language game, of the form of life—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a practice, and the framework leaves the practice
to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Wittgenstein’s practice
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
32.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      349


Wittgenstein must accept that the framework’s structure is not a metaphysical entity; it is a
structural condition that the practice presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is
the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and
each is incomplete without the other.


32.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Wittgen-
   stein’s term “the language game.” If one substitutes “the language game” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Wittgenstein’s language
   game is the practice of the community, and it is not manifested, because it is the practice.
   The framework’s identity is multiple; Wittgenstein’s language game is the practice. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term
  “expression” is not substitutable for Wittgenstein’s term “the form of life.” If one substitutes
  “the form of life” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements change:
   the framework’s expression is a structural relation; Wittgenstein’s form of life is the
   practice of the community. The framework’s expression is structural; Wittgenstein’s form
   of life is practical. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Wittgenstein is re-
   semblance: both critique metaphysics, and they differ on whether the critique is of the
   metaphysical entity or of the metaphysical confusion. Both hold that the practice is
   prior to the theory, and they differ on whether the practice is the ground or the reading.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Wittgenstein would be refuted by showing that Wittgenstein’s practice cannot
   be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and practice—by
   showing, that is, that Wittgenstein already distinguishes the structural condition from the
   practice, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Wittgenstein’s own.



32.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Wittgenstein’s language game,
or is it a departure from Wittgenstein? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Wittgenstein’s language game is already a
structural condition, not a practice, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.
350                                                                     Chapter 32. Wittgenstein


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Tractatus and the Investigations do
justice to the texts? The chapter has used the picture theory, the saying/showing distinction, the
limits, the silence, the language games, the forms of life, the family resemblance, the meaning as
use, the rule-following consideration, the private language argument, the aspect-seeing, and the
critique of metaphysics, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a practice and a structure—a language, a tradition, a
form of life. Is the thing the practice that is played, or the structure that is presupposed? Is the
meaning the use in the game, or the condition of the game? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Wittgenstein’s language game and the framework’s structure?
