Quine and Davidson


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Willard Van Orman Quine and Donald Davidson,
the two great figures of post-war analytic philosophy. It states Quine’s critique of the two
dogmas of empiricism (the analytic/synthetic distinction and reductionism), the web of belief
and confirmation holism, the indeterminacy of translation and the gavagai case, ontological
relativity, and naturalized epistemology, with reference to “Two Dogmas of Empiricism,” Word
and Object, Ontological Relativity, and “Epistemology Naturalized”; and Davidson’s account
of radical interpretation, the principle of charity, truth-conditional semantics, the critique of
the scheme/content distinction, anomalous monism, and the coherence theory of truth without
confrontation, with reference to “Truth and Meaning,” “Radical Interpretation,” “On the Very
Idea of a Conceptual Scheme,” and “Mental Events”; it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of Quine and Davidson; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of translation and interpretation is the nearest contemporary analogue
to theirs; it presents the objections that Quine and Davidson would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind
of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “web of belief,” “indeterminacy,”
“gavagai,” “radical interpretation,” “charity,” “anomalous monism,” or “the scheme/content
distinction,” these are Quine’s and Davidson’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the essays and
by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


33.1     A Scene
Consider a linguist who is dropped into a culture whose language she does not know. A rabbit
runs past; the native says “gavagai.” The linguist notes the utterance, and she forms a hypothesis:
“gavagai” means “rabbit.” But the evidence does not decide the hypothesis; the same evidence
would be compatible with “gavagai” meaning “undetached rabbit part,” or “rabbit stage,” or
“there is rabbithood here.” The linguist can never know which of these is the native’s meaning;
the translation is indeterminate. This is Quine’s image of the indeterminacy of translation.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what “gavagai” means, but what makes
the translation possible at all. The translation is possible because the native is a rational agent;
her utterances are governed by beliefs and desires; and the linguist can attribute beliefs and
desires to her only by assuming that most of her beliefs are true. She must read the native
as believing what is, by her own lights, true; she must extend the principle of charity. This is
Davidson’s image of radical interpretation: the interpretation of a language is possible only if
the interpreter assumes that the speaker is mostly right.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the translation is, or

                                                352
33.2. The Question                                                                                353


what makes it possible, but what the relation is between language and reality. The relation is
not a scheme on one side and a content on the other; it is not a conceptual scheme organizing an
unconceptualized given. There is no given; there is no scheme; there is only the web of belief,
which is at once language and theory, and which faces the tribunal of experience as a whole.
This is the image that Quine and Davidson share: the image of knowledge as a web, not as a
foundation.
   The scene poses the question that Quine and Davidson were the first to pose in its full form.
What is the meaning of an utterance? Is it determinate, or is it indeterminate? What is the
relation between language and reality? Is it scheme and content, or is it a web without a given?
And what is the structure of interpretation? Is it a method, or a condition of possibility? The
present chapter states Quine’s and Davidson’s answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


33.2      The Question

The previous chapter stated Wittgenstein’s position: the picture theory, the saying/showing
distinction, the limits of language, the silence, the language games, the forms of life, the family
resemblance, the meaning as use, the rule-following consideration, the private language argument,
and the critique of metaphysics. Quine and Davidson are the great inheritors of Wittgenstein’s
later philosophy, and they are the great critics of the empiricist tradition. Quine criticizes the two
dogmas of empiricism; Davidson criticizes the scheme/content distinction. The present chapter
states their critiques, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
   The question is not whether Quine and Davidson were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Quine and Davidson hold? The chapter states Quine’s
critique of the two dogmas, the web of belief, the indeterminacy of translation, the gavagai case,
ontological relativity, and naturalized epistemology; and Davidson’s radical interpretation, the
principle of charity, truth-conditional semantics, the critique of the scheme/content distinction,
anomalous monism, and the coherence theory of truth without confrontation.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two philosophers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Quine and Davidson would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Quine and
Davidson? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


33.3      Quine’s Position
354                                                             Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


33.3.1      The Two Dogmas of Empiricism
Quine’s critique of the two dogmas of empiricism is stated in “Two Dogmas of Empiricism”
(1951). The essay is the most influential critique of logical positivism; it is the origin of the
post-positivist philosophy of science.
      The critique has three features.

First feature: the critique of the analytic/synthetic distinction. The distinction
between analytic and synthetic judgments is one of the dogmas of empiricism. An analytic
judgment is true in virtue of meaning; a synthetic judgment is true in virtue of fact. Quine
argues that the distinction cannot be drawn: every attempt to define analyticity presupposes
analyticity; every attempt to define synonymy presupposes synonymy; the distinction is a circle.

Second feature: the critique of reductionism. The second dogma is reductionism: the
belief that every meaningful proposition is equivalent to a logical construction out of terms that
refer to immediate experience. Quine argues that reductionism fails: the propositions of science
are not equivalent to constructions out of experience; they face experience as a corporate body,
not one by one.

Third feature: the web of belief. The alternative is the web of belief: knowledge is a web of
propositions, interconnected, with no privileged foundation; the web faces experience as a whole;
when experience conflicts with the web, we can revise any proposition, if we make compensatory
revisions elsewhere. The web has no analytic propositions; it has no synthetic propositions; it
has only propositions, more or less central, more or less peripheral.
      The critique is the foundation of Quine’s philosophy. It is the end of the analytic/synthetic
distinction; it is the beginning of holism; it is the source of the indeterminacy of translation.

   From the Tradition

   “Any statement can be held true come what may, if we make drastic enough adjustments
   elsewhere in the system. Even a statement very close to the periphery can be held true
   in the face of recalcitrant experience by pleading hallucination or by amending certain
   statements of the kind called logical laws.” (Quine, “Two Dogmas of Empiricism,” in From
   a Logical Point of View, p. 43)


33.3.2      The Indeterminacy of Translation and the Gavagai Case
Quine’s indeterminacy of translation is stated in Word and Object (1960), Chapter 2. The
indeterminacy is the thesis that translation between languages is not uniquely determined by
the evidence; two incompatible translation manuals can both be compatible with all possible
evidence.
      The indeterminacy has three features.

First feature: the gavagai case. A native says “gavagai” when a rabbit runs past. The
linguist can translate it as “rabbit,” or as “undetached rabbit part,” or as “rabbit stage,” or as
33.3. Quine’s Position                                                                              355


“there is rabbithood here.” All are compatible with the evidence; none is uniquely determined by
the evidence.


Second feature: the behavioral criterion. The evidence is behavioral: the native’s disposi-
tions to assent and dissent. The linguist has only the behavior; she has no access to the native’s
meanings. The meanings are not in the behavior; they are posited by the linguist; and the posits
are not uniquely determined.


Third feature: the indeterminacy is not skepticism. The indeterminacy is not skepticism;
it is not the claim that translation is impossible; it is the claim that translation is not unique.
The linguist can translate; she cannot translate uniquely; the choice among manuals is a choice
of convenience, not of truth.
   The indeterminacy is the key to Quine’s philosophy of language. It is the consequence of
holism; it is the consequence of behaviorism; it is the source of ontological relativity.

   From the Tradition

   “The word ’gavagai’ might be translated as ’rabbit,’ or as ’undetached rabbit part,’ or as
   ’rabbit stage,’ and the native’s behavior would be the same in all three cases.” (Quine,
   Word and Object, §12)


33.3.3     Ontological Relativity

Quine’s ontological relativity is stated in Ontological Relativity (1969) and in Word and Object.
The relativity is the thesis that ontology is relative to a background theory; there is no absolute
ontology; there is only ontology relative to a framework.
   The relativity has three features.


First feature: to be is to be the value of a variable. Quine’s criterion of ontological
commitment is the quantifier: to be is to be the value of a bound variable. The ontology of a
theory is the range of its quantifiers; the entities the theory is committed to are the entities over
which its variables range.


Second feature: the relativity. The relativity is the thesis that the ontology is not absolute;
it is relative to the background theory; the same phenomenon can be described in different
ontologies, and no ontology is uniquely correct. The choice among ontologies is a choice of
framework, not a choice of fact.


Third feature: the instrumentalism. The relativity leads to instrumentalism: the ontology
is an instrument; it is not a description of reality; it is a way of organizing the evidence. The
instrumentalism is not skepticism; it is the recognition of the relativity.
   The ontological relativity is the consequence of the indeterminacy of translation. If translation
is indeterminate, then ontology is relative; if ontology is relative, then there is no absolute ontology;
there is only ontology relative to a framework.
356                                                              Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


33.3.4      Naturalized Epistemology

Quine’s naturalized epistemology is stated in “Epistemology Naturalized” (1969). The naturalized
epistemology is the replacement of traditional epistemology by empirical psychology; it is the
continuity of philosophy and science.
      The naturalized epistemology has three features.


First feature: the replacement. Traditional epistemology asks for the foundations of
knowledge; it asks how knowledge is possible; it asks for the justification of belief. Naturalized
epistemology replaces the question of justification by the question of description: how do we
acquire knowledge? How do we form beliefs? The question is empirical; it is answered by
psychology.


Second feature: the continuity. Naturalized epistemology is continuous with science; it is
part of science; it is not a foundational discipline; it is not a tribunal above science. Philosophy
is not the queen of the sciences; it is a branch of the sciences; it is continuous with them.


Third feature: the replacement of normativity. Naturalized epistemology replaces
the normative question (how ought we to believe?) by the descriptive question (how do we
believe?). The replacement is controversial; it is the source of the debate about the normativity
of epistemology.
      The naturalized epistemology is the key to Quine’s later philosophy. It is the consequence of
holism; it is the consequence of the rejection of the given; it is the source of the naturalism that
dominates contemporary analytic philosophy.


33.4       Davidson’s Position

33.4.1      Radical Interpretation

Davidson’s radical interpretation is stated in “Radical Interpretation” (1973) and in “Truth and
Meaning” (1967). The radical interpretation is the interpretation of a language from scratch; it is
the interpretation of the utterances of a speaker whose language the interpreter does not know.
      The radical interpretation has three features.


First feature: the evidence is the speaker’s behavior. The evidence for interpretation
is the speaker’s behavior: her utterances, her dispositions to assent and dissent, her actions.
The interpreter has only the behavior; she has no access to the speaker’s meanings; she must
construct the meanings from the behavior.


Second feature: the principle of charity. The interpreter must assume that the speaker
is mostly right; she must attribute to the speaker mostly true beliefs; she must interpret the
speaker’s utterances as expressing beliefs that are true by the interpreter’s own lights. The
principle of charity is not a courtesy; it is a condition of interpretation.
33.4. Davidson’s Position                                                                          357


Third feature: the truth-conditional semantics. The interpretation is a truth theory: a
theory that specifies the truth conditions of every sentence of the language. The truth theory is
a Tarski-style theory: it specifies, for each sentence, the conditions under which the sentence is
true. The truth theory is the core of the interpretation; the meaning is the truth condition.
   The radical interpretation is the foundation of Davidson’s philosophy of language. It is the
account of how interpretation is possible; it is the account of the conditions of meaning; it is the
account that leads to the critique of the scheme/content distinction.

   From the Tradition

   “Radical interpretation is interpretation of a language from scratch; it is the interpretation of
   the utterances of a speaker whose language the interpreter does not know. The interpreter
   has only the speaker’s behavior; she must construct the meanings from the behavior.”
   (Davidson, “Radical Interpretation,” in Inquiries into Truth and Interpretation, p. 125)


33.4.2    The Principle of Charity
Davidson’s principle of charity is stated in “Radical Interpretation” and in “On the Very Idea of
a Conceptual Scheme” (1974). The principle is the assumption that the speaker is mostly right;
it is the condition of interpretation.
   The principle has three features.

First feature: the charity. The charity is the assumption that the speaker’s beliefs are
mostly true; it is the assumption that the speaker’s utterances are mostly correct. The charity
is not a courtesy; it is a condition of interpretation; without it, the interpreter cannot assign
meanings to the utterances.

Second feature: the optimality. The charity is optimal: the interpreter maximizes the
truth of the speaker’s beliefs; she interprets the utterances in the way that makes the speaker
most rational. The optimality is not a choice; it is a constraint; it is the constraint that makes
interpretation possible.

Third feature: the community. The charity is social: it is the assumption that the speaker
is a member of the same community of belief; it is the assumption that the speaker’s beliefs are
the beliefs of the community. The charity is the ground of the community; it is the condition of
the common world.
   The principle of charity is the key to Davidson’s philosophy. It is what makes interpretation
possible; it is what grounds the common world; it is what makes meaning public.

33.4.3    Truth-Conditional Semantics
Davidson’s truth-conditional semantics is stated in “Truth and Meaning” (1967) and in the essays
that follow. The semantics is the theory of meaning as truth conditions; it is the theory that the
meaning of a sentence is its truth condition.
   The semantics has three features.
358                                                             Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


First feature: the truth theory. The truth theory is a Tarski-style theory: it specifies, for
each sentence, the conditions under which the sentence is true. The theory is compositional:
the truth conditions of complex sentences are determined by the truth conditions of the simple
sentences and the logical connectives.


Second feature: the meaning as truth condition. The meaning of a sentence is its truth
condition: to know what a sentence means is to know the conditions under which it is true. The
meaning is not a mental entity; it is not a picture; it is the truth condition; it is the relation
between language and world.


Third feature: the holism. The truth-conditional semantics is holistic: the truth conditions
of a sentence depend on the truth conditions of the other sentences; the meaning of a sentence is
determined by its role in the language. The holism is the condition of interpretation; it is the
condition of meaning.
      The truth-conditional semantics is the foundation of Davidson’s philosophy of language. It
is the theory of meaning; it is the alternative to the mentalist theories; it is the source of the
critique of the scheme/content distinction.


33.4.4      The Critique of the Scheme/Content Distinction

Davidson’s critique of the scheme/content distinction is stated in “On the Very Idea of a
Conceptual Scheme” (1974). The critique is the rejection of the distinction between a conceptual
scheme (on one side) and an unconceptualized content (on the other); it is the rejection of the
"third dogma" of empiricism.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the third dogma. The third dogma is the scheme/content distinction: the
belief that there is a conceptual scheme that organizes an unconceptualized content. The
distinction is the heir of the analytic/synthetic distinction; it is the last dogma of empiricism.


Second feature: the incoherence. The distinction is incoherent: the content cannot be
identified independently of the scheme; the scheme cannot be identified independently of the
content. The two are not separable; they are two aspects of one thing; they are the two sides of
one coin.


Third feature: the rejection. The rejection is the rejection of the third dogma; it is the
rejection of the idea that there are alternative conceptual schemes; it is the rejection of the idea
that there is an unconceptualized given. The rejection leaves the web of belief: the web without
a given, the web without a scheme, the web without a content.
      The critique of the scheme/content distinction is the culmination of Davidson’s philosophy
of language. It is the rejection of the last dogma; it is the affirmation of the web; it is the new
beginning of the philosophy of language.
33.4. Davidson’s Position                                                                       359


33.4.5    Anomalous Monism

Davidson’s anomalous monism is stated in “Mental Events” (1970). The anomalous monism is
the theory of the relation between the mental and the physical: it is monism (there is only one
kind of substance), but it is anomalous (the mental is not reducible to the physical).
   The anomalous monism has three features.


First feature: the monism. The monism is the thesis that there is only one kind of substance:
every mental event is a physical event; every mental event is identical with a physical event. The
monism is not a reductionism: the identity is not a reduction; it is not a definitional identity; it
is a token identity.


Second feature: the anomaly. The anomaly is the thesis that the mental is not reducible to
the physical: there are no strict psychophysical laws; there are no laws connecting mental types
with physical types. The mental is anomalous; it is not law-governed; it is not predictable from
the physical.


Third feature: the compatibilism. The compatibilism is the thesis that freedom is compati-
ble with determinism: the mental is anomalous, but it is also physical; the freedom is the freedom
of the anomalous; the determinism is the determinism of the physical. The compatibilism is the
consequence of the anomalous monism.
   The anomalous monism is the key to Davidson’s philosophy of mind. It is the alternative to
the identity theory and to the dualism; it is the affirmation of the monism and of the anomaly; it
is the source of the debate about mental causation.


33.4.6    The Coherence Theory of Truth Without Confrontation

Davidson’s coherence theory of truth without confrontation is stated in “A Coherence Theory of
Truth and Knowledge” (1983). The theory is the thesis that truth is coherence, but not coherence
without confrontation; it is the thesis that truth is the coherence of the web of belief, but the
web faces the world.
   The theory has three features.


First feature: the coherence. The coherence is the coherence of the web of belief: the beliefs
are true when they cohere with one another; the truth is the coherence; the truth is not the
correspondence with an unconceptualized given.


Second feature: the without confrontation. The "without confrontation" is the rejection
of the idea that the truth is the confrontation with the given: there is no given; there is no
confrontation; there is only the web. The truth is the coherence of the web, not the correspondence
with the world.
360                                                              Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


Third feature: the facing the world. The web faces the world: the beliefs are about the
world; the truth is the truth of the world; the coherence is the coherence of the beliefs about the
world. The facing is not the confrontation; it is the condition of the web; it is the ground of the
coherence.
      The coherence theory without confrontation is the culmination of Davidson’s philosophy. It
is the rejection of the given; it is the affirmation of the web; it is the new beginning of the theory
of truth.


33.5        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Quine and Davidson is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the indeterminacy. The traditional reading takes the indeterminacy of
translation to be a real thesis: the translation is not uniquely determined by the evidence;
there are many manuals, none of which is uniquely correct. A revisionary reading takes it to
be a consequence of behaviorism: the indeterminacy is not a fact about translation; it is a
consequence of the behaviorist methodology; if we drop the behaviorism, the indeterminacy
disappears. The two readings disagree on whether Quine is a realist or a behaviorist about
meaning, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
meaning is a structural relation, not a behavioral disposition.


Second dispute: the charity. The traditional reading takes the principle of charity to be a
methodological principle: it is a principle of interpretation; it is a constraint on the interpreter.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a structural principle: it is the condition of possibility of
interpretation; it is the structure of the common world. The two readings disagree on whether
Davidson is a methodologist or a structuralist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural condition, not a methodological
maxim.


Third dispute: the anomalous monism. The traditional reading takes anomalous monism
to be a metaphysical theory: it is a theory about the relation between the mental and the physical.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a semantic theory: it is a theory about the language of the
mental; it is a way of speaking about the mental, not a way of being. The two readings disagree
on whether Davidson is a metaphysician or a semanticist, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s distinction between identity and manifestation is
a structural distinction, not a semantic one.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Quine is a behaviorist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a behaviorist instrumentalism.
If Davidson is a methodologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
methodological interpretivism. The framework holds that the second readings are closer to the
texts, but it does not rest its case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.
33.6. Points of Convergence                                                                    361


33.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Quine. The framework shares three structural features with Quine’s position.

       1. The holism of belief. Quine holds that the web of belief is holistic: the beliefs are
         interconnected; no belief is immune to revision; the web faces experience as a whole.
         The framework holds that the structure of identity and manifestation is holistic: the
         four columns are interconnected; no column is immune to revision; the structure faces
         the manifestations as a whole. Both hold that knowledge is holistic, not foundational,
         and that no belief is privileged.

       2. The critique of the given. Quine holds that there is no unconceptualized given;
         there is no immediate experience; there is only the web. The framework holds that
         there is no direct access to the identity; there is only the reconstruction from the
         manifestations. Both hold that the given is a myth, and that knowledge is mediated.

       3. The naturalized epistemology. Quine holds that philosophy is continuous with science;
         it is not a tribunal above science; it is a branch of the sciences. The framework holds
         that its structure is continuous with the inquiries it describes; it is not a tribunal
         above them; it is a structural description. Both hold that philosophy is continuous
         with science, and that it is not a foundation.

   With Davidson. The framework shares three structural features with Davidson’s position.

       1. The principle of charity. Davidson holds that interpretation requires the assumption
         that the speaker is mostly right; the charity is the condition of interpretation. The
         framework holds that reconstruction requires the assumption that the manifestations
         are mostly coherent; the coherence is the condition of reconstruction. Both hold
         that interpretation requires a structural assumption, and that the assumption is the
         condition of the common world.

       2. The critique of the scheme/content distinction. Davidson holds that there is no
         scheme without content, no content without scheme; there is only the web. The
         framework holds that there is no identity without manifestation, no manifestation
         without identity; there is only the structure. Both hold that the dualism of scheme
         and content is a mistake, and that the structure is a unity.

       3. The truth as coherence. Davidson holds that truth is coherence, but not coherence
         without confrontation; the web faces the world. The framework holds that the recon-
         struction is coherence, but not coherence without confrontation; the reconstruction
         faces the manifestations. Both hold that truth is coherence, and that the coherence
         is grounded in the world.
362                                                              Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


33.7      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Quine. The framework diverges from Quine in three respects.

       1. The indeterminacy of translation. Quine holds that translation is indeterminate: there
          is no unique manual; the manuals are not uniquely correct. The framework holds that
          reconstruction is determinate: the identity is the invariance; the reconstruction is the
          reading of the invariance; the reconstruction is not unique, but it is not indeterminate.
         The framework’s reconstruction is a structural reading, not a behavioral posit.

       2. The behaviorism. Quine holds that the evidence for translation is behavioral: the
          dispositions to assent and dissent. The framework holds that the evidence for
          reconstruction is structural: the manifestations, not the dispositions. The frame-
         work’s evidence is the manifestation, not the behavior; the behavior is one of the
          manifestations, not the only one.

       3. The ontological relativity. Quine holds that ontology is relative to the background
          theory; there is no absolute ontology. The framework holds that the structure of
          identity and manifestation is not relative to a background theory; it is the condition
          of possibility of the theory. The framework’s structure is not an ontology; it is the
          structure that every ontology presupposes.

  With Davidson. The framework diverges from Davidson in three respects.

       1. The charity. Davidson holds that charity is the condition of interpretation; the
          interpreter must assume that the speaker is mostly right. The framework holds
          that charity is the condition of reconstruction; the reconstructor must assume that
          the manifestations are mostly coherent. The framework’s charity is structural, not
          methodological; it is the condition of the structure, not a maxim of the method.

       2. The anomalous monism. Davidson holds that the mental is anomalous: there are no
          strict psychophysical laws. The framework holds that the realms are differentiated:
          each realm has its own rules; the rules are not reducible to one another; the
          differentiation is structural, not anomalous. The framework’s differentiation is a
          structure, not an anomaly.

       3. The coherence without confrontation. Davidson holds that truth is coherence, but
          not coherence without confrontation; the web faces the world. The framework
          holds that reconstruction is coherence, but not coherence without confrontation;
          the reconstruction faces the manifestations. The framework’s confrontation is the
          manifestation, not the world; the world is the manifestation, and the manifestation
          is the confrontation.
33.8. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 363


33.8     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Quine’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
   its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is a posit; it is
   a theoretical entity; it is not given in experience. Quine’s indeterminacy of translation
   shows that the posit is not unique; the same evidence would support many incompatible
   posits. The framework’s identity is one posit among many; it is not uniquely determined;
   it is not real. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of posits, not of invariants.
   Davidson’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   a scheme; it is a conceptual framework that organizes the manifestations. Davidson’s
   critique of the scheme/content distinction shows that the scheme cannot be separated
   from the content; the scheme is not a structure above the content; it is one with the
   content. The framework’s identity is a scheme; it is the third dogma in disguise; it is the
   last remnant of the given.
   Davidson’s second objection. The framework says that the realms are differentiated,
   and that each realm has its own rules. But a differentiation without a difference is an
   anomaly; an anomaly without a law is a mystery. Davidson’s anomalous monism shows
   that the differentiation is compatible with the monism; the differentiation is not a structure,
   but an anomaly. The framework’s differentiation is a mystery; it is not a structure; it is
   an anomaly in disguise.



33.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Quine’s objection. The framework agrees that a structural invariance is a
   posit, and it agrees that the posit is not uniquely determined by the evidence. But the
   framework denies that its identity is a posit among many. The framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment
   is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a posit; it is the
   structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition
   is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a posit (a theoretical entity)
   and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   The indeterminacy of translation is a fact about the evidence; it is not a fact about the
   identity; the identity is the source, not the posit.
   Reply to Davidson’s first objection. The framework agrees that the scheme cannot
   be separated from the content, and it agrees that the scheme is not a structure above
   the content. But the framework denies that its identity is a scheme. The framework’s
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not a conceptual framework; it is
364                                                            Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


   not a way of organizing the manifestations; it is the structure of the manifestations. The
   distinction is between a scheme (a conceptual framework) and a structure (the invariant of
   the manifestations); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework
   does not posit an unconceptualized given; it posits a manifested structure; the structure is
   not separate from the manifestations.
   Reply to Davidson’s second objection. The framework agrees that a differentiation
   without a difference is an anomaly, and it agrees that an anomaly without a law is a
   mystery. But the framework denies that its differentiation is an anomaly. The framework’s
   differentiation is a structure: each realm has its own rules; the rules are the structure
   of the realm; the structure is the differentiation. The distinction is between an anomaly
   (a difference without a law) and a structure (a difference with a rule); the framework’s
   differentiation is the second, not the first.



33.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Quine’s cost. If Quine accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
indeterminacy of translation is a fact about meaning. He must accept that the indeterminacy is
a fact about the evidence, and that the identity is not a posit but an enactment. The cost is the
loss of the radical behaviorism: the meaning is no longer behavior; the meaning is the structure;
the behavior is one of the manifestations.


Davidson’s cost. If Davidson accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the scheme is not separable from the content. He must accept that the structure is separable
from the manifestations, and that the structure is not a scheme. The cost is the loss of the
radical coherentism: the truth is no longer coherence without confrontation; the truth is the
coherence of the structure, and the structure is confronted by the manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Quine and Davidson, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the evidence, of the behavior, of the coherence—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a posit and not a scheme, and the framework
leaves the posit and the scheme to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Quine’s indeterminacy and
Davidson’s coherentism are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Quine and Davidson must accept that the framework’s structure is
not a posit and not a scheme; it is a structural condition that the evidence and the coherence
presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
33.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                     365


opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.



33.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Quine). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Quine’s term “the web of belief.” If one substitutes “the web of belief” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Quine’s web of belief is the holistic
   system of beliefs, and it is not manifested, because it is the web. The framework’s identity
   is multiple; Quine’s web is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Quine’s term
   “the observation sentence.” If one substitutes “the observation sentence” for “manifestation”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s manifestation is
   the appearance of the identity in a realm; Quine’s observation sentence is the sentence at
   the periphery of the web, and it is not an appearance. The framework’s manifestation
   is ontological; Quine’s observation sentence is linguistic. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Davidson). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Davidson’s term “the truth condition.” If one substitutes “the truth condition” for
   “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source; Davidson’s truth condition is the condition
   under which a sentence is true. The framework’s identity is ontological; Davidson’s
   truth condition is semantic. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Davidson’s term
   “radical interpretation.” If one substitutes “radical interpretation” for “expression” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural
   relation; Davidson’s radical interpretation is the interpretation of a language from scratch.
   The framework’s expression is ontological; Davidson’s interpretation is methodological.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Quine is resemblance:
   both reject the given, and they differ on whether the web is one or many. The relation
   between the framework and Davidson is resemblance: both reject the scheme/content
   distinction, and they differ on whether the structure is separable from the manifestations.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Quine and Davidson would be refuted by showing that their positions cannot
   be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and web, or between
   structure and interpretation—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the
   structural condition from the web and the interpretation, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of their own.
366                                                            Chapter 33. Quine and Davidson


33.12      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Quine’s web or Davidson’s truth
condition, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but
the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Quine’s web is already a structural
condition, or that Davidson’s truth condition is already a structural relation, has a question the
chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the essays of Quine and Davidson do justice
to the texts? The chapter has used the two dogmas, the web of belief, the indeterminacy, the
gavagai case, the ontological relativity, the naturalized epistemology, the radical interpretation,
the charity, the truth-conditional semantics, the critique of the scheme/content distinction, the
anomalous monism, and the coherence theory, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A
reader who holds that the essays support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.
