A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a web and a structure—a language, a body of knowledge,
a tradition. Is the thing the web that coheres, or the structure that persists? Is the meaning the
use in the web, or the truth condition of the sentence? What does your answer tell you about
the relation between Quine’s web, Davidson’s truth condition, and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Kripke and Lewis. It states Kripke’s causal theory of reference, the
necessary a posteriori, the rigid designator, and Naming and Necessity; and Lewis’s modal
realism, the possible worlds, the counterpart theory, and the counterfactuals. It identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Kripke and Lewis; and it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of necessity and possible worlds
is the nearest contemporary analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated Quine’s and
Davidson’s answers to the problem of meaning; the next chapter states Kripke’s and Lewis’s
answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
Chapter 34

Kripke and Lewis


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Saul Kripke and David Lewis, the two great figures of
post-war modal metaphysics. It states Kripke’s causal theory of reference, the rigid designator,
the necessary a posteriori, the distinction between epistemic and metaphysical modality, and
the Naming and Necessity arguments (the Gödel/Schmidt case, the meter-stick case, the Hespe-
rus/Phosphorus case); and Lewis’s modal realism, the plurality of worlds, the counterpart theory,
the indexical analysis of actuality, and the counterfactual analysis of causation, with reference to
Naming and Necessity, On the Plurality of Worlds, Counterfactuals, and Philosophical Papers; it
identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Kripke and Lewis; it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of necessity and possible
worlds is the nearest contemporary analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that Kripke and
Lewis would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “rigid
designator,” “necessary a posteriori,” “possible world,” “counterpart,” or “counterfactual,” these
are Kripke’s and Lewis’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


34.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a photograph of a child. The photograph was taken in 1950;
the child is now an adult. The person says: "That is the same person." What does she mean?
She does not mean that the child in the photograph and the adult before her share all their
properties; they do not. She does not mean that the child in the photograph is qualitatively
identical to the adult; the two are different. She means that the name she uses for the adult, and
the name she uses for the child, both refer to the same individual; the individual is the same
across time, across the changes, across the worlds. This is Kripke’s image of the rigid designator:
the name refers to the same individual in every possible world in which the individual exists.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the name refers to, but what makes
the name refer. The name refers by a causal chain: the name was given at a baptism, and the
chain of uses, from speaker to speaker, carries the reference to the same individual. The name is
not a description; it is not a cluster of properties; it is a label; it is a tag; it is a rigid designator.
This is Kripke’s image of the causal theory of reference: the name refers in virtue of its causal
history, not in virtue of its descriptive content.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the name refers to, or
what makes it refer, but what the world is in which the name refers. The world is not the actual
world alone; it is the plurality of possible worlds; it is the totality of ways things could have

                                                   368
34.2. The Question                                                                                369


been. Each possible world is a concrete, real entity; each is as real as the actual world; each is
a way the world could be. This is Lewis’s image of modal realism: the possible worlds are not
abstractions, not fictions, not linguistic constructs; they are real; they are the plurality of worlds.
   The scene is the image that Kripke and Lewis share and divide: the image of modality.
Kripke draws the image from the side of language: the name is a rigid designator; the necessity
is metaphysical, not epistemic; the possible worlds are the ways the referent could be. Lewis
draws the image from the side of reality: the worlds are real; the individuals are counterparts;
the actuality is indexical. Both are modal realists, in different senses; both reject the reduction
of modality to language or to psychology; both affirm the objectivity of the possible.
   The scene poses the question that Kripke and Lewis were the first to pose in its full form. What
is a name? Is it a description, or a label? What is necessity? Is it epistemic, or metaphysical?
And what are the possible worlds? Are they linguistic constructs, or concrete realities? The
present chapter states Kripke’s and Lewis’s answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


34.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Quine’s and Davidson’s positions: the two dogmas, the web of belief,
the indeterminacy of translation, the radical interpretation, the charity, the truth-conditional
semantics, the critique of the scheme/content distinction, the anomalous monism, and the
coherence theory. Quine and Davidson are the great critics of the modal tradition; they reject
the analytic/synthetic distinction; they reject the possible worlds as a metaphysical posit. Kripke
and Lewis are the great restorers of modality; they defend the necessary a posteriori; they defend
the possible worlds as a metaphysical framework. The present chapter states their restoration,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Kripke and Lewis were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the positions. What did Kripke and Lewis hold? The chapter states Kripke’s
causal theory of reference, the rigid designator, the necessary a posteriori, and the epis-
temic/metaphysical distinction; and Lewis’s modal realism, the plurality of worlds, the counterpart
theory, the indexical analysis of actuality, and the counterfactual analysis.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two philosophers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Kripke and Lewis would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Kripke
and Lewis? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


34.3      Kripke’s Position
370                                                                Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


34.3.1       The Causal Theory of Reference

Kripke’s causal theory of reference is stated in Naming and Necessity (1980), the published
version of the lectures of 1970. The theory is a rejection of the descriptivist theory of names; it
is the affirmation of the causal chain.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: the rejection of descriptivism. The descriptivist theory holds that a name
is equivalent to a description, or a cluster of descriptions; the name refers to whatever satisfies
the description. Kripke rejects the theory: the name is not a description; the name refers by a
causal chain; the description is not the meaning of the name; it is at most a way of fixing the
reference.


Second feature: the baptism. The reference is fixed at a baptism, an initial act of naming;
the name is attached to the object; the chain of uses, from speaker to speaker, carries the
reference; each use refers to the same object, in virtue of the causal chain, not in virtue of the
description.


Third feature: the Gödel/Schmidt case. Suppose Gödel is not the man who proved the
incompleteness theorem; suppose Schmidt is. Still, when we use the name "Gödel," we refer
to Gödel, not to Schmidt; the name refers by the causal chain, not by the description. The
descriptivist theory would say that "Gödel" refers to whoever proved the theorem; Kripke’s theory
says that "Gödel" refers to the man baptized "Gödel," whatever he did.
      The causal theory is the foundation of Kripke’s philosophy of language. It is the rejection of
descriptivism; it is the affirmation of the causal chain; it is the source of the rigid designator.

   From the Tradition

   “A rough statement of a theory might be the following: An initial ’baptism’ takes place.
   Here the object may be named by ostension, or the reference of the name may be fixed by
   a description. When the name is ’introduced,’ it is used to refer to the object. The name
   is then passed from link to link.” (Kripke, Naming and Necessity, p. 96)


34.3.2       The Rigid Designator

Kripke’s rigid designator is stated in Naming and Necessity. A rigid designator is a term that
refers to the same object in every possible world in which the object exists; a non-rigid designator
is a term that refers to different objects in different worlds.
      The rigid designator has three features.


First feature: the rigidity. The name is rigid: it refers to the same object in every possible
world; the description is non-rigid: it refers to different objects in different worlds. The name
"Aristotle" refers to Aristotle in every world; the description "the teacher of Alexander" refers to
whoever taught Alexander in each world; the two are not equivalent.
34.3. Kripke’s Position                                                                            371


Second feature: the identity across worlds. The identity across worlds is the identity of
the individual, not of the properties. The individual is the same in every world; the properties
may vary; the name tracks the individual, not the properties.

Third feature: the essential properties. The essential properties are the properties that the
individual has in every world in which it exists; the accidental properties are the properties that
the individual has in some worlds and not in others. The essential properties are the properties
that the individual cannot lack; the accidental properties are the properties that the individual
can lack.
    The rigid designator is the key to Kripke’s philosophy of language. It is what distinguishes
the name from the description; it is what grounds the identity across worlds; it is what makes
the necessary a posteriori possible.


34.3.3       The Necessary A Posteriori
Kripke’s necessary a posteriori is stated in Naming and Necessity, Lecture III. The necessary a
posteriori is the combination of necessity (the proposition is true in all possible worlds) and a
posteriority (the proposition is known by experience); it is the rejection of the Kantian dichotomy
between the a priori and the necessary.
    The necessary a posteriori has three features.

First feature: the identity statements. The identity statements between names are
necessary a posteriori: "Hesperus is Phosphorus" is necessary (the two names refer to the
same object, the evening star and the morning star, which is Venus, in every world); but it
is a posteriori (it was discovered by astronomical observation). The identity is necessary; the
discovery is empirical.

Second feature: the theoretical identifications. The theoretical identifications are neces-
sary a posteriori: "Water is H2O" is necessary (in every world in which water exists, it is H2O);
but it is a posteriori (it was discovered by chemistry). The identity is necessary; the discovery is
empirical.

Third feature: the meter-stick case. The meter-stick case illustrates the distinction between
the epistemic and the metaphysical: the meter stick in Paris is one meter long; the proposition
"the meter stick is one meter long" is a priori (it is true by definition); but it is not necessary (in
another world, the meter stick could be longer or shorter than one meter). The a priori is not
the necessary; the necessary is not the a priori.
    The necessary a posteriori is the key to Kripke’s metaphysics. It is what breaks the Kantian
dichotomy; it is what affirms the metaphysical necessity; it is what grounds the essentialism.


34.3.4       The Epistemic/Metaphysical Distinction
Kripke’s epistemic/metaphysical distinction is stated throughout Naming and Necessity. The
distinction is between the epistemic modality (what we can know a priori or a posteriori) and
372                                                                  Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


the metaphysical modality (what is necessary or contingent in itself).
      The distinction has three features.


First feature: the epistemic modality. The epistemic modality concerns our knowledge: a
proposition is a priori if it can be known independently of experience; a posteriori if it can be
known only through experience. The epistemic modality is about us, not about the world.


Second feature: the metaphysical modality. The metaphysical modality concerns the
world: a proposition is necessary if it is true in all possible worlds; contingent if it is true in some
and false in others. The metaphysical modality is about the world, not about us.


Third feature: the independence. The two modalities are independent: a proposition can
be a priori and contingent (the meter-stick case); a proposition can be a posteriori and necessary
(Hesperus is Phosphorus); the a priori is not the necessary; the necessary is not the a priori.
      The epistemic/metaphysical distinction is the key to Kripke’s philosophy. It is what breaks
the Kantian identification of the a priori with the necessary; it is what opens the space for the
necessary a posteriori; it is what grounds the essentialism.


34.4       Lewis’s Position

34.4.1      Modal Realism

Lewis’s modal realism is stated in On the Plurality of Worlds (1986), Chapter 1. The modal
realism is the thesis that the possible worlds are real; they are not fictions, not abstractions, not
linguistic constructs; they are concrete entities, as real as the actual world.
      The modal realism has three features.


First feature: the plurality of worlds. There are many possible worlds; each is a concrete,
spatiotemporal entity; each is as real as the actual world; each is a way the world could be. The
actual world is not privileged; it is one world among many; it is the world we inhabit.


Second feature: the isolation. The worlds are isolated; they are spatiotemporally discon-
nected; no individual exists in more than one world; no causal relation crosses the worlds. Each
world is a closed system; each is complete in itself.


Third feature: the theoretical utility. The modal realism is justified by its theoretical
utility: it provides a unified account of modality, of counterfactuals, of propositions, of properties,
of contents, of what is possible and necessary. The utility is the justification; the utility is the
reason to believe.
      The modal realism is the foundation of Lewis’s philosophy. It is what grounds modality; it is
what grounds counterfactuals; it is what grounds the possible worlds.
34.4. Lewis’s Position                                                                           373


   From the Tradition

   “The world we live in is a very small part of a very much larger reality. There are many
   other worlds, and they are not mere possibilities, not fictions, not abstractions. They are
   as real as the world we live in.” (Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds, p. 2)


34.4.2      The Counterpart Theory
Lewis’s counterpart theory is stated in On the Plurality of Worlds, Chapter 4. The counterpart
theory is the alternative to the trans-world identity; it is the account of how an individual exists
in many worlds without being the same individual.
    The counterpart theory has three features.

First feature: the trans-world identity is rejected. The trans-world identity is rejected:
no individual exists in more than one world; the individual is world-bound; the individual is
confined to its world. The trans-world identity is a mistake; it treats the individual as if it could
exist in many worlds; but the individual is world-bound.

Second feature: the counterpart. The counterpart is the individual in another world that
resembles the individual in the actual world; it is not the same individual; it is a counterpart.
The counterpart relation is the relation of similarity; the similarity is the ground of the modal
predication.

Third feature: the modal predication. The modal predication is the predication of the
counterpart: "Humphrey could have won the election" means that there is a world in which a
counterpart of Humphrey wins the election; it does not mean that Humphrey exists in that world
and wins; it means that a counterpart does.
    The counterpart theory is the key to Lewis’s philosophy. It is what replaces the trans-world
identity; it is what grounds the modal predication; it is what grounds the possible worlds.

34.4.3      The Indexical Analysis of Actuality
Lewis’s indexical analysis of actuality is stated in On the Plurality of Worlds, Chapter 1, and in
“Anselm and Actuality” (1970). The indexical analysis is the thesis that actuality is indexical; it
is like "here" and "now"; it refers to the world in which the speaker is.
    The indexical analysis has three features.

First feature: the actuality is indexical. The actuality is indexical: "the actual world"
means "this world," the world in which the speaker is; it does not mean "the world that is
privileged"; it does not mean "the world that is more real." The actuality is a perspective, not a
property.

Second feature: the plurality is not hierarchical. The plurality of worlds is not hierarchical:
no world is more real than another; no world is privileged; each is as real as the others. The
actuality is not a degree of reality; it is a position.
374                                                                Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


Third feature: the objectivity. The indexical analysis is objective: the actuality is not a
subjective projection; it is the position of the speaker in the plurality of worlds. The objectivity
is the recognition of the plurality; the subjectivity is the recognition of the position.
      The indexical analysis is the key to Lewis’s philosophy of actuality. It is what distinguishes
the actuality from the reality; it is what grounds the plurality; it is what grounds the objectivity.

34.4.4      The Counterfactual Analysis
Lewis’s counterfactual analysis is stated in Counterfactuals (1973). The analysis is the account
of the truth conditions of the counterfactual: a counterfactual is true if the consequent is true in
the closest possible world in which the antecedent is true.
      The counterfactual analysis has three features.

First feature: the closest world. The closest world is the world most similar to the
actual world; the similarity is the ground of the counterfactual; the counterfactual is true if the
consequent is true in the closest world.

Second feature: the similarity. The similarity is a matter of degree; the similarity is the
ground of the counterfactual; the counterfactual is true if the consequent is true in the closest
world; the counterfactual is false if the consequent is false in the closest world.

Third feature: the causation. The causation is analyzed in terms of the counterfactual:
a cause is the event such that if it had not occurred, the effect would not have occurred; the
counterfactual is the ground of the causation; the causation is the counterfactual.
      The counterfactual analysis is the key to Lewis’s philosophy of causation. It is what grounds
the counterfactuals; it is what grounds the causation; it is what grounds the possible worlds.


34.5        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Kripke and Lewis is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the possible worlds (Kripke). The traditional reading takes
Kripke’s possible worlds to be a heuristic device: they are ways of speaking about modality;
they are not real; they are not entities. A revisionary reading takes them to be a metaphysical
framework: they are the objective ways things could be; they are not fictions; they are the
structure of modality. The two readings disagree on whether Kripke is a modal realist or a
modal conceptualist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s realms are real levels, not possible worlds.

Second dispute: the status of the counterpart (Lewis). The traditional reading takes
the counterpart to be a similarity relation: the counterpart is the individual in another world
that resembles the individual; the similarity is the ground. A revisionary reading takes the
counterpart to be a structural relation: the counterpart is the position in the structure of worlds;
the similarity is the description. The two readings disagree on whether Lewis is a reductionist
34.6. Points of Convergence                                                                        375


or a structuralist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s structure is a structural condition, not a similarity.


Third dispute: the status of the actuality (Lewis). The traditional reading takes the
actuality to be indexical: "the actual world" means "this world"; the indexicality is the ground.
A revisionary reading takes the actuality to be a structural position: "the actual world" is the
world we inhabit; the position is the ground. The two readings disagree on whether Lewis is
an indexicalist or a structuralist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s structure is a structural position, not an indexical.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Kripke and Lewis are realists, the framework’s
dialogue with them is a dialogue between a structural realism and a modal realism. If they are
conceptualists, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to the texts, but it does
not rest its case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


34.6       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Kripke. The framework shares three structural features with Kripke’s position.

       1. The rigidity of the identity. Kripke holds that the name is a rigid designator: it
           refers to the same object in every possible world; the identity is rigid; the identity is
           not the description. The framework holds that the identity is a structural invariance:
           it is the same in every manifestation; the identity is rigid; the identity is not the
           description. Both hold that the identity is rigid, and that the rigidity is not the
           descriptive content.

       2. The primitive thisness. Kripke’s rigid designator presupposes a primitive thisness:
           the name refers to the this, whatever its properties; the this is the individual, not the
           cluster of properties. The framework’s primitive thisness is an individuating feature
           that is not qualitative; the this is the individual, not the pattern. Both hold that
           the individual is irreducible to the pattern; both hold that the this is the ground of
           the identity.

       3. The necessary a posteriori. Kripke holds that some identities are necessary a
           posteriori: they are necessary, but they are discovered empirically. The framework
           holds that the structure of identity and manifestation is necessary a posteriori: the
           structure is necessary, but it is discovered by philosophical analysis. Both hold that
           necessity and discovery are compatible; both hold that the necessary is not the a
           priori.

   With Lewis. The framework shares three structural features with Lewis’s position.
376                                                                  Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


       1. The plurality of worlds. Lewis holds that there are many possible worlds; each is a
          concrete entity; each is a way the world could be. The framework holds that there
          are many realms; each is a real level; each is a mode of manifestation. Both hold
          that reality is plural, and that the plurality is not a fiction.

       2. The structural analysis of modality. Lewis holds that modality is analyzed struc-
          turally: the possible worlds are the framework; the counterparts are the ground;
          the counterfactuals are the truth conditions. The framework holds that modality
          is analyzed structurally: the realms are the framework; the manifestations are the
          ground; the expression is the truth condition. Both hold that modality is structural,
          not psychological.

       3. The structural analysis of actuality. Lewis holds that actuality is indexical: "the
          actual world" means "this world"; the indexicality is the ground. The framework
          holds that actuality is structural: "the actual realm" is the realm we inhabit; the
          position is the ground. Both hold that actuality is a position, not a degree of reality.



34.7      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Kripke. The framework diverges from Kripke in three respects.

       1. The status of the possible worlds. Kripke holds that the possible worlds are the ways
          things could be; they are not concrete entities; they are the objective structure of
          modality. The framework holds that the realms are real levels; they are concrete;
          they are the structure of manifestation. The framework’s realms are real; Kripke’s
          possible worlds are modal; the two are different.

       2. The status of the essential properties. Kripke holds that the essential properties are
          the properties the individual has in every world; the essentialism is the ground. The
          framework holds that the identity is not the essential properties; the identity is the
          invariance under a class of transformations; the invariance is not the essence. The
          framework’s identity is structural; Kripke’s essence is modal.

       3. The status of the naming. Kripke holds that the naming is the baptism; the causal
          chain is the reference. The framework holds that the naming is the manifestation;
          the expression is the reference. The framework’s naming is structural; Kripke’s
          naming is causal.

  With Lewis. The framework diverges from Lewis in three respects.

       1. The status of the worlds. Lewis holds that the possible worlds are concrete, spa-
          tiotemporal entities; they are isolated; they are real. The framework holds that the
34.8. The Tradition’s Objections                                                               377


         realms are not spatiotemporal; they are not isolated; they are related by expression.
         The framework’s realms are structural; Lewis’s worlds are concrete.

       2. The status of the counterpart. Lewis holds that the counterpart is the individual
         in another world that resembles the individual; the similarity is the ground. The
         framework holds that the manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm;
         the expression is the ground. The framework’s manifestation is structural; Lewis’s
         counterpart is similar.

       3. The status of the actuality. Lewis holds that the actuality is indexical: "the actual
         world" means "this world"; the indexicality is the ground. The framework holds that
         the actuality is the realm we inhabit; the position is the ground. The framework’s
         actuality is structural; Lewis’s actuality is indexical.




34.8      The Tradition’s Objections


   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Kripke’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is a
   description; it is not a rigid designator. The name refers to the object by the causal
   chain; the name is rigid; the name is not the description. The framework’s identity is a
   description; it is not a name; it is not rigid. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
   descriptions, not of names.
   Lewis’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
   real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not possible worlds;
   the realms are not concrete entities; the realms are not isolated. Lewis’s modal realism
   shows that the possible worlds are concrete, isolated, real; the framework’s realms are not
   concrete, not isolated, not real in Lewis’s sense. The framework’s ontology is an ontology
   of abstractions, not of worlds.
   Lewis’s second objection. The framework says that the identity is the invariance; the
   manifestation is the appearance. But the identity is not the counterpart; the manifestation
   is not the similarity. Lewis’s counterpart theory shows that the counterpart is the
   individual in another world that resembles the individual; the similarity is the ground.
   The framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the identity; the expression is the
   ground. The framework’s manifestation is not the counterpart; it is a different relation.
378                                                                 Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


34.9      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Kripke’s objection. The framework agrees that a description is not a name,
   and it agrees that the name is rigid. But the framework denies that its identity is a
   description. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*,
   in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
   framework’s identity is not a description; it is the structural condition under which a thing
   is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The
   distinction is between a description (a cluster of properties) and an enactment (a concrete
   act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework’s identity is
   rigid; it is not a description; it is the this.
   Reply to Lewis’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not
   possible worlds, and it agrees that the realms are not concrete entities in Lewis’s sense.
   But the framework denies that its realms are abstractions. The framework’s realms are
   real levels; they are the modes of manifestation; they are the structure of reality. The
   distinction is between a possible world (a concrete, isolated entity) and a realm (a real level
   of manifestation); the framework’s realms are the second, not the first. The framework’s
   realms are real; they are not concrete in Lewis’s sense; they are not isolated; they are
   related by expression.
   Reply to Lewis’s second objection. The framework agrees that the manifestation is not
   the counterpart, and it agrees that the expression is not the similarity. But the framework
   denies that its manifestation is only an appearance. The framework’s manifestation is
   the appearance of the identity in a realm; the expression is the structural relation; the
   manifestation is the enactment of the identity. The distinction is between a counterpart
   (a similar individual in another world) and a manifestation (the appearance of the identity
   in a realm); the framework’s manifestation is the second, not the first.



34.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Kripke’s cost. If Kripke accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
possible worlds are the objective structure of modality. He must accept that the realms are the
real structure of manifestation, and that the possible worlds are a description of the structure.
The cost is the loss of the modal realism: the possible worlds are no longer the objective structure;
they are descriptions of the structure.

Lewis’s cost. If Lewis accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
possible worlds are concrete, spatiotemporal entities. He must accept that the realms are real
levels, and that the possible worlds are the structure of the realms. The cost is the loss of the
modal realism: the possible worlds are no longer concrete; they are structural.
34.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                    379


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Kripke and Lewis, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the possible worlds, of the counterparts, of the rigid designators—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a rigid designator, and the
framework leaves the possible worlds to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Kripke’s rigid designator
and Lewis’s possible worlds are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Kripke and Lewis must accept that the framework’s structure is
not a description; it is a structural condition that the rigid designator and the possible worlds
presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.


34.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Kripke). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Kripke’s term “the rigid designator.” If one substitutes “the rigid designator” for
   “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source; the Kripkean rigid designator is the name
   that refers to the same object in every possible world. The framework’s identity is the
   structure; the Kripkean rigid designator is the name. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not
   substitutable for Kripke’s term “the possible world.” If one substitutes “the possible world”
   for “manifestation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm; the Kripkean possible world
   is a way the world could be. The framework’s manifestation is the actual; the Kripkean
   possible world is the possible. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The substitution test (Lewis). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Lewis’s term “the counterpart.” If one substitutes “the counterpart” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source; the Lewisian counterpart is the individual in another world that
   resembles the individual. The framework’s identity is one; the Lewisian counterpart is
   many. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The
   framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Lewis’s term “the counterfactual.”
   If one substitutes “the counterfactual” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural relation; the Lewisian
380                                                              Chapter 34. Kripke and Lewis


   counterfactual is the truth condition of a conditional. The framework’s expression is
   ontological; the Lewisian counterfactual is semantic. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Kripke is resemblance:
   both hold that identity is rigid, and they differ on whether the rigidity is the name
   or the structure. The relation between the framework and Lewis is resemblance: both
   hold that modality is structural, and they differ on whether the structure is concrete or
   abstract. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of Kripke and Lewis would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and name,
   or between structure and world—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the
   structural condition from the name and the world, and that the framework’s distinction is
   a development of their own.




34.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Kripke’s rigid designator or
Lewis’s counterpart, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a
development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Kripke’s rigid
designator is already a structural condition, or that Lewis’s counterpart is already a structural
relation, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Naming and Necessity and On the Plurality
of Worlds do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the causal theory of reference, the rigid
designator, the necessary a posteriori, the epistemic/metaphysical distinction, the modal realism,
the counterpart theory, the indexical analysis, and the counterfactual analysis, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has
a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a this and a world—a person, a tradition, a work of art.
Is the thing the rigid designator that names it, or the possible worlds in which it exists? Is the
truth the counterpart that resembles, or the manifestation that enacts? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between Kripke’s rigid designator, Lewis’s possible worlds, and the
framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Foucault and Habermas. It states the archaeology, the genealogy, and
the doctrine of power/knowledge in the one, and communicative action, validity claims, and the
lifeworld in the other; it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of both; and it states
the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of context and of the
conditions of a valid claim is the nearest analogue to their accounts of discourse and of validity.
The present chapter has stated the answer of Kripke and Lewis; the next chapter states the answer
of the theory of discourse and of validity, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 35

Foucault and Habermas


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Michel Foucault (1926–1984 CE) and Jürgen Habermas
(born 1929 CE), the two thinkers who made the relation between knowledge, power, and
rationality the central question of late twentieth-century continental philosophy. It states
Foucault’s archaeology and genealogy, the episteme and the discursive formation, the doctrine of
power/knowledge, and the late studies of subjectivation and the care of the self, with reference to
The Order of Things (1966), The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), Discipline and Punish (1975),
and The History of Sexuality (1976–1984); it states Habermas’s theory of communicative action,
his distinction between communicative and strategic action, the validity claims of speech, the
lifeworld and the system, and the ideal speech situation, with reference to Knowledge and Human
Interests (1968), The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), and The Philosophical Discourse
of Modernity (1985). It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of both; it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of context and of the
conditions of a valid claim is the nearest analogue to their accounts of discourse and of validity;
it presents the objections that each would raise; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what
each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “episteme,” “power/knowledge,” “communicative action,” or “validity claims,” these
are the terms of the two thinkers, and their sense is fixed by their works, not by the framework.


35.1      A Scene
Consider a physician of the early nineteenth century who looks at a patient. What she sees is not
what a physician of the seventeenth century saw: where the earlier physician read a pattern of
qualities across the body, she sees a lesion in an organ, and she can say where it is. The patient
is the same, and the disease is called by the same name, yet the objects, the concepts, the rules
for what may be said, and the persons authorized to say it have all changed. Nothing in the later
knowledge corrects the earlier one; the two are separated by a rearrangement of what counts as
a statement about the body.
   Consider next two people who disagree about whether a bridge is safe. Each gives reasons. If
the disagreement is to be settled and not merely endured, they must assume that the other can
be moved by a better argument, that each is saying what she believes, and that the matter is
one on which an argument can bear. Without these assumptions the exchange is a contest of
force, and the one who prevails does not thereby show that she is right.
   The two scenes pose opposite versions of one question. In the first, knowledge is inseparable
from the arrangements of power and discourse that make it possible, and no neutral point stands
outside them. In the second, speech carries a claim to validity that cannot be reduced to the

                                                382
35.2. The Question                                                                             383


power of whoever speaks. The framework also states conditions under which a claim is valid,
and it asks what a claim’s validity is. The chapter asks how the framework stands to a thinker
who historicizes validity and to one who defends its irreducibility.


35.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated the pragmatists’ account of inquiry. Foucault and Habermas take
the question of the conditions of knowledge in a different direction: toward the historical and
social arrangements in which knowledge is produced and, in Habermas’s case, toward the rational
structure of communication that those arrangements presuppose.
   The question is not whether Foucault or Habermas was right. The question is what each
held, what each can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to each. The two
are treated together because they were the principal contestants in a long debate on whether
critique can claim a standpoint that is not itself an effect of power. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Foucault and Habermas hold? The chapter states the
archaeology, the genealogy, and the doctrine of power/knowledge in the one, and communicative
action, validity claims, and the lifeworld in the other.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and
presents the objections that each would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and each
thinker? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


35.3     Foucault’s Position
Foucault’s early work, which he called archaeology, describes the historical a priori of a period
of knowledge: the set of rules that determine what can appear as an object of discourse, what
concepts can be formed, and which statements count as serious. In The Order of Things he
identifies three such arrangements, the Renaissance, the classical age, and the modern, and he
argues that the modern figure of Man as both the object and the subject of knowledge is of
recent date and may be erased.


35.3.1    Genealogy and Power/Knowledge

In the later work Foucault turns from the rules of discourse to the practices and institutions in
which discourse is bound up with power. Genealogy is the history of the present: it traces how
current forms of knowledge and of the self came to be, without assuming an origin or a continuous
progress. Power is not, for Foucault, primarily a possession or a prohibition; it is a field of
relations that produces objects, bodies, and subjects. Knowledge and power imply one another:
384                                                          Chapter 35. Foucault and Habermas


there is no body of knowledge that does not constitute and presuppose relations of power, and
no exercise of power that does not give rise to knowledge. Discipline and Punish studies the
prison, the school, and the barracks as sites where this relation produces the individual as an
object of discipline and as a subject.


35.3.2    Subjectivation and the Care of the Self

In the last works Foucault asks how an individual is led to recognize himself as a subject of
desire, and he studies ancient practices of the care of the self. The self is not given; it is formed
through techniques that a person applies to himself in a relation to truth. Foucault does not
return to a founding subject, but he opens a space in which a subject’s relation to itself can be
examined as a practice and not only as an effect.



35.4     Habermas’s Position

Habermas holds that the critique of reason must itself be carried out by reason. In Knowledge and
Human Interests he argues that the sciences are guided by cognitive interests, technical, practical,
and emancipatory, and that critique is guided by the last. In The Theory of Communicative
Action he locates the rational core of human life in language: whoever speaks, by the act of
speaking, raises claims that can be redeemed or contested.


35.4.1    Communicative Action and Validity Claims

Habermas distinguishes communicative action, oriented to mutual understanding, from strategic
action, oriented to success. In communicative action a speaker raises three validity claims: that
what she says is true, that it is right in the normative context in which she says it, and that
she is sincere. A hearer can accept or reject the claim on the strength of reasons. The claim to
truth and the claim to rightness can be redeemed only in discourse, an argumentative practice in
which the force of the better argument is the only admissible force.


35.4.2    Lifeworld and System

Habermas distinguishes the lifeworld, the background of shared meanings and solidarities that
make communication possible, from the systems, economic and administrative, that coordinate
action through money and power without requiring agreement. Modernity, he holds, is an
unfinished project in which the rationalization of the lifeworld has been overtaken by the
colonization of the lifeworld by the systems. The ideal speech situation is a regulative idea of
discourse free from distortion, not a state of affairs to be reached.



35.5     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of both thinkers is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
35.6. Points of Convergence                                                                     385


First dispute: Foucault and critique. One reading takes Foucault to hold that critique
is impossible, because every standpoint is an effect of power. Another takes him to hold that
critique is possible as a historical attitude, an interrogation of the limits imposed on us, without
a universal ground. The disagreement matters for the framework because the framework’s claim
to state conditions of validity differs in its relation to each reading.


Second dispute: the status of the ideal speech situation. One reading takes the ideal
speech situation to be a quasi-transcendental presupposition of all speech. Another takes it to be
a historically specific ideal of modern Western reason. The disagreement matters because the
framework’s own claims to universality must be distinguished from either.


Third dispute: Habermas’s reading of Foucault. Habermas charged Foucault with
cryptonormativism: with relying on a normative standard of critique that he disavows. Foucault’s
defenders reply that the charge misreads the genealogical method. The disagreement matters
because the framework must say whether a structural account can be critical without a normative
one.


35.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Foucault and Habermas. The framework shares four structural features with
   the two positions.

       1. The conditions of a claim. Foucault holds that what can be said depends on a
         historical a priori, and Habermas holds that speech presupposes validity claims. The
         framework holds that a claim is valid only under a context and a structure. All three
         hold that a claim has conditions that are not themselves among the claims.

       2. The plurality of regimes of knowledge. Foucault describes several epistemes, Habermas
         several kinds of cognitive interest and validity claim. The framework holds that
         contexts are infinite and that each has its own criteria of validity. All three hold
         that no one regime of knowledge is the measure of all.

       3. The structure of the subject. Foucault holds that the subject is formed in practices,
         and Habermas holds that the subject is formed in intersubjective communication.
         The framework holds that a subject is itself a manifestation in a realm and is
         not outside what it knows. All three reject the subject as an isolated founding
         consciousness.

       4. The refusal of a final standpoint. Foucault denies any standpoint outside discourse,
         and Habermas holds that the ideal speech situation is regulative and never reached.
         The framework holds that no context is the context of all contexts. All three hold
         that no inquirer occupies a final position.
386                                                        Chapter 35. Foucault and Habermas


35.7      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Foucault and Habermas. The framework diverges from the two positions in four
  respects.

       1. The ground of validity. Foucault historicizes validity into regimes, and Habermas
         grounds it in the structure of communication. The framework grounds it in the
         structure of identity, realm, and context. The ground of validity is not discourse for
         the framework.

       2. The status of power. For Foucault power is constitutive of knowledge and of the
         subject. The framework states no doctrine of power and does not make relations of
         power constitutive of identity.

       3. The role of agreement. For Habermas, validity is redeemed in the agreement of an
         unlimited communication community under ideal conditions. For the framework,
         validity is a structural relation and is not constituted by agreement.

       4. The relation to critique. Both thinkers practice and theorize a critique of present
         arrangements. The framework makes no normative or critical claim and treats its
         structural account as descriptive.



35.8      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Foucault’s objection. The framework claims to state the conditions of a valid claim
  from a structural register that is neutral. But no statement is neutral. The framework’s
  categories, identity, manifestation, realm, light, have a history and serve to order and to
  authorize what may be said about what is. A claim to a structural neutrality is the oldest
  form of power’s self-concealment, and the framework is a discourse among others, not a
  view of the conditions of discourse.
  Habermas’s first objection. The framework claims that its principles are argued and
  open to criticism. But it provides no account of the practice of argument in which criticism
  takes place. An argument is redeemed only in a discourse whose participants accept the
  force of the better reason, and the framework’s structural statements presuppose this
  practice without stating it. The framework has a performative contradiction in claiming
  validity while denying that validity is a communicative achievement.
  Habermas’s second objection. The framework’s refusal of normative claims is itself a
  normative stance, since it excludes the question of what is right. A philosophy that says
  nothing on the practical question leaves the lifeworld to the systems.
35.9. The Framework’s Reply                                                                   387


35.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Foucault. The framework agrees that its categories have a history and that no
   statement is neutral in the sense of being without a context. It denies that this entails
   that the structural register is merely one discourse among others. A claim that all claims
   are effects of discourse must itself be treated as an effect, and the framework asks for the
   conditions under which any claim, including this one, can be assessed. Foucault’s own
   genealogy distinguishes better from worse historical accounts and so presupposes such
   conditions.
   Reply to Habermas’s first objection. The framework agrees that argument is a
   practice with its own presuppositions and does not deny that validity is redeemed in it.
   It denies that validity is constituted by the redemption. The framework’s claim is that
   a claim is valid or not under a structure, and that argument is the way in which the
   structure is shown. Habermas’s own account distinguishes validity from acceptance, and
   the framework draws the same distinction at the level of structure.
   Reply to Habermas’s second objection. The framework agrees that its abstention is
   a stance, and it states it in the open: it makes no normative claim because its subject is
   structure. It denies that the abstention leaves the lifeworld to the systems; the practical
   question is left to a separate inquiry that the framework neither prejudges nor forbids.



35.10         The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Foucault and Habermas’s cost. If Foucault and Habermas accept the framework’s reply,
they must allow that validity has a structural condition that is neither an effect of discourse
nor the achievement of a communication community. Foucault must grant that a claim can be
assessed under conditions that do not themselves belong to a regime. Habermas must grant that
the validity of a claim is not constituted by its redeemability. The cost is the loss of the claim
that validity is wholly a matter of discourse.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its structural register is independent of the practices in which structure is stated. It must
accept that its categories have a history and that its neutrality about the practical is a stance
that has consequences. The cost is the loss of the innocence of the structural register and of its
abstention.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about the possibility of valid knowledge. The framework must take the historicity of
its categories seriously. Foucault and Habermas must take structure as a way of stating what a
388                                                          Chapter 35. Foucault and Habermas


valid claim presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between structure
and discourse.


35.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Foucault and Habermas.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “context” is not substitutable for Foucault’s
   term “episteme.” If one substitutes “episteme” for “context,” the statements change: an
   episteme is a historical a priori that governs what can be said in a period, while a context
   is a structural condition of validity that is not confined to a period. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “validity” is not substitutable for Habermas’s
   term “validity claim.” If one substitutes “validity claim” for “validity,” the statements
   change: a validity claim is raised by a speaker and redeemed in discourse, while the
   framework’s validity is a relation under a structure. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Foucault’s
   term “discursive formation.” If one substitutes “discursive formation” for “manifestation,”
   the statements change: a discursive formation is a regularity of statements, while a
   manifestation is the appearance of an identity in a realm. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Foucault is resemblance:
   both hold that a claim has conditions that are not among the claims and that no final
   standpoint is available, and they differ on whether the conditions are historical or structural.
   The relation between the framework and Habermas is resemblance of another kind: both
   hold that a claim to validity cannot be reduced to power, and they differ on whether
   validity is constituted by communication. Neither relation is equivalence, agreement, or
   identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Foucault’s historical
   a priori cannot be stated without a structural condition of the framework’s kind, or
   that Habermas’s validity claims cannot be redeemed without the framework’s distinction
   between validity and acceptance.



35.12      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Can the framework state conditions of validity without presupposing a practice
of argument? The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive, and a
reader who holds that every statement of conditions is a communicative act has a question the
chapter leaves open.
35.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               389


Second question. Is the framework’s abstention from normative claims stable? The chapter
has argued that it is, but a reader who holds that a description of validity already contains a
norm has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the late Foucault do justice to the care of
the self? The chapter has treated it as a practice in which a subject relates to truth, and a reader
who holds that this reading brings back the founding subject has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Think of a rule of speech in a profession you know, what may be said in a clinic, a court, or a
classroom, and who may say it. Is the rule there because it is true, or is it taken to be true
because it is there? If you try to criticize it, from where do you criticize? What does your answer
tell you about whether validity can be separated from the arrangements in which it is claimed?

The next chapter turns to Derrida and Deleuze. It states Derrida’s deconstruction, the différance,
the trace, the supplement, and the critique of the metaphysics of presence; and Deleuze’s difference
and repetition, the rhizome, the fold, the virtual/actual, and the critique of the dogmatic image of
thought. It identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Derrida and Deleuze; and
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of difference
and structure is the nearest contemporary analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated the
answer of the theory of discourse and of validity; the next chapter states the answer of Derrida
and Deleuze, and the framework’s dialogue with it.

Derrida and Deleuze


Scope. This chapter closes Part V, the dialogues with the contemporary West, and it closes it with
Jacques Derrida and Gilles Deleuze, the two great figures of post-structuralism. It states Derrida’s
deconstruction, the différance, the trace, the supplement, the critique of the metaphysics of
presence, the undecidable, and the hauntology, with reference to De la grammatologie, L’écriture
et la différence, Marges de la philosophie, and Spectres de Marx; and Deleuze’s philosophy of
difference, the différence en elle-même, the repetition, the rhizome, the fold, the virtual and the
