Différence et répétition, Mille plateaux (with Guattari), Le pli, and Qu’est-ce que la philosophie?
(with Guattari); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Derrida and
Deleuze; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of
difference and structure is the nearest contemporary analogue to theirs; it presents the objections
that Derrida and Deleuze would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply;
it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “différance,” “trace,” “supplement,” “deconstruction,” “difference,” “repetition,”
“rhizome,” “fold,” or “the virtual,” these are Derrida’s and Deleuze’s terms, and their sense is
fixed by the works and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


36.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is reading a text. She reads the first sentence; she reads the second;
she reads the third. Each sentence refers to the previous one; each sentence prepares the next
one; the meaning of each sentence is deferred, postponed, never fully present in the moment of
reading. The meaning is not in the sentence; it is in the difference between the sentences; it is in
the spacing that separates them; it is in the trace of what has been said and the anticipation of
what is to come. This is Derrida’s image of différance: the movement of difference and deferral
that makes meaning possible, and that prevents meaning from ever being fully present.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the meaning is, or how it is deferred,
but what the text is. The text is not a system of signs; it is not a structure; it is not a closed
whole. The text is an assemblage; it is a rhizome; it is a multiplicity that has no center and no
end; it is connected to other texts, to other practices, to other assemblages, in a network that
has no privileged point. This is Deleuze’s image of the rhizome: the multiplicity without center,
the network without hierarchy, the difference without identity.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the text is, or how it
works, but what reality is. Reality is not a system of identities; it is not a structure of presence;
it is not a hierarchy of substances. Reality is difference; it is the difference that differs from

                                                390
36.2. The Question                                                                                391


itself; it is the repetition that produces the new; it is the virtual that is actualized in the actual
without being exhausted by it. This is the image that Derrida and Deleuze share: the image of
difference as the fundamental character of reality.
   The scene poses the question that Derrida and Deleuze were the first to pose in its full form.
What is meaning? Is it presence, or is it deferral? What is the text? Is it a structure, or is it
a rhizome? And what is reality? Is it identity, or is it difference? The present chapter states
Derrida’s and Deleuze’s answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


36.2       The Question
The previous chapters stated the positions of Husserl, Heidegger, Whitehead, Wittgenstein, Quine
and Davidson, and Kripke and Lewis. Husserl posed the problem of consciousness; Heidegger
posed the problem of being; Whitehead posed the problem of process; Wittgenstein posed the
problem of language; Quine and Davidson posed the problem of meaning; Kripke and Lewis
posed the problem of modality. Derrida and Deleuze are the great critics of the entire tradition;
they reject the metaphysics of presence; they reject the priority of identity over difference; they
affirm difference as the fundamental character of reality. The present chapter states their critique,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Derrida and Deleuze were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Derrida and Deleuze hold? The chapter states Derrida’s
deconstruction, the différance, the trace, the supplement, the critique of the metaphysics of
presence, and the undecidable; and Deleuze’s philosophy of difference, the repetition, the rhizome,
the fold, the virtual and the actual, the agencement, and the critique of the dogmatic image of
thought.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two philosophers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Derrida and Deleuze would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Derrida
and Deleuze? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


36.3       Derrida’s Position

36.3.1     Deconstruction

Derrida’s deconstruction is stated in De la grammatologie (1967), L’écriture et la différence
(1967), and Marges de la philosophie (1972). The deconstruction is not a method; it is not a
392                                                               Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


critique; it is not a destruction. It is a way of reading; it is a way of showing the internal tensions
of a text; it is a way of opening the text to what it excludes.
      The deconstruction has three features.


First feature: the reading. The deconstruction is a reading: it reads the text closely; it
reads the text in its details; it reads the text in its margins. The reading is not a summary; it is
not a paraphrase; it is not a commentary. The reading is a displacement: it shows what the text
says and what the text does not say; it shows what the text includes and what the text excludes.


Second feature: the internal tension. The deconstruction shows the internal tension of
the text: the tension between what the text claims and what the text presupposes; the tension
between the explicit and the implicit; the tension between the center and the margin. The
tension is not a defect; it is the condition of the text; it is what makes the text a text.


Third feature: the opening. The deconstruction opens the text to what it excludes: the
other; the outside; the difference. The opening is not a completion; it is not a synthesis; it is
not a resolution. The opening is the recognition of the undecidable; it is the recognition of the
impossibility of closure.
      The deconstruction is the foundation of Derrida’s philosophy. It is the reading of the tradition;
it is the critique of the metaphysics of presence; it is the affirmation of difference.

   From the Tradition

   “Deconstruction is not a method, and cannot be transformed into one. It is not a critique,
   either, in the general sense of the word. It is not an analysis, and it is not a demolition.
   It is a reading, a displacement, an affirmation.” (Derrida, “Letter to a Japanese Friend,”
   trans. after Kamuf)



36.3.2      The Différance

Derrida’s différance is stated in Marges de la philosophie (1972) and in L’écriture et la différence
(1967). The différance is the movement of difference and deferral; it is the movement that makes
meaning possible and prevents meaning from ever being fully present.
      The différance has three features.


First feature: the difference. The différance is the difference: it is the spacing between
signs; it is the distinction between terms; it is what makes a sign different from another sign.
The difference is not a thing; it is a movement; it is a relation; it is what makes the sign a sign.


Second feature: the deferral. The différance is the deferral: it is the postponement of
meaning; it is the delay of presence; it is what makes meaning never fully present. The deferral
is not a defect; it is the condition of meaning; it is what makes meaning possible.
36.3. Derrida’s Position                                                                          393


Third feature: the movement. The différance is the movement: it is the movement of
difference and deferral; it is the movement that is not a thing; it is the movement that is not a
presence; it is the movement that cannot be named. The movement is the condition of meaning;
it is the condition of the sign; it is the condition of the text.
   The différance is the key to Derrida’s philosophy. It is what replaces the presence; it is what
replaces the identity; it is what affirms the difference.


36.3.3    The Trace

Derrida’s trace is stated in De la grammatologie (1967) and in L’écriture et la différence (1967).
The trace is the mark of what has been; it is the mark of the absent; it is the mark of the other.
   The trace has three features.


First feature: the mark. The trace is the mark: it is the mark of what has passed; it is the
mark of what is no longer present; it is the mark of the absent. The mark is not a presence; it is
the trace of a presence; it is what remains when the presence has gone.


Second feature: the absence. The trace is the absence: it is the absence of the origin; it is
the absence of the presence; it is the absence of the signified. The absence is not a lack; it is the
condition of the trace; it is what makes the trace a trace.


Third feature: the other. The trace is the other: it is the trace of the other; it is the trace
of what is not the same; it is the trace of what is different. The other is not a presence; it is the
trace of a presence; it is what makes the trace a trace.
   The trace is the key to Derrida’s philosophy of language. It is what replaces the sign; it is
what replaces the presence; it is what affirms the absence.


36.3.4    The Supplement

Derrida’s supplement is stated in De la grammatologie (1967), in the reading of Rousseau. The
supplement is what is added to something to complete it; but the addition reveals that the thing
was not complete; the supplement is both an addition and a substitute.
   The supplement has three features.


First feature: the addition. The supplement is the addition: it is what is added to the
thing; it is what completes the thing. The addition is not a part of the thing; it is an extra; it is
what comes after.


Second feature: the substitute. The supplement is the substitute: it is what replaces the
thing; it is what stands in for the thing. The substitute is not the thing; it is a replacement; it is
what takes the place of the thing.
394                                                               Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


Third feature: the lack. The supplement is the lack: it is what reveals the lack of the thing;
it is what shows that the thing was not complete. The lack is not a defect; it is the condition of
the supplement; it is what makes the supplement possible.
      The supplement is the key to Derrida’s reading of the tradition. It is what shows the
incompleteness of the tradition; it is what shows the lack of the presence; it is what opens the
tradition to the other.


36.3.5      The Critique of the Metaphysics of Presence

Derrida’s critique of the metaphysics of presence is stated throughout his works, but most clearly
in De la grammatologie and in L’écriture et la différence. The critique is the diagnosis of the
tradition’s assumption: the assumption that being is presence; the assumption that meaning is
presence; the assumption that truth is presence.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the presence. The presence is the assumption: the assumption that what is,
is present; the assumption that what is, is fully present; the assumption that what is, is present
to consciousness. The presence is the ground of the tradition; it is the ground of the metaphysics;
it is the ground of the philosophy.


Second feature: the critique. The critique is the deconstruction of the presence: it shows
that the presence is not given; it shows that the presence is deferred; it shows that the presence
is the effect of the difference. The critique is not a denial; it is a displacement; it is a reading.


Third feature: the alternative. The alternative is the difference: it is the difference that is
not a presence; it is the difference that is not an identity; it is the difference that is not a ground.
The alternative is the affirmation of the difference; it is the affirmation of the trace; it is the
affirmation of the other.
      The critique is the key to Derrida’s philosophy. It is what replaces the presence; it is what
replaces the identity; it is what affirms the difference.


36.3.6      The Undecidable

Derrida’s undecidable is stated in Marges de la philosophie (1972) and in Limited Inc (1988).
The undecidable is what cannot be decided; it is what is neither this nor that; it is what escapes
the binary opposition.
      The undecidable has three features.


First feature: the binary opposition. The binary opposition is the structure of the tradition:
the opposition between presence and absence; between speech and writing; between inside and
outside; between the same and the other. The binary opposition is the ground of the tradition;
it is the ground of the metaphysics.
36.4. Deleuze’s Position                                                                            395


Second feature: the undecidable. The undecidable is what escapes the binary opposition:
it is what is neither this nor that; it is what is both this and that; it is what is the condition of
the opposition. The undecidable is the difference; it is the trace; it is the supplement.


Third feature: the decision. The decision is what follows the undecidable: it is the act that
cuts through the undecidable; it is the act that decides. The decision is not a conclusion; it is
not a deduction; it is an act; it is a leap.
   The undecidable is the key to Derrida’s ethics and politics. It is what makes the decision
possible; it is what makes the decision necessary; it is what makes the decision responsible.


36.3.7    The Hauntology

Derrida’s hauntology is stated in Spectres de Marx (1993). The hauntology is the logic of the
specter; it is the logic of what haunts; it is the logic of what is neither present nor absent.
   The hauntology has three features.


First feature: the specter. The specter is what haunts: it is what is neither present nor
absent; it is what is between the presence and the absence; it is what is the trace of the other.
The specter is not a presence; it is not an absence; it is a haunting.


Second feature: the haunting. The haunting is the effect of the specter: it is the effect
of what haunts; it is the effect of what is neither present nor absent. The haunting is not a
presence; it is not an absence; it is a haunting.


Third feature: the hauntology. The hauntology is the logic of the haunting: it is the logic
of what haunts; it is the logic of what is neither present nor absent. The hauntology is not an
ontology; it is not a metaphysics; it is a haunting.
   The hauntology is the key to Derrida’s later philosophy. It is what replaces the ontology; it is
what replaces the metaphysics; it is what affirms the specter.


36.4      Deleuze’s Position

36.4.1    The Philosophy of Difference

Deleuze’s philosophy of difference is stated in Différence et répétition (1968). The philosophy
of difference is the affirmation of difference as the fundamental character of reality; it is the
rejection of the priority of identity over difference.
   The philosophy of difference has three features.


First feature: the difference in itself. The difference is not a difference between two things;
it is not a difference between two identities; it is not a difference between two presences. The
difference is in itself; it is the difference that differs from itself; it is the difference that is the
ground of the things.
396                                                               Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


Second feature: the repetition. The repetition is not the return of the same; it is not the
reproduction of the identical; it is not the copy of the original. The repetition is the production
of the new; it is the difference that returns; it is the return of the difference.


Third feature: the affirmation. The affirmation is not the negation of the negation; it is
not the dialectic of the negative; it is not the reconciliation of the opposites. The affirmation is
the affirmation of the difference; it is the affirmation of the multiplicity; it is the affirmation of
the creative.
      The philosophy of difference is the foundation of Deleuze’s philosophy. It is the rejection of
the identity; it is the rejection of the presence; it is the affirmation of the difference.

   From the Tradition

   “Difference is not diversity. Diversity is given, but difference is that by which the given
   is given. Difference is not phenomenon but the noumenon closest to the phenomenon.”
   (Deleuze, Différence et répétition, p. 222, trans. after Patton)



36.4.2      The Repetition

Deleuze’s repetition is stated in Différence et répétition (1968). The repetition is the production
of the new; it is the return of the difference; it is the repetition that differs.
      The repetition has three features.


First feature: the repetition and the same. The repetition is not the return of the same;
it is not the reproduction of the identical; it is not the copy of the original. The repetition is the
return of the different; it is the production of the new; it is the affirmation of the difference.


Second feature: the repetition and the time. The repetition is not the repetition of the
past; it is not the return to the past; it is not the memory of the past. The repetition is the
repetition of the future; it is the return of the new; it is the affirmation of the future.


Third feature: the repetition and the eternal return. The repetition is the eternal
return; it is the return of the different; it is the affirmation of the difference. The eternal return
is not the return of the same; it is the return of the different; it is the affirmation of the creative.
      The repetition is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy. It is what replaces the identity; it is what
replaces the presence; it is what affirms the difference.


36.4.3      The Rhizome

Deleuze’s rhizome is stated in Mille plateaux (1980), with Guattari. The rhizome is the multiplicity
without center; it is the network without hierarchy; it is the difference without identity.
      The rhizome has three features.
36.4. Deleuze’s Position                                                                              397


First feature: the multiplicity. The rhizome is the multiplicity: it is the many that is not
reduced to the one; it is the many that is not unified; it is the many that is not totalized. The
multiplicity is not a defect; it is the condition of the rhizome; it is what makes the rhizome a
rhizome.

Second feature: the connection. The rhizome is the connection: it is the network of
connections; it is the web of relations; it is the assemblage of elements. The connection is not a
hierarchy; it is not a center; it is not a ground. The connection is the rhizome; the rhizome is
the connection.

Third feature: the heterogeneity. The rhizome is the heterogeneity: it is the many that
is not the same; it is the many that is different; it is the many that is heterogeneous. The
heterogeneity is not a defect; it is the condition of the rhizome; it is what makes the rhizome a
rhizome.
   The rhizome is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy of multiplicity. It is what replaces the
structure; it is what replaces the hierarchy; it is what affirms the multiplicity.


36.4.4     The Fold
Deleuze’s fold is stated in Le pli: Leibniz et le baroque (1988). The fold is the inside of the
outside; it is the folding of the outside into the inside; it is the inflection of the line.
   The fold has three features.

First feature: the inside and the outside. The fold is the relation between the inside and
the outside: it is the folding of the outside into the inside; it is the inflection of the line; it is the
creation of the inside. The inside is not a substance; it is a fold; it is the folding of the outside.

Second feature: the inflection. The fold is the inflection: it is the bending of the line; it is
the curvature of the surface; it is the inflection of the point. The inflection is not a point; it is
not a line; it is not a surface. The inflection is the fold; the fold is the inflection.

Third feature: the monad. The fold is the monad: it is the individual; it is the point of
view; it is the perspective. The monad is not a substance; it is a fold; it is the folding of the
outside into the inside; it is the inflection of the line.
   The fold is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy of the subject. It is what replaces the substance;
it is what replaces the subject; it is what affirms the fold.


36.4.5     The Virtual and the Actual
Deleuze’s virtual and actual is stated in Différence et répétition (1968) and in Bergsonisme (1966).
The virtual and the actual are the two modes of the real; the virtual is the problematic; the
actual is the solution; the actual is the actualization of the virtual without being the resemblance
of the virtual.
   The virtual and actual have three features.
398                                                               Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


First feature: the virtual. The virtual is not the possible; it is not the abstract; it is not the
unreal. The virtual is the real; it is the problematic; it is the multiplicity; it is the structure.
The virtual is not the actual; it is not the present; it is not the given.


Second feature: the actual. The actual is not the realization of the possible; it is not the
copy of the virtual; it is not the resemblance of the virtual. The actual is the actualization of
the virtual; it is the solution of the problem; it is the creation of the new. The actual is not the
virtual; it is not the problematic; it is not the multiplicity.


Third feature: the actualization. The actualization is the process: it is the process by
which the virtual becomes actual; it is the process by which the problem becomes solution; it is
the process by which the new is created. The actualization is not a resemblance; it is not a copy;
it is a creation.
      The virtual and actual is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy of reality. It is what replaces the
possible; it is what replaces the real; it is what affirms the creative.


36.4.6      The Agencement
Deleuze’s agencement is stated in Mille plateaux (1980), with Guattari. The agencement is the
assemblage; it is the arrangement; it is the composition of heterogeneous elements.
      The agencement has three features.


First feature: the assemblage. The agencement is the assemblage: it is the arrangement of
heterogeneous elements; it is the composition of different things; it is the coming together of the
many. The assemblage is not a structure; it is not a system; it is not a totality. The assemblage
is a composition; it is a coming together; it is a agencement.


Second feature: the heterogeneous. The agencement is the heterogeneous: it is the many
that is different; it is the many that is not the same; it is the many that is heterogeneous.
The heterogeneous is not a defect; it is the condition of the agencement; it is what makes the
agencement an agencement.


Third feature: the territorialization. The agencement is the territorialization: it is the
marking of the territory; it is the delimitation of the space; it is the creation of the inside. The
territorialization is not a closure; it is not a boundary; it is an opening.
      The agencement is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy of the social. It is what replaces the
structure; it is what replaces the system; it is what affirms the composition.


36.4.7      The Critique of the Dogmatic Image of Thought
Deleuze’s critique of the dogmatic image of thought is stated in Différence et répétition (1968),
Chapter 3. The critique is the diagnosis of the image of thought that dominates the tradition:
the image of thought as recognition; the image of thought as representation; the image of thought
as the natural exercise of a faculty.
36.5. Internal Disputes                                                                            399


   The critique has three features.

First feature: the dogmatic image. The dogmatic image is the image of thought as
recognition: the image of thought as the recognition of the same; the image of thought as the
representation of the identical; the image of thought as the natural exercise of a faculty. The
dogmatic image is the ground of the tradition; it is the ground of the philosophy; it is the ground
of the metaphysics.

Second feature: the critique. The critique is the deconstruction of the dogmatic image: it
shows that thought is not recognition; it shows that thought is not representation; it shows that
thought is not the natural exercise of a faculty. The critique is not a denial; it is a displacement;
it is a reading.

Third feature: the thought without image. The thought without image is the alternative:
it is the thought that is not the recognition; it is the thought that is not the representation; it is
the thought that is the creation. The thought without image is the thought of the difference; it
is the thought of the multiplicity; it is the thought of the new.
   The critique is the key to Deleuze’s philosophy of thought. It is what replaces the recognition;
it is what replaces the representation; it is what affirms the creation.


36.5      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Derrida and Deleuze is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the relation between Derrida and Deleuze. The traditional reading
takes Derrida and Deleuze to be allies: both are post-structuralists; both reject the metaphysics
of presence; both affirm difference. A revisionary reading takes them to be rivals: Derrida’s
difference is the deferral; Deleuze’s difference is the affirmation; Derrida’s difference is negative;
Deleuze’s difference is positive. The two readings disagree on whether the two are allies or rivals,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s difference
is structural, not negative and not affirmative.

Second dispute: the status of deconstruction. The traditional reading takes deconstruction
to be a method: it is a way of reading; it is a technique; it is a procedure. A revisionary reading
takes it to be an event: it is what happens to the text; it is what the text does; it is not
a method, but an event. The two readings disagree on whether Derrida is a methodologist
or an event-thinker, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s structure is an event, not a method.

Third dispute: the status of the rhizome. The traditional reading takes the rhizome to be
a metaphor: it is a figure of speech; it is an image; it is a representation. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a concept: it is a concept of multiplicity; it is a concept of the real; it is a concept
of the world. The two readings disagree on whether Deleuze is a metaphysician or a poet, and
400                                                               Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a
concept, not a metaphor.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Derrida and Deleuze are allies, the framework’s
dialogue with them is a dialogue between a structural realism and a post-structuralist difference.
If they are rivals, the dialogue is a dialogue between three positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to the texts, but it does
not rest its case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


36.6        Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Derrida. The framework shares three structural features with Derrida’s position.

        1. The critique of the metaphysics of presence. Derrida holds that the tradition assumes
           that being is presence; that meaning is presence; that truth is presence. The
           framework holds that the tradition assumes that identity is presence; that the
           manifestation is presence; that the reconstruction is presence. Both hold that the
           presence is a mistake, and that the mistake is the source of the crisis.

        2. The difference. Derrida holds that the difference is the movement of difference and
           deferral; it is what makes meaning possible and prevents meaning from ever being
           fully present. The framework holds that the difference is the structural relation
           between identity and manifestation; it is what makes manifestation possible and
           prevents manifestation from ever being fully identical with the identity. Both hold
           that the difference is the condition of meaning, and that the difference is not a
           presence.

        3. The undecidable. Derrida holds that the undecidable is what escapes the binary
           opposition; it is what makes the decision possible. The framework holds that the
           undecidable is the structural condition of the reconstruction; it is what makes the
           reconstruction a decision. Both hold that the undecidable is the condition of the
           decision, and that the decision is not a conclusion.

   With Deleuze. The framework shares three structural features with Deleuze’s position.

        1. The priority of difference over identity. Deleuze holds that difference is the funda-
           mental character of reality; identity is the effect of difference; the difference is in
           itself. The framework holds that the difference is the structural relation between
           identity and manifestation; the identity is not the ground of the difference; the
           difference is the ground of the manifestation. Both hold that the difference is prior
           to the identity, and that the identity is not the ground.

        2. The multiplicity. Deleuze holds that the multiplicity is irreducible; it is not the
           many that is reduced to the one; it is the many that is not unified. The framework
36.7. Points of Divergence                                                                        401


          holds that the realms are plural; they are not reducible to one another; they are the
          multiplicity of the manifestation. Both hold that the multiplicity is irreducible, and
          that the plurality is not a defect.

       3. The virtual and the actual. Deleuze holds that the virtual is the real; the actual is
          the actualization of the virtual; the actualization is the creation of the new. The
          framework holds that the identity is the virtual; the manifestation is the actual; the
          expression is the actualization of the identity. Both hold that the virtual and the
          actual are the two modes of the real, and that the actualization is a creation.



36.7      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Derrida. The framework diverges from Derrida in three respects.

       1. The status of the difference. Derrida holds that the différance is the movement of
          difference and deferral; it is not a structure; it is not a ground; it is not a presence.
         The framework holds that the difference is the structural relation between identity
          and manifestation; it is a structure; it is a ground; it is a structural condition. The
          framework’s difference is structural; Derrida’s difference is not.

       2. The status of the deconstruction. Derrida holds that the deconstruction is a reading;
          it is an event; it is a displacement. The framework holds that the reconstruction
          is a reading; it is an interpretation; it is a displacement. But the framework’s
          reconstruction is structural; it is not an event; it is not a deconstruction.

       3. The status of the undecidable. Derrida holds that the undecidable is the condition of
          the decision; it is what makes the decision possible. The framework holds that the
          undecidable is the condition of the reconstruction; it is what makes the reconstruction
          a decision. But the framework’s reconstruction is structural; it is not undecidable; it
          is decidable in principle, undecidable in practice.

   With Deleuze. The framework diverges from Deleuze in three respects.

       1. The status of the difference. Deleuze holds that the difference is in itself; it is the
          ground of the things; it is the affirmation of the difference. The framework holds
          that the difference is the structural relation between identity and manifestation; it
          is the ground of the manifestation; it is the structural condition. The framework’s
          difference is structural; Deleuze’s difference is affirmative.

       2. The status of the rhizome. Deleuze holds that the rhizome is the multiplicity without
          center; it is the network without hierarchy. The framework holds that the realms are
          multiple; but the multiplicity is structured; it is not the rhizome; it is the hierarchy;
          it is not the network.
402                                                              Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


       3. The status of the virtual. Deleuze holds that the virtual is the real; the actual is the
          actualization of the virtual. The framework holds that the identity is the virtual; the
          manifestation is the actual. But the framework’s identity is not the real in Deleuze’s
          sense; it is the structural condition; it is the invariance; it is the enactment.



36.8      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Derrida’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is a
  presence; it is a ground; it is an origin. The deconstruction shows that there is no presence;
  there is no ground; there is no origin; there is only the difference; there is only the trace;
  there is only the supplement. The framework’s identity is a presence; it is the metaphysics
  of presence in disguise. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of presence, not of
  difference.
  Deleuze’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is an
  identity; it is the priority of the identity over the difference. Deleuze’s philosophy of
  difference shows that the difference is prior to the identity; the identity is the effect of
  the difference; the difference is in itself. The framework’s identity is a mistake; it is the
  dogmatic image of thought; it is the representation of the same. The framework’s ontology
  is an ontology of identity, not of difference.
  Deleuze’s second objection. The framework says that the realms are structured; they
  are hierarchical; they are ordered. But the rhizome is the multiplicity without center; it
  is the network without hierarchy; it is the difference without identity. The framework’s
  realms are the tree; they are the root; they are the hierarchy. The framework’s ontology is
  an ontology of the tree, not of the rhizome.



36.9      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to Derrida’s objection. The framework agrees that a presence is a mistake, and
  it agrees that the deconstruction shows the mistake. But the framework denies that its
  identity is a presence. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
  *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its
  realm. The framework’s identity is not a presence; it is the structural condition under
  which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
  calls *act*. The distinction is between a presence (a full presence) and an enactment
  (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework’s
  identity is not the metaphysics of presence; it is the structural condition that the presence
36.10. The Cost of Each Side                                                                          403


   presupposes.
   Reply to Deleuze’s first objection. The framework agrees that an identity is not the
   ground of the difference, and it agrees that the difference is prior to the identity. But the
   framework denies that its identity is the priority of the identity over the difference. The
   framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not the identity that is
   prior to the difference; it is the identity that is the effect of the difference; it is the identity
   that is enacted in the manifestation. The distinction is between an identity (a ground)
   and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Deleuze’s second objection. The framework agrees that the rhizome is
   the multiplicity without center, and it agrees that the rhizome is the network without
   hierarchy. But the framework denies that its realms are the tree. The framework’s realms
   are the levels of manifestation; they are the structure of the manifestation; they are the
   enactment of the identity. The distinction is between a tree (a hierarchy) and a structure
   (a level of manifestation); the framework’s realms are the second, not the first.



36.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Derrida’s cost. If Derrida accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that there
is no presence. He must accept that there is a structural condition, and that the structural
condition is not a presence but an enactment. The cost is the loss of the radical deconstruction:
the deconstruction is no longer the only reading; the structure is also a reading; the difference is
not the only ground.


Deleuze’s cost. If Deleuze accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
difference is prior to identity. He must accept that the identity is the enactment of the difference,
and that the enactment is not the priority of the identity. The cost is the loss of the radical
affirmation: the difference is no longer the only ground; the structure is also a ground; the
difference is not the only creative.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Derrida and Deleuze, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension
of reality—the dimension of the trace, of the undecidable, of the rhizome, of the fold—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a presence, and the framework
leaves the difference to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Derrida’s difference
and Deleuze’s difference are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Derrida and Deleuze must accept that the framework’s structure is
404                                                             Chapter 36. Derrida and Deleuze


not a presence; it is a structural condition that the difference presupposes as its condition. The
cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they
are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.



36.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Derrida). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Derrida’s term “différance.” If one substitutes “différance” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source; the Derridean différance is the movement of difference and deferral.
   The framework’s identity is a structure; the Derridean différance is a movement. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term
   “manifestation” is not substitutable for Derrida’s term “the trace.” If one substitutes “the
   trace” for “manifestation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm; the Derridean trace
   is the mark of the absent. The framework’s manifestation is the actual; the Derridean
   trace is the absent. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Deleuze). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Deleuze’s term “difference.” If one substitutes “difference” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source; the Deleuzian difference is the difference in itself. The framework’s
   identity is one; the Deleuzian difference is many. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for
   Deleuze’s term “the actualization.” If one substitutes “the actualization” for “expression”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a
   structural relation; the Deleuzian actualization is the process of the virtual becoming
   actual. The framework’s expression is ontological; the Deleuzian actualization is virtual.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Derrida is resemblance:
   both critique the metaphysics of presence, and they differ on whether the difference is a
   structure or a movement. The relation between the framework and Deleuze is resemblance:
   both affirm the priority of difference over identity, and they differ on whether the difference
   is a structure or an affirmation. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Derrida and Deleuze would be refuted by
   showing that their positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and movement, or between structure and affirmation—by showing, that
   is, that they already distinguish the structural condition from the movement and the
   affirmation, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of their own.
36.12. Open Questions                                                                           405


36.12      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Derrida’s différance or Deleuze’s
difference, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Derrida’s différance is already a
structure, or that Deleuze’s difference is already an affirmation, has a question the chapter leaves
open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of De la grammatologie, Marges de la philoso-
phie, Différence et répétition, and Mille plateaux do justice to the texts? The chapter has used
the deconstruction, the différance, the trace, the supplement, the critique of the metaphysics
of presence, the undecidable, the hauntology, the philosophy of difference, the repetition, the
rhizome, the fold, the virtual and actual, the agencement, and the critique of the dogmatic image
of thought, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts
support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection

Consider a thing you know that is both a structure and a difference—a person, a tradition, a text.
Is the thing the structure that persists, or the difference that differs? Is the truth the presence
that is deferred, or the multiplicity that is affirmed? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between Derrida’s différance, Deleuze’s difference, and the framework’s identity?

Part V is now complete. The dialogues with the seven great figures of the contemporary West—
Husserl, Heidegger, Whitehead, Wittgenstein, Quine and Davidson, Kripke and Lewis, and
Derrida and Deleuze—have been stated. Part VI turns to the Islamic tradition. The first dialogue
is with al-Kindi, on the first philosophy and the creation of the world; the next with al-Farabi,
on emanation and the virtuous city; the next with Ibn Sina, on essence and existence, necessary
being, and the human soul; the next with al-Ghazali, on the incoherence of the philosophers
and the causality of God; the next with Ibn Rushd, on the harmony of philosophy and religion;
the next with the Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya, on divine attributes, justice, and free will; the
next with Suhrawardi, on light, illumination, and the imaginal realm; the next with Ibn Arabi,
on manifestation, the barzakh, and the unity of being; the next with Mulla Sadra, on existence,
36.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 407


substantial motion, and the unity of the intellect and the intelligible; and the last with Ibn
Khaldun, on the science of civilization and the cycles of history. The contemporary West has
questioned the question itself; the Islamic tradition will recover the question that the tradition has
forgotten.

Chapter 37

al-Kindi


Scope. This chapter opens Part VI, the dialogues with the Islamic tradition, and it opens it with
Abu Yusuf Ya’qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi, the first philosopher of the Arabs. It states al-Kindi’s
account of first philosophy as the knowledge of the First Cause, his argument for the createdness
of the world against the Aristotelian eternity of the world, his doctrine of the absolute unity of
God, his account of the agent intellect, his analysis of the five essences, and his reconciliation of
philosophy and religion, with reference to Fi al-Falsafa al-Ula (On First Philosophy), Fi Huduth
al-Alam (On the Createdness of the World), Fi Wahdaniyyat Allah (On the Unity of God), Fi
al-’Aql (On the Intellect), and Fi al-Mahiyyat al-Khams (On the Five Essences); it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of al-Kindi; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the First Determination and of expression is
the nearest classical Islamic analogue to al-Kindi’s; it presents the objections that al-Kindi would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “first philosophy,”
“First Cause,” “createdness,” “agent intellect,” or “the five essences,” these are al-Kindi’s terms,
and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.



37.1       A Scene

Consider a person who is walking in the desert. She sees a stone; she sees a plant; she sees a
star. Each of them has a cause: the stone was formed by water; the plant was grown from a
seed; the star was formed from cosmic dust. Each cause has a cause: the water was carried by
wind; the seed was produced by another plant; the cosmic dust was formed by a supernova. She
follows the chain of causes backward, and the chain never ends. Each cause has a cause; each
explanation needs an explanation; the regress is infinite.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what causes the stone, or the plant, or
the star, but what causes the whole chain. The chain cannot be infinite; an actual infinite is
impossible; the regress must stop. The chain must stop at a cause that has no cause; at a cause
that is not caused; at a cause that is the cause of itself. This is what al-Kindi calls the First
Cause: the cause that is not caused, the principle that is not principled, the source that is not
sourced.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the First Cause is, or
how it causes the chain, but what the world is in relation to the First Cause. The world is not
eternal; it is created; it has a beginning. The world is not the First Cause; it is the effect of the
First Cause. The world is not one; it is many; the First Cause is one. The world is not necessary;

                                                409
410                                                                           Chapter 37. al-Kindi


it is possible; the First Cause is necessary. The world is created from nothing by the First Cause,
and the First Cause is not diminished by the creation.
      The scene is al-Kindi’s image, in On First Philosophy and in On the Createdness of the World,
of the structure of reality. The stone is the effect; the chain is the series of causes; the First
Cause is the source. The world is the effect of the First Cause; the First Cause is the creator of
the world; the creation is the beginning of the world. The scene poses the question that al-Kindi
was the first to pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What is the First Cause? How does
it cause the world? And what is the world in relation to it? The present chapter states al-Kindi’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


37.2       The Question
The previous part stated the positions of the contemporary West: Husserl, Heidegger, White-
head, Wittgenstein, Quine and Davidson, Kripke and Lewis, and Derrida and Deleuze. The
contemporary West has questioned the metaphysical tradition; it has questioned the priority
of presence; it has questioned the priority of identity. Al-Kindi is the first philosopher of the
Islamic tradition, and he is the philosopher who introduces the Greek philosophical tradition
into the Islamic world: he translates, he comments, he reconciles. The present chapter states
al-Kindi’s reconciliation, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether al-Kindi was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did al-Kindi hold? The chapter states the first philosophy,
the createdness of the world, the unity of God, the agent intellect, the five essences, and the
reconciliation of philosophy and religion, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and al-Kindi converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that al-Kindi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and al-
Kindi? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


37.3       The Position

37.3.1      First Philosophy

Al-Kindi’s account of first philosophy is stated in Fi al-Falsafa al-Ula (On First Philosophy).
First philosophy is the knowledge of the first cause; it is the highest part of philosophy; it is the
science of the principle of all things.
      The first philosophy has three features.
37.3. The Position                                                                                    411


First feature: philosophy is the knowledge of causes. Philosophy is the knowledge of
things in their essences and causes; it is the knowledge of what things are and why they are. The
highest part of philosophy is the knowledge of the first cause; it is the knowledge of the cause
that is not caused.


Second feature: the first cause is the cause of all things. The first cause is the cause of
all things; it is the source of all multiplicity; it is the principle of all being. The first cause is not
a cause among causes; it is the cause of the chain of causes; it is the cause that is not caused.


Third feature: the first cause is one. The first cause is one; it is absolutely simple; it has
no multiplicity; it has no parts; it has no distinctions. The first cause is the one; it is the source
of the many; it is the principle of the multiplicity.
    The first philosophy is the foundation of al-Kindi’s philosophy. It is the science of the first
cause; it is the knowledge of the principle; it is the reconciliation of philosophy and religion.

   From the Tradition

   “Philosophy is the knowledge of things in their essences and causes. The highest part of
   philosophy is the knowledge of the First Cause, which is the cause of all things.” (al-Kindi,
   Fi al-Falsafa al-Ula, trans. after Ivry)



37.3.2     The Createdness of the World

Al-Kindi’s account of the createdness of the world is stated in Fi Huduth al-Alam (On the
Createdness of the World). The world is not eternal; it is created; it has a beginning; it is brought
into being by the First Cause.
    The createdness has three features.


First feature: the world is finite. The world is finite in magnitude and in time; it is not
infinite; it is not eternal. The world has a beginning; it has a first moment; it has a first state.
The finite world is created; the infinite world is impossible.


Second feature: the actual infinite is impossible. The actual infinite is impossible; the
infinite regress is impossible; the infinite chain is impossible. The world cannot be eternal; the
chain of causes cannot be infinite; the regress must stop at a first cause.


Third feature: the first cause is the creator. The first cause is the creator of the world; it
is the cause of the beginning; it is the source of the creation. The creation is not a change in the
creator; it is a bringing into being of the world; it is a giving of existence to the world.
    The createdness is the key to al-Kindi’s cosmology. It is the rejection of the Aristotelian
eternity of the world; it is the affirmation of the creation; it is the reconciliation of philosophy
and religion.
412                                                                             Chapter 37. al-Kindi


   From the Tradition

   “The world is created; it has a beginning; it is brought into being by the First Cause. The
   eternity of the world is impossible; the infinite regress is impossible; the actual infinite is
   impossible.” (al-Kindi, Fi Huduth al-Alam, trans. after Ivry)


37.3.3      The Unity of God
Al-Kindi’s account of the unity of God is stated in Fi Wahdaniyyat Allah (On the Unity of God).
God is absolutely one; God has no multiplicity; God has no parts; God has no distinctions. The
unity of God is the most radical unity; it is the unity that excludes all multiplicity.
      The unity has three features.

First feature: God is one. God is one; God is not many; God is not a composite; God is
not a whole of parts. God is the one that is not divided; God is the one that is not multiplied;
God is the one that is not distinguished.

Second feature: the divine attributes are not distinct from the essence. The divine
attributes (knowledge, power, life, etc.) are not distinct from the divine essence; they are not
added to the essence; they are not separate from the essence. The attributes are the essence; the
essence is the attributes; the distinction is only in our way of speaking.

Third feature: the unity is the source of multiplicity. The unity is the source of
multiplicity; the one is the source of the many; the simple is the source of the composite. The
multiplicity is not in God; the multiplicity is from God; the creation is the multiplicity that
comes from the one.
      The unity is the key to al-Kindi’s theology. It is the affirmation of the divine simplicity; it is
the rejection of the divine multiplicity; it is the reconciliation of philosophy and religion.

37.3.4      The Agent Intellect
Al-Kindi’s account of the agent intellect is stated in Fi al-’Aql (On the Intellect). The agent
intellect is the lowest of the celestial intellects; it is the mediator between the material world and
the intelligible world; it is the source of human knowledge.
      The agent intellect has three features.

First feature: the agent intellect is the mediator. The agent intellect is the mediator
between the material world and the intelligible world; it is the bridge between the senses and the
intellect; it is the source of the abstract concepts. The agent intellect illuminates the material
images and makes them intelligible.

Second feature: the agent intellect is the source of knowledge. The agent intellect is
the source of human knowledge; it is the active principle that actualizes the potential intellect; it
is the light that makes the intelligible visible. The human intellect is potential; the agent intellect
is actual; the two are related as the eye is related to the light.
37.3. The Position                                                                                   413


Third feature: the agent intellect is one. The agent intellect is one; it is not many; it is
the same for all human beings. The agent intellect is the single source of all human knowledge;
it is the single light that illuminates all minds.
    The agent intellect is the key to al-Kindi’s epistemology. It is the mediator between the
material and the intelligible; it is the source of knowledge; it is the light that makes the intelligible
visible.


37.3.5     The Five Essences

Al-Kindi’s account of the five essences is stated in Fi al-Mahiyyat al-Khams (On the Five
Essences). The five essences are matter, form, motion, time, and place; they are the five
principles of the material world; they are the five categories of the material manifestation.
    The five essences have three features.


First feature: the five essences are the principles. The five essences are the principles of
the material world; they are the conditions of the material manifestation; they are the structure
of the material realm. Without them, there is no material world; with them, the material world
is what it is.


Second feature: the five essences are interrelated. The five essences are interrelated;
matter needs form; form needs matter; motion needs time and place; time needs motion; place
needs matter. The five are not separate; they are the aspects of one structure; they are the
structure of the material realm.


Third feature: the five essences are created. The five essences are created; they are not
eternal; they are brought into being by the First Cause. The material world is created; the five
essences are created; the whole is created.
    The five essences are the key to al-Kindi’s philosophy of nature. They are the structure of
the material world; they are the principles of the material manifestation; they are the categories
of the material realm.


37.3.6     Faith and Reason

Al-Kindi’s account of faith and reason is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in Fi
al-Falsafa al-Ula. Faith and reason are not enemies; they are complements; they are two ways of
knowing the same truth.
    The reconciliation has three features.


First feature: the truth is one. The truth is one; the truth is not many; the truth is not
divided. Faith and reason both lead to the truth; both are ways of knowing the truth; both are
legitimate.
414                                                                           Chapter 37. al-Kindi


Second feature: the prophet and the philosopher. The prophet and the philosopher
both receive the truth; the prophet receives it directly; the philosopher receives it through reason.
The prophet communicates it in symbols; the philosopher communicates it in concepts. The two
are not in conflict; they are complementary.


Third feature: the reconciliation. The reconciliation is the recognition that faith and reason
are two ways of knowing the same truth; the reconciliation is the recognition that philosophy
and religion are not enemies; the reconciliation is the recognition that the truth is one.
      The reconciliation is the key to al-Kindi’s philosophy. It is the affirmation of the unity of
truth; it is the affirmation of the compatibility of faith and reason; it is the reconciliation of
philosophy and religion.


37.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of al-Kindi is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the world’s eternity. The traditional reading takes al-Kindi’s
argument for the createdness of the world to be a philosophical argument: it is based on the
impossibility of the actual infinite; it is based on the finitude of the world. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a theological argument: it is based on the revelation; it is based on the Qur’an; it
is not a philosophical argument, but a theological one. The two readings disagree on whether
al-Kindi is a philosopher or a theologian, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, not a creation.


Second dispute: the status of the divine attributes. The traditional reading takes
al-Kindi’s denial of the distinctness of the attributes to be a radical divine simplicity: God has
no attributes distinct from the essence. A revisionary reading takes it to be a linguistic thesis:
the attributes are not distinct in reality, but they are distinct in language; the distinction is
only in our way of speaking. The two readings disagree on whether al-Kindi is a simplist or a
linguistic philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a God with attributes.


Third dispute: the status of the agent intellect. The traditional reading takes the agent
intellect to be a cosmic entity: it is the lowest of the celestial intellects; it is a real being. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a structural principle: it is the condition of knowledge; it is not
a being, but a structure. The two readings disagree on whether al-Kindi is a cosmologist or a
structuralist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
light is a structural conveyor, not a cosmic entity.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If al-Kindi is a philosopher, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a philosophical theology. If
al-Kindi is a theologian, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does
37.5. Points of Convergence                                                                         415


not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


37.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With al-Kindi. The framework shares four structural features with al-Kindi’s position.

       1. The priority of the first cause. Al-Kindi holds that the first cause is the source of
           all things; it is the cause of the chain of causes; it is the principle of all being. The
           framework holds that the First Determination is the realm of pure unity; it is the
           source of all multiplicity; it is the principle of all manifestation. Both hold that there
           is a first principle that is the source of all things.

       2. The hierarchy of being. Al-Kindi holds that reality is stratified: the first cause, the
           celestial intellects, the human intellect, the material world. The framework holds
           that reality is stratified: the seven realms, from the First Determination to the
           Material Manifestation. Both hold that reality is hierarchical, and that the hierarchy
           is the structure of the real.

       3. The mediator. Al-Kindi holds that the agent intellect is the mediator between
           the material and the intelligible; it is the light that makes the intelligible visible.
           The framework holds that light is the conveyor of effect between identity and
           manifestation; it is the condition of possibility of relation. Both hold that there is a
           mediator between the higher and the lower, and that the mediator is the condition
           of knowledge.

       4. The unity of truth. Al-Kindi holds that faith and reason are two ways of knowing
           the same truth; the truth is one; the truth is not divided. The framework holds that
           its structure is compatible with any inquiry that does not contradict it; the truth is
           one; the truth is not divided. Both hold that truth is one, and that different ways of
           knowing it must be compatible.



37.6       Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With al-Kindi. The framework diverges from al-Kindi in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Al-Kindi’s first cause is God; God is the creator; God is the one;
           God is the source of all things. The framework has no God; its First Determination
           is a realm of pure unity; it is not a creator; it is not a person; it is not a God. The
           framework is a metaphysics without God.
416                                                                            Chapter 37. al-Kindi


       2. The status of creation. Al-Kindi holds that the world is created; it has a beginning;
          it is brought into being by the First Cause. The framework holds that expression is a
          structural tendency; it is the enactment of the identity; it is not a creation ex nihilo;
          the world is not created, but expressed. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
          expression, not of creation.

       3. The status of the agent intellect. Al-Kindi holds that the agent intellect is a cosmic
          entity; it is the lowest of the celestial intellects; it is a real being. The framework
          holds that light is a structural conveyor; it is the condition of possibility of relation;
          it is not a cosmic entity. The framework’s light is structural, not cosmic.

       4. The status of the five essences. Al-Kindi holds that the five essences (matter, form,
          motion, time, place) are the principles of the material world. The framework holds
          that the material realm is structured by the rules of the Material Manifestation
         (causality, temporality, discreteness), not by the five essences. The framework’s
          material realm is structured by the rules, not by the essences.




37.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  al-Kindi’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
  a cause; it is a pattern. The world is caused by the First Cause; the world is not just
  expressed from an identity; the world is created by God. The framework has no creator;
  the framework has no creation; the framework’s world is a world without a cause. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of causes.
  al-Kindi’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are created by
  God; they are not just levels of manifestation; they are the creation of the First Cause.
  The framework has no creation; the framework’s realms are not created; the framework’s
  realms are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of creation.
  al-Kindi’s third objection. The framework says that light is a structural conveyor; it is
  the condition of possibility of relation. But light is the agent intellect; it is the mediator
  between the material and the intelligible; it is a cosmic entity. The framework has no
  agent intellect; the framework’s light is not a cosmic entity; the framework’s light is a
  structure. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of structures, not of intellects.
37.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      417


37.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world has a cause, and it
   agrees that the cause is not the world. But the framework denies that the cause must be
   a creator. The framework’s expression is a structural tendency; it is the enactment of the
   identity; it is the cause of the manifestation. The cause is structural, not personal. The
   distinction is between a creator (a personal cause) and a structural cause (a condition of
   possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are real, and it
   agrees that the realms are structured. But the framework denies that the realms must be
   created. The framework’s realms are levels of manifestation; they are the structure of the
   manifestation; they are not created; they are the condition of possibility of the creation.
   The distinction is between a creation (a bringing into being) and a condition of possibility
   (a structural level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that there is a mediator between
   the material and the intelligible, and it agrees that the mediator is the condition of
   knowledge. But the framework denies that the mediator must be a cosmic entity. The
   framework’s light is the structural conveyor of effect; it is the condition of possibility of
   relation; it is not a cosmic entity. The distinction is between a cosmic entity (an intellect)
   and a structural condition (a light); the framework holds the second, not the first.



37.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

al-Kindi’s cost. If al-Kindi accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
world is created by God. He must accept that the world is expressed from the identity; that the
expression is a structural tendency; that the world is not created; that the world is enacted. The
cost is the loss of the creation: the world is no longer created; the world is expressed; the creator
is no longer a creator; the creator is a structural condition.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts al-Kindi’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the creation, of the creator, of the agent intellect—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is
the enactment of a structure, but not a creation, and the framework leaves the creation to a
separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that al-Kindi’s creation is not
a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. al-Kindi
418                                                                          Chapter 37. al-Kindi


must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
creation presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


37.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for al-
   Kindi’s term “the First Cause.” If one substitutes “the First Cause” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; al-Kindi’s First Cause is the
   cause of all things, and it is not manifested, because it is the source. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; al-Kindi’s First Cause is one. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence. The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable
   for al-Kindi’s term “the creation.” If one substitutes “the creation” for “expression” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural
   relation; al-Kindi’s creation is an act of the First Cause. The framework’s expression
   is structural; al-Kindi’s creation is personal. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and al-Kindi is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a first principle that is the source of all things, and they differ
   on whether the principle is a creator or a structure. Both hold that reality is stratified,
   and they differ on whether the strata are created or expressed. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of al-Kindi
   would be refuted by showing that al-Kindi’s creation cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and creation—by showing, that is, that al-Kindi
   already distinguishes the structural condition from the creation, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of al-Kindi’s own.



37.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of al-Kindi’s First Cause, or is it a
departure from al-Kindi? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that al-Kindi’s First Cause is already a structural condition,
not a creator, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.
37.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                419


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Fi al-Falsafa al-Ula and Fi Huduth al-Alam
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the first philosophy, the createdness of the world,
the unity of God, the agent intellect, the five essences, and the reconciliation of faith and reason,
and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a
different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
