A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a cause and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the cause that brings into being, or the structure that makes possible? Is the
truth the creation that begins, or the expression that enacts? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between al-Kindi’s First Cause and the framework’s First Determination?

The next chapter turns to al-Farabi. It states the emanation of the ten intellects and the nine
spheres, the distinction between the First and the Second, the theory of prophecy, the virtuous
city, and the harmony of philosophy and religion; it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of al-Farabi; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of emanation and of the political order is the nearest classical Islamic
analogue to al-Farabi’s. The present chapter has stated al-Kindi’s answer to the problem of the
First Cause; the next chapter states al-Farabi’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 38

al-Farabi


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Tarkhan ibn
Awzalagh al-Farabi (c. 872–950 CE), known in the tradition as the “Second Teacher” (al-mu’allim
al-thani), after Aristotle. It states al-Farabi’s cosmology of emanation, the hierarchy of the ten
intellects and the nine spheres, the distinction between the First and the Second, the theory of
the active intellect, the theory of prophecy, the political philosophy of the virtuous city, and
the harmony of philosophy and religion, with reference to Ara’ Ahl al-Madina al-Fadila (The
Opinions of the Inhabitants of the Virtuous City), al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya (The Political Regime),
Falsafat Aristutalis (The Philosophy of Aristotle), Kitab al-Huruf (The Book of Letters), and
Ihsa’ al-’Ulum (The Enumeration of the Sciences); it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of al-Farabi; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of emanation, of light, and of the realms is the nearest classical Islamic analogue
to al-Farabi’s; it presents the objections that al-Farabi would raise against the framework; it
presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “emanation,” “intellect,” “sphere,” “active
intellect,” “prophecy,” or “virtuous city,” these are al-Farabi’s terms, and their sense is fixed by
the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


38.1     A Scene
Consider a philosopher in tenth-century Baghdad. He is translating Aristotle from Greek into
Arabic, and as he translates, he notices that Aristotle speaks of “God” as the “First Mover,” but
does not speak of “creation from nothing.” He reads Plato, and finds the “Forms” and the “Good
beyond being.” He reads the Qur’an, which says that God created the heavens and the earth in
six days. He reads Plotinus, whose Enneads have been paraphrased in Arabic as the Theology
of Aristotle, and he finds there a hierarchy of emanation: the One, the Intellect, the Soul, the
material world.
   Al-Farabi stands before four traditions: the Aristotelian, the Platonic, the Qur’anic, and
the Neoplatonic. Can the four be reconciled? His answer: yes, if “creation” is interpreted as
“emanation.” God is one; from the one, only one proceeds. So God brings forth the First Intellect;
the First Intellect, by thinking its own essence, brings forth the Second Intellect and the First
Heaven; the Second Intellect, by thinking its own essence, brings forth the Third Intellect and the
Second Heaven; and the series continues down to the Tenth Intellect—the Active Intellect—which
mediates between heaven and earth, and which is the source of human knowledge and of prophecy.
   Now a harder case. The philosopher asks what “existence” is. Aristotle said that being
is divided into ten categories. But al-Farabi says: existence, in one sense, is a second-order

                                                420
38.2. The Question                                                                              421


concept—“existence” in the sense of truth—and in another sense, it is identical with the essence
of an existent. Possible beings receive their existence from another; only God is that whose
existence is identical with its essence.
   And the hardest case. The philosopher asks how knowledge is possible. The human being
is born with a potential intellect; but the potential intellect alone cannot grasp universals. It
needs the Active Intellect—the Tenth Intellect—which, from without, emanates the universal
forms into the human intellect. And if the Active Intellect conveys its emanation to the human
being in a complete way, the human becomes a prophet: one who receives divine truths through
imagination, in the form of symbols and parables, and who conveys them to the multitude in the
form that the multitude can receive.
   The scene poses three questions. First: what is the relation between the one and the many,
and how does the many proceed from the one? Second: what is the relation between existence
and essence, and is existence a real predicate or a mental concept? Third: how is universal
knowledge possible, and what is the relation between the human intellect and the Active Intellect?
The present chapter states al-Farabi’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


38.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated al-Kindi’s position: the first philosophy, the createdness of the world,
the unity of God, the agent intellect, the five essences, and the reconciliation of faith and reason.
Al-Kindi is the first philosopher of the Islamic tradition; he introduces the Greek tradition into
the Islamic world, and he reconciles it with the Qur’an. Al-Farabi is his successor, and he is the
great systematizer: he systematizes the Neoplatonic emanationism, he articulates the hierarchy
of the ten intellects, and he develops the political philosophy of the virtuous city. The present
chapter states al-Farabi’s systematization, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether al-Farabi was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did al-Farabi hold? The chapter states the cosmology of
emanation, the hierarchy of the ten intellects and the nine spheres, the distinction between the
First and the Second, the theory of the active intellect, the theory of prophecy, the political
philosophy of the virtuous city, and the harmony of philosophy and religion, with reference to
the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and al-Farabi converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that al-Farabi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and al-
Farabi? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.
422                                                                            Chapter 38. al-Farabi


38.3        The Position

38.3.1      Emanation and the Ten Intellects

Al-Farabi’s cosmology is stated in Ara’ Ahl al-Madina al-Fadila and in al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya.
The cosmology is a hierarchical emanationism, derived from Plotinus and from the Arabic
Aristotle, but modified in important ways.
      The First Principle. God is absolutely one. God is not a substance, not a body, not an
intellect, not a soul. God is pure unity, and from pure unity only one thing can proceed. This is
the principle of min al-wahid la yasduru illa wahid (from the one, only one proceeds). God is
the First, the One, the Necessary Being, the uncaused cause of all things.
      The First Intellect. From God proceeds the First Intellect. The First Intellect is one, but it
has three acts: it thinks God, it thinks itself, and it thinks the possible. From these three acts
proceed three things: the Second Intellect, the First Heaven, and the matter of the First Heaven.
This triadic structure is repeated at each level of the hierarchy, down to the Tenth Intellect.
      The Ten Intellects. The hierarchy has ten intellects, each corresponding to a celestial sphere:
the First Intellect (the sphere of the fixed stars), the Second (Saturn), the Third (Jupiter), the
Fourth (Mars), the Fifth (the Sun), the Sixth (Venus), the Seventh (Mercury), the Eighth (the
Moon), the Ninth (the sphere of fire), and the Tenth (the Active Intellect, which governs the
sublunar world). Each intellect emanates its sphere and the next intellect; the hierarchy is a
chain of emanations, from the highest to the lowest.
      The Active Intellect. The Tenth Intellect is the Active Intellect (al-’aql al-fa”al). It is the
lowest of the separate intellects, and it is the mediator between the celestial and the sublunar
worlds. It is the source of the forms of material things, and it is the source of human knowledge.
In the framework’s terms, the Active Intellect is the light that conveys the effect of the higher
realms to the lower realm.

   From the Tradition

   “From the First, which is one, proceeds a single intellect. This intellect thinks the First,
   and in thinking it, it thinks itself, and in thinking itself, it thinks the possible. From these
   three acts proceed the Second Intellect, the First Heaven, and the matter of the First
   Heaven. And so on, down to the Tenth Intellect, which is the Active Intellect.” (al-Farabi,
   al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya, ch. 1, trans. after Najjar, adapted)



38.3.2      Existence and Essence

Al-Farabi’s account of existence and essence is stated in Kitab al-Huruf and in Falsafat Aristutalis.
The account distinguishes three senses of existence.
      First sense: existence as a category. Existence in this sense is one of the ten categories; it is
the existence of a substance or an accident. It is not what al-Farabi means by existence in the
primary sense.
      Second sense: existence as truth. Existence in this sense is the truth of a proposition. To say
that something exists is to say that the proposition that asserts it is true. This is a second-order
38.3. The Position                                                                                  423


concept, not a real predicate.
   Third sense: existence as the act of existing. Existence in this sense is the act by which a
thing is. It is not a category, and it is not a concept; it is the very act of being. In possible
beings, existence is received from another; in God, existence is identical with essence.
   The distinction between essence and existence is real in possible beings. A possible being’s
essence does not include its existence; its existence is received from the First Principle, through
the chain of emanation. The essence is what the thing is; the existence is the act by which the
thing is; the two are distinct in the creature, and identical in God.

   From the Tradition

   “Existence, in one sense, is the truth of a proposition; in another sense, it is the act by
   which a thing is. In possible beings, the act is received from another; in God, the act
   is identical with the essence.” (al-Farabi, Kitab al-Huruf, §10–11, trans. after Mahdi,
   adapted)



38.3.3    The Active Intellect and Prophecy

Al-Farabi’s theory of cognition and prophecy is stated in al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya and in Ara’.
The theory has three parts.
   The potential intellect. The human being is born with a potential intellect (al-’aql al-hayulani).
The potential intellect is the capacity to grasp universals, but it does not yet possess them.
   The actual intellect. When the potential intellect grasps the first intelligibles (the axioms of
thought), it becomes the actual intellect (al-’aql bi-al-fi’l). But the actual intellect still needs the
Active Intellect to grasp the higher intelligibles.
   The acquired intellect. When the human intellect is united with the Active Intellect, it
becomes the acquired intellect (al-’aql al-mustafad). This is the highest level of human cognition,
and it is the level at which the human being becomes a philosopher or a prophet.
   Prophecy. Prophecy is the highest form of the acquired intellect. The prophet receives the
emanation of the Active Intellect not only in his intellect, but also in his imagination. The truths
that the philosopher grasps in abstract concepts, the prophet grasps in symbols and parables.
The prophet is the one who conveys the truths of the intellect to the multitude, in the form that
the multitude can receive. Prophecy is not a suspension of the intellect; it is its completion; it is
the intellect and the imagination working together.

   From the Tradition

   “The prophet is the one who receives the emanation of the Active Intellect in his intellect
   and in his imagination. The truths that the philosopher grasps in concepts, the prophet
   grasps in symbols. The prophet is the mediator between the intellectual and the political
   orders.” (al-Farabi, al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya, ch. 2, trans. after Najjar, adapted)
424                                                                           Chapter 38. al-Farabi


38.3.4      The Virtuous City
Al-Farabi’s political philosophy is stated in Ara’ and in al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya. The virtuous
city (al-madina al-fadila) is the city whose inhabitants are ordered toward the highest human
perfection, which is the knowledge of God and of the hierarchy of being.
      The virtuous city has three features. First, it is a city in which each inhabitant fulfills the
function for which he or she is suited by nature. Second, it is a city governed by a philosopher-
prophet, who has attained the highest level of cognition. Third, it is a city whose institutions
are ordered to the cultivation of virtue, not merely to the satisfaction of desires.
      The virtuous city is the political analogue of the cosmic hierarchy. As the cosmos is ordered by
emanation from the First Principle, so the city is ordered by the rule of the philosopher-prophet,
who is the mediator between the divine and the human. The city is the image of the cosmos; the
ruler is the image of the Active Intellect; the citizens are the image of the celestial spheres.

   From the Tradition

   “The virtuous city is the city whose inhabitants are ordered toward the highest perfection.
   Its ruler is the philosopher-prophet, who is the mediator between the divine and the
   human, as the Active Intellect is the mediator between the celestial and the sublunar.”
   (al-Farabi, Ara’, ch. 15, trans. after Walzer, adapted)


38.3.5      Faith and Reason
Al-Farabi’s account of faith and reason is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in Kitab
al-Huruf and in Ihsa’ al-’Ulum. Faith and reason are not enemies; they are complements; they
are two ways of knowing the same truth.
      The reconciliation has three features. First, the truth is one; the truth is not many; the truth
is not divided. Faith and reason both lead to the truth; both are ways of knowing the truth;
both are legitimate.
      Second, the prophet and the philosopher. The prophet and the philosopher both receive the
truth; the prophet receives it through the Active Intellect in his imagination; the philosopher
receives it through the Active Intellect in his intellect. The prophet communicates it in symbols;
the philosopher communicates it in concepts. The two are not in conflict; they are complementary.
      Third, the reconciliation. The reconciliation is the recognition that faith and reason are two
ways of knowing the same truth; the reconciliation is the recognition that philosophy and religion
are not enemies; the reconciliation is the recognition that the truth is one. The reconciliation is
not a subordination of one to the other; it is the recognition that the two are two modes of one
knowledge.


38.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of al-Farabi is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of emanation. The traditional reading takes emanation to be a
necessary process: the First Intellect, by its nature, emanates the Second Intellect, and so on. A
38.5. Points of Convergence                                                                     425


revisionary reading takes emanation to be a free act of God, in which God creates the hierarchy of
intellects by an act of will. The two readings disagree on whether al-Farabi is a necessitarian or a
voluntarist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
expression is a structural tendency, neither necessary in the necessitarian sense nor free in the
voluntarist sense.


Second dispute: the status of the active intellect. The traditional reading takes the
Active Intellect to be a separate substance, one of the ten intellects, and the source of human
knowledge. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphorical name for the human capacity
to grasp universals, or for the divine light that illuminates the human mind. The two readings
disagree on whether al-Farabi is a realist or a conceptualist about the Active Intellect, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s light is neither a
separate substance nor a metaphor, but a structural conveyor.


Third dispute: the status of prophecy. The traditional reading takes prophecy to be a
real phenomenon, in which the prophet receives divine truths through the Active Intellect. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a political phenomenon, in which the prophet is the one who
conveys philosophical truths to the multitude in symbolic form. The two readings disagree on
whether al-Farabi is a mystic or a political philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no prophecy, and its account of knowledge is
structural, not prophetic.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If al-Farabi is a necessitarian, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a necessitarian emanationism.
If al-Farabi is a voluntarist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of al-Farabi,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.


38.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With al-Farabi. The framework shares four structural features with al-Farabi’s position.

       1. The priority of unity. Al-Farabi holds that God is absolutely one, and that from
         the one only one proceeds. The framework holds that the First Determination is
         the realm of pure unity, and that multiplicity is derived from unity. Both hold that
         unity is prior to multiplicity, and that multiplicity is derived from unity.

       2. The hierarchy of levels. Al-Farabi’s cosmos is a hierarchy of ten intellects, each
         derived from the level above. The framework’s ontology is a hierarchy of seven
         realms, each related to the others by expression. Both hold that reality is stratified,
         and that the strata are not reducible to one another.
426                                                                       Chapter 38. al-Farabi


       3. The distinction between essence and existence. Al-Farabi holds that in possible
         beings, essence and existence are distinct; in God alone, they are identical. The
         framework holds that identity and manifestation are distinct: the identity is the
         invariance; the manifestation is the appearance. Both hold that what a thing is
         and that it is are distinct, and that the distinction is the key to understanding the
         creature.

       4. Light as the mediator. Al-Farabi’s Active Intellect is the mediator between the
         celestial and the sublunar worlds; it is the source of the forms of material things,
         and the source of human knowledge. The framework’s light is the conveyor of effect
         between identity and manifestation, and the condition of possibility of relation.
         Both hold that there is a mediator between the higher and the lower, and that the
         mediator is the condition of both knowledge and being.




38.6      Points of Divergence
38.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 427


   Points of Divergence

   With al-Farabi. The framework diverges from al-Farabi in four respects.

       1. The nature of emanation. Al-Farabi’s emanation is a necessary process: from the one,
          only one proceeds, and the hierarchy unfolds by necessity. The framework’s expression
          is a structural tendency: every identity, by its nature, tends toward expression, and
          expression is the enactment of the identity’s structure. The framework’s expression
          is not an emanation from a transcendent source; it is the structure of identity itself.
          The two are structurally different: emanation is a giving from a transcendent source,
          expression is the enactment of an immanent structure.

       2. The status of the Active Intellect. Al-Farabi holds that the Active Intellect is a
          separate substance, one of the ten intellects, and the source of human knowledge.
          The framework holds that light is a structural conveyor, not a separate substance; it
          is the condition of possibility of relation, not a being among beings. The framework’s
          light is structural, not substantial.

       3. The status of prophecy. Al-Farabi holds that prophecy is a real phenomenon, in which
          the prophet receives divine truths through the Active Intellect. The framework has
          no prophecy; its knowledge is reconstruction, not revelation; its truth is structural,
          not prophetic. The framework is a metaphysics without prophecy.

       4. The status of the virtuous city. Al-Farabi holds that the virtuous city is the political
          analogue of the cosmic hierarchy, and that it is governed by a philosopher-prophet.
          The framework has no political philosophy; its subject is the structure of identity
          and manifestation, and it leaves the political question to a separate inquiry. The
          framework is a metaphysics without a political philosophy.



38.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   al-Farabi’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its expression is a structural tendency. But a structural invariance is not a source;
   it is a pattern. A pattern does not give rise to anything; it does not emanate; it does not
   produce. If the framework’s identity is only an invariance, then the framework has no
   account of why anything exists at all. al-Farabi’s First Principle is a source, because it is
   the absolute one that gives being to everything else. The framework’s identity is a pattern,
   and a pattern is not a source. The framework’s ontology is a description of structures
   without a source, and a description without a source is not a metaphysics.
   al-Farabi’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction
   from manifestations. But a reconstruction without the Active Intellect is a reconstruction
   without a foundation. The human intellect, by itself, cannot grasp universals; it needs the
428                                                                          Chapter 38. al-Farabi


  emanation of the Active Intellect. The framework’s reconstruction is a human construction,
  without the illumination of the Active Intellect; it is a knowledge without a foundation,
  and a knowledge without a foundation is not knowledge. The framework’s epistemology is
  a skepticism in disguise.
  al-Farabi’s third objection. The framework says that there are seven realms, each with
  its own mode of existence. But the realms are not just levels; they are the emanations of the
  First Principle. The realms are not independent; they are dependent on the First Principle;
  they are the effects of the emanation. The framework’s realms are not emanations; they
  are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of emanation.




38.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a source, and
  it agrees that a metaphysics should account for existence. But the framework denies that
  its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
  source—a this, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is not a pattern, but the act
  of the source. The framework’s identity is not a universal, not a relation, not a separate
  thing; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of
  that condition is what the framework calls existence. The distinction is between a pattern
  (a description) and an enactment (a reality); the framework’s identity is the second, not
  the first. al-Farabi’s First Principle is a source of a different kind: it is a transcendent one,
  and its emanation is an overflow. The framework’s identity is a source of a different kind:
  it is an immanent structure, and its expression is an enactment. The two are different
  kinds of source, and the framework does not claim to be the first.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that knowledge needs a
  foundation, and it agrees that a reconstruction without a foundation is not knowledge. But
  the framework denies that its reconstruction is without a foundation. The framework’s
  reconstruction is anchored in the manifestations themselves; the manifestations are given,
  and the reconstruction is the mind’s reading of them. The manifestations are the foundation;
  the reconstruction is the structure that the mind builds on them. The distinction is between
  the Active Intellect (which emanates the forms from without) and the manifestations
  (which are given from within the realm). The framework holds that the second is the
  foundation, and it holds that the second is sufficient for knowledge. The framework does
  not deny that there is a light that makes knowledge possible; it denies that the light is a
  separate substance. The framework’s light is a structural conveyor, and it is the condition
  of possibility of knowledge, not its source.
  Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just levels,
  and it agrees that they are dependent on the First Determination. But the framework
  denies that the dependence is emanation. The framework’s dependence is expression: the
38.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                       429


   realms are the expressions of the First Determination, and the expression is the structure
   of the dependence. The distinction is between an emanation (a giving from a transcendent
   source) and an expression (the enactment of an immanent structure); the framework holds
   the second, not the first. The realms are not emanations; they are expressions, and the
   expression is a structural relation, not an overflow.



38.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

al-Farabi’s cost. If al-Farabi accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the First Principle is a transcendent source. He must accept that the source is an immanent
structure, and that the expression of the source is an enactment, not an overflow. The cost is the
loss of the transcendence of the One: the source is no longer beyond being, and the emanation
is no longer an overflow. He must also give up the claim that the Active Intellect is a separate
substance; he must accept that the light is a structural conveyor, not a being among beings. The
cost is the loss of the hierarchy of intellects as separate substances.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts al-Farabi’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the transcendent source, of the emanation of the many from the one, of the
illumination of the Active Intellect—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss
of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s expression is the enactment of
identity, but not the emanation from the One, and the framework leaves the emanation to a
separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that al-Farabi’s One is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s identity does not capture. al-Farabi
must accept that the framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is a structural source that al-Farabi’s
One presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


38.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for al-
   Farabi’s term “the First Principle.” If one substitutes “the First Principle” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; al-Farabi’s First Principle
430                                                                          Chapter 38. al-Farabi


   is the absolute one, and it is not manifested, because it is beyond all manifestation. The
   framework’s identity is multiple (there are many identities); al-Farabi’s First Principle is
   one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for al-Farabi’s term “emanation.” If
   one substitutes “emanation” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, enacted by an identity in
   a realm; al-Farabi’s emanation is an overflow of the One’s perfection, and it is not an
   enactment by the source in a realm. The framework’s expression is non-teleological;
   al-Farabi’s emanation is the expression of the Good. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for al-Farabi’s term “the Active Intellect.”
   If one substitutes “the Active Intellect” for “light” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s light is a structural conveyor, and it is not a separate
   substance; al-Farabi’s Active Intellect is a separate intellect, one of the ten, and the source
   of human knowledge. The framework’s light is impersonal; al-Farabi’s Active Intellect is a
   cosmic entity. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and al-Farabi is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is a hierarchy of levels, and they differ on whether the source is
   a transcendent one or an immanent structure. Both hold that light is the medium of
   emanation or expression, and they differ on what the light carries (perfection vs. effect).
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of al-Farabi would be refuted by showing that al-Farabi’s First Principle cannot be
   formulated without the framework’s distinction between identity and manifestation—by
   showing, that is, that al-Farabi already distinguishes the source from its emanations in a
   way that the framework’s distinction develops, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of al-Farabi’s own.



38.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of al-Farabi’s First Principle, or is it
a departure from al-Farabi? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that al-Farabi’s First Principle is already a structural
source, not a transcendent one, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of emanation?
The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that
expression requires the notion of emanation has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Ara’ and the al-Siyasa al-Madaniyya
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the emanation, the ten intellects, the distinction
38.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 431


between essence and existence, the Active Intellect, the prophecy, and the virtuous city, and it

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a source and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the source a perfection that overflows, or a structure that is enacted? Is the source
beyond being, or is it the being of what it sources? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between al-Farabi’s First Principle and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Ibn Sina. It states the distinction between essence and existence, the
proof of the necessary being, the theory of the ten intellects and the celestial spheres, the account
of the human soul and its faculties, the theory of prophecy, and the harmony of philosophy and
religion; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ibn Sina; and it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of essence and existence
and of the hierarchy of being is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Ibn Sina’s. The present
chapter has stated al-Farabi’s answer to the problem of emanation; the next chapter states Ibn
Sina’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 39

Ibn Sina


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Sina (980–1037
CE), known in the Latin West as Avicenna and in the Islamic tradition as al-Shaykh al-Ra’is
(the Chief Master). It states Ibn Sina’s distinction between essence and existence, his proof of
the Necessary Being, his account of the ten intellects and the celestial spheres, his theory of the
human soul and its faculties, his account of prophecy and the imagination, and his reconciliation
of philosophy and religion, with reference to al-Shifa’ (The Healing), al-Najat (The Salvation),
al-Isharat wa-al-Tanbihat (The Pointers and Reminders), and al-Risala al-Adhawiyya fi al-Ma’ad
(The Treatise on the Afterlife); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ibn
Sina; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of
essence and existence and of the hierarchy of being is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Ibn
Sina’s; it presents the objections that Ibn Sina would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “essence,” “existence,” “necessary being,” “possible being,”
“the soul,” “the active intellect,” “prophecy,” or “the afterlife,” these are Ibn Sina’s terms, and
their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


39.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is thinking about a triangle. She has the concept of a triangle: three
sides, three angles, the sum of the angles equal to two right angles. The concept is in her mind;
it is one concept; it is universal; it applies to every triangle. But the concept is not a triangle; it
is the concept of a triangle. And the triangle is not the concept; it is the thing that the concept
represents. The essence of the triangle is its being three-sided; its existence is its being in the
world, or its being in the mind. The essence does not include the existence; the existence is
added to the essence.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what a triangle is, or whether it exists, but
what makes it exist. The triangle in the world exists because someone drew it, or because the
material world is arranged in a triangular way. The triangle in the mind exists because she is
thinking it. The existence of the triangle is not self- explanatory; it is received from another; it
is caused. The triangle is a possible being: it can exist or not exist; its existence is not necessary;
it is contingent.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks whether there is a being whose
existence is not received from another—a being whose essence is its existence, a being that
cannot not exist. The chain of possible beings cannot be infinite; an infinite regress of causes
is impossible; the chain must terminate in a being that is necessary in itself. This is what Ibn

                                                 432
39.2. The Question                                                                                433


Sina calls the Necessary Being (wajib al-wujud): the being whose existence is identical with its
essence, the being that is the cause of all possible beings, the being that is one, simple, and
beyond all determination.
   The scene is Ibn Sina’s image, in al-Shifa’ and in al-Isharat, of the structure of reality. The
triangle is the possible being; the concept is the essence; the existence is the act; the Necessary
Being is the source. The possible being is composed of essence and existence; the Necessary
Being is not composed; it is pure existence. The scene poses the question that Ibn Sina was the
first to pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What is the distinction between essence
and existence? What is the proof of the Necessary Being? And what is the relation between the
Necessary Being and the possible beings? The present chapter states Ibn Sina’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


39.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated al-Farabi’s position: the emanation of the ten intellects, the distinction
between essence and existence, the theory of the active intellect, the theory of prophecy, the
political philosophy of the virtuous city, and the harmony of philosophy and religion. Al-Farabi
is the great systematizer of the Neoplatonic emanationism in the Islamic tradition; he articulates
the hierarchy of the ten intellects, and he develops the political philosophy of the virtuous city.
Ibn Sina is his successor, and he is the great metaphysician: he distinguishes essence and existence
with unprecedented precision, he proves the existence of the Necessary Being, and he develops
the theory of the soul and of prophecy. The present chapter states Ibn Sina’s metaphysics, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Ibn Sina was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ibn Sina hold? The chapter states the distinction between
essence and existence, the proof of the Necessary Being, the ten intellects and the celestial spheres,
the human soul and its faculties, the theory of prophecy, and the reconciliation of philosophy
and religion, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ibn Sina converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Ibn Sina would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ibn
Sina? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


39.3      The Position
434                                                                            Chapter 39. Ibn Sina


39.3.1      Essence and Existence
Ibn Sina’s distinction between essence and existence is stated in al-Shifa’: al-Ilahiyyat (The
Healing: Metaphysics) and in al-Isharat. The distinction is one of the most influential in the
history of philosophy, and it is the foundation of Ibn Sina’s metaphysics.
      The distinction has three features.

First feature: the essence is what a thing is. The essence (inniyya or quiddity, mahiyya)
is what a thing is; it is the whatness of the thing; it is the definition. The essence of a triangle is
three-sidedness; the essence of a human being is rational animality. The essence does not include
the existence; a thing’s essence can be conceived without conceiving its existence.

Second feature: the existence is the act by which a thing is. The existence (wujud) is
the act by which the essence is; it is not a property added to the essence; it is not a predicate;
it is the very act of being. In possible beings, the existence is received from another; in the
Necessary Being, the existence is identical with the essence.

Third feature: the distinction is real in possible beings. In possible beings, essence and
existence are really distinct: the essence does not include the existence; the existence is added
to the essence. In the Necessary Being, essence and existence are identical: God’s essence is to
exist; God is existence itself.
      The distinction is the foundation of Ibn Sina’s metaphysics. It is what distinguishes the
possible from the necessary; it is what explains the contingency of the world; it is what grounds
the proof of the Necessary Being.

   From the Tradition

   “The essence of a thing is not its existence. The essence is what the thing is; the existence
   is the act by which it is. In possible beings, the two are distinct; in the Necessary Being,
   they are identical.” (Ibn Sina, al-Shifa’: al-Ilahiyyat, I.5, trans. after Marmura, adapted)


39.3.2      The Proof of the Necessary Being
Ibn Sina’s proof of the Necessary Being is stated in al-Shifa’: al-Ilahiyyat and in al-Najat. The
proof is one of the most famous in the history of Islamic philosophy, and it is known as the
“proof from contingency” (burhan al-imkan).
      The proof has three steps.

First step: the possible being. Whatever exists is either necessary in itself or possible in
itself. A possible being is a being whose existence is not necessary; it can exist or not exist; its
existence is received from another.

Second step: the regress. The possible being depends on another for its existence; the other
is either necessary or possible; if possible, it depends on another; and so on. An infinite regress
of possible beings is impossible; an actual infinite is impossible; the regress must terminate.
39.3. The Position                                                                               435


Third step: the Necessary Being. The regress must terminate in a being that is necessary
in itself; a being whose existence is not received from another; a being whose essence is its
existence. This is the Necessary Being (wajib al-wujud), and it is God.
   The proof is not a proof from the world to God in the manner of the cosmological argument;
it is a proof from the structure of existence to its ground. The proof does not begin with the
world as a contingent fact; it begins with the distinction between essence and existence, and it
shows that the distinction requires a being in which the two are identical.

   From the Tradition

   “The possible being needs a cause for its existence. The chain of causes cannot be infinite.
   Therefore, the chain must terminate in a being that is necessary in itself, and this is the
   Necessary Being, which is God.” (Ibn Sina, al-Najat, II.1, trans. after Fakhry, adapted)


39.3.3    The Ten Intellects and the Celestial Spheres
Ibn Sina’s cosmology is stated in al-Shifa’: al-Ilahiyyat and in al-Najat. The cosmology is a
hierarchical emanationism, derived from al-Farabi, but modified in important ways.
   The First Principle. God is absolutely one. From the one, only one proceeds. God is the
Necessary Being; God is pure unity; God is beyond all determination.
   The First Intellect. From God proceeds the First Intellect. The First Intellect is one, but it
has three acts: it thinks God, it thinks itself, and it thinks the possible. From these three acts
proceed three things: the Second Intellect, the First Heaven, and the matter of the First Heaven.
   The Ten Intellects. The hierarchy has ten intellects, each corresponding to a celestial sphere:
the First Intellect (the sphere of the fixed stars), the Second (Saturn), the Third (Jupiter), the
Fourth (Mars), the Fifth (the Sun), the Sixth (Venus), the Seventh (Mercury), the Eighth (the
Moon), the Ninth (the sphere of fire), and the Tenth (the Active Intellect, which governs the
sublunar world).
   The Active Intellect. The Tenth Intellect is the Active Intellect (al-’aql al-fa”al). It is the
lowest of the separate intellects, and it is the mediator between the celestial and the sublunar
worlds. It is the source of the forms of material things, and it is the source of human knowledge.
It is the “giver of forms” (wahib al-suwar), and it is the light that illuminates the human intellect.

39.3.4    The Human Soul and Its Faculties
Ibn Sina’s theory of the soul is stated in al-Shifa’: al-Nafs (The Healing: On the Soul) and in
al-Isharat. The theory is one of the most detailed in the history of philosophy, and it is the
foundation of Ibn Sina’s psychology.
   The soul has three faculties.

First faculty: the vegetative soul. The vegetative soul (al-nafs al-nabatiyya) is the lowest
faculty; it is the principle of nutrition, growth, and reproduction. It is shared with plants.

Second faculty: the animal soul. The animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawaniyya) is the middle
faculty; it is the principle of perception, movement, and appetite. It is shared with animals. It
436                                                                              Chapter 39. Ibn Sina


has two powers: the power of perception (the external senses and the internal senses) and the
power of movement (the appetitive and the motive powers).

Third faculty: the rational soul. The rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqa) is the highest faculty;
it is the principle of thought and knowledge. It is unique to human beings. It has two powers: the
practical intellect (which governs action) and the theoretical intellect (which grasps universals).
      The theoretical intellect has four levels: the potential intellect (al-’aql al-hayulani), the actual
intellect (al-’aql bi-al-fi’l), the acquired intellect (al-’aql al-mustafad), and the active intellect
(al-’aql al-fa”al). The human intellect is potential; the Active Intellect is actual; the two are
related as the eye is related to the light.

   From the Tradition

   “The soul is a substance, not a body, not an accident. It is the form of the body, and it is
   the principle of life. It has three faculties: the vegetative, the animal, and the rational.”
   (Ibn Sina, al-Shifa’: al-Nafs, I.1, trans. after Rahman, adapted)


39.3.5       Prophecy and the Imagination
Ibn Sina’s theory of prophecy is stated in al-Shifa’: al-Nafs and in al-Isharat. The theory is a
development of al-Farabi’s theory, but it is more detailed.
      The prophet. The prophet is the one who receives the emanation of the Active Intellect in
his intellect and in his imagination. The prophet grasps the truths of the intellect in concepts,
and he conveys them to the multitude in symbols and parables.
      The imagination. The imagination (al-khayal) is the faculty that retains the images of the
senses and combines them in new ways. The prophet’s imagination is exceptionally powerful; it
can receive the emanation of the Active Intellect in the form of images and symbols.
      The three kinds of prophecy. Ibn Sina distinguishes three kinds of prophecy: the prophecy of
the intellect (the prophet grasps the truths of the intellect), the prophecy of the imagination (the
prophet receives the truths in images), and the prophecy of the practical intellect (the prophet
guides the community in action).
      The prophet is the mediator between the intellectual and the political orders. He is the
philosopher-king of Plato, but he is also the prophet of the Qur’an. Prophecy is not a suspension
of the intellect; it is its completion.

39.3.6       The Afterlife
Ibn Sina’s theory of the afterlife is stated in al-Risala al-Adhawiyya and in al-Shifa’: al-Ilahiyyat.
The theory is one of the most controversial in the Islamic tradition, because it departs from the
literal reading of the Qur’an.
      The immortality of the soul. The soul is a substance, not a body; it is immortal. The soul
does not die with the body; it survives the death of the body; it returns to its source.
      The happiness of the soul. The happiness of the soul is the knowledge of the intelligibles, and
especially the knowledge of God. The soul that has attained this knowledge in this life attains it
more fully in the next; the soul that has not attained it is deprived of it.
39.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             437


   The resurrection of the body. Ibn Sina does not deny the resurrection of the body, but he
interprets it symbolically. The resurrection is not a physical event; it is a spiritual event; it is
the return of the soul to its source. The literal reading of the Qur’an is for the multitude; the
philosophical reading is for the elite.
   The theory of the afterlife is the foundation of Ibn Sina’s eschatology. It is what distinguishes
him from the literalists; it is what makes him a philosopher, not a theologian.



39.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Ibn Sina is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the distinction between essence and existence. The
traditional reading takes the distinction to be a real distinction: in possible beings, essence and
existence are really distinct; the existence is added to the essence. A revisionary reading takes it
to be a conceptual distinction: the distinction is in our way of thinking, not in the thing; the
essence and the existence are the same thing under two descriptions. The two readings disagree
on whether Ibn Sina is a realist or a conceptualist about the distinction, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s distinction between identity and
manifestation is a real distinction, not a conceptual one.


Second dispute: the status of the Necessary Being. The traditional reading takes the
Necessary Being to be God, the creator of the world, the source of all existence. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a philosophical principle, the ground of the contingency of the world, not
a personal God. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Sina is a theist or a deist, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no God, and its
First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a personal creator.


Third dispute: the status of the afterlife. The traditional reading takes Ibn Sina’s theory
of the afterlife to be a philosophical interpretation of the Qur’anic doctrine, consistent with
the revelation. A revisionary reading takes it to be a departure from the Qur’anic doctrine,
inconsistent with the revelation. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Sina is a Muslim
philosopher or a secular philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework has no afterlife in the religious sense, and its account of death is structural,
not eschatological.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ibn Sina is a realist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between two realist metaphysics. If Ibn Sina is a conceptualist, the dialogue
is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct. The framework holds
that the first reading is closer to the texts of Ibn Sina, but it does not rest its case on this reading;
it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
438                                                                            Chapter 39. Ibn Sina


39.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Ibn Sina. The framework shares four structural features with Ibn Sina’s position.

       1. The distinction between essence and existence. Ibn Sina holds that in possible beings,
          essence and existence are distinct; in the Necessary Being, they are identical. The
          framework holds that identity and manifestation are distinct: the identity is the
          invariance; the manifestation is the appearance. Both hold that what a thing is
          and that it is are distinct, and that the distinction is the key to understanding the
          creature.

       2. The priority of the necessary over the possible. Ibn Sina holds that the Necessary
          Being is prior to the possible beings; the possible beings depend on the Necessary
          Being for their existence. The framework holds that the First Determination is prior
          to the other realms; the other realms depend on the First Determination for their
          manifestation. Both hold that there is a first principle that is the source of all things.

       3. The hierarchy of being. Ibn Sina holds that reality is stratified: the Necessary
          Being, the ten intellects, the celestial spheres, the human soul, the material world.
         The framework holds that reality is stratified: the seven realms, from the First
          Determination to the Material Manifestation. Both hold that reality is hierarchical,
          and that the hierarchy is the structure of the real.

       4. The active intellect as mediator. Ibn Sina holds that the Active Intellect is the
          mediator between the celestial and the sublunar worlds; it is the source of the forms
          of material things, and the source of human knowledge. The framework holds that
          light is the conveyor of effect between identity and manifestation; it is the condition
          of possibility of relation. Both hold that there is a mediator between the higher and
          the lower, and that the mediator is the condition of knowledge.



39.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Ibn Sina. The framework diverges from Ibn Sina in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being is God; God is the creator; God is
          the source of all existence. The framework has no God; its First Determination is
          a realm of pure unity; it is not a creator; it is not a person; it is not a God. The
          framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of creation. Ibn Sina holds that the world is created; it is brought into
          being by the Necessary Being; it has a beginning in essence, though not in time.
39.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                   439


          The framework holds that expression is a structural tendency; it is the enactment of
          the identity; it is not a creation ex nihilo; the world is not created, but expressed.
          The framework’s ontology is an ontology of expression, not of creation.

       3. The status of the active intellect. Ibn Sina holds that the Active Intellect is a separate
          substance; it is the lowest of the ten intellects; it is the source of human knowledge.
          The framework holds that light is a structural conveyor; it is the condition of
          possibility of relation; it is not a separate substance. The framework’s light is
          structural, not substantial.

       4. The status of the afterlife. Ibn Sina holds that the soul is immortal; it survives the
          death of the body; it attains happiness in the next life. The framework holds that
          death is the zeroing of manifestation functions; the identity is conserved; there is no
          afterlife in the religious sense. The framework’s account of death is structural, not
          eschatological.




39.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ibn Sina’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not a cause; it is a pattern. The world is caused by the Necessary Being; the world is
   not just expressed from an identity; the world is created by God. The framework has no
   Necessary Being; the framework has no creation; the framework’s world is a world without
   a cause. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of causes.
   Ibn Sina’s second objection. The framework says that the identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source. But the enactment is not the invariance; it is an act of the source,
   and the act is not the pattern. The framework’s identity is a pattern plus an act, and the
   act is not explained by the pattern. The framework’s identity is either a pattern (and then
   not a source) or a pattern plus an unexplained act (and then not a complete account).
   The framework’s ontology is incomplete.
   Ibn Sina’s third objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
   are the emanations of the Necessary Being. The realms are not independent; they are
   dependent on the Necessary Being; they are the effects of the emanation. The framework’s
   realms are not emanations; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology
   of levels, not of emanation.
440                                                                       Chapter 39. Ibn Sina


39.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world has a cause, and it
   agrees that the cause is not the world. But the framework denies that the cause must be
   a creator. The framework’s expression is a structural tendency; it is the enactment of the
   identity; it is the cause of the manifestation. The cause is structural, not personal. The
   distinction is between a creator (a personal cause) and a structural cause (a condition of
   possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the enactment is not the
   invariance, and it agrees that the act is not the pattern. But the framework denies that
   the act is unexplained. The act is the tendency to express (the principle of expression),
   and the tendency is a structural feature of the identity. The act is not an add-on to
   the pattern; it is the pattern’s own tendency to manifest. The distinction is between
   an unexplained act (which the framework rejects) and a structural tendency (which the
   framework affirms). The framework’s identity is a pattern with a structural tendency, not
   a pattern plus an unexplained act.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just levels,
   and it agrees that they are dependent on the First Determination. But the framework
   denies that the dependence is emanation. The framework’s dependence is expression: the
   realms are the expressions of the First Determination, and the expression is the structure
   of the dependence. The distinction is between an emanation (a giving from a transcendent
   source) and an expression (the enactment of an immanent structure); the framework holds
   the second, not the first. The realms are not emanations; they are expressions, and the
   expression is a structural relation, not an overflow.



39.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Ibn Sina’s cost. If Ibn Sina accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
Necessary Being is a creator. He must accept that the source is an immanent structure, and
that the expression of the source is an enactment, not an overflow. The cost is the loss of the
transcendence of the Necessary Being: the source is no longer beyond being, and the emanation
is no longer an overflow. He must also give up the claim that the Active Intellect is a separate
substance; he must accept that the light is a structural conveyor, not a being among beings.
The cost is the loss of the hierarchy of intellects as separate substances. And he must give up
the claim that the soul is immortal; he must accept that death is the zeroing of manifestation
functions, and that the identity is conserved, but not in an afterlife.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ibn Sina’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
39.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                   441


dimension of the Necessary Being, of the creation, of the Active Intellect, of the afterlife—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s expression is the enactment of identity, but not the creation from the Necessary
Being, and the framework leaves the creation to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s identity does not capture.
Ibn Sina must accept that the framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is a structural source
that the Necessary Being presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


39.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ibn
   Sina’s term “the Necessary Being.” If one substitutes “the Necessary Being” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Ibn Sina’s Necessary
   Being is the being whose essence is its existence, and it is not manifested, because it is
   beyond all manifestation. The framework’s identity is multiple (there are many identities);
   Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Ibn Sina’s term “emanation.” If
   one substitutes “emanation” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, enacted by an identity in
   a realm; Ibn Sina’s emanation is an overflow of the Necessary Being, and it is not an
   enactment by the source in a realm. The framework’s expression is non-teleological; Ibn
   Sina’s emanation is the expression of the Good. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ibn Sina’s term “the soul.” If
   one substitutes “the soul” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source; Ibn Sina’s soul is
   a substance, immortal, the form of the body. The framework’s identity is not a substance;
   Ibn Sina’s soul is a substance. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ibn Sina is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a first principle that is the source of all things, and they differ
   on whether the principle is a necessary being or a structural condition. Both hold that
   reality is stratified, and they differ on whether the strata are emanations or expressions.
442                                                                       Chapter 39. Ibn Sina


   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Ibn Sina would be refuted by showing that Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being cannot
   be formulated without the framework’s distinction between identity and manifestation—by
   showing, that is, that Ibn Sina already distinguishes the source from its emanations in a
   way that the framework’s distinction develops, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of Ibn Sina’s own.




39.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being, or is
it a departure from Ibn Sina? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being is already a structural
source, not a personal God, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of emanation?
The chapter has argued that it can, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that
expression requires the notion of emanation has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of al-Shifa’ and al-Isharat do justice to the
texts? The chapter has used the distinction between essence and existence, the proof of the
Necessary Being, the ten intellects, the human soul, the prophecy, and the afterlife, and it has
stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
