A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an essence and an existence—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the essence that is, or the existence that enacts the essence? Is the
thing necessary in itself, or possible in itself? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Ibn Sina’s Necessary Being and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to al-Ghazali. It states the critique of the philosophers in Tahafut al-
Falasifa ( The Incoherence of the Philosophers), the doctrine of occasionalism, the critique of
causality, the account of the divine attributes, and the relation between philosophy and theology;
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of al-Ghazali; and it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of causality and of the relation
between philosophy and theology is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to al-Ghazali’s. The
present chapter has stated Ibn Sina’s answer to the problem of essence and existence; the next
chapter states al-Ghazali’s critique, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 40

al-Ghazali


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Abu Hamid Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Ghazali
(c. 1058–1111 CE), known in the Islamic tradition as Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam) and
in the Latin West as Algazel. It states al-Ghazali’s critique of the philosophers in Tahafut
al-Falasifa (The Incoherence of the Philosophers), his doctrine of occasionalism, his critique of
causality, his account of the divine attributes, his account of the relation between philosophy
and theology, and his mystical turn in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (The Deliverance from Error)
and Ihya’ ’Ulum al-Din (The Revival of the Religious Sciences); it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of al-Ghazali; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of causality and of the relation between philosophy and theology
is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to al-Ghazali’s; it presents the objections that al-Ghazali
would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side
costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of
“occasionalism,” “causality,” “the divine attributes,” “the incoherence of the philosophers,” or
“the deliverance from error,” these are al-Ghazali’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


40.1      A Scene
Consider a person who sees a piece of cotton placed near a fire. The cotton catches fire; it burns;
it turns to ash. The ordinary explanation is that the fire caused the burning; the fire is the
cause; the burning is the effect; the connection between them is necessary. But al-Ghazali asks:
is the connection really necessary? Have we ever observed the fire causing the burning? We have
observed the fire and the burning occurring together; we have not observed the causal power
itself. The connection is not observed; it is inferred; it is a habit of the mind.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose the fire is not the cause; suppose God is the cause.
God creates the burning at the moment the cotton touches the fire; God creates the connection
between them; God is the only cause. The fire is not a cause; it is an occasion; it is the occasion
on which God creates the burning. This is what al-Ghazali calls occasionalism: the doctrine that
God is the only cause, and that the things we call causes are only occasions.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose the person asks not what causes the
burning, or how the cause works, but what the philosophers have claimed. The philosophers
have claimed that the world is eternal; that God does not know particulars; that the soul is
immortal; that the resurrection is spiritual, not physical. Al-Ghazali responds in the Tahafut: he
shows that the philosophers’ arguments are incoherent; he shows that their claims contradict the
Qur’an; he shows that their philosophy is not necessary, and that the revelation is sufficient.

                                                444
40.2. The Question                                                                              445


   The scene is al-Ghazali’s image, in the Tahafut and in the Munqidh, of the structure of reality.
The fire is the occasion; the burning is the effect; God is the cause; the philosophers are the
critics. The scene poses the question that al-Ghazali was the first to pose in its full form in the
Islamic tradition. What is causality? Is the connection between cause and effect necessary, or
is it a habit? And what is the relation between philosophy and theology? The present chapter
states al-Ghazali’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


40.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Ibn Sina’s position: the distinction between essence and existence,
the proof of the Necessary Being, the ten intellects, the human soul, the prophecy, and the
afterlife. Ibn Sina is the great metaphysician of the Islamic tradition; he systematizes the
Neoplatonic emanationism, and he develops the theory of the soul and of prophecy. Al-Ghazali is
his greatest critic; he attacks the philosophers’ claims; he defends the Qur’anic doctrine; he turns
to mysticism. The present chapter states al-Ghazali’s critique, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
   The question is not whether al-Ghazali was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did al-Ghazali hold? The chapter states the critique of the
philosophers, the doctrine of occasionalism, the critique of causality, the account of the divine
attributes, the relation between philosophy and theology, and the mystical turn, with reference
to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and al-Ghazali converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that al-Ghazali would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and al-
Ghazali? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


40.3       The Position

40.3.1     The Critique of the Philosophers

Al-Ghazali’s critique of the philosophers is stated in Tahafut al-Falasifa (The Incoherence of
the Philosophers, 1095). The critique is not a rejection of philosophy; it is a rejection of the
philosophers’ claims to certainty. Al-Ghazali accepts logic and mathematics; he rejects the
metaphysical claims that go beyond the limits of reason.
   The critique has three features.
446                                                                      Chapter 40. al-Ghazali


First feature: the twenty propositions. Al-Ghazali identifies twenty propositions in which
the philosophers (especially Ibn Sina and al-Farabi) depart from the Qur’an. Three of these are
kufr (unbelief): the eternity of the world, the claim that God does not know particulars, and the
denial of the resurrection of the body. The other seventeen are bid’a (innovation), not unbelief.

Second feature: the method of the critique. Al-Ghazali’s method is dialectical: he shows
that the philosophers’ arguments are incoherent; he shows that their conclusions do not follow
from their premises; he shows that their claims are not demonstrated. The critique is not a
refutation from first principles; it is a deconstruction of the philosophers’ arguments.

Third feature: the purpose of the critique. The purpose is not to destroy philosophy;
it is to defend the faith. Al-Ghazali accepts the tools of philosophy (logic, demonstration) but
rejects the metaphysical conclusions that go beyond the limits of reason. The faith is sufficient;
the philosophy is a tool; the tool is not the master.

   From the Tradition

   “The philosophers have claimed that their arguments are demonstrations. But their
   arguments are not demonstrations; they are conjectures. We will show that their claims
   are incoherent, and that the truth is in the revelation.” (al-Ghazali, Tahafut al-Falasifa,
   Introduction, trans. after Marmura, adapted)


40.3.2      Occasionalism
Al-Ghazali’s doctrine of occasionalism is stated in the Tahafut, in the seventeenth discussion.
The doctrine is the claim that God is the only cause; the things we call causes are only occasions.
      The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the denial of necessary connection. The connection between cause and
effect is not necessary; it is not observed; it is a habit of the mind. We see the fire and the
burning occurring together; we do not see the fire causing the burning. The connection is not in
the things; it is in our minds.

Second feature: God as the only cause. God is the only cause; God creates the burning
at the moment the cotton touches the fire; God creates the connection between them. The fire is
not a cause; it is an occasion; it is the occasion on which God creates the burning.

Third feature: the possibility of miracles. If God is the only cause, then miracles are
possible: God can create the burning without the fire; God can create the fire without the
burning; God can create any effect without its usual occasion. The possibility of miracles is the
consequence of occasionalism.
      The doctrine is the foundation of al-Ghazali’s philosophy of nature. It is the rejection of
the Aristotelian necessary connection; it is the affirmation of the divine omnipotence; it is the
ground of the possibility of miracles.
40.3. The Position                                                                                 447


   From the Tradition

   “The connection between what is habitually believed to be a cause and what is habitually
   believed to be an effect is not necessary. God is the only cause; the fire is only an occasion.”
   (al-Ghazali, Tahafut al-Falasifa, Discussion 17, trans. after Marmura, adapted)



40.3.3      The Critique of Causality

Al-Ghazali’s critique of causality is a development of his occasionalism. The critique has three
features.


First feature: the empiricist premise. All knowledge comes from experience; we have no
knowledge of causal powers; we have only the observation of constant conjunction. The premise
is similar to Hume’s; al-Ghazali anticipates Hume by six centuries.


Second feature: the logical gap. From the observation of constant conjunction, we cannot
infer necessary connection; the inference is not deductive; it is not inductive; it is a habit of the
mind. The gap between the observation and the inference is the foundation of the critique.


Third feature: the theological conclusion. The gap is filled by God; God is the only cause;
God creates the connection between the cause and the effect. The theological conclusion is the
alternative to the philosophical claim of necessary connection.
   The critique is the foundation of al-Ghazali’s epistemology. It is the rejection of the Aristotelian
necessary connection; it is the affirmation of the divine omnipotence; it is the ground of the
possibility of miracles.


40.3.4      The Divine Attributes

Al-Ghazali’s account of the divine attributes is stated in al-Iqtisad fi al-I’tiqad (The Middle Path
in Belief ) and in Ihya’. The account is a middle path between the philosophers’ denial of the
attributes and the literalists’ affirmation of the attributes.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the reality of the attributes. The divine attributes (knowledge, power, life,
will, hearing, sight, speech) are real; they are not identical with the essence; they are not separate
from the essence. The attributes are eternal; they are not created; they are not accidents.


Second feature: the rejection of the literal reading. The literal reading of the attributes
(the hand of God, the eye of God, the face of God) is rejected; the attributes are not bodily; they
are not spatial; they are not temporal. The literal reading is for the multitude; the allegorical
reading is for the elite.
448                                                                          Chapter 40. al-Ghazali


Third feature: the rejection of the philosophical reading. The philosophical reading
(the attributes are identical with the essence) is rejected; the attributes are real; they are not
just names. The middle path is the affirmation of the reality of the attributes without the literal
reading.
      The account is the foundation of al-Ghazali’s theology. It is the reconciliation of the Qur’anic
doctrine with the philosophical critique; it is the middle path between the literalists and the
philosophers.


40.3.5      Philosophy and Theology

Al-Ghazali’s account of the relation between philosophy and theology is stated in the Munqidh
and in the Tahafut. The account is a middle path between the philosophers’ claim to certainty
and the literalists’ rejection of philosophy.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the acceptance of logic and mathematics. Al-Ghazali accepts logic and
mathematics; they are neutral tools; they are not tied to any metaphysical claim. The Muslim
should learn them; they are useful for the defense of the faith.


Second feature: the rejection of metaphysics. Al-Ghazali rejects metaphysics; it goes
beyond the limits of reason; it makes claims that cannot be demonstrated. The metaphysical
claims of the philosophers (the eternity of the world, the denial of the resurrection) are not
demonstrated; they are conjectures.


Third feature: the priority of the revelation. The revelation is the foundation; the
philosophy is a tool; the tool is not the master. The truth is in the revelation; the philosophy is
a way of defending the truth, not a way of discovering it. The faith is sufficient; the philosophy
is a servant.
      The account is the foundation of al-Ghazali’s reconciliation. It is the acceptance of the
philosophical tools; it is the rejection of the philosophical claims; it is the priority of the
revelation.


40.3.6      The Mystical Turn

Al-Ghazali’s mystical turn is stated in the Munqidh and in the Ihya’. After the Tahafut, al-Ghazali
turned to Sufism; he sought the direct experience of God; he sought the certainty that philosophy
could not give.
      The mystical turn has three features.


First feature: the dissatisfaction with philosophy. Philosophy gives knowledge, but not
certainty; it gives concepts, but not experience. The philosopher knows about God, but does not
know God. The knowledge of the philosophers is not the knowledge of the saints.
40.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         449


Second feature: the Sufi path. The Sufi path is the path of purification, of detachment,
of the remembrance of God. The path leads to the direct experience of God; it leads to the
certainty that philosophy could not give.


Third feature: the return to the tradition. After the mystical experience, al-Ghazali
returned to the tradition; he wrote the Ihya’; he taught the people; he defended the faith. The
mystical experience is not a rejection of the tradition; it is its completion.
   The mystical turn is the culmination of al-Ghazali’s philosophy. It is the recognition of the
limits of reason; it is the affirmation of the experience; it is the return to the tradition.



40.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of al-Ghazali is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the critique of causality. The traditional reading takes
al-Ghazali’s critique to be a destruction of causality: the connection between cause and effect is
not necessary; God is the only cause. A revisionary reading takes it to be a defense of the divine
omnipotence: the critique is not a denial of causality; it is a denial of the philosophers’ claim
to necessity. The two readings disagree on whether al-Ghazali is a skeptic or a theologian, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s causality is a
structural relation, not a divine action.


Second dispute: the status of occasionalism. The traditional reading takes occasionalism
to be a metaphysical doctrine: God is the only cause; the things we call causes are only occasions.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a theological doctrine: the doctrine is not a metaphysics; it
is a confession of the divine omnipotence. The two readings disagree on whether al-Ghazali is
a metaphysician or a theologian, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s causality is a structural relation, not a divine action.


Third dispute: the status of the mystical turn. The traditional reading takes the mystical
turn to be a rejection of philosophy: al-Ghazali abandoned philosophy for mysticism. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a completion of philosophy: al-Ghazali did not abandon philosophy; he
completed it with the mystical experience. The two readings disagree on whether al-Ghazali is a
philosopher or a mystic, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework has no mysticism, and its knowledge is reconstruction, not experience.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If al-Ghazali is a theologian, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a theological occasionalism. If
al-Ghazali is a skeptic, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a philosophical
skepticism. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of al-Ghazali, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.
450                                                                           Chapter 40. al-Ghazali


40.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With al-Ghazali. The framework shares four structural features with al-Ghazali’s
  position.

       1. The critique of necessary connection. Al-Ghazali holds that the connection between
          cause and effect is not necessary; it is a habit of the mind; the necessity is not observed.
         The framework holds that the connection between identity and manifestation is not
          necessary; it is a structural tendency; the necessity is not observed. Both hold that
          the connection is not a necessary connection, and that the necessity is not in the
          things.

       2. The limits of reason. Al-Ghazali holds that reason has limits; it cannot demonstrate
          the metaphysical claims; it cannot know God. The framework holds that reason
          has limits; it cannot know the identity completely; it can only reconstruct a pseudo-
          identity. Both hold that reason has limits, and that the recognition of the limits is
          the condition of wisdom.

       3. The priority of the revelation. Al-Ghazali holds that the revelation is the foundation;
          the philosophy is a tool; the tool is not the master. The framework holds that its
          structure is autonomous; it does not depend on any revelation; its truth is structural,
          not revealed. But the framework shares with al-Ghazali the recognition that the
          ultimate truth is not exhausted by philosophy; the philosophy is a way, not the end.

       4. The mystical turn. Al-Ghazali holds that the mystical experience is the completion
          of philosophy; the experience gives the certainty that philosophy could not give.
         The framework holds that the reconstruction is the condition of knowledge; the
          reconstruction is not the experience, but the reading of the manifestations. Both
          hold that the ultimate truth is not exhausted by the concepts, and that there is a
          dimension of the real that the concepts do not capture.



40.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With al-Ghazali. The framework diverges from al-Ghazali in four respects.

       1. The status of causality. Al-Ghazali holds that the connection between cause and
          effect is not necessary; God is the only cause; the things we call causes are only
          occasions. The framework holds that causality is a structural relation; the connection
          between cause and effect is a structural tendency; it is not a divine action. The
          framework’s causality is structural, not occasionalist.
40.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 451


       2. The status of reason. Al-Ghazali holds that reason has limits; it cannot demonstrate
         the metaphysical claims; it cannot know God. The framework holds that reason
         has limits; it cannot know the identity completely; but it can reconstruct a pseudo-
         identity with increasing adequacy. The framework’s reason is reconstructive, not
         mystical.

       3. The status of the revelation. Al-Ghazali holds that the revelation is the foundation;
         the philosophy is a tool. The framework holds that its structure is autonomous;
         it does not depend on any revelation; its truth is structural, not revealed. The
         framework’s autonomy is the rejection of the priority of the revelation.

       4. The status of the mystical experience. Al-Ghazali holds that the mystical experience
         is the completion of philosophy; the experience gives the certainty that philosophy
         could not give. The framework holds that the mystical experience is not a category
         of the framework; its knowledge is reconstruction, not experience; its certainty is
         structural, not mystical. The framework is a metaphysics without mysticism.




40.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   al-Ghazali’s first objection. The framework says that causality is a structural relation,
   and that the connection between cause and effect is a structural tendency. But a structural
   tendency is not a cause; it is a pattern. The world is caused by God; the world is not
   just structured; the world is created by the divine will. The framework has no God;
   the framework has no creation; the framework’s world is a world without a cause. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of causes.
   al-Ghazali’s second objection. The framework says that reason can reconstruct a
   pseudo-identity. But a reconstruction is not knowledge; it is a conjecture; it is a hypothesis.
   The only certainty is the mystical experience; the only knowledge is the revelation. The
   framework’s reconstruction is a knowledge without certainty; it is a skepticism in disguise.
   The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of doubt, not of faith.
   al-Ghazali’s third objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
   they are the creation of God. The realms are not independent; they are dependent on
   God; they are the effects of the divine will. The framework’s realms are not creations;
   they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of creation.
452                                                                        Chapter 40. al-Ghazali


40.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world has a cause, and
   it agrees that the cause is not the world. But the framework denies that the cause must
   be a divine will. The framework’s causality is a structural relation; it is the tendency
   of the identity to manifest; it is the cause of the manifestation. The cause is structural,
   not personal. The distinction is between a divine will (a personal cause) and a structural
   cause (a condition of possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that reconstruction is not
   certainty, and it agrees that the only certainty is the mystical experience. But the framework
   denies that reconstruction is therefore skepticism. The framework’s reconstruction is fallible,
   but it is not arbitrary; it is anchored in the manifestations; it is checked by the criteria
   of adequacy; it is open to revision. The distinction is between a reconstruction (which is
   fallible but not arbitrary) and a skepticism (which denies the possibility of knowledge);
   the framework holds the first, not the second.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just levels,
   and it agrees that they are dependent on the First Determination. But the framework
   denies that the dependence is creation. The framework’s dependence is expression: the
   realms are the expressions of the First Determination, and the expression is the structure
   of the dependence. The distinction is between a creation (a bringing into being) and an
   expression (a structural relation); the framework holds the second, not the first. The
   realms are not creations; they are expressions, and the expression is a structural relation,
   not a divine act.



40.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


al-Ghazali’s cost. If al-Ghazali accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that God is the only cause. He must accept that causality is a structural relation, and that the
connection between cause and effect is a structural tendency, not a divine action. The cost is the
loss of the divine omnipotence: the world is no longer a direct creation of God; the world is an
expression of the identity; the cause is no longer a divine will, but a structural condition. He
must also give up the claim that the mystical experience is the only certainty; he must accept
that the reconstruction is a kind of knowledge, fallible but not arbitrary. The cost is the loss of
the mystical certainty.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts al-Ghazali’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the divine will, of the mystical experience, of the revelation—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
40.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                    453


causality is a structural relation, but not a divine action, and the framework leaves the divine
action to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that al-Ghazali’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. al-Ghazali
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
divine action presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity
of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the other.


40.10        The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for al-
   Ghazali’s term “God.” If one substitutes “God” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; al-Ghazali’s God is the only cause, the creator of the
   world, and it is not manifested, because it is beyond all manifestation. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; al-Ghazali’s God is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for al-Ghazali’s term “the divine ac-
   tion.” If one substitutes “the divine action” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; al-Ghazali’s
   divine action is a free act of God. The framework’s expression is structural; al-Ghazali’s
   divine action is personal. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for al-Ghazali’s term “the
   mystical experience.” If one substitutes “the mystical experience” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is
   a reading of the manifestations; al-Ghazali’s mystical experience is a direct union with
   God. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; al-Ghazali’s mystical experience is
   existential. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and al-Ghazali is resemblance:
   both hold that the connection between cause and effect is not a necessary connection,
   and they differ on whether the connection is a divine action or a structural tendency.
   Both hold that reason has limits, and they differ on whether the limits are the mystical
   experience or the reconstruction. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of al-Ghazali would be refuted by showing
   that al-Ghazali’s divine action cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and action—by showing, that is, that al-Ghazali already distinguishes
454                                                                        Chapter 40. al-Ghazali


   the structural condition from the divine action, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of al-Ghazali’s own.



40.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s causality a development of al-Ghazali’s critique of causality,
or is it a departure from al-Ghazali? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that al-Ghazali’s critique is already a structural
critique, not a theological one, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Tahafut and the Munqidh do justice to
the texts? The chapter has used the critique of the philosophers, occasionalism, the critique of
causality, the divine attributes, the relation between philosophy and theology, and the mystical
turn, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support
a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.



40.12      Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a cause and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the cause that acts, or the structure that makes possible? Is the truth the
certainty of the experience, or the fallibility of the reconstruction? What does your answer tell
you about the relation between al-Ghazali’s God and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Ibn Rushd. It states the harmony of philosophy and religion in Fasl
al-Maqal ( The Decisive Treatise) and Tahafut al-Tahafut ( The Incoherence of the Incoherence),
the defense of Aristotle against al-Ghazali, the doctrine of the twofold truth, the account of the
eternity of the world, and the theory of the intellect; it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of Ibn Rushd; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of the relation between philosophy and religion is the nearest classical
Islamic analogue to Ibn Rushd’s. The present chapter has stated al-Ghazali’s critique of the
philosophers; the next chapter states Ibn Rushd’s defense, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 41

Ibn Rushd


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Rushd
(1126–1198 CE), known in the Latin West as Averroes and in the Islamic tradition as al-Hafid
(the Grandson). It states Ibn Rushd’s defense of Aristotle against al-Ghazali, his account of
the harmony of philosophy and religion in Fasl al-Maqal (The Decisive Treatise) and al-Kashf
’an Manahij al-Adilla (The Exposition of the Methods of Proof ), his response to al-Ghazali in
Tahafut al-Tahafut (The Incoherence of the Incoherence), his account of the eternity of the
world, his theory of the intellect (the material intellect, the agent intellect, and the unity of
the intellect), and his political philosophy in Talkhis al-Siyasa (The Commentary on Plato’s
Republic); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ibn Rushd; it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the relation between
philosophy and religion is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Ibn Rushd’s; it presents the
objections that Ibn Rushd would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply;
it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “the harmony of philosophy and religion,” “the twofold truth,” “the eternity of
the world,” “the material intellect,” “the agent intellect,” or “the unity of the intellect,” these
are Ibn Rushd’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.


41.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the Qur’an. She reads the verse: “He it is who has sent down
to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear—they are the foundation of the Book—and others
that are allegorical” (Q 3:7). She asks: what does the allegorical verse mean? The literal reading
gives one meaning; the allegorical reading gives another; the two readings seem to conflict. She
asks: which reading is correct? And who has the authority to decide?
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she reads the philosophers: they say that the world is
eternal; the Qur’an says that God created the world in six days. The philosophers say that the
soul is immortal; the Qur’an says that the body will be resurrected. The two seem to conflict.
She asks: can the two be reconciled? Ibn Rushd’s answer: yes, if we distinguish three classes of
people. The multitude, who are capable only of rhetorical persuasion, should take the literal
reading. The theologians, who are capable of dialectical argument, should take the allegorical
reading. The philosophers, who are capable of demonstrative proof, should take the philosophical
reading. The three readings are not in conflict; they are three levels of one truth, accommodated
to three levels of capacity.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the verse means, or how

                                                456
41.2. The Question                                                                                457


the readings are reconciled, but what the intellect is. The philosophers say that the intellect
is one; the theologians say that each person has their own intellect. Ibn Rushd’s answer: the
material intellect is one for all human beings; the agent intellect is one for all human beings; the
individual intellect is not a substance, but a disposition. The unity of the intellect is what makes
knowledge possible; the plurality of individuals is what makes knowledge actual.
   The scene is Ibn Rushd’s image, in the Fasl al-Maqal and in the Tahafut al-Tahafut, of the
structure of reality. The verse is the revelation; the reading is the interpretation; the intellect is
the knower. The scene poses the question that Ibn Rushd was the first to pose in its full form
in the Islamic tradition. What is the relation between philosophy and religion? Can the two
be reconciled? And what is the nature of the intellect? The present chapter states Ibn Rushd’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.



41.2         The Question

The previous chapter stated al-Ghazali’s position: the critique of the philosophers, occasionalism,
the critique of causality, the divine attributes, the relation between philosophy and theology,
and the mystical turn. Al-Ghazali is the great critic of the philosophers; he attacks their claims;
he defends the Qur’anic doctrine; he turns to mysticism. Ibn Rushd is his greatest opponent;
he defends Aristotle against al-Ghazali; he defends the harmony of philosophy and religion; he
defends the demonstrative method. The present chapter states Ibn Rushd’s defense, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Ibn Rushd was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ibn Rushd hold? The chapter states the harmony of
philosophy and religion, the twofold truth, the defense of Aristotle against al-Ghazali, the eternity
of the world, the theory of the intellect, and the political philosophy, with reference to the
treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ibn Rushd converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Ibn Rushd would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ibn
Rushd? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.



41.3         The Position
458                                                                          Chapter 41. Ibn Rushd


41.3.1      The Harmony of Philosophy and Religion

Ibn Rushd’s account of the harmony of philosophy and religion is stated in Fasl al-Maqal (The
Decisive Treatise, c. 1179) and in al-Kashf ’an Manahij al-Adilla (The Exposition of the Methods of
Proof ). The account is a defense of philosophy against the charge of unbelief; it is a reconciliation
of philosophy and religion; it is a theory of the three classes of people.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the truth is one. The truth is one; the truth is not many; the truth is not
divided. Philosophy and religion both lead to the truth; both are ways of knowing the truth;
both are legitimate. The truth that the philosopher demonstrates is the same truth that the
prophet reveals; the two are not in conflict.


Second feature: the three classes of people. The people are divided into three classes:
the multitude, who are capable only of rhetorical persuasion; the theologians, who are capable of
dialectical argument; and the philosophers, who are capable of demonstrative proof. The three
classes have three ways of knowing the truth; the three ways are not in conflict; they are three
levels of one truth, accommodated to three levels of capacity.


Third feature: the allegorical interpretation. The Qur’an contains verses that are clear
and verses that are allegorical. The clear verses are the foundation of the Book; the allegorical
verses require interpretation. The multitude should take the literal reading; the theologians
should take the allegorical reading; the philosophers should take the philosophical reading. The
allegorical interpretation is not a denial of the literal reading; it is a deepening of it.
      The account is the foundation of Ibn Rushd’s philosophy. It is the defense of philosophy; it is
the reconciliation of philosophy and religion; it is the theory of the three classes of people.

   From the Tradition

   “The truth does not contradict the truth. The truth that the philosopher demonstrates is
   the same truth that the prophet reveals; the two are not in conflict. The three classes
   of people have three ways of knowing the same truth.” (Ibn Rushd, Fasl al-Maqal, trans.
   after Hourani, adapted)



41.3.2      The Twofold Truth

Ibn Rushd’s doctrine of the twofold truth is a development of his account of the harmony of
philosophy and religion. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the two truths. There are two truths: the truth of philosophy and the truth
of religion. The two truths are not in conflict; they are two aspects of one truth. The truth of
philosophy is the truth of demonstration; the truth of religion is the truth of revelation. The two
are different in method, not in content.
41.3. The Position                                                                                 459


Second feature: the two methods. The two methods are different: the method of philosophy
is demonstration; the method of religion is persuasion. The philosopher demonstrates; the prophet
persuades. The two methods are not in conflict; they are two ways of communicating the same
truth.

Third feature: the two audiences. The two audiences are different: the audience of
philosophy is the elite; the audience of religion is the multitude. The elite can grasp the
demonstration; the multitude can grasp only the persuasion. The two audiences are not in
conflict; they are two levels of capacity.
   The doctrine is the key to Ibn Rushd’s reconciliation. It is the acceptance of the two truths;
it is the acceptance of the two methods; it is the acceptance of the two audiences. The doctrine
is not a relativism; it is a hierarchy of levels of knowledge.


41.3.3    The Defense of Aristotle Against al-Ghazali
Ibn Rushd’s defense of Aristotle against al-Ghazali is stated in Tahafut al-Tahafut (The Incoher-
ence of the Incoherence, c. 1180). The defense is a point-by-point response to al-Ghazali’s Tahafut
al-Falasifa; it is a defense of the Aristotelian philosophy; it is a defense of the demonstrative
method.
   The defense has three features.

First feature: the response to occasionalism. Al-Ghazali had argued that the connection
between cause and effect is not necessary; God is the only cause. Ibn Rushd responds: the
connection is necessary; the cause is a real cause; the effect is a real effect. The necessity is not a
logical necessity; it is a natural necessity; it is the necessity of the natures of things.

Second feature: the response to the critique of causality. Al-Ghazali had argued that
the connection between cause and effect is not observed; it is a habit of the mind. Ibn Rushd
responds: the connection is not observed, but it is known by demonstration; the demonstration
is not a habit; it is a proof. The proof is based on the natures of things; it is not based on the
observation of constant conjunction.

Third feature: the response to the critique of the philosophers. Al-Ghazali had argued
that the philosophers’ claims are not demonstrated; they are conjectures. Ibn Rushd responds:
the philosophers’ claims are demonstrated; the demonstrations are valid; the claims are not
conjectures. The demonstrations are not the arguments of the mutakallimun; they are the
demonstrations of Aristotle; they are the demonstrations of the philosophers.
   The defense is the key to Ibn Rushd’s philosophy. It is the defense of Aristotle; it is the
defense of the demonstrative method; it is the defense of the philosophical tradition.


41.3.4    The Eternity of the World
Ibn Rushd’s account of the eternity of the world is stated in Tahafut al-Tahafut and in al-Kashf.
The account is a middle path between the philosophers’ claim of eternity and the theologians’
460                                                                          Chapter 41. Ibn Rushd


claim of creation in time.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the world is eternal in its matter. The world is eternal in its matter; the
matter is not created in time; it is the eternal substrate of the changes. The world is not created
ex nihilo; it is the eternal matter, formed by the eternal forms.


Second feature: the world is created in its form. The world is created in its form; the
forms are not eternal; they are brought into being by the agent intellect. The world is created in
its form, but eternal in its matter.


Third feature: the reconciliation. The reconciliation is the recognition that the world is
both eternal and created: eternal in its matter, created in its form. The philosophers’ claim is
true of the matter; the theologians’ claim is true of the form. The two claims are not in conflict;
they are two aspects of one truth.
      The account is the key to Ibn Rushd’s cosmology. It is the reconciliation of the philosophers
and the theologians; it is the middle path between the eternity and the creation; it is the
affirmation of the eternity of matter and the createdness of form.


41.3.5      The Theory of the Intellect

Ibn Rushd’s theory of the intellect is stated in Talkhis al-Nafs (The Commentary on the Soul)
and in Tahafut al-Tahafut. The theory is one of the most influential in the history of philosophy;
it is the foundation of the Latin Averroism.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: the material intellect. The material intellect (al-’aql al-hayulani) is the
capacity to receive the intelligibles; it is the pure potentiality; it is the same for all human beings.
The material intellect is one; it is not divided among individuals; it is the common capacity of
the species.


Second feature: the agent intellect. The agent intellect (al-’aql al-fa”al) is the active
principle that actualizes the intelligibles; it is the lowest of the ten separate intellects; it is the
same for all human beings. The agent intellect is one; it is not divided among individuals; it is
the common light of the species.


Third feature: the unity of the intellect. The material intellect and the agent intellect are
one for all human beings. The individual intellect is not a substance; it is a disposition; it is
the individual’s capacity to receive the intelligibles. The unity of the intellect is what makes
knowledge possible; the plurality of individuals is what makes knowledge actual. The immortality
of the intellect is not the immortality of the individual; it is the immortality of the species.
      The theory is the key to Ibn Rushd’s psychology. It is the unity of the intellect; it is the
plurality of individuals; it is the immortality of the species. The theory is the foundation of the
41.4. Internal Disputes                                                                               461


Latin Averroism; it is the subject of the controversy with Aquinas; it is the alternative to the
Avicennian theory of the individual intellect.

41.3.6     The Political Philosophy
Ibn Rushd’s political philosophy is stated in Talkhis al-Siyasa (The Commentary on Plato’s
Republic). The political philosophy is a development of Plato’s Republic; it is the application of
the philosophical theory to the political order.
    The political philosophy has three features.

First feature: the virtuous city. The virtuous city is the city whose inhabitants are ordered
toward the highest perfection, which is the knowledge of God and of the hierarchy of being. The
virtuous city is the city of the philosophers; it is the city of the elite; it is the city of the virtuous.

Second feature: the ruler. The ruler is the philosopher- king; he is the one who has attained
the highest level of cognition; he is the one who governs by wisdom. The ruler is the mediator
between the divine and the human; he is the image of the agent intellect; he is the image of the
divine law.

Third feature: the law. The law is the foundation of the city; it is the law that orders the
city toward the highest perfection. The law is not the positive law of the multitude; it is the
natural law of the philosophers; it is the law of the virtuous city.
    The political philosophy is the key to Ibn Rushd’s practical philosophy. It is the continuation
of Plato; it is the application of the theory; it is the foundation of the virtuous city.


41.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Ibn Rushd is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the twofold truth. The traditional reading takes the twofold
truth to be a relativism: the truth of philosophy and the truth of religion are two different
truths; the two are not in conflict because they are different. A revisionary reading takes it to be
a hierarchy: the truth of philosophy and the truth of religion are two levels of one truth; the
two are not in conflict because they are the same truth at different levels. The two readings
disagree on whether Ibn Rushd is a relativist or a hierarchist, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s truth is one, not relative.

Second dispute: the status of the eternity of the world. The traditional reading takes
Ibn Rushd’s account to be a defense of the eternity of the world: the world is eternal in its
matter; the matter is not created. A revisionary reading takes it to be a reconciliation: the world
is both eternal and created; eternal in its matter, created in its form. The two readings disagree
on whether Ibn Rushd is an Aristotelian or a reconciler, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s expression is neither eternal nor created; it is a
structural tendency.
462                                                                        Chapter 41. Ibn Rushd


Third dispute: the status of the unity of the intellect. The traditional reading takes
Ibn Rushd’s account to be a denial of individual immortality: the material intellect is one; the
individual intellect is a disposition; the individual is not immortal. A revisionary reading takes it
to be a theory of knowledge: the unity of the intellect is what makes knowledge possible; the
plurality of individuals is what makes knowledge actual; the immortality of the species is the
immortality of knowledge. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Rushd is a materialist or a
rationalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
identity is conserved, but its manifestations are not immortal.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ibn Rushd is a hierarchist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a hierarchical rationalism. If
Ibn Rushd is a relativist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a relativistic
rationalism. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts of Ibn Rushd,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.


41.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Ibn Rushd. The framework shares four structural features with Ibn Rushd’s
   position.

        1. The harmony of philosophy and religion. Ibn Rushd holds that philosophy and
           religion are not in conflict; they are two ways of knowing the same truth. The
           framework holds that its structure is compatible with any inquiry that does not
           contradict it; the truth is one; the truth is not divided. Both hold that truth is one,
           and that different ways of knowing it must be compatible.

        2. The levels of knowledge. Ibn Rushd holds that there are three levels of knowledge: the
           rhetorical, the dialectical, and the demonstrative. The framework holds that there
           are different levels of reconstruction: the partial, the approximate, and the adequate.
           Both hold that knowledge is stratified, and that the strata are accommodated to the
           capacity of the knower.

        3. The defense of the demonstrative method. Ibn Rushd holds that the demonstrative
           method is the highest method; it is the method of the philosophers; it is the method
           of the elite. The framework holds that the structural method is the highest method;
           it is the method of the framework; it is the method of the structural reconstruction.
           Both hold that there is a highest method, and that the highest method is the method
           of the elite.

        4. The unity of the intellect. Ibn Rushd holds that the material intellect and the agent
           intellect are one for all human beings; the unity of the intellect is what makes
           knowledge possible. The framework holds that the light is the conveyor of effect
41.6. Points of Divergence                                                                           463


          between identity and manifestation; the unity of the light is what makes relation
          possible. Both hold that there is a unity that makes knowledge possible, and that
          the unity is not the plurality of individuals.



41.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Ibn Rushd. The framework diverges from Ibn Rushd in four respects.

       1. The status of the twofold truth. Ibn Rushd holds that there are two truths: the truth
          of philosophy and the truth of religion. The framework holds that there is one truth:
          the structural truth; the truth of philosophy and the truth of religion are two ways
          of knowing the same structural truth. The framework’s truth is one, not twofold.

       2. The status of the eternity of the world. Ibn Rushd holds that the world is eternal
          in its matter and created in its form. The framework holds that the expression is
          a structural tendency; it is neither eternal nor created; it is the enactment of the
          identity. The framework’s world is not eternal in its matter; it is the expression of
          the identity; it is the manifestation of the structure.

       3. The status of the intellect. Ibn Rushd holds that the material intellect and the agent
          intellect are one for all human beings. The framework holds that the light is a
          structural conveyor; it is not an intellect; it is the condition of possibility of relation.
         The framework’s light is not an intellect; it is a structure.

       4. The status of the political philosophy. Ibn Rushd holds that the virtuous city is the
          city of the philosophers; it is the city of the elite; it is the city of the virtuous. The
          framework has no political philosophy; its subject is the structure of identity and
          manifestation; it leaves the political question to a separate inquiry. The framework
          is a metaphysics without a political philosophy.



41.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ibn Rushd’s first objection. The framework says that the identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not a substance; it is a pattern. The world is composed of substances; the
   world is not just structured; the world is a plurality of substances. The framework has
   no substances; the framework has no plurality of substances; the framework’s world is a
   world without substances. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of
   substances.
464                                                                         Chapter 41. Ibn Rushd


   Ibn Rushd’s second objection. The framework says that there is one truth: the
   structural truth. But there are two truths: the truth of philosophy and the truth of
   religion. The truth of philosophy is the truth of demonstration; the truth of religion is
   the truth of revelation. The two truths are not the same; they are two levels of one truth.
   The framework’s one truth is a reduction of the two truths; it is a denial of the plurality
   of truths. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of one truth, not of two truths.
   Ibn Rushd’s third objection. The framework says that the light is a structural conveyor;
   it is not an intellect. But the light is the agent intellect; it is the active principle that
   actualizes the intelligibles; it is the same for all human beings. The framework’s light is
   not an intellect; it is a structure. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of structures,
   not of intellects.



41.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is composed of
   substances, and it agrees that the world is a plurality. But the framework denies that the
   substances are the ultimate reality. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source; it is not a substance; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one
   thing. The distinction is between a substance (a thing among things) and an identity (a
   structural condition); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework
   does not deny the plurality of substances; it denies that the plurality is the ultimate reality.
   The ultimate reality is the structure of identity and manifestation.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that there are two truths: the
   truth of philosophy and the truth of religion. But the framework denies that the two
   truths are not the same. The two truths are two ways of knowing the same structural
   truth; they are not two different truths. The distinction is between a plurality of truths
   (which the framework rejects) and a plurality of ways of knowing one truth (which the
   framework affirms). The framework’s one truth is not a reduction of the two truths; it is
   the recognition that the two truths are the same truth at different levels.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that there is an active principle
   that actualizes the intelligibles, and it agrees that the principle is the same for all human
   beings. But the framework denies that the principle must be an intellect. The framework’s
   light is the structural conveyor of effect; it is the condition of possibility of relation; it
   is not an intellect. The distinction is between an intellect (a substance) and a light (a
   structure); the framework holds the second, not the first. The light is not an intellect; it
   is a structure, and the structure is the condition of knowledge, not its source.



41.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
41.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     465


Ibn Rushd’s cost. If Ibn Rushd accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that there are two truths. He must accept that there is one truth: the structural truth; the truth
of philosophy and the truth of religion are two ways of knowing the same structural truth. The
cost is the loss of the twofold truth: the truth is no longer twofold; it is one; the two truths are
two ways of knowing one truth. He must also give up the claim that the world is eternal in its
matter; he must accept that the world is an expression of the identity; it is neither eternal nor
created; it is the manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the eternity of matter:
the world is no longer eternal; the world is an expression.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ibn Rushd’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the substance, of the twofold truth, of the agent intellect—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a substance, and the framework leaves the
substance to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ibn Rushd’s substance is
not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Ibn
Rushd must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition
that the substance presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.



41.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ibn
   Rushd’s term “substance.” If one substitutes “substance” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Ibn Rushd’s substance is the ultimate subject
   of predication, and it is not manifested, because it is the substrate. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; Ibn Rushd’s substance is multiple. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Ibn Rushd’s term “the eternity
   of the world.” If one substitutes “the eternity of the world” for “expression” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural
   tendency; Ibn Rushd’s eternity of the world is the eternity of matter. The framework’s
   expression is structural; Ibn Rushd’s eternity is material. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
466                                                                      Chapter 41. Ibn Rushd


   The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for Ibn Rushd’s term “the agent intellect.”
   If one substitutes “the agent intellect” for “light” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s light is a structural conveyor; Ibn Rushd’s agent
   intellect is a separate intellect. The framework’s light is structural; Ibn Rushd’s agent
   intellect is substantial. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ibn Rushd is resemblance:
   both hold that philosophy and religion are not in conflict, and they differ on whether the
   truth is twofold or one. Both hold that there is a unity that makes knowledge possible, and
   they differ on whether the unity is an intellect or a light. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Ibn Rushd would
   be refuted by showing that Ibn Rushd’s twofold truth cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structure and truth—by showing, that is, that Ibn
   Rushd already distinguishes the structural condition from the twofold truth, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of Ibn Rushd’s own.




41.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ibn Rushd’s substance, or is it a
departure from Ibn Rushd? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ibn Rushd’s substance is already a structural condition,
not a substrate, has a question the chapter leaves open.



Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.



Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Fasl al-Maqal, the Tahafut al-Tahafut,
and the Talkhis al-Nafs do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the harmony of philosophy
and religion, the twofold truth, the defense of Aristotle, the eternity of the world, the theory of
the intellect, and the political philosophy, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A
reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.
