A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a philosophy and a religion—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the philosophy that demonstrates, or the religion that persuades? Is the
truth the twofold truth of the two, or the one truth of the structure? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between Ibn Rushd’s twofold truth and the framework’s one truth?

The next chapter turns to the Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya. It states the five principles of the
Mutazila (divine unity, divine justice, the promise and the threat, the intermediate position, the
commanding of right and the forbidding of wrong), the doctrine of the created Qur’an, the doctrine
of free will, and the Ash’arite response: the doctrine of the divine attributes, the doctrine of
acquisition ( kasb), the doctrine of the uncreated Qur’an, and the doctrine of divine determinism;
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the two schools; and it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the divine attributes
and of free will is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated
Ibn Rushd’s defense of the philosophers; the next chapter states the theological schools’ response,
and the framework’s dialogue with them.
Chapter 42

The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with the two great theological schools of classical Islam: the
Mu’tazila, the rationalist school that flourished in Basra and Baghdad from the eighth to the
eleventh century, and the Ash’ariyya, the school founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash’ari (873–935
CE) that became the dominant Sunni theology. It states the five principles of the Mu’tazila
(divine unity, divine justice, the promise and the threat, the intermediate position, and the
commanding of right and forbidding of wrong), their doctrine of the created Qur’an, their doctrine
of free will, and their account of the divine attributes; and it states the Ash’arite response: the
doctrine of the divine attributes, the doctrine of acquisition (kasb), the doctrine of the uncreated
Qur’an, the doctrine of divine determinism, and the doctrine of occasionalism, with reference
to the Kitab al-Usul al-Khamsa of Abd al-Jabbar, the Maqalat al-Islamiyyin of al-Ash’ari, the
al-Ibanah of al-Ash’ari, the Kitab al-Luma’ of al-Ash’ari, and the al-Mawaqif of al-Iji and the
Sharh al-Mawaqif of al-Jurjani; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
the two schools; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of the divine attributes and of free will is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to theirs;
it presents the objections that the two schools would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “divine unity,” “divine justice,” “acquisition,” “the created
Qur’an,” “the divine attributes,” or “free will,” these are the terms of the two schools, and their
sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


42.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the Qur’an. She reads the verse: “God does not burden a soul
beyond its capacity” (Q 2:286). She reads another verse: “God guides whom He wills, and He
leads astray whom He wills” (Q 14:4). The two verses seem to conflict: the first suggests that
the human being has a capacity and is responsible for what is within that capacity; the second
suggests that God is the one who guides and leads astray, and that the human being has no
independent power. She asks: which verse is to be taken literally? Which is to be interpreted?
And what is the relation between divine power and human responsibility?
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she reads the philosophers: they say that God is
absolutely one; God has no attributes distinct from the essence; God does not know particulars.
The Qur’an says that God is knowing, powerful, living, willing, hearing, seeing, speaking. The
two seem to conflict. She asks: are the divine attributes real? Are they distinct from the essence?
Are they eternal? The Mu’tazila say: the attributes are identical with the essence; the Qur’an is
created; the human being is free. The Ash’ariyya say: the attributes are real and eternal; the

                                                468
42.2. The Question                                                                              469


Qur’an is uncreated; the human being acquires (kasb) what God creates.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the attributes are, or
how the Qur’an is created, but what the human being is. Is the human being the author of their
actions? Or is God the author of all actions, and the human being only the locus of acquisition?
The Mu’tazila say: the human being is the author of their actions; God is just, and God does not
will evil. The Ash’ariyya say: God is the creator of all actions, including evil; the human being
acquires the action, but does not create it; God is just, but the divine justice is not measured by
human standards.
   The scene is the image of the two schools, in the Kitab al-Usul al-Khamsa and in the al-Ibanah,
of the structure of reality. The verse is the revelation; the reading is the interpretation; the
human being is the actor. The scene poses the question that the two schools were the first to
pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What is the relation between divine power and
human responsibility? What is the status of the divine attributes? And what is the relation
between reason and revelation? The present chapter states the two schools’ answers, and the
framework’s dialogue with them.


42.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated Ibn Rushd’s position: the harmony of philosophy and religion, the
twofold truth, the defense of Aristotle against al-Ghazali, the eternity of the world, the theory of
the intellect, and the political philosophy. Ibn Rushd is the great defender of the philosophers;
he defends the demonstrative method; he defends the harmony of philosophy and religion. The
Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya are the two great theological schools; they are not philosophers in
the strict sense; they are theologians (mutakallimun) who use the tools of philosophy to defend
the faith. The present chapter states their positions, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
   The question is not whether the Mu’tazila or the Ash’ariyya were right. The question is what
they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The
question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did the Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya hold? The chapter
states the five principles of the Mu’tazila, their doctrine of the created Qur’an, their doctrine of
free will, and their account of the divine attributes; and it states the Ash’arite response: the
doctrine of the divine attributes, the doctrine of acquisition (kasb), the doctrine of the uncreated
Qur’an, the doctrine of divine determinism, and the doctrine of occasionalism.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two schools converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two schools would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
schools? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.
470                                                 Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


42.3        The Position of the Mu’tazila

42.3.1      The Five Principles

The Mu’tazila’s five principles are stated in the Kitab al-Usul al-Khamsa of Abd al-Jabbar
(d. 1025). The five principles are the foundation of the Mu’tazilite theology; they are the mark
of the Mu’tazilite identity; they are the five doctrines that distinguish the Mu’tazila from the
other schools.
      The five principles are:


First principle: divine unity (al-tawhid). God is one; God has no partner; God has no
multiplicity; God has no attributes distinct from the essence. The divine attributes (knowledge,
power, life, will, hearing, sight, speech) are identical with the essence; they are not added to the
essence; they are not eternal in themselves. The denial of the distinctness of the attributes is the
foundation of the Mu’tazilite theology.


Second principle: divine justice (al-’adl). God is just; God does not will evil; God does
not command evil; God does not punish the innocent. The human being is the author of their
actions; the human being is free; the human being is responsible. The divine justice requires
that the human being be free, because a just God would not punish a being that has no power
over its actions.


Third principle: the promise and the threat (al-wa’d wa-al-wa’id). God has promised
reward for the obedient and threat of punishment for the disobedient. The promise and the
threat are real; they are not empty; they are the foundation of the moral order. The human
being who obeys will be rewarded; the human being who disobeys will be punished; the divine
justice requires that the promise and the threat be fulfilled.


Fourth principle: the intermediate position (al-manzila bayna al-manzilatayn). The
grave sinner (murtakib al-kabira) is neither a believer nor an unbeliever; they are in an intermediate
position. The Mu’tazila distinguish themselves from the Kharijites, who consider the grave sinner
an unbeliever, and from the Murji’a, who consider the grave sinner a believer. The intermediate
position is the mark of the Mu’tazilite moderation.


Fifth principle: the commanding of right and the forbidding of wrong (al-amr
bi-al-ma’ruf wa-al-nahy ’an al-munkar). The Muslim is obligated to command the right
and to forbid the wrong; the obligation is not merely individual; it is social; it is political. The
Mu’tazila are the advocates of the moral activism; they are the critics of the unjust ruler; they
are the defenders of the moral order.
      The five principles are the foundation of the Mu’tazilite theology. They are the five doctrines
that distinguish the Mu’tazila from the other schools; they are the five commitments that define
the Mu’tazilite identity.
42.3. The Position of the Mu’tazila                                                            471


   From the Tradition

   “The five principles are the foundation of our doctrine: divine unity, divine justice, the
   promise and the threat, the intermediate position, and the commanding of right and
   forbidding of wrong. Whoever holds these five is a Mu’tazilite.” (Abd al-Jabbar, Kitab
   al-Usul al-Khamsa, trans. after Martin et al., adapted)


42.3.2     The Created Qur’an

The Mu’tazila’s doctrine of the created Qur’an is a consequence of their doctrine of divine unity.
The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the Qur’an is created. The Qur’an is the word of God; it is created; it is
not eternal. If the Qur’an were eternal, it would be a second eternal beside God; it would be a
multiplicity in God; it would contradict the divine unity.


Second feature: the word of God is created. The word of God is an attribute of action,
not an attribute of essence; it is created, not eternal. The word of God is the expression of the
divine will; it is not the divine essence; it is not eternal.


Third feature: the recitation is created. The recitation of the Qur’an is created; the ink
is created; the paper is created; the letters are created. The Qur’an that we recite is the created
word; the divine word is the attribute of action; the two are not the same.
   The doctrine is the mark of the Mu’tazilite theology. It is the denial of the eternity of the
Qur’an; it is the affirmation of the divine unity; it is the source of the controversy with the
traditionalists.


42.3.3     Free Will

The Mu’tazila’s doctrine of free will is a consequence of their doctrine of divine justice. The
doctrine has three features.


First feature: the human being is free. The human being is free; the human being is the
author of their actions; the human being is responsible. The freedom is not a gift of God; it is a
constitutive feature of the human being; it is what makes the human being a moral agent.


Second feature: God does not will evil. God does not will evil; God does not command
evil; God does not create evil. Evil is the act of the human being; it is not the act of God. The
divine justice requires that God not will evil, because a just God would not will evil.


Third feature: the human being is responsible. The human being is responsible for
their actions; the human being will be rewarded for their good actions; the human being will be
punished for their evil actions. The responsibility is the foundation of the moral order; it is the
foundation of the divine justice.
472                                                 Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


      The doctrine is the mark of the Mu’tazilite ethics. It is the affirmation of the human freedom;
it is the affirmation of the divine justice; it is the source of the controversy with the Ash’ariyya.



42.4        The Position of the Ash’ariyya

42.4.1       The Divine Attributes

The Ash’ariyya’s doctrine of the divine attributes is stated in al-Ibanah and in Kitab al-Luma’ of
al-Ash’ari. The doctrine is a middle path between the Mu’tazilite denial of the attributes and
the traditionalist affirmation of the attributes.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the attributes are real. The divine attributes (knowledge, power, life, will,
hearing, sight, speech) are real; they are not identical with the essence; they are not the essence;
they are not the creatures. The attributes are eternal; they are not created; they are not
accidents.


Second feature: the attributes are not the essence. The attributes are not the essence;
they are not identical with the essence; they are added to the essence. The distinction is real;
the attributes are real; the essence is real; the two are not the same.


Third feature: the attributes are not the creatures. The attributes are not the creatures;
they are not created; they are not the same as the human attributes. The divine knowledge is
not the human knowledge; the divine power is not the human power; the divine speech is not the
human speech. The two are not the same; the two are not even analogous.
      The doctrine is the mark of the Ash’arite theology. It is the affirmation of the reality of the
attributes; it is the denial of the identity of the attributes with the essence; it is the source of
the controversy with the Mu’tazila.

   From the Tradition

   “The attributes are real; they are eternal; they are not the essence; they are not the
   creatures. The knowledge of God is not the knowledge of the human being; the power of
   God is not the power of the human being.” (al-Ash’ari, al-Ibanah, trans. after McCarthy,
   adapted)



42.4.2       Acquisition (Kasb)

The Ash’ariyya’s doctrine of acquisition (kasb) is stated in Kitab al-Luma’ and in the later
Ash’arite manuals. The doctrine is a middle path between the Mu’tazilite affirmation of free will
and the Jabrite denial of free will.
      The doctrine has three features.
42.4. The Position of the Ash’ariyya                                                            473


First feature: God creates all actions. God creates all actions; the human being does
not create their actions; the human being acquires (yaksib) the actions that God creates. The
creation is the act of God; the acquisition is the act of the human being.


Second feature: the human being acquires. The human being acquires the action; the
acquisition is real; it is not a metaphor. The human being is responsible for the action; the
human being will be rewarded or punished for the action.


Third feature: the acquisition is not creation. The acquisition is not the creation; the
human being does not create the action; the human being only acquires it. The distinction is
between the creation (the act of God) and the acquisition (the act of the human being); the two
are not the same.
   The doctrine is the mark of the Ash’arite ethics. It is the affirmation of the divine omnipotence;
it is the affirmation of the human responsibility; it is the source of the controversy with the
Mu’tazila.


42.4.3    The Uncreated Qur’an
The Ash’ariyya’s doctrine of the uncreated Qur’an is a consequence of their doctrine of the divine
attributes. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the Qur’an is uncreated. The Qur’an is the word of God; it is uncreated; it
is eternal. If the Qur’an were created, it would be a creature; it would not be the word of God;
it would not be eternal.


Second feature: the word of God is an attribute of essence. The word of God is an
attribute of essence, not an attribute of action; it is eternal, not created. The word of God is the
divine speech; it is the divine attribute; it is eternal.


Third feature: the recitation is created. The recitation of the Qur’an is created; the ink
is created; the paper is created; the letters are created. The Qur’an that we recite is the created
recitation; the divine word is the uncreated attribute; the two are not the same.
   The doctrine is the mark of the Ash’arite theology. It is the affirmation of the eternity of
the Qur’an; it is the affirmation of the reality of the divine attribute; it is the source of the
controversy with the Mu’tazila.


42.4.4    Divine Determinism
The Ash’ariyya’s doctrine of divine determinism is a consequence of their doctrine of divine
omnipotence. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: God wills all things. God wills all things; God wills the good and the evil;
God wills the obedience and the disobedience. The divine will is universal; it is not limited; it is
not restricted.
474                                                Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


Second feature: God creates all things. God creates all things; God creates the good and
the evil; God creates the obedience and the disobedience. The divine creation is universal; it is
not limited; it is not restricted.


Third feature: the human being acquires. The human being acquires the action; the
acquisition is real; the human being is responsible. The divine determinism is not a denial of the
human responsibility; it is the affirmation of the divine omnipotence and the human acquisition.
      The doctrine is the mark of the Ash’arite theology. It is the affirmation of the divine
omnipotence; it is the affirmation of the human responsibility; it is the source of the controversy
with the Mu’tazila.


42.4.5      Occasionalism

The Ash’ariyya’s doctrine of occasionalism is a consequence of their doctrine of divine omnipotence.
The doctrine has three features.


First feature: God is the only cause. God is the only cause; the things we call causes are
only occasions; they are not real causes. The fire does not burn; God creates the burning at the
moment the fire touches the cotton.


Second feature: the connection is not necessary. The connection between cause and
effect is not necessary; it is a habit of the mind; it is not a real connection. The necessity is not
in the things; it is in the divine will.


Third feature: the possibility of miracles. If God is the only cause, then miracles are
possible: God can create the burning without the fire; God can create the fire without the
burning. The possibility of miracles is the consequence of occasionalism.
      The doctrine is the mark of the Ash’arite philosophy of nature. It is the affirmation of the
divine omnipotence; it is the denial of the natural causality; it is the source of the controversy
with the philosophers.


42.5       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of the Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya is disputed, and the disputes matter for
the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the divine attributes. The traditional reading takes the
Mu’tazilite denial of the distinctness of the attributes to be a radical divine simplicity: God has
no attributes distinct from the essence. A revisionary reading takes it to be a linguistic thesis:
the attributes are not distinct in reality, but they are distinct in language; the distinction is only
in our way of speaking. The two readings disagree on whether the Mu’tazila are simplists or
linguistic philosophers, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a God with attributes.
42.6. Points of Convergence                                                                        475


Second dispute: the status of acquisition. The traditional reading takes the Ash’arite
acquisition to be a theological doctrine: God creates all actions; the human being acquires them.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophical doctrine: the acquisition is a real relation
between the human being and the action; it is not a mere metaphor. The two readings disagree
on whether the Ash’ariyya are determinists or compatibilists, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s freedom is structural, not theological.


Third dispute: the status of occasionalism. The traditional reading takes the Ash’arite
occasionalism to be a metaphysical doctrine: God is the only cause; the things we call causes
are only occasions. A revisionary reading takes it to be a theological doctrine: the doctrine is
not a metaphysics; it is a confession of the divine omnipotence. The two readings disagree on
whether the Ash’ariyya are metaphysicians or theologians, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s causality is a structural relation, not a divine
action.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the Mu’tazila are simplists, the framework’s
dialogue with them is a dialogue between a structural realism and a radical simplism. If the
Ash’ariyya are determinists, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
theological determinism. The framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to the
texts, but it does not rest its case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.



42.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the Mu’tazila. The framework shares three structural features with the Mu’tazilite
   position.

       1. The priority of unity. The Mu’tazila hold that God is one; God has no multiplicity;
          God has no attributes distinct from the essence. The framework holds that the First
          Determination is the realm of pure unity; multiplicity is derived from unity. Both
          hold that unity is prior to multiplicity, and that multiplicity is derived from unity.

       2. The reality of the human responsibility. The Mu’tazila hold that the human being is
          free; the human being is the author of their actions; the human being is responsible.
          The framework holds that the identity is enacted by one source; the source is
          responsible for its manifestations. Both hold that there is a responsibility, and that
          the responsibility is real.

       3. The reality of the divine justice. The Mu’tazila hold that God is just; God does not
          will evil; God does not command evil. The framework holds that the structure is
          just; the structure is the condition of possibility of the manifestation; the structure
          is not arbitrary. Both hold that there is a justice, and that the justice is real.
476                                               Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


  With the Ash’ariyya. The framework shares three structural features with the Ash’arite
  position.

       1. The reality of the divine attributes. The Ash’ariyya hold that the divine attributes
         are real; they are not identical with the essence; they are not the creatures. The
         framework holds that the identity is real; it is not identical with the manifestation;
         it is not the appearance. Both hold that there is a reality that is not identical with
         the appearance, and that the reality is real.

       2. The reality of the divine omnipotence. The Ash’ariyya hold that God is omnipotent;
         God creates all things; God wills all things. The framework holds that the structure
         is universal; the structure is the condition of possibility of all manifestations; the
         structure is not limited. Both hold that there is a universality, and that the
         universality is real.

       3. The reality of the human acquisition. The Ash’ariyya hold that the human being
         acquires the action; the acquisition is real; the human being is responsible. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the reading
         is real; the reconstruction is responsible. Both hold that there is an acquisition, and
         that the acquisition is real.



42.7      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With the Mu’tazila. The framework diverges from the Mu’tazilite position in three
  respects.

       1. The status of God. The Mu’tazila hold that God is one; God has no attributes
         distinct from the essence; God is the creator of the world. The framework has no
         God; its First Determination is a realm of pure unity; it is not a creator; it is not a
         person; it is not a God. The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the divine justice. The Mu’tazila hold that God is just; the divine
         justice is the foundation of the moral order; the human being is responsible. The
         framework holds that the structure is just; the structure is the condition of possibility
         of the manifestation; the structure is not the foundation of a moral order. The
         framework’s justice is structural, not moral.

       3. The status of the created Qur’an. The Mu’tazila hold that the Qur’an is created; the
         word of God is created; the recitation is created. The framework has no Qur’an; its
         structure is not a revelation; its truth is structural, not revealed. The framework is
         a metaphysics without a revelation.

  With the Ash’ariyya. The framework diverges from the Ash’arite position in three
42.8. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                    477


   respects.

       1. The status of the divine attributes. The Ash’ariyya hold that the divine attributes
         are real; they are not identical with the essence; they are not the creatures. The
         framework holds that the identity is real; it is not identical with the manifestation;
         it is not the appearance. But the framework’s identity is not an attribute of God; it
         is a structural condition; the framework has no God.

       2. The status of divine determinism. The Ash’ariyya hold that God wills all things;
         God creates all things; the human being acquires. The framework holds that the
         structure is universal; the structure is the condition of possibility of all manifestations;
         the structure is not a divine will. The framework’s universality is structural, not
         personal.

       3. The status of occasionalism. The Ash’ariyya hold that God is the only cause; the
         things we call causes are only occasions. The framework holds that causality is a
         structural relation; the connection between cause and effect is a structural tendency;
         it is not a divine action. The framework’s causality is structural, not occasionalist.



42.8      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   The Mu’tazilite objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not a divine unity; it is a pattern. The world is created by God; the world is not just
   expressed from an identity; the world is created by the divine will. The framework has no
   God; the framework has no creation; the framework’s world is a world without a creator.
   The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of creation.
   The Mu’tazilite second objection. The framework says that the identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source. But the enactment is not the invariance; it is an act
   of the source, and the act is not the pattern. The framework’s identity is a pattern plus
   an act, and the act is not explained by the pattern. The framework’s identity is either
   a pattern (and then not a source) or a pattern plus an unexplained act (and then not a
   complete account).
   The Ash’arite objection. The framework says that causality is a structural relation,
   and that the connection between cause and effect is a structural tendency. But a structural
   tendency is not a cause; it is a pattern. The world is caused by God; the world is not
   just structured; the world is created by the divine will. The framework has no God;
   the framework has no creation; the framework’s world is a world without a cause. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of causes.
   The Ash’arite second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
478                                               Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


   they are the creation of God. The realms are not independent; they are dependent on
   God; they are the effects of the divine will. The framework’s realms are not creations;
   they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of creation.



42.9        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the Mu’tazilite first objection. The framework agrees that the world has a
   cause, and it agrees that the cause is not the world. But the framework denies that the
   cause must be a divine will. The framework’s expression is a structural tendency; it is the
   enactment of the identity; it is the cause of the manifestation. The cause is structural, not
   personal. The distinction is between a creator (a personal cause) and a structural cause
   (a condition of possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the Mu’tazilite second objection. The framework agrees that the enactment
   is not the invariance, and it agrees that the act is not the pattern. But the framework
   denies that the act is unexplained. The act is the tendency to express (the principle of
   expression), and the tendency is a structural feature of the identity. The act is not an
   add-on to the pattern; it is the pattern’s own tendency to manifest. The distinction is
   between an unexplained act (which the framework rejects) and a structural tendency
   (which the framework affirms).
   Reply to the Ash’arite first objection. The framework agrees that the world has a
   cause, and it agrees that the cause is not the world. But the framework denies that the
   cause must be a divine will. The framework’s causality is a structural relation; it is the
   tendency of the identity to manifest; it is the cause of the manifestation. The cause is
   structural, not personal. The distinction is between a divine will (a personal cause) and a
   structural cause (a condition of possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the Ash’arite second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
   not just levels, and it agrees that they are dependent on the First Determination. But
   the framework denies that the dependence is creation. The framework’s dependence is
   expression: the realms are the expressions of the First Determination, and the expression
   is the structure of the dependence. The distinction is between a creation (a bringing into
   being) and an expression (a structural relation); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.



42.10        The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


The Mu’tazila’s cost. If the Mu’tazila accept the framework’s reply, they must give up the
claim that God is the creator. They must accept that the source is an immanent structure, and
that the expression of the source is an enactment, not a creation. The cost is the loss of the
42.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                     479


divine unity: the source is no longer God; it is a structure. They must also give up the claim that
the human being is free in the Mu’tazilite sense; they must accept that the freedom is structural,
not theological.

The Ash’ariyya’s cost. If the Ash’ariyya accept the framework’s reply, they must give up
the claim that God is the only cause. They must accept that causality is a structural relation,
and that the connection between cause and effect is a structural tendency, not a divine action.
The cost is the loss of the divine omnipotence: the world is no longer a direct creation of God;
the world is an expression of the identity; the cause is no longer a divine will, but a structural
condition. They must also give up the claim that the divine attributes are real; they must accept
that the identity is a structural condition, not a divine attribute.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the two schools, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the divine unity, of the divine justice, of the divine attributes, of the
divine omnipotence—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness
of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a
divine attribute, and the framework leaves the divine attributes to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the Mu’tazilite God
and the Ash’arite God are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. The two schools must accept that the framework’s structure is not a
pattern; it is a structural condition that the divine attributes presuppose as their condition. The
cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they
are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.


42.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the
   Mu’tazilite term “the divine unity.” If one substitutes “the divine unity” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the Mu’tazilite divine
   unity is the oneness of God, and it is not manifested, because it is the essence. The
   framework’s identity is multiple; the Mu’tazilite divine unity is one. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for the Ash’arite term “the divine
   creation.” If one substitutes “the divine creation” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   the Ash’arite divine creation is an act of God. The framework’s expression is structural;
   the Ash’arite creation is personal. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
480                                               Chapter 42. The Mutazila and the Ash’ariyya


   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “causality” is not substitutable for the Ash’arite term “occasionalism.”
   If one substitutes “occasionalism” for “causality” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s causality is a structural relation; the Ash’arite
   occasionalism is a divine action. The framework’s causality is structural; the Ash’arite
   occasionalism is personal. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the Mu’tazila is
   resemblance: both hold that unity is prior to multiplicity, and they differ on whether the
   unity is a divine essence or a structural condition. The relation between the framework and
   the Ash’ariyya is resemblance: both hold that there is a reality that is not identical with
   the appearance, and they differ on whether the reality is a divine attribute or a structural
   condition. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of the two schools would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and attribute,
   or between structure and creation—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish
   the structural condition from the divine attribute and the divine creation, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of their own.




42.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Mu’tazilite divine unity or
the Ash’arite divine attributes, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it
is a development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the Mu’tazilite
divine unity is already a structural condition, or that the Ash’arite divine attributes are already
a structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Kitab al-Usul al-Khamsa, the al-Ibanah,
and the Kitab al-Luma’ do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the five principles,
the created Qur’an, free will, the divine attributes, acquisition, the uncreated Qur’an, divine
determinism, and occasionalism, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a unity and a multiplicity—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the unity that precedes the multiplicity, or the multiplicity that follows the
unity? Is the truth the divine justice that rewards and punishes, or the divine omnipotence that
creates and wills? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the Mu’tazilite
unity, the Ash’arite omnipotence, and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Suhrawardi. It states the philosophy of illumination ( ishraq), the
hierarchy of lights, the light of lights, the imaginal realm ( ’alam al-mithal), the critique of the
Peripatetic philosophy, and the doctrine of the master of the two orders; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Suhrawardi; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of light and of the imaginal realm is the nearest
classical Islamic analogue to Suhrawardi’s. The present chapter has stated the two theological
schools’ answers to the problem of the divine attributes and free will; the next chapter states
Suhrawardi’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 43

Suhrawardi


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Shihab al-Din Yahya ibn Habash ibn Amirak al-
Suhrawardi (1154–1191 CE), known in the Islamic tradition as Shaykh al-Ishraq (the Master of
Illumination) and in the West as Sohravardi. It states Suhrawardi’s philosophy of illumination
(ishraq), the hierarchy of lights, the Light of Lights (nur al-anwar), the imaginal realm (’alam
al-mithal), the critique of the Peripatetic philosophy, and the doctrine of the master of the two
orders, with reference to Hikmat al-Ishraq (The Philosophy of Illumination), al-Talwihat (The
Intimations), al-Mashari’ wa al-Mutarahat (The Paths and the Places of Rest), and Hayakil
al-Nur (The Temples of Light); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Suhrawardi; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of light and of the imaginal realm is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Suhrawardi’s; it
presents the objections that Suhrawardi would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “illumination,” “light,” “the Light of Lights,” “the imaginal
realm,” “the master of the two orders,” or “the critique of the Peripatetic philosophy,” these are
Suhrawardi’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.


43.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is in a dark room. She cannot see anything; the room is dark; the objects
are invisible. Then a lamp is lit; the room is illuminated; the objects become visible. The lamp
is not one of the objects; it is the source of the light that makes the objects visible. The light is
not the lamp; it is the effect of the lamp; it is the medium through which the objects are seen.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the lamp is, or how the light
illuminates the objects, but what the light itself is. The light is not a body; it is not a substance;
it is not an accident in the ordinary sense. The light is the very act of manifestation; it is
the condition under which the objects appear; it is the reality that makes the visible visible.
Suhrawardi says: the light is the fundamental reality; everything that exists is a degree of light;
the Light of Lights is the source of all lights; the material world is the lowest degree of light, the
light that is mixed with darkness.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the light is, or how it
illuminates, but what the imaginal realm is. The imaginal realm (’alam al-mithal) is the realm
of the images; it is the realm of the forms that are not material; it is the realm of the visions and
the dreams. The imaginal realm is not the material world; it is not the intelligible world; it is a
third realm, between the two, where the images have their own reality. Suhrawardi says: the

                                                 482
43.2. The Question                                                                               483


imaginal realm is the realm of the suspended images (suwar mu’allaqa); it is the realm of the
prophetic visions; it is the realm of the afterlife.
   The scene is Suhrawardi’s image, in the Hikmat al-Ishraq, of the structure of reality. The
lamp is the Light of Lights; the light is the hierarchy of lights; the objects are the material world;
the imaginal realm is the third realm between the material and the intelligible. The scene poses
the question that Suhrawardi was the first to pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What
is the fundamental reality? Is it being, or is it light? What is the imaginal realm? And what is
the relation between philosophy and mysticism? The present chapter states Suhrawardi’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.


43.2         The Question
The previous chapter stated the positions of the Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya: the five principles
of the Mu’tazila, the created Qur’an, free will, the divine attributes, acquisition, the uncreated
Qur’an, divine determinism, and occasionalism. The two schools are the great theological schools
of classical Islam; they are not philosophers in the strict sense; they are theologians who use the
tools of philosophy to defend the faith. Suhrawardi is the founder of the school of illumination;
he is the philosopher who turns from the Peripatetic philosophy to the philosophy of light; he is
the philosopher who brings together the Greek philosophy, the Islamic theology, and the ancient
Persian wisdom. The present chapter states Suhrawardi’s philosophy of illumination, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Suhrawardi was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Suhrawardi hold? The chapter states the philosophy of
illumination, the hierarchy of lights, the Light of Lights, the imaginal realm, the critique of the
Peripatetic philosophy, and the doctrine of the master of the two orders, with reference to the
treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Suhrawardi converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Suhrawardi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Suhrawardi?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


43.3         The Position

43.3.1       The Philosophy of Illumination

Suhrawardi’s philosophy of illumination (ishraq) is stated in Hikmat al-Ishraq (The Philosophy
of Illumination, 1186). The philosophy is not a system of concepts; it is a way of knowing; it is
484                                                                        Chapter 43. Suhrawardi


the knowledge that comes from the light; it is the knowledge that is present to the knower.
      The philosophy of illumination has three features.


First feature: the light is the fundamental reality. The light is the fundamental reality;
everything that exists is a degree of light; the light is the principle of all things. The light is not
a body; it is not a substance; it is not an accident; it is the very act of manifestation; it is the
condition under which the things appear.


Second feature: the knowledge is presence. The knowledge is presence; it is the presence
of the known to the knower; it is not the representation of the known; it is not the concept of
the known; it is the presence itself. The knowledge by presence (’ilm huduri) is the highest form
of knowledge; it is the knowledge that the soul has of itself; it is the knowledge that the soul has
of its Lord.


Third feature: the illumination is the method. The illumination is the method; it is the
way of knowing; it is the way of the light. The illumination is not the reasoning; it is not the
demonstration; it is the direct experience of the light; it is the presence of the light to the soul.
      The philosophy of illumination is the foundation of Suhrawardi’s philosophy. It is the
knowledge that comes from the light; it is the knowledge that is present; it is the knowledge that
is illuminated.

   From the Tradition

   “The light is the fundamental reality; everything that exists is a degree of light. The
   knowledge is presence; the knowledge by presence is the highest form of knowledge. The
   illumination is the method; it is the way of the light.” (Suhrawardi, Hikmat al-Ishraq,
   trans. after Walbridge-Ziai, adapted)



43.3.2      The Hierarchy of Lights

Suhrawardi’s hierarchy of lights is stated in Hikmat al-Ishraq and in al-Talwihat. The hierarchy is
a stratification of reality by the degree of light; it is the fundamental ontology of the philosophy
of illumination.
      The hierarchy has three features.


First feature: the Light of Lights. The Light of Lights (nur al-anwar) is the highest light;
it is the source of all lights; it is the light that is pure; it is the light that is not mixed with
darkness. The Light of Lights is God; it is the necessary being; it is the principle of all things.


Second feature: the separate lights. The separate lights are the intellects; they are the
lights that are not mixed with matter; they are the lights that are pure; they are the lights that
are the causes of the material world. The separate lights are the angels; they are the intelligences;
they are the ten intellects of the Peripatetic cosmology.
43.3. The Position                                                                               485


Third feature: the accidental lights. The accidental lights are the lights that are mixed
with matter; they are the lights that are the forms of the material things; they are the lights
that are the souls of the living beings. The accidental lights are the lowest degree of light; they
are the light that is obscured by the darkness of matter.
    The hierarchy is the key to Suhrawardi’s ontology. It is the stratification of reality by light;
it is the affirmation of the light as the fundamental reality; it is the rejection of the darkness as
the fundamental reality.


43.3.3    The Imaginal Realm
Suhrawardi’s imaginal realm (’alam al-mithal) is stated in Hikmat al-Ishraq and in al-Mashari’.
The imaginal realm is a third realm between the material world and the intelligible world; it is
the realm of the images; it is the realm of the suspended images (suwar mu’allaqa).
    The imaginal realm has three features.

First feature: the third realm. The imaginal realm is the third realm; it is not the material
world; it is not the intelligible world; it is between the two. The imaginal realm is the realm of
the forms that are not material; it is the realm of the images that have their own reality.

Second feature: the suspended images. The suspended images (suwar mu’allaqa) are the
images that are not in the material world; they are the images that are in the imaginal realm;
they are the images that are the forms of the prophetic visions. The suspended images are not
the material images; they are the imaginal images; they are the images that are the reality of the
imagination.

Third feature: the prophetic vision. The prophetic vision is the vision of the imaginal
realm; it is the vision of the suspended images; it is the vision of the forms that are not material.
The prophet sees the imaginal realm; the prophet receives the revelation in the imaginal realm;
the prophet conveys the revelation in the material world.
    The imaginal realm is the key to Suhrawardi’s epistemology. It is the realm of the prophetic
vision; it is the realm of the imagination; it is the realm of the afterlife.


43.3.4    The Critique of the Peripatetic Philosophy
Suhrawardi’s critique of the Peripatetic philosophy is stated in Hikmat al-Ishraq and in al-Talwihat.
The critique is not a rejection of the Peripatetic philosophy; it is a critique of the limits of the
Peripatetic philosophy; it is the recognition that the Peripatetic philosophy cannot grasp the
light.
    The critique has three features.

First feature: the limits of the definition. The Peripatetic philosophy defines the things
by their essences; it defines the light by its essence; it defines the light as a body or a substance.
But the light cannot be defined; the light is the fundamental reality; the light is the presence;
the light is not the essence; the light is the very act of manifestation.
486                                                                        Chapter 43. Suhrawardi


Second feature: the limits of the reasoning. The Peripatetic philosophy reasons; it
demonstrates; it argues. But the reasoning cannot grasp the light; the reasoning cannot grasp
the presence; the reasoning can only grasp the concepts. The light is known by the presence; it
is not known by the reasoning.


Third feature: the limits of the philosophy. The Peripatetic philosophy is a philosophy;
it is a system of concepts; it is a knowledge that is mediated. But the philosophy cannot replace
the illumination; the philosophy cannot replace the presence; the philosophy can only prepare
the soul for the illumination.
      The critique is the key to Suhrawardi’s philosophy. It is the recognition of the limits of the
philosophy; it is the affirmation of the illumination; it is the turn from the Peripatetic philosophy
to the philosophy of illumination.


43.3.5      The Master of the Two Orders

Suhrawardi’s doctrine of the master of the two orders is stated in Hikmat al-Ishraq. The master
of the two orders (sahib al-kiyamatan) is the one who combines the two orders: the order of the
philosophers and the order of the mystics.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the two orders. The two orders are the order of the philosophers (the
Peripatetic philosophy) and the order of the mystics (the Sufi path). The two orders are not in
conflict; they are complementary; they are two ways of knowing the same truth.


Second feature: the master of the two orders. The master of the two orders is the one
who combines the two orders; the one who knows the philosophy and the mysticism; the one
who has the demonstration and the illumination. The master of the two orders is the perfect
philosopher; the master of the two orders is the perfect mystic.


Third feature: the historical claim. The historical claim is that the two orders have always
existed; the order of the philosophers (the Greek tradition) and the order of the mystics (the
Persian tradition) are two streams of one tradition; the master of the two orders is the one who
combines them. Suhrawardi claims that he is the master of the two orders; he claims that he
has received the illumination; he claims that he has the authority to teach the philosophy of
illumination.
      The doctrine is the key to Suhrawardi’s claim. It is the claim to the authority; it is the claim
to the knowledge; it is the claim to the illumination.



43.4        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Suhrawardi is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
43.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      487


First dispute: the status of the light. The traditional reading takes the light to be the
fundamental reality: everything that exists is a degree of light; the light is the principle of all
things. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphor: the light is a figure of speech; it is
a way of speaking about the intelligibility of things. The two readings disagree on whether
Suhrawardi is a realist or a metaphorist about the light, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s light is a structural conveyor, neither a substance
nor a metaphor.

Second dispute: the status of the imaginal realm. The traditional reading takes the
imaginal realm to be a real realm: the realm of the suspended images; the realm of the prophetic
vision. A revisionary reading takes it to be a psychological state: the imaginal realm is the
imagination; it is not a realm but a faculty. The two readings disagree on whether Suhrawardi
is a realist or a psychologist about the imaginal realm, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are real levels, not psychological states.

Third dispute: the status of the illumination. The traditional reading takes the illumina-
tion to be a real experience: the presence of the light to the soul; the knowledge by presence.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a way of speaking about the intuition: the illumination
is not a real experience; it is a way of speaking about the non-discursive knowledge. The two
readings disagree on whether Suhrawardi is a mystic or a philosopher, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no mysticism; its knowledge is
reconstruction, not presence.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Suhrawardi is a realist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a realist illuminationism. If
Suhrawardi is a metaphorist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework
treats as distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of Suhrawardi,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.


43.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Suhrawardi. The framework shares four structural features with Suhrawardi’s
   position.

       1. The priority of light. Suhrawardi holds that the light is the fundamental reality;
         everything that exists is a degree of light; the light is the principle of all things.
         The framework holds that light is the condition of possibility of relation; it is the
         conveyor of effect; it is the principle of the manifestation. Both hold that light is the
         fundamental principle, and that reality is structured by light.

       2. The hierarchy of lights. Suhrawardi holds that reality is a hierarchy of lights; the
         Light of Lights is the highest; the separate lights are the middle; the accidental lights
488                                                                      Chapter 43. Suhrawardi


         are the lowest. The framework holds that reality is a hierarchy of realms; the First
         Determination is the highest; the Material Manifestation is the lowest; the seven
         realms are the levels of the hierarchy. Both hold that reality is stratified, and that
         the strata are the degrees of light.

       3. The knowledge by presence. Suhrawardi holds that the knowledge by presence is
         the highest form of knowledge; the presence is the direct experience of the light;
         the presence is the knowledge that the soul has of itself. The framework holds that
         the reconstruction is the knowledge of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the
         reading of the appearances. Both hold that knowledge is not merely conceptual, and
         that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not capture.

       4. The imaginal realm. Suhrawardi holds that the imaginal realm is a real realm; the
         realm of the suspended images; the realm of the prophetic vision. The framework
         holds that the realms are real levels; the Relational Manifestation is the realm of
         the meanings and the relations; the imaginal realm is the realm of the images that
         are the forms of the relation. Both hold that there is a realm between the material
         and the intelligible, and that the images have their own reality.



43.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Suhrawardi. The framework diverges from Suhrawardi in four respects.

       1. The status of the light. Suhrawardi holds that the light is the fundamental reality;
         the light is the principle of all things; the light is the source of all existence. The
         framework holds that light is a structural conveyor; it is the condition of possibility
         of relation; it is not the principle of existence. The framework’s light is structural,
         not substantial.

       2. The status of the knowledge by presence. Suhrawardi holds that the knowledge by
         presence is the highest form of knowledge; the presence is the direct experience of the
         light. The framework holds that the knowledge is reconstruction; it is the reading of
         the manifestations; it is not the presence. The framework’s knowledge is structural,
         not presence.

       3. The status of the imaginal realm. Suhrawardi holds that the imaginal realm is a
         real realm; the realm of the suspended images; the realm of the prophetic vision.
         The framework holds that the realms are real levels; but the imaginal realm is not
         a separate realm in the framework’s ontology; it is a dimension of the Relational
         Manifestation. The framework’s realms are seven, not eight.

       4. The status of the illumination. Suhrawardi holds that the illumination is the method;
         it is the way of the light; it is the direct experience of the light. The framework
43.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 489


         holds that the method is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations;
         it is not the illumination. The framework’s method is structural, not mystical.



43.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Suhrawardi’s first objection. The framework says that light is a structural conveyor;
   it is the condition of possibility of relation. But the light is not a structure; it is the
   fundamental reality; it is the very act of manifestation. The framework’s light is a structure,
   and a structure is not the light. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of structures,
   not of lights.
   Suhrawardi’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But the knowledge by presence is the highest
   form of knowledge; the presence is the direct experience of the light; the presence is the
   knowledge that the soul has of itself. The framework’s knowledge is a mediation, and
   a mediation is not the presence. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of
   mediation, not of presence.
   Suhrawardi’s third objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the imaginal realm is a real
   realm; it is the realm of the suspended images; it is the realm of the prophetic vision. The
   framework’s realms are seven; they do not include the imaginal realm. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of seven realms, not of eight. The framework has no place for the
   imaginal realm.



43.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the light is not a structure,
   and it agrees that the light is the fundamental principle. But the framework denies that
   the light must be a substance. The framework’s light is the structural conveyor of effect;
   it is the condition of possibility of relation; it is the principle of the manifestation. The
   light is not a structure; it is a conveyor. The distinction is between a structure (a pattern)
   and a conveyor (a condition of possibility); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge by presence
   is a form of knowledge, and it agrees that the presence is the direct experience of the light.
   But the framework denies that the presence is the only form of knowledge. The framework
   holds that the reconstruction is a form of knowledge; it is a fallible, partial, and revisable
   knowledge; it is the reading of the manifestations. The distinction is between a presence
  (a direct experience) and a reconstruction (a reading of the manifestations); the framework
   holds both, and it does not deny the presence.
490                                                                      Chapter 43. Suhrawardi


   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the imaginal realm is a real
   realm, and it agrees that the images have their own reality. But the framework denies that
   the imaginal realm is a separate realm in the framework’s ontology. The framework holds
   that the imaginal realm is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation; it is the realm of
   the images that are the forms of the relation. The distinction is between a separate realm
   (a level of being) and a dimension of a realm (an aspect of a level); the framework holds
   the second, not the first. The framework’s realms are seven, but the imaginal realm is not
   absent; it is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation.




43.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Suhrawardi’s cost. If Suhrawardi accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the light is a substance. He must accept that the light is a structural conveyor, and that
the light is a condition of possibility of relation, not a substance. The cost is the loss of the
substantiality of the light: the light is no longer a substance; the light is a structure. He must
also give up the claim that the imaginal realm is a separate realm; he must accept that the
imaginal realm is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation. The cost is the loss of the separate
realm: the imaginal realm is no longer a separate level; it is a dimension of a level.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Suhrawardi’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the light as a fundamental reality, of the knowledge by presence, of the imaginal
realm as a separate realm—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the
completeness of the structural account: the framework’s light is a structural conveyor, but not
the fundamental reality, and the framework leaves the fundamental reality to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Suhrawardi’s light is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Suhrawardi
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
light presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.
43.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                   491


43.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “light” is not substitutable for Suhrawardi’s
   term “the Light of Lights.” If one substitutes “the Light of Lights” for “light” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s light is a structural
   conveyor, and it is not the source of all things; Suhrawardi’s Light of Lights is the source
   of all things, and it is not a conveyor. The framework’s light is structural; Suhrawardi’s
   Light of Lights is substantial. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “knowledge” is not substitutable for Suhrawardi’s term “the knowl-
   edge by presence.” If one substitutes “the knowledge by presence” for “knowledge” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s knowledge is recon-
   struction; Suhrawardi’s knowledge by presence is the direct experience. The framework’s
   knowledge is mediated; Suhrawardi’s knowledge by presence is immediate. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “realm” is not substitutable for Suhrawardi’s term “the imaginal
   realm.” If one substitutes “the imaginal realm” for “realm” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s realm is a level of being; Suhrawardi’s imaginal
   realm is the realm of the suspended images. The framework’s realm is ontological;
   Suhrawardi’s imaginal realm is imaginal. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Suhrawardi is resemblance:
   both hold that light is the fundamental principle, and they differ on whether light is a
   substance or a structure. Both hold that reality is stratified, and they differ on whether
   the strata are degrees of light or levels of manifestation. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Suhrawardi would
   be refuted by showing that Suhrawardi’s Light of Lights cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structure and substance—by showing, that is, that
   Suhrawardi already distinguishes the structural condition from the substance, and that
   the framework’s distinction is a development of Suhrawardi’s own.




43.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s light a development of Suhrawardi’s light, or is it a
departure from Suhrawardi? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Suhrawardi’s light is already a structural condition,
not a substance, has a question the chapter leaves open.
492                                                                         Chapter 43. Suhrawardi


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Hikmat al-Ishraq and the al-Talwihat
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the philosophy of illumination, the hierarchy of
lights, the Light of Lights, the imaginal realm, the critique of the Peripatetic philosophy, and
the doctrine of the master of the two orders, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A
reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a light and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the light that illuminates, or the structure that makes the illumination possible?
Is the truth the presence that is immediate, or the reconstruction that is mediated? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between Suhrawardi’s Light of Lights and the framework’s
light?
