Chapter 44

Ibn Arabi


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Muhyi al-Din Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Arabi (1165–1240
CE), known in the Islamic tradition as al-Shaykh al-Akbar (the Greatest Master) and in the West
as Ibn Arabi or Ibn al-Arabi. It states Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud),
the manifestation of the divine names (tajalli al-asma’ al-ilahiyya), the barzakh, the imaginal
realm (’alam al-mithal), the perfect human being (al-insan al-kamil), and the dialectical theology
of the divine attributes, with reference to al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya (The Meccan Openings), Fusus
al-Hikam (The Bezels of Wisdom), and The Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (The Interpreter of Desires);
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ibn Arabi; it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of manifestation and of the
realms is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Ibn Arabi’s; it presents the objections that Ibn
Arabi would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the
unity of being,” “manifestation,” “the divine names,” “the barzakh,” “the imaginal realm,” “the
perfect human being,” or “the dialectical theology,” these are Ibn Arabi’s terms, and their sense
is fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


44.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a mirror. She sees her own face; she sees the reflection;
she sees the image. The image is not her face; it is the reflection of her face; it is the face as it
appears in the mirror. The mirror is not the face; the mirror is the medium; the image is the
appearance. The face, the mirror, and the image are three things, and they are not the same.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the image is, or how the mirror
reflects, but what the face is. The face is not the image; the face is the reality; the face is the
source; the image is the appearance. But the face is not known except through the image; the
face is not seen except in the mirror; the face is not present except in the reflection. The face is
hidden in its manifestation; the face is manifest in its hiddenness.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the face is, or how it
appears, but what the being is. The being is one; the being is the Real (al-Haqq); the being is
God. The things are not the being; the things are the manifestations of the being; the things are
the names of the being. The being is one; the names are many; the manifestations are many; the
being is not multiplied by the manifestations. This is what Ibn Arabi calls the unity of being
(wahdat al-wujud): the being is one, and the things are its manifestations.
   The scene is Ibn Arabi’s image, in the Futuhat and in the Fusus, of the structure of reality.
The face is the being; the mirror is the manifestation; the image is the appearance. The scene

                                                494
44.2. The Question                                                                            495


poses the question that Ibn Arabi was the first to pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition.
What is the being? How does the one manifest in the many? And what is the relation between
God and the world? The present chapter states Ibn Arabi’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.


44.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Suhrawardi’s position: the philosophy of illumination, the hierarchy
of lights, the Light of Lights, the imaginal realm, the critique of the Peripatetic philosophy,
and the doctrine of the master of the two orders. Suhrawardi is the founder of the school of
illumination; he turns from the Peripatetic philosophy to the philosophy of light; he brings
together the Greek philosophy, the Islamic theology, and the ancient Persian wisdom. Ibn Arabi
is the greatest master of the Sufi tradition; he develops the doctrine of the unity of being; he
articulates the manifestation of the divine names; he describes the imaginal realm and the perfect
human being. The present chapter states Ibn Arabi’s doctrine, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
   The question is not whether Ibn Arabi was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ibn Arabi hold? The chapter states the unity of being,
the manifestation of the divine names, the barzakh, the imaginal realm, the perfect human being,
and the dialectical theology of the divine attributes, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ibn Arabi converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Ibn Arabi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ibn
Arabi? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


44.3       The Position

44.3.1     The Unity of Being

Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud) is stated in al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya
and in Fusus al-Hikam. The doctrine is the foundation of Ibn Arabi’s metaphysics; it is the key
to his theology; it is the source of the controversy that surrounds his name.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the being is one. The being is one; the being is the Real (al-Haqq); the being
is God. There is no being other than the being; the things are not beings; the things are the
496                                                                             Chapter 44. Ibn Arabi


manifestations of the being. The being is not multiplied by the manifestations; the being is one
in its essence; the manifestations are many in their appearances.


Second feature: the manifestations are the names. The manifestations are the names
of the being; they are the divine names (al-asma’ al-ilahiyya); they are the attributes of the
being. The names are many; the being is one; the names are not the being; the names are the
manifestations of the being. The names are the relations between the being and the things; they
are the aspects under which the being appears.


Third feature: the manifestation is the self-disclosure. The manifestation is the self-
disclosure (tajalli) of the being; it is the being’s knowledge of itself; it is the being’s love of itself.
The being manifests itself in the things; the being knows itself in the things; the being loves itself
in the things. The manifestation is not a creation from nothing; it is the self-disclosure of the
being in the forms.
      The doctrine is the foundation of Ibn Arabi’s philosophy. It is the affirmation of the unity
of being; it is the affirmation of the manifestation of the names; it is the affirmation of the
self-disclosure of the being.

   From the Tradition

   “The being is one; the things are its manifestations. The being is not multiplied by
   the manifestations; the being is one in its essence; the manifestations are many in their
   appearances. The being manifests itself in the things; the being knows itself in the things;
   the being loves itself in the things.” (Ibn Arabi, Fusus al-Hikam, trans. after Austin,
   adapted)


44.3.2      The Manifestation of the Divine Names

Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the manifestation of the divine names is a development of his doctrine of
the unity of being. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the divine names. The divine names are the attributes of God; they are
the aspects under which God appears; they are the relations between God and the world. The
names are many; the being is one; the names are not the being; the names are the manifestations
of the being. The names are the names of God; they are the names of the being; they are the
names of the Real.


Second feature: the manifestation. The manifestation is the appearance of the name in
the thing; it is the name’s determination in the thing; it is the name’s self-disclosure in the form.
The name manifests itself in the thing; the thing is the manifestation of the name; the thing is
the name in its determinate form.


Third feature: the hierarchy of the names. The names are hierarchically ordered; some
names are more universal; some names are more particular. The name “the Merciful” is more
44.3. The Position                                                                             497


universal than the name “the Provider”; the name “the Living” is more universal than the name
“the Knowing.” The hierarchy of the names is the hierarchy of the manifestations; it is the
hierarchy of the worlds.
   The doctrine is the key to Ibn Arabi’s cosmology. It is the manifestation of the names; it is
the hierarchy of the worlds; it is the self-disclosure of the being.


44.3.3    The Barzakh
Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the barzakh is stated in the Futuhat and in the Fusus. The barzakh is
the isthmus; it is the intermediate realm; it is the realm between the spiritual and the material.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the isthmus. The barzakh is the isthmus; it is the intermediate realm; it is
the realm between the spiritual and the material. The barzakh is not the spiritual; it is not the
material; it is between the two; it is the realm of the imagination; it is the realm of the images.


Second feature: the mirror. The barzakh is the mirror; it is the mirror in which the spiritual
appears as material; it is the mirror in which the material appears as spiritual. The barzakh is
the realm of the symbolic; it is the realm of the visions; it is the realm of the dreams.


Third feature: the imagination. The barzakh is the imagination (khayal); it is the faculty
of the images; it is the faculty of the symbolic. The imagination is not the reason; it is not the
sense; it is between the two; it is the faculty of the barzakh.
   The doctrine is the key to Ibn Arabi’s epistemology. It is the realm of the symbolic; it is the
realm of the visions; it is the realm of the dreams.


44.3.4    The Imaginal Realm
Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the imaginal realm is a development of his doctrine of the barzakh. The
doctrine has three features.


First feature: the imaginal realm. The imaginal realm (’alam al-mithal) is the realm of
the images; it is the realm of the forms that are not material; it is the realm of the suspended
images. The imaginal realm is the realm of the barzakh; it is the realm of the intermediate; it is
the realm between the spiritual and the material.


Second feature: the vision. The vision is the perception of the imaginal realm; it is the
perception of the images; it is the perception of the forms. The vision is not the sense; it is not
the reason; it is the imagination; it is the faculty of the imaginal realm.


Third feature: the prophecy. The prophecy is the vision of the imaginal realm; it is the
vision of the divine names; it is the vision of the being. The prophet sees the imaginal realm; the
prophet receives the revelation in the imaginal realm; the prophet conveys the revelation in the
material world.
498                                                                         Chapter 44. Ibn Arabi


      The doctrine is the key to Ibn Arabi’s prophecy. It is the realm of the vision; it is the realm
of the revelation; it is the realm of the imaginal.


44.3.5      The Perfect Human Being

Ibn Arabi’s doctrine of the perfect human being is stated in the Futuhat and in the Fusus. The
perfect human being (al-insan al-kamil) is the one who has realized the unity of being; the one
who has realized the manifestation of the names; the one who has realized the imaginal realm.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the microcosm. The perfect human being is the microcosm; the human being
is the image of the cosmos; the human being is the summary of the divine names. The human
being is the mirror in which the being sees itself; the human being is the knowledge in which the
being knows itself; the human being is the love in which the being loves itself.


Second feature: the vicegerent. The perfect human being is the vicegerent (khalifa) of
God; the human being is the representative of the being; the human being is the manifestation
of the names. The human being is the image of God; the human being is the form of the being;
the human being is the perfect manifestation.


Third feature: the pole. The perfect human being is the pole (qutb) of the world; the human
being is the axis of the cosmos; the human being is the center of the manifestation. The perfect
human being is the one through whom the world is sustained; the one through whom the world
is known; the one through whom the world is loved.
      The doctrine is the key to Ibn Arabi’s anthropology. It is the microcosm; it is the vicegerent;
it is the pole.


44.3.6      The Dialectical Theology of the Divine Attributes

Ibn Arabi’s dialectical theology of the divine attributes is stated in the Futuhat and in the Fusus.
The theology is a dialectic; it is a way of speaking about the divine attributes; it is a way of
reconciling the transcendence and the immanence of God.
      The theology has three features.


First feature: the transcendence. God is transcendent; God is beyond all attributes; God
is beyond all names; God is beyond all manifestations. God is the hidden treasure; God is the
unknown; God is the absolute.


Second feature: the immanence. God is immanent; God is in all attributes; God is in all
names; God is in all manifestations. God is the manifest; God is the known; God is the relative.


Third feature: the dialectic. The dialectic is the recognition that God is both transcendent
and immanent; God is both hidden and manifest; God is both absolute and relative. The dialectic
44.4. Internal Disputes                                                                          499


is not a contradiction; it is a unity; it is the unity of the opposites; it is the coincidence of the
contraries.
    The theology is the key to Ibn Arabi’s dialectic. It is the transcendence; it is the immanence;
it is the dialectic.



44.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Ibn Arabi is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the unity of being. The traditional reading takes the unity
of being to be a pantheism: God is the world; the world is God; there is no distinction between
the creator and the creature. A revisionary reading takes it to be a panentheism: God is in the
world; the world is in God; the distinction is real, but the two are not separate. The two readings
disagree on whether Ibn Arabi is a pantheist or a panentheist, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework is a structural realism, neither pantheistic nor
panentheistic in Ibn Arabi’s sense.



Second dispute: the status of the manifestation. The traditional reading takes the
manifestation to be a creation: God creates the world; the world is the creature; the world is
not God. A revisionary reading takes the manifestation to be a self-disclosure: God manifests
Himself in the world; the world is the manifestation of God; the world is not other than God.
The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Arabi is a creationist or a manifestationist, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s expression is a
structural tendency, not a creation and not a self-disclosure.



Third dispute: the status of the perfect human being. The traditional reading takes
the perfect human being to be a human being: the perfect human being is a person; the perfect
human being is a prophet or a saint. A revisionary reading takes it to be a symbol: the perfect
human being is the image of God; the perfect human being is the microcosm; the perfect human
being is the pole. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Arabi is an anthropologist or a
symbolist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework
has no perfect human being; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation.
    The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ibn Arabi is a pantheist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a pantheistic monism. If Ibn
Arabi is a panentheist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a panentheistic
monism. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts of Ibn Arabi, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.
500                                                                        Chapter 44. Ibn Arabi


44.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Ibn Arabi. The framework shares four structural features with Ibn Arabi’s position.

       1. The priority of the one over the many. Ibn Arabi holds that the being is one;
          the things are the manifestations of the being; the being is not multiplied by the
          manifestations. The framework holds that the identity is one; the manifestations are
          the appearances of the identity; the identity is not multiplied by the manifestations.
          Both hold that the one is prior to the many, and that the many is real in the one.

       2. The manifestation of the names. Ibn Arabi holds that the manifestations are the
          names of the being; the names are the aspects under which the being appears.
         The framework holds that the manifestations are the expressions of the identity;
          the expressions are the modes in which the identity appears. Both hold that the
          manifestations are the expressions of the source, and that the expressions are real.

       3. The imaginal realm. Ibn Arabi holds that the imaginal realm is a real realm; the
          realm of the images; the realm of the suspended images. The framework holds that
          the Relational Manifestation is the realm of the meanings and the relations; the
          imaginal realm is the realm of the images that are the forms of the relation. Both
          hold that there is a realm between the material and the intelligible, and that the
          images have their own reality.

       4. The perfect human being. Ibn Arabi holds that the perfect human being is the
          microcosm; the human being is the image of the cosmos; the human being is the
          summary of the divine names. The framework holds that the human being is the
          manifestation of the identity; the human being is the reconstruction of the pseudo-
          identity; the human being is the subject of the knowledge. Both hold that the human
          being is the image of the cosmos, and that the human being is the subject of the
          knowledge.



44.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Ibn Arabi. The framework diverges from Ibn Arabi in four respects.

       1. The status of the being. Ibn Arabi holds that the being is one; the being is the Real;
          the being is God; the things are the manifestations of the being. The framework
          holds that the identity is multiple; the identity is the invariance enacted by one
          source; the identity is not the being. The framework’s identity is not the being; it is
          the structural condition of the manifestation.
44.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                               501


       2. The status of the manifestation. Ibn Arabi holds that the manifestation is the
         self-disclosure of the being; the manifestation is the being’s knowledge of itself; the
         manifestation is the being’s love of itself. The framework holds that the manifestation
         is the expression of the identity; the manifestation is the appearance of the identity
         in a realm; the manifestation is not the self-disclosure of the being. The framework’s
         manifestation is structural, not self-disclosive.

       3. The status of the imaginal realm. Ibn Arabi holds that the imaginal realm is a real
         realm; the realm of the images; the realm of the suspended images. The framework
         holds that the realms are real levels; but the imaginal realm is not a separate realm
         in the framework’s ontology; it is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation. The
         framework’s realms are seven, not eight.

       4. The status of the perfect human being. Ibn Arabi holds that the perfect human being
         is the microcosm; the human being is the image of the cosmos; the human being is
         the pole. The framework holds that the human being is the manifestation of the
         identity; the human being is not the microcosm; the human being is not the pole.
         The framework has no perfect human being; its subject is the structure of identity
         and manifestation.



44.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ibn Arabi’s first objection. The framework says that the identity is multiple; the
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source; the identity is not the being. But the
   being is one; the things are the manifestations of the being; the being is not multiplied by
   the manifestations. The framework’s identity is a multiplicity; it is not the being; it is a
   plurality of identities. The framework has no being; the framework has no unity of being;
   the framework’s ontology is an ontology of plurality, not of unity.
   Ibn Arabi’s second objection. The framework says that the manifestation is the
   expression of the identity; the manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm.
   But the manifestation is the self-disclosure of the being; the manifestation is the being’s
   knowledge of itself; the manifestation is the being’s love of itself. The framework’s
   manifestation is a structural relation; it is not the self-disclosure of the being. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of relations, not of self-disclosure.
   Ibn Arabi’s third objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the imaginal realm is a
   real realm; it is the realm of the images; it is the realm of the suspended images. The
   framework’s realms are seven; they do not include the imaginal realm. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of seven realms, not of eight. The framework has no place for the
   imaginal realm.
502                                                                       Chapter 44. Ibn Arabi


44.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the being is one, and it agrees
   that the unity of being is a fundamental principle. But the framework denies that the
   being must be the only reality. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source; it is not the being; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. The
   distinction is between the being (the absolute unity) and the identity (the structural
   condition); the framework holds the second, not the first. The framework does not deny
   the unity of being; it denies that the unity of being is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the manifestation is
   the self-disclosure of the being, and it agrees that the self-disclosure is a fundamental
   principle. But the framework denies that the manifestation must be the self-disclosure.
   The framework’s manifestation is the expression of the identity; it is the appearance of the
   identity in a realm; it is not the self-disclosure of the being. The distinction is between
   a self- disclosure (a revelation of the being) and an expression (a manifestation of the
   identity); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the imaginal realm is a real
   realm, and it agrees that the images have their own reality. But the framework denies that
   the imaginal realm is a separate realm in the framework’s ontology. The framework holds
   that the imaginal realm is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation; it is the realm of
   the images that are the forms of the relation. The distinction is between a separate realm
   (a level of being) and a dimension of a realm (an aspect of a level); the framework holds
   the second, not the first. The framework’s realms are seven, but the imaginal realm is not
   absent; it is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation.



44.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Ibn Arabi’s cost. If Ibn Arabi accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the being is the only reality. He must accept that there is a plurality of identities, and that the
identities are the structural conditions of the manifestation. The cost is the loss of the unity of
being: the being is no longer the only reality; the identities are the structural conditions; the
multiplicity is real. He must also give up the claim that the imaginal realm is a separate realm;
he must accept that the imaginal realm is a dimension of the Relational Manifestation. The
cost is the loss of the separate realm: the imaginal realm is no longer a separate level; it is a
dimension of a level.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ibn Arabi’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the unity of being, of the self-disclosure, of the imaginal realm as a separate
44.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     503


realm—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the
structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the being,
and the framework leaves the unity of being to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ibn Arabi’s being is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Ibn Arabi
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a plurality; it is a structural condition that the
unity of being presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity
of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the other.


44.10        The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ibn
   Arabi’s term “the being.” If one substitutes “the being” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Ibn Arabi’s being is the one reality, and it is
   not manifested, because it is the source. The framework’s identity is multiple; Ibn Arabi’s
   being is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Ibn Arabi’s term “the self-
   disclosure.” If one substitutes “the self-disclosure” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   Ibn Arabi’s self-disclosure is the being’s knowledge of itself. The framework’s expression is
   structural; Ibn Arabi’s self- disclosure is personal. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “realm” is not substitutable for Ibn Arabi’s term “the imaginal
   realm.” If one substitutes “the imaginal realm” for “realm” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s realm is a level of being; Ibn Arabi’s imaginal
   realm is the realm of the suspended images. The framework’s realm is ontological; Ibn
   Arabi’s imaginal realm is imaginal. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ibn Arabi is resemblance:
   both hold that the one is prior to the many, and they differ on whether the one is the
   being or the identity. Both hold that the manifestations are the expressions of the source,
   and they differ on whether the expressions are self- disclosures or structural expressions.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Ibn Arabi would be refuted by showing that Ibn Arabi’s unity of being cannot be
   formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and being—by showing,
   that is, that Ibn Arabi already distinguishes the structural condition from the being, and
504                                                                    Chapter 44. Ibn Arabi


   that the framework’s distinction is a development of Ibn Arabi’s own.



44.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ibn Arabi’s being, or is it a
departure from Ibn Arabi? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ibn Arabi’s being is already a structural condition,
not a personal God, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Futuhat and the Fusus do justice to
the texts? The chapter has used the unity of being, the manifestation of the divine names, the
barzakh, the imaginal realm, the perfect human being, and the dialectical theology, and it has
stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a unity and a multiplicity—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the unity that manifests itself in the multiplicity, or the multiplicity
that manifests the unity? Is the truth the self-disclosure of the being, or the expression of the
identity? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Ibn Arabi’s unity of being
and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Mulla Sadra. It states the primacy of existence ( asalat al-wujud), the
gradation of existence ( tashkik al-wujud), the substantial motion ( al-haraka al-jawhariyya), the
union of the intellect and the intelligible ( ittihad al-’aql wa-al-ma’qul), and the transcendent
philosophy ( al-hikma al-muta’aliya); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of Mulla Sadra; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of existence and of motion is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Mulla Sadra’s.
The present chapter has stated Ibn Arabi’s answer to the problem of the one and the many; the
next chapter states Mulla Sadra’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 45

Mulla Sadra


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Sadr al-Din Muhammad ibn Ibrahim Shirazi (c. 1571–
1640 CE), known in the Islamic tradition as Mulla Sadra and Sadr al-Muta’allihin (the Foremost
of the Theosophers). It states Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the primacy of existence (asalat al-wujud),
the gradation of existence (tashkik al-wujud), substantial motion (al-haraka al-jawhariyya), the
union of the intellect and the intelligible (ittihad al-’aql wa-al-ma’qul), the trans-substantial
becoming of the soul, and the transcendent philosophy (al-hikma al-muta’aliya), with reference
to al-Asfar al-Arba’a (The Four Journeys), al-Shawahid al-Rububiyya (The Divine Witnesses),
al-Mabda’ wa-al-Ma’ad (The Origin and the Return), and Mafatih al-Ghayb (The Keys of the
Unseen); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Mulla Sadra; it states
the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of existence and
of motion is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Mulla Sadra’s; it presents the objections
that Mulla Sadra would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states
what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “the primacy of existence,” “the gradation of existence,” “substantial motion,” “the
union of the intellect and the intelligible,” “the trans-substantial becoming of the soul,” or “the
transcendent philosophy,” these are Mulla Sadra’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the treatises
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


45.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is watching a flame. The flame is not the same from one moment to the
next; the fire consumes the fuel; the smoke rises; the light flickers; the flame changes at every
instant. And yet the flame is one flame; it is the same fire; it is the same process of combustion.
The identity of the flame is not the identity of a substance that persists unchanged; it is the
identity of a process that persists through change. The flame is a substantial motion (al-haraka
al-jawhariyya): it changes in its very substance, not merely in its accidents.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the flame is, or how it changes, but
what existence is. The flame exists; the smoke exists; the light exists. The existence is not a
concept; it is not a predicate; it is not an accident added to the essence. The existence is the
very act of being; it is the reality that makes the thing to be; it is the most fundamental of all
things. The existence is one; the things are its gradations; the things are the degrees of existence.
This is what Mulla Sadra calls the primacy of existence (asalat al-wujud) and the gradation of
existence (tashkik al-wujud): existence is the fundamental reality, and the things are its degrees.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the flame is, or what
existence is, but what the soul is. The soul is not a substance that is created once and remains

                                                506
45.2. The Question                                                                                507


unchanged; the soul is a substance that becomes; it moves from one level to another; it passes
from the mineral to the plant, from the plant to the animal, from the animal to the human, from
the human to the angelic. The soul is a substantial motion; it is the trans-substantial becoming
of the soul. And at the highest level, the soul is united with the intelligible; the intellect and the
intelligible are one. This is what Mulla Sadra calls the union of the intellect and the intelligible
(ittihad al-’aql wa-al-ma’qul): the knower and the known are not two; they are one.
   The scene is Mulla Sadra’s image, in the Asfar and in the Shawahid, of the structure of
reality. The flame is the substantial motion; the existence is the fundamental reality; the soul is
the trans-substantial becoming. The scene poses the question that Mulla Sadra was the first to
pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What is existence? Is it the fundamental reality,
or is it a concept? What is motion? Is it a change of accidents, or is it a change of substance?
And what is the soul? Is it a static substance, or a becoming? The present chapter states Mulla
Sadra’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


45.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Ibn Arabi’s position: the unity of being, the manifestation of the
divine names, the barzakh, the imaginal realm, the perfect human being, and the dialectical
theology of the divine attributes. Ibn Arabi is the greatest master of the Sufi tradition; he
develops the doctrine of the unity of being; he articulates the manifestation of the divine names.
Mulla Sadra is the great systematizer of the Islamic philosophical tradition; he brings together
the Peripatetic philosophy, the illuminationist philosophy, and the Sufi metaphysics; he develops
the doctrine of the primacy of existence and substantial motion. The present chapter states
Mulla Sadra’s synthesis, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Mulla Sadra was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the position. What did Mulla Sadra hold? The chapter states the primacy
of existence, the gradation of existence, substantial motion, the union of the intellect and the
intelligible, the trans-substantial becoming of the soul, and the transcendent philosophy, with
reference to the treatises.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Mulla Sadra converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Mulla Sadra would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Mulla
Sadra? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


45.3      The Position
508                                                                       Chapter 45. Mulla Sadra


45.3.1      The Primacy of Existence

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the primacy of existence (asalat al-wujud) is stated in al-Asfar al-Arba’a
and in al-Shawahid al-Rububiyya. The doctrine is the foundation of Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics;
it is the key to his theology; it is the source of the controversy with the Peripatetic philosophy.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: existence is the fundamental reality. Existence is the fundamental reality;
it is not a concept; it is not a predicate; it is not an accident added to the essence. Existence is
the very act of being; it is the reality that makes the thing to be; it is the most fundamental of
all things. The essence is not the fundamental reality; the essence is a limitation of existence;
the essence is the mode in which existence appears.


Second feature: the primacy of existence over essence. The primacy of existence over
essence is the claim that existence is prior to essence; the essence is derived from existence;
the essence is the determination of existence. The Peripatetic philosophy holds the primacy of
essence; the essence is the fundamental reality; the existence is added to the essence. Mulla
Sadra reverses this: existence is the fundamental reality; the essence is a limitation of existence.


Third feature: the reality of existence. Existence is real; it is not a mental construct; it
is not a logical category; it is the very reality of the thing. The existence is not a universal; it
is not a genus; it is not a category; it is the act of being; it is the most real of all things. The
existence is not known by the concept; it is known by the presence; it is known by the intuition.
      The doctrine is the foundation of Mulla Sadra’s philosophy. It is the affirmation of the
primacy of existence; it is the affirmation of the reality of existence; it is the affirmation of the
act of being.

   From the Tradition

   “Existence is the most fundamental of all things; it is the very act of being; it is the reality
   that makes the thing to be. The essence is not the fundamental reality; the essence is a
   limitation of existence; the essence is the mode in which existence appears.” (Mulla Sadra,
   al-Asfar al-Arba’a, I.1, trans. after Rahman, adapted)



45.3.2      The Gradation of Existence

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the gradation of existence (tashkik al-wujud) is a development of his
doctrine of the primacy of existence. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the gradation. Existence is one; but it has degrees; it has gradations; it
has levels. The existence of God is the highest; the existence of the intellects is the next; the
existence of the souls is the next; the existence of the material things is the lowest. The existence
is one; the degrees are many; the degrees are the gradations of one existence.
45.3. The Position                                                                               509


Second feature: the unity in multiplicity. The gradation of existence is the unity in
multiplicity; it is the one in the many; it is the many in the one. The existence is one; the things
are many; the things are the degrees of existence; the existence is not multiplied by the degrees.
The gradation is the reconciliation of the unity and the multiplicity; it is the reconciliation of
the one and the many.


Third feature: the reality of the degrees. The degrees are real; they are not illusions;
they are not mental constructs; they are the real gradations of the real existence. The degrees
are the determinations of existence; they are the modes in which existence appears; they are the
levels of the manifestation.
   The doctrine is the key to Mulla Sadra’s cosmology. It is the gradation of existence; it is the
unity in multiplicity; it is the reconciliation of the one and the many.


45.3.3    Substantial Motion

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of substantial motion (al-haraka al-jawhariyya) is stated in al-Asfar and
in al-Mabda’ wa-al-Ma’ad. The doctrine is one of the most original in the history of Islamic
philosophy; it is the key to Mulla Sadra’s philosophy of nature.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the motion is substantial. The motion is substantial; it is not merely
accidental; it is not merely a change of accidents; it is a change of the substance itself. The
substance is not static; the substance is in motion; the substance is a process; the substance is a
becoming. The motion is not a change in the substance; it is a change of the substance.


Second feature: the motion is continuous. The motion is continuous; it is not a series of
discrete states; it is a continuous process; it is a continuous becoming. The substance is not a
series of static states; it is a continuous flow; it is a continuous motion. The continuity is the
reality of the motion; the discreteness is the appearance of the motion.


Third feature: the motion is universal. The motion is universal; it is not confined to the
material things; it is the reality of all things. The material things are in motion; the souls are in
motion; the intellects are in motion; the whole cosmos is in motion. The motion is the reality of
the cosmos; the cosmos is a process; the cosmos is a becoming.
   The doctrine is the key to Mulla Sadra’s philosophy of nature. It is the substantial motion; it
is the continuous motion; it is the universal motion.


45.3.4    The Union of the Intellect and the Intelligible

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the union of the intellect and the intelligible (ittihad al-’aql wa-al-
ma’qul) is stated in al-Asfar and in al-Shawahid. The doctrine is one of the most controversial in
the history of Islamic philosophy; it is the key to Mulla Sadra’s epistemology.
   The doctrine has three features.
510                                                                       Chapter 45. Mulla Sadra


First feature: the union. The intellect and the intelligible are one; they are not two; they
are not separate. The knower and the known are not two things; they are one thing; they are
one act; they are one reality. The union is not a conjunction; it is not a relation; it is an identity;
it is the identity of the intellect and the intelligible.


Second feature: the knowledge by presence. The knowledge by presence is the foundation
of the union; it is the presence of the known to the knower; it is the presence of the intelligible
to the intellect. The knowledge by presence is not a representation; it is not a concept; it is the
presence itself; it is the union itself.


Third feature: the gradation of the union. The union has degrees; it has gradations; it
has levels. The union of the human intellect with the intelligible is partial; the union of the
divine intellect with the intelligible is complete. The union is the gradation of knowledge; it is
the gradation of presence; it is the gradation of existence.
      The doctrine is the key to Mulla Sadra’s epistemology. It is the union; it is the knowledge by
presence; it is the gradation of the union.


45.3.5      The Trans-Substantial Becoming of the Soul

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the trans-substantial becoming of the soul is a development of his
doctrine of substantial motion. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the soul is a becoming. The soul is not a static substance; the soul is a
becoming; the soul is a process; the soul is a motion. The soul is not created once and remains
unchanged; the soul is created continuously; the soul is in continuous becoming. The soul is a
substantial motion; the soul is a trans-substantial becoming.


Second feature: the levels of the soul. The soul has levels; it has gradations; it has stages.
The soul begins as a material soul; it becomes a vegetative soul; it becomes an animal soul; it
becomes a human soul; it becomes an angelic soul. The soul is not a substance that has accidents;
the soul is a substance that becomes; the soul is the becoming itself.


Third feature: the immortality of the soul. The immortality of the soul is not the
persistence of a static substance; it is the continuation of the becoming; it is the continuation of
the motion. The soul does not die with the body; the soul continues in the becoming; the soul
continues in the motion; the soul continues in the levels.
      The doctrine is the key to Mulla Sadra’s psychology. It is the becoming; it is the levels; it is
the immortality.


45.3.6      The Transcendent Philosophy

Mulla Sadra’s doctrine of the transcendent philosophy (al-hikma al-muta’aliya) is the synthesis
of his philosophy. The transcendent philosophy has three features.
45.4. Internal Disputes                                                                           511


First feature: the synthesis. The transcendent philosophy is the synthesis of the Peripatetic
philosophy, the illuminationist philosophy, and the Sufi metaphysics. It is not a rejection of the
three; it is a synthesis; it is a development; it is a transcendence. The Peripatetic philosophy gives
the demonstration; the illuminationist philosophy gives the illumination; the Sufi metaphysics
gives the unity of being.

Second feature: the method. The method of the transcendent philosophy is the combination
of the demonstration and the intuition. The demonstration gives the knowledge; the intuition
gives the presence; the two are not in conflict; they are complementary; they are the two wings
of the philosophy.

Third feature: the goal. The goal of the transcendent philosophy is the knowledge of God; it
is the knowledge of the existence; it is the knowledge of the unity. The goal is not the knowledge
of the concepts; it is the knowledge of the reality; it is the knowledge of the presence.
   The doctrine is the key to Mulla Sadra’s philosophy. It is the synthesis; it is the method; it
is the goal.


45.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Mulla Sadra is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the primacy of existence. The traditional reading takes
the primacy of existence to be a metaphysical doctrine: existence is the fundamental reality;
the essence is a limitation of existence. A revisionary reading takes it to be a phenomenological
doctrine: the primacy of existence is the primacy of the act of being; it is the primacy of the
presence; it is the primacy of the intuition. The two readings disagree on whether Mulla Sadra
is a metaphysician or a phenomenologist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s identity is a structural condition, neither a metaphysical
substance nor a phenomenological presence.

Second dispute: the status of substantial motion. The traditional reading takes sub-
stantial motion to be a physical doctrine: the substance is in motion; the substance is a process;
the substance is a becoming. A revisionary reading takes it to be a metaphysical doctrine: the
motion is the reality of the cosmos; the motion is the reality of the existence; the motion is the
reality of the being. The two readings disagree on whether Mulla Sadra is a philosopher of nature
or a metaphysician, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s expression is a structural tendency, not a substantial motion.

Third dispute: the status of the union of the intellect and the intelligible. The
traditional reading takes the union to be an epistemological doctrine: the knower and the known
are one; the intellect and the intelligible are one; the knowledge is the union. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a metaphysical doctrine: the union is the reality of the existence; the union
is the reality of the being; the union is the reality of the presence. The two readings disagree on
512                                                                       Chapter 45. Mulla Sadra


whether Mulla Sadra is an epistemologist or a metaphysician, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s knowledge is reconstruction, not union.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Mulla Sadra is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysical existentialism.
If Mulla Sadra is a phenomenologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of
Mulla Sadra, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.



45.5        Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Mulla Sadra. The framework shares four structural features with Mulla Sadra’s
   position.

        1. The priority of existence. Mulla Sadra holds that existence is the fundamental reality;
           it is the very act of being; it is the reality that makes the thing to be. The framework
           holds that the identity is the fundamental reality; it is the invariance enacted by one
           source; it is the reality that makes the thing to be one thing. Both hold that there
           is a fundamental reality, and that the fundamental reality is the act of being.

        2. The gradation of existence. Mulla Sadra holds that existence is one; but it has
           degrees; it has gradations; it has levels. The framework holds that identity is one;
           but it has degrees; it has gradations; it has levels. The framework’s realms are
           the degrees of the manifestation; the framework’s identities are the degrees of the
           invariance. Both hold that reality is stratified, and that the strata are the degrees of
           the fundamental reality.

        3. The substantial motion. Mulla Sadra holds that the substance is in motion; the
           substance is a process; the substance is a becoming. The framework holds that the
           identity is in expression; the identity is a tendency; the identity is an enactment.
           Both hold that reality is dynamic, not static, and that the dynamic is the truth of
           the static.

        4. The union of the intellect and the intelligible. Mulla Sadra holds that the knower
           and the known are one; the intellect and the intelligible are one; the knowledge
           is the union. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the
           manifestations; the reconstruction is the presence of the identity to the subject.
           Both hold that knowledge is not merely conceptual, and that there is a dimension of
           knowledge that the concepts do not capture.
45.6. Points of Divergence                                                                      513


45.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Mulla Sadra. The framework diverges from Mulla Sadra in four respects.

       1. The status of existence. Mulla Sadra holds that existence is the fundamental reality;
         it is the very act of being; it is the reality that makes the thing to be. The framework
         holds that the identity is the fundamental reality; it is the invariance enacted by one
         source; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. The framework’s identity
         is not existence; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. The framework’s
         metaphysics is a metaphysics of identity, not of existence.

       2. The status of substantial motion. Mulla Sadra holds that the substance is in motion;
         the substance is a process; the substance is a becoming. The framework holds
         that the expression is a structural tendency; the expression is the enactment of
         the identity; the expression is the manifestation of the identity. The framework’s
         expression is structural, not substantial.

       3. The status of the union. Mulla Sadra holds that the knower and the known are one;
         the intellect and the intelligible are one; the knowledge is the union. The framework
         holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction
         is the pseudo-identity of the identity. The framework’s knowledge is reconstructive,
         not union.

       4. The status of the transcendent philosophy. Mulla Sadra holds that the transcendent
         philosophy is the synthesis of the Peripatetic philosophy, the illuminationist philoso-
         phy, and the Sufi metaphysics. The framework holds that its structure is autonomous;
         it does not depend on any tradition; its truth is structural, not synthetic. The
         framework’s philosophy is a systematic reconstruction, not a transcendent synthesis.



45.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Mulla Sadra’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not existence; it is a pattern. The world is composed of existences; the world
   is not just structured; the world is a plurality of acts of being. The framework has no
   existence; the framework has no act of being; the framework’s world is a world without
   existence. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of existence.
   Mulla Sadra’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms;
   the realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the degrees of existence; they are the gradations of the act of being. The
514                                                                     Chapter 45. Mulla Sadra


   framework’s realms are not degrees of existence; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of existence.
   Mulla Sadra’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the union of the intellect and the
   intelligible; the knower and the known are one. The framework’s knowledge is a mediation;
   it is not the union. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of mediation, not of
   union.



45.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is composed of
   existences, and it agrees that the existence is the act of being. But the framework denies
   that the existence must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition of the manifestation; it is
   the act of being of the thing. The distinction is between an existence (an act of being) and
   an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not the first. The
   framework does not deny the existence; it denies that the existence is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are degrees. But the framework denies that the degrees are
   degrees of existence. The framework’s degrees are degrees of manifestation; the degrees
   are the levels of the expression; the degrees are the modes in which the identity appears.
   The distinction is between a degree of existence (an ontological degree) and a degree of
   manifestation (a structural degree); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the union. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a union (an identity)
   and a presence (a relation); the framework holds the second, not the first.



45.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Mulla Sadra’s cost. If Mulla Sadra accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the
claim that the existence is the fundamental reality. He must accept that the identity is the
structural condition, and that the existence is the act of being of the thing. The cost is the loss
of the primacy of existence: the existence is no longer the fundamental reality; the identity is
the structural condition. He must also give up the claim that the knowledge is the union; he
45.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                   515


must accept that the knowledge is the reconstruction; the reconstruction is the reading of the
manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Mulla Sadra’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the existence, of the substantial motion, of the union—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the existence, and the framework leaves the
existence to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Mulla Sadra’s existence
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Mulla Sadra must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural
condition that the existence presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss
of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is
incomplete without the other.



45.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Mulla
   Sadra’s term “existence.” If one substitutes “existence” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Mulla Sadra’s existence is the act of being,
   and it is not manifested, because it is the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity
   is multiple; Mulla Sadra’s existence is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Mulla Sadra’s term “substantial
   motion.” If one substitutes “substantial motion” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   Mulla Sadra’s substantial motion is the motion of the substance. The framework’s
   expression is structural; Mulla Sadra’s substantial motion is substantial. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “knowledge” is not substitutable for Mulla Sadra’s term “the
   union of the intellect and the intelligible.” If one substitutes “the union” for “knowledge”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s knowledge is
   reconstruction; Mulla Sadra’s knowledge is the union of the knower and the known.
   The framework’s knowledge is mediated; Mulla Sadra’s knowledge is immediate. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
516                                                                     Chapter 45. Mulla Sadra


   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Mulla Sadra is resem-
   blance: both hold that there is a fundamental reality, and they differ on whether the
   fundamental reality is existence or identity. Both hold that reality is dynamic, and they
   differ on whether the dynamic is substantial motion or structural expression. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Mulla Sadra would be refuted by showing that Mulla Sadra’s existence cannot be formu-
   lated without the framework’s distinction between structure and existence—by showing,
   that is, that Mulla Sadra already distinguishes the structural condition from the existence,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Mulla Sadra’s own.




45.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Mulla Sadra’s existence, or
is it a departure from Mulla Sadra? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but
the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Mulla Sadra’s existence is already a
structural condition, not an act of being, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Asfar and the Shawahid do justice to
the texts? The chapter has used the primacy of existence, the gradation of existence, substantial
motion, the union of the intellect and the intelligible, the trans-substantial becoming of the soul,
and the transcendent philosophy, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
