A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an existence and a structure—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the existence that acts, or the structure that persists? Is the truth
the substantial motion that becomes, or the structural expression that enacts? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between Mulla Sadra’s primacy of existence and the
framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Ibn Khaldun. It states the science of civilization ( ’ilm al-’umran), the
cycles of history, the distinction between the Bedouin and the sedentary, the concept of social
solidarity ( ’asabiyya), and the critique of the philosophers’ political philosophy; it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Ibn Khaldun; and it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of the realms and of the cycles of manifestation
is the nearest classical Islamic analogue to Ibn Khaldun’s. The present chapter has stated Mulla
Sadra’s answer to the problem of existence; the next chapter states Ibn Khaldun’s answer, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 46

Ibn Khaldun


Scope. This chapter closes Part VI, the dialogues with classical Islamic philosophy, and it
closes it with Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Khaldun al-Hadrami (1332–1406 CE), the
historian, sociologist, and philosopher of history. It states Ibn Khaldun’s science of civilization
(’ilm al-’umran), the distinction between the Bedouin and the sedentary, the concept of social
solidarity (’asabiyya), the cycles of dynastic rise and decline, the critique of the philosophers’
political philosophy, and the methodology of history, with reference to the Muqaddima (The
Introduction) and the Kitab al-’Ibar (The Book of Lessons); it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of Ibn Khaldun; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of the realms and of the cycles of manifestation is the nearest
classical Islamic analogue to Ibn Khaldun’s; it presents the objections that Ibn Khaldun would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the science of
civilization,” “social solidarity,” “the Bedouin and the sedentary,” “the cycles of dynastic rise
and decline,” or “the methodology of history,” these are Ibn Khaldun’s terms, and their sense is
fixed by the treatises and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


46.1      A Scene
Consider a city that has grown wealthy through trade. Its merchants have become rich; its
scholars have become famous; its palaces have become grand; its armies have become large. The
city is at the height of its power; it is the center of the world; it is the envy of its neighbors.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose the city asks: how did we get here? The city has grown
from a small settlement; it has grown from a tribe; it has grown from a group of families that
shared a common purpose. The city has grown through the solidarity of its people; it has grown
through the ’asabiyya of its tribe; it has grown through the willingness of its people to fight and
to die for one another. The city is not the product of a single individual; it is the product of a
group; it is the product of a solidarity; it is the product of a history.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose the city asks: what will become of us?
The city has grown wealthy; the city has grown soft; the city has grown complacent. The
solidarity that built the city has weakened; the ’asabiyya that defended the city has dissolved;
the willingness to fight and to die has been replaced by the willingness to enjoy and to consume.
The city is on the path of decline; the city is on the path of decay; the city is on the path of
death. And the cycle will begin again: a new tribe will rise; a new city will be built; a new
solidarity will be formed. This is what Ibn Khaldun calls the cycle of dynastic rise and decline:
the cycle of the ’asabiyya, the cycle of the city, the cycle of the civilization.

                                                 518
46.2. The Question                                                                                    519


   The scene is Ibn Khaldun’s image, in the Muqaddima, of the structure of history. The city is
the civilization; the solidarity is the ’asabiyya; the cycle is the dynastic cycle. The scene poses
the question that Ibn Khaldun was the first to pose in its full form in the Islamic tradition. What
is the science of civilization? What is the ’asabiyya? And what is the cycle of the dynastic rise
and decline? The present chapter states Ibn Khaldun’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.


46.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Mulla Sadra’s position: the primacy of existence, the gradation of
existence, substantial motion, the union of the intellect and the intelligible, the trans-substantial
becoming of the soul, and the transcendent philosophy. Mulla Sadra is the great systematizer of the
Islamic philosophical tradition; he brings together the Peripatetic philosophy, the illuminationist
philosophy, and the Sufi metaphysics. Ibn Khaldun is his contemporary, but he is not a philosopher
in the strict sense; he is a historian, a sociologist, and a philosopher of history. He is the founder
of the science of civilization; he is the first to study the cycles of history; he is the first to analyze
the social solidarity. The present chapter states Ibn Khaldun’s science of civilization, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Ibn Khaldun was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ibn Khaldun hold? The chapter states the science
of civilization, the distinction between the Bedouin and the sedentary, the concept of social
solidarity (’asabiyya), the cycles of dynastic rise and decline, the critique of the philosophers’
political philosophy, and the methodology of history, with reference to the treatises.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ibn Khaldun converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Ibn Khaldun would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ibn
Khaldun? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


46.3       The Position

46.3.1     The Science of Civilization

Ibn Khaldun’s science of civilization (’ilm al-’umran) is stated in the Muqaddima (The Intro-
duction, 1377). The science is the foundation of Ibn Khaldun’s philosophy of history; it is the
first attempt to study the human society as a natural phenomenon; it is the first attempt to
formulate the laws of the social life.
520                                                                       Chapter 46. Ibn Khaldun


      The science has three features.


First feature: the subject. The subject of the science is the human society; it is the
civilization; it is the ’umran. The ’umran is the social life; it is the life of the human beings in a
society; it is the life of the human beings in a city. The ’umran is not the individual; it is the
collective; it is the social.


Second feature: the method. The method of the science is the empirical method; it is the
method of the observation; it is the method of the historical evidence. The science is not the
philosophy; it is not the metaphysics; it is the empirical study of the social life. The science
is based on the observation of the historical facts; it is based on the evidence of the historical
sources.


Third feature: the laws. The science formulates the laws of the social life; it formulates
the laws of the ’umran; it formulates the laws of the history. The laws are not the laws of the
philosophy; they are the laws of the empirical science; they are the laws of the social life.
      The science is the foundation of Ibn Khaldun’s philosophy. It is the science of civilization; it
is the empirical study of the social life; it is the formulation of the laws of the history.

   From the Tradition

   “The science of civilization is the science of the social life; it is the empirical study of the
   ’umran; it is the formulation of the laws of the history.” (Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddima, I.1,
   trans. after Rosenthal, adapted)


46.3.2      The Bedouin and the Sedentary

Ibn Khaldun’s distinction between the Bedouin and the sedentary is stated in the Muqaddima.
The distinction is the foundation of Ibn Khaldun’s sociology; it is the distinction between the
two modes of the social life.
      The distinction has three features.


First feature: the Bedouin. The Bedouin is the nomadic; the Bedouin lives in the desert;
the Bedouin lives by the pastoralism; the Bedouin lives by the raid. The Bedouin is hard; the
Bedouin is brave; the Bedouin is solidary. The Bedouin has the ’asabiyya; the Bedouin has the
solidarity; the Bedouin has the willingness to fight and to die.


Second feature: the sedentary. The sedentary is the urban; the sedentary lives in the city;
the sedentary lives by the trade; the sedentary lives by the craft. The sedentary is soft; the
sedentary is cultured; the sedentary is refined. The sedentary has the luxury; the sedentary has
the comfort; the sedentary has the civilization.


Third feature: the cycle. The cycle is the relation between the Bedouin and the sedentary.
The Bedouin conquers the city; the Bedouin becomes sedentary; the Bedouin becomes soft; the
46.3. The Position                                                                                  521


Bedouin loses the ’asabiyya; the Bedouin is conquered by a new Bedouin. The cycle is the cycle
of the ’umran; it is the cycle of the civilization; it is the cycle of the history.
   The distinction is the key to Ibn Khaldun’s sociology. It is the Bedouin and the sedentary; it
is the desert and the city; it is the cycle of the two.


46.3.3     The Social Solidarity (’Asabiyya)

Ibn Khaldun’s concept of social solidarity (’asabiyya) is stated in the Muqaddima. The ’asabiyya
is the foundation of Ibn Khaldun’s political philosophy; it is the bond that holds the society
together; it is the force that drives the history.
   The concept has three features.


First feature: the solidarity. The ’asabiyya is the solidarity; it is the bond that holds
the group together; it is the force that makes the group act as one. The ’asabiyya is not the
individual; it is not the family; it is the group; it is the tribe; it is the nation.


Second feature: the group. The ’asabiyya is the force of the group; it is the force of the
tribe; it is the force of the nation. The ’asabiyya is the willingness to fight and to die for the
group; it is the willingness to sacrifice for the group; it is the willingness to defend the group.


Third feature: the cycle. The ’asabiyya is the force that drives the cycle; it is the force that
builds the civilization; it is the force that destroys the civilization. The ’asabiyya is strong in
the Bedouin; it is weak in the sedentary; it is the force that builds the city; it is the force that
destroys the city. The cycle is the cycle of the ’asabiyya; it is the cycle of the solidarity; it is the
cycle of the history.
   The concept is the key to Ibn Khaldun’s political philosophy. It is the solidarity; it is the
group; it is the cycle.


46.3.4     The Cycles of Dynastic Rise and Decline

Ibn Khaldun’s doctrine of the cycles of dynastic rise and decline is a development of his concept
of the ’asabiyya. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the rise. The rise is the rise of the ’asabiyya; it is the rise of the solidarity; it
is the rise of the Bedouin. The Bedouin has the ’asabiyya; the Bedouin has the solidarity; the
Bedouin conquers the city; the Bedouin builds the dynasty. The rise is the rise of the cycle; it is
the rise of the civilization; it is the rise of the history.


Second feature: the decline. The decline is the decline of the ’asabiyya; it is the decline of
the solidarity; it is the decline of the sedentary. The sedentary has the luxury; the sedentary has
the comfort; the sedentary has the civilization. The sedentary loses the ’asabiyya; the sedentary
loses the solidarity; the sedentary is conquered by a new Bedouin. The decline is the decline of
the cycle; it is the decline of the civilization; it is the decline of the history.
522                                                                        Chapter 46. Ibn Khaldun


Third feature: the cycle. The cycle is the cycle of the rise and the decline; it is the cycle
of the ’asabiyya; it is the cycle of the civilization. The cycle has three generations: the first
generation builds the dynasty; the second generation maintains the dynasty; the third generation
destroys the dynasty. The cycle is the cycle of the three generations; it is the cycle of the history;
it is the cycle of the civilization.
      The doctrine is the key to Ibn Khaldun’s philosophy of history. It is the cycle of the rise and
the decline; it is the cycle of the ’asabiyya; it is the cycle of the civilization.


46.3.5      The Critique of the Philosophers’ Political Philosophy

Ibn Khaldun’s critique of the philosophers’ political philosophy is stated in the Muqaddima. The
critique is not a rejection of the philosophy; it is a critique of the limits of the philosophy; it is
the recognition that the philosophy cannot grasp the social life.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the limits of the philosophy. The philosophers (Plato, al-Farabi) have
developed a political philosophy; they have described the ideal city; they have described the
virtuous city. But the philosophers’ political philosophy is not the science of the social life; it is
the description of the ideal; it is not the description of the real. The philosophers’ city is not the
city of the ’umran; it is the city of the ideal.


Second feature: the limits of the ideal. The ideal city is not the real city; the ideal city is
the city that should be; the real city is the city that is. The philosophers’ political philosophy
is the description of the ideal; it is not the description of the real; it is not the science of the
’umran. The science of the ’umran is the science of the real; it is the science of the actual; it is
the science of the historical.


Third feature: the need for the empirical method. The science of the ’umran needs the
empirical method; it needs the observation; it needs the historical evidence. The philosophers’
political philosophy uses the speculative method; it uses the demonstration; it uses the deduction.
The science of the ’umran uses the empirical method; it uses the observation; it uses the induction.
The distinction is between the speculative and the empirical; the distinction is between the ideal
and the real.
      The critique is the key to Ibn Khaldun’s methodology. It is the critique of the speculative
political philosophy; it is the affirmation of the empirical science; it is the foundation of the
science of the ’umran.


46.3.6      The Methodology of History

Ibn Khaldun’s methodology of history is stated in the Muqaddima. The methodology is the
foundation of Ibn Khaldun’s science of civilization; it is the method by which the history is
studied; it is the method by which the facts are verified.
      The methodology has three features.
46.4. Internal Disputes                                                                              523


First feature: the critique of the sources. The critique of the sources is the first step; it is
the examination of the sources; it is the verification of the facts. The historian must not accept
the sources blindly; the historian must examine the sources critically; the historian must verify
the facts.


Second feature: the natural laws. The natural laws are the second step; they are the laws
of the social life; they are the laws of the ’umran. The historian must understand the natural
laws; the historian must apply the natural laws; the historian must explain the facts by the
natural laws.


Third feature: the science of the ’umran. The science of the ’umran is the third step; it
is the science of the social life; it is the science of the civilization. The science of the ’umran is
the foundation of the history; it is the foundation of the sociology; it is the foundation of the
philosophy of history.
   The methodology is the key to Ibn Khaldun’s history. It is the critique of the sources; it is
the natural laws; it is the science of the ’umran.


46.4         Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Ibn Khaldun is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the science of the ’umran. The traditional reading takes
the science of the ’umran to be a sociology: it is the empirical study of the social life; it is the
formulation of the laws of the social life. A revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophy of
history: it is the speculative study of the historical process; it is the formulation of the laws of
the historical process. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Khaldun is a sociologist or a
philosopher of history, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s realms are ontological levels, not social facts.


Second dispute: the status of the ’asabiyya. The traditional reading takes the ’asabiyya
to be a social bond: it is the solidarity of the group; it is the force that holds the society together.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a psychological bond: it is the feeling of solidarity; it is the
emotion of belonging. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Khaldun is a sociologist or a
psychologist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural relation, not a psychological feeling.


Third dispute: the status of the cycles. The traditional reading takes the cycles to be a
historical law: the cycles of the rise and the decline; the cycles of the civilization; the cycles of the
history. A revisionary reading takes them to be a heuristic device: they are a way of organizing
the historical facts; they are not a law of the history. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn
Khaldun is a determinist or a heuristicist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s cycles are structural recurrences, not historical laws.
524                                                                         Chapter 46. Ibn Khaldun


      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ibn Khaldun is a sociologist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a sociological empiricism. If
Ibn Khaldun is a philosopher of history, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that
the framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the
texts of Ibn Khaldun, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way
that is compatible with either reading.




46.5       Points of Convergence


   Points of Convergence

   With Ibn Khaldun. The framework shares four structural features with Ibn Khaldun’s
   position.

        1. The study of the social life. Ibn Khaldun holds that the social life is a subject of the
           science; it is the ’umran; it is the civilization. The framework holds that the social
           life is a subject of the science; it is the manifestation of the identity in the Relational
           Manifestation; it is the expression of the identity in the society. Both hold that the
           social life is a subject of the science, and that the social life is a real phenomenon.

        2. The importance of the solidarity. Ibn Khaldun holds that the solidarity is the force
           that holds the society together; it is the ’asabiyya; it is the bond of the group. The
           framework holds that the relation is the force that holds the society together; it is
           the expression of the identity; it is the bond of the manifestation. Both hold that
           there is a force that holds the society together, and that the force is real.

        3. The cycle of the rise and the decline. Ibn Khaldun holds that the civilization has the
           cycle of the rise and the decline; the cycle of the ’asabiyya; the cycle of the history.
           The framework holds that the expression has the cycle of the manifestation and the
           cessation; the cycle of the light; the cycle of the relation. Both hold that there is a
           cycle, and that the cycle is real.

        4. The critique of the ideal. Ibn Khaldun holds that the philosophers’ political philosophy
           is the description of the ideal; it is not the description of the real. The framework
           holds that the philosophy is the description of the structure; it is not the description
           of the historical facts. Both hold that the philosophy is not the history, and that
           the philosophy is not the empirical science.
46.6. Points of Divergence                                                                          525


46.6        Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Ibn Khaldun. The framework diverges from Ibn Khaldun in four respects.

       1. The status of the science. Ibn Khaldun holds that the science of the ’umran is the
            empirical science; it is the study of the social facts; it is the study of the historical
            facts. The framework holds that the science of the structure is the philosophical
            science; it is the study of the structural conditions; it is the study of the ontological
            levels. The framework’s science is philosophical, not empirical.

       2. The status of the solidarity. Ibn Khaldun holds that the ’asabiyya is the social bond;
            it is the force of the group; it is the willingness to fight and to die. The framework
            holds that the relation is the structural bond; it is the expression of the identity; it
            is the condition of the manifestation. The framework’s relation is structural, not
            psychological.

       3. The status of the cycle. Ibn Khaldun holds that the cycle is the historical law; it is
            the cycle of the rise and the decline; it is the cycle of the civilization. The framework
            holds that the cycle is the structural recurrence; it is the cycle of the manifestation
            and the cessation; it is the cycle of the light. The framework’s cycle is structural,
            not historical.

       4. The status of the history. Ibn Khaldun holds that the history is the subject of the
            science; it is the ’umran; it is the civilization. The framework holds that the history
            is the manifestation of the identity in the Material Manifestation; it is the expression
            of the identity in time; it is the succession of the manifestations. The framework’s
            history is structural, not sociological.



46.7        The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ibn Khaldun’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not a social fact; it is a pattern. The social life is composed of social facts; the
   social life is not just structured; the social life is a plurality of social facts. The framework
   has no social facts; the framework has no sociology; the framework’s world is a world
   without social facts. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of social
   facts.
   Ibn Khaldun’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
   they are the levels of the social life; they are the levels of the ’umran. The framework’s
526                                                                      Chapter 46. Ibn Khaldun


   realms are not levels of the social life; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of levels, not of the social life.
   Ibn Khaldun’s third objection. The framework says that the cycle is the structural
   recurrence; it is the cycle of the manifestation and the cessation. But the cycle is the
   historical law; it is the cycle of the rise and the decline; it is the cycle of the ’asabiyya.
   The framework’s cycle is structural; it is not historical. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of structures, not of history.



46.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the social life is composed of
   social facts, and it agrees that the social facts are real. But the framework denies that the
   social facts are the ultimate reality. The framework’s identity is the structural condition
   of the social facts; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition
   under which the social facts are what they are. The distinction is between a social fact (an
   empirical fact) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second,
   not the first. The framework does not deny the social facts; it denies that the social facts
   are the ultimate reality.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of manifestation. But the framework denies that
   the realms are levels of the social life. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they
   are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the social life.
   The distinction is between a level of the social life (a sociological level) and a level of
   manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the cycle is the historical
   law, and it agrees that the cycle of the rise and the decline is a real phenomenon. But
   the framework denies that the cycle must be the historical law. The framework’s cycle is
   the structural recurrence; it is the cycle of the manifestation and the cessation; it is the
   cycle of the light. The distinction is between a historical law (a law of the social life) and
   a structural recurrence (a law of the manifestation); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.



46.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Ibn Khaldun’s cost. If Ibn Khaldun accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the
claim that the social facts are the ultimate reality. He must accept that the social facts are the
manifestations of the identity, and that the identity is the structural condition of the social facts.
The cost is the loss of the sociological empiricism: the social facts are no longer the ultimate
46.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     527


reality; the identity is the structural condition. He must also give up the claim that the cycle is
the historical law; he must accept that the cycle is the structural recurrence; the cycle is the law
of the manifestation, not the law of the social life.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ibn Khaldun’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the social facts, of the ’asabiyya, of the historical cycle—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a social fact, and the framework leaves the
social facts to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ibn Khaldun’s social
facts are not a mistake; they are a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does
not capture. Ibn Khaldun must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a
structural condition that the social facts presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue
is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and
each is incomplete without the other.



46.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ibn
   Khaldun’s term “the social fact.” If one substitutes “the social fact” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Ibn Khaldun’s social fact is the
   empirical fact, and it is not manifested, because it is the social fact. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; Ibn Khaldun’s social fact is multiple. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Ibn Khaldun’s term “the
  ’asabiyya.” If one substitutes “the ’asabiyya” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; Ibn Khaldun’s
  ’asabiyya is the social bond. The framework’s expression is structural; Ibn Khaldun’s
  ’asabiyya is social. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “cycle” is not substitutable for Ibn Khaldun’s term “the dynastic
   cycle.” If one substitutes “the dynastic cycle” for “cycle” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s cycle is the structural recurrence; Ibn Khaldun’s
   dynastic cycle is the cycle of the rise and the decline. The framework’s cycle is structural;
   Ibn Khaldun’s cycle is historical. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
528                                                                     Chapter 46. Ibn Khaldun


   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ibn Khaldun is resem-
   blance: both hold that there is a force that holds the society together, and they differ on
   whether the force is a social bond or a structural condition. Both hold that there is a cycle,
   and they differ on whether the cycle is a historical law or a structural recurrence. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Ibn Khaldun would be refuted by showing that Ibn Khaldun’s social facts cannot be
   formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and social fact—by
   showing, that is, that Ibn Khaldun already distinguishes the structural condition from the
   social fact, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Ibn Khaldun’s own.




46.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ibn Khaldun’s social fact, or
is it a departure from Ibn Khaldun? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ibn Khaldun’s social fact is already a
structural condition, not an empirical fact, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Muqaddima do justice to the text? The
chapter has used the science of civilization, the Bedouin and the sedentary, the social solidarity,
the cycles of dynastic rise and decline, the critique of the philosophers’ political philosophy, and
the methodology of history, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the text supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a social fact and a structure—a city, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the social fact that is observed, or the structure that makes the observation
possible? Is the truth the historical cycle that rises and declines, or the structural recurrence that
manifests and ceases? What does your answer tell you about the relation between Ibn Khaldun’s
’asabiyya and the framework’s expression?

Part VI is now complete. The dialogues with the ten great figures of classical Islamic philosophy—
al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, al-Ghazali, Ibn Rushd, the Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya, Suhrawardi,
Ibn Arabi, Mulla Sadra, and Ibn Khaldun—have been stated. Part VII turns to contemporary
Islamic philosophy. The first dialogue is with Iqbal, on the reconstruction of Islamic thought and
the self; the next with Tabatabai, on the principles of philosophy and the method of realism; the
next with Nasr, on traditionalism and the sacred science; the next with Soroush, on the theoretical
contraction and expansion of religious knowledge; and the last with Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman,
on the critique of Arab reason and the renewal of the Islamic tradition. The classical Islamic
tradition has posed the problem of the one and the many, of essence and existence, of light and
manifestation; the contemporary Islamic tradition will ask whether the tradition can be renewed.

Contemporary Islamic Philosophy

Chapter 47

Iqbal


Scope. This chapter opens Part VII, the dialogues with contemporary Islamic philosophy, and it
opens it with Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938 CE), the poet, philosopher, and reformer of modern
Islamic thought. It states Iqbal’s reconstruction of religious thought in Islam, his critique of
Greek philosophy and of the static conception of the universe, his doctrine of the self (khudi),
his dynamic conception of God and of the universe, his account of ijtihad as the principle of
movement in Islam, and his vision of the perfect human being (insan al-kamil) as the vicegerent
of God on earth, with reference to The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam (1930),
Asrar-i-Khudi (The Secrets of the Self, 1915), Rumuz-i-Bekhudi (The Mysteries of Selflessness,
1917), and Payam-i-Mashriq (The Message of the East, 1923); it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of Iqbal; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of identity, of expression, and of the dynamism of the real is the
nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Iqbal’s; it presents the objections that Iqbal would raise
against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other;
it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes
no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the reconstruction of
religious thought,” “the self,” “khudi,” “ijtihad,” “the perfect human being,” or “the dynamic
universe,” these are Iqbal’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


47.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the Qur’an. She reads the verse: “God does not change the
condition of a people until they change what is in themselves” (Q 13:11). She reads another
verse: “And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge” (Q 20:114). She reads a third: “We have
made you a middle nation” (Q 2:143). The three verses seem to point in different directions:
the first to the inner transformation, the second to the pursuit of knowledge, the third to the
collective responsibility. She asks: what is the relation between the inner self and the outer
world? What is the relation between knowledge and action? And what is the relation between
the individual and the community?
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she reads the philosophers of the Greek tradition: they
say that the universe is eternal, that change is an illusion, that the perfect is the unchanging.
She reads the modern philosophers: they say that the universe is in process, that change is real,
that the perfect is the creative advance. She asks: which view is true to the Qur’an? Iqbal’s
answer: neither the Greek nor the modern view is true to the Qur’an, but the modern view is
closer. The Qur’an presents a dynamic universe, a universe that is in motion, a universe that is
creative. The Greek view is static; the Qur’anic view is dynamic. The task of the Muslim thinker

                                               531
532                                                                                 Chapter 47. Iqbal


is to reconstruct the Islamic thought in the light of the modern knowledge, and to recover the
dynamic spirit of the Qur’an from the static crust of the tradition.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the universe is, or how
it changes, but what the self is. The self is not a static substance; the self is an act; the self is
a becoming; the self is an ego. The self is not a thing that is; the self is a thing that becomes;
the self is a thing that strives. The self is khudi: the selfhood, the ego-hood, the individuality.
And the self is not a solitary ego; the self is a self in relation to other selves; the self is a self in
relation to God. The perfect self is the one who has realized the divine attributes within itself;
the perfect self is the vicegerent of God on earth.
      The scene is Iqbal’s image, in The Reconstruction and in Asrar-i-Khudi, of the structure of
reality. The verse is the revelation; the universe is the dynamic process; the self is the khudi.
The scene poses the question that Iqbal was the first to pose in its full form in the contemporary
Islamic tradition. What is the self? How does the self relate to God and to the universe? And
what is the task of the Muslim thinker in the modern world? The present chapter states Iqbal’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.



47.2       The Question

The previous part stated the positions of classical Islamic philosophy: al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn
Sina, al-Ghazali, Ibn Rushd, the Mu’tazila and the Ash’ariyya, Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Mulla
Sadra, and Ibn Khaldun. The classical tradition posed the problem of the one and the many, of
essence and existence, of light and manifestation, of the cycles of history. Iqbal is the first great
figure of the contemporary Islamic tradition, and he is the philosopher who asks whether the
tradition can be renewed: he reconstructs the religious thought in the light of modern knowledge;
he recovers the dynamic spirit of the Qur’an; he develops the doctrine of the self. The present
chapter states Iqbal’s reconstruction, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Iqbal was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Iqbal hold? The chapter states the reconstruction of
religious thought, the critique of Greek philosophy, the doctrine of khudi, the dynamic conception
of God and the universe, the principle of ijtihad, and the perfect human being, with reference to
the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Iqbal converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Iqbal would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Iqbal? The
chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.
47.3. The Position                                                                                  533


47.3      The Position

47.3.1    The Reconstruction of Religious Thought
Iqbal’s reconstruction of religious thought is stated in The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in
Islam (1930), a series of lectures delivered in Madras, Hyderabad, and Aligarh. The reconstruction
is not a rejection of the tradition; it is a renewal of the tradition; it is the recovery of the dynamic
spirit of the Qur’an from the static crust of the tradition.
   The reconstruction has three features.

First feature: the critique of the static conception. The reconstruction begins with a
critique of the static conception of the universe, which Iqbal attributes to the Greek influence
on Islamic thought. The Greek philosophers held that the universe is eternal, that change is an
illusion, and that the perfect is the unchanging. Iqbal argues that this view is incompatible with
the Qur’an, which presents a dynamic universe, a universe that is in motion, a universe that is
creative. The task of the reconstruction is to recover the Qur’anic view from the Greek crust.

Second feature: the engagement with modern knowledge. The reconstruction engages
with modern knowledge, especially with modern physics, biology, and psychology. Iqbal draws
on the work of Bergson, Whitehead, and Einstein to develop a dynamic conception of the
universe. The reconstruction is not a rejection of modern knowledge; it is an integration of
modern knowledge into the Islamic worldview.

Third feature: the recovery of the Qur’anic spirit. The reconstruction recovers the
Qur’anic spirit, which is the spirit of movement, of change, of creativity. The Qur’an presents
a God who creates, who acts, who responds; it presents a human being who strives, who acts,
who becomes; it presents a universe that is in process, that is dynamic, that is alive. The
reconstruction is the recovery of this spirit from the static crust of the tradition.
   The reconstruction is the foundation of Iqbal’s philosophy. It is the renewal of the tradition;
it is the integration of modern knowledge; it is the recovery of the Qur’anic spirit.

   From the Tradition

   “The Qur’an presents a dynamic universe, a universe that is in motion, a universe that is
   creative. The Greek view is static; the Qur’anic view is dynamic. The task of the Muslim
   thinker is to reconstruct the Islamic thought in the light of modern knowledge, and to
   recover the dynamic spirit of the Qur’an from the static crust of the tradition.” (Iqbal,
   The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, Lecture I, adapted)


47.3.2    The Critique of Greek Philosophy
Iqbal’s critique of Greek philosophy is stated in The Reconstruction and in his poetry. The
critique is not a rejection of Greek philosophy; it is a critique of the Greek influence on Islamic
thought; it is the recognition that the Greek view of the universe is static, and that the Qur’anic
view is dynamic.
534                                                                                  Chapter 47. Iqbal


      The critique has three features.

First feature: the static universe. The Greek philosophers held that the universe is eternal,
that change is an illusion, and that the perfect is the unchanging. This view is incompatible
with the Qur’an, which presents a universe that is created, that is in motion, that is dynamic.
The Greek view is the view of being; the Qur’anic view is the view of becoming.

Second feature: the critique of Plato. Iqbal criticizes Plato for his theory of Forms, which
he sees as the source of the static conception. The Forms are eternal, unchanging, separate from
the world; the world is a shadow of the Forms. Iqbal argues that this view is incompatible with
the Qur’anic view of a dynamic, creative universe. He calls Plato the “leader of the old herd of
sheep,” though this is a poet’s hyperbole rather than a philosopher’s judgment.

Third feature: the recovery of the Qur’anic dynamism. The critique is not merely
negative; it is also positive. Iqbal recovers the Qur’anic dynamism, which is the view of a universe
that is in process, that is creative, that is alive. The Qur’anic view is the view of becoming, not
of being; it is the view of movement, not of stasis; it is the view of life, not of death.
      The critique is the key to Iqbal’s philosophy. It is the rejection of the static conception; it is
the affirmation of the dynamic conception; it is the recovery of the Qur’anic spirit.

47.3.3       The Doctrine of Khudi
Iqbal’s doctrine of khudi is stated in Asrar-i-Khudi (The Secrets of the Self, 1915) and in The
Reconstruction. The khudi is the selfhood, the ego-hood, the individuality; it is the self as an act,
as a becoming, as a striving.
      The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the self as an act. The self is not a static substance; the self is an act; the self
is a becoming; the self is a striving. The self is not a thing that is; the self is a thing that becomes;
the self is a thing that strives. The self is khudi: the selfhood, the ego-hood, the individuality.

Second feature: the self and the other. The self is not a solitary ego; the self is a self in
relation to other selves; the self is a self in relation to God. The self is not a monad; the self is a
relation; the self is a dialogue. The self is not a closed system; the self is an open system; the self
is a process of becoming.

Third feature: the perfection of the self. The perfection of the self is not the annihilation
of the self; it is the intensification of the self. The perfect self is the one who has realized the
divine attributes within itself; the perfect self is the one who has become the vicegerent of God on
earth; the perfect self is the one who has attained the khudi in its highest form. The perfection
is not the loss of the self; it is the fulfillment of the self.
      The doctrine is the key to Iqbal’s philosophy. It is the self as an act; it is the self in relation;
it is the perfection of the self.
47.3. The Position                                                                                   535


   From the Tradition

   “The self is not a static substance; the self is an act; the self is a becoming; the self is a
   striving. The perfection of the self is not the annihilation of the self; it is the intensification
   of the self. The perfect self is the one who has realized the divine attributes within itself.”
   (Iqbal, Asrar-i-Khudi, trans. after Nicholson, adapted)


47.3.4    The Dynamic Conception of God and the Universe

Iqbal’s dynamic conception of God and the universe is stated in The Reconstruction and in his
poetry. The conception is the foundation of Iqbal’s theology; it is the alternative to the static
conception of the Greek philosophers.
   The conception has three features.


First feature: the dynamic God. God is not a static being; God is a dynamic being; God
is a creative being; God is a living being. God creates, God acts, God responds. God is not the
unmoved mover; God is the mover who moves; God is the creator who creates. The dynamic
God is the God of the Qur’an, not the God of the philosophers.


Second feature: the dynamic universe. The universe is not a static order; the universe is
a dynamic process; the universe is a creative advance. The universe is not a finished product;
the universe is an ongoing process; the universe is a becoming. The universe is not a machine;
the universe is an organism; the universe is a life.


Third feature: the relation between God and the universe. The relation between God
and the universe is not the relation between the unmoved mover and the moved; it is the relation
between the creator and the creation; it is the relation between the living God and the living
universe. The universe is not God; the universe is not separate from God; the universe is the
creation of God, and it is sustained by God.
   The conception is the key to Iqbal’s theology. It is the dynamic God; it is the dynamic
universe; it is the relation between the two.


47.3.5    The Principle of Ijtihad

Iqbal’s principle of ijtihad is stated in The Reconstruction, Lecture VI. The ijtihad is the principle
of movement in the structure of Islam; it is the exercise of independent judgment in matters of
law; it is the dynamic principle that keeps the Islamic law alive.
   The principle has three features.


First feature: the rejection of taqlid. Iqbal rejects taqlid, the blind following of the past
jurists. He argues that the completion of the Qur’anic message does not mean that the details
worked out by the past jurists are binding for all times. The past jurists worked under different
conditions; their judgments were for their time; the Muslim of the modern world must exercise
ijtihad to apply the principles to the new conditions.
536                                                                                 Chapter 47. Iqbal


Second feature: the exercise of ijtihad. The ijtihad is the exercise of independent judgment;
it is the right of the qualified jurist to interpret the law in the light of the Qur’an and the Sunnah,
and in the light of the modern conditions. The ijtihad is not the rejection of the tradition; it is
the renewal of the tradition; it is the application of the principles to the new conditions.

Third feature: the collective ijtihad. Iqbal proposes that the ijtihad should be exercised
collectively, by an assembly of qualified jurists, rather than individually. The collective ijtihad is
the democratic principle; it is the principle of the consultation; it is the principle of the consensus.
The collective ijtihad is the way to keep the Islamic law alive in the modern world.
      The principle is the key to Iqbal’s reformism. It is the rejection of taqlid; it is the exercise of
ijtihad; it is the collective ijtihad.

47.3.6       The Perfect Human Being
Iqbal’s doctrine of the perfect human being (insan al-kamil) is stated in Asrar-i-Khudi and in
The Reconstruction. The perfect human being is the one who has realized the divine attributes
within himself; the perfect human being is the vicegerent of God on earth; the perfect human
being is the goal of humanity.
      The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the divine attributes. The perfect human being is the one who has realized
the divine attributes within himself; he is the one who has become the mirror of God; he is the
one in whom the divine names are manifested. The perfect human being is not God; he is the
vicegerent of God; he is the representative of God on earth.

Second feature: the vicegerent. The perfect human being is the vicegerent (khalifa) of
God; he is the ruler of the earth; he is the trustee of the divine authority. The vicegerent is not
the slave of God; he is the partner of God; he is the co-worker with God in the creation and the
ordering of the world.

Third feature: the goal of humanity. The perfect human being is the goal of humanity; he
is the end of the evolution; he is the acme of life. The evolution of humanity is the evolution
toward the perfect human being; the history of humanity is the history of the approach to the
perfect human being. The perfect human being is the ideal; he is the model; he is the hope.
      The doctrine is the key to Iqbal’s anthropology. It is the divine attributes; it is the vicegerent;
it is the goal of humanity.


47.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Iqbal is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of khudi. The traditional reading takes khudi to be the ego, the
self, the individuality. A revisionary reading takes it to be the principle of individuation, the
principle of uniqueness, the principle of creativity. The two readings disagree on whether Iqbal is
47.5. Points of Convergence                                                                         537


an individualist or a personalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s identity is a structural condition, not an ego.

Second dispute: the status of the perfect human being. The traditional reading takes
the perfect human being to be a real human being, a prophet or a saint, the model of the Muslim
life. A revisionary reading takes it to be an ideal, a symbol, a goal of the evolution. The two
readings disagree on whether Iqbal is a mystic or a philosopher, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no perfect human being; its subject is
the structure of identity and manifestation.

Third dispute: the status of ijtihad. The traditional reading takes ijtihad to be the legal
principle, the exercise of independent judgment in matters of law. A revisionary reading takes it
to be the principle of movement, the principle of change, the principle of renewal in all matters
of thought. The two readings disagree on whether Iqbal is a jurist or a reformer, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no legal principle;
its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Iqbal is an individualist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an individualist personalism.
If Iqbal is a reformer, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a reformist
modernism. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts of Iqbal, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.


47.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Iqbal. The framework shares four structural features with Iqbal’s position.

       1. The priority of the dynamic over the static. Iqbal holds that the universe is dynamic,
          not static; it is in process, not at rest; it is creative, not fixed. The framework holds
          that reality is expression, not substance; it is the enactment of the identity, not the
          static form. Both hold that reality is dynamic, and that the dynamic is the truth of
          the static.

       2. The critique of the static conception. Iqbal holds that the Greek view of the universe
          is static, and that the Qur’anic view is dynamic. The framework holds that the
          tradition has conflated identity with manifestation; it has reduced the identity to
          its manifestations; it has collapsed the structural difference. Both hold that the
          tradition has made a mistake, and that the mistake is the collapse of a distinction.

       3. The reality of the self. Iqbal holds that the self is real; it is an act; it is a becoming;
          it is a striving. The framework holds that the identity is real; it is the invariance
          enacted by one source; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. Both hold
538                                                                                Chapter 47. Iqbal


          that the self is real, and that the self is not a static substance.

       4. The perfection of the self. Iqbal holds that the perfection of the self is not the
          annihilation of the self; it is the intensification of the self. The framework holds that
          the expression of the identity is not the loss of the identity; it is the manifestation of
          the identity. Both hold that the perfection is not the loss, but the fulfillment.



47.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Iqbal. The framework diverges from Iqbal in four respects.

       1. The status of God. Iqbal holds that God is a dynamic being, a creative being, a
          living being. The framework has no God; its First Determination is a realm of pure
          unity; it is not a creator; it is not a person; it is not a God. The framework is a
          metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the self. Iqbal holds that the self is an ego, a becoming, a striving; the
          self is khudi. The framework holds that the identity is a structural condition; it is
          the invariance enacted by one source; it is not an ego. The framework’s identity is
          not a self; it is a structure.

       3. The status of ijtihad. Iqbal holds that ijtihad is the principle of movement in Islam;
          it is the exercise of independent judgment; it is the dynamic principle of the law.
          The framework has no law; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation;
          it leaves the legal question to a separate inquiry. The framework is a metaphysics
          without a legal principle.

       4. The status of the perfect human being. Iqbal holds that the perfect human being is
          the vicegerent of God; he is the goal of humanity; he is the model of the Muslim life.
          The framework has no perfect human being; its subject is the structure of identity
          and manifestation; it leaves the ethical and the political question to a separate
          inquiry. The framework is a metaphysics without a perfect human being.



47.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Iqbal’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not a
  self; it is a pattern. The self is an act; the self is a becoming; the self is a striving. The
  framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not a self. The framework’s ontology is
  an ontology of patterns, not of selves.
47.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      539


  Iqbal’s second objection. The framework says that there is one truth: the structural
  truth. But the truth is dynamic; it is creative; it is alive. The framework’s truth is
  static; it is a structure; it is a pattern. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of static
  structures, not of dynamic truths.
  Iqbal’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not value.
  But a metaphysics without value is an incomplete metaphysics; the question of value
  is the fundamental question; the question of the meaning of existence is the question
  of philosophy. The framework’s silence on value is not a boundary; it is a gap. The
  framework’s philosophy is a philosophy without value, and a philosophy without value is a
  philosophy without life.




47.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a self, and
  it agrees that the self is an act, a becoming, a striving. But the framework denies that
  its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
  source—a this, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the act of the identity in
  its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
  which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
  calls act. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
  concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first. The framework does
  not claim that its identity is a self; it claims that its identity is a structure, and it leaves
  the self to a separate inquiry.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the truth is dynamic,
  and it agrees that the truth is creative. But the framework denies that the truth is only
  dynamic. The framework’s truth is structural; it is the truth of the structure; it is the
  truth of the invariance. The truth is not a static pattern; it is the structural condition
  of the dynamic manifestation. The distinction is between a static pattern (which the
  framework rejects) and a structural truth (which the framework affirms). The framework’s
  truth is structural, not static.
  Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without value
  is incomplete, and it agrees that the question of value is fundamental. But the framework
  denies that its silence on value is a gap. The framework is a work of metaphysics, not of
  ethics; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation, not the value of existence.
  The framework states the structural condition of reality; it leaves the question of value to
  a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics and an ethics; the framework
  keeps it, and it holds that keeping it is not a gap, but a boundary.
540                                                                             Chapter 47. Iqbal


47.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Iqbal’s cost. If Iqbal accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the self
is an ego. He must accept that the identity is a structural condition, and that the self is a
manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of the individuality: the self is no longer an
ego; the self is a structure. He must also give up the claim that God is a dynamic being; he must
accept that the First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a God. The cost is the loss of
the dynamic God: the God is no longer a creator; the God is a structural condition.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Iqbal’s objections, it must give up the claim
that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the dimension
of the self, of the dynamic God, of the value—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the
loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a
structure, but not a self, and the framework leaves the self to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Iqbal’s self is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Iqbal
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that
the self presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


47.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Iqbal’s
   term “khudi.” If one substitutes “khudi” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; Iqbal’s khudi is the self, the ego, the individuality. The
   framework’s identity is a structure; Iqbal’s khudi is a self. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Iqbal’s term “the dynamic
   process.” If one substitutes “the dynamic process” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   Iqbal’s dynamic process is the creative advance. The framework’s expression is structural;
   Iqbal’s dynamic process is creative. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “structure” is not substitutable for Iqbal’s term “the perfect human
   being.” If one substitutes “the perfect human being” for “structure” in the framework’s
47.11. Open Questions                                                                          541


   statements, the statements change: the framework’s structure is the condition of possibility
   of the manifestation; Iqbal’s perfect human being is the vicegerent of God on earth.
   The framework’s structure is impersonal; Iqbal’s perfect human being is personal. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Iqbal is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is dynamic, and they differ on whether the dynamic is a structure
   or a self. Both hold that the self is real, and they differ on whether the self is an ego or
   a structural condition. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is
   identity. The framework’s reading of Iqbal would be refuted by showing that Iqbal’s khudi
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and self—by
   showing, that is, that Iqbal already distinguishes the structural condition from the self,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Iqbal’s own.




47.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Iqbal’s khudi, or is it a departure
from Iqbal? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not conclusive.
A reader who holds that Iqbal’s khudi is already a structural condition, not an ego, has a question
the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of The Reconstruction and Asrar-i-Khudi do
justice to the texts? The chapter has used the reconstruction of religious thought, the critique of
Greek philosophy, the doctrine of khudi, the dynamic conception of God and the universe, the
principle of ijtihad, and the perfect human being, and it has stated what would refute its reading.
A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.
