A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a self and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the self that strives, or the structure that persists? Is the truth the dynamic
process that creates, or the structural condition that enacts? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Iqbal’s khudi and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Tabatabai. It states the principles of philosophy ( usul al-falsafa), the
method of realism, the primacy of existence, the gradation of existence, the theory of knowledge,
and the interpretation of the Qur’an; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of Tabatabai; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of existence and of knowledge is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Tabatabai’s.
The present chapter has stated Iqbal’s answer to the problem of the self; the next chapter states
Tabatabai’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 48

Tabatabai


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Muhammad Husayn Tabatabai (1903–1981 CE), the
Iranian philosopher, Qur’anic commentator, and teacher of the generation of contemporary
Islamic philosophers in Iran. It states Tabatabai’s principles of philosophy (usul al-falsafa), the
method of realism, the primacy of existence (asalat al-wujud), the gradation of existence (tashkik
al-wujud), the theory of knowledge (’ilm huduri and ’ilm husuli), the doctrine of the soul, and the
interpretation of the Qur’an in al-Mizan fi Tafsir al-Qur’an (The Balance in the Interpretation of
the Qur’an), with reference to Usul-i Falsafa wa Ravish-i Ri’alism (The Principles of Philosophy
and the Method of Realism), Bidayat al-Hikma (The Beginning of Wisdom), Nihayat al-Hikma
(The End of Wisdom), and al-Mizan; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Tabatabai; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of existence and of knowledge is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Tabatabai’s;
it presents the objections that Tabatabai would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the principles of philosophy,” “the method of realism,”
“the primacy of existence,” “the gradation of existence,” “the knowledge by presence,” or “the
knowledge by acquisition,” these are Tabatabai’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


48.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a tree. She sees the trunk, the branches, the leaves, the
green color, the shadow on the ground. She sees the tree as a thing; she sees it as a substance;
she sees it as something that exists. But what is the tree? Is it the trunk, the branches, the
leaves? Is it the green color? Is it the shadow? The tree is not any of these; the tree is the thing
that has these; the tree is the substance that underlies these; the tree is the existence that makes
these to be.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the tree is, or how it appears, but
what existence is. The existence is not a concept; it is not a predicate; it is not an accident added
to the essence. The existence is the very act of being; it is the reality that makes the tree to be;
it is the most fundamental of all things. The existence is one; the things are its gradations; the
things are the degrees of existence. This is what Tabatabai calls the primacy of existence and
the gradation of existence: existence is the fundamental reality, and the things are its degrees.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the tree is, or what
existence is, but what knowledge is. The knowledge is not the concept of the tree; the knowledge
is not the image of the tree; the knowledge is not the representation of the tree. The knowledge

                                                543
544                                                                         Chapter 48. Tabatabai


is the presence of the tree to the knower; the knowledge is the union of the knower and the
known; the knowledge is the ’ilm huduri, the knowledge by presence. And the knowledge by
presence is the foundation of all knowledge; it is the knowledge that the soul has of itself; it is
the knowledge that the soul has of its Lord.
      The scene is Tabatabai’s image, in the Usul-i Falsafa and in the al-Mizan, of the structure
of reality. The tree is the thing; the existence is the fundamental reality; the knowledge is the
presence. The scene poses the question that Tabatabai was the first to pose in its full form in
the contemporary Islamic tradition. What is existence? What is knowledge? And what is the
relation between the two? The present chapter states Tabatabai’s answer, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.


48.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Iqbal’s position: the reconstruction of religious thought, the critique
of Greek philosophy, the doctrine of khudi, the dynamic conception of God and the universe, the
principle of ijtihad, and the perfect human being. Iqbal is the great reformer of modern Islamic
thought; he reconstructs the tradition in the light of modern knowledge; he recovers the dynamic
spirit of the Qur’an. Tabatabai is the great systematizer of contemporary Islamic philosophy
in Iran; he is the teacher of the generation of contemporary Islamic philosophers; he develops
the principles of philosophy and the method of realism. The present chapter states Tabatabai’s
principles, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Tabatabai was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Tabatabai hold? The chapter states the principles of
philosophy, the method of realism, the primacy of existence, the gradation of existence, the
theory of knowledge, the doctrine of the soul, and the interpretation of the Qur’an, with reference
to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Tabatabai converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Tabatabai would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Tabatabai?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


48.3       The Position

48.3.1      The Principles of Philosophy

Tabatabai’s principles of philosophy (usul al-falsafa) are stated in Usul-i Falsafa wa Ravish-i
Ri’alism (The Principles of Philosophy and the Method of Realism, 1950s), a work that Tabatabai
48.3. The Position                                                                               545


dictated to his student Murtada Mutahhari. The principles are the foundation of Tabatabai’s
philosophy; they are the systematic articulation of the Islamic philosophical tradition.
   The principles have three features.


First feature: the realism. The principles are realist; they affirm the reality of the external
world; they affirm the reality of the things; they affirm the reality of the existence. The realism
is the foundation of Tabatabai’s philosophy; it is the alternative to the idealism of the modern
Western philosophy.


Second feature: the primacy of existence. The principles affirm the primacy of existence
(asalat al-wujud); existence is the fundamental reality; the essence is a limitation of existence.
The primacy of existence is the foundation of Tabatabai’s metaphysics; it is the inheritance of
Mulla Sadra’s philosophy.


Third feature: the gradation of existence. The principles affirm the gradation of existence
(tashkik al-wujud); existence is one, but it has degrees; the things are the degrees of existence.
The gradation of existence is the foundation of Tabatabai’s cosmology; it is the reconciliation of
the one and the many.
   The principles are the foundation of Tabatabai’s philosophy. They are the realism; they are
the primacy of existence; they are the gradation of existence.

   From the Tradition

   “The principles of philosophy are the principles of realism: the reality of the external world,
   the primacy of existence, and the gradation of existence. These are the foundations of the
   Islamic philosophical tradition, and they are the answer to the idealism of the modern
   Western philosophy.” (Tabatabai, Usul-i Falsafa, trans. after Rizvi, adapted)



48.3.2    The Method of Realism

Tabatabai’s method of realism (ravish-i ri’alism) is a development of his principles of philosophy.
The method is the way of knowing the reality; it is the method of the philosophical realism.
   The method has three features.


First feature: the affirmation of reality. The method affirms the reality of the external
world; it affirms the reality of the things; it affirms the reality of the existence. The affirmation
is not a proof; it is a starting point; it is a commitment. The realism is the foundation; the proof
is the consequence.


Second feature: the rejection of idealism. The method rejects the idealism of the modern
Western philosophy; it rejects the claim that the world is a construction of the mind; it rejects the
claim that the existence is a concept. The realism is the alternative; the reality is the foundation;
the existence is the act.
546                                                                          Chapter 48. Tabatabai


Third feature: the combination of the demonstration and the intuition. The method
combines the demonstration and the intuition; the demonstration gives the knowledge by
acquisition; the intuition gives the knowledge by presence. The two are not in conflict; they are
complementary; they are the two wings of the philosophy.
      The method is the key to Tabatabai’s philosophy. It is the affirmation of reality; it is the
rejection of idealism; it is the combination of the demonstration and the intuition.


48.3.3      The Primacy of Existence

Tabatabai’s doctrine of the primacy of existence is the inheritance of Mulla Sadra’s philosophy.
The doctrine has three features.


First feature: existence is the fundamental reality. Existence is the fundamental reality;
it is not a concept; it is not a predicate; it is not an accident. Existence is the very act of being;
it is the reality that makes the thing to be; it is the most fundamental of all things.


Second feature: the primacy of existence over essence. The primacy of existence over
essence is the claim that existence is prior to essence; the essence is derived from existence;
the essence is the determination of existence. The Peripatetic philosophy holds the primacy of
essence; Tabatabai holds the primacy of existence.


Third feature: the reality of existence. Existence is real; it is not a mental construct; it is
not a logical category; it is the very reality of the thing. The existence is not a universal; it is
not a genus; it is not a category; it is the act of being; it is the most real of all things.
      The doctrine is the key to Tabatabai’s metaphysics. It is the primacy of existence; it is the
reality of existence; it is the act of being.


48.3.4      The Gradation of Existence

Tabatabai’s doctrine of the gradation of existence is a development of his doctrine of the primacy
of existence. The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the gradation. Existence is one; but it has degrees; it has gradations; it
has levels. The existence of God is the highest; the existence of the intellects is the next; the
existence of the souls is the next; the existence of the material things is the lowest. The existence
is one; the degrees are many; the degrees are the gradations of one existence.


Second feature: the unity in multiplicity. The gradation of existence is the unity in
multiplicity; it is the one in the many; it is the many in the one. The existence is one; the things
are many; the things are the degrees of existence; the existence is not multiplied by the degrees.


Third feature: the reality of the degrees. The degrees are real; they are not illusions;
they are not mental constructs; they are the real gradations of the real existence. The degrees
48.3. The Position                                                                               547


are the determinations of existence; they are the modes in which existence appears; they are the
levels of the manifestation.
   The doctrine is the key to Tabatabai’s cosmology. It is the gradation of existence; it is the
unity in multiplicity; it is the reconciliation of the one and the many.


48.3.5    The Theory of Knowledge
Tabatabai’s theory of knowledge is stated in Usul-i Falsafa and in al-Mizan. The theory
distinguishes two kinds of knowledge: the knowledge by presence (’ilm huduri) and the knowledge
by acquisition (’ilm husuli).
   The theory has three features.

First feature: the knowledge by presence. The knowledge by presence is the direct
knowledge; it is the presence of the known to the knower; it is the knowledge that the soul has of
itself; it is the knowledge that the soul has of its states; it is the knowledge that the soul has of
its Lord. The knowledge by presence is the foundation of all knowledge; it is the most certain
knowledge.

Second feature: the knowledge by acquisition. The knowledge by acquisition is the
indirect knowledge; it is the knowledge through the concepts; it is the knowledge through the
images; it is the knowledge of the external world. The knowledge by acquisition is derived from
the knowledge by presence; it is mediated; it is fallible.

Third feature: the correspondence. The knowledge by acquisition corresponds to the
reality; it is the correspondence between the concept and the thing; it is the correspondence
between the image and the object. The correspondence is the criterion of the truth; it is the
foundation of the knowledge by acquisition.
   The theory is the key to Tabatabai’s epistemology. It is the knowledge by presence; it is the
knowledge by acquisition; it is the correspondence.


48.3.6    The Doctrine of the Soul
Tabatabai’s doctrine of the soul is stated in Usul-i Falsafa and in al-Mizan. The doctrine is the
inheritance of Mulla Sadra’s philosophy; it is the foundation of Tabatabai’s psychology.
   The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the soul is a substance. The soul is a substance; it is not a body; it is not
an accident; it is the form of the body; it is the principle of life. The soul is a substance that
becomes; it is a substantial motion; it is a trans-substantial becoming.

Second feature: the levels of the soul. The soul has levels; it has gradations; it has stages.
The soul begins as a material soul; it becomes a vegetative soul; it becomes an animal soul; it
becomes a human soul; it becomes an angelic soul. The soul is not a substance that has accidents;
the soul is a substance that becomes; the soul is the becoming itself.
548                                                                          Chapter 48. Tabatabai


Third feature: the immortality of the soul. The immortality of the soul is not the
persistence of a static substance; it is the continuation of the becoming; it is the continuation of
the motion. The soul does not die with the body; the soul continues in the becoming; the soul
continues in the motion; the soul continues in the levels.
      The doctrine is the key to Tabatabai’s psychology. It is the substance; it is the levels; it is
the immortality.


48.3.7      The Interpretation of the Qur’an

Tabatabai’s interpretation of the Qur’an is stated in al-Mizan fi Tafsir al-Qur’an (The Balance
in the Interpretation of the Qur’an, 20 volumes, 1956–1972). The interpretation is the foundation
of Tabatabai’s Qur’anic scholarship; it is the interpretation of the Qur’an by the Qur’an; it is
the interpretation of the Qur’an in the light of the philosophical principles.
      The interpretation has three features.


First feature: the interpretation by the Qur’an. The interpretation is by the Qur’an; it
is the interpretation of the verse by the verse; it is the interpretation of the verse in the light of
the other verses. The Qur’an is the guide; the Qur’an is the criterion; the Qur’an is the source.


Second feature: the use of the philosophical principles. The interpretation uses the
philosophical principles; it uses the realism; it uses the primacy of existence; it uses the gradation
of existence. The philosophy is the tool; it is the instrument; it is the servant of the interpretation.


Third feature: the balance. The balance (al-mizan) is the criterion of the interpretation; it
is the balance between the reason and the revelation; it is the balance between the philosophy
and the faith. The balance is the harmony; it is the reconciliation; it is the unity.
      The interpretation is the key to Tabatabai’s Qur’anic scholarship. It is the interpretation by
the Qur’an; it is the use of the philosophical principles; it is the balance.



48.4        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Tabatabai is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the primacy of existence. The traditional reading takes
the primacy of existence to be a metaphysical doctrine: existence is the fundamental reality;
the essence is a limitation of existence. A revisionary reading takes it to be a phenomenological
doctrine: the primacy of existence is the primacy of the act of being; it is the primacy of the
presence; it is the primacy of the intuition. The two readings disagree on whether Tabatabai is a
metaphysician or a phenomenologist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s identity is a structural condition, neither a metaphysical substance nor
a phenomenological presence.
48.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      549


Second dispute: the status of the knowledge by presence. The traditional reading takes
the knowledge by presence to be a certain knowledge: it is the knowledge that the soul has of
itself; it is the knowledge that the soul has of its Lord; it is the foundation of all knowledge.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a form of knowledge: it is one kind of knowledge among
others; it is not more certain than the knowledge by acquisition; it is not the foundation of all
knowledge. The two readings disagree on whether Tabatabai is a foundationalist or a coherentist,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s knowledge
is neither foundationalist nor coherentist, but structural.

Third dispute: the status of the interpretation. The traditional reading takes the
interpretation to be a philosophical interpretation: it is the interpretation of the Qur’an in the
light of the philosophical principles; it is the reconciliation of the philosophy and the faith. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a traditional interpretation: it is the interpretation of the
Qur’an in the light of the tradition; it is the interpretation of the Qur’an by the Qur’an; it
is not the philosophy, but the tradition. The two readings disagree on whether Tabatabai is
a philosopher or a traditionalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework is a philosophy, not a tradition.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Tabatabai is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysical existentialism.
If Tabatabai is a traditionalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
traditionalist philosophy. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of
Tabatabai, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


48.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Tabatabai. The framework shares four structural features with Tabatabai’s
   position.

       1. The realism. Tabatabai holds that the external world is real; the things are real; the
          existence is real. The framework holds that the manifestations are real; the realms
          are real; the structure is real. Both hold that reality is real, and that the realism is
          the foundation of the philosophy.

       2. The primacy of existence. Tabatabai holds that existence is the fundamental reality;
          the essence is a limitation of existence. The framework holds that the identity is the
          fundamental reality; the manifestation is the appearance of the identity. Both hold
          that there is a fundamental reality, and that the fundamental reality is the act of
          being.

       3. The knowledge by presence. Tabatabai holds that the knowledge by presence is the
          direct knowledge; it is the presence of the known to the knower. The framework
550                                                                         Chapter 48. Tabatabai


          holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction
          is the presence of the identity to the subject. Both hold that knowledge is not merely
          conceptual, and that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not
          capture.

       4. The interpretation of the Qur’an. Tabatabai holds that the interpretation is by the
          Qur’an; it is the interpretation of the verse by the verse. The framework holds that
          the structure is interpreted by the structure; the structure is the interpretation of
          the manifestation by the manifestation. Both hold that the interpretation is by the
          source, and that the source is the criterion.




48.6      Points of Divergence


  Points of Divergence

  With Tabatabai. The framework diverges from Tabatabai in four respects.

       1. The status of existence. Tabatabai holds that existence is the fundamental reality; it
          is the very act of being. The framework holds that the identity is the fundamental
          reality; it is the invariance enacted by one source. The framework’s identity is
          not existence; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. The framework’s
          metaphysics is a metaphysics of identity, not of existence.

       2. The status of the knowledge by presence. Tabatabai holds that the knowledge
          by presence is the certain knowledge; it is the foundation of all knowledge. The
          framework holds that the reconstruction is the fallible knowledge; it is the reading
          of the manifestations. The framework’s knowledge is structural, not presential.

       3. The status of the interpretation. Tabatabai holds that the interpretation is by the
          Qur’an; it is the interpretation of the verse by the verse. The framework holds that
          the interpretation is by the structure; it is the interpretation of the manifestation by
          the manifestation. The framework’s interpretation is structural, not Qur’anic.

       4. The status of the tradition. Tabatabai holds that the tradition is the foundation; the
          philosophy is the tool; the philosophy is the servant of the tradition. The framework
          holds that its structure is autonomous; it does not depend on any tradition; its
          truth is structural, not traditional. The framework’s autonomy is the rejection of
          the priority of the tradition.
48.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                              551


48.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Tabatabai’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not existence; it is a pattern. The world is composed of existences; the world is not just
   structured; the world is a plurality of acts of being. The framework has no existence; the
   framework has no act of being; the framework’s world is a world without existence. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of existence.
   Tabatabai’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the degrees of existence; they are the gradations of the act of being. The
   framework’s realms are not degrees of existence; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of existence.
   Tabatabai’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
   is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the knowledge by presence; it is the
   presence of the known to the knower; it is the certainty. The framework’s knowledge is a
   mediation; it is not the presence. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of
   mediation, not of presence.



48.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is composed of
   existences, and it agrees that the existence is the act of being. But the framework denies
   that the existence must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition of the manifestation; it is
   the act of being of the thing. The distinction is between an existence (an act of being) and
   an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not the first. The
   framework does not deny the existence; it denies that the existence is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are degrees. But the framework denies that the degrees are
   degrees of existence. The framework’s degrees are degrees of manifestation; the degrees
   are the levels of the expression; the degrees are the modes in which the identity appears.
   The distinction is between a degree of existence (an ontological degree) and a degree of
   manifestation (a structural degree); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the presence. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it
552                                                                       Chapter 48. Tabatabai


   is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a presence (an
   identity) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



48.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Tabatabai’s cost. If Tabatabai accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the existence is the fundamental reality. He must accept that the identity is the structural
condition, and that the existence is the act of being of the thing. The cost is the loss of the
primacy of existence: the existence is no longer the fundamental reality; the identity is the
structural condition. He must also give up the claim that the knowledge is the presence; he
must accept that the knowledge is the reconstruction; the reconstruction is the reading of the
manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Tabatabai’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the existence, of the knowledge by presence, of the tradition—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the existence, and the framework leaves the
existence to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Tabatabai’s existence
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Tabatabai must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition
that the existence presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


48.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Tabatabai’s term “existence.” If one substitutes “existence” for “identity” in the frame-
   work’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Tabatabai’s existence is the act of
   being, and it is not manifested, because it is the fundamental reality. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; Tabatabai’s existence is one. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
48.11. Open Questions                                                                         553


   The framework’s term “knowledge” is not substitutable for Tabatabai’s term “the knowl-
   edge by presence.” If one substitutes “the knowledge by presence” for “knowledge” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s knowledge is reconstruc-
   tion; Tabatabai’s knowledge by presence is the presence. The framework’s knowledge is
   mediated; Tabatabai’s knowledge by presence is immediate. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “interpretation” is not substitutable for Tabatabai’s term “the
   interpretation by the Qur’an.” If one substitutes “the interpretation by the Qur’an” for
  “interpretation” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   interpretation is the reading of the manifestations; Tabatabai’s interpretation by the
   Qur’an is the reading of the verse by the verse. The framework’s interpretation is
   structural; Tabatabai’s interpretation is Qur’anic. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Tabatabai is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a fundamental reality, and they differ on whether the fundamental
   reality is existence or identity. Both hold that knowledge is not merely conceptual, and
   they differ on whether the knowledge is presence or reconstruction. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Tabatabai
   would be refuted by showing that Tabatabai’s existence cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structure and existence—by showing, that is, that
   Tabatabai already distinguishes the structural condition from the existence, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of Tabatabai’s own.



48.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Tabatabai’s existence, or is it a
departure from Tabatabai? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Tabatabai’s existence is already a structural condition,
not an act of being, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Usul-i Falsafa and al-Mizan do justice to
the texts? The chapter has used the principles of philosophy, the method of realism, the primacy
of existence, the gradation of existence, the theory of knowledge, the doctrine of the soul, and
the interpretation of the Qur’an, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an existence and a structure—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the existence that acts, or the structure that persists? Is the truth the
presence that is immediate, or the reconstruction that is mediated? What does your answer tell
you about the relation between Tabatabai’s primacy of existence and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Motahhari. It states his realism, his critique of materialism, the
doctrines of the primordial nature and of divine justice, and his account of the permanent and the
changing in the law; it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Motahhari; and it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the invariant
and the changing is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to his. The present chapter has
stated Tabatabai’s answer to the problem of existence; the next chapter states Motahhari’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 49

Motahhari


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Morteza Motahhari (1919–1979 CE), the Iranian
philosopher, theologian, and student of Tabatabai who became the most influential public
interpreter of Islamic philosophy in modern Iran. It states Motahhari’s realist theory of knowledge,
his critique of materialism, his doctrine of the primordial nature (fitra), his theodicy of divine
justice (’adl-i ilahi), and his account of the permanent and the changing in Islamic law and of
the dynamism of ijtihad, with reference to his explanatory notes on Usul-i Falsafa va Ravish-i
Ri’alism, to Mas’ala-yi Shinakht (The Problem of Knowledge), ’Adl-i Ilahi (Divine Justice),
’Ilal-i Gharayish bi Maddigari (The Causes of the Inclination to Materialism), and Khadamat-i
Muta’qabil-i Islam va Iran (The Mutual Services of Islam and Iran). It identifies the internal
disputes in the interpretation of Motahhari; it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of the invariant and the changing is the nearest contemporary
Islamic analogue to Motahhari’s account of the permanent and the changing; it presents the
objections that Motahhari would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply;
it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “the primordial nature,” “divine justice,” “the permanent and the changing,” or
“ijtihad,” these are Motahhari’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his works and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.


49.1      A Scene
Consider a physician in a village who has treated the same family for forty years. Medicines
have changed under her hands, techniques have been replaced, and the diseases of the village
have shifted with the roads and the wells. Yet there is something in her work that she would not
change for any new instrument: that the patient is to be healed, that the body has a nature that
she serves and does not make, and that some things done to it are wrong whatever the fashion.
She cannot say exactly where the line between what stays and what goes is drawn, but she draws
it every day.
    Consider now a student in a seminary who is asked a question that no earlier jurist faced: a
question about a technology, a market, a medical procedure that did not exist when the sources
were written. He cannot find the answer in a text, and he cannot invent one. He must find in
the sources the principles that the new case falls under, and he must see that the principles are
constant while the case is not. The dignity of his work lies in holding both.
    The two scenes pose one question: how can there be something permanent in a world that
changes, and how can what is permanent be applied to what is not? Motahhari held that
this question is the main question of Islamic thought in modern times, and that the answer

                                                555
556                                                                        Chapter 49. Motahhari


lies in a realist philosophy of knowledge and of being joined to a dynamic jurisprudence. The
framework poses the same question in its own register, as the relation of an invariant identity to
its manifestations. The chapter asks how the two answers stand to each other.


49.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Tabatabai’s principles of philosophy. Motahhari was his student,
and a large part of his work is the explanation, defense, and application of his teacher’s doctrines
to the questions of the modern age. But he is also an original thinker in his own right, and in
the dialogue he is not to be treated as a commentary on Tabatabai.
      The question is not whether Motahhari was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Motahhari hold? The chapter states his realism, his
critique of materialism, his doctrines of the primordial nature and of divine justice, and his
account of the permanent and the changing.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Motahhari converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Motahhari would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Motahhari?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


49.3       Motahhari’s Position
Motahhari’s thought begins from the claim that human beings are able to know reality as it is,
and that every serious alternative, in the form of skepticism, relativism, or an idealism that denies
the independence of the world, is both self-undermining and corrosive of religious and social life.
His philosophy is thus a defense of realism, which he takes from Tabatabai and develops in a
broader polemical and pedagogical direction.


49.3.1      Knowledge and the Critique of Materialism

In Mas’ala-yi Shinakht Motahhari discusses the problem of knowledge in its Islamic and Western
forms. He argues that sense experience alone cannot ground the certainty of the first principles of
reason, such as the principle of non-contradiction, and that there are primary rational propositions
that are known without proof and that every proof presupposes. In ’Ilal-i Gharayish bi Maddigari
he turns to the history of materialism and argues that its appeal is to be explained by social and
psychological causes and not by the strength of its arguments. He treats dialectical materialism,
which was a live option among Iranian intellectuals of his generation, as a philosophy whose own
principles cannot be justified within it.
49.4. Internal Disputes                                                                       557


49.3.2    The Primordial Nature

Motahhari holds, with the Qur’anic and philosophical tradition, that human beings have a
primordial nature (fitra), an original disposition toward truth, toward the good, and toward
God, that precedes culture and education. The nature is not a set of acquired opinions; it is a
structure of the human being that education may nourish or obscure. He uses the doctrine to
answer the claim that all human values are products of social conditions.


49.3.3    Divine Justice and the Permanent and the Changing

In ’Adl-i Ilahi Motahhari defends the Imamite and Mu’tazili thesis that God’s acts are just, in
the sense that they conform to a reality of the good that is not constituted by the divine will,
against the Ash’arite thesis that justice is what God wills. He holds that the problem of evil is
to be answered by the doctrine that evil is a privation and that the good of the whole includes
what appears as evil in a part. In his writings on jurisprudence he distinguishes the permanent
from the changing in the law: the foundations of the law rest on constant human needs and on
constant principles, and the rulings that apply them change with circumstances. Ijtihad is the
discipline by which a jurist relates the two, and it is the mechanism by which Islam remains alive.



49.4     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Motahhari is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: philosopher or populariser. One reading takes Motahhari to be an original
philosopher who developed the realism of his teacher in a creative direction. Another takes him
to be an unusually gifted populariser who explained Tabatabai and the philosophical tradition
to a wide public. The disagreement matters for the framework because the dialogue is with a
position, and the reading decides whether the position is Motahhari’s or his teacher’s.


Second dispute: the relation of philosophy and politics. Motahhari was an adviser to
the revolutionary movement of 1979 and was assassinated in the same year. One reading takes
his philosophy to be inseparable from his political commitment. Another takes the philosophy to
stand on its own. The disagreement matters because the framework makes no normative claim,
and the dialogue must decide what part of the position it takes up.


Third dispute: the dynamism of ijtihad. One reading takes Motahhari to hold that the law
can change substantially with circumstances. Another takes him to hold that only applications
change, and the principles are fixed. The disagreement matters because the framework’s relation
to the position depends on how much change the permanent is allowed to bear.
558                                                                        Chapter 49. Motahhari


49.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Motahhari. The framework shares four structural features with Motahhari’s
  position.

       1. The realism. Motahhari holds that reality can be known as it is and that the denial
          of this is self-undermining. The framework holds that identities are real and that
          reconstruction is of what is. Both hold that the realism is the foundation of the
          philosophy.

       2. The distinction of the permanent and the changing. Motahhari distinguishes the
          permanent principles of the law from the changing rulings. The framework distin-
          guishes the conserved identity from the changing manifestations. Both hold that
         what changes is intelligible only in relation to what does not.

       3. The primary rational propositions. Motahhari holds that there are primary proposi-
          tions that every proof presupposes. The framework holds that some principles are
          axioms that every argument presupposes and marks them as such. Both hold that
          not everything can be proved.

       4. The resistance to reduction. Motahhari resists the reduction of human values to social
          conditions, and the framework resists the reduction of identity to its manifestations.
          Both hold that there is something that the reductive account leaves out.



49.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Motahhari. The framework diverges from Motahhari’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of the primordial nature. Motahhari holds that human beings have a
          primordial nature with a content directed to God. The framework states the identity
          of a subject as a structural condition and does not give it a determinate content.

       2. The status of the good. Motahhari holds that there is a reality of the good that
          the divine justice conforms to. The framework makes no claim about the good and
          treats viability as descriptive.

       3. The status of revelation. For Motahhari the sources of the law are the Qur’an and
          the Sunna, and philosophy serves the understanding of them. The framework treats
          the autonomy of philosophical justification as basic.

       4. The explanation of error. Motahhari explains the appeal of materialism by social
          and psychological causes. The framework gives no causal account of the errors it
49.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                               559


        opposes and treats them as positions to be answered by argument.



49.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Motahhari’s first objection. The framework says that an identity is invariant and that
   its manifestations change. But it gives no account of what makes the invariant relevant to
   the changing: no account of how a principle governs a case. A distinction between the
   permanent and the changing that does not state how the permanent is applied is idle. The
   law lives by ijtihad, and the framework has no ijtihad.
   Motahhari’s second objection. The framework abstains from the good. But a
   philosophy that states the structure of the human being without stating its orientation to
   the good has abstracted from what the human being is. The primordial nature is not an
   addition to the structure; it is the structure’s direction. The framework’s abstention is an
   amputation.
   Motahhari’s third objection. The framework claims the autonomy of philosophical
   justification. But the revealed sources are the highest source of knowledge, and a philosophy
   that does not stand in their light is a philosophy that has not completed its task. The
   framework’s autonomy is the autonomy of an incomplete reason.



49.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a distinction between the
   permanent and the changing must state how the first bears on the second, and it holds
   that it does: the invariant identity is the condition under which a manifestation is a
   manifestation of that identity, and the application of a principle to a case is the reading
   of the case under that condition. The framework does not state the method of ijtihad
   because its subject is the structure that ijtihad presupposes. It does not deny that a
   method is needed.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the human being is oriented,
   and it does not deny that the orientation is real. It holds that the orientation is to be
   stated in a separate inquiry, because the structure of a subject can be stated without
   the claim that the subject’s orientation is to the good. The abstention is a division of
   labor and not an amputation; it states what the structure is and leaves its direction to a
   treatment that does not presuppose the framework’s claims.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that revelation may be a source
   of knowledge for one who accepts it, and it makes no claim against it. The autonomy that
   it asserts is the autonomy of the justification of its own claims: they are to be assessed by
   their premises and arguments, and not by the authority of any source. This does not entail
560                                                                        Chapter 49. Motahhari


   that no other source of knowledge exists, and Motahhari’s own use of rational argument
   to defend the possibility of revelation shows that he too assesses claims about revelation
   by argument.



49.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Motahhari’s cost. If Motahhari accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the structure
of identity can be stated without its orientation to the good or to God, and that the permanent
in the law has a structural condition that is not itself a content of the primordial nature. The cost
is the loss of the claim that the structure of the human being and its orientation are inseparable
in philosophical statement.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its structural account is complete as an account of the human being. It must accept that
the question of orientation is internal to the question of identity, and that the abstention from
the good has a cost in the completeness of the account. The cost is the loss of the sufficiency of
the structural register.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what a complete account of the human being must contain. The framework
must take the primordial nature as a claim about the structure’s direction. Motahhari must take
the structure as a claim about what the direction presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the
loss of the opposition between structure and orientation.


49.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Motahhari.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Motahhari’s
   term “primordial nature.” If one substitutes “primordial nature” for “identity,” the
   statements change: the primordial nature has a content, an orientation to truth and to
   God, while the framework’s identity is a structural invariance without a determinate
   content. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “invariance” is not substitutable for Motahhari’s
   term “the permanent.” If one substitutes “the permanent” for “invariance,” the statements
   change: the permanent in the law is a set of principles grounded in constant needs, while
   the framework’s invariance is the condition of a manifestation’s belonging to an identity.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
49.11. Open Questions                                                                         561


   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Mo-
   tahhari’s term “ijtihad.” If one substitutes “ijtihad” for “reconstruction,” the statements
   change: ijtihad is the derivation of rulings from the sources by a qualified jurist, while
   reconstruction is the reading of manifestations. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Motahhari is resemblance:
   both hold that reality can be known, that what changes is intelligible only in relation
   to what does not, and that the reduction of the human to its conditions fails, and they
   differ on whether the invariant has a content directed to the good. The relation is not
   equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing
   that Motahhari’s distinction between the permanent and the changing cannot be stated
   without an invariance of the framework’s kind, or that the framework’s invariance cannot
   be stated without the orientation that Motahhari ascribes to the primordial nature.




49.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s invariance a development of Motahhari’s permanent, or a
departure from it? The chapter has argued that it is a structural counterpart, but the argument
is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that the permanent in the law is already a structural
condition has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework state the structure of the human being without stating
its direction? The chapter has argued that it can, but a reader who holds that structure and
direction are one has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to Motahhari as distinct from
Tabatabai? The chapter has treated him as a thinker in his own right, and a reader who holds
that his philosophy is wholly derived has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Think of an institution you know that has lasted a long time, a craft, a school, a legal tradition.
What in it has stayed the same, and what has changed? Who decides, and by what, which is
which? What does your answer tell you about whether the permanent can be stated apart from
the practice of applying it?

The next chapter turns to Shariati. It states the worldview of unity, the account of the human
being between clay and spirit, the return to the self, the reading of history, and the conception
of the committed intellectual; it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Shariati;
and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of
the identity of a subject and of its expression in a context is the nearest contemporary Islamic
analogue to his account of the self and of its return. The present chapter has stated Motahhari’s
answer; the next chapter states Shariati’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 50

Shariati


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Ali Shariati (1933–1977 CE), the Iranian sociologist of
religion, writer, and lecturer who trained in Mashhad and Paris and became one of the most
widely read Muslim intellectuals of the twentieth century. It states Shariati’s worldview of unity
(jahan-bini-yi tawhidi), his account of the human being as a being composed of clay and of spirit,
his doctrine of the return to the self (bazgasht bi khishtan), his reading of history as a conflict
between the way of Cain and the way of Abel, his distinction between religion as a living force
and religion as a closed institution, and his conception of the committed intellectual (raushanfikr),
with reference to Hajj, Din bar Din (Religion against Religion), Bazgasht (Return), Islamshinasi
(Islamology), and Marxism and Other Western Fallacies. It identifies the internal disputes in the
interpretation of Shariati; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of the identity of a subject and of its expression in a context is the nearest
contemporary Islamic analogue to Shariati’s account of the self and of its return; it presents the
objections that Shariati would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “the worldview of unity,” “the return to the self,” “clay and spirit,” or “the
committed intellectual,” these are Shariati’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his works and by
the interpretive literature, not by the framework.


50.1     A Scene
Consider a pilgrim in the great circle of the pilgrimage, moving with a crowd of a million people
in white cloth. In this garment no one is rich or poor, no one is of a race or a class; each is a
body in a motion that has no individual author. And yet the experience, as those who have
undergone it often say, is not a loss of the self but a finding of it: in the circling one is both
nothing and, for the first time, oneself.
   Consider next a young person from a provincial town who has gone to the capital to study
and has come back changed. He speaks the language of the place he studied, he is ashamed of
the customs of his parents, and he is at home in neither world. He can acquire a new self from
the west, or he can return to the one he left. But the self he left is no longer the one he can
return to; it must be recovered and rebuilt, and in the rebuilding it is not the same.
   The two scenes pose a question that Shariati held to be the central question of his age: what
is the self that is to be returned to, and how can it be found without being either an inheritance
that one passively accepts or an invention that has no root? The framework poses the same
question in another register: what is an identity, how is it manifested, and how is it read? The
chapter asks how the two answers stand to each other.

                                                563
564                                                                            Chapter 50. Shariati


50.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Motahhari’s realism and his account of the permanent and the
changing. Shariati belongs to the same generation and the same revolutionary moment, but
his thought comes from a different direction, from sociology and the philosophy of history, and
he is often placed in opposition to Motahhari on the question of the relation of religion to the
intellectual’s task.
      The question is not whether Shariati was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Shariati hold? The chapter states the worldview of unity,
the account of the human being, the return to the self, the reading of history, and the conception
of the committed intellectual.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Shariati converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Shariati would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Shariati?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


50.3       Shariati’s Position
Shariati’s work is a sociology of religion, in the sense that it treats Islam as a force in history and
not primarily as a system of doctrines or of laws. He draws on the Qur’an and on the tradition
of the Imams, on the sociology of Durkheim and Gurvitch, on the phenomenology of religion,
and on the existentialism that he met in Paris, and he joins these to make a program of cultural
and political renewal.


50.3.1      The Worldview of Unity
Shariati holds that the core of Islam is tawhid, not only as the doctrine that God is one but as
a worldview in which existence is one: there is no split between the world and the hereafter,
between spirit and matter, between the individual and society. Each of the great dualisms of
other worldviews, he argues, is a form of the polytheism that tawhid rejects. The worldview of
unity is therefore at once a metaphysics, a sociology, and a practice of life.


50.3.2      The Human Being between Clay and Spirit
In a celebrated essay Shariati reads the creation of Adam from clay and the breath of God as
the symbol of a being who is constituted by two poles, one of baseness and immobility and the
other of elevation, and who lives in the tension between them. The human being is not given a
nature; he is a being who must choose his direction between the poles. The essay is influenced
by existentialism and is also anchored in the Qur’anic story.
50.4. Internal Disputes                                                                        565


50.3.3     The Return to the Self
Against colonial domination and the cultural subservience to the west that he thought it produced,
Shariati calls for a return to the self: to the authentic culture of the community, understood
not as the nostalgic repetition of the past but as the recovery and the reconstruction of its
own resources for the sake of its own freedom. He distinguishes religion as an institution of the
established clergy, which he thinks has often served power, from religion as the living ideology of
movement, which he identifies with the tradition of the Imams and above all with the martyrdom
of Husayn. In history the conflict is between the way of Cain, which is the way of power and of
possession, and the way of Abel, which is the way of the sacrificed. The intellectual’s role is to
articulate the ideology of the second and to bring it to the people.


50.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Shariati is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: sociologist or theologian. One reading takes Shariati to be a sociologist who
used religious language to give a social analysis. Another takes him to be a religious thinker who
used sociology as a tool. The disagreement matters for the framework because the framework’s
dialogue is with a philosophical position, and the reading decides whether there is one.

Second dispute: the status of ideology. Shariati called Islam an ideology and thought
that an ideology was a necessary guide for a people’s movement. One reading takes this to be a
rigorous position. Another takes it to be a rhetorical use of a term that he did not define with
care. The disagreement matters because the framework’s relation to any position that states a
commitment depends on how the commitment is stated.

Third dispute: his relation to the clergy and to the tradition. Some readers take
Shariati to have rejected the established scholarly tradition. Others take him to have criticized
only its institutional complacency while relying heavily on its sources. The disagreement matters
because the framework’s relation to the tradition depends on whether Shariati stands within it.


50.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Shariati. The framework shares four structural features with Shariati’s position.

       1. The unity of the real. Shariati holds that existence is one and that the dualisms of
         other worldviews are errors. The framework holds that an identity is enacted by
         one source and that the realms are not separate worlds. Both resist the division of
         reality into unrelated orders.

       2. The self as not simply given. Shariati holds that the human being is a being that
566                                                                            Chapter 50. Shariati


         must determine its own direction. The framework holds that an identity is expressed
         in a context and is read by reconstruction. Both hold that the self is not simply
         present to itself as a datum.

       3. The return as reconstruction. Shariati’s return to the self is not the repetition of
         the past but its recovery and reconstruction. The framework’s reconstruction is the
         reading of manifestations under a structure. Both hold that access to what one is
         requires a work and not a mere inheritance.

       4. The situated character of thought. Shariati holds that ideas are carried by social
         forces and have a social bearing. The framework holds that every claim is made
         within a context. Both hold that thought is not detached from the situation in which
         it is thought.



50.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Shariati. The framework diverges from Shariati’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of ideology. Shariati holds that a people needs an ideology, a committed
         vision that mobilizes. The framework makes no normative claim and states a
         structure without a mobilizing purpose.

       2. The account of the self. Shariati’s self is a being between two poles that chooses
         its direction. The framework’s identity is an invariance that is conserved and
         non-duplicable, and it is not chosen.

       3. The role of history. Shariati reads history as the conflict of Cain and Abel and
         gives it a direction. The framework states no philosophy of history and assigns no
         direction to the course of events.

       4. The relation to a community. Shariati’s return is the return of a community to its
         own culture. The framework’s identity is not a community’s and is not specific to a
         culture.



50.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Shariati’s first objection. The framework describes the structure of identity and of
  its manifestation, but it says nothing about the one who is subjected to domination. A
  philosophy that describes the self without asking whether the self is free to be itself describes
  an abstraction. The framework’s neutrality is a neutrality in the face of oppression, and
50.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      567


   neutrality in the face of oppression sides with the oppressor.
   Shariati’s second objection. The framework says that an identity is conserved and
   enacted by one source. But a human being is not a conserved identity; he is a project, a
   being whose being is at stake in his choices. The framework’s identity is the clay without
   the spirit, the pole of the given without the pole of freedom.
   Shariati’s third objection. The framework’s detachment is the detachment of the
   academic who stands outside the struggle of his people. The intellectual’s task is to be
   committed. A philosophy without commitment is not a higher kind of knowledge; it is an
   evasion.



50.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a description that ignores
   the conditions of freedom is abstract, and it does not deny that domination is real. It
   holds that its abstention from normative claims is a division of subject matter and not a
   verdict about oppression. A structural account of identity and manifestation may be used
   by anyone who wishes to understand the structure of what domination distorts, and the
   framework does not prevent its use for that purpose. It does not hold that neutrality in
   the structural register entails neutrality in life.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that a human being is not only
   a given, and it does not deny that choice is real. It holds that the manifestations of an
   identity are the field in which choices are made and that the identity is the condition under
   which a choice is the choice of one. Shariati’s own account of the human being as a being
   between two poles presupposes a being who is the same across the tension; the framework
   states that sameness as a structural condition without claiming that it determines the
   direction of the choice.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that commitment is a mode
   of intellectual life, and it holds that it is not the only one. A distinction between the
   structural account and the practice of commitment is a division of labor that Shariati’s
   own work respects, since his sociology is distinguished from his preaching. The framework
   does not claim that detachment is higher; it claims that it is a different task.



50.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Shariati’s cost. If Shariati accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the structure of
the self can be stated apart from the commitment, and that the return to the self has a structural
condition that is not itself an ideology. The cost is the loss of the claim that the structure of the
human being and the call to freedom are inseparable.
568                                                                         Chapter 50. Shariati


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its abstention from normative claims is innocent in a world of domination. It must accept
that a structural account has a social location and effects. The cost is the loss of the innocence
of the abstention.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about what an account of the self must answer to. The framework must take freedom
from domination as a condition of the self’s expression. Shariati must take structure as a way
of stating what the return presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition
between description and commitment.


50.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Shariati.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Shariati’s
   term “the self” (khish). If one substitutes “the self” for “identity,” the statements change:
   Shariati’s self is the authentic culture of a community to which one returns, while the
   framework’s identity is a structural invariance of any subject. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Shariati’s
   term “return.” If one substitutes “return” for “reconstruction,” the statements change:
   the return is a practical and political movement, while reconstruction is a reading of
   manifestations. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “one source” is not substitutable for Shariati’s
   term “tawhid.” If one substitutes “tawhid” for “one source,” the statements change: tawhid
   is a worldview that has sociological and practical implications, while the framework’s one
   source is a structural condition. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Shariati is resemblance:
   both hold that reality is one, that the self is not simply given but must be recovered
   through a work, and that thought is situated, and they differ on whether the account of
   the self is accompanied by a call to action. The relation is not equivalence, agreement,
   or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Shariati’s return
   to the self cannot be stated without an invariance of the framework’s kind, or that the
   framework’s invariance presupposes the commitment that Shariati holds to be inseparable
   from the account of the self.



50.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.
50.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                            569


First question. Is Shariati’s self a development of the framework’s identity or a departure
from it? The chapter has argued that it is a different notion with a structural counterpart,
but the argument is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that Shariati’s self is only a social
category has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can a structural account of the self be offered without taking a position
on freedom from domination? The chapter has argued that it can, but a reader who holds that
every account of the self is political has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to Shariati’s essays as essays? The
chapter has treated them as the source of a philosophical position, and a reader who holds that
they are only rhetoric has a question the chapter leaves open.
