A Question for Reflection
Think of a part of your own inheritance that you have both received and changed, a language,
a craft, a faith, a way of cooking. When you recover it, what exactly do you recover? If you
rebuild it, in what sense is it still the same? What does your answer tell you about whether a
self can be returned to?

The next chapter turns to Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. It states his theory of knowledge, his
critique of empiricism and of dialectical materialism, and his probabilistic theory of induction;
it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of al-Sadr; and it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the status of a claim and of
reconstruction under uncertainty is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to his account
of the logical structure of induction. The present chapter has stated Shariati’s answer; the next
chapter states al-Sadr’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 51

Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr (1935–1980 CE), the Iraqi
Shi’i jurist and philosopher, founder of a systematic Islamic response to the philosophies and
economic doctrines of his time, who was executed by the Iraqi state in 1980. It states al-Sadr’s
theory of knowledge, his critique of empiricism and of dialectical materialism, his account of
the rational and the empirical sources of knowledge, and his probabilistic theory of induction,
with reference to Falsafatuna (Our Philosophy, 1959), Iqtisaduna (Our Economics, 1961), and
al-Usus al-Mantiqiyya lil-Istiqra’ (The Logical Foundations of Induction, 1972), and, for the
method of jurisprudence, Durus fi ’Ilm al-Usul (Lessons in the Science of Principles). It identifies
the internal disputes in the interpretation of al-Sadr; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the status of a claim and of reconstruction
under uncertainty is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to al-Sadr’s account of the logical
structure of induction; it presents the objections that al-Sadr would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the subjective and the objective foundations
of knowledge,” “the logical foundations of induction,” or “the necessary knowledge,” these are
al-Sadr’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his works and by the interpretive literature, not by
the framework.


51.1     A Scene
Consider a person who has seen the sun rise every morning of her life and who expects it
tomorrow. She has no proof that it will; the past does not entail the future. Yet she is not
irrational, and she would think a person who denied the expectation to be odd. What is it that
she knows, and on what does the expectation rest?
   Consider now a scientist who has repeated an experiment a hundred times with the same
result and writes a general law. Every observation confirms the law, and the law goes far beyond
any observation. The more observations there are, the more confident she is, but never certain.
How does the confirmation of a law by its instances increase its probability, and what must be
assumed for it to do so?
   The two scenes pose a question that al-Sadr treated as the foundation of all his philosophy: if
all knowledge of the world beyond one’s immediate states rests on generalization from experience,
what grounds the generalization? If the answer is experience itself, the argument is circular, and
if the answer is nothing, then science and religion alike are groundless. Al-Sadr’s answer was
a theory in which certain rational principles are known without experience and in which the
probability of a generalization is derived from them. The framework poses a related question in

                                                570
51.2. The Question                                                                              571


its own register: how is a reconstruction justified, and what status does it have? The chapter
asks how the two answers stand to each other.


51.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Shariati’s worldview of unity and his reading of history. Al-Sadr was
a contemporary of both Shariati and Motahhari, but he worked in the Iraqi seminary of Najaf,
and his philosophy has a character that differs from theirs: it is a technical, logical inquiry into
the structure of knowledge, undertaken in order to defend a religious and social vision against
materialism.
   The question is not whether al-Sadr was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did al-Sadr hold? The chapter states his theory of knowledge,
his critique of empiricism and materialism, and his probabilistic theory of induction.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and al-Sadr converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that al-Sadr would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and al-
Sadr? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


51.3      Al-Sadr’s Position
Al-Sadr’s Falsafatuna is a book written for a wide readership and a vigorous critique of the
philosophies in circulation in the Arab world at his time. Its first part treats the theory of
knowledge and its second the metaphysical question of the world, and it is built on the claim
that the dispute between idealism, materialism, and theism is at bottom a dispute about the
sources of knowledge.


51.3.1    The Theory of Knowledge

Al-Sadr holds that knowledge has two kinds, conceptions (tasawwurat) and assents (tasdiqat),
and that each kind has a primary and a derived part. Conceptions are derived from sense
experience by a process of abstraction and are in this sense empirical. Assents are of two kinds:
those that are inferred from others and those that are primary and need no proof. He argues
against the empiricist that the primary assents, among them the principle of non-contradiction
and the principle of causality, cannot themselves be derived from experience, since any derivation
would already use them. Against the rationalist who holds that all knowledge is innate, he argues
that conceptions begin in sense experience. His position is therefore a mixed one: concepts are
empirical in origin, and the first principles of assent are rational.
572                                                       Chapter 51. Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr


51.3.2     The Critique of Dialectical Materialism

Al-Sadr’s critique of dialectical materialism proceeds on the ground of this theory. He argues that
materialism cannot account for the knowledge it presupposes, since the knowledge of the primary
principles is not a material effect, and that the dialectical laws, such as the transformation of
quantity into quality, are not established by the empirical evidence that is cited for them. The
argument is not only a polemic but a model of how a philosophy should be assessed: by whether
its own claims can be justified on its own account of knowledge.


51.3.3     The Logical Foundations of Induction

The late work al-Usus al-Mantiqiyya lil-Istiqra’ gives the technical development of the theory.
Al-Sadr takes up the problem of induction and the application of the calculus of probability,
and he argues that the increase of the probability of a generalization by the accumulation of
confirming instances can be explained only if two kinds of foundation are distinguished. The
objective foundation is the application of the calculus of probability, which has the property that
the confirmation of a hypothesis by an instance that would be improbable without it raises its
probability. The subjective foundation is the initial degree of belief that a generalization has
before the evidence, which cannot be derived from the evidence and rests on a principle that he
identifies with a primary rational assent, namely that there is some finite initial probability for
the generalization. In the final part of the book he extends the result to the knowledge of God
and the argument from design, holding that the same structure of probabilistic confirmation
applies to it.


51.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of al-Sadr is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the novelty of the theory of induction. One reading takes the theory to
be an original contribution that anticipates later work in confirmation theory. Another takes it
to be a reformulation of the Bayesian tradition of Laplace and Keynes in an Islamic framework.
The disagreement matters for the framework because the dialogue is with the position, and
whether it is original or a reformulation affects what it is a position of.


Second dispute: foundationalism. One reading takes al-Sadr to be a strict foundationalist
who holds that all knowledge rests on certain primary assents. Another takes the theory of
induction to show that most knowledge is probable and that only the primary assents are certain.
The disagreement matters because the framework’s own marking of claims by status stands in a
different relation to each.


Third dispute: philosophy and jurisprudence. Al-Sadr was also a leading jurist who
reformed the science of the principles of jurisprudence. One reading takes the philosophical works
and the jurisprudential works to form a single system. Another takes them to be separate. The
51.5. Points of Convergence                                                                    573


disagreement matters because the framework’s dialogue is with the philosophical works, and the
reading decides how far they are autonomous.


51.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With al-Sadr. The framework shares four structural features with al-Sadr’s position.

       1. The status of claims. Al-Sadr distinguishes certain assents from probable ones.
         The framework marks each claim with an epistemic status, distinguishing axioms,
          theorems, and other kinds. Both hold that a claim’s status is part of what is to be
          known about it.

       2. The unprovable first principles. Al-Sadr holds that the primary assents are known
         without proof and that every proof presupposes them. The framework holds that
          some principles are axioms that every argument presupposes. Both hold that a
          philosophy begins from what it cannot prove.

       3. The justification of a position on its own terms. Al-Sadr assesses materialism by
         whether it can justify its own claims. The framework holds that a position is assessed
          by its premises and arguments and that a position that cannot justify its own
          presuppositions is open to criticism. Both treat internal justification as a test.

       4. The role of the calculus of probability. Al-Sadr treats the confirmation of a general-
          ization as a matter that the calculus of probability regulates. The framework holds
          that reconstruction is revisable and that confidence may be graded. Both hold that
          the support of a claim is a matter of degree and has a structure.



51.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With al-Sadr. The framework diverges from al-Sadr’s position in four respects.

       1. The register. Al-Sadr’s account is a logical and epistemological account of induction.
         The framework’s account is a metaphysical and structural account of identity and
          manifestation, and it does not treat induction as its central problem.

       2. The foundation. Al-Sadr holds that the primary assents are rational necessities and
          that the probability of a generalization rests on one of them. The framework labels
          its axioms as axioms and does not claim that they are necessities of reason.

       3. The application to God. Al-Sadr extends the theory of induction to the knowledge of
          God. The framework does not apply its structure to the question of God’s existence.
574                                                     Chapter 51. Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr


       4. The relation to the social order. Al-Sadr’s philosophy is joined to an economic and
         legal program. The framework makes no such program.



51.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Al-Sadr’s first objection. The framework speaks of reconstruction and of epistemic
  statuses, but it gives no account of how a reconstruction is confirmed by its manifestations.
  Without a logical account of the support that an instance gives to a generalization, the
  framework’s claim that a reconstruction is revisable is empty: it does not say in what way,
  or by how much, evidence revises it.
  Al-Sadr’s second objection. The framework treats its axioms as axioms and leaves
  them without ground. But an axiom without a ground is an arbitrary stipulation, and the
  framework cannot distinguish its axioms from those of materialism. The only defense is
  that the axioms are primary rational assents, and the framework does not say so.
  Al-Sadr’s third objection. The framework’s metaphysics of identity and source makes
  no connection to the question of God. If it does not, it is a metaphysics that stops short
  of its own conclusion. The structure of confirmation that supports generalizations also
  supports the inference to a source, and the framework leaves that inference unstated.



51.8      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a claim of revisability
  requires an account of how evidence revises, and it accepts that its own statement of
  this is incomplete. It holds that the logical account of confirmation is an inquiry that
  supplements the structural account and does not conflict with it, and al-Sadr’s calculus
  can serve as such an account. The framework does not commit to a particular theory of
  confirmation and is compatible with his.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that an axiom without ground
  is not arbitrary when its role in every argument can be shown, and it holds that this is
  the case for its own. It does not claim that the axioms are necessities of reason, because it
  does not wish to claim more than it can show. Al-Sadr’s own argument that the primary
  assents are known without proof does not distinguish them from other candidates except
  by their role, and the framework makes the same appeal to role.
  Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the inference from structure
  to a source is a question that its principles raise, and it holds that it answers it at the
  level of structure: an identity is enacted by one source. It does not extend the inference to
  the question of God, because that question has a theological content that the structural
  account does not supply. It leaves the extension to a separate inquiry and does not forbid
51.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     575


   it.



51.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

al-Sadr’s cost. If al-Sadr accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the structural
account of identity and manifestation can be stated without a logical account of confirmation
and that its axioms need not be claimed as necessities of reason. The cost is the loss of the claim
that a complete philosophy must begin from a theory of the sources of knowledge.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that the structural account is independent of a theory of knowledge. It must accept that its
statements of status and revisability require a logic of confirmation and that its axioms require
an account of their rational standing. The cost is the loss of the independence of the structural
register from epistemology.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim as
a claim about what justifies a philosophy. The framework must take the logic of confirmation as
a condition of its own claims. Al-Sadr must take structure as a way of stating what confirmation
concerns. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between structure and logic.


51.10         The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   al-Sadr.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “axiom” is not substitutable for al-Sadr’s term
   “primary assent.” If one substitutes “primary assent” for “axiom,” the statements change:
   a primary assent is a proposition known without proof and held to be a necessity of
   reason, while an axiom is a proposition taken as a starting point and labeled as such. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for al-Sadr’s
   term “induction.” If one substitutes “induction” for “reconstruction,” the statements
   change: induction is the inference from instances to a generalization, while reconstruction
   is the reading of manifestations as manifestations of an identity. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “epistemic status” is not substitutable for al-
   Sadr’s term “degree of probability.” If one substitutes “degree of probability” for “epistemic
   status,” the statements change: a degree of probability is a number in a calculus, while a
   status is a classification of the kind of warrant a claim has. The substitution fails, and the
576                                                     Chapter 51. Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr


   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and al-Sadr is resemblance:
   both hold that a philosophy rests on principles that it does not prove, that a position is
   tested by its own account of justification, and that the support of a claim has a structure,
   and they differ on whether the starting points are rational necessities and on whether
   the account of confirmation is part of the philosophy. The relation is not equivalence,
   agreement, or identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that al-Sadr’s
   theory of induction cannot be stated without a structure of identity and manifestation
   of the framework’s kind, or that the framework’s statuses cannot be stated without a
   probabilistic logic of the kind al-Sadr gives.




51.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Can the framework’s epistemic statuses be given a probabilistic interpretation
of al-Sadr’s kind? The chapter has argued that they can be compatible with one, but the
argument is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that a status is not a degree has a question
the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Are the framework’s axioms primary rational assents? The chapter has
argued that the framework does not claim this, but a reader who holds that an axiom that is not
a necessity of reason is arbitrary has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to the technical argument of al-Usus
al-Mantiqiyya? The chapter has stated it at the level of its main structure, and a reader who
holds that the argument depends on details the chapter omits has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Think of a generalization you rely on without proof, that the next bridge you cross will hold,
that people mean what they say most of the time. What makes you more confident of it after
each instance? Is there a starting confidence that no instance gave you? What does your answer
tell you about whether a philosophy can begin from nothing it does not prove?

The next chapter turns to Nasr. It states the traditionalism, the sacred science, the critique of
modernity, the doctrine of the unity of being, and the interpretation of the Islamic tradition;
it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Nasr; and it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of tradition and of modernity is
the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Nasr’s. The present chapter has stated al-Sadr’s
answer; the next chapter states Nasr’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 52

Nasr


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Seyyed Hossein Nasr (born 1933 CE), the Iranian
philosopher, traditionalist, and scholar of comparative religion, known in the Islamic tradition
as Sayyid Hossein Nasr and in the West as one of the foremost spokesmen of the traditionalist
school (perennialism). It states Nasr’s traditionalism, the doctrine of the philosophia perennis
(the perennial philosophy), the sacred science (scientia sacra), the critique of modernity, the
doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud), the hierarchy of being, and the interpretation of
the Islamic tradition, with reference to Knowledge and the Sacred (1981), The Need for a Sacred
Science (1968), Islamic Science: An Illustrated Study (1976), Sufi Essays (1972), and The Garden
of Truth (2007); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Nasr; it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of tradition and of
modernity is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Nasr’s; it presents the objections that
Nasr would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of
“traditionalism,” “the perennial philosophy,” “sacred science,” “the critique of modernity,” “the
unity of being,” or “the hierarchy of being,” these are Nasr’s terms, and their sense is fixed by
the works and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


52.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing in a traditional mosque. The mosque is not a building; it is a
sacred space; it is a symbol of the cosmos; it is a reflection of the divine order. The columns of
the mosque are the pillars of the cosmos; the dome is the vault of heaven; the mihrab is the axis
of the world; the call to prayer is the voice of the angel. The mosque is not a construction of the
human will; it is a manifestation of the sacred; it is a symbol of the eternal.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the mosque is, or how it is built, but
what makes the mosque sacred. The mosque is sacred because it is built according to the sacred
science; it is built according to the traditional knowledge; it is built according to the perennial
philosophy. The sacred science is not the modern science; it is not the empirical science; it is the
knowledge of the sacred; it is the knowledge of the eternal; it is the knowledge of the divine. The
sacred science is the foundation of the traditional civilization; it is the foundation of the Islamic
art; it is the foundation of the Islamic architecture.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the mosque is, or what
makes it sacred, but what modernity is. Modernity is not the progress; it is not the liberation; it
is not the enlightenment. Modernity is the forgetting of the sacred; it is the loss of the tradition;
it is the reduction of the knowledge to the empirical; it is the reduction of the human being to

                                                578
52.2. The Question                                                                                 579


the economic animal. Modernity is the crisis; it is the disease; it is the death. The traditionalism
is the response; it is the recovery of the sacred; it is the return to the tradition; it is the revival
of the perennial philosophy.
   The scene is Nasr’s image, in Knowledge and the Sacred and in The Need for a Sacred Science,
of the structure of reality. The mosque is the sacred space; the sacred science is the traditional
knowledge; modernity is the forgetting of the sacred. The scene poses the question that Nasr was
the first to pose in its full form in the contemporary Islamic tradition. What is the tradition?
What is modernity? And what is the relation between the two? The present chapter states
Nasr’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


52.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Tabatabai’s position: the principles of philosophy, the method
of realism, the primacy of existence, the gradation of existence, the theory of knowledge, the
doctrine of the soul, and the interpretation of the Qur’an. Tabatabai is the great systematizer of
contemporary Islamic philosophy in Iran; he is the teacher of the generation of contemporary
Islamic philosophers; he develops the principles of philosophy and the method of realism. Nasr is
his student and his successor, but he is not a philosopher in the strict sense; he is a traditionalist;
he is a scholar of comparative religion; he is the spokesman of the traditionalist school. The
present chapter states Nasr’s traditionalism, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Nasr was right. The question is what he held, what he can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Nasr hold? The chapter states the traditionalism, the
perennial philosophy, the sacred science, the critique of modernity, the unity of being, the
hierarchy of being, and the interpretation of the Islamic tradition, with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Nasr converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Nasr would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Nasr? The
chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


52.3      The Position

52.3.1    The Traditionalism

Nasr’s traditionalism is stated in Knowledge and the Sacred (1981) and in The Need for a Sacred
Science (1968). The traditionalism is not a conservatism; it is not a fundamentalism; it is not a
return to the past. The traditionalism is the affirmation of the tradition; it is the affirmation of
the perennial philosophy; it is the affirmation of the sacred.
580                                                                                 Chapter 52. Nasr


      The traditionalism has three features.


First feature: the tradition. The tradition is not the past; it is not the historical; it is not
the temporal. The tradition is the sacred; it is the eternal; it is the divine. The tradition is
the transmission of the sacred knowledge from the origin to the present; it is the chain of the
prophets and the sages; it is the perennial philosophy.


Second feature: the perennial philosophy. The perennial philosophy (philosophia perennis)
is the universal philosophy; it is the philosophy that is present in all the traditions; it is the
philosophy that is the same in all the ages. The perennial philosophy is not a system; it is not a
doctrine; it is the wisdom; it is the knowledge of the sacred; it is the knowledge of the divine.


Third feature: the traditionalist school. The traditionalist school is the school of the
thinkers who affirm the perennial philosophy; it is the school of René Guénon, Ananda
Coomaraswamy, Frithjof Schuon, Titus Burckhardt, and Seyyed Hossein Nasr. The school
is not a sect; it is not a party; it is the school of the traditional knowledge; it is the school of the
sacred science.
      The traditionalism is the foundation of Nasr’s philosophy. It is the affirmation of the tradition;
it is the affirmation of the perennial philosophy; it is the affirmation of the sacred.

   From the Tradition

   “The tradition is not the past; it is the sacred. The perennial philosophy is the universal
   wisdom; it is present in all the traditions. The traditionalist school is the school of the
   thinkers who affirm the perennial philosophy.” (Nasr, Knowledge and the Sacred, ch. 1,
   adapted)


52.3.2      The Sacred Science

Nasr’s doctrine of the sacred science (scientia sacra) is stated in The Need for a Sacred Science
and in Islamic Science: An Illustrated Study. The sacred science is not the modern science; it is
not the empirical science; it is the knowledge of the sacred; it is the knowledge of the cosmic
order.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the sacred science. The sacred science is the knowledge of the sacred; it
is the knowledge of the cosmic order; it is the knowledge of the correspondences between the
macrocosm and the microcosm. The sacred science is not the empirical science; it is not the
profane science; it is the traditional science; it is the science of the sages.


Second feature: the cosmic order. The cosmic order is the order of the cosmos; it is the
hierarchy of the being; it is the degrees of the existence. The cosmic order is not a mechanism; it
is not a machine; it is a symbol; it is a theophany; it is the manifestation of the divine. The
sacred science is the knowledge of the cosmic order; it is the knowledge of the theophany.
52.3. The Position                                                                                   581


Third feature: the critique of the modern science. The modern science is the profane
science; it is the science that has lost the sacred; it is the science that has reduced the cosmos to
the matter; it is the science that has reduced the human being to the economic animal. The
modern science is the crisis; it is the disease; it is the death. The sacred science is the response;
it is the recovery of the sacred; it is the return to the tradition.
   The doctrine is the key to Nasr’s philosophy of science. It is the sacred science; it is the
cosmic order; it is the critique of the modern science.


52.3.3     The Critique of Modernity

Nasr’s critique of modernity is stated in Knowledge and the Sacred and in The Garden of Truth.
The critique is not a rejection of the modern world; it is a critique of the modern worldview; it is
the recognition that the modern worldview has lost the sacred.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the forgetting of the sacred. Modernity is the forgetting of the sacred; it is
the loss of the tradition; it is the reduction of the knowledge to the empirical; it is the reduction
of the human being to the economic animal. Modernity is the crisis; it is the disease; it is the
death.


Second feature: the secularization. The secularization is the process by which the sacred
is removed from the public life; it is the process by which the religion is confined to the private
life; it is the process by which the world is desacralized. The secularization is the consequence of
the modernity; it is the cause of the crisis; it is the source of the death.


Third feature: the traditional response. The traditional response is the recovery of the
sacred; it is the return to the tradition; it is the revival of the perennial philosophy. The traditional
response is not a rejection of the modern world; it is a critique of the modern worldview; it is
the affirmation of the sacred in the modern world.
   The critique is the key to Nasr’s philosophy of modernity. It is the forgetting of the sacred; it
is the secularization; it is the traditional response.


52.3.4     The Unity of Being

Nasr’s doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud) is stated in Knowledge and the Sacred
and in Sufi Essays. The doctrine is the inheritance of Ibn Arabi and Mulla Sadra; it is the
foundation of Nasr’s metaphysics.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the being is one. The being is one; the being is the Real (al-Haqq); the being
is God. There is no being other than the being; the things are not beings; the things are the
manifestations of the being. The being is not multiplied by the manifestations; the being is one
in its essence; the manifestations are many in their appearances.
582                                                                                 Chapter 52. Nasr


Second feature: the manifestation. The manifestation is the appearance of the being in
the things; it is the theophany; it is the self-disclosure of the being. The manifestation is not a
creation from nothing; it is the self-disclosure of the being in the forms.


Third feature: the hierarchy of being. The hierarchy of being is the gradation of the
existence; it is the degrees of the manifestation; it is the levels of the theophany. The hierarchy
of being is the order of the cosmos; it is the structure of the manifestation; it is the reflection of
the divine.
      The doctrine is the key to Nasr’s metaphysics. It is the unity of being; it is the manifestation;
it is the hierarchy of being.


52.3.5      The Hierarchy of Being
Nasr’s doctrine of the hierarchy of being is a development of his doctrine of the unity of being.
The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the levels. The hierarchy of being has levels; it has gradations; it has stages.
The levels are: the divine essence, the divine names, the universal intellect, the universal soul,
the material world. The hierarchy of being is the order of the cosmos; it is the structure of the
manifestation.


Second feature: the correspondence. The hierarchy of being is the correspondence between
the macrocosm and the microcosm; it is the correspondence between the cosmos and the human
being; it is the correspondence between the divine and the human. The correspondence is the
key to the sacred science; it is the key to the traditional knowledge.


Third feature: the return. The hierarchy of being is the return to the source; it is the ascent
from the material world to the divine essence; it is the journey of the soul to God. The return is
the goal of the hierarchy; it is the goal of the cosmos; it is the goal of the human being.
      The doctrine is the key to Nasr’s cosmology. It is the levels; it is the correspondence; it is the
return.


52.3.6      The Interpretation of the Islamic Tradition
Nasr’s interpretation of the Islamic tradition is stated throughout his works, but most clearly in
Islamic Science, Sufi Essays, and The Garden of Truth. The interpretation is the traditionalist
interpretation; it is the interpretation of the Islamic tradition in the light of the perennial
philosophy.
      The interpretation has three features.


First feature: the tradition. The Islamic tradition is not a historical phenomenon; it is not
a social phenomenon; it is the sacred tradition; it is the transmission of the prophetic knowledge;
it is the chain of the prophets and the saints. The Islamic tradition is the manifestation of the
perennial philosophy in the Islamic form.
52.4. Internal Disputes                                                                           583


Second feature: the sufism. The Sufism is the inner dimension of the Islamic tradition; it is
the esoteric dimension; it is the dimension of the spiritual path. The Sufism is the manifestation
of the perennial philosophy in the Islamic form; it is the heart of the Islamic tradition.

Third feature: the sacred art. The sacred art is the manifestation of the sacred in the
artistic form; it is the manifestation of the divine in the Islamic art. The sacred art is the
reflection of the divine order; it is the symbol of the eternal; it is the theophany.
   The interpretation is the key to Nasr’s Islamic scholarship. It is the tradition; it is the Sufism;
it is the sacred art.


52.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Nasr is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the traditionalism. The traditional reading takes the tra-
ditionalism to be a perennial philosophy: it is the universal wisdom; it is present in all the
traditions; it is the same in all the ages. A revisionary reading takes it to be a comparative
method: it is a way of studying the traditions; it is not a doctrine; it is a method. The two
readings disagree on whether Nasr is a traditionalist or a comparativist, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a traditionalism nor a comparativism.

Second dispute: the status of the sacred science. The traditional reading takes the
sacred science to be a real science: it is the knowledge of the sacred; it is the knowledge of the
cosmic order. A revisionary reading takes it to be a poetic knowledge: it is the knowledge of
the symbols; it is the knowledge of the images; it is not the science, but the poetry. The two
readings disagree on whether Nasr is a scientist or a poet, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, neither a science
nor a poetry.

Third dispute: the status of the critique of modernity. The traditional reading takes the
critique of modernity to be a metaphysical critique: it is the critique of the modern worldview; it
is the critique of the secularization. A revisionary reading takes it to be a cultural critique: it is
the critique of the modern culture; it is the critique of the modern society. The two readings
disagree on whether Nasr is a metaphysician or a cultural critic, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, neither a
metaphysics nor a cultural critique.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Nasr is a traditionalist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a traditionalist perennialism. If
Nasr is a comparativist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a comparative
traditionalism. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts of Nasr, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.
584                                                                               Chapter 52. Nasr


52.5      Points of Convergence

  Points of Convergence

  With Nasr. The framework shares four structural features with Nasr’s position.

       1. The critique of modernity. Nasr holds that modernity is the forgetting of the sacred;
          it is the reduction of the knowledge to the empirical; it is the reduction of the human
          being to the economic animal. The framework holds that the tradition has conflated
          identity with manifestation; it has reduced the identity to its manifestations; it has
          collapsed the structural difference. Both hold that the modern worldview has made
          a mistake, and that the mistake is the collapse of a distinction.

       2. The hierarchy of being. Nasr holds that reality is a hierarchy of levels; the levels are
          the degrees of the manifestation; the levels are the theophany. The framework holds
          that reality is a hierarchy of realms; the realms are the levels of the manifestation;
          the realms are the expression of the identity. Both hold that reality is stratified, and
          that the strata are not reducible to one another.

       3. The unity of being. Nasr holds that the being is one; the things are the manifestations
          of the being; the being is not multiplied by the manifestations. The framework holds
          that the identity is one; the manifestations are the appearances of the identity; the
          identity is not multiplied by the manifestations. Both hold that the one is prior to
          the many, and that the many is real in the one.

       4. The critique of the secular. Nasr holds that the secularization is the process by
          which the sacred is removed from the public life; it is the source of the crisis. The
          framework holds that the secularization is the process by which the structure is
          reduced to the manifestation; it is the source of the crisis. Both hold that the secular
          is a mistake, and that the mistake is the loss of the structure.



52.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Nasr. The framework diverges from Nasr in four respects.

       1. The status of the tradition. Nasr holds that the tradition is the sacred; it is the
          transmission of the sacred knowledge; it is the perennial philosophy. The framework
          holds that the structure is the condition of possibility of the tradition; the structure
          is not the tradition; the structure is the condition. The framework’s structure is
          autonomous; it does not depend on any tradition.

       2. The status of the sacred science. Nasr holds that the sacred science is the knowledge
          of the sacred; it is the knowledge of the cosmic order. The framework holds that the
52.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 585


         science is the reconstruction of the structure; it is the reading of the manifestations.
         The framework’s science is structural, not sacred.

       3. The status of the critique of modernity. Nasr holds that modernity is the forgetting
         of the sacred; it is the loss of the tradition. The framework holds that modernity is
         the reduction of the structure to the manifestation; it is the collapse of the structural
         difference. The framework’s critique is structural, not traditional.

       4. The status of the unity of being. Nasr holds that the being is one; the things are
         the manifestations of the being. The framework holds that the identity is multiple;
         the identity is the invariance enacted by one source; the identity is not the being.
         The framework’s identity is not the being; it is the structural condition of the
         manifestation.




52.7      The Tradition’s Objections


   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Nasr’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
   a sacred; it is a pattern. The world is composed of theophanies; the world is not just
   structured; the world is a theophany. The framework has no sacred; the framework has
   no theophany; the framework’s world is a world without the sacred. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of theophanies.
   Nasr’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
   are the degrees of the manifestation; they are the levels of the theophany. The framework’s
   realms are not levels of the theophany; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is
   an ontology of levels, not of the theophany.
   Nasr’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not the
   sacred. But a metaphysics without the sacred is an incomplete metaphysics; the sacred
   is the fundamental reality; the question of the sacred is the question of philosophy. The
   framework’s silence on the sacred is not a boundary; it is a gap. The framework’s philosophy
   is a philosophy without the sacred, and a philosophy without the sacred is a philosophy
   without the reality.
586                                                                              Chapter 52. Nasr


52.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is composed of
   theophanies, and it agrees that the theophany is a real phenomenon. But the framework
   denies that the theophany must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity
   is the structural condition of the theophany; it is the invariance enacted by one source;
   it is the structural condition under which the theophany is what it is. The distinction
   is between a theophany (a manifestation of the sacred) and an identity (a structural
   condition); the framework holds the second, not the first. The framework does not deny
   the sacred; it denies that the sacred is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the theophany. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   theophany. The distinction is between a level of the theophany (a sacred level) and a level
   of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without the
   sacred is incomplete, and it agrees that the question of the sacred is fundamental. But
   the framework denies that its silence on the sacred is a gap. The framework is a work of
   metaphysics, not of theology; its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation,
   not the sacred. The framework states the structural condition of reality; it leaves the
   question of the sacred to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics
   and a theology; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it is not a gap, but a
   boundary.



52.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Nasr’s cost. If Nasr accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the tradition
is the sacred. He must accept that the structure is the condition of possibility of the tradition,
and that the tradition is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the sacred
tradition: the tradition is no longer the sacred; the tradition is a manifestation. He must also
give up the claim that the sacred science is the knowledge of the sacred; he must accept that the
science is the reconstruction of the structure; the science is the reading of the manifestations.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Nasr’s objections, it must give up the claim
that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the dimension
of the sacred, of the tradition, of the theophany—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is
the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment
of a structure, but not the sacred, and the framework leaves the sacred to a separate inquiry.
52.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      587


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Nasr’s sacred is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Nasr
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
sacred presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.



52.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Nasr’s
   term “the sacred.” If one substitutes “the sacred” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Nasr’s sacred is the divine reality, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the sacred. The framework’s identity is multiple; Nasr’s sacred is
   one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Nasr’s term “the theophany.”
   If one substitutes “the theophany” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; Nasr’s theophany is
   the manifestation of the sacred. The framework’s expression is structural; Nasr’s theophany
   is sacred. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Nasr’s term “the sacred
   science.” If one substitutes “the sacred science” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; Nasr’s sacred science is the knowledge of the sacred. The framework’s
   reconstruction is structural; Nasr’s sacred science is sacred. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Nasr is resemblance: both
   hold that reality is a hierarchy of levels, and they differ on whether the levels are sacred or
   structural. Both hold that there is a fundamental reality, and they differ on whether the
   fundamental reality is the sacred or the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither
   is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Nasr would be refuted by
   showing that Nasr’s sacred cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and the sacred—by showing, that is, that Nasr already distinguishes the
   structural condition from the sacred, and that the framework’s distinction is a development
   of Nasr’s own.



52.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
588                                                                             Chapter 52. Nasr


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Nasr’s sacred, or is it a departure
from Nasr? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not conclusive.
A reader who holds that Nasr’s sacred is already a structural condition, not a divine reality, has
a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Knowledge and the Sacred, The Need
for a Sacred Science, and Islamic Science do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the
traditionalism, the perennial philosophy, the sacred science, the critique of modernity, the unity
of being, the hierarchy of being, and the interpretation of the Islamic tradition, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has
a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection

Consider a thing you know that is both a sacred and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the sacred that manifests, or the structure that makes the manifestation
possible? Is the truth the theophany that is revealed, or the expression that is enacted? What
does your answer tell you about the relation between Nasr’s sacred science and the framework’s
structure?
