Chapter 53

Fazlur Rahman


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Fazlur Rahman (1919–1988 CE), the Pakistani-American
philosopher, Qur’anic scholar, and reformer of modern Islamic thought. It states Fazlur Rahman’s
hermeneutics of the Qur’an, his theory of the double movement (al-haraka al-muzdawaja), his
account of revelation as the word of God and the word of the Prophet, his distinction between
the general principles and the specific responses of the Qur’an, his concept of the living Sunnah
(al-sunnah al-hayya), and his critique of both the traditionalist and the secularist responses to
modernity, with reference to Islam and Modernity: Transformation of an Intellectual Tradition
(1982), Major Themes of the Qur’an (1980), Prophecy in Islam: Philosophy and Orthodoxy (1958),
Islamic Methodology in History (1965), and Revival and Reform in Islam (1999, posthumous); it
identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Fazlur Rahman; it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of expression and of the
relation between structure and manifestation is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to
Rahman’s; it presents the objections that Rahman would raise against the framework; it presents
the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation;
and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or
evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the double movement,” “the living Sunnah,”
“revelation,” “the general principles,” “the specific responses,” or “the neo-modernist project,”
these are Rahman’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.


53.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the Qur’anic verse on inheritance: “Allah instructs you
concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females” (Q 4:11). She
reads the verse in its seventh-century context: a society in which women had no independent
economic standing, in which the male was the sole provider, in which the inheritance of the male
was the inheritance of the family. She asks: is this verse a timeless law, binding on all societies
in all ages? Or is it a specific response to a specific historical situation, expressing a general
principle that must be applied differently in different conditions?
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she reads another verse: “And do not approach the
property of the orphan except in the best manner” (Q 6:152). She sees that the Qur’an does
not abolish the institution of inheritance; it reforms it. It gives the female a share that she did
not have before; it protects the orphan’s property; it establishes a principle of justice in the
distribution of wealth. The verse is not a timeless law; it is a response to a historical situation,
and the response expresses a principle. The principle is the moral spirit of the Qur’an: justice,
equity, the protection of the weak. The specific response is the form that the principle took in

                                                590
53.2. The Question                                                                               591


the seventh century. The task of the modern Muslim is not to repeat the specific response, but
to recover the principle and to apply it to the modern condition.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the verse means, or how
it is applied, but what the Qur’an is. The Qur’an is the word of God; it is revealed; it is the
guidance for humanity. But the Qur’an is also the word of the Prophet: it came through his
heart, through his mind, through his language, through his historical situation. The Qur’an is
entirely the word of God and, in an ordinary sense, also entirely the word of Muhammad. The
revelation is not a dictation; it is a creative process, in which the divine word takes form in the
human heart, and the human heart gives form to the divine word. This is what Fazlur Rahman
calls the double movement: the movement from the divine to the human, and the movement
from the human back to the divine.
   The scene is Rahman’s image, in Islam and Modernity and in Major Themes of the Qur’an,
of the structure of revelation. The verse is the specific response; the principle is the moral
spirit; the Qur’an is the word of God and the word of the Prophet. The scene poses the
question that Rahman was the first to pose in its full form in the contemporary Islamic tradition.
What is revelation? How does the divine word become a human text? And how is the text to
be interpreted for the modern world? The present chapter states Rahman’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


53.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Nasr’s position: the traditionalism, the perennial philosophy, the
sacred science, the critique of modernity, the unity of being, the hierarchy of being, and the
interpretation of the Islamic tradition. Nasr is the great spokesman of the traditionalist school;
he affirms the perennial philosophy; he critiques the modern worldview. Fazlur Rahman is his
contemporary, but he is not a traditionalist; he is a neo-modernist; he is the reformer who
seeks to reconstruct Islamic thought in the light of modern knowledge, without abandoning the
Qur’anic foundation. The present chapter states Rahman’s neo-modernism, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Rahman was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the position. What did Rahman hold? The chapter states the double movement,
the account of revelation, the distinction between the general principles and the specific responses,
the living Sunnah, and the critique of traditionalism and secularism, with reference to the works.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Rahman converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Rahman would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Rahman?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.
592                                                                    Chapter 53. Fazlur Rahman


53.3       The Position

53.3.1      The Double Movement

Rahman’s theory of the double movement (al-haraka al-muzdawaja) is stated in Islam and
Modernity (1982) and in Islamic Methodology in History (1965). The double movement is the
hermeneutical structure of Rahman’s interpretation of the Qur’an; it is the method by which the
Qur’an is to be understood and applied to the modern world.
      The double movement has three features.


First feature: the first movement. The first movement is from the specific to the general;
it is the movement from the specific responses of the Qur’an to the general principles that the
responses express. The Qur’an was revealed in a specific historical situation; it responded to
specific problems; it gave specific answers. But the specific answers express general principles.
The first movement is the movement from the verse to the principle, from the response to the
spirit, from the letter to the meaning. The interpreter must understand the historical situation of
the revelation, the problems to which the Qur’an responded, and the principles that the responses
express.


Second feature: the second movement. The second movement is from the general to the
specific; it is the movement from the general principles to the specific application in the modern
situation. The principles are eternal; the applications are historical. The interpreter must apply
the principles to the modern condition, to the problems of the modern world, to the needs of the
modern society. The second movement is the movement from the principle to the application,
from the spirit to the form, from the meaning to the law. The interpreter must be creative; the
interpreter must be faithful to the principle, and free in the application.


Third feature: the unity of the two movements. The two movements are not separate;
they are the two moments of one hermeneutical act. The first movement without the second is
antiquarianism; the second without the first is subjectivism. The two together are the double
movement: the movement from the text to the principle, and the movement from the principle
to the modern world. The double movement is the way to keep the Qur’an alive; it is the way to
be faithful to the text and relevant to the world.
      The double movement is the foundation of Rahman’s hermeneutics. It is the movement from
the specific to the general; it is the movement from the general to the specific; it is the unity of
the two.

   From the Tradition

   “The Qur’an was revealed in a specific historical situation, but it expresses general principles.
   The task of the interpreter is to move from the specific to the general, and then from the
   general to the specific application in the modern world. This is the double movement.”
   (Rahman, Islam and Modernity, ch. 1, adapted)
53.3. The Position                                                                               593


53.3.2    The Account of Revelation

Rahman’s account of revelation is stated in Islam and Modernity and in Prophecy in Islam.
The account is one of the most controversial in the contemporary Islamic tradition; it is the
foundation of Rahman’s theology.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the Qur’an as the word of God. The Qur’an is the word of God; it is
revealed; it is the guidance for humanity. The Qur’an is not a human production; it is not a
human invention; it is the divine word. The Qur’an is the word of God in the full sense; it is the
revelation of the divine will.


Second feature: the Qur’an as the word of the Prophet. The Qur’an is also the word
of the Prophet; it came through his heart; through his mind; through his language; through
his historical situation. The Qur’an is entirely the word of God and, in an ordinary sense, also
entirely the word of Muhammad. The revelation is not a dictation; it is a creative process. The
divine word takes form in the human heart, and the human heart gives form to the divine word.
The Qur’an is the divine word in human language; it is the eternal in time; it is the absolute in
the relative.


Third feature: the creative process. The creative process is the process by which the
divine word becomes the human text. The Prophet is not a passive receiver; he is an active
participant; he is the one through whom the divine word takes form. The Prophet’s personality,
his language, his culture, his historical situation are not obstacles to the revelation; they are the
conditions of the revelation. The revelation is not despite the human; it is through the human.
The Qur’an is the word of God and the word of the Prophet; the two are not in conflict; they
are the two aspects of one revelation.
   The account is the key to Rahman’s theology. It is the Qur’an as the word of God; it is the
Qur’an as the word of the Prophet; it is the creative process.


53.3.3    The General Principles and the Specific Responses

Rahman’s distinction between the general principles and the specific responses is stated in
Islam and Modernity and in Major Themes of the Qur’an. The distinction is the foundation of
Rahman’s hermeneutics; it is the key to the double movement.
   The distinction has three features.


First feature: the specific responses. The specific responses are the verses of the Qur’an
that respond to specific problems in specific historical situations. The verse on inheritance, the
verse on the orphan, the verse on the poor, the verse on the stranger: each is a response to a
specific problem in the seventh-century Arabian society. The specific responses are historical;
they are conditioned by the situation; they are not timeless laws.
594                                                                     Chapter 53. Fazlur Rahman


Second feature: the general principles. The general principles are the moral spirit that
the specific responses express. The principles are justice, equity, the protection of the weak,
the care for the poor, the dignity of the human being. The principles are eternal; they are not
conditioned by the situation; they are the timeless core of the Qur’an. The specific responses are
the form; the general principles are the spirit.

Third feature: the relation between the two. The relation between the two is the relation
between the form and the spirit, between the historical and the eternal, between the specific and
the general. The specific responses are the application of the general principles to the historical
situation; the general principles are the meaning of the specific responses. The interpreter must
move from the specific to the general, and from the general to the specific. The double movement
is the movement between the two.
      The distinction is the key to Rahman’s hermeneutics. It is the specific responses; it is the
general principles; it is the relation between the two.


53.3.4      The Living Sunnah
Rahman’s concept of the living Sunnah (al-sunnah al-hayya) is stated in Islamic Methodology in
History (1965). The concept is one of Rahman’s most original contributions to Islamic thought;
it is the foundation of his account of the tradition.
      The concept has three features.

First feature: the Sunnah as a living tradition. The Sunnah is not a fixed text; it is not
a collection of hadith; it is not a set of rules. The Sunnah is a living tradition; it is the practice
of the community; it is the ongoing interpretation of the Prophet’s example. The Sunnah is not
the past; it is the present; it is the living voice of the community.

Second feature: the Sunnah as the interpretation of the Qur’an. The Sunnah is the
interpretation of the Qur’an; it is the way the community has understood and applied the Qur’an.
The Sunnah is not separate from the Qur’an; it is the Qur’an in practice; it is the Qur’an in the
life of the community. The Sunnah is the living interpretation of the living word.

Third feature: the Sunnah as the basis of ijtihad. The Sunnah is the basis of ijtihad; it
is the foundation of the independent judgment. The ijtihad is not the rejection of the Sunnah;
it is the continuation of the Sunnah; it is the living interpretation of the living tradition. The
ijtihad is the way to keep the Sunnah alive; it is the way to apply the Sunnah to the modern
world.
      The concept is the key to Rahman’s account of the tradition. It is the living Sunnah; it is
the interpretation of the Qur’an; it is the basis of ijtihad.


53.3.5      The Critique of Traditionalism and Secularism
Rahman’s critique of traditionalism and secularism is stated in Islam and Modernity. The critique
is the diagnosis of the two errors that have impeded the development of Islamic thought; it is the
53.4. Internal Disputes                                                                       595


foundation of Rahman’s reformism.
   The critique has three features.

First feature: the critique of traditionalism. The traditionalists have failed to recognize
the difference between the general principles and the specific responses. They have treated the
specific responses as timeless laws; they have frozen the Qur’an in the seventh century; they have
made the Qur’an irrelevant to the modern world. The traditionalism is the first error; it is the
error of rigidity; it is the error of the letter without the spirit.

Second feature: the critique of secularism. The secularists have accepted the traditional-
ists’ rigid reading; they have concluded that the Qur’an is irrelevant to the modern world; they
have abandoned the Qur’anic foundation. The secularism is the second error; it is the error of
the spirit without the letter; it is the error of the modern world without the Qur’an.

Third feature: the neo-modernist alternative. The neo-modernist alternative is the
double movement; it is the recognition of the difference between the general principles and the
specific responses; it is the application of the principles to the modern world. The neo-modernism
is the way between the two errors; it is the way to be faithful to the Qur’an and relevant to the
modern world. Rahman calls himself a neo-modernist; he is the one who seeks to reconstruct the
Islamic thought in the light of the Qur’an and the modern knowledge.
   The critique is the key to Rahman’s reformism. It is the critique of traditionalism; it is the
critique of secularism; it is the neo-modernist alternative.


53.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Rahman is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of revelation. The traditional reading takes Rahman’s account
of revelation to be a denial of the verbal revelation: the Qur’an is not the word of God in the
literal sense; it is the word of the Prophet in the full sense. A revisionary reading takes it to
be an affirmation of the verbal revelation: the Qur’an is the word of God in the full sense, and
the human participation is the mode of the divine revelation, not its denial. The two readings
disagree on whether Rahman is a modernist or a traditionalist, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s expression is a structural tendency, neither a
verbal revelation nor a human production.

Second dispute: the status of the double movement. The traditional reading takes the
double movement to be a hermeneutical method: it is a way of interpreting the Qur’an; it is a
technique; it is a procedure. A revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophical anthropology:
it is a way of understanding the human condition; it is a way of understanding the relation
between the eternal and the historical. The two readings disagree on whether Rahman is a
methodologist or a philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, neither a method nor an anthropology.
596                                                                      Chapter 53. Fazlur Rahman


Third dispute: the status of the living Sunnah. The traditional reading takes the living
Sunnah to be a historical concept: it is the practice of the community; it is the living tradition. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophical concept: it is the structure of the tradition; it is
the condition of the continuity. The two readings disagree on whether Rahman is a historian or a
philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, neither a history nor a philosophy.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Rahman is a modernist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a modernist reformism. If
Rahman is a traditionalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
traditionalist reformism. The framework holds that the revisionary reading is closer to the texts
of Rahman, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


53.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Rahman. The framework shares four structural features with Rahman’s position.

        1. The distinction between the principle and the application. Rahman holds that
           the Qur’an contains general principles and specific responses; the principles are
           eternal; the responses are historical. The framework holds that the identity is the
           invariance and the manifestation is the appearance; the identity is the structure; the
           manifestation is the historical form. Both hold that there is a distinction between
           the eternal and the historical, and that the eternal is expressed in the historical.

        2. The critique of the static conception. Rahman holds that the traditionalists have
           frozen the Qur’an in the seventh century; they have made the Qur’an irrelevant to
           the modern world. The framework holds that the tradition has conflated identity
          with manifestation; it has reduced the identity to its manifestations; it has collapsed
           the structural difference. Both hold that the tradition has made a mistake, and that
           the mistake is the collapse of a distinction.

        3. The dynamic conception of the tradition. Rahman holds that the Sunnah is a living
           tradition; it is the ongoing interpretation of the Qur’an; it is the living voice of the
           community. The framework holds that the tradition is a living structure; it is the
           ongoing expression of the identity; it is the living manifestation of the structure.
           Both hold that the tradition is dynamic, not static, and that the dynamic is the
           truth of the static.

        4. The reformist project. Rahman holds that the task of the modern Muslim is to
           reconstruct the Islamic thought in the light of the Qur’an and the modern knowledge;
           it is the neo-modernist project. The framework holds that the task of the philosopher
           is to reconstruct the structure of identity and manifestation in the light of the tradition
53.6. Points of Divergence                                                                     597


         and the modern knowledge. Both hold that there is a task of reconstruction, and
         that the task is the way to keep the tradition alive.



53.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Rahman. The framework diverges from Rahman in four respects.

       1. The status of revelation. Rahman holds that the Qur’an is the word of God and the
         word of the Prophet; the revelation is a creative process; the divine word takes form
         in the human heart. The framework has no revelation; its structure is not a divine
         word; its truth is structural, not revealed. The framework is a metaphysics without
         revelation.

       2. The status of the Qur’an. Rahman holds that the Qur’an is the guidance for humanity;
         it is the source of the principles; it is the foundation of the reform. The framework
         has no Qur’an; its structure is not a text; its guidance is structural, not scriptural.
         The framework is a metaphysics without a scripture.

       3. The status of the community. Rahman holds that the community is the bearer
         of the living Sunnah; it is the interpreter of the Qur’an; it is the agent of the
         reform. The framework has no community; its subject is the structure of identity
         and manifestation; it leaves the community to a separate inquiry. The framework is
         a metaphysics without a community.

       4. The status of the modern world. Rahman holds that the modern world is the context
         of the reform; it is the situation to which the principles are to be applied; it is the
         challenge that the tradition must meet. The framework holds that the modern world
         is the context of the reconstruction; it is the situation in which the structure is to
         be understood; it is the challenge that the philosophy must meet. The framework’s
         modern world is structural, not historical.



53.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Rahman’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
   a principle; it is a pattern. The Qur’an contains principles; the principles are the moral
   spirit; the principles are the guidance for humanity. The framework has no principles;
   the framework has no guidance; the framework’s world is a world without guidance. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of principles.
598                                                                  Chapter 53. Fazlur Rahman


   Rahman’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
   they are the levels of the divine revelation; they are the levels of the divine guidance. The
   framework’s realms are not levels of revelation; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of revelation.
   Rahman’s third objection. The framework says that its subject is structure, not the
   community. But a metaphysics without the community is an incomplete metaphysics; the
   community is the bearer of the tradition; the community is the interpreter of the text; the
   community is the agent of the reform. The framework’s silence on the community is not a
   boundary; it is a gap. The framework’s philosophy is a philosophy without the community,
   and a philosophy without the community is a philosophy without the tradition.



53.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the Qur’an contains principles,
   and it agrees that the principles are the moral spirit. But the framework denies that the
   principles must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the structural
   condition of the principles; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural
   condition under which the principles are what they are. The distinction is between a
   principle (a moral spirit) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds
   the second, not the first. The framework does not deny the principles; it denies that the
   principles are the only reality.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of manifestation. But the framework denies that
   the realms are levels of revelation. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they are
   the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the revelation. The
   distinction is between a level of revelation (a scriptural level) and a level of manifestation
   (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that a metaphysics without the
   community is incomplete, and it agrees that the community is the bearer of the tradition.
   But the framework denies that its silence on the community is a gap. The framework
   is a work of metaphysics, not of sociology; its subject is the structure of identity and
   manifestation, not the community. The framework states the structural condition of reality;
   it leaves the community to a separate inquiry. The distinction is between a metaphysics
   and a sociology; the framework keeps it, and it holds that keeping it is not a gap, but a
   boundary.



53.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
53.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      599


Rahman’s cost. If Rahman accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the Qur’an is the guidance for humanity in the full sense. He must accept that the Qur’an is a
manifestation of the structure, and that the guidance is a structural condition, not a scriptural
revelation. The cost is the loss of the scriptural guidance: the Qur’an is no longer the guidance;
the structure is the guidance. He must also give up the claim that the community is the bearer
of the living Sunnah; he must accept that the community is a manifestation of the structure; the
structure is the bearer of the tradition.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Rahman’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of revelation, of the Qur’an, of the community—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is
the enactment of a structure, but not a revelation, and the framework leaves the revelation to a
separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Rahman’s revelation is not
a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Rahman
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
revelation presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of
the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


53.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Rah-
   man’s term “the general principle.” If one substitutes “the general principle” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Rahman’s general prin-
   ciple is the moral spirit of the Qur’an, and it is not manifested, because it is the principle.
   The framework’s identity is multiple; Rahman’s principle is one. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Rahman’s term “the double
   movement.” If one substitutes “the double movement” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   Rahman’s double movement is the hermeneutical method. The framework’s expression is
   ontological; Rahman’s double movement is hermeneutical. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “tradition” is not substitutable for Rahman’s term “the living
   Sunnah.” If one substitutes “the living Sunnah” for “tradition” in the framework’s
600                                                                 Chapter 53. Fazlur Rahman


   statements, the statements change: the framework’s tradition is the structure of the
   manifestation; Rahman’s living Sunnah is the practice of the community. The framework’s
   tradition is structural; Rahman’s living Sunnah is communal. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Rahman is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a distinction between the eternal and the historical, and they
   differ on whether the eternal is a principle or a structure. Both hold that the tradition is
   dynamic, and they differ on whether the dynamic is a hermeneutical method or a structural
   tendency. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of Rahman would be refuted by showing that Rahman’s general
   principle cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and
   principle—by showing, that is, that Rahman already distinguishes the structural condition
   from the principle, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Rahman’s
   own.




53.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Rahman’s general principle, or is
it a departure from Rahman? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Rahman’s general principle is already a structural
condition, not a moral spirit, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of Islam and Modernity, Major Themes of
the Qur’an, and Islamic Methodology in History do justice to the texts? The chapter has used
the double movement, the account of revelation, the distinction between the general principles
and the specific responses, the living Sunnah, and the critique of traditionalism and secularism,
and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a
different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a principle and a structure—a tradition, a text, a practice.

Chapter 54

Arkoun


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Mohammed Arkoun (1928–2010 CE), the Algerian-French
historian of Islamic thought who taught at the Sorbonne and who proposed a critique of Islamic
reason (critique de la raison islamique). It states Arkoun’s project of an applied Islamology, his
distinction between the unthinkable (l’impensable) and the unthought (l’impensé) in Islamic
thought, his analysis of the social imaginary and of the closed official corpus, his account of
the Qur’an as an open linguistic corpus and of the event of revelation, and his critique of both
orthodoxy and orientalism, with reference to Pour une critique de la raison islamique (1984),
Rethinking Islam (1994), L’islam: morale et politique, and The Unthought in Contemporary
Islamic Thought (2002). It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Arkoun; it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of context
and of the autonomy of justification is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Arkoun’s
account of the historicity of reason; it presents the objections that Arkoun would raise against
the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it
states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes
no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the unthought,” “the
social imaginary,” “the closed official corpus,” or “applied Islamology,” these are Arkoun’s terms,
and their sense is fixed by his works and by the interpretive literature, not by the framework.


54.1      A Scene
Consider a student in a university lecture hall, taking notes on the history of Islamic law. The
lecturer speaks of the formation of the schools, the compilation of the traditions, the great jurists.
The account is learned and coherent, and every statement in it can be verified. Yet the student
notices that there are questions that the account never asks, and that no one in the room would
think to ask: how the criteria by which a tradition was counted sound were themselves formed,
and who decided what the questions might be.
   Consider next a believer who recites a verse that she has known since childhood. She hears it
as the speech of God, and she does not hear the grammar or the history of the word. If she were
told that the verse was uttered at a particular moment to a particular audience in a particular
language, she might feel that the verse was made smaller. If she were told that it could be read
in no way except as the speech of God, she might feel that the historical moment was erased.
   The two scenes pose a single question: what lies beneath the surface of what a tradition says,
the unasked questions, the unseen conditions of its sayings, and how can they be brought to light
without destroying what the tradition holds sacred? Arkoun held that this is the central task of
a critique of Islamic reason. The framework also asks for the conditions of a claim, in its own
register. The chapter asks how the two stand to each other.

                                                602
54.2. The Question                                                                               603


54.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Fazlur Rahman’s hermeneutics of the Qur’an and his double
movement. Arkoun’s project is akin to Rahman’s in its historical seriousness but differs in
its method, which draws on structural linguistics, on the history of mentalities, and on the
philosophy of the human sciences in France, and which carries the historical critique of reason
further than Rahman does.
   The question is not whether Arkoun was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Arkoun hold? The chapter states the project of the
critique of Islamic reason, the unthought, the social imaginary, the open corpus, and the critique
of orthodoxy and orientalism.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Arkoun converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Arkoun would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Arkoun?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


54.3      Arkoun’s Position
Arkoun’s project, as he states it in Pour une critique de la raison islamique, is to carry out for
Islamic thought what the critique of reason has done for the thought of the West: to examine the
conditions, the instruments, and the limits of the reason that has produced its knowledge. He
calls the project applied Islamology, and he distinguishes it both from classical Islamic theology,
which takes the revealed text as given, and from orientalism, which takes it as an object of
philology and leaves the categories of the investigator unexamined.


54.3.1    The Unthinkable and the Unthought
Arkoun distinguishes what is unthinkable in a given state of a tradition, what cannot be thought
because the conceptual tools are lacking or forbidden, from what is unthought, what could
have been thought but was not, because the tradition’s attention was directed elsewhere or its
institutions did not allow it. The critique of reason is the work of identifying the unthought
and of showing how it came to be unthought. Arkoun holds that the history of Islamic thought
contains large regions of the unthought, in particular the historical and social conditions of the
formation of the canon.


54.3.2    The Social Imaginary and the Closed Corpus
Arkoun holds that a community lives by an imaginary, a body of images, beliefs, and ideals
that structure what its members can perceive and desire, and that the imaginary is ordinarily
604                                                                          Chapter 54. Arkoun


invisible to those who live by it. In the case of Islam he argues that the early sources were closed
into an official corpus by a process of selection and canonization that served the needs of an
emergent political order, and that the closure is a historical event and not a necessity of faith.
The Qur’an itself, in the stage of its oral proclamation, was an open corpus, rich in possibilities
of meaning that the later corpus restricted.

54.3.3     The Event of Revelation
Arkoun distinguishes the revelation as an event, the prophetic discourse in its origin, from the
Qur’an as a book and from the commentary on it. He holds that the first can be approached
only through the second and third, and that the historical and linguistic study of the latter is
not a hostile attack on the former but the only way of approaching it responsibly. He calls for a
rethinking of the status of the sacred in a way that neither reduces it to a social function nor
protects it from inquiry.


54.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Arkoun is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: critique or relativism. One reading takes Arkoun’s critique to be a rational
examination that leaves the possibility of truth intact. Another takes it to reduce every claim
to its historical conditions and so to relativism. The disagreement matters for the framework
because the framework’s claim to state conditions of validity stands in a different relation to
each.

Second dispute: the accessibility of his work. Arkoun wrote in a dense and allusive
French, and many of his works are collections of essays and lectures, not systematic treatises.
One reading takes this to be an essential feature of a thought that resists system. Another takes
it to be a limitation. The disagreement matters because the framework’s dialogue is with a
position, and the reading decides whether there is a stable one.

Third dispute: his place in Islamic thought. Some readers take Arkoun to stand within
the tradition as a reformer. Others take him to stand outside it as a critic. The disagreement
matters because the framework’s relation to him depends on whether he speaks from within the
community of faith.


54.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Arkoun. The framework shares four structural features with Arkoun’s position.

        1. The conditions of a claim. Arkoun holds that every claim is made under conditions
          that are not themselves among the claims. The framework holds that a claim is
54.6. Points of Divergence                                                                      605


         valid only under a context and a structure. Both hold that the conditions of a claim
          are a proper object of inquiry.

       2. The plurality of contexts. Arkoun holds that the same text has been read in many
         ways under many conditions and that no reading has exhausted it. The framework
          holds that contexts are infinite. Both hold that a text or a structure is not exhausted
          by any one reading.

       3. The refusal of an unexamined standpoint. Arkoun criticizes both orthodoxy and
          orientalism for leaving their own categories unexamined. The framework holds that
          no context is the context of all contexts. Both refuse the privilege of an unexamined
          standpoint.

       4. The distinction between event and record. Arkoun distinguishes the event of revelation
          from the book. The framework distinguishes the identity from its manifestations.
          Both hold that what is the source is not simply identical with what records it.



54.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Arkoun. The framework diverges from Arkoun’s position in four respects.

       1. The register. Arkoun’s critique is historical, linguistic, and sociological. The frame-
         work’s is structural and does not appeal to a history of the conditions of its claims.

       2. The status of the sacred. Arkoun treats the sacred as a historical category that is to
          be rethought. The framework makes no claim about the sacred.

       3. The claim to autonomy. Arkoun holds that every claim is conditioned by a social
          imaginary. The framework holds the autonomy of philosophical justification.

       4. The account of the source. Arkoun’s event of revelation is a historical event. The
          framework’s one source is a structural condition of an identity.



54.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Arkoun’s first objection. The framework claims the autonomy of philosophical justifi-
   cation. But there is no justification that is not carried out in a language and an imaginary,
   and the framework’s claim to autonomy is the unexamined imaginary of a particular
   philosophical tradition, the tradition of the system. The framework has an unthought,
   and it does not know what it is.
606                                                                             Chapter 54. Arkoun


   Arkoun’s second objection. The framework’s structure, with its identity, its source,
   and its realms, is a construction of reason presented as a description of what is. But the
   critique of reason shows that every such construction is the product of a history. The
   framework should begin by examining the history of its own categories, and it does not.
   Arkoun’s third objection. The framework takes no position on the sacred. But a
   position that says nothing of the sacred is a position that takes the secular as given, and
   the secular is itself a historical formation. The framework’s silence is not neutrality but a
   decision.



54.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that every justification is carried
   out in a language and a tradition, and it agrees that it has an unthought. It denies that
   this refutes the claim to autonomy, which is the claim that a claim is assessed by its
   premises and arguments and not by its origin. Arkoun’s own critique asks that the claims
   of orthodoxy and of orientalism be assessed on these grounds, and it is therefore itself an
   appeal to the autonomy that the objection denies.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that its categories have a
   history and that an examination of the history is a legitimate and valuable inquiry. It
   holds that the examination is a different task from the statement of the structure and that
   it does not need to precede it. A structure may be stated and assessed before its history
   is written, and the history, when written, may modify the structure. The framework does
   not close that possibility.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that silence is a position and not
   a neutrality, and it states its silence as a position: it makes no claim about the sacred
   because its subject is structure. It does not take the secular as given; it takes no view
   on the secular either. The distinction between a silence that excludes and a silence that
   abstains is one that Arkoun’s own project of rethinking the sacred requires.



54.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Arkoun’s cost. If Arkoun accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that a claim can be
assessed by its premises and arguments independently of an inquiry into its social imaginary,
and that a structure can be stated before its history is written. The cost is the loss of the claim
that the critique of conditions must always precede the assessment of a claim.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim that
its structural register is innocent of a history, and it must accept that a historical inquiry into its
54.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      607


categories is a necessary complement of its argument. The cost is the loss of the self-sufficiency
of the structural register.


The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about the conditions of a valid account. The framework must take the unthought as
a limit of its own statements. Arkoun must take structure as a way of stating what a critique
presupposes. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between history and structure.



54.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Arkoun.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “context” is not substitutable for Arkoun’s term
   “social imaginary.” If one substitutes “social imaginary” for “context,” the statements
   change: a social imaginary is a body of images and beliefs that a community lives by,
   while a context is a structural condition of validity. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “manifestation” is not substitutable for Arkoun’s
   term “corpus.” If one substitutes “corpus” for “manifestation,” the statements change:
   a corpus is a body of texts that has been selected and closed, while a manifestation
   is the appearance of an identity in a realm. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Arkoun’s term
   “the event of revelation.” If one substitutes “the event of revelation” for “identity,” the
   statements change: the event is a historical occurrence of prophetic discourse, while the
   identity is a structural invariance. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Arkoun is resemblance:
   both hold that a claim has conditions that are not among the claims, that no standpoint
   is unexamined, and that what is a source is not identical with what records it, and they
   differ on whether the conditions are historical or structural and on whether justification is
   autonomous. The relation is not equivalence, agreement, or identity. The framework’s
   reading would be refuted by showing that Arkoun’s unthought cannot be stated without a
   structural condition of the framework’s kind, or that the framework’s structure cannot be
   stated without an appeal to the history that Arkoun holds to be its condition.



54.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
608                                                                             Chapter 54. Arkoun


First question. Does the framework’s claim to autonomy survive Arkoun’s critique of reason?
The chapter has argued that it does as the claim that a claim is assessed by its grounds, but
the argument is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that every ground is conditioned has a
question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can a structure be stated before its history is written? The chapter has
argued that it can, but a reader who holds that the history is internal to the structure has a
question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to Arkoun’s essays, which resist
system? The chapter has stated their main lines, and a reader who holds that this reading
imposes a unity they do not have has a question the chapter leaves open.

Think of a question that no one in your family, your profession, or your community ever asks.
