Chapter 55

Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


Scope. This chapter closes Part VII, the dialogues with contemporary Islamic philosophy, and
it closes it with two Moroccan thinkers whose projects stand in stark opposition: Mohammed
Abed al-Jabri (1935–2010 CE) and Taha Abdurrahman (born 1944 CE). It states al-Jabri’s
critique of Arab reason (naqd al-’aql al-’arabi), the tripartite division of the epistemic systems
into demonstration (burhan), rhetoric (bayan), and gnosis (’irfan), the critique of the Andalusian-
Averroist tradition as the model for renewal, and the project of epistemological rupture; and it
states Taha Abdurrahman’s critique of al-Jabri’s fragmentation of the tradition, his tripartite
hierarchy of reason (abstract reason, sustained reason, confirmed reason), the primacy of the
ethical and the pragmatic over the theoretical, and the project of renewing the method of
assessing the tradition (tajdid al-manhaj fi taqwim al-turath), with reference to al-Jabri’s Takwin
al-’Aql al-’Arabi (The Formation of Arab Reason, 1982), Bunyat al-’Aql al-’Arabi (The Structure
of Arab Reason, 1986), and al-’Aql al-Siyasi al-’Arabi (The Political Arab Reason, 1990); and
Taha Abdurrahman’s Tajdid al-Manhaj fi Taqwim al-Turath (The Renewal of Method in the
Assessment of the Tradition, 1994), al-’Amal al-Dini wa-Tajdid al-’Aql (Religious Practice and
the Renewal of Reason, 1989), Su’al al-Akhlaq (The Question of Ethics, 2000), and Ruh al-Din
(The Spirit of Religion, 2012); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
each thinker; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of reason and of tradition is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to theirs; it
presents the objections that each thinker would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the critique of Arab reason,” “demonstration,” “rhetoric,”
“gnosis,” “abstract reason,” “sustained reason,” “confirmed reason,” “the renewal of method,” or
“the ethics of dialogue,” these are the thinkers’ terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and
by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


55.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the history of Islamic philosophy. She reads Ibn Rushd, and
she sees a rationalist, a defender of Aristotle, a critic of al-Ghazali. She reads Ibn Arabi, and
she sees a mystic, a visionary, a spokesman of the unity of being. She reads al-Ghazali, and she
sees a critic of the philosophers, a defender of the faith, a Sufi. She asks: which of these is the
authentic Islamic tradition? Which of these should the modern Muslim recover?
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she reads al-Jabri. Al-Jabri tells her: the authentic
Islamic tradition is the Andalusian tradition, the tradition of Ibn Rushd, the tradition of
demonstration (burhan). The Eastern tradition, the tradition of Ibn Sina and al-Ghazali and Ibn

                                               609
610                                                    Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


Arabi, is the tradition of rhetoric (bayan) and gnosis (’irfan), and it is the tradition of decline.
The modern Muslim must recover the Andalusian tradition, the Averroist spirit, the rationalist
project, and must break with the Eastern tradition, the mystical project, the tradition of decline.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she reads Taha Abdurrahman. Taha tells
her: al-Jabri is wrong. The tradition is not divided into three independent systems; it is a unity,
and the attempt to divide it is a fragmentation (tajzi’a) that destroys the tradition. And the
hierarchy is wrong: the highest form of reason is not the abstract reason of the demonstration,
but the confirmed reason (al-’aql al-mu’ayyad) of the gnosis, the reason that is illuminated by
the divine. The ethical and the pragmatic are prior to the theoretical; the practice is prior to the
concept; the tradition is a living unity, not a collection of systems.
      The scene is the image of the two projects, in Takwin al-’Aql al-’Arabi and in Tajdid al-Manhaj,
of the structure of the tradition. The tradition is the subject; al-Jabri is the epistemologist; Taha
is the ethicist. The scene poses the question that the two thinkers were the first to pose in its
full form in the contemporary Moroccan tradition. What is the Arab reason? How is it to be
critiqued? And what is the relation between the tradition and modernity? The present chapter
states the two answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


55.2        The Question
The previous chapter stated Fazlur Rahman’s position: the double movement, the account of
revelation, the general principles and the specific responses, the living Sunnah, and the critique
of traditionalism and secularism. Rahman is the neo-modernist who seeks to reconstruct Islamic
thought in the light of the Qur’an and modern knowledge. Al-Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman
are his contemporaries, and they are the two great figures of the contemporary Moroccan
philosophical scene. Al-Jabri is the epistemologist who critiques the Arab reason; Taha is the
ethicist who critiques al-Jabri and renews the method. The present chapter states the two
projects, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
      The question is not whether al-Jabri or Taha was right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did al-Jabri and Taha hold? The chapter states al-Jabri’s
critique of Arab reason, the tripartite division, and the Averroist project; and Taha’s critique of
al-Jabri, the tripartite hierarchy of reason, the primacy of the ethical, and the renewal of method.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that each thinker would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and each
thinker? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.
55.3. Al-Jabri’s Position                                                                        611


55.3      Al-Jabri’s Position

55.3.1    The Critique of Arab Reason
Al-Jabri’s critique of Arab reason is stated in the trilogy Naqd al-’Aql al-’Arabi (The Critique of
Arab Reason): Takwin al-’Aql al-’Arabi (The Formation of Arab Reason, 1982), Bunyat al-’Aql
al-’Arabi (The Structure of Arab Reason, 1986), and al-’Aql al-Siyasi al-’Arabi (The Political
Arab Reason, 1990). The critique is not a critique of the products of Arab reason; it is a critique
of the apparatus that produces them; it is an epistemological critique.
   The critique has three features.

First feature: the object of the critique. The object of the critique is not the tradition
as a body of ideas; it is the epistemic system that governs the production of ideas in the Arab
culture. Al-Jabri distinguishes between the tradition as a product (al-turath) and the reason
that produces it (al-’aql). The critique is directed at the latter, not the former. The question is
not what the Arab thinkers said; it is how they thought, what concepts and methods governed
their thinking.

Second feature: the epistemological rupture. The critique aims at an epistemological
rupture (qat’i’a epistemologiyya); it aims at breaking with the epistemic systems that have
dominated Arab thought since the Age of Codification (’asr al-tadwin). The rupture is not a
rejection of the tradition; it is a break with the epistemological structures that have made the
tradition stagnant. The goal is to recover the rationalist spirit of the Andalusian tradition, the
spirit of Ibn Rushd, and to use it as the foundation for a modern Arab thought.

Third feature: the historical method. The critique uses the historical method; it studies the
formation of the Arab reason in its historical context; it identifies the external influences (Greek,
Persian, Indian) and the internal dynamics that shaped it. The method is not philosophical in
the traditional sense; it is epistemological and historical. It asks: what were the conditions under
which the Arab reason was formed? What were the systems that governed it? And how can it
be transformed?
   The critique is the foundation of al-Jabri’s project. It is the critique of the apparatus; it is
the epistemological rupture; it is the historical method.

   From the Tradition

   “The critique of Arab reason is not a critique of the tradition as a product, but of the
   apparatus that produces it. The goal is an epistemological rupture that breaks with the
   systems that have made the Arab thought stagnant, and recovers the rationalist spirit of
   the Andalusian tradition.” (al-Jabri, Takwin al-’Aql al-’Arabi, Introduction, adapted)


55.3.2    The Tripartite Division
Al-Jabri’s tripartite division of the Arab epistemic systems is stated in the trilogy. The division
is the analytical core of his project; it is the key to his reading of the tradition.
612                                                      Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


      The division has three features.

First feature: the demonstration (burhan). The demonstration is the epistemic system
of the philosophers; it is the system of Aristotle and his Arab followers (al-Farabi, Ibn Sina,
Ibn Rushd). Its model is logic; its criterion is demonstration; its paradigm is the syllogism.
The demonstration is the system of the rationalists; it is the system that al-Jabri considers the
highest, and the Andalusian tradition is its highest manifestation.

Second feature: the rhetoric (bayan). The rhetoric is the epistemic system of the jurists,
the theologians, and the linguists; it is the system of the Arabic language and the Islamic sciences.
Its model is the Arabic language; its criterion is the linguistic convention; its paradigm is the
analogy (qiyas). The rhetoric is the system of the majority; it is the system that has dominated
Arab thought, and it is the system that al-Jabri considers the source of the stagnation.

Third feature: the gnosis (’irfan). The gnosis is the epistemic system of the Sufis and the
esoteric thinkers; it is the system of Ibn Arabi and the illuminationists. Its model is the inner
experience; its criterion is the unveiling (kashf ); its paradigm is the symbolic interpretation. The
gnosis is the system of the mystics; it is the system that al-Jabri considers the lowest, and it is
the system that he associates with the decline of Arab thought.
      The division is the key to al-Jabri’s reading of the tradition. It is the demonstration; it is the
rhetoric; it is the gnosis.

55.3.3      The Averroist Project
Al-Jabri’s recovery of the Averroist tradition is the constructive side of his project. The project
has three features.

First feature: the Andalusian tradition. The Andalusian tradition is the tradition of
Ibn Rushd, Ibn Bajja, and Ibn Tufayl; it is the tradition of the demonstration, the rationalism,
the Aristotelianism. Al-Jabri argues that the Andalusian tradition is the authentic rationalist
tradition of Islam, and that it was suppressed by the Eastern tradition, the tradition of al-Ghazali
and Ibn Arabi. The recovery of the Andalusian tradition is the recovery of the rationalist spirit
of Islam.

Second feature: the critique of the Eastern tradition. The Eastern tradition is the
tradition of Ibn Sina and al-Ghazali and Ibn Arabi; it is the tradition of the rhetoric and the
gnosis. Al-Jabri argues that the Eastern tradition is the source of the stagnation of Arab thought;
it is the tradition that replaced the rationalism of the Andalusian tradition with the mysticism
of the gnosis and the authoritarianism of the rhetoric. The critique of the Eastern tradition is
the liberation from the stagnation.

Third feature: the modern project. The modern project is the project of a modern Arab
thought that is founded on the Averroist tradition. It is not a rejection of the tradition; it is
a recovery of the authentic tradition. It is not a rejection of modernity; it is a recovery of the
55.4. Taha Abdurrahman’s Position                                                                613


rationalist spirit that is the condition of modernity. The modern project is the synthesis of the
Averroist tradition and the modern reason.
   The project is the constructive side of al-Jabri’s critique. It is the Andalusian tradition; it is
the critique of the Eastern tradition; it is the modern project.


55.4      Taha Abdurrahman’s Position

55.4.1    The Critique of al-Jabri

Taha Abdurrahman’s critique of al-Jabri is stated in Tajdid al-Manhaj fi Taqwim al-Turath
(The Renewal of Method in the Assessment of the Tradition, 1994) and in Su’al al-Akhlaq (The
Question of Ethics, 2000). The critique is the foundation of Taha’s project; it is the diagnosis of
the errors of the epistemological approach.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the fragmentation (tajzi’a). Taha argues that al-Jabri’s tripartite division
fragments the tradition into three independent systems, and that the fragmentation destroys
the unity of the tradition. The tradition is not three systems; it is a unity, and the systems are
aspects of the unity. The fragmentation is the first error; it is the error of the analytical method
that loses the whole in the parts.


Second feature: the criterion confusion. Taha argues that al-Jabri’s division is marred
by a confusion of criteria: the demonstration is judged by logic, the rhetoric by language, and
the gnosis by inner experience, but the division should use a single criterion to distinguish the
systems. The confusion is the second error; it is the error of the method that does not distinguish
between the criteria of the systems.


Third feature: the neglect of the ethical. Taha argues that al-Jabri’s project neglects the
ethical dimension of the tradition; it treats the tradition as an epistemological problem, and it
forgets that the tradition is, before all, an ethical and practical reality. The neglect is the third
error; it is the error of the project that reduces the tradition to knowledge.
   The critique is the foundation of Taha’s project. It is the fragmentation; it is the criterion
confusion; it is the neglect of the ethical.


55.4.2    The Tripartite Hierarchy of Reason

Taha Abdurrahman’s tripartite hierarchy of reason is stated in al-’Amal al-Dini wa-Tajdid al-’Aql
(Religious Practice and the Renewal of Reason, 1989) and in Tajdid al-Manhaj. The hierarchy is
the alternative to al-Jabri’s division; it is the key to Taha’s epistemology.
   The hierarchy has three features.


First feature: the abstract reason (al-’aql al-mujarrad). The abstract reason is the
reason of the demonstration, the logic, the theoretical thought. It is the reason that al-Jabri
614                                                    Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


considers the highest, but Taha considers it the lowest. The abstract reason is the reason of the
philosophers, and it is necessary, but it is not sufficient.


Second feature: the sustained reason (al-’aql al-musaddad). The sustained reason is
the reason of the rhetoric, the language, the jurisprudence. It is the reason that is guided by the
revelation and the tradition; it is the reason of the jurists and the theologians. Taha considers it
higher than the abstract reason, because it is guided by the divine.


Third feature: the confirmed reason (al-’aql al-mu’ayyad). The confirmed reason is
the reason of the gnosis, the inner experience, the spiritual practice. It is the reason that is
confirmed by the divine light; it is the reason of the Sufis and the saints. Taha considers it the
highest, because it is the reason that is united with the divine.
      The hierarchy is the key to Taha’s epistemology. It is the abstract reason; it is the sustained
reason; it is the confirmed reason.


55.4.3      The Primacy of the Ethical and the Pragmatic
Taha Abdurrahman’s primacy of the ethical and the pragmatic is stated in Su’al al-Akhlaq and
in Ruh al-Din. The primacy is the foundation of Taha’s philosophy; it is the alternative to the
theoretical approach of al-Jabri.
      The primacy has three features.


First feature: the ethical as the foundation. The ethical is not a branch of philosophy; it
is the foundation of philosophy. The human being is an ethical being before being a knowing
being; the practice is prior to the theory; the ethics is prior to the epistemology. Taha argues
that the Arab thought must be renewed on the basis of the ethical, not on the basis of the
epistemological.


Second feature: the pragmatic as the criterion. The pragmatic is the criterion of the
truth; the truth is what works in the practice; the theory is validated by the practice. Taha
argues that the Arab thought must be pragmatic, not theoretical; it must be concerned with the
practice, not with the concept.


Third feature: the trusteeship (al-i’timan). The trusteeship is the ethical relation between
the human being and the divine; it is the responsibility of the human being before God. Taha
argues that the modern Arab thought must be founded on the trusteeship, not on the secular
autonomy; it must be ethical, not secular.
      The primacy is the key to Taha’s philosophy. It is the ethical; it is the pragmatic; it is the
trusteeship.


55.4.4      The Renewal of Method
Taha Abdurrahman’s renewal of method (tajdid al-manhaj) is the constructive side of his project.
The renewal has three features.
55.5. Internal Disputes                                                                           615


First feature: the holistic view. The renewal begins with a holistic view of the tradition; it
refuses the fragmentation of the tradition into systems; it treats the tradition as a living unity.
The holistic view is the condition of the correct assessment; the fragmentation is the error that
must be avoided.


Second feature: the internal productivity. The renewal studies the internal productivity
of the tradition; it asks how the tradition produces its concepts and its practices; it does not
impose external categories on the tradition. The internal productivity is the condition of the
authentic understanding; the external categories are the source of the distortion.


Third feature: the dialogue. The renewal is a dialogue with the tradition; it is a conversation
with the ancestors; it is a living relation with the past. The dialogue is not a rejection; it is not
a repetition; it is a renewal. The dialogue is the condition of the living tradition; the repetition
is the death of the tradition.
   The renewal is the constructive side of Taha’s project. It is the holistic view; it is the internal
productivity; it is the dialogue.


55.5        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of al-Jabri and Taha is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of al-Jabri’s project. The traditional reading takes al-Jabri’s
project to be an epistemological critique: it is a critique of the Arab reason; it is an analysis
of the epistemic systems. A revisionary reading takes it to be an ideological project: it is a
defense of the Andalusian tradition; it is a critique of the Eastern tradition; it is a political
intervention. The two readings disagree on whether al-Jabri is an epistemologist or an ideologue,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is
a structural realism, neither an epistemology nor an ideology.


Second dispute: the status of Taha’s project. The traditional reading takes Taha’s project
to be an ethical critique: it is a critique of the epistemological approach; it is a defense of the
ethical and the pragmatic. A revisionary reading takes it to be a theological project: it is a
defense of the Sufi tradition; it is a critique of the secular modernity. The two readings disagree
on whether Taha is an ethicist or a theologian, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, neither an ethics nor a
theology.


Third dispute: the relation between the two. The traditional reading takes the two to be
rivals: al-Jabri is the rationalist, Taha is the mystic; al-Jabri is the epistemologist, Taha is the
ethicist; the two projects are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary:
al-Jabri critiques the apparatus, Taha critiques the ethics; the two are the two sides of one renewal.
The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement
616                                                      Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a rival nor a complement.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If al-Jabri is an epistemologist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an epistemological critique. If
Taha is an ethicist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and an ethical critique.
The framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to the texts, but it does not rest its
case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


55.6       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With al-Jabri. The framework shares three structural features with al-Jabri’s position.

        1. The critique of the static tradition. Al-Jabri holds that the Arab reason has been
           stagnant since the Age of Codification; it has been dominated by the rhetoric and the
           gnosis; it has lost the rationalist spirit. The framework holds that the tradition has
           conflated identity with manifestation; it has reduced the identity to its manifestations;
           it has collapsed the structural difference. Both hold that the tradition has made a
           mistake, and that the mistake is the collapse of a distinction.

        2. The tripartite division. Al-Jabri divides the Arab epistemic systems into the demon-
           stration, the rhetoric, and the gnosis. The framework distinguishes the realms into
           the First Determination, the Structural Determination, the Relational Manifestation,
           and the Material Manifestation. Both hold that reality is stratified, and that the
           strata are distinct.

        3. The recovery of the rationalist spirit. Al-Jabri seeks to recover the rationalist spirit of
           the Andalusian tradition; he seeks to found a modern Arab thought on the Averroist
           tradition. The framework seeks to recover the structural spirit of the tradition; it
           seeks to found a modern philosophy on the structural realism. Both hold that there
           is a spirit to be recovered, and that the recovery is the condition of the renewal.

   With Taha. The framework shares three structural features with Taha’s position.

        1. The critique of fragmentation. Taha holds that al-Jabri’s division fragments the
           tradition; it loses the unity of the tradition; it destroys the whole in the parts. The
           framework holds that the tradition is a unity; it is the unity of the structure; it is
           not a collection of systems. Both hold that the fragmentation is a mistake, and that
           the unity is the truth.

        2. The primacy of the ethical. Taha holds that the ethical is the foundation of philosophy;
           the practice is prior to the theory; the ethics is prior to the epistemology. The
           framework holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation; the identity
           is the condition of the appearance; the structure is prior to the manifestation. Both
           hold that there is a foundation, and that the foundation is not the theoretical.
55.7. Points of Divergence                                                                         617


       3. The holistic view. Taha holds that the renewal must begin with a holistic view of the
          tradition; it must treat the tradition as a living unity; it must not impose external
          categories on the tradition. The framework holds that the structure is a holistic
          structure; it is the structure of the whole; it is not a collection of parts. Both hold
          that the whole is prior to the parts, and that the holistic view is the condition of
          the understanding.




55.7      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With al-Jabri. The framework diverges from al-Jabri in three respects.

       1. The status of the tradition. Al-Jabri holds that the tradition is divided into three
          epistemic systems; it is the demonstration, the rhetoric, and the gnosis. The
          framework holds that the tradition is a unity; it is the unity of the structure; it is not
          a collection of systems. The framework’s tradition is a structure, not a collection.

       2. The status of the reason. Al-Jabri holds that the reason is the apparatus that
          produces the tradition; it is the epistemic system; it is the object of the critique.
         The framework holds that the reason is the reconstruction of the structure; it is the
          reading of the manifestations; it is the condition of the knowledge. The framework’s
          reason is structural, not epistemological.

       3. The status of the modern project. Al-Jabri holds that the modern project is the
          recovery of the Averroist tradition; it is the synthesis of the Andalusian tradition
          and the modern reason. The framework holds that the modern project is the
          reconstruction of the structure; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is the
          condition of the philosophy. The framework’s modern project is structural, not
         Averroist.

   With Taha. The framework diverges from Taha in three respects.

       1. The status of the ethical. Taha holds that the ethical is the foundation of philosophy;
          the ethics is prior to the epistemology. The framework holds that the structure is the
          foundation of the philosophy; the structure is prior to the ethics. The framework’s
          foundation is structural, not ethical.

       2. The status of the gnosis. Taha holds that the confirmed reason is the highest form of
          reason; it is the reason of the gnosis; it is the reason that is united with the divine.
         The framework has no gnosis; its knowledge is reconstruction; its highest form of
          knowledge is the structural reconstruction. The framework’s knowledge is structural,
          not gnostic.
618                                                   Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


       3. The status of the trusteeship. Taha holds that the trusteeship is the ethical relation
          between the human being and the divine; it is the foundation of the modern Arab
          thought. The framework has no trusteeship; its structure is not a relation to the
          divine; its ethics is left to a separate inquiry. The framework’s metaphysics is without
          the trusteeship.



55.8      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Al-Jabri’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
  a tradition; it is a pattern. The tradition is the epistemic system; it is the apparatus that
  produces the knowledge; it is the object of the critique. The framework has no tradition;
  the framework has no apparatus; the framework’s world is a world without tradition. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of tradition.
  Al-Jabri’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
  they are the levels of the epistemic systems; they are the levels of the demonstration, the
  rhetoric, and the gnosis. The framework’s realms are not levels of the epistemic systems;
  they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the epistemic
  systems.
  Taha’s first objection. The framework says that the structure is the foundation; the
  structure is prior to the ethics. But the ethical is the foundation; the practice is prior to
  the theory; the ethics is prior to the epistemology. The framework’s structure is a theory;
  it is not the practice. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of theories, not of practices.
  Taha’s second objection. The framework says that the knowledge is reconstruction;
  it is the reading of the manifestations. But the knowledge is the confirmed reason; it
  is the reason that is united with the divine; it is the knowledge that comes from the
  practice. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the confirmed reason.
  The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of confirmation.



55.9      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to al-Jabri’s first objection. The framework agrees that the tradition is an
  apparatus that produces knowledge, and it agrees that the apparatus is the object of
  the critique. But the framework denies that the tradition must be the only object. The
  framework’s identity is the structural condition of the tradition; it is the invariance enacted
  by one source; it is the structural condition under which the tradition is what it is. The
  distinction is between a tradition (an apparatus) and an identity (a structural condition);
55.10. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     619


   the framework holds the second, not the first. The framework does not deny the tradition;
   it denies that the tradition is the only principle.
   Reply to al-Jabri’s second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not
   just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the epistemic systems. The framework’s realms are
   ontological levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of
   possibility of the epistemic systems. The distinction is between a level of the epistemic
   system (an epistemological level) and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the
   framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Taha’s first objection. The framework agrees that the ethical is a foundation,
   and it agrees that the practice is prior to the theory. But the framework denies that the
   ethical is the foundation of the structure. The framework’s structure is the condition of
   possibility of the ethics; the ethics is a manifestation of the structure; the structure is not
   a manifestation of the ethics. The distinction is between a structure (a condition) and an
   ethics (a manifestation); the framework holds the first, not the second.
   Reply to Taha’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is
   not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the
   confirmed reason. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of
   the manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is
   between a confirmation (a union) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds
   the second, not the first.




55.10      The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Al-Jabri’s cost. If al-Jabri accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
tradition is divided into three systems. He must accept that the tradition is a unity, and that the
unity is the structure. The cost is the loss of the tripartite division: the tradition is no longer
three systems; the tradition is one structure. He must also give up the claim that the reason is
the apparatus; he must accept that the reason is the reconstruction; the reason is the reading of
the manifestations.


Taha’s cost. If Taha accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the ethical
is the foundation. He must accept that the structure is the foundation, and that the ethics is a
manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the ethical foundation: the ethics is no
longer the foundation; the structure is the foundation. He must also give up the claim that the
knowledge is the confirmed reason; he must accept that the knowledge is the reconstruction; the
knowledge is the reading of the manifestations.
620                                                  Chapter 55. Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of al-Jabri and Taha, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the tradition, of the ethics, of the confirmed reason—that its ontology
does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the
framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the tradition, and the framework
leaves the tradition to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that al-Jabri’s tradition and
Taha’s ethics are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Al-Jabri and Taha must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern;
it is a structural condition that the tradition and the ethics presuppose as their condition. The
cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they
are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.


55.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (al-Jabri). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for al-Jabri’s term “the epistemic system.” If one substitutes “the epistemic system” for
   “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; al-Jabri’s epistemic
   system is the apparatus that produces the knowledge, and it is not manifested, because it
   is the apparatus. The framework’s identity is a structure; al-Jabri’s epistemic system is
   an apparatus. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for al-Jabri’s term “the tradition.”
   If one substitutes “the tradition” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; al-Jabri’s tradition
   is the product of the epistemic system. The framework’s expression is structural; al-Jabri’s
   tradition is epistemological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The substitution test (Taha). The framework’s term “structure” is not substitutable
   for Taha’s term “the ethical.” If one substitutes “the ethical” for “structure” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s structure is the condition
   of possibility of the manifestation; Taha’s ethical is the foundation of the philosophy. The
   framework’s structure is ontological; Taha’s ethical is ethical. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Taha’s term “the confirmed
   reason.” If one substitutes “the confirmed reason” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; Taha’s confirmed reason is the reason united with the divine. The frame-
55.12. Open Questions                                                                          621


   work’s reconstruction is structural; Taha’s confirmed reason is mystical. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and al-Jabri is resemblance:
   both hold that the tradition has made a mistake, and they differ on whether the mistake
   is the collapse of a distinction or the stagnation of the apparatus. The relation between
   the framework and Taha is resemblance: both hold that the whole is prior to the parts,
   and they differ on whether the whole is a structure or an ethics. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of al-Jabri
   and Taha would be refuted by showing that their positions cannot be formulated without
   the framework’s distinction between structure and apparatus, or between structure and
   ethics—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the structural condition from
   the apparatus and the ethics, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of
   their own.




55.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of al-Jabri’s epistemic system or
Taha’s ethical, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that al-Jabri’s epistemic system is
already a structural condition, or that Taha’s ethical is already a structural condition, has a
question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Naqd al-’Aql al-’Arabi and Tajdid
al-Manhaj do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the critique of Arab reason, the tripartite
division, the Averroist project, the critique of al-Jabri, the tripartite hierarchy of reason, the
primacy of the ethical, and the renewal of method, and it has stated what would refute its
reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter
leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an apparatus and a structure—a tradition, a text, a
practice. Is the thing the apparatus that produces, or the structure that persists? Is the truth
the ethical that founds, or the structure that enacts? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between al-Jabri’s epistemic system, Taha’s ethical, and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Soroush. It states the distinction between religion and religious
knowledge, the theory of contraction and expansion, the account of the prophetic experience, and
the arguments on reason and freedom; it identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation
of Soroush; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of the relation between an identity and its reconstruction is the nearest contemporary
Islamic analogue to his account of the relation between religion and religious knowledge. The
present chapter has stated the answer of Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman; the next chapter states
Soroush’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 56

Soroush


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Abdolkarim Soroush (born 1945 CE), the Iranian
philosopher of religion and of science, whose distinction between religion and religious knowledge
has been among the most discussed proposals in contemporary Islamic thought. It states Soroush’s
theory of the contraction and expansion of religious knowledge (qabz va bast-i ti’urik-i shari’at),
his distinction between the essential and the accidental in religion, his account of the prophetic
experience and of the Qur’an as the speech of the Prophet in the experience of revelation, his
philosophy of the human sciences, and his arguments concerning reason, freedom, and the religious
state, with reference to Qabz va Bast-i Ti’urik-i Shari’at (1990), Bast-i Tajriba-yi Nabavi (The
Expansion of Prophetic Experience, 1999), and the collection Reason, Freedom, and Democracy
in Islam (2000). It identifies the internal disputes in the interpretation of Soroush; it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the relation between
an identity and its reconstruction is the nearest contemporary Islamic analogue to Soroush’s
account of the relation between religion and religious knowledge; it presents the objections that
Soroush would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of
“religion,” “religious knowledge,” “contraction and expansion,” or “prophetic experience,” these
are Soroush’s terms, and their sense is fixed by his works and by the interpretive literature, not
by the framework.


56.1      A Scene
Consider a mountain that many people have tried to describe. A geologist describes its strata; a
painter, the light on its face; a poet, what it is to stand beneath it; a guide, the routes across it.
Each description is true of the mountain and each is shaped by the describer: by the instruments,
the vocabulary, the habits of attention that she brings. If a new instrument is invented, the
geologist’s description changes, and the guide’s does not, and the painter’s changes for other
reasons. The mountain has not changed. Yet no one describes the mountain except through
descriptions.
   Consider next a religious community that has been reading a sacred text for fourteen centuries.
In the first century its readers had the physics, the medicine, and the social order of their time
and read the text in their light. Today its readers have another physics, another medicine,
another social order, and they read the same text differently. Some say that the text has been
understood better, some that it has been understood worse, and some that the question of better
and worse does not arise. What is the relation between the text and the understandings?
   The two scenes pose a single question. If what is known is distinguishable from the knowing

                                                623
624                                                                           Chapter 56. Soroush


of it, then the knowing may change without what is known changing, and the question is how to
state the relation. Soroush’s answer is the distinction between religion, which he holds to be
sacred and fixed, and religious knowledge, which he holds to be human, historical, and revisable.
The framework’s answer is the distinction between an identity and its reconstruction. The
chapter asks how the two answers stand to each other.


56.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated Jabri’s critique of the Arab reason and Taha Abdurrahman’s critique
of the philosophy of modernity. Soroush belongs to the same period but works in the Iranian
tradition, and his thought is shaped by the philosophy of science of Karl Popper and by the
Persian mystical tradition, especially Rumi, in an unusual combination.
      The question is not whether Soroush was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts.


First part: the position. What did Soroush hold? The chapter states the distinction between
religion and religious knowledge, the theory of contraction and expansion, the account of the
prophetic experience, and the arguments about reason and freedom.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Soroush converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence and presents the
objections that Soroush would raise.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Soroush?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


56.3       Soroush’s Position
Soroush trained in pharmacy and in the history and philosophy of science in London, and he
returned to Iran to teach and to write. His central work, Qabz va Bast-i Ti’urik-i Shari’at, began
as a series of articles in which he drew a distinction that he took to be the key to the relation
between religion and the modern world.


56.3.1      Religion and Religious Knowledge

Soroush distinguishes religion (din), the body of the revealed message, from religious knowledge
(ma’rifat-i dini), the human understanding of it. Religion is sacred, complete, and unchanging,
as the divine message in itself. Religious knowledge is a human product: it is formed in the
minds of jurists, theologians, and commentators, and it depends on the other knowledge that
they possess, philosophical, scientific, and social. Because that other knowledge changes, religious
knowledge changes with it. No one possesses religion as such; everyone possesses a knowledge of
it.
56.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         625


56.3.2     Contraction and Expansion

Religious knowledge, Soroush argues, is in a continual process of contraction and expansion. It
contracts when other knowledge, being revised, forces the reinterpretation of what was thought
to be religious doctrine and so shrinks the domain assigned to it. It expands when new questions
are addressed and new answers are found. The process is a necessary feature of the relation
between religious knowledge and the human sciences, and it is neither a decline nor a progress in
itself. He draws on Popper’s account of the growth of knowledge by conjecture and refutation,
and he holds that religious knowledge, as human knowledge, is subject to the same logic.


56.3.3     The Prophetic Experience

In the later work Soroush turns to the origin of religion and develops a theory of the prophetic
experience. The Prophet’s experience of revelation, he holds, was a real experience of the divine,
and the Qur’an is the Prophet’s expression of it in the language and the images available to
him. The words are therefore at once the divine message and the Prophet’s own speech, and the
experience is the source of both. The experience was not closed at the death of the Prophet:
its fruits, in the form of interpretation, continue to grow, and the religious experience of later
believers is a continuation of the prophetic one, in a lesser form.


56.3.4     Reason, Freedom, and the State

Soroush draws from the distinction political conclusions: since no one possesses religion as such,
no one has a claim to rule in its name, and a state that rules in the name of a particular religious
knowledge imposes a human opinion as if it were divine. He therefore argues for a democratic
state that respects the plurality of religious understanding. The argument is a part of his work
and is outside the strict philosophical register of the framework, but the distinction on which it
rests is within it.


56.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Soroush is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: realism. One reading takes Soroush to be a realist about religion: religion is a
determinate reality that human knowledge approximates. Another takes him to be an antirealist:
there is no access to religion except through religious knowledge, and the notion of religion in
itself has no work to do. The disagreement matters for the framework because the framework’s
identity is real and the reading decides whether Soroush’s religion is its analogue.


Second dispute: the account of revelation. The theory of the prophetic experience was
criticized by many religious authorities as reducing revelation to the Prophet’s own speech.
Soroush’s defenders hold that he distinguished the source of the experience from the words in
which it was expressed. The disagreement matters because the framework’s structure of source
and manifestation is analogous.
626                                                                         Chapter 56. Soroush


Third dispute: the essential and the accidental. Soroush distinguishes the essential from
the accidental in religion, but his account of how the distinction is to be drawn varies. One
reading takes it to be a distinction drawn by reason. Another takes it to be drawn by the
community’s practice. The disagreement matters because the framework’s invariant is not drawn
by either.


56.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Soroush. The framework shares four structural features with Soroush’s position.

       1. The distinction between what is and what is known. Soroush distinguishes religion
         from religious knowledge. The framework distinguishes an identity from its re-
         construction. Both hold that what is known is not identical with the knowing of
         it.

       2. The revisability of the knowing. Soroush holds that religious knowledge changes with
         other knowledge. The framework holds that reconstruction is revisable. Both hold
         that the knowing is revisable without the known being thereby revised.

       3. The source as prior to its expression. Soroush holds that the prophetic experience is
         the source of the words. The framework holds that an identity is enacted by one
         source and expressed in manifestations. Both hold that the expression depends on a
         source that it does not exhaust.

       4. The plurality of readings. Soroush holds that there are many religious knowledges
         and that none is final. The framework holds that contexts are infinite. Both hold
         that the plurality of readings is not a defect.



56.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Soroush. The framework diverges from Soroush’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of the invariant. Soroush’s religion is a sacred message, the content of
         which is a divine word. The framework’s identity is a structural invariance and has
         no such content.

       2. The origin of change. Soroush explains the change of religious knowledge by the
         change of the other sciences. The framework explains the change of reconstruction
         by the structure of manifestation and context.

       3. The role of Popper. Soroush uses the logic of conjecture and refutation. The
         framework does not adopt a particular philosophy of science.
56.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                   627


       4. The political consequence. Soroush draws a political conclusion from the distinction.
         The framework draws none.



56.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Soroush’s first objection. The framework says that an identity is invariant and that its
   reconstruction is revisable. But it gives no criterion by which one reconstruction is better
   than another. Without a criterion the distinction between identity and reconstruction is
   idle, since any reconstruction could be said to be of the identity. The framework needs a
   theory of the growth of knowledge, and it has none.
   Soroush’s second objection. The framework states its own structure as though it
   were the identity and not a reconstruction. But the framework is itself a reconstruction
   and is subject to contraction and expansion. A philosophy that does not apply its own
   distinction to itself claims for its own knowledge the status of religion.
   Soroush’s third objection. The framework is silent on the consequences of the distinction
   for the common life. But the distinction between what is and what is known is not a mere
   theoretical result; it has consequences for who may speak for the real. A philosophy that
   does not draw them leaves the claim to speak for the real to the powerful.



56.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a distinction between identity
   and reconstruction requires a criterion for the assessment of reconstructions, and it holds
   that it has one: a reconstruction is assessed by its coherence with the manifestations
   under the structure and by its revisability in the light of further manifestations. It does
   not commit to a particular philosophy of science, and Popper’s logic of conjecture and
   refutation is compatible with the criterion. The framework holds that Soroush’s own
   criterion for the growth of religious knowledge has this form.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that it is a reconstruction and
   that its distinction applies to itself. It marks its claims by status for that reason, and it
   states that its structure is subject to revision. It denies that this is a claim to the status of
   religion: it holds its principles as reconstructions of an identity that they do not exhaust,
   and not as the identity.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the distinction has conse-
   quences for the common life, and it does not deny that they are important. It holds that
   drawing them is a task that depends on further premises about the common life that the
   structural account does not supply. It states the distinction and leaves the consequences
   to an inquiry that can supply them.
628                                                                          Chapter 56. Soroush


56.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Soroush’s cost. If Soroush accepts the framework’s reply, he must allow that the relation
between religion and religious knowledge has a structural condition that is not itself a piece of
religious knowledge, and that the criterion of the growth of knowledge is a structural matter.
The cost is the loss of the claim that the distinction between religion and religious knowledge is
itself a result of the philosophy of science.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections, it must give up the claim
that its distinction between identity and reconstruction is complete without a theory of the
growth of knowledge, and it must accept that its own statements are subject to contraction and
expansion and that the distinction has consequences it leaves undrawn. The cost is the loss of
the completeness and the neutrality of the structural account.

The cost of the dialogue. A dialogue requires that each side take the other’s central claim
as a claim about the relation between what is and what is known. The framework must take the
revisability of its own reconstruction as a structural feature of its statements. Soroush must take
the invariant as a structural condition of the distinction on which his theory rests. The cost of
the dialogue is the loss of the opposition between structure and history of knowledge.


56.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s central terms are not substitutable for those of
   Soroush.
   Substitution 1. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Soroush’s
   term “religion” (din). If one substitutes “religion” for “identity,” the statements change:
   religion is a divine message with a content, while the identity is a structural invariance
   without a determinate content. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   Substitution 2. The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Soroush’s
   term “religious knowledge.” If one substitutes “religious knowledge” for “reconstruction,”
   the statements change: religious knowledge is the human understanding of a revealed
   message, while reconstruction is the reading of manifestations under a structure. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   Substitution 3. The framework’s term “one source” is not substitutable for Soroush’s
   term “the prophetic experience.” If one substitutes “the prophetic experience” for “one
   source,” the statements change: the prophetic experience is a historical experience of a
   person, while the one source is a structural condition of an identity. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
56.11. Open Questions                                                                       629


   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Soroush is resemblance
   of a close kind: both hold that what is known is distinct from the knowing of it, that the
   knowing is revisable, that the expression depends on a source that it does not exhaust,
   and that readings are plural, and they differ on whether the invariant is a divine message
   with a content or a structural condition. The relation is not equivalence, agreement, or
   identity. The framework’s reading would be refuted by showing that Soroush’s distinction
   cannot be stated without an invariance of the framework’s kind, or that the framework’s
   distinction between identity and reconstruction collapses into a distinction between two
   kinds of knowledge.




56.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is Soroush’s religion a realist notion? The chapter has argued that it can
be read so and that on this reading it has a structural counterpart in the framework’s identity,
but the argument is not conclusive, and a reader who holds that Soroush’s religion is only a
regulative idea has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s criterion for the assessment of reconstructions be
stated without a philosophy of science? The chapter has argued that it can be stated in a form
compatible with Popper’s, but a reader who holds that the criterion depends on a particular
theory has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading do justice to the theory of the prophetic
experience? The chapter has treated it as a theory of source and expression, and a reader who
holds that it is primarily a theory of the Qur’an’s authorship has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Think of a body of knowledge you hold about something you are sure is real, a place, a person,
an illness. How much of what you know about it has changed in your lifetime? Did the thing
change, or only your knowledge of it? If the knowledge keeps changing, what is it that you are
claiming to know? What does your answer tell you about the relation between what is and what
is known?

Part VII is now complete. The dialogues with the ten figures of contemporary Islamic philosophy—
Iqbal, Tabatabai, Motahhari, Shariati, al-Sadr, Nasr, Fazlur Rahman, Arkoun, Jabri and Taha
Abdurrahman, and Soroush—have been stated. Part VIII turns to Indian philosophy. The first
dialogue is with the Upanishads, on the self and the absolute; the next with Samkhya and Yoga,
on the dualism of consciousness and nature; the next with Nyaya and Vaisheshika, on logic
and ontology; the next with Shankara, on non-dualism; the next with Ramanuja, on qualified
non-dualism; and the last with Aurobindo, on the integral yoga. The contemporary Islamic
tradition has asked whether the tradition can be renewed; the Indian tradition will ask what the
self is, and what the absolute is.

Indian Philosophy
