Chapter 57

The Upanishads


Scope. This chapter opens Part VIII, the dialogues with Indian philosophy, and it opens it
with the Upanishads, the foundational texts of the Vedanta tradition. It states the Upanishadic
account of Brahman (the absolute), Atman (the self), the identity of Brahman and Atman (tat
tvam asi, “that thou art”), the doctrine of the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming,
deep sleep, and the fourth, turiya), the doctrine of the five sheaths (panca-kosa), and the doctrine
of maya (cosmic illusion), with reference to the Brhadaranyaka Upanishad, the Chandogya
Upanishad, the Mundaka Upanishad, the Katha Upanishad, and the Mandukya Upanishad; it
identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the Upanishads; it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of identity and manifestation is
the nearest Indian analogue to the Upanishadic identity of Brahman and Atman; it presents the
objections that the Upanishads would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s
reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what
would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where
the chapter speaks of “Brahman,” “Atman,” “maya,” “turiya,” “the sheaths,” or “the identity of
Brahman and Atman,” these are the Upanishadic terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts
and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


57.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a clay pot. The pot is a thing; it has a shape, a color, a use.
But what is the pot? The pot is clay; it is nothing but clay; the shape is the shape of clay; the
color is the color of clay; the use is the use of clay. The pot is a name and a form (nama-rupa);
the reality is the clay. When the pot is broken, the name and the form are gone, but the clay
remains. The pot is not other than the clay; the clay is the reality of the pot.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the pot is, but what the clay is. The
clay is earth; the earth is matter; the matter is the material cause. But what is the material
cause of the earth? The Upanishads say: the material cause of all things is Brahman; the reality
of all things is Brahman; the being of all things is Brahman. The pot is the name and the form
of the clay; the clay is the name and the form of the earth; the earth is the name and the form
of Brahman. Everything is Brahman; Brahman is the only reality; the world is a name and a
form of Brahman.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the pot is, or what the
clay is, but what she is. She is the body; she is the mind; she is the intellect; she is the ego.
But the Upanishads say: she is not the body; she is not the mind; she is not the intellect; she
is not the ego. She is the Atman; she is the self; she is the innermost reality; she is the reality
that is the same as Brahman. Tat tvam asi: that thou art. The Atman is Brahman; the self is

                                                632
57.2. The Question                                                                           633


the absolute; the innermost is the ultimate. This is the Upanishadic identity of Brahman and
Atman.
   The scene is the Upanishadic image, in the Chandogya and in the Mundaka, of the structure
of reality. The pot is the name and the form; the clay is the reality; the Atman is the Brahman.
The scene poses the question that the Upanishads were the first to pose in its full form. What is
the absolute? What is the self? And what is the relation between the two? The present chapter
states the Upanishadic answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.



57.2      The Question

The previous part stated the positions of contemporary Islamic philosophy: Iqbal, Tabatabai,
Nasr, Fazlur Rahman, and Jabri and Taha Abdurrahman. The contemporary Islamic tradition
has asked whether the tradition can be renewed. The present part turns to Indian philosophy,
and its first dialogue is with the Upanishads, the foundational texts of the Vedanta tradition.
The Upanishads are not a single system; they are a collection of texts, composed over centuries,
which present a variety of doctrines. But they share a common core: the identity of Brahman
and Atman.
   The question is not whether the Upanishads were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What do the Upanishads hold? The chapter states the doctrine
of Brahman, the doctrine of Atman, the identity of Brahman and Atman, the four states of
consciousness, the five sheaths, and the doctrine of maya, with reference to the texts.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the Upanishads converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the Upanishads would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the
Upanishads? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.



57.3      The Position

57.3.1    Brahman

The Upanishadic doctrine of Brahman is stated in the Brhadaranyaka Upanishad, the Chandogya
Upanishad, and the Mundaka Upanishad. Brahman is the absolute; it is the ultimate reality; it is
the source of all things.
   The doctrine has three features.
634                                                                     Chapter 57. The Upanishads


First feature: Brahman is the reality of all things. Brahman is the reality of all things;
the things are not other than Brahman; the things are the names and forms of Brahman. As the
clay is the reality of the pot, so Brahman is the reality of the world. The world is not nothing; it
is real as a name and a form; but its reality is Brahman.


Second feature: Brahman is one. Brahman is one; Brahman has no multiplicity; Brahman
has no parts; Brahman has no distinctions. The multiplicity of the world is not in Brahman; the
multiplicity is the name and the form; the reality is one. Brahman is the one without a second
(ekam evadvitiyam).


Third feature: Brahman is the source. Brahman is the source of all things; it is that from
which all things originate, by which all things are sustained, and into which all things return.
Brahman is the material cause, the efficient cause, and the final cause of the world; it is the
origin, the ground, and the goal.
      The doctrine is the foundation of the Upanishadic philosophy. It is the reality of all things; it
is the one without a second; it is the source of the world.

   From the Tradition

   “Brahman is the reality of all things; the things are the names and forms of Brahman. As
   the clay is the reality of the pot, so Brahman is the reality of the world. Brahman is one,
   without a second.” (Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1, trans. after Radhakrishnan, adapted)


57.3.2      Atman

The Upanishadic doctrine of Atman is stated in the Brhadaranyaka Upanishad, the Chandogya
Upanishad, and the Katha Upanishad. Atman is the self; it is the innermost reality of the human
being; it is the reality that is the same as Brahman.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: Atman is the innermost self. Atman is the innermost self; it is not the
body; it is not the mind; it is not the intellect; it is not the ego. Atman is the reality that
underlies all the sheaths; it is the self that is the witness of all the states; it is the reality that is
never an object, but always the subject.


Second feature: Atman is not the ego. Atman is not the empirical ego; it is not the "I"
that is the subject of the experiences. The empirical ego is a construction; it is the name and the
form; the Atman is the reality. The Atman is the self that remains when the ego is dissolved; it
is the self that is realized in the state of turiya.


Third feature: Atman is the same as Brahman. Atman is the same as Brahman; the
self is the absolute; the innermost is the ultimate. Tat tvam asi: that thou art. The identity is
not a similarity; it is an identity; the Atman is not like Brahman; the Atman is Brahman. The
realization of this identity is the goal of the Upanishadic teaching; it is the liberation (moksha).
57.3. The Position                                                                               635


    The doctrine is the foundation of the Upanishadic psychology. It is the innermost self; it is
not the ego; it is the same as Brahman.


57.3.3      The Identity of Brahman and Atman

The Upanishadic doctrine of the identity of Brahman and Atman is stated in the Chandogya
Upanishad (6.8.7), in the Brhadaranyaka Upanishad (1.4.10), and in the Mandukya Upanishad.
The identity is the central teaching of the Upanishads; it is the foundation of the Vedanta.
    The doctrine has three features.


First feature: tat tvam asi. The formula tat tvam asi (that thou art) states the identity.
Tat is Brahman; tvam is the Atman; asi is the identity. The teaching is not that the Atman is
like Brahman; it is that the Atman is Brahman. The identity is the truth; the distinction is the
ignorance.


Second feature: the four great sayings. The Upanishads contain four great sayings
(mahavakyas): prajnanam brahma (consciousness is Brahman), aham brahmasmi (I am Brahman),
tat tvam asi (that thou art), and ayam atma brahma (this self is Brahman). The four sayings
state the same identity; they are the four formulations of the one truth.


Third feature: the realization. The identity is not a concept; it is a reality that is to be
realized. The realization is not a matter of knowledge; it is a matter of experience; it is the
direct experience of the self as Brahman. The realization is the liberation; it is the end of the
ignorance; it is the end of the suffering.
    The doctrine is the foundation of the Upanishadic teaching. It is the identity; it is the four
sayings; it is the realization.


57.3.4      The Four States of Consciousness

The Upanishadic doctrine of the four states of consciousness is stated in the Mandukya Upanishad.
The four states are the waking state, the dreaming state, the deep sleep state, and the fourth
(turiya).
    The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the waking state. The waking state (jagrat) is the state in which the self is
aware of the external world; it is the state of the senses; it is the state of the gross body. The
self in the waking state is visva; it is the self that experiences the external world.


Second feature: the dreaming state. The dreaming state (svapna) is the state in which
the self is aware of the inner world; it is the state of the mind; it is the state of the subtle body.
The self in the dreaming state is taijasa; it is the self that experiences the inner world.
636                                                                   Chapter 57. The Upanishads


Third feature: the deep sleep state and the fourth. The deep sleep state (susupti) is
the state in which the self is without any experience; it is the state of the causal body; it is the
state of the seed. The self in the deep sleep state is prajna; it is the self that is the seed of all
experiences. The fourth (turiya) is not a state; it is the reality that underlies all the states; it is
the Atman; it is Brahman. The fourth is not the waking, not the dreaming, not the deep sleep;
it is the silent witness of all the states.
      The doctrine is the key to the Upanishadic psychology. It is the waking state; it is the
dreaming state; it is the deep sleep state and the fourth.


57.3.5        The Five Sheaths

The Upanishadic doctrine of the five sheaths (panca-kosa) is stated in the Taittiriya Upanishad.
The five sheaths are the layers that cover the Atman; they are the layers that the self mistakes
for itself.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the five sheaths. The five sheaths are: the sheath of food (annamaya-kosa),
the sheath of breath (pranamaya-kosa), the sheath of mind (manomaya-kosa), the sheath of
intellect (vijnanamaya-kosa), and the sheath of bliss (anandamaya-kosa). Each sheath is a layer;
each layer is a name and a form; the Atman is the reality that underlies all the layers.


Second feature: the neti neti. The Upanishad teaches the method of neti neti (not this,
not this). The self is not the sheath of food; it is not the sheath of breath; it is not the sheath of
mind; it is not the sheath of intellect; it is not the sheath of bliss. The self is the reality that
remains when all the sheaths are negated; it is the self that cannot be described by any name or
form.


Third feature: the self beyond the sheaths. The self is beyond the sheaths; it is the
witness of the sheaths; it is the reality that the sheaths cover. The self is not the sheaths; the
sheaths are not the self. The realization of the self is the realization of the reality that is beyond
all the sheaths.
      The doctrine is the key to the Upanishadic method. It is the five sheaths; it is the neti neti;
it is the self beyond the sheaths.


57.3.6        The Doctrine of Maya

The Upanishadic doctrine of maya is stated in the Brhadaranyaka Upanishad, the Svetasvatara
Upanishad, and the Mundaka Upanishad. Maya is the cosmic illusion; it is the power that makes
the one appear as many; it is the power that makes the real appear as the unreal.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the illusion. Maya is the illusion; it is the appearance; it is the name and the
form. The world is not nothing; it is real as an appearance; but its reality is not the reality of
57.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         637


Brahman. The world is the appearance of Brahman; it is not Brahman; it is the name and the
form of Brahman.


Second feature: the power. Maya is the power of Brahman; it is the power by which
Brahman creates the world; it is the power by which the one appears as many. The power is not
separate from Brahman; it is the power of Brahman; it is the sakti of Brahman.


Third feature: the ignorance. Maya is the ignorance; it is the ignorance that makes the
self mistake the appearance for the reality; it is the ignorance that makes the self mistake the
ego for the Atman. The liberation is the end of the ignorance; it is the realization of the reality
that is beyond the appearance.
   The doctrine is the key to the Upanishadic cosmology. It is the illusion; it is the power; it is
the ignorance.


57.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of the Upanishads is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of Brahman. The traditional reading takes Brahman to be a
personal God, the Lord (Ishvara), the creator and the sustainer of the world. A revisionary
reading takes Brahman to be an impersonal absolute, the ground of being, the reality beyond
all names and forms. The two readings disagree on whether the Upanishads are theistic or
monistic, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
First Determination is a realm of pure unity, not a personal God.


Second dispute: the status of the world. The traditional reading takes the world to be
real, the creation of Brahman, the manifestation of the divine. A revisionary reading takes the
world to be an illusion (maya), the appearance of Brahman, the name and the form that covers
the reality. The two readings disagree on whether the Upanishads are realistic or illusionistic, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is
real, not an illusion.


Third dispute: the status of the self. The traditional reading takes the self to be the
individual soul, the jiva, the empirical ego that is the subject of the experiences. A revisionary
reading takes the self to be the Atman, the innermost reality, the reality that is the same
as Brahman. The two readings disagree on whether the Upanishads are individualistic or
universalistic, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
identity is the individual identity, not the universal self.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Brahman is a personal God, the framework’s
dialogue with the Upanishads is a dialogue between a structural realism and a theistic monism.
If Brahman is an impersonal absolute, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the
framework treats as distinct. The framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to
638                                                                Chapter 57. The Upanishads


the texts, but it does not rest its case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


57.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the Upanishads. The framework shares four structural features with the Upan-
   ishadic position.

       1. The distinction between the reality and the appearance. The Upanishads hold that
         Brahman is the reality, and the world is the name and the form; the pot is the name
         and the form of the clay. The framework holds that the identity is the reality, and
         the manifestation is the appearance; the manifestation is the name and the form
         of the identity. Both hold that there is a distinction between the reality and the
         appearance, and that the reality is not exhausted by the appearance.

       2. The priority of the one over the many. The Upanishads hold that Brahman is one,
         and the many are the names and forms of the one. The framework holds that the
         identity is one, and the manifestations are the appearances of the one. Both hold
         that the one is prior to the many, and that the many is real in the one.

       3. The innermost self. The Upanishads hold that the Atman is the innermost self, the
         reality that underlies the sheaths. The framework holds that the identity is the
         innermost reality, the invariance that underlies the manifestations. Both hold that
         there is an innermost reality, and that the innermost reality is not the empirical ego.

       4. The limits of language. The Upanishads hold that the self is beyond the sheaths,
         and that it cannot be described by any name or form; the method is neti neti. The
         framework holds that the identity is beyond the manifestations, and that it cannot
         be exhausted by any description; the method is reconstruction. Both hold that
         language has limits, and that the mind must recognize them.



57.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With the Upanishads. The framework diverges from the Upanishadic position in four
   respects.

       1. The status of the world. The Upanishads hold that the world is the name and the
         form of Brahman; it is real as an appearance, but its reality is not the reality of
         Brahman. The framework holds that the manifestation is real in its own realm;
         it is not an appearance of the identity; it is the expression of the identity. The
         framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.
57.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  639


       2. The status of the self. The Upanishads hold that the Atman is the same as Brahman;
          the self is the absolute. The framework holds that the identity is the individual
          identity; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not the absolute. The
          framework’s identity is individual, not universal.

       3. The status of the realization. The Upanishads hold that the realization of the identity
          is the goal; it is the direct experience of the self as Brahman. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the knowledge; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
          not the experience. The framework’s knowledge is structural, not experiential.

       4. The status of maya. The Upanishads hold that the world is maya, the cosmic
          illusion. The framework holds that the manifestation is real; it is not maya; it is the
          expression of the identity. The framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.



57.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   The Upanishads’ first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not Brahman; it is a pattern. The world is the name and the form of Brahman;
   the world is not just structured; the world is the appearance of Brahman. The framework
   has no Brahman; the framework has no absolute; the framework’s world is a world without
   the absolute. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the absolute.
   The Upanishads’ second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms;
   the realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the levels of the appearance of Brahman; they are the levels of maya. The
   framework’s realms are not levels of maya; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology
   is an ontology of levels, not of maya.
   The Upanishads’ third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruc-
   tion; it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the realization of the identity;
   it is the direct experience of the self as Brahman; it is the liberation. The framework’s
   knowledge is a mediation; it is not the realization. The framework’s epistemology is an
   epistemology of mediation, not of realization.



57.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is the appearance
   of the absolute, and it agrees that the appearance is real. But the framework denies
   that the appearance must be the only reality. The framework’s identity is the structural
640                                                                 Chapter 57. The Upanishads


   condition of the appearance; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural
   condition under which the appearance is what it is. The distinction is between an absolute
   (a reality) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not
   the first. The framework does not deny the absolute; it denies that the absolute is the
   only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the appearance. But the framework denies that
   the realms are levels of maya. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they are the
   levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the appearance. The
   distinction is between a level of maya (an illusion) and a level of manifestation (a real
   level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the realization. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a realization (an
   experience) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.



57.9        The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


The Upanishads’ cost. If the Upanishads accept the framework’s reply, they must give up
the claim that the world is an illusion. They must accept that the manifestation is real, and that
the world is the expression of the identity, not the illusion of Brahman. The cost is the loss of
maya: the world is no longer an illusion; the world is a real manifestation. They must also give
up the claim that the realization is the goal; they must accept that the reconstruction is the
knowledge; the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the Upanishads’ objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of Brahman, of the Atman, of the realization—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is
the enactment of a structure, but not the absolute, and the framework leaves the absolute to a
separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the Upanishads’ Brahman
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
The Upanishads must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural
condition that Brahman presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
57.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                    641


simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


57.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the Up-
   anishadic term “Brahman.” If one substitutes “Brahman” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
   by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Brahman is the absolute, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the reality of all things. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   Brahman is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for the Upanishadic term “maya.”
   If one substitutes “maya” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; maya is the cosmic illusion.
   The framework’s expression is real; maya is an illusion. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Upanishadic term “the
   realization.” If one substitutes “the realization” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the Upanishadic realization is the direct experience of the self as Brahman.
   The framework’s reconstruction is mediated; the Upanishadic realization is immediate.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the Upanishads is
   resemblance: both hold that there is a distinction between the reality and the appearance,
   and they differ on whether the appearance is real or an illusion. Both hold that there is
   an innermost reality, and they differ on whether the innermost reality is the absolute or
   the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of the Upanishads would be refuted by showing that the Upanishadic
   Brahman cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure
   and absolute—by showing, that is, that the Upanishads already distinguish the structural
   condition from the absolute, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of the
   Upanishads’ own.



57.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Upanishadic Atman, or
is it a departure from the Upanishads? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but
the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the Upanishadic Atman is already a
structural condition, not the absolute, has a question the chapter leaves open.
642                                                               Chapter 57. The Upanishads


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Brhadaranyaka, the Chandogya, the
Mundaka, the Katha, and the Mandukya do justice to the texts? The chapter has used Brahman,
the Atman, the identity, the four states, the five sheaths, and maya, and it has stated what
would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a
question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an appearance and a reality—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the appearance that covers, or the reality that underlies? Is the truth
the realization that is immediate, or the reconstruction that is mediated? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between the Upanishadic Atman and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Samkhya and Yoga. It states the dualism of consciousness ( purusha)
and nature ( prakriti), the twenty-five categories, the three qualities ( gunas), the eight limbs
of Yoga, and the goal of liberation ( kaivalya); it identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of Samkhya and Yoga; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of consciousness and of nature is the nearest Indian analogue to
theirs. The present chapter has stated the Upanishadic answer to the problem of the absolute and
the self; the next chapter states the Samkhya and Yoga answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
Chapter 58

Samkhya and Yoga


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Samkhya and Yoga, the two foundational schools of Indian
philosophy that share a common metaphysics but differ in their methods. It states the Samkhya
dualism of consciousness (purusha) and nature (prakriti), the twenty-five categories (tattvas),
the three qualities (gunas), the theory of causation (satkaryavada), and the goal of liberation
(kaivalya); and it states the Yoga account of the eight limbs (ashtanga), the modifications of
the mind (vritti), the practice of cessation (nirodha), and the goal of isolation (kaivalya), with
reference to the Samkhya Karika of Ishvarakrishna and the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, together
with their major commentaries; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
the two schools; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of consciousness and of nature is the nearest Indian analogue to theirs; it presents the
objections that the two schools would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s
reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what
would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where
the chapter speaks of “purusha,” “prakriti,” “guna,” “vritti,” “nirodha,” “kaivalya,” or “the eight
limbs,” these are the schools’ terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive
tradition, not by the framework.



58.1     A Scene

Consider a person who is sitting in meditation. She closes her eyes; she attends to her breath;
she watches the thoughts that arise and pass. A thought arises: a memory of yesterday. Another
thought arises: a plan for tomorrow. Another thought arises: a judgment about herself. The
thoughts are many; the mind is restless; the consciousness is scattered among the objects of the
thoughts. She is not the master of her mind; the mind is the master of her.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the thoughts are, or how they arise,
but what the witness of the thoughts is. The witness is not a thought; the witness is not a
memory; the witness is not a plan; the witness is not a judgment. The witness is the consciousness
that is aware of the thoughts; it is the purusha; it is the self; it is the pure consciousness. The
purusha is not the mind; the mind is the prakriti; the purusha is the witness; the prakriti is the
witnessed.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the witness is, or what
the mind is, but what the relation between the two is. The purusha and the prakriti are two;
they are not one; they are not the same. The purusha is pure consciousness; it is inactive; it is
the witness. The prakriti is nature; it is active; it is the witnessed. The two are independent; the
two are eternal; the two are the ultimate categories. The liberation (kaivalya) is the realization

                                                643
644                                                               Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


of the distinction between the two; it is the realization that the purusha is not the prakriti; it is
the cessation of the confusion that binds the purusha to the prakriti.
      The scene is the image of the two schools, in the Samkhya Karika and in the Yoga Sutras, of
the structure of reality. The thoughts are the vrittis; the witness is the purusha; the mind is
the prakriti. The scene poses the question that the two schools were the first to pose in its full
form in the Indian tradition. What is consciousness? What is nature? And what is the relation
between the two? The present chapter states the two schools’ answers, and the framework’s
dialogue with them.


58.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the Upanishadic position: Brahman, the Atman, the identity of
Brahman and Atman, the four states of consciousness, the five sheaths, and the doctrine of maya.
The Upanishads are the foundational texts of the Vedanta; they teach the identity of the self and
the absolute. Samkhya and Yoga are the two foundational schools of Indian philosophy that share
a common metaphysics but differ in their methods. Samkhya is the school of discrimination; Yoga
is the school of practice. The two are the classical formulations of the dualism of consciousness
and nature, and they are the foundation of the later Indian philosophy. The present chapter
states the two schools’ positions, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
      The question is not whether Samkhya or Yoga was right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Samkhya and Yoga hold? The chapter states the
Samkhya dualism of purusha and prakriti, the twenty-five categories, the three gunas, the theory
of causation, and the goal of kaivalya; and it states the Yoga account of the eight limbs, the
modifications of the mind, the practice of cessation, and the goal of isolation.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two schools converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two schools would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
schools? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


58.3       The Position of Samkhya

58.3.1      The Dualism of Purusha and Prakriti

The Samkhya dualism of purusha and prakriti is stated in the Samkhya Karika of Ishvarakrishna
(c. 350 CE) and in the commentaries. The dualism is the foundation of the Samkhya metaphysics;
it is the key to the Samkhya theory of liberation.
58.3. The Position of Samkhya                                                                     645


   The dualism has three features.


First feature: purusha. Purusha is pure consciousness; it is the self; it is the witness; it is
the spectator. Purusha is not the mind; it is not the body; it is not the intellect; it is not the ego.
Purusha is inactive; it is unchanging; it is eternal. Purusha is many; each purusha is a distinct
center of consciousness; each purusha is an independent witness.


Second feature: prakriti. Prakriti is nature; it is the material principle; it is the source
of the body, the mind, and the world. Prakriti is active; it is changing; it is the cause of the
manifestations. Prakriti is one; it is the common material cause of all the individual bodies and
minds.


Third feature: the relation. The relation between purusha and prakriti is not a relation of
identity; the two are distinct; the two are independent. The relation is the relation of witness
and witnessed; the purusha is the witness; the prakriti is the witnessed. The confusion of the
two is the cause of bondage; the discrimination of the two is the cause of liberation.
   The dualism is the foundation of the Samkhya philosophy. It is the purusha; it is the prakriti;
it is the distinction between the two.

   From the Tradition

   “Purusha is pure consciousness; it is the witness; it is the spectator. Prakriti is nature;
   it is the material principle; it is the source of the world. The two are distinct; the two
   are independent. The liberation is the discrimination of the two.” (Samkhya Karika, 2–3,
   trans. after Larson, adapted)



58.3.2    The Twenty-Five Categories

The Samkhya twenty-five categories (tattvas) are stated in the Samkhya Karika. The categories
are the constituents of reality; they are the levels of the manifestation of prakriti.
   The categories have three features.


First feature: the categories. The twenty-five categories are: purusha, prakriti, mahat (the
great, intellect), ahamkara (the ego), manas (the mind), the five senses (jnanendriyas), the five
organs of action (karmendriyas), the five subtle elements (tanmatras), and the five gross elements
(mahabhutas). The categories are the constituents of the individual and the world; they are the
levels of the manifestation.


Second feature: the evolution. The categories evolve from prakriti; the evolution is the
manifestation of the prakriti into the categories. The evolution is not a creation; it is a
transformation; the prakriti is the material cause of the categories; the categories are the
modifications of the prakriti.
646                                                               Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


Third feature: the discrimination. The discrimination (viveka) is the knowledge of the
categories; it is the knowledge of the distinction between the purusha and the prakriti; it is the
knowledge of the distinction between the categories and the self. The discrimination is the path
to liberation; it is the path to the kaivalya.
      The categories are the foundation of the Samkhya cosmology. They are the twenty-five; they
are the evolution; they are the discrimination.


58.3.3      The Three Gunas

The Samkhya three gunas are stated in the Samkhya Karika. The gunas are the three constituents
of the prakriti; they are the three qualities that are present in everything.
      The three gunas have three features.


First feature: sattva. Sattva is the quality of lightness, clarity, and goodness. Sattva is the
quality of the intellect; it is the quality that makes the mind clear; it is the quality that leads to
knowledge.


Second feature: rajas. Rajas is the quality of activity, passion, and motion. Rajas is the
quality of the will; it is the quality that makes the mind active; it is the quality that leads to
action.


Third feature: tamas. Tamas is the quality of darkness, inertia, and ignorance. Tamas is
the quality of the body; it is the quality that makes the mind dull; it is the quality that leads to
ignorance.
      The gunas are the foundation of the Samkhya psychology. They are sattva; they are rajas;
they are tamas.


58.3.4      The Theory of Causation

The Samkhya theory of causation (satkaryavada) is stated in the Samkhya Karika. The theory is
the doctrine that the effect is pre-existent in the cause; it is the doctrine that the effect is the
manifestation of what is latent in the cause.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: the effect is pre-existent. The effect is pre-existent in the cause; the effect
is not a new creation; the effect is the manifestation of what is latent. The pot is pre-existent in
the clay; the pot is the manifestation of the clay; the pot is not a new creation.


Second feature: the manifestation. The manifestation is the process by which the latent
becomes manifest; it is the process by which the cause becomes the effect. The manifestation is
not a creation; it is a transformation; the effect is the transformation of the cause.
58.4. The Position of Yoga                                                                        647


Third feature: the identity. The identity of the cause and the effect is the identity of the
substance; the effect is the same substance as the cause; the effect is the cause in a new form.
The identity is not a numerical identity; it is a substantial identity; the effect is the cause in the
form of the effect.
   The theory is the foundation of the Samkhya philosophy of nature. It is the pre-existence; it
is the manifestation; it is the identity.


58.3.5     The Goal of Kaivalya

The Samkhya goal of kaivalya is stated in the Samkhya Karika. Kaivalya is the isolation; it is
the liberation; it is the state in which the purusha is isolated from the prakriti.
   The goal has three features.


First feature: the isolation. The isolation is the separation of the purusha from the prakriti;
it is the realization that the purusha is not the prakriti; it is the end of the confusion.


Second feature: the cessation. The cessation is the cessation of the suffering; it is the
cessation of the bondage; it is the end of the cycle of rebirth. The purusha is free; it is no longer
bound; it is no longer suffering.


Third feature: the liberation. The liberation is not a state of bliss; it is not a state of
union; it is a state of isolation; the purusha is alone, in its own nature, as pure consciousness.
The liberation is the kaivalya; it is the goal of the Samkhya.
   The goal is the foundation of the Samkhya soteriology. It is the isolation; it is the cessation;
it is the liberation.


58.4      The Position of Yoga

58.4.1     The Eight Limbs

The Yoga eight limbs (ashtanga) are stated in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali (c. 400 CE). The
eight limbs are the path to the liberation; they are the method of the Yoga.
   The eight limbs have three features.


First feature: the eight limbs. The eight limbs are: yama (restraints), niyama (observances),
asana (posture), pranayama (breath control), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana
(concentration), dhyana (meditation), and samadhi (absorption). The eight limbs are the stages
of the path; they are the method of the Yoga.


Second feature: the path. The path is not a linear progression; the path is a holistic
discipline; the eight limbs are interdependent; the practice of one supports the practice of the
others. The path is the way to the cessation of the modifications of the mind; it is the way to
the kaivalya.
648                                                                  Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


Third feature: the goal. The goal is kaivalya; it is the isolation of the purusha from the
prakriti; it is the same goal as the Samkhya. The Yoga adds the method to the Samkhya
metaphysics; it is the practical side of the same dualism.
      The eight limbs are the foundation of the Yoga. They are the eight; they are the path; they
are the goal.

   From the Tradition

   “The eight limbs are: yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, and
   samadhi. The eight limbs are the path to the kaivalya.” (Yoga Sutras, 2.29, trans. after
   Bryant, adapted)


58.4.2      The Modifications of the Mind
The Yoga modifications of the mind (vritti) are stated in the Yoga Sutras. The vrittis are the
activities of the mind; they are the thoughts, the memories, the plans, the judgments.
      The vrittis have three features.

First feature: the five vrittis. The five vrittis are: pramana (right knowledge), viparyaya
(wrong knowledge), vikalpa (imagination), nidra (sleep), and smriti (memory). The five are the
activities of the mind; they are the modifications of the mind.

Second feature: the restlessness. The vrittis are the cause of the restlessness; they are the
cause of the suffering; they are the cause of the bondage. The mind is restless; it is scattered; it
is not at peace.

Third feature: the cessation. The cessation (nirodha) is the cessation of the vrittis; it is
the stillness of the mind; it is the state in which the mind is without the modifications. The
cessation is the goal of the Yoga; it is the condition of the kaivalya.
      The vrittis are the foundation of the Yoga psychology. They are the five; they are the
restlessness; they are the cessation.


58.4.3      The Practice of Cessation
The Yoga practice of cessation (nirodha) is stated in the Yoga Sutras. The practice is the method
of the cessation; it is the method of the stillness of the mind.
      The practice has three features.

First feature: the practice. The practice (abhyasa) is the repeated effort; it is the sustained
effort; it is the discipline of the mind. The practice is not a single act; it is a long discipline; it is
the cultivation of the stillness.

Second feature: the detachment. The detachment (vairagya) is the letting go; it is the
freedom from the desire; it is the freedom from the attachment. The detachment is not the
suppression of the desire; it is the freedom from the desire; it is the peace of the mind.
58.5. Internal Disputes                                                                           649


Third feature: the cessation. The cessation (nirodha) is the state of the stillness; it is the
state in which the vrittis have ceased; it is the state of the pure consciousness. The cessation is
the goal of the practice; it is the condition of the kaivalya.
   The practice is the foundation of the Yoga. It is the practice; it is the detachment; it is the
cessation.


58.4.4       The Goal of Kaivalya

The Yoga goal of kaivalya is stated in the Yoga Sutras. The goal is the isolation; it is the same
goal as the Samkhya; it is the state in which the purusha is isolated from the prakriti.
   The goal has three features.


First feature: the isolation. The isolation is the separation of the purusha from the prakriti;
it is the realization that the purusha is not the prakriti; it is the end of the confusion.


Second feature: the cessation. The cessation is the cessation of the suffering; it is the
cessation of the bondage; it is the end of the cycle of rebirth. The purusha is free; it is no longer
bound; it is no longer suffering.


Third feature: the liberation. The liberation is the isolation; the purusha is alone, in its
own nature, as pure consciousness. The liberation is the kaivalya; it is the goal of the Yoga.
   The goal is the foundation of the Yoga soteriology. It is the isolation; it is the cessation; it is
the liberation.



58.5     Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Samkhya and Yoga is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of purusha. The traditional reading takes purusha to be the
pure consciousness, the witness, the inactive spectator. A revisionary reading takes it to be the
self, the person, the individual soul, the one who experiences. The two readings disagree on
whether the Samkhya is a dualism of consciousness and nature or a dualism of self and nature,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is
the individual identity, not the pure consciousness.


Second dispute: the status of prakriti. The traditional reading takes prakriti to be the
material principle, the source of the world, the active cause. A revisionary reading takes it to
be the nature, the physical world, the realm of the manifestations. The two readings disagree
on whether the Samkhya is a materialism or a dualism, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are levels of the manifestation, not the
material principle.
650                                                               Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


Third dispute: the status of kaivalya. The traditional reading takes kaivalya to be the
isolation, the separation of the purusha from the prakriti, the state of the pure consciousness.
A revisionary reading takes it to be the liberation, the freedom from the suffering, the end of
the bondage. The two readings disagree on whether the Samkhya is a dualism of liberation or a
dualism of isolation, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework has no liberation in the Samkhya sense, and its account of the cessation is structural,
not soteriological.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the Samkhya is a dualism of consciousness and
nature, the framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a dualism
of consciousness. If the Samkhya is a dualism of self and nature, the dialogue is a dialogue
between a structural realism and a dualism of self. The framework holds that the second reading
is closer to the texts, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way
that is compatible with either reading.


58.6       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Samkhya and Yoga. The framework shares four structural features with the two
   schools’ position.

        1. The distinction between consciousness and its objects. Samkhya holds that purusha
           is the witness and the prakriti is the witnessed; the two are distinct. The framework
           holds that the identity is the source and the manifestation is the appearance; the
           two are distinct. Both hold that there is a distinction between the subject and the
           object, and that the distinction is the condition of knowledge.

        2. The reality of the manifestations. Samkhya holds that the prakriti is real; the
           manifestations are real; they are the transformations of the prakriti. The framework
           holds that the manifestations are real; they are the expressions of the identity. Both
           hold that the manifestations are real, and that they are not an illusion.

        3. The theory of causation. Samkhya holds that the effect is pre-existent in the cause;
           the effect is the manifestation of what is latent in the cause. The framework holds
           that the manifestation is the expression of the identity; the manifestation is the
           enactment of what is latent in the identity. Both hold that the manifestation is the
           actualization of what is latent, and that there is a continuity between the cause and
           the effect.

        4. The discipline of the mind. Yoga holds that the cessation of the modifications of
           the mind is the goal; the discipline is the method. The framework holds that the
           reconstruction is the knowledge; the discipline is the method. Both hold that there
           is a discipline, and that the discipline is the condition of the knowledge.
58.7. Points of Divergence                                                                      651


58.7      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Samkhya and Yoga. The framework diverges from the two schools’ position in
   four respects.

       1. The status of purusha. Samkhya holds that purusha is pure consciousness; it is
         inactive; it is the witness. The framework holds that the identity is the invariance
         enacted by one source; it is active; it is the tendency to express. The framework’s
         identity is not pure consciousness; it is the structural condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of prakriti. Samkhya holds that prakriti is the material principle; it
         is the source of the world; it is the active cause. The framework holds that the
         realms are levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of the expression. The
         framework’s realms are not the material principle; they are the structural levels.

       3. The status of kaivalya. Samkhya and Yoga hold that kaivalya is the goal; it is the
         isolation of the purusha from the prakriti; it is the state of the pure consciousness.
         The framework holds that the expression is a structural tendency; it is the enactment
         of the identity; it is not the liberation. The framework has no kaivalya; its goal is
         the understanding of the structure.

       4. The status of the discipline. Yoga holds that the cessation of the modifications
         of the mind is the goal; the discipline is the method. The framework holds that
         the reconstruction is the knowledge; the reading is the method. The framework’s
         discipline is structural, not yogic.



58.8      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Samkhya’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not consciousness; it is a pattern. The purusha is pure consciousness; it is the witness; it
   is the spectator. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not consciousness.
   The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of consciousness.
   Samkhya’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
   they are the levels of the prakriti; they are the levels of the manifestation of the prakriti.
   The framework’s realms are not levels of the prakriti; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the prakriti.
   Yoga’s objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is the reading
   of the manifestations. But knowledge is the cessation of the modifications of the mind; it
652                                                               Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


   is the stillness; it is the kaivalya. The framework’s knowledge is a mediation; it is not the
   cessation. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of mediation, not of cessation.



58.9     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Samkhya’s first objection. The framework agrees that consciousness is not
   a pattern, and it agrees that the purusha is the witness. But the framework denies that
   the purusha must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the structural
   condition of the witness; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural
   condition under which the witness is what it is. The distinction is between a consciousness
   (a witness) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not
   the first. The framework does not deny the consciousness; it denies that the consciousness
   is the only principle.
   Reply to Samkhya’s second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
   not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the prakriti. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   prakriti. The distinction is between a level of the prakriti (a material level) and a level of
   manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Yoga’s objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the cessation. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it
   is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a cessation (a
   stillness) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



58.10      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Samkhya and Yoga’s cost. If the two schools accept the framework’s reply, they must give up
the claim that purusha is pure consciousness. They must accept that the identity is a structural
condition, and that the consciousness is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of
the purusha: the pure consciousness is no longer the fundamental reality; the identity is the
structural condition. They must also give up the claim that kaivalya is the goal; they must accept
that the expression is the structural tendency; the expression is the enactment of the identity.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the two schools, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the purusha, of the prakriti, of the kaivalya—that its ontology does
58.11. The Kind of Relation                                                                    653


not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the pure consciousness, and the framework
leaves the pure consciousness to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the purusha of the two
schools is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not
capture. The two schools must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a
structural condition that the purusha presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is
the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and
each is incomplete without the others.


58.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the
   Samkhya term “purusha.” If one substitutes “purusha” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the purusha is pure consciousness, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the witness. The framework’s identity is multiple; the purusha is
   multiple. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for the Samkhya term “the
   manifestation of the prakriti.” If one substitutes “the manifestation of the prakriti” for
   “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   expression is a structural tendency; the manifestation of the prakriti is the transformation
   of the material principle. The framework’s expression is structural; the manifestation
   of the prakriti is material. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Yoga term “the cessation
   of the modifications of the mind.” If one substitutes “the cessation” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is the
   reading of the manifestations; the cessation is the stillness of the mind. The framework’s
   reconstruction is mediated; the cessation is immediate. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the two schools is
   resemblance: both hold that there is a distinction between the consciousness and the
   objects of consciousness, and they differ on whether the consciousness is the witness or
   the identity. Both hold that the manifestations are real, and they differ on whether the
   manifestations are the transformations of the prakriti or the expressions of the identity.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of the two schools would be refuted by showing that the purusha cannot be
654                                                             Chapter 58. Samkhya and Yoga


   formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and consciousness—by
   showing, that is, that the two schools already distinguish the structural condition from
   the consciousness, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of their own.




58.12      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the purusha, or is it a departure
from the two schools? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not
conclusive. A reader who holds that the purusha is already a structural condition, not a pure
consciousness, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Samkhya Karika and the Yoga Sutras do
justice to the texts? The chapter has used the dualism of purusha and prakriti, the twenty-five
categories, the three gunas, the theory of causation, the goal of kaivalya, the eight limbs, the
modifications of the mind, the practice of cessation, and the goal of isolation, and it has stated
what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has
a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a consciousness and a structure—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the consciousness that witnesses, or the structure that persists? Is the
truth the cessation of the modifications of the mind, or the reconstruction of the manifestations?
What does your answer tell you about the relation between the Samkhya purusha and the
framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Nyaya and Vaisheshika. It states the logic of inference ( anumana), the
theory of perception ( pratyaksha), the categories of Vaisheshika ( padarthas), the theory of atoms,
and the goal of liberation; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Nyaya and
Vaisheshika; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of logic and of categories is the nearest Indian analogue to theirs. The present chapter
has stated the Samkhya and Yoga answer to the problem of consciousness; the next chapter states
the Nyaya and Vaisheshika answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 59

Nyaya and Vaisheshika


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Nyaya and Vaisheshika, the two foundational schools of
Indian philosophy that share a common ontology and a common epistemology but differ in their
emphasis: Nyaya is the school of logic and epistemology, Vaisheshika is the school of ontology
and category theory. It states the Nyaya account of the four means of knowledge (pramanas)—
perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana), comparison (upamana), and testimony (shabda)—,
the five-membered syllogism (panchavayava), the theory of inference, and the critique of the
skeptical positions; and it states the Vaisheshika account of the six categories (padarthas)—
substance (dravya), quality (guna), action (karma), universal (samanya), particularity (vishesha),
and inherence (samavaya)—, the atomic theory, and the goal of liberation (moksha), with
reference to the Nyaya Sutras of Gautama, the Vaisheshika Sutras of Kanada, the Nyaya-Bhashya
of Vatsyayana, and the Tattvarthadhigama Sutra of Prashastapada; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of the two schools; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of categories and of logic is the nearest Indian
analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that the two schools would raise against the
framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the
kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “pramana,” “anumana,” “padartha,”
“dravya,” “guna,” “karma,” “samanya,” “vishesha,” or “samavaya,” these are the schools’ terms,
and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


59.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a fire on a distant hill. She sees the smoke; she does not
see the fire; but she infers the fire from the smoke. The inference is not a perception; it is not a
testimony; it is not a comparison; it is an inference. The inference has a structure: there is a
reason (the smoke), there is a conclusion (the fire), and there is an invariable connection between
the two (where there is smoke, there is fire). The inference is valid because the connection is
invariable; it is invalid if the connection is not invariable.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the inference is, or how it works, but
what the categories of reality are. She sees a pot; she sees the clay; she sees the shape; she sees
the action of the potter; she sees the potness that the pot shares with other pots; she sees the
particularity that makes this pot this pot; she sees the inherence that holds the shape in the
clay. The categories are six: substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, and inherence.
The pot is a substance; its color is a quality; its making is an action; its potness is a universal;
its thisness is a particularity; its shape in the clay is an inherence. The six categories are the
ultimate kinds of reality; they are the padarthas.

                                                 656
59.2. The Question                                                                               657


   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the inference is, or what
the categories are, but what knowledge is. Knowledge is not a belief; it is not an opinion; it is not
a conviction. Knowledge is a true cognition; it is a cognition that corresponds to the reality; it is
a cognition that is produced by a valid means of knowledge. The valid means of knowledge are
four: perception, inference, comparison, and testimony. Knowledge is the cognition that arises
from one of these four; it is the cognition that is true and that is produced by a valid means.
This is the Nyaya account of knowledge: knowledge is true cognition produced by a pramana.
   The scene is the image of the two schools, in the Nyaya Sutras and in the Vaisheshika Sutras,
of the structure of reality. The smoke is the reason; the fire is the conclusion; the categories
are the six; knowledge is the true cognition. The scene poses the question that the two schools
were the first to pose in its full form in the Indian tradition. What is knowledge? What are the
categories of reality? And what is the relation between the two? The present chapter states the
two schools’ answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.



59.2      The Question

The previous chapter stated the positions of Samkhya and Yoga: the dualism of purusha and
prakriti, the twenty-five categories, the three gunas, the theory of causation, the goal of kaivalya,
the eight limbs, the modifications of the mind, the practice of cessation, and the goal of isolation.
The two schools are the classical formulations of the dualism of consciousness and nature; they are
the foundation of the later Indian philosophy. Nyaya and Vaisheshika are the two foundational
schools of Indian philosophy that share a common ontology and a common epistemology but
differ in their emphasis: Nyaya is the school of logic and epistemology, Vaisheshika is the school
of ontology and category theory. The present chapter states the two schools’ positions, and the
framework’s dialogue with them.
   The question is not whether Nyaya or Vaisheshika was right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Nyaya and Vaisheshika hold? The chapter states the
Nyaya account of the four means of knowledge, the five-membered syllogism, and the theory of
inference; and it states the Vaisheshika account of the six categories, the atomic theory, and the
goal of liberation.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two schools converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two schools would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
schools? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.
