59.3       The Position of Nyaya

59.3.1      The Four Means of Knowledge
The Nyaya four means of knowledge (pramanas) are stated in the Nyaya Sutras of Gautama
(c. 200 CE) and in the Nyaya-Bhashya of Vatsyayana (c. 450 CE). The four means are the
foundation of the Nyaya epistemology; they are the valid sources of knowledge.
      The four means have three features.

First feature: perception (pratyaksha). Perception is the cognition that arises from the
contact between the senses and the objects; it is the direct cognition; it is the cognition of the
particular. Perception is the foundation of the other means; it is the source of the empirical
knowledge.

Second feature: inference (anumana). Inference is the cognition that arises from the
knowledge of the invariable connection (vyapti) between the reason (hetu) and the conclusion
(sadhya). The inference is the cognition of the general from the particular; it is the cognition of
the fire from the smoke. The inference is the foundation of the rational knowledge.

Third feature: comparison and testimony (upamana and shabda). Comparison is
the cognition that arises from the resemblance between two things; it is the cognition of the
word from the resemblance with the object. Testimony is the cognition that arises from the
reliable assertion of a trustworthy person; it is the cognition of the truth from the words of the
trustworthy. The comparison and the testimony are the foundation of the linguistic and the
traditional knowledge.
      The four means are the foundation of the Nyaya epistemology. They are perception; they are
inference; they are comparison and testimony.

   From the Tradition

   “The four means of knowledge are perception, inference, comparison, and testimony.
   Knowledge is the true cognition that is produced by one of these four; it is the cognition
   that corresponds to the reality.” (Nyaya Sutras, 1.1.3, trans. after Jha, adapted)


59.3.2      The Five-Membered Syllogism
The Nyaya five-membered syllogism (panchavayava) is stated in the Nyaya Sutras and in the
Nyaya-Bhashya. The syllogism is the form of the inference; it is the method of the demonstration.
      The syllogism has three features.

First feature: the five members. The five members are: pratijna (the thesis), hetu (the
reason), udaharana (the example), upanaya (the application), and nigamana (the conclusion).
The thesis is the statement to be proved; the reason is the ground of the proof; the example is
the instance of the invariable connection; the application is the application of the connection to
the case; the conclusion is the restatement of the thesis as proved.
59.3. The Position of Nyaya                                                                        659


Second feature: the invariable connection. The invariable connection (vyapti) is the
foundation of the syllogism; it is the relation between the reason and the conclusion; it is the
relation that holds in all cases. The example is the instance of the connection; it is the evidence of
the connection. The syllogism is valid if the connection is invariable; it is invalid if the connection
is not invariable.


Third feature: the inference. The inference is the cognition that arises from the syllogism;
it is the cognition of the conclusion from the reason. The inference is the application of the
invariable connection to the case; it is the demonstration of the thesis.
    The syllogism is the foundation of the Nyaya logic. It is the five members; it is the invariable
connection; it is the inference.


59.3.3     The Theory of Inference

The Nyaya theory of inference is stated in the Nyaya Sutras and in the Nyaya-Bhashya. The
theory is the account of the inference; it is the account of the cognition of the general from the
particular.
    The theory has three features.


First feature: the three kinds of inference. The three kinds of inference are: purvavat
(inference from cause to effect), sheshavat (inference from effect to cause), and samanyato-drishta
(inference from the general to the particular). The three kinds are the three directions of the
inference; they are the three applications of the invariable connection.


Second feature: the five fallacies. The five fallacies (hetvabhasa) are: savyabhichara (the
inconclusive reason), viruddha (the contradictory reason), prakaranasama (the reason that is the
same as the question), sadhyasama (the reason that is the same as the conclusion), and kalatita
(the reason that is out of time). The five fallacies are the five ways the inference can fail; they
are the five ways the reason can be invalid.


Third feature: the validity. The validity of the inference is the invariable connection; it is
the relation between the reason and the conclusion. The inference is valid if the connection is
invariable; it is invalid if the connection is not invariable. The validity is not a matter of the
form; it is a matter of the connection.
    The theory is the foundation of the Nyaya logic. It is the three kinds; it is the five fallacies;
it is the validity.


59.3.4     The Critique of the Skeptical Positions

The Nyaya critique of the skeptical positions is stated in the Nyaya Sutras and in the Nyaya-
Bhashya. The critique is the defense of knowledge against the skeptics; it is the defense of the
pramanas against the critics.
    The critique has three features.
660                                                           Chapter 59. Nyaya and Vaisheshika


First feature: the critique of the universal doubt. The skeptic argues that nothing can
be known, because every cognition can be doubted. Nyaya responds: the universal doubt is
impossible; the doubt presupposes the knowledge; the act of doubting is itself a cognition that is
not doubted. The doubt is not a refutation of knowledge; it is a confirmation of knowledge.


Second feature: the critique of the momentariness. The Buddhist argues that everything
is momentary, and that there is no permanent substance. Nyaya responds: the momentariness
is not established; the perception of the enduring object is not refuted; the inference of the
momentariness is not valid. The enduring object is real; the momentariness is a philosophical
construction.


Third feature: the critique of the no-self. The Buddhist argues that there is no self, and
that the self is a construction. Nyaya responds: the self is not a construction; the self is the
substance that is the substratum of the cognition; the self is the one who knows, who feels, who
acts. The self is real; the no-self is a philosophical construction.
      The critique is the foundation of the Nyaya defense. It is the critique of the universal doubt;
it is the critique of the momentariness; it is the critique of the no-self.


59.4        The Position of Vaisheshika

59.4.1      The Six Categories

The Vaisheshika six categories (padarthas) are stated in the Vaisheshika Sutras of Kanada
(c. 200 BCE–100 CE) and in the Tattvarthadhigama Sutra of Prashastapada (c. 500 CE). The six
categories are the ultimate kinds of reality; they are the structure of the world.
      The six categories have three features.


First feature: substance (dravya). Substance is the substratum of the qualities and the
actions; it is the thing that has the qualities and the actions. The substances are nine: earth,
water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind. The substance is the foundation of the other
categories; it is the thing that the other categories inhere in.


Second feature: quality, action, and universal (guna, karma, and samanya). Quality
is the attribute of the substance; it is the color, the taste, the smell, the touch, the number, the
measure, the separation, the conjunction, the priority, the posteriority, the cognition, the pleasure,
the pain, the desire, the aversion, and the effort. Action is the movement of the substance; it is
the upward, the downward, the contraction, the expansion, and the going. Universal is the class
that the substance belongs to; it is the potness, the humanness, the horseness.


Third feature: particularity and inherence (vishesha and samavaya). Particularity
is the ultimate distinguishing feature of the substance; it is what makes this substance this
substance, and not another. Inherence is the relation between the substance and the qualities,
the actions, and the universals; it is the relation that holds the qualities in the substance.
59.4. The Position of Vaisheshika                                                              661


    The six categories are the foundation of the Vaisheshika ontology. They are the substance;
they are the quality, the action, and the universal; they are the particularity and the inherence.

   From the Tradition

   “The six categories are substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, and inherence.
   They are the ultimate kinds of reality; they are the structure of the world.” (Vaisheshika
   Sutras, 1.1.4, trans. after Sinha, adapted)



59.4.2    The Atomic Theory

The Vaisheshika atomic theory is stated in the Vaisheshika Sutras and in the Tattvarthadhigama
Sutra. The theory is the account of the material world; it is the account of the composition of
the material substances.
    The theory has three features.


First feature: the atoms. The atoms are the ultimate particles of the material substances;
they are the indivisible, eternal, and infinitesimal particles. The atoms are of four kinds: earth,
water, fire, and air. The atoms are the material causes of the material world.


Second feature: the dyads and the triads. The atoms combine into dyads; the dyads
combine into triads; the triads combine into the gross elements. The dyads are the first
combination; the triads are the second; the gross elements are the third. The world is the
composition of the atoms; it is the aggregation of the atoms.


Third feature: the creation and the dissolution. The creation is the combination of
the atoms; the dissolution is the separation of the atoms. The creation and the dissolution are
the cycles of the cosmos; they are the cycles of the material world. The atoms are eternal; the
combinations are temporary; the world is the temporary combination of the eternal atoms.
    The theory is the foundation of the Vaisheshika physics. It is the atoms; it is the dyads and
the triads; it is the creation and the dissolution.


59.4.3    The Goal of Liberation

The Vaisheshika goal of liberation (moksha) is stated in the Vaisheshika Sutras and in the
Tattvarthadhigama Sutra. The goal is the liberation from the suffering; it is the end of the cycle
of rebirth.
    The goal has three features.


First feature: the knowledge of the categories. The liberation is the knowledge of the
categories; it is the knowledge of the six padarthas; it is the knowledge of the structure of the
world. The knowledge is the means to the liberation; it is the condition of the freedom.
662                                                              Chapter 59. Nyaya and Vaisheshika


Second feature: the cessation of the suffering. The liberation is the cessation of the
suffering; it is the end of the pain; it is the end of the bondage. The self is free; it is no longer
bound; it is no longer suffering.


Third feature: the isolation of the self. The liberation is the isolation of the self; it is the
state in which the self is alone, in its own nature, as pure consciousness. The liberation is the
moksha; it is the goal of the Vaisheshika.
      The goal is the foundation of the Vaisheshika soteriology. It is the knowledge of the categories;
it is the cessation of the suffering; it is the isolation of the self.



59.5        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Nyaya and Vaisheshika is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the pramanas. The traditional reading takes the four
pramanas to be the valid means of knowledge: perception, inference, comparison, and testimony.
A revisionary reading takes them to be the four kinds of cognition: the four ways the mind relates
to the world. The two readings disagree on whether Nyaya is an epistemology or a psychology,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s knowledge
is reconstruction, not a pramana.


Second dispute: the status of the categories. The traditional reading takes the six
categories to be the ultimate kinds of reality: substance, quality, action, universal, particularity,
and inherence. A revisionary reading takes them to be the six ways of describing reality: the six
ways the language relates to the world. The two readings disagree on whether Vaisheshika is an
ontology or a grammar, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s categories are analytical roles, not ontological kinds.


Third dispute: the status of the atomic theory. The traditional reading takes the atoms
to be the ultimate particles of the material world: the indivisible, eternal, and infinitesimal
particles. A revisionary reading takes them to be the theoretical constructs: the hypothetical
entities that explain the material world. The two readings disagree on whether Vaisheshika
is a realism or a conventionalism, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s material realm is structured by the rules, not by the atoms.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Nyaya is an epistemology, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and an epistemology. If Vaisheshika
is an ontology, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and an ontology. The
framework holds that the revisionary readings are closer to the texts, but it does not rest its
case on these readings; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
59.6. Points of Convergence                                                                         663


59.6      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

  With Nyaya and Vaisheshika. The framework shares four structural features with the
   two schools’ position.

       1. The reality of knowledge. Nyaya holds that knowledge is real; it is the true cognition; it
          is the cognition that corresponds to the reality. The framework holds that knowledge
          is real; it is the reconstruction of the identity; it is the reading of the manifestations.
          Both hold that knowledge is real, and that it is not a mere opinion.

       2. The structure of inference. Nyaya holds that the inference has a structure: the reason,
          the conclusion, and the invariable connection between the two. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction has a structure: the manifestations, the identity, and the
          structural relation between the two. Both hold that there is a structure, and that
          the structure is the condition of knowledge.

       3. The reality of the categories. Vaisheshika holds that the categories are real; they are
          the ultimate kinds of reality; they are the structure of the world. The framework
          holds that the columns are real; they are the analytical roles; they are the structure
          of the explanation. Both hold that there are categories, and that the categories are
          the condition of the understanding.

       4. The goal of liberation. Nyaya and Vaisheshika hold that the liberation is the goal; it
          is the knowledge of the categories; it is the cessation of the suffering. The framework
          holds that the understanding of the structure is the goal; it is the reading of the
          manifestations; it is the cessation of the confusion. Both hold that there is a goal,
          and that the goal is the knowledge of the structure.



59.7      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

  With Nyaya and Vaisheshika. The framework diverges from the two schools’ position
   in four respects.

       1. The status of the pramanas. Nyaya holds that the four pramanas are the valid
          means of knowledge; they are the sources of the true cognition. The framework
          holds that the reconstruction is the only means of knowledge; it is the reading of the
          manifestations; it is not a pramana. The framework’s knowledge is structural, not
          pramanic.

       2. The status of the categories. Vaisheshika holds that the six categories are the ultimate
          kinds of reality; they are the structure of the world. The framework holds that
664                                                         Chapter 59. Nyaya and Vaisheshika


         the columns are analytical roles; they are not the ultimate kinds of reality. The
         framework’s categories are analytical, not ontological.

       3. The status of the atoms. Vaisheshika holds that the atoms are the ultimate particles
         of the material world; they are the material causes of the world. The framework
         holds that the material realm is structured by the rules; it is not composed of atoms.
         The framework’s material realm is structural, not atomic.

       4. The status of the liberation. Nyaya and Vaisheshika hold that the liberation is
         the goal; it is the knowledge of the categories; it is the cessation of the suffering.
         The framework holds that the understanding is the goal; it is the reading of the
         manifestations; it is the comprehension of the structure. The framework’s goal is
         structural, not soteriological.



59.8      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Nyaya’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance
  is not a cognition; it is a pattern. Knowledge is a true cognition; it is the cognition
  that is produced by a pramana. The framework’s reconstruction is a cognition, but it is
  not produced by a pramana; it is not knowledge. The framework’s epistemology is an
  epistemology of patterns, not of cognitions.
  Nyaya’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
  are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
  are the levels of the cognition; they are the levels of the pramanas. The framework’s
  realms are not levels of the cognition; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an
  ontology of levels, not of cognitions.
  Vaisheshika’s objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
  the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the knowledge of the categories; it is
  the knowledge of the six padarthas; it is the knowledge of the structure of the world. The
  framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the knowledge of the categories. The
  framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of categories.



59.9      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to Nyaya’s first objection. The framework agrees that knowledge is a true
  cognition, and it agrees that knowledge is produced by a means of knowledge. But the
  framework denies that the means must be a pramana. The framework’s reconstruction is
59.10. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     665


   the means of knowledge; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is the cognition that
   is produced by the contact between the mind and the manifestations. The distinction is
   between a pramana (a scriptural means) and a reconstruction (a structural means); the
   framework holds the second, not the first. The framework does not deny the pramanas; it
   denies that they are the only means.
   Reply to Nyaya’s second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not
   just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the cognition. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   cognition. The distinction is between a level of the cognition (an epistemological level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to Vaisheshika’s objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge of the
   categories is a form of knowledge, and it agrees that the categories are real. But the
   framework denies that the knowledge must be the knowledge of the six padarthas. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction of the structure; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the comprehension of the categories. The distinction is between
   a knowledge of the six categories (a categorial knowledge) and a reconstruction of the
   structure (a structural knowledge); the framework holds the second, not the first.



59.10       The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Nyaya and Vaisheshika’s cost. If the two schools accept the framework’s reply, they must
give up the claim that the pramanas are the only means of knowledge. They must accept that
the reconstruction is a means of knowledge, and that the reconstruction is the reading of the
manifestations. The cost is the loss of the pramanas: the four means are no longer the only
means; the reconstruction is the means. They must also give up the claim that the categories
are the ultimate kinds of reality; they must accept that the columns are analytical roles; the
categories are analytical, not ontological.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the two schools, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the pramanas, of the categories, of the atoms—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a pramana, and the framework leaves the
pramanas to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the pramanas and the
categories of the two schools are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
666                                                          Chapter 59. Nyaya and Vaisheshika


structure does not capture. The two schools must accept that the framework’s structure is not a
pattern; it is a structural condition that the pramanas presuppose as their condition. The cost
of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they are
complements, and each is incomplete without the others.



59.11      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the
   Nyaya term “the pramana.” If one substitutes “the pramana” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the pramana is the means of
   knowledge, and it is not manifested, because it is the means. The framework’s identity is a
   structure; the pramana is a means. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for the Nyaya term “the inference.”
   If one substitutes “the inference” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the inference is
   the cognition of the conclusion from the reason. The framework’s expression is ontological;
   the inference is epistemological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “category” is not substitutable for the Vaisheshika term “the
   padartha.” If one substitutes “the padartha” for “category” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s category is an analytical role; the padartha is the
   ultimate kind of reality. The framework’s category is analytical; the padartha is ontological.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Nyaya is resemblance:
   both hold that knowledge is real, and they differ on whether the means is a pramana or a
   reconstruction. The relation between the framework and Vaisheshika is resemblance: both
   hold that there are categories, and they differ on whether the categories are ontological or
   analytical. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of the two schools would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and cognition,
   or between structure and category—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish
   the structural condition from the cognition and the category, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of their own.




59.12      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
59.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 667


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Nyaya pramana or the
Vaisheshika padartha, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a
development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the pramana is already
a structural condition, or that the padartha is already a structural condition, has a question the
chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Nyaya Sutras and the Vaisheshika Sutras
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the four pramanas, the five-membered syllogism,
the theory of inference, the six categories, the atomic theory, and the goal of liberation, and it
has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a cognition and a structure—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the cognition that knows, or the structure that persists? Is the truth
the inference that concludes, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between the Nyaya pramana and the framework’s identity?

the theory of maya, and the path of knowledge ( jnana); it identifies the internal disputes within

the interpretation of Shankara; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with

Shankara’s. The present chapter has stated the Nyaya and Vaisheshika answer to the problem of

Chapter 60

Shankara


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Adi Shankara (c. 788–820 CE), the founder of the Advaita
Vedanta school of Indian philosophy. It states Shankara’s non-dualism (advaita), the doctrine that
Brahman is the only reality and that the world is maya (appearance), the identity of Brahman
and Atman, the two levels of reality (the absolute, paramarthika, and the empirical, vyavaharika),
the doctrine of superimposition (adhyasa), the theory of maya, and the path of knowledge (jnana)
as the means to liberation (moksha), with reference to the Brahmasutrabhashya (Commentary on
the Brahma Sutras), the Upadesasahasri (A Thousand Teachings), the Vivekachudamani (The
Crest-Jewel of Discrimination), and the commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita,
and the Brahma Sutras; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Shankara;
it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of identity
and manifestation is the nearest Indian analogue to Shankara’s; it presents the objections that
Shankara would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what
each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “advaita,” “Brahman,” “Atman,” “maya,” “adhyasa,” “moksha,” “jnana,” or “the two
levels of reality,” these are Shankara’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the
interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


60.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is walking in the desert at noon. She sees a rope on the ground, and she
mistakes it for a snake. Her heart races; she jumps back; she is afraid. Then she looks more
closely; she sees that it is a rope, not a snake; her fear subsides; she laughs at herself. The snake
was not real; it was a superimposition (adhyasa) on the rope; it was the rope mistaken for a
snake. The rope was real all along; the snake was an appearance; the fear was real, but it was
based on an illusion.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the snake is, or how she mistook it,
but what the rope is. The rope is not the snake; the rope is the reality; the rope is what was
there all along. But the rope is also not the ultimate reality; the rope is a name and a form;
the rope is a bundle of fibers; the fibers are a bundle of molecules; the molecules are a bundle
of atoms; the atoms are a bundle of particles. The rope is real at the empirical level, but it is
not the ultimate reality. The ultimate reality is Brahman; the rope is a name and a form of
Brahman; the rope is Brahman in the empirical mode.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the snake is, or what
the rope is, but what she is. She is the body; she is the mind; she is the intellect; she is the ego.
But Shankara says: she is not the body; she is not the mind; she is not the intellect; she is not

                                                669
670                                                                          Chapter 60. Shankara


the ego. She is the Atman; she is the self; she is the witness; she is the reality that is the same
as Brahman. Tat tvam asi: that thou art. The Atman is Brahman; the self is the absolute; the
innermost is the ultimate. This is the Advaita teaching: there is only one reality, Brahman, and
the self is that reality.
      The scene is Shankara’s image, in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in the Vivekachudamani, of
the structure of reality. The snake is the maya; the rope is the empirical reality; the Atman is
the Brahman. The scene poses the question that Shankara was the first to pose in its full form
in the Indian tradition. What is the ultimate reality? What is the world? And what is the self?
The present chapter states Shankara’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


60.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the positions of Nyaya and Vaisheshika: the four pramanas, the
five-membered syllogism, the theory of inference, the six categories, the atomic theory, and
the goal of liberation. The two schools are the classical formulations of the realist and the
pluralist Indian philosophy; they affirm the reality of the world and the plurality of the categories.
Shankara is the founder of the Advaita Vedanta, and he is the great critic of the realist and the
pluralist schools; he affirms the non-duality of Brahman and the illusoriness of the world. The
present chapter states Shankara’s non-dualism, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Shankara was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Shankara hold? The chapter states the non-dualism, the
identity of Brahman and Atman, the two levels of reality, the doctrine of superimposition, the
theory of maya, and the path of knowledge, with reference to the texts.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Shankara converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Shankara would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Shankara?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


60.3       The Position

60.3.1      The Non-Dualism (Advaita)

Shankara’s non-dualism (advaita) is stated in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in the Upadesasahasri.
The non-dualism is the foundation of Shankara’s philosophy; it is the teaching that there is only
one reality, Brahman, and that the plurality of the world is an appearance.
      The non-dualism has three features.
60.3. The Position                                                                                    671


First feature: Brahman is the only reality. Brahman is the only reality; there is no second;
there is no other. The world is not a second reality; the world is an appearance of Brahman; the
world is Brahman in the empirical mode. The plurality of the world is not a plurality of realities;
it is a plurality of appearances; the reality is one.


Second feature: the world is maya. The world is maya; it is the appearance; it is the name
and the form. The world is not nothing; it is real as an appearance; but its reality is not the
reality of Brahman. The world is the appearance of Brahman; it is not Brahman; it is the name
and the form of Brahman.


Third feature: the self is Brahman. The self is Brahman; the Atman is the absolute; the
innermost is the ultimate. Tat tvam asi: that thou art. The identity is not a similarity; it is an
identity; the Atman is not like Brahman; the Atman is Brahman. The realization of this identity
is the goal of the Advaita teaching; it is the liberation (moksha).
    The non-dualism is the foundation of Shankara’s philosophy. It is Brahman; it is the world
as maya; it is the self as Brahman.

   From the Tradition

   “Brahman is the only reality; the world is an appearance; the self is Brahman. There is
   no second; there is no other. The plurality of the world is a plurality of appearances;
   the reality is one.” (Shankara, Brahmasutrabhashya, 1.1.4, trans. after Gambhirananda,
   adapted)



60.3.2     The Two Levels of Reality

Shankara’s doctrine of the two levels of reality is stated in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in the
Upadesasahasri. The two levels are the absolute (paramarthika) and the empirical (vyavaharika).
    The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the absolute level. The absolute level (paramarthika) is the level of Brahman;
it is the level of the only reality; it is the level of the non-dual. At this level, there is no plurality;
there is no world; there is no self; there is only Brahman. The absolute level is the truth; the
empirical level is the appearance.


Second feature: the empirical level. The empirical level (vyavaharika) is the level of the
world; it is the level of the plurality; it is the level of the selves. At this level, there is the world;
there are the selves; there is the suffering; there is the liberation. The empirical level is real as
an appearance; it is not the absolute reality.


Third feature: the relation between the two levels. The relation between the two levels
is the relation between the reality and the appearance. The absolute is the reality; the empirical
is the appearance. The two are not the same; the two are not different; the two are the two
672                                                                          Chapter 60. Shankara


aspects of one reality. The empirical is the appearance of the absolute; the absolute is the reality
of the empirical.
      The doctrine is the key to Shankara’s philosophy. It is the absolute level; it is the empirical
level; it is the relation between the two.


60.3.3      The Doctrine of Superimposition (Adhyasa)

Shankara’s doctrine of superimposition (adhyasa) is stated in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in
the Upadesasahasri. The doctrine is the account of the error; it is the account of the confusion
between the self and the not-self.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the superimposition. The superimposition (adhyasa) is the error by which
the self is confused with the not-self; it is the error by which the Atman is confused with the
body, the mind, the intellect, the ego. The error is the cause of the bondage; it is the cause of
the suffering; it is the cause of the cycle of rebirth.


Second feature: the rope and the snake. The classical example is the rope and the snake:
the rope is mistaken for a snake; the snake is superimposed on the rope. The rope is the reality;
the snake is the appearance; the error is the confusion of the two. The Atman is the rope; the
body is the snake; the error is the confusion of the two.


Third feature: the removal of the superimposition. The removal of the superimposition
is the goal; it is the knowledge of the reality; it is the realization that the Atman is not the body,
not the mind, not the intellect, not the ego. The removal is the liberation; it is the moksha.
      The doctrine is the key to Shankara’s epistemology. It is the superimposition; it is the rope
and the snake; it is the removal.


60.3.4      The Theory of Maya

Shankara’s theory of maya is stated in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in the Vivekachudamani.
Maya is the power of Brahman; it is the power by which the one appears as many; it is the power
by which the reality appears as the appearance.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: maya as the power. Maya is the power of Brahman; it is the sakti of
Brahman; it is the power by which Brahman creates the world. The power is not separate from
Brahman; it is the power of Brahman; it is the sakti of Brahman.


Second feature: maya as the illusion. Maya is the illusion; it is the appearance; it is the
name and the form. The world is not nothing; it is real as an appearance; but its reality is not
the reality of Brahman. The world is the appearance of Brahman; it is not Brahman; it is the
name and the form of Brahman.
60.4. Internal Disputes                                                                          673


Third feature: maya as the ignorance. Maya is the ignorance; it is the ignorance that
makes the self mistake the appearance for the reality; it is the ignorance that makes the self
mistake the ego for the Atman. The liberation is the end of the ignorance; it is the realization of
the reality that is beyond the appearance.
   The theory is the key to Shankara’s cosmology. It is maya; it is the illusion; it is the ignorance.

60.3.5    The Path of Knowledge (Jnana)
Shankara’s path of knowledge (jnana) is stated in the Brahmasutrabhashya and in the Vivekachu-
damani. The path is the means to the liberation; it is the knowledge of the reality.
   The path has three features.

First feature: the knowledge. The knowledge (jnana) is the knowledge of Brahman; it
is the knowledge of the identity of the Atman and Brahman; it is the direct experience of the
reality. The knowledge is not a concept; it is not a belief; it is the realization.

Second feature: the discrimination. The discrimination (viveka) is the discrimination
between the real and the unreal; it is the discrimination between the Atman and the not-self.
The discrimination is the condition of the knowledge; it is the method of the path.

Third feature: the liberation. The liberation (moksha) is the end of the suffering; it is the
end of the bondage; it is the realization of the identity. The liberation is not a state; it is not a
place; it is the realization of what one always was. The liberation is the goal of the path; it is
the moksha.
   The path is the key to Shankara’s soteriology. It is the knowledge; it is the discrimination; it
is the liberation.


60.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Shankara is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of maya. The traditional reading takes maya to be a real power
of Brahman: it is the power by which Brahman creates the world; it is the sakti of Brahman. A
revisionary reading takes maya to be a metaphorical expression: it is a way of speaking about
the appearance; it is not a real power. The two readings disagree on whether Shankara is a
realist or a metaphorist about maya, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.

Second dispute: the status of the world. The traditional reading takes the world to be an
illusion: it is maya; it is the appearance; it is not the reality. A revisionary reading takes the
world to be real at the empirical level: it is real as an appearance; it is not the absolute reality,
but it is real in its own level. The two readings disagree on whether Shankara is an illusionist
or a phenomenalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.
674                                                                            Chapter 60. Shankara


Third dispute: the status of the path. The traditional reading takes the path of knowledge
to be the only path: it is the knowledge of Brahman; it is the direct experience. A revisionary
reading takes the path of knowledge to be one path among others: it is the path of the elite;
it is not the only path; the path of devotion (bhakti) and the path of action (karma) are also
paths. The two readings disagree on whether Shankara is an exclusivist or an inclusivist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no path of
knowledge; its knowledge is reconstruction.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Shankara is an illusionist, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an illusionism. If Shankara is a
phenomenalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does not rest
its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.



60.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Shankara. The framework shares four structural features with Shankara’s position.

        1. The distinction between the reality and the appearance. Shankara holds that Brahman
           is the reality, and the world is the appearance; the rope is the reality, and the snake
           is the appearance. The framework holds that the identity is the reality, and the
           manifestation is the appearance; the manifestation is the name and the form of the
           identity. Both hold that there is a distinction between the reality and the appearance,
           and that the reality is not exhausted by the appearance.

        2. The priority of the one over the many. Shankara holds that Brahman is one, and the
           many are the names and forms of the one. The framework holds that the identity is
           one, and the manifestations are the appearances of the one. Both hold that the one
           is prior to the many, and that the many is real in the one.

        3. The identity of the self and the absolute. Shankara holds that the Atman is Brahman;
           the self is the absolute; the innermost is the ultimate. The framework holds that the
           identity is the innermost reality; it is the invariance that underlies the manifestations.
           Both hold that there is an innermost reality, and that the innermost reality is not
           the empirical ego.

        4. The limits of language. Shankara holds that Brahman is beyond the words; it is not
           sat (being), not asat (non-being), not both, not neither; the method is neti neti.
           The framework holds that the identity is beyond the manifestations, and that it
           cannot be exhausted by any description; the method is reconstruction. Both hold
           that language has limits, and that the mind must recognize them.
60.6. Points of Divergence                                                                        675


60.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Shankara. The framework diverges from Shankara’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of the world. Shankara holds that the world is an illusion; it is maya; it
         is the appearance; it is not the reality. The framework holds that the manifestation
         is real in its own realm; it is not an illusion; it is the expression of the identity. The
         framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.

       2. The status of the self. Shankara holds that the Atman is the same as Brahman; the
         self is the absolute. The framework holds that the identity is the individual identity;
         it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not the absolute. The framework’s
         identity is individual, not universal.

       3. The status of the path. Shankara holds that the path of knowledge is the means
         to the liberation; it is the knowledge of Brahman; it is the direct experience. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is the knowledge; it is the reading of the
         manifestations; it is not the experience. The framework’s knowledge is structural,
         not experiential.

       4. The status of maya. Shankara holds that the world is maya, the cosmic illusion. The
         framework holds that the manifestation is real; it is not maya; it is the expression of
         the identity. The framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.



60.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Shankara’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not Brahman; it is a pattern. The world is the name and the form of Brahman; the world
   is not just structured; the world is the appearance of Brahman. The framework has no
   Brahman; the framework has no absolute; the framework’s world is a world without the
   absolute. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the absolute.
   Shankara’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the levels of the appearance of Brahman; they are the levels of maya. The
   framework’s realms are not levels of maya; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology
   is an ontology of levels, not of maya.
   Shankara’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the realization of the identity;
   it is the direct experience of the self as Brahman; it is the liberation. The framework’s
676                                                                        Chapter 60. Shankara


   knowledge is a mediation; it is not the realization. The framework’s epistemology is an
   epistemology of mediation, not of realization.



60.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is the appearance
   of the absolute, and it agrees that the appearance is real. But the framework denies
   that the appearance must be the only reality. The framework’s identity is the structural
   condition of the appearance; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural
   condition under which the appearance is what it is. The distinction is between an absolute
   (a reality) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not
   the first. The framework does not deny the absolute; it denies that the absolute is the
   only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the appearance. But the framework denies that
   the realms are levels of maya. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they are the
   levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the appearance. The
   distinction is between a level of maya (an illusion) and a level of manifestation (a real
   level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the realization. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a realization (an
   experience) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.



60.9        The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Shankara’s cost. If Shankara accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the world is an illusion. He must accept that the manifestation is real, and that the world is
the expression of the identity, not the illusion of Brahman. The cost is the loss of maya: the
world is no longer an illusion; the world is a real manifestation. He must also give up the claim
that the realization is the goal; he must accept that the reconstruction is the knowledge; the
reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Shankara’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
60.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     677


dimension of Brahman, of the Atman, of the realization—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is
the enactment of a structure, but not the absolute, and the framework leaves the absolute to a
separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Shankara’s Brahman is
not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Shankara must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition
that Brahman presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity
of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the other.


60.10        The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Shankara’s term “Brahman.” If one substitutes “Brahman” for “identity” in the frame-
   work’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Brahman is the absolute, and it is
   not manifested, because it is the reality of all things. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   Brahman is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Shankara’s term “maya.” If
   one substitutes “maya” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; maya is the cosmic illusion.
   The framework’s expression is real; maya is an illusion. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Shankara’s term “the
   realization.” If one substitutes “the realization” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the Shankaran realization is the direct experience of the self as Brahman.
   The framework’s reconstruction is mediated; the Shankaran realization is immediate. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Shankara is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a distinction between the reality and the appearance, and they
   differ on whether the appearance is real or an illusion. Both hold that there is an innermost
   reality, and they differ on whether the innermost reality is the absolute or the identity.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Shankara would be refuted by showing that the Shankaran Brahman cannot
   be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and absolute—by
   showing, that is, that Shankara already distinguishes the structural condition from the
678                                                                     Chapter 60. Shankara


   absolute, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Shankara’s own.



60.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Shankara’s Brahman, or is it a
departure from Shankara? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Shankara’s Brahman is already a structural condition,
not the absolute, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Brahmasutrabhashya and the Vivekachu-
damani do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the non-dualism, the identity of Brahman
and Atman, the two levels of reality, the doctrine of superimposition, the theory of maya, and
the path of knowledge, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that
the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
