A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an appearance and a reality—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the appearance that covers, or the reality that underlies? Is the truth
the realization that is immediate, or the reconstruction that is mediated? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between the Shankaran Atman and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Ramanuja. It states the qualified non-dualism ( visishtadvaita), the
doctrine that Brahman is the unity of the self and the world, the critique of Shankara’s illusionism,
the doctrine of the three realities (Brahman, the self, and the world), and the path of devotion
( bhakti); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Ramanuja; and it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of unity and multiplicity
is the nearest Indian analogue to Ramanuja’s. The present chapter has stated Shankara’s answer
to the problem of the absolute and the self; the next chapter states Ramanuja’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 61

Ramanuja


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Ramanuja (c. 1017–1137 CE), the founder of the
Visishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) school of Vedanta. It states Ramanuja’s qualified non-
dualism (visishtadvaita), the doctrine that Brahman is the unity of the self and the world, the
critique of Shankara’s illusionism, the doctrine of the three realities (Brahman, the self, and the
world), the doctrine of the divine attributes, and the path of devotion (bhakti) as the means to
liberation (moksha), with reference to the Sri Bhashya (Commentary on the Brahma Sutras),
the Vedartha Sangraha (The Essence of the Vedas), the Gita Bhashya (Commentary on the
Bhagavad Gita), and the Saranagati Gadya (The Prose on Surrender); it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of Ramanuja; it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of unity and multiplicity is the nearest Indian analogue to
Ramanuja’s; it presents the objections that Ramanuja would raise against the framework; it
presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “visishtadvaita,” “Brahman,” “chit,” “achit,”
“bhakti,” “prapatti,” or “the three realities,” these are Ramanuja’s terms, and their sense is fixed
by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


61.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at her own body. She sees her hand; she sees her foot; she sees
her face in the mirror. The hand is not the person; the foot is not the person; the face is not
the person. And yet the hand is hers; the foot is hers; the face is hers. The body is not the self,
and the body is not other than the self; the body is the self’s body; the body is the self in its
embodied form. The relation between the self and the body is the relation of inseparability: the
two are distinct, and the two are not separate.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the body is, or how it relates to the
self, but what the world is. The world is not the self; the world is not other than the self; the
world is the body of God. The world is the manifestation of Brahman; the world is the form of
Brahman; the world is the chit and the achit of Brahman. The world is real; the world is not
an illusion; the world is the expression of Brahman. This is what Ramanuja calls the qualified
non-dualism (visishtadvaita): Brahman is one, and the world is the qualified form of Brahman;
the two are not the same, and the two are not separate.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the body is, or what
the world is, but what God is. God is not a bare unity; God is not a qualityless absolute; God is
the Lord; God is the personal God; God is the one who has the divine attributes; God is the one
who is the inner self of all things. God is Brahman; God is the Isvara; God is the one who is the

                                                680
61.2. The Question                                                                               681


unity of the self and the world. And the path to God is not the path of knowledge alone; it is
the path of devotion (bhakti); it is the path of love; it is the path of surrender (prapatti). The
devotee is not the knower; the devotee is the lover; the devotee is the one who surrenders.
   The scene is Ramanuja’s image, in the Sri Bhashya and in the Vedartha Sangraha, of the
structure of reality. The body is the self’s body; the world is God’s body; the self is the servant
of God. The scene poses the question that Ramanuja was the first to pose in its full form in the
Indian tradition. What is the relation between God and the world? What is the relation between
God and the self? And what is the path to liberation? The present chapter states Ramanuja’s
answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


61.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated Shankara’s position: the non-dualism, the identity of Brahman and
Atman, the two levels of reality, the doctrine of superimposition, the theory of maya, and the
path of knowledge. Shankara is the founder of the Advaita Vedanta, and he is the great critic of
the realist and the pluralist schools; he affirms the non-duality of Brahman and the illusoriness
of the world. Ramanuja is his successor, and he is the great critic of Shankara; he affirms the
qualified non-dualism, the reality of the world, and the path of devotion. The present chapter
states Ramanuja’s qualified non-dualism, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Ramanuja was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Ramanuja hold? The chapter states the qualified
non-dualism, the critique of Shankara, the three realities, the divine attributes, and the path of
devotion, with reference to the texts.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Ramanuja converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Ramanuja would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Ramanuja?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


61.3      The Position

61.3.1     The Qualified Non-Dualism (Visishtadvaita)

Ramanuja’s qualified non-dualism (visishtadvaita) is stated in the Sri Bhashya and in the
Vedartha Sangraha. The qualified non-dualism is the foundation of Ramanuja’s philosophy; it
is the teaching that Brahman is one, and that the world and the self are the qualified forms of
Brahman.
   The qualified non-dualism has three features.
682                                                                       Chapter 61. Ramanuja


First feature: Brahman is one. Brahman is one; there is no second; there is no other.
Brahman is the ultimate reality; it is the source of all things; it is the Lord. The unity of
Brahman is not the bare unity of Shankara; it is the unity that includes the world and the self
as its qualified forms.


Second feature: the world and the self are the qualified forms. The world and the self
are not Brahman; they are not other than Brahman; they are the qualified forms of Brahman.
As the body is the qualified form of the self, so the world is the qualified form of Brahman;
the world is the body of God. The world is real; the world is not an illusion; the world is the
expression of Brahman.


Third feature: the inseparability. The relation between Brahman and the world is the
relation of inseparability (apritthak-siddhi). The two are distinct; the two are not separate; the
two are the two aspects of one reality. The world is not Brahman, and the world is not other
than Brahman; the world is the qualified form of Brahman.
      The qualified non-dualism is the foundation of Ramanuja’s philosophy. It is Brahman; it is
the world and the self; it is the inseparability.

   From the Tradition

   “Brahman is one; the world and the self are the qualified forms of Brahman. As the body
   is the qualified form of the self, so the world is the qualified form of Brahman. The two are
   distinct; the two are not separate.” (Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya, 1.1.1, trans. after Thibaut,
   adapted)



61.3.2       The Critique of Shankara

Ramanuja’s critique of Shankara is stated in the Sri Bhashya and in the Vedartha Sangraha.
The critique is the foundation of Ramanuja’s qualified non-dualism; it is the diagnosis of the
errors of the Advaita.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the critique of maya. Shankara holds that the world is maya, the cosmic
illusion; the world is not real. Ramanuja responds: the world is real; the world is the expression
of Brahman; the world is the body of God. The illusionism of Shankara is a denial of the reality
of the world; it is a denial of the reality of the experience; it is a denial of the reality of the
scripture.


Second feature: the critique of the qualityless Brahman. Shankara holds that Brahman
is without attributes; Brahman is the qualityless absolute; Brahman is nirguna. Ramanuja
responds: Brahman is not without attributes; Brahman is the Lord; Brahman is the personal
God; Brahman is saguna. The qualityless Brahman of Shankara is an abstraction; it is not the
God of the scripture; it is not the God of the devotion.
61.3. The Position                                                                             683


Third feature: the critique of the path of knowledge. Shankara holds that the path of
knowledge is the only path; the knowledge of Brahman is the liberation. Ramanuja responds:
the path of knowledge is not the only path; the path of devotion is the higher path; the love of
God is the liberation. The knowledge of Brahman without the love of God is a cold knowledge;
it is not the liberation.
   The critique is the foundation of Ramanuja’s qualified non-dualism. It is the critique of maya;
it is the critique of the qualityless Brahman; it is the critique of the path of knowledge.


61.3.3     The Three Realities

Ramanuja’s doctrine of the three realities is stated in the Sri Bhashya and in the Vedartha
Sangraha. The three realities are Brahman, the self (chit), and the world (achit).
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: Brahman. Brahman is the Lord; it is the personal God; it is the one who has
the divine attributes; it is the inner self of all things. Brahman is the unity of the self and the
world; it is the ground of the two; it is the source of the two.


Second feature: the self (chit). The self (chit) is the individual soul; it is the conscious
entity; it is the one who knows, who feels, who acts. The self is not Brahman; the self is not
other than Brahman; the self is the qualified form of Brahman; the self is the body of Brahman.


Third feature: the world (achit). The world (achit) is the non-conscious entity; it is the
material world; it is the object of the experience. The world is not Brahman; the world is not
other than Brahman; the world is the qualified form of Brahman; the world is the body of
Brahman.
   The doctrine is the key to Ramanuja’s ontology. It is Brahman; it is the self; it is the world.


61.3.4     The Divine Attributes

Ramanuja’s doctrine of the divine attributes is stated in the Sri Bhashya and in the Vedartha
Sangraha. The doctrine is the affirmation of the personal God; it is the affirmation of the
attributes of Brahman.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the attributes. Brahman has the divine attributes; it has knowledge, power,
love, mercy, justice, and beauty. The attributes are real; they are not illusions; they are not
the products of the ignorance. The attributes are the perfections of Brahman; they are the
perfections of the Lord.


Second feature: the inseparability. The attributes are inseparable from Brahman; they
are not separate entities; they are not the parts of Brahman. The attributes are the modes of
Brahman; they are the ways Brahman is; they are the qualified forms of Brahman.
684                                                                          Chapter 61. Ramanuja


Third feature: the knowledge of the attributes. The knowledge of the attributes is the
knowledge of Brahman; it is the knowledge of the Lord; it is the knowledge that leads to the
devotion. The knowledge of the attributes is not the knowledge of the qualityless absolute; it is
the knowledge of the personal God.
      The doctrine is the key to Ramanuja’s theology. It is the attributes; it is the inseparability;
it is the knowledge.

61.3.5      The Path of Devotion (Bhakti)
Ramanuja’s path of devotion (bhakti) is stated in the Sri Bhashya and in the Gita Bhashya. The
path is the means to the liberation; it is the love of God; it is the surrender to God.
      The path has three features.

First feature: the devotion. The devotion (bhakti) is the love of God; it is the attachment
to God; it is the dedication to God. The devotion is not a mere feeling; it is a practice; it is the
cultivation of the love; it is the discipline of the heart.

Second feature: the surrender (prapatti). The surrender (prapatti) is the self-surrender
to God; it is the trust in God; it is the reliance on God. The surrender is the highest form of the
devotion; it is the way of the Saranagati Gadya; it is the way of the one who has no other refuge.

Third feature: the liberation. The liberation (moksha) is the union with God; it is the
service of God; it is the enjoyment of God. The liberation is not the isolation of the self; it is the
community of the self with God; it is the service of the Lord.
      The path is the key to Ramanuja’s soteriology. It is the devotion; it is the surrender; it is the
liberation.


61.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Ramanuja is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the world. The traditional reading takes the world to be real:
it is the qualified form of Brahman; it is the body of God; it is not an illusion. A revisionary
reading takes the world to be a mode of Brahman: it is the mode of the divine; it is not a separate
reality; it is the expression of the divine. The two readings disagree on whether Ramanuja is a
realist or a modalist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s manifestation is real, not an illusion.

Second dispute: the status of the self. The traditional reading takes the self to be a real
entity: it is the individual soul; it is the conscious entity; it is the servant of God. A revisionary
reading takes the self to be a mode of Brahman: it is the mode of the divine; it is not a separate
reality; it is the expression of the divine. The two readings disagree on whether Ramanuja is a
pluralist or a monist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s identity is the individual identity, not the mode of the absolute.
61.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      685


Third dispute: the status of the devotion. The traditional reading takes the devotion to be
the path to the liberation: it is the love of God; it is the surrender to God. A revisionary reading
takes the devotion to be the end of the liberation: it is the service of God; it is the enjoyment of
God. The two readings disagree on whether Ramanuja is a devotionalist or a service-theorist, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework has no devotion;
its knowledge is reconstruction.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ramanuja is a realist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a qualified non-dualism. If Ramanuja
is a modalist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as
distinct. The framework holds that the second reading is closer to the texts, but it does not rest
its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.




61.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Ramanuja. The framework shares four structural features with Ramanuja’s
   position.

       1. The reality of the world. Ramanuja holds that the world is real; it is the qualified
         form of Brahman; it is the body of God. The framework holds that the manifestation
         is real; it is the expression of the identity; it is the appearance of the identity. Both
         hold that the world is real, and that it is not an illusion.

       2. The relation between the one and the many. Ramanuja holds that Brahman is one,
         and the world and the self are the qualified forms of Brahman. The framework holds
         that the identity is one, and the manifestations are the qualified forms of the identity.
         Both hold that the one is prior to the many, and that the many is real in the one.

       3. The personal God. Ramanuja holds that Brahman is the Lord; it is the personal
         God; it is the one who has the divine attributes. The framework holds that the
         First Determination is a realm of pure unity; it is not a personal God. But the
         framework shares with Ramanuja the recognition that the ultimate reality is not a
         bare abstraction; it is the structure of the manifestation.

       4. The path of devotion. Ramanuja holds that the path of devotion is the means to the
         liberation; it is the love of God; it is the surrender to God. The framework holds
         that the reconstruction is the knowledge; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
         not the devotion. But the framework shares with Ramanuja the recognition that
         knowledge is not merely conceptual; it is the relation of the self to the structure.
686                                                                         Chapter 61. Ramanuja


61.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Ramanuja. The framework diverges from Ramanuja’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of Brahman. Ramanuja holds that Brahman is the Lord; it is the personal
          God; it is the one who has the divine attributes. The framework holds that the First
          Determination is a realm of pure unity; it is not a personal God; it is not the Lord.
         The framework is a metaphysics without God.

       2. The status of the self. Ramanuja holds that the self is the individual soul; it is the
          servant of God; it is the body of Brahman. The framework holds that the identity
          is the invariance enacted by one source; it is not the individual soul; it is not the
          servant of God. The framework’s identity is individual, not devotional.

       3. The status of the world. Ramanuja holds that the world is the body of God; it is
          the qualified form of Brahman. The framework holds that the manifestation is the
          expression of the identity; it is not the body of God; it is the appearance of the
          identity. The framework’s manifestation is structural, not theological.

       4. The status of the devotion. Ramanuja holds that the path of devotion is the means to
          the liberation; it is the love of God; it is the surrender to God. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the knowledge; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
          not the devotion. The framework’s knowledge is structural, not devotional.



61.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Ramanuja’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
  Brahman; it is a pattern. The world is the body of God; the world is not just structured;
  the world is the expression of Brahman. The framework has no Brahman; the framework
  has no God; the framework’s world is a world without God. The framework’s ontology is
  an ontology of patterns, not of God.
  Ramanuja’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
  they are the levels of the body of God; they are the levels of the expression of Brahman.
  The framework’s realms are not levels of the body of God; they are just levels. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of God.
  Ramanuja’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the love of God; it is the devotion;
  it is the surrender. The framework’s knowledge is a mediation; it is not the devotion. The
61.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      687


   framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of mediation, not of devotion.



61.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is the expression
   of God, and it agrees that the expression is real. But the framework denies that the
   expression must be the body of God. The framework’s identity is the structural condition
   of the expression; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition
   under which the expression is what it is. The distinction is between a God (a personal
   reality) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the second, not the
   first. The framework does not deny God; it denies that God is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the body of God. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   expression. The distinction is between a level of the body of God (a theological level) and
   a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the devotion. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a devotion (a love)
   and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



61.9        The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Ramanuja’s cost. If Ramanuja accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
God is the only reality. He must accept that the identity is the structural condition, and that
the world is the expression of the identity. The cost is the loss of the personal God: God is no
longer the Lord; God is the structural condition. He must also give up the claim that devotion is
the path; he must accept that reconstruction is the knowledge; the reconstruction is the reading
of the manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Ramanuja’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of God, of the self, of the world—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the
688                                                                       Chapter 61. Ramanuja


loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a
structure, but not God, and the framework leaves God to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ramanuja’s God is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Ramanuja
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that
God presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


61.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Ra-
   manuja’s term “Brahman.” If one substitutes “Brahman” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Ramanuja’s Brahman is the Lord, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the inner self of all things. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   Ramanuja’s Brahman is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Ramanuja’s term “the body of
   God.” If one substitutes “the body of God” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the body
   of God is the qualified form of Brahman. The framework’s expression is structural; the
   body of God is theological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Ramanuja’s term “the
   devotion.” If one substitutes “the devotion” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the devotion is the love of God. The framework’s reconstruction is mediated;
   the devotion is immediate. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ramanuja is resemblance:
   both hold that the world is real, and they differ on whether the world is the body of God or
   the expression of the identity. Both hold that the one is prior to the many, and they differ
   on whether the one is Brahman or the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is
   agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Ramanuja would be refuted
   by showing that Ramanuja’s Brahman cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and God—by showing, that is, that Ramanuja already
   distinguishes the structural condition from God, and that the framework’s distinction is a
61.11. Open Questions                                                                            689


   development of Ramanuja’s own.



61.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ramanuja’s Brahman, or is it a
departure from Ramanuja? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ramanuja’s Brahman is already a structural condition,
not a personal God, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Sri Bhashya and the Vedartha Sangraha
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the qualified non-dualism, the critique of Shankara,
the three realities, the divine attributes, and the path of devotion, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

Consider a thing you know that is both a unity and a multiplicity—a person, a tradition, a work

unity? Is the truth the devotion that loves, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your

Scope. This chapter closes Part VIII, the dialogues with Indian philosophy, and it closes it with Sri
Aurobindo (1872–1950 CE), the Indian philosopher, poet, and yogi. It states Aurobindo’s integral
yoga (purna yoga), the doctrine of the Supermind (vijnana), the evolution of consciousness, the
ascent and the descent, the transformation of the human being, the doctrine of the planes of
consciousness, and the goal of the supramental transformation, with reference to The Life Divine
(1939–1940), The Synthesis of Yoga (1941–1951), The Secret of the Veda (1914–1916), and Savitri:
A Legend and a Symbol (1950); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Aurobindo; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account

objections that Aurobindo would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply;
it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “integral yoga,” “the Supermind,” “the evolution of consciousness,” “the ascent
and the descent,” “the supramental transformation,” or “the planes of consciousness,” these are
Aurobindo’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the works and by the interpretive tradition, not by
the framework.



62.1      A Scene

Consider a person who is standing on a mountain. Below her is the valley: the villages, the
rivers, the fields. Above her is the peak: the snow, the clouds, the sky. She is between the two;
she is on the slope; she is climbing. The climb is not a flight; it is not a jump; it is a step-by-step
ascent, from the valley to the peak, from the lower to the higher.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the mountain is, or how she climbs it,
but what the climb is. The climb is not a movement in space; it is a movement in consciousness;
it is the ascent from the lower planes of consciousness to the higher planes. The lower planes are
the physical, the vital, the mental; the higher planes are the higher mind, the illumined mind,
the intuitive mind, the overmind, and the Supermind. The climb is the ascent of consciousness;
it is the yoga of the integral path.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the climb is, or how it
is done, but what the peak is. The peak is not a place; it is a state; it is the Supermind; it is the
consciousness that is beyond the mental. The Supermind is not a negation of the world; it is the
transformation of the world; it is the descent of the higher consciousness into the lower; it is the
divine life on earth. The goal is not to escape the world; it is to transform the world; it is to
bring the Supermind into the earth; it is the supramental transformation.

                                                 691
692                                                                        Chapter 62. Aurobindo


      The scene is Aurobindo’s image, in The Life Divine and in The Synthesis of Yoga, of the
structure of reality. The mountain is the planes of consciousness; the climb is the ascent; the
peak is the Supermind. The scene poses the question that Aurobindo was the first to pose in
its full form in the Indian tradition. What is consciousness? What is evolution? And what is
the goal of human life? The present chapter states Aurobindo’s answer, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.



62.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated Ramanuja’s position: the qualified non-dualism, the critique of
Shankara, the three realities, the divine attributes, and the path of devotion. Ramanuja is the
founder of the Visishtadvaita, and he is the great critic of Shankara; he affirms the reality of
the world and the path of devotion. Aurobindo is his successor in a different line, and he is the
great synthesizer of the Indian tradition; he affirms the evolution of consciousness, the reality of
the world, and the transformation of the human being. The present chapter states Aurobindo’s
integral yoga, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Aurobindo was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Aurobindo hold? The chapter states the integral yoga,
the Supermind, the evolution of consciousness, the ascent and the descent, the transformation of
the human being, the planes of consciousness, and the goal of the supramental transformation,
with reference to the works.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Aurobindo converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Aurobindo would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Aurobindo?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.



62.3       The Position

62.3.1      The Integral Yoga

Aurobindo’s integral yoga (purna yoga) is stated in The Synthesis of Yoga (1941–1951) and in
The Life Divine (1939–1940). The integral yoga is the foundation of Aurobindo’s philosophy; it
is the path that integrates the three traditional yogas: the yoga of knowledge (jnana), the yoga
of devotion (bhakti), and the yoga of action (karma).
      The integral yoga has three features.
62.3. The Position                                                                               693


First feature: the integration. The integral yoga integrates the three traditional yogas; it
does not reject them; it includes them; it transforms them. The knowledge is not the rejection of
the world; it is the understanding of the world; the devotion is not the escape from the world; it
is the love of the world; the action is not the bondage to the world; it is the service of the world.
The three are the three aspects of one path.


Second feature: the transformation. The integral yoga is not the escape from the world; it
is the transformation of the world. The goal is not the liberation from the world; it is the divine
life in the world; it is the supramental transformation. The transformation is the descent of the
higher consciousness into the lower; it is the divinization of the world.


Third feature: the evolution. The integral yoga is the evolution of consciousness; it is the
ascent from the lower planes to the higher planes; it is the descent of the higher planes into the
lower. The evolution is not a blind process; it is the conscious ascent; it is the collaboration with
the divine.
   The integral yoga is the foundation of Aurobindo’s philosophy. It is the integration; it is the
transformation; it is the evolution.

   From the Tradition

   “The integral yoga is not the rejection of the world; it is the transformation of the world.
   The goal is not the liberation from the world; it is the divine life in the world; it is the
   supramental transformation.” (Aurobindo, The Synthesis of Yoga, ch. 1, adapted)



62.3.2    The Supermind

Aurobindo’s doctrine of the Supermind (vijnana) is stated in The Life Divine. The Supermind is
the highest plane of consciousness; it is the consciousness that is beyond the mental; it is the
consciousness that is the source of the world.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the Supermind as the highest plane. The Supermind is the highest plane
of consciousness; it is the plane that is beyond the mental; it is the plane that is the source of
the world. The Supermind is not a negation of the world; it is the truth of the world; it is the
consciousness that sees the world as the expression of the divine.


Second feature: the Supermind as the source. The Supermind is the source of the world;
it is the consciousness that creates the world; it is the consciousness that is the ground of the
world. The Supermind is not a thing; it is a consciousness; it is the consciousness that is the
source of all things.


Third feature: the Supermind as the goal. The Supermind is the goal of the evolution;
it is the plane that the evolution is moving toward; it is the plane that the human being is to
694                                                                        Chapter 62. Aurobindo


realize. The realization of the Supermind is the supramental transformation; it is the divinization
of the human being.
      The doctrine is the key to Aurobindo’s cosmology. It is the Supermind; it is the source; it is
the goal.


62.3.3      The Evolution of Consciousness

Aurobindo’s doctrine of the evolution of consciousness is stated in The Life Divine. The evolution
is the ascent from the lower planes of consciousness to the higher planes; it is the movement from
the matter to the life to the mind to the Supermind.
      The evolution has three features.


First feature: the planes. The planes of consciousness are the levels of the evolution; they
are the stages of the ascent. The planes are: the physical, the vital, the mental, the higher mind,
the illumined mind, the intuitive mind, the overmind, and the Supermind. Each plane is a level
of consciousness; each level is a stage of the evolution.


Second feature: the ascent. The ascent is the movement from the lower planes to the higher
planes; it is the movement from the matter to the life to the mind to the Supermind. The
ascent is not a movement in space; it is a movement in consciousness; it is the evolution of the
consciousness.


Third feature: the descent. The descent is the movement from the higher planes to the
lower planes; it is the movement from the Supermind to the mind to the life to the matter.
The descent is the involution of the consciousness; it is the source of the evolution. The two
movements are the two aspects of one process; the ascent is the return of the descent; the descent
is the condition of the ascent.
      The doctrine is the key to Aurobindo’s philosophy of evolution. It is the planes; it is the
ascent; it is the descent.


62.3.4      The Ascent and the Descent

Aurobindo’s doctrine of the ascent and the descent is stated in The Life Divine. The ascent and
the descent are the two movements of the evolution; they are the two aspects of one process.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the ascent. The ascent is the movement from the lower to the higher; it is
the evolution of the consciousness; it is the return to the source. The ascent is the path of the
integral yoga; it is the path of the transformation.


Second feature: the descent. The descent is the movement from the higher to the lower; it
is the involution of the consciousness; it is the creation of the world. The descent is the condition
of the ascent; it is the source of the evolution.
62.3. The Position                                                                                 695


Third feature: the unity. The unity of the ascent and the descent is the unity of the
evolution; the two are the two aspects of one process; the two are the two movements of one
consciousness. The unity is the key to the integral yoga; it is the key to the transformation.
   The doctrine is the key to Aurobindo’s cosmology. It is the ascent; it is the descent; it is the
unity.


62.3.5     The Transformation of the Human Being

Aurobindo’s doctrine of the transformation of the human being is stated in The Life Divine
and in The Synthesis of Yoga. The transformation is the goal of the integral yoga; it is the
divinization of the human being.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the transformation. The transformation is the change of the human being;
it is the change of the body, the life, the mind, and the Supermind. The transformation is not
the escape from the world; it is the divinization of the world; it is the divine life in the world.


Second feature: the human being. The human being is the transitional being; it is the
being that is between the animal and the divine; it is the being that is to be transformed. The
human being is not the end of the evolution; it is the transition to the next stage.


Third feature: the superman. The superman is the being that is to come; it is the being
that has realized the Supermind; it is the being that has transformed the human being. The
superman is not the Übermensch of Nietzsche; it is the being of the supramental transformation;
it is the being of the divine life.
   The doctrine is the key to Aurobindo’s anthropology. It is the transformation; it is the human
being; it is the superman.


62.3.6     The Goal of the Supramental Transformation

Aurobindo’s doctrine of the goal of the supramental transformation is stated in The Life Divine.
The goal is the divinization of the world; it is the divine life on earth; it is the realization of the
Supermind in the world.
   The goal has three features.


First feature: the divinization. The divinization is the transformation of the world; it is
the descent of the Supermind into the world; it is the divine life on earth. The divinization is
not the escape from the world; it is the transformation of the world.


Second feature: the divine life. The divine life is the life of the Supermind; it is the life of
the consciousness that is beyond the mental; it is the life of the transformation. The divine life
is not the life of the world; it is the life of the world transformed.
696                                                                            Chapter 62. Aurobindo


Third feature: the realization. The realization is the goal of the evolution; it is the goal
of the integral yoga; it is the goal of the human being. The realization is the supramental
transformation; it is the divinization of the world.
      The goal is the key to Aurobindo’s soteriology. It is the divinization; it is the divine life; it is
the realization.




62.4        Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Aurobindo is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.



First dispute: the status of the Supermind. The traditional reading takes the Supermind
to be a real plane of consciousness: it is the highest plane; it is the source of the world; it is the
goal of the evolution. A revisionary reading takes it to be a symbol: it is a way of speaking
about the highest consciousness; it is not a real plane. The two readings disagree on whether
Aurobindo is a realist or a symbolist about the Supermind, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a symbolism.



Second dispute: the status of the evolution. The traditional reading takes the evolution
to be a real process: it is the ascent from the lower to the higher; it is the evolution of the
consciousness. A revisionary reading takes it to be a phenomenological description: it is a way of
speaking about the experience of the transformation; it is not a real process. The two readings
disagree on whether Aurobindo is an evolutionist or a phenomenologist, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a phenomenology.



Third dispute: the status of the transformation. The traditional reading takes the
transformation to be a real possibility: it is the divinization of the world; it is the divine life on
earth. A revisionary reading takes it to be an ideal: it is a goal that is not yet realized; it is a
hope; it is a vision. The two readings disagree on whether Aurobindo is a realist or an idealist
about the transformation, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because
the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not an idealism.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Aurobindo is a realist, the framework’s dialogue
with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and an integral realism. If Aurobindo is a
symbolist, the dialogue is a dialogue between two positions that the framework treats as distinct.
The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the texts, but it does not rest its case on
this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
62.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      697


62.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

  With Aurobindo. The framework shares four structural features with Aurobindo’s
   position.

       1. The reality of the world. Aurobindo holds that the world is real; it is not an illusion;
          it is the expression of the divine. The framework holds that the manifestation is real;
          it is not an illusion; it is the expression of the identity. Both hold that the world is
          real, and that it is not an illusion.

       2. The reality of evolution. Aurobindo holds that the evolution is real; it is the ascent
          from the lower to the higher; it is the evolution of the consciousness. The framework
          holds that the expression is real; it is the enactment of the identity; it is the
          manifestation of the identity. Both hold that there is a process, and that the process
          is real.

       3. The planes of consciousness. Aurobindo holds that there are planes of consciousness;
          they are the levels of the evolution; they are the stages of the ascent. The framework
          holds that there are realms of manifestation; they are the levels of the expression;
          they are the stages of the manifestation. Both hold that reality is stratified, and
          that the strata are the levels of the consciousness.

       4. The transformation. Aurobindo holds that the goal of the evolution is the transforma-
          tion; it is the divinization of the world; it is the divine life on earth. The framework
          holds that the goal of the expression is the manifestation; it is the enactment of the
          identity; it is the expression of the structure. Both hold that there is a goal, and
          that the goal is the transformation.



62.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

  With Aurobindo. The framework diverges from Aurobindo’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of the Supermind. Aurobindo holds that the Supermind is the highest
          plane of consciousness; it is the source of the world; it is the goal of the evolution.
          The framework holds that the First Determination is a realm of pure unity; it is not
          a plane of consciousness; it is not the Supermind. The framework’s metaphysics is a
          metaphysics of structure, not of consciousness.

       2. The status of the evolution. Aurobindo holds that the evolution is a real process; it is
          the ascent from the lower to the higher; it is the evolution of the consciousness. The
          framework holds that the expression is a structural tendency; it is the enactment of
698                                                                       Chapter 62. Aurobindo


         the identity; it is not the evolution of the consciousness. The framework’s expression
         is structural, not evolutionary.

       3. The status of the transformation. Aurobindo holds that the goal of the evolution is
         the transformation; it is the divinization of the world; it is the divine life on earth.
         The framework holds that the goal of the expression is the manifestation; it is the
         enactment of the identity; it is not the transformation. The framework’s goal is
         structural, not transformative.

       4. The status of the superman. Aurobindo holds that the superman is the being that is
         to come; it is the being that has realized the Supermind; it is the being that has
         transformed the human being. The framework has no superman; its subject is the
         structure of identity and manifestation; it leaves the superman to a separate inquiry.
         The framework is a metaphysics without a superman.




62.7      The Tradition’s Objections


  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Aurobindo’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
  a consciousness; it is a pattern. The world is the expression of the divine consciousness;
  the world is not just structured; the world is the evolution of the consciousness. The
  framework has no consciousness; the framework has no evolution; the framework’s world is
  a world without the consciousness. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns,
  not of consciousness.
  Aurobindo’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
  they are the planes of consciousness; they are the stages of the evolution. The framework’s
  realms are not planes of consciousness; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is
  an ontology of levels, not of consciousness.
  Aurobindo’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
  it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the transformation; it is the
  divinization; it is the divine life. The framework’s knowledge is a mediation; it is not the
  transformation. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of mediation, not of
  transformation.
62.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      699


62.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is the expression
   of consciousness, and it agrees that the consciousness is real. But the framework denies
   that the consciousness must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the
   structural condition of the consciousness; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it
   is the structural condition under which the consciousness is what it is. The distinction
   is between a consciousness (an experience) and an identity (a structural condition); the
   framework holds the second, not the first. The framework does not deny the consciousness;
   it denies that the consciousness is the only principle.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are planes of consciousness. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   consciousness. The distinction is between a plane of consciousness (an experiential level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not
   capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the transformation. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a transformation
   (an experience) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.



62.9        The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Aurobindo’s cost. If Aurobindo accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the Supermind is the highest plane of consciousness. He must accept that the First Determination
is a realm of pure unity, not a plane of consciousness. The cost is the loss of the Supermind: the
Supermind is no longer the highest plane; the structure is the highest principle. He must also
give up the claim that the transformation is the goal; he must accept that the manifestation is
the goal; the manifestation is the expression of the identity.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Aurobindo’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the Supermind, of the evolution, of the transformation—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
700                                                                         Chapter 62. Aurobindo


identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the Supermind, and the framework leaves the
Supermind to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Aurobindo’s Supermind
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Aurobindo must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition
that the Supermind presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


62.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Au-
   robindo’s term “the Supermind.” If one substitutes “the Supermind” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the Supermind is the highest
   plane of consciousness, and it is not manifested, because it is the source. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; the Supermind is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Aurobindo’s term “the evolution.”
   If one substitutes “the evolution” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the evolution is
   the ascent from the lower to the higher. The framework’s expression is structural; the
   evolution is evolutionary. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Aurobindo’s term “the
   transformation.” If one substitutes “the transformation” for “reconstruction” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a
   reading of the manifestations; the transformation is the divinization of the world. The
   framework’s reconstruction is mediated; the transformation is immediate. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Aurobindo is resemblance:
   both hold that the world is real, and they differ on whether the world is the expression of
   the divine or the expression of the identity. Both hold that there is a process, and they differ
   on whether the process is the evolution of consciousness or the enactment of the structure.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Aurobindo would be refuted by showing that Aurobindo’s Supermind cannot be
   formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and consciousness—by
   showing, that is, that Aurobindo already distinguishes the structural condition from the
62.11. Open Questions                                                                       701


   consciousness, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Aurobindo’s own.



62.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Aurobindo’s Supermind, or is it a
departure from Aurobindo? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Aurobindo’s Supermind is already a structural condition,
not a plane of consciousness, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of The Life Divine and The Synthesis of Yoga
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the integral yoga, the Supermind, the evolution of
consciousness, the ascent and the descent, the transformation of the human being, the planes of
consciousness, and the goal of the supramental transformation, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a consciousness and a structure—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the consciousness that evolves, or the structure that persists? Is the
truth the transformation that divinizes, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between Aurobindo’s Supermind and the framework’s identity?

Part VIII is now complete. The dialogues with the six great figures of Indian philosophy—the
Upanishads, Samkhya and Yoga, Nyaya and Vaisheshika, Shankara, Ramanuja, and Aurobindo—
have been stated. Part IX turns to Buddhist and Jain philosophy. The first dialogue is with
Nagarjuna, on emptiness and the middle way; the next with Yogacara, on consciousness-only; the
next with Buddhist logic, on inference and the criteria of truth; and the last with Jainism, on the
many-sidedness of reality. The Indian tradition has asked what the self is, and what the absolute
is; the Buddhist tradition will ask whether the self is real, and whether the absolute is empty.

Chapter 63

Nāgārjuna


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE), the founder of the
Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism, known in the tradition as the Second Buddha and in
the West as the philosopher of emptiness. It states Nāgārjuna’s doctrine of dependent origination
(pratı̄tyasamutpāda), his identification of dependent origination with emptiness (śūnyatā) and
with the middle way (madhyamā-pratipad), his critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the
tetralemma (catus.kot.i) and the fourfold negation, and the doctrine of the two truths (satya-
dvaya), with reference to the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (Fundamental Verses on the Middle
Way), the Vigrahavyāvartanı̄ (Refutation of Objections), the Śūnyatāsaptati (Seventy Verses
on Emptiness), and the Ratnāvalı̄ (Precious Garland); it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of Nāgārjuna; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of identity and manifestation is the nearest Buddhist analogue to
Nāgārjuna’s emptiness and dependent origination; it presents the objections that Nāgārjuna
would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side
costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of
“emptiness,” “dependent origination,” “intrinsic nature,” “the middle way,” “the two truths,” or
“the tetralemma,” these are Nāgārjuna’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the
interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


63.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a chariot. She sees the wheels, the axle, the pole, the reins,
the body. She asks: what is the chariot? Is it the wheels? No, the wheels are not the chariot. Is
it the axle? No. Is it the body? No. Is it the collection of the parts? The collection is not the
chariot; the chariot is not the collection. Is the chariot something other than the parts? If it
were other than the parts, it could not be found among the parts; but it is found among the
parts, and nowhere else. The chariot is not the parts, and it is not other than the parts. It is a
dependent designation (prajñapti): it is designated in dependence on the parts, and it has no
intrinsic nature of its own.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the chariot is, but what anything is.
A pot is not the clay; a cloth is not the threads; a person is not the aggregates. Every thing is
dependent on its parts, and every part is dependent on its parts, and so on without end. Nothing
is found that has intrinsic nature (svabhāva); nothing is found that exists in itself, by itself,
independently. Everything is empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature. Emptiness is not nothingness; it
is the absence of intrinsic nature. The thing exists conventionally, as a dependent designation; it
does not exist ultimately, as an intrinsic nature.

                                                704
63.2. The Question                                                                                 705


   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the chariot is, or what
anything is, but what the middle way is. The middle way is the way between eternalism and
nihilism. Eternalism holds that things exist with intrinsic nature, permanently and independently.
Nihilism holds that things do not exist at all, that emptiness is nothingness. The middle way holds
that things are dependently originated: they exist conventionally, as dependent designations,
and they are empty of intrinsic nature. They are not eternal, and they are not nothing. This is
the teaching of the Buddha, and it is the teaching of Nāgārjuna.
   The scene is Nāgārjuna’s image, in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, of the structure of reality.
The chariot is the dependent designation; the parts are the dependently originated elements;
the middle way is the path between eternalism and nihilism. The scene poses the question that
Nāgārjuna was the first to pose in its full form in the Buddhist tradition. What is a thing? Does
it exist with intrinsic nature, or is it empty? And what is the middle way between existence and
non-existence? The present chapter states Nāgārjuna’s answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.


63.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the position of Aurobindo: the integral yoga, the Supermind, the
evolution of consciousness, the ascent and the descent, and the transformation of the human
being. Aurobindo is the great synthesizer of the Indian tradition; he affirms the evolution of
consciousness and the reality of the world. Nāgārjuna is the founder of the Madhyamaka, and he
is the great critic of all the schools of Indian philosophy: he critiques the substantialist ontologies
                                 . khya, and the Vedānta; he critiques the Abhidharma’s theory of
of the Nyāya-Vaiśes.ika, the Sām
dharmas; he critiques the very notion of intrinsic nature. The present chapter states Nāgārjuna’s
critique, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Nāgārjuna was right. The question is what he held, what he can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the position. What did Nāgārjuna hold? The chapter states the doctrine of
dependent origination, the identification of dependent origination with emptiness and with the
middle way, the critique of intrinsic nature, the tetralemma and the fourfold negation, and the
doctrine of the two truths, with reference to the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Nāgārjuna converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Nāgārjuna would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Nāgārjuna?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.
