706                                                                         Chapter 63. Nāgārjuna


63.3.1      Dependent Origination (Pratı̄tyasamutpāda)

Nāgārjuna’s doctrine of dependent origination is stated in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, especially
in the first chapter and in the twenty-fourth chapter. The doctrine is the foundation of Nāgārjuna’s
philosophy; it is the teaching that all things arise in dependence on conditions, and that nothing
arises independently.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the arising in dependence. All things arise in dependence on conditions;
nothing arises from itself, from another, from both, or from no cause. The sprout arises in
dependence on the seed, the soil, the water, the sunlight; the seed arises in dependence on the
plant, the flower, the fruit. The chain of conditions is without beginning; there is no first cause;
there is no self-caused being.


Second feature: the absence of intrinsic nature. Because things arise in dependence on
conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Intrinsic nature is what a thing would have if it
existed in itself, by itself, independently of all conditions. Nothing has such a nature; everything
is dependently originated; everything is empty of intrinsic nature.


Third feature: the conventional existence. The absence of intrinsic nature does not mean
the absence of existence. Things exist conventionally; they are dependently designated; they are
effective; they arise and pass away; they cause and are caused. The conventional existence is
real; the ultimate existence is empty. The two are not contradictory; they are the two truths.

   From the Tradition

   “Whatever arises dependently, that we declare to be emptiness. That is a dependent
   designation; that is the middle way.” (Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.18, trans.
   after Garfield)


63.3.2      Emptiness (Śūnyatā)

Nāgārjuna’s doctrine of emptiness is stated in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, especially in the
twenty-fourth chapter, and in the Śūnyatāsaptati. Emptiness is the absence of intrinsic nature; it
is the dependently originated character of all things.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: emptiness is not nothingness. Emptiness is not the absence of existence; it
is the absence of intrinsic nature. Things exist conventionally; they are dependently originated;
they are empty of intrinsic nature. To say that things are empty is not to say that they do not
exist; it is to say that they do not exist independently.


Second feature: emptiness is dependently originated. Emptiness itself is dependently
originated; it is not a substance; it is not a thing; it is not an intrinsic nature. Emptiness is the
63.3. The Position                                                                                707


absence of intrinsic nature, and the absence is dependently originated; it is dependent on the
things that are empty. Emptiness is empty; it is the emptiness of emptiness.


Third feature: emptiness is the middle way. Emptiness is the middle way between
eternalism and nihilism. Eternalism holds that things exist with intrinsic nature; nihilism holds
that things do not exist at all. Emptiness holds that things exist conventionally and are empty
ultimately; it avoids both extremes. The middle way is the teaching of the Buddha; it is the
teaching of Nāgārjuna.


63.3.3    The Critique of Intrinsic Nature (Svabhāva)

Nāgārjuna’s critique of intrinsic nature is stated throughout the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. The
critique is the foundation of the doctrine of emptiness; it is the diagnosis of the error of all the
substantialist schools.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the definition of intrinsic nature. Intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is what a
thing has in itself, by itself, independently of all conditions. It is the essence of the thing; it is
what makes the thing be what it is; it is what the thing would be if nothing else existed. Intrinsic
nature is the ground of the substantialist ontologies; it is what the Nyāya-Vaiśes.ika calls the
                             . khya calls the prakr.ti; it is what the Abhidharma calls the dharma.
substance; it is what the Sām


Second feature: the critique. Intrinsic nature is impossible; nothing can have it. If a thing
had intrinsic nature, it would not depend on anything; it would not arise; it would not change; it
would not cease. But everything arises, changes, and ceases; everything depends on conditions;
nothing is independent. Therefore nothing has intrinsic nature; everything is empty.


Third feature: the consequence. The critique of intrinsic nature is not a nihilism; it is not
the denial of existence. It is the denial of independent existence; it is the affirmation of dependent
existence. Things exist dependently; they are empty of intrinsic nature; they are dependently
originated. The critique is the middle way between eternalism and nihilism.


63.3.4    The Tetralemma (Catus.kot.i) and the Fourfold Negation

Nāgārjuna’s tetralemma is stated in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, especially in the first chapter
and in the twenty-fifth chapter. The tetralemma is the fourfold negation: the negation of the
four alternatives.
   The tetralemma has three features.


First feature: the four alternatives. The four alternatives are: (1) the thing exists; (2) the
thing does not exist; (3) the thing both exists and does not exist; (4) the thing neither exists nor
does not exist. The four alternatives are the four possible positions on the existence of a thing;
they are the four extremes that the middle way avoids.
708                                                                           Chapter 63. Nāgārjuna


Second feature: the fourfold negation. Nāgārjuna negates all four alternatives. He does
not say that the thing exists; he does not say that it does not exist; he does not say that it both
exists and does not exist; he does not say that it neither exists nor does not exist. The fourfold
negation is not a fifth alternative; it is the negation of all the alternatives; it is the silence of the
middle way.


Third feature: the purpose of the tetralemma. The purpose of the tetralemma is not to
establish a new position; it is to destroy all positions. The tetralemma is a therapeutic device;
it is a medicine for the disease of views; it is the cure for the clinging to opinions. The one
who understands the tetralemma is freed from all views; the one who is freed from all views is
liberated.


63.3.5       The Two Truths (Satya-Dvaya)

Nāgārjuna’s doctrine of the two truths is stated in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, especially in
                                                                        . vr.ti-satya) and the
the twenty-fourth chapter. The two truths are the conventional truth (sam
ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the conventional truth. The conventional truth is the truth of the world; it
is the truth of the dependently originated things; it is the truth of the conventional designations.
The conventional truth is real; it is not an illusion; it is the truth of the everyday life. The
conventional truth is the truth of the chariot, the pot, the person; it is the truth of the causes
and the effects; it is the truth of the suffering and the liberation.


Second feature: the ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is the truth of emptiness; it is the
truth of the absence of intrinsic nature; it is the truth of the dependently originated character of
all things. The ultimate truth is not a thing; it is not a substance; it is not an intrinsic nature; it
is the emptiness of all things. The ultimate truth is the truth of the middle way; it is the truth
of the Buddha.


Third feature: the relation between the two truths. The two truths are not two separate
realities; they are two aspects of one reality. The conventional truth is the truth of the things
that are empty; the ultimate truth is the truth of the emptiness of the things. The two are not
contradictory; they are complementary. The one who understands the two truths understands
the middle way; the one who understands the middle way is liberated.

   From the Tradition

   “The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is based on two truths: a truth of worldly
   convention and an ultimate truth. Those who do not understand the distinction between
   these two truths do not understand the Buddha’s profound teaching.” (Nāgārjuna,
   Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.8–9, trans. after Garfield)
63.4. Internal Disputes                                                                         709


63.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Nāgārjuna is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of emptiness. The traditional reading takes emptiness to be the
ultimate truth: it is the absence of intrinsic nature; it is the dependently originated character of
all things. A revisionary reading takes emptiness to be a therapeutic device: it is a medicine for
the disease of views; it is not a truth; it is not a doctrine. The two readings disagree on whether
Nāgārjuna is a metaphysician or a therapeutic philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a real structure, not a therapeutic
device.

Second dispute: the status of the two truths. The traditional reading takes the two truths
to be two realities: the conventional reality and the ultimate reality. A revisionary reading takes
them to be two descriptions: the conventional description and the ultimate description; they are
not two realities, but two ways of describing one reality. The two readings disagree on whether
Nāgārjuna is a realist or a conventionalist about the two truths, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s realms are real levels, not descriptions.

Third dispute: the status of the tetralemma. The traditional reading takes the tetralemma
to be a logical device: it is the fourfold negation; it is the negation of all the alternatives. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a mystical silence: it is the silence of the middle way; it is
the ineffable. The two readings disagree on whether Nāgārjuna is a logician or a mystic, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s method is a
structural reconstruction, not a logical negation or a mystical silence.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Nāgārjuna is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of emptiness. If
Nāgārjuna is a therapeutic philosopher, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism
and a therapeutic philosophy. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the
Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a
way that is compatible with either reading.


63.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Nāgārjuna. The framework shares four structural features with Nāgārjuna’s
   position.

       1. The rejection of intrinsic nature. Nāgārjuna holds that nothing has intrinsic nature;
          everything is empty of intrinsic nature; everything is dependently originated. The
          framework holds that identity is not a substance; it is not an intrinsic nature; it is
          the invariance enacted by one source, and the enactment is a structural tendency.
710                                                                          Chapter 63. Nāgārjuna


          Both reject the substantialist ontologies; both reject the notion of a self-existent
          thing.

       2. The reality of the conventional. Nāgārjuna holds that the conventional truth is real;
          the dependently originated things are real; they are effective; they arise and pass
          away. The framework holds that the manifestation is real; it is the appearance of
          the identity in a realm; it is not an illusion. Both hold that the conventional reality
          is real, and that it is not to be dismissed.

       3. The middle way. Nāgārjuna holds that the middle way is between eternalism and
          nihilism; it is the way of dependent origination. The framework holds that the
          middle way is between the substantialism of the tradition and the nihilism of the
          deconstruction; it is the way of the structural realism. Both hold that the middle
          way is the path, and that it avoids the extremes.

       4. The two truths. Nāgārjuna holds that there are two truths: the conventional truth and
          the ultimate truth. The framework holds that there are two levels: the manifestation
          and the identity; the manifestation is the conventional level; the identity is the
          ultimate level. Both hold that there are two levels, and that the two are related.



63.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Nāgārjuna. The framework diverges from Nāgārjuna in four respects.

       1. The status of emptiness. Nāgārjuna holds that emptiness is the absence of intrinsic
          nature; it is the ultimate truth; it is the dependently originated character of all things.
          The framework holds that the identity is not emptiness; it is the invariance enacted
          by one source; it is the structural condition of the manifestation. The framework’s
          identity is not empty; it is real; it is the structure that the manifestations exhibit.

       2. The status of the two truths. Nāgārjuna holds that the two truths are the conventional
          and the ultimate; the ultimate truth is emptiness. The framework holds that the
          two levels are the manifestation and the identity; the identity is not emptiness; it is
          the invariance. The framework’s ultimate level is not the emptiness of all things; it
          is the structure of the identity.

       3. The status of the tetralemma. Nāgārjuna holds that the tetralemma is the fourfold
          negation; it is the negation of all the alternatives; it is the silence of the middle way.
          The framework holds that the tetralemma is not the method; the method is the
          structural reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations. The framework’s
          method is not the negation; it is the reconstruction.

       4. The status of the liberation. Nāgārjuna holds that the liberation is the cessation of
63.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                 711


         the suffering; it is the freedom from the views; it is the realization of emptiness. The
         framework holds that the liberation is not the goal; the goal is the understanding
         of the structure; it is the comprehension of the identity. The framework’s goal is
         structural, not soteriological.



63.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Nāgārjuna’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is an
   intrinsic nature; it is what a thing has in itself, by itself, independently of all conditions.
   The framework’s identity is an intrinsic nature; it is the svabhāva that Nāgārjuna refutes.
   The framework’s ontology is an ontology of intrinsic natures, not of emptiness.
   Nāgārjuna’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the levels of the intrinsic nature; they are the levels of the svabhāva. The
   framework’s realms are not levels of emptiness; they are levels of intrinsic nature. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of intrinsic natures, not of emptiness.
   Nāgārjuna’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
   is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the realization of emptiness; it is the
   freedom from the views; it is the liberation. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction
   of the intrinsic nature; it is not the realization of emptiness. The framework’s epistemology
   is an epistemology of intrinsic nature, not of emptiness.



63.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a structural invariance is not
   a substance, and it agrees that the intrinsic nature is to be rejected. But the framework
   denies that its identity is an intrinsic nature. The framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the
  *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not an intrinsic nature; it
   is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that
   condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between an intrinsic nature
  (a self-existent thing) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of intrinsic nature. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
712                                                                        Chapter 63. Nāgārjuna


   intrinsic nature. The distinction is between a level of intrinsic nature (a substantial level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the realization of
   emptiness. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a realization (an experience) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.




63.9      The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Nāgārjuna’s cost. If Nāgārjuna accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that everything is empty of intrinsic nature. He must accept that the identity is a structural
condition, and that the identity is not an intrinsic nature, but a real structure. The cost is the
loss of emptiness: the identity is no longer empty; the identity is a structural condition. He must
also give up the claim that the liberation is the goal; he must accept that the understanding is
the goal; the understanding is the comprehension of the structure.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Nāgārjuna’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of emptiness, of the two truths, of the tetralemma—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not the emptiness, and the framework leaves the emptiness to a
separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Nāgārjuna’s emptiness
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Nāgārjuna must accept that the framework’s structure is not an intrinsic nature; it is a structural
condition that emptiness presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.
63.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                    713


63.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Nāgārjuna’s term “emptiness.” If one substitutes “emptiness” for “identity” in the frame-
   work’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Nāgārjuna’s emptiness is the
   absence of intrinsic nature, and it is not manifested, because it is the absence. The
   framework’s identity is multiple; Nāgārjuna’s emptiness is one. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Nāgārjuna’s term “dependent
   origination.” If one substitutes “dependent origination” for “expression” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency;
   Nāgārjuna’s dependent origination is the arising in dependence on conditions. The
   framework’s expression is structural; Nāgārjuna’s dependent origination is conditional.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Nāgārjuna’s term “the real-
   ization of emptiness.” If one substitutes “the realization of emptiness” for “reconstruction”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction
   is a reading of the manifestations; Nāgārjuna’s realization of emptiness is the freedom
   from the views. The framework’s reconstruction is mediated; Nāgārjuna’s realization is
   immediate. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Nāgārjuna is resemblance:
   both reject the intrinsic nature, and they differ on whether the rejection leaves a structure
   or an emptiness. Both hold that the conventional is real, and they differ on whether
   the conventional is the manifestation or the dependent origination. Neither relation
   is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of
   Nāgārjuna would be refuted by showing that Nāgārjuna’s emptiness cannot be formulated
   without the framework’s distinction between structure and emptiness—by showing, that
   is, that Nāgārjuna already distinguishes the structural condition from the emptiness, and
   that the framework’s distinction is a development of Nāgārjuna’s own.




63.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Nāgārjuna’s emptiness, or is it a
departure from Nāgārjuna? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is
not conclusive. A reader who holds that Nāgārjuna’s emptiness is already a structural condition,
not an absence, has a question the chapter leaves open.
714                                                                         Chapter 63. Nāgārjuna


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā do justice to
the text? The chapter has used dependent origination, emptiness, the critique of intrinsic nature,
the tetralemma, and the two truths, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader
who holds that the text supports a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an appearance and a reality—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the appearance that is empty, or the reality that underlies? Is the truth
the emptiness that is realized, or the structure that is reconstructed? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between Nāgārjuna’s emptiness and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Yogācāra. It states the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā),
the three natures (trisvabhāva), the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), and the theory of
the āśraya-parāvr.tti (the transformation of the basis); it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of Yogācāra; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of consciousness and of the manifestation is the nearest Buddhist
analogue to Yogācāra’s. The present chapter has stated Nāgārjuna’s answer to the problem of
emptiness; the next chapter states the Yogācāra answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.

Lùn (The Demonstration of Consciousness-Only); it identifies the internal disputes within the

64.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is dreaming. In the dream, she sees a snake; her heart races; she is afraid.
The snake is not there; there is no snake in the room; there is only the mind that is dreaming
the snake. The fear is real; the snake is not. When she wakes, she sees that the snake was a
projection of the mind; the snake was consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā); it was the mind
appearing as a snake.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the dream is, or how it arises, but
what the waking world is. The waking world seems different from the dream; the objects seem
solid; the causes seem real. But the Yogācārin asks: is the waking world really different from the
dream? In the dream, the objects seemed solid; the causes seemed real; the fear was real. In
the waking world, the objects seem solid; the causes seem real; the suffering is real. What is
the difference? The difference is not in the structure of the experience; the difference is in the
stability and the intersubjectivity of the experience. The waking world is a stable, intersubjective
projection of the storehouse consciousness; the dream is an unstable, private projection of the
storehouse consciousness. Both are consciousness-only; both are projections of the mind.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the dream is, or what
the waking world is, but what the mind is. The mind is not a single thing; it is a stream

                                                715
716                                                                           Chapter 64. Yogācāra


of consciousness; it is a series of moments; it is a flow of projections. The mind has eight
consciousnesses: the five sense consciousnesses, the mind consciousness (mano-vijñāna), the
defiled mind consciousness (klis..ta-manas), and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). The
storehouse consciousness is the foundation; it is the reservoir of the seeds (bı̄ja) that project the
world; it is the ground of the three natures; it is the basis of the transformation of the basis
(āśraya-parāvr.tti). The transformation of the basis is the goal; it is the turning of the storehouse
consciousness from the defiled to the pure; it is the realization of the three bodies of the Buddha.
                                                   . śikā and in the Chéng Wéishì Lùn, of the
      The scene is the Yogācāra image, in the Trim
structure of reality. The dream is the projection; the waking world is the stable projection; the
mind is the stream of consciousness. The scene poses the question that the Yogācāra was the first
to pose in its full form in the Buddhist tradition. What is consciousness? What is the world?
And what is the relation between the two? The present chapter states the Yogācāra answer, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.



64.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated Nāgārjuna’s position: dependent origination, emptiness, the critique
of intrinsic nature, the tetralemma, and the two truths. Nāgārjuna is the founder of the
Madhyamaka, and he is the great critic of all the substantialist ontologies. Yogācāra is the other
great school of Mahāyāna Buddhism, and it is the great systematic philosophy of consciousness:
it affirms the reality of consciousness, the consciousness-only doctrine, and the three natures.
The present chapter states the Yogācāra position, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Yogācāra was right. The question is what it held, what it can
say to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts, and
the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Yogācāra hold? The chapter states the doctrine of
consciousness-only, the three natures, the storehouse consciousness, the seven consciousnesses,
                                                                                . śikā, the Vim
the transformation of the basis, and the three bodies, with reference to the Trim              . śikā,
and the Chéng Wéishì Lùn.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Yogācāra converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Yogācāra would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Yogācāra?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.



64.3       The Position
64.3. The Position                                                                                717


64.3.1    Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātratā)

                                                                  . śikā and in the Vim
The Yogācāra doctrine of consciousness-only is stated in the Trim                    . śikā of
Vasubandhu, and in the Chéng Wéishì Lùn. The doctrine is the foundation of the Yogācāra
philosophy; it is the teaching that the world is a projection of consciousness, and that there is no
external object apart from the consciousness that projects it.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the projection. The world is a projection of consciousness; the objects are
not external; they are the appearances of the consciousness. The consciousness projects the
world; the world is the projection; the two are not separate. The projection is not a creation
from nothing; it is the self-manifestation of the consciousness; it is the consciousness appearing
as the world.


Second feature: the absence of external objects. There are no external objects; there is
no world apart from the consciousness; there is no matter apart from the mind. The objects that
seem external are the projections of the storehouse consciousness; they are the seeds that ripen
into the appearances. The absence of external objects is the meaning of consciousness-only; it is
the rejection of the subject-object duality.


Third feature: the reality of consciousness. The consciousness is real; it is not empty; it
is the ground of the projection. The consciousness is not a substance; it is a stream; it is a flow;
it is a series of moments. The consciousness is the only reality; the world is its projection; the
two are not separate.

   From the Tradition

   “There is no external object; there is only consciousness. The world is a projection of
                                                                                  . śikā 1,
   consciousness; it is the consciousness appearing as the world.” (Vasubandhu, Vim
   trans. after Anacker)



64.3.2    The Three Natures (Trisvabhāva)

                                                                 . śikā and in the Madhyāntavibhāga.
The Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures is stated in the Trim
The three natures are the three aspects of the projected world; they are the three ways the
consciousness appears.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva). The imagined nature is the
nature that the world seems to have; it is the nature of the external object; it is the nature of the
subject-object duality. The imagined nature is not real; it is the projection of the consciousness;
it is the appearance that the consciousness takes for reality.
718                                                                           Chapter 64. Yogācāra


Second feature: the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). The dependent nature is
the nature that the world actually has; it is the nature of the dependently originated projection;
it is the nature of the stream of consciousness. The dependent nature is real; it is the flow of the
consciousness; it is the ground of the imagined nature.


Third feature: the perfected nature (parinis.panna-svabhāva). The perfected nature is
the nature that the world has when it is seen as it is; it is the nature of the emptiness of the
imagined nature; it is the nature of the consciousness-only. The perfected nature is the goal; it is
the realization of the emptiness; it is the transformation of the basis.


64.3.3      The Storehouse Consciousness (Ālayavijñāna)

                                                                            . śikā and in the Chéng
The Yogācāra doctrine of the storehouse consciousness is stated in the Trim
Wéishì Lùn. The storehouse consciousness is the eighth consciousness; it is the foundation of the
other seven; it is the reservoir of the seeds.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the reservoir. The storehouse consciousness is the reservoir of the seeds (bı̄ja);
it is the storehouse of the impressions; it is the ground of the projections. The seeds are the
latent tendencies; they are the traces of the past experiences; they ripen into the appearances.
The storehouse consciousness is the foundation of the world; it is the ground of the three natures.


Second feature: the ripening. The storehouse consciousness ripens into the appearances; it
projects the world; it manifests the objects. The ripening is not a creation; it is the maturation
of the seeds; it is the unfolding of the latent tendencies. The ripening is the process of the
projection; it is the process of the consciousness-only.


Third feature: the transformation. The storehouse consciousness is transformed by the
practice; it is turned from the defiled to the pure; it is the basis of the transformation of the basis.
The transformation is the goal; it is the realization of the perfected nature; it is the attainment
of the three bodies.


64.3.4      The Seven Consciousnesses

                                                                         . śikā and in the Chéng
The Yogācāra doctrine of the seven consciousnesses is stated in the Trim
Wéishì Lùn. The seven consciousnesses are the five sense consciousnesses, the mind consciousness,
and the defiled mind consciousness.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the five sense consciousnesses. The five sense consciousnesses are the con-
sciousnesses of the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body. They are the consciousnesses
that perceive the external objects; they are the consciousnesses that arise in dependence on the
senses and the objects. They are the surface consciousnesses; they are the consciousnesses of the
everyday experience.
64.4. Internal Disputes                                                                           719


Second feature: the mind consciousness (mano-vijñāna). The mind consciousness is the
sixth consciousness; it is the consciousness that organizes the sense data; it is the consciousness
that thinks, imagines, and remembers. The mind consciousness is the consciousness of the
concepts; it is the consciousness of the internal world.


Third feature: the defiled mind consciousness (klis..ta-manas). The defiled mind
consciousness is the seventh consciousness; it is the consciousness that clings to the self; it is the
consciousness that takes the storehouse consciousness for the self. The defiled mind consciousness
is the source of the ego; it is the source of the suffering; it is the source of the clinging.


64.3.5    The Transformation of the Basis (Āśraya-Parāvr.tti)

                                                                               . śikā and in the
The Yogācāra doctrine of the transformation of the basis is stated in the Trim
Chéng Wéishì Lùn. The transformation of the basis is the goal of the Yogācāra path; it is the
turning of the storehouse consciousness from the defiled to the pure.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the turning. The turning is the transformation of the basis; it is the turning
of the storehouse consciousness from the defiled to the pure. The turning is not a destruction; it
is a transformation; it is the purification of the seeds; it is the ripening of the pure seeds.


Second feature: the realization. The realization is the realization of the perfected nature; it
is the realization of the emptiness of the imagined nature; it is the realization of the consciousness-
only. The realization is the goal; it is the liberation; it is the freedom from the suffering.


Third feature: the three bodies. The three bodies are the three aspects of the Buddha;
they are the three aspects of the realization. The three bodies are the dharmakāya (the truth
body), the sambhogakāya (the enjoyment body), and the nirmān.akāya (the emanation body).
The three bodies are the realization of the transformation of the basis; they are the fruit of the
path.

   From the Tradition

   “The transformation of the basis is the turning of the storehouse consciousness from the
   defiled to the pure; it is the realization of the perfected nature; it is the attainment of the
                                  . śikā 29–30, trans. after Anacker)
   three bodies.” (Vasubandhu, Trim



64.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Yogācāra is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of consciousness-only. The traditional reading takes consciousness-
only to be a metaphysical doctrine: there are no external objects; there is only consciousness;
the world is a projection. A revisionary reading takes it to be a phenomenological doctrine: it
720                                                                          Chapter 64. Yogācāra


is a description of the structure of experience; it is not a denial of the external world; it is the
recognition that the world is experienced through the consciousness. The two readings disagree
on whether Yogācāra is a metaphysics or a phenomenology, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a projection.

Second dispute: the status of the three natures. The traditional reading takes the three
natures to be three realities: the imagined nature, the dependent nature, and the perfected
nature. A revisionary reading takes them to be three descriptions: the descriptions of the same
experience from three perspectives. The two readings disagree on whether Yogācāra is a realism
or a conventionalism, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s realms are real levels, not descriptions.

Third dispute: the status of the storehouse consciousness. The traditional reading
takes the storehouse consciousness to be a real entity: it is the eighth consciousness; it is the
reservoir of the seeds; it is the ground of the projections. A revisionary reading takes it to be a
theoretical construct: it is a way of explaining the continuity of the karmic traces; it is not a
real entity. The two readings disagree on whether Yogācāra is a realism or a conceptualism, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is a
structural condition, not a theoretical construct.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Yogācāra is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of consciousness. If
Yogācāra is a phenomenologist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
                                                                              . śikā, but it does
phenomenology. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Trim
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


64.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Yogācāra. The framework shares four structural features with the Yogācāra
   position.

        1. The rejection of the subject-object duality. Yogācāra holds that there is no external
           object apart from the consciousness; the object is the projection of the consciousness;
           the subject and the object are not two separate things. The framework holds that the
           manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm; the manifestation is not a
           separate thing; it is the expression of the identity. Both reject the subject-object
           duality; both hold that the world is a manifestation.

        2. The reality of consciousness. Yogācāra holds that the consciousness is real; it is
           the ground of the projection; it is the only reality. The framework holds that the
           identity is real; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the ground of the
           manifestation. Both hold that there is a reality, and that the reality is the ground of
64.6. Points of Divergence                                                                         721


          the world.

       3. The three natures. Yogācāra holds that there are three natures: the imagined, the
          dependent, and the perfected. The framework holds that there are two levels: the
          manifestation and the identity; the manifestation is the imagined and the dependent;
          the identity is the perfected. Both hold that there are levels, and that the levels are
          related.

       4. The transformation. Yogācāra holds that the goal is the transformation of the
          basis; it is the turning of the storehouse consciousness from the defiled to the pure.
          The framework holds that the goal is the understanding of the structure; it is the
          reconstruction of the identity from the manifestations. Both hold that there is a
          goal, and that the goal is the transformation.




64.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Yogācāra. The framework diverges from the Yogācāra position in four respects.

       1. The status of consciousness. Yogācāra holds that the consciousness is the only reality;
          the world is its projection; there is no external object. The framework holds that
          the identity is not the consciousness; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is
          the structural condition of the manifestation. The framework’s identity is not the
          consciousness; it is the structure.

       2. The status of the world. Yogācāra holds that the world is a projection of consciousness;
          it is not external; it is not real in the way that consciousness is real. The framework
          holds that the manifestation is real; it is the appearance of the identity in a realm;
          it is not a projection. The framework’s manifestation is real, not a projection.

       3. The status of the storehouse consciousness. Yogācāra holds that the storehouse
          consciousness is the reservoir of the seeds; it is the ground of the projections. The
          framework holds that the identity is the ground of the manifestations; there is no
          storehouse consciousness; there is the structural condition. The framework’s identity
          is structural, not a reservoir.

       4. The status of the transformation. Yogācāra holds that the transformation of the
          basis is the goal; it is the turning of the storehouse consciousness from the defiled to
          the pure. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the goal; it is the reading
          of the manifestations; it is not the transformation of the basis. The framework’s
          goal is structural, not transformative.
722                                                                       Chapter 64. Yogācāra


64.7       The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Yogācāra’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  not a consciousness; it is a pattern. The world is a projection of consciousness; the world
  is not just structured; the world is a projection. The framework has no consciousness; the
  framework has no projection; the framework’s world is a world without the consciousness.
  The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of consciousness.
  Yogācāra’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
  levels; they are the levels of the projection; they are the levels of the consciousness. The
  framework’s realms are not levels of the projection; they are just levels. The framework’s
  ontology is an ontology of levels, not of consciousness.
  Yogācāra’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the transformation of the basis;
  it is the turning of the storehouse consciousness; it is the realization of the three bodies.
  The framework’s knowledge is a mediation; it is not the transformation. The framework’s
  epistemology is an epistemology of mediation, not of transformation.



64.8       The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the world is a projection
  of consciousness, and it agrees that the consciousness is real. But the framework denies
  that the consciousness must be the fundamental reality. The framework’s identity is the
  structural condition of the projection; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the
  structural condition under which the projection is what it is. The distinction is between a
  consciousness (a projection) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework holds
  the second, not the first. The framework does not deny the consciousness; it denies that
  the consciousness is the only principle.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
  levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
  that the realms are levels of the projection. The framework’s realms are ontological levels;
  they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
  projection. The distinction is between a level of the projection (a consciousness level) and
  a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the
  first.
  Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
  conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
64.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                       723


   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the transformation
   of the basis. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a transformation (a turning) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.



64.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Yogācāra’s cost. If Yogācāra accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the
consciousness is the only reality. It must accept that the identity is the structural condition, and
that the consciousness is a projection of the identity. The cost is the loss of the consciousness-only:
the consciousness is no longer the only reality; the identity is the structural condition. It must
also give up the claim that the transformation of the basis is the goal; it must accept that the
reconstruction is the knowledge; the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Yogācāra’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the consciousness, of the projection, of the transformation—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the consciousness, and the framework leaves the
consciousness to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Yogācāra’s consciousness
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Yogācāra must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition
that the consciousness presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the
simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete
without the other.


64.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Yogācāra’s term “the storehouse consciousness.” If one substitutes “the storehouse con-
   sciousness” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a
   realm; the storehouse consciousness is the reservoir of the seeds, and it is not manifested,
   because it is the ground of the projections. The framework’s identity is multiple; the
724                                                                        Chapter 64. Yogācāra


   storehouse consciousness is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Yogācāra’s term “the projection.”
   If one substitutes “the projection” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the projection
   is the appearance of the consciousness. The framework’s expression is structural; the
   projection is conscious. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Yogācāra’s term “the
   transformation of the basis.” If one substitutes “the transformation of the basis” for
   “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the transformation of the basis is the
   turning of the storehouse consciousness. The framework’s reconstruction is mediated;
   the transformation of the basis is immediate. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Yogācāra is resemblance:
   both reject the subject-object duality, and they differ on whether the world is a projection
   or a manifestation. Both hold that there is a reality, and they differ on whether the reality
   is the consciousness or the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Yogācāra would be refuted by showing that
   Yogācāra’s consciousness cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between
   structure and consciousness—by showing, that is, that Yogācāra already distinguishes
   the structural condition from the consciousness, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of Yogācāra’s own.



64.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Yogācāra’s consciousness, or is it
a departure from Yogācāra? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Yogācāra’s consciousness is already a structural
condition, not a projection, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a consciousness and a structure—a person, a tradition,
a work of art. Is the thing the consciousness that projects, or the structure that persists? Is
the truth the transformation of the basis, or the reconstruction of the manifestations? What
does your answer tell you about the relation between Yogācāra’s consciousness-only and the
framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Buddhist Logic. It states the account of perception (pratyaks.a) and
inference (anumāna), the theory of the svabhāva-hetu and the kārya-hetu, the doctrine of the
apoha (exclusion), and the criteria of truth (pramān.a); it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of Buddhist Logic; and it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of logic and of the criteria of truth is the nearest Buddhist
analogue to Buddhist Logic. The present chapter has stated the Yogācāra answer to the problem
of consciousness; the next chapter states the Buddhist Logic answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.

Buddhist Logic


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with the Buddhist logico-epistemological school, founded
by Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE) and developed by Dharmakı̄rti (c. 600–660 CE), and known in the
tradition as the school of valid cognition (pramān.a). It states the account of the two means
of knowledge (pramān.a)—perception (pratyaks.a) and inference (anumāna)—, the theory of
the three kinds of logical reason (liṅga), the doctrine of exclusion (apoha), the account of the
svalaks.an.a (the particular) and the sāmānyalaks.an.a (the universal), and the critique of the realist
theories of universals, with reference to the Pramān.asamuccaya of Dignāga, the Pramān.avārttika
                                                     . graha of Śāntaraks.ita; it identifies the
and the Nyāyabindu of Dharmakı̄rti, and the Tattvasam
internal disputes within the interpretation of Buddhist Logic; it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of logic and of the criteria of truth is the
nearest Buddhist analogue to Buddhist Logic; it presents the objections that the school would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading.
It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “perception,”
“inference,” “exclusion,” “the particular,” “the universal,” or “valid cognition,” these are the
school’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the
framework.


65.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a fire on a distant hill. She sees the smoke; she does not
see the fire; but she infers the fire from the smoke. The inference is not a perception; it is not a
testimony; it is not a comparison; it is an inference. The inference has a structure: there is a
reason (the smoke), there is a conclusion (the fire), and there is an invariable connection between
the two (where there is smoke, there is fire). The inference is valid because the connection is
invariable; it is invalid if the connection is not invariable.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the inference is, or how it works, but
what the perception is. The perception is the cognition that arises from the contact between
the senses and the objects; it is the direct cognition; it is the cognition of the particular. The
perception is not the inference; the perception is not the concept; the perception is the pure
sensation, before the conceptualization. The perception is the foundation of the inference; it is
the source of the empirical knowledge.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the inference is, or
what the perception is, but what the universal is. The universal is not a real thing; it is not
a substance; it is not a property that exists in the particulars. The universal is an exclusion
(apoha); it is the exclusion of the other; it is the determination of the particular by the negation

                                                  726
65.2. The Question                                                                              727


of what it is not. The word “cow” does not refer to a real universal cow; it refers to the exclusion
of the non-cow. The universal is a construction of the mind; it is not a reality in the world. This
is the doctrine of apoha: the universal is the exclusion.
   The scene is the Buddhist Logic image, in the Pramān.asamuccaya and in the Pramān.avārttika,
of the structure of knowledge. The smoke is the reason; the fire is the conclusion; the perception
is the particular; the universal is the exclusion. The scene poses the question that the Buddhist
Logic was the first to pose in its full form in the Buddhist tradition. What is knowledge? What
are the means of knowledge? And what is the relation between the particular and the universal?
The present chapter states the Buddhist Logic answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.


65.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated the Yogācāra position: consciousness-only, the three natures, the
storehouse consciousness, the seven consciousnesses, the transformation of the basis, and the
three bodies. Yogācāra is the great systematic philosophy of consciousness; it affirms the reality
of consciousness, the consciousness-only doctrine, and the three natures. Buddhist Logic is the
great systematic philosophy of knowledge; it affirms the two means of knowledge, the theory of
inference, and the doctrine of exclusion. The present chapter states the Buddhist Logic position,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Buddhist Logic was right. The question is what it held, what it
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Buddhist Logic hold? The chapter states the two means
of knowledge, the theory of the three kinds of logical reason, the doctrine of exclusion, the
account of the particular and the universal, and the critique of the realist theories of universals,
with reference to the Pramān.asamuccaya, the Pramān.avārttika, and the Nyāyabindu.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Buddhist Logic converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Buddhist Logic would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Buddhist
Logic? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.


65.3     The Position

65.3.1                                      . a)
          The Two Means of Knowledge (Pramān

The Buddhist Logic account of the two means of knowledge is stated in the Pramān.asamuccaya of
Dignāga and in the Pramān.avārttika of Dharmakı̄rti. The two means are perception (pratyaks.a)
and inference (anumāna).
728                                                                  Chapter 65. Buddhist Logic


      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: perception (pratyaks.a). Perception is the cognition that arises from the
contact between the senses and the objects; it is the direct cognition; it is the cognition of
the particular (svalaks.an.a). Perception is free from conceptualization (kalpanā); it is the pure
sensation; it is the given. Perception is the foundation of the other means; it is the source of the
empirical knowledge.


Second feature: inference (anumāna). Inference is the cognition that arises from the
knowledge of the invariable connection (vyāpti) between the reason (liṅga) and the conclusion
(sādhya). Inference is conceptual; it is the cognition of the universal (sāmānyalaks.an.a); it is
the cognition of the general from the particular. Inference is the foundation of the rational
knowledge.


Third feature: the exclusion of the third means. Buddhist Logic admits only two means
of knowledge; it rejects the other means that the Nyāya admits. It rejects comparison (upamāna),
because comparison is a kind of inference; it rejects testimony (śabda), because testimony is a
kind of inference; it rejects presumption (arthāpatti), because presumption is a kind of inference.
The two means are the only means; the other means are reducible to the two.

   From the Tradition

   “The means of knowledge are two: perception and inference. Perception is the cognition
   of the particular, free from conceptualization. Inference is the cognition of the universal,
   through the invariable connection.” (Dignāga, Pramān.asamuccaya 1.2–3, trans. after
   Hattori)



65.3.2      The Three Kinds of Logical Reason (Liṅga)

The Buddhist Logic theory of the three kinds of logical reason is stated in the Nyāyabindu of
Dharmakı̄rti. The three kinds are the three ways the reason is connected to the conclusion.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: the identity reason (svabhāva-hetu). The identity reason is the reason
that is identical with the conclusion; it is the reason that is the same nature as the conclusion.
The reason “it is a tree” proves the conclusion “it is a plant,” because being a tree is identical
with being a plant; the tree is a kind of plant.


Second feature: the effect reason (kārya-hetu). The effect reason is the reason that is the
effect of the conclusion; it is the reason that is produced by the conclusion. The reason “there
is smoke” proves the conclusion “there is fire,” because smoke is the effect of fire; the smoke is
produced by the fire.
65.3. The Position                                                                               729


Third feature: the non-perception reason (anupalabdhi-hetu). The non-perception
reason is the reason that is the absence of the perception of the conclusion; it is the reason that
is the non-apprehension of the conclusion. The reason “there is no pot” proves the conclusion
“there is no pot on the table,” because the pot is not perceived; the non-perception of the pot is
the reason for the non-existence of the pot.


65.3.3    The Doctrine of Exclusion (Apoha)

The Buddhist Logic doctrine of exclusion is stated in the Pramān.asamuccaya and in the
Pramān.avārttika. The doctrine is the account of the universal; it is the account of the meaning
of the word.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the universal is not real. The universal is not a real thing; it is not a
substance; it is not a property that exists in the particulars. The universal is a construction of
the mind; it is a concept; it is a determination of the particular. The realist schools (Nyāya,
                  . sā) hold that the universal is real; the Buddhist Logic holds that the universal
Vaiśes.ika, Mı̄mām
is not real.


Second feature: the universal is the exclusion. The universal is the exclusion (apoha); it
is the exclusion of the other; it is the determination of the particular by the negation of what it
is not. The word “cow” does not refer to a real universal cow; it refers to the exclusion of the
non-cow. The universal is the negative determination; it is the exclusion of the other.


Third feature: the two levels of meaning. The word has two levels of meaning: the direct
meaning (śakya) and the indirect meaning (lāks.an.ika). The direct meaning is the exclusion; the
word directly refers to the exclusion; the word indirectly refers to the particular. The word “cow”
directly refers to the exclusion of the non-cow; it indirectly refers to the particular cow. The two
levels are the two aspects of the meaning.

          The Particular (Svalaks.an                                      . a)
The Buddhist Logic account of the particular and the universal is stated in the Pramān.asamuccaya
and in the Nyāyabindu. The account is the foundation of the epistemology; it is the key to the
two means of knowledge.
   The account has three features.

Third feature: the relation between the two. The relation between the particular and
