not separate; they are the two aspects of the knowledge.


65.3.5       The Critique of the Realist Theories of Universals

The Buddhist Logic critique of the realist theories of universals is stated in the Pramān.asamuccaya
and in the Pramān.avārttika. The critique is the foundation of the doctrine of exclusion; it is the
diagnosis of the error of the realist schools.
      The critique has three features.


First feature: the critique of the real universal. The realist schools hold that the universal
is real; it is a substance; it is a property that exists in the particulars. The Buddhist Logic
responds: the universal is not real; it is not a substance; it is not a property. If the universal were
real, it would be either identical with the particular or different from the particular. If it were
identical, it would not be universal; it would be particular. If it were different, it would not be in
the particular; it would be separate. The universal is neither identical nor different; it is not real.


Second feature: the critique of the relation of inherence. The realist schools hold
that the universal inheres in the particular; it is connected to the particular by the relation of
inherence (samavāya). The Buddhist Logic responds: the relation of inherence is not real; it is
not perceived; it is not inferred. The relation of inherence is a construction; it is a concept; it is
not a reality. The universal is not connected to the particular by inherence; it is the exclusion of
the other.


Third feature: the critique of the word. The realist schools hold that the word refers to
the real universal; the word “cow” refers to the real universal cow. The Buddhist Logic responds:
the word does not refer to the real universal; it refers to the exclusion of the non-cow. The
word is a construction; it is a convention; it is not a reality. The word does not reveal the real
universal; it reveals the exclusion.



65.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Buddhist Logic is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
65.5. Points of Convergence                                                                        731


First dispute: the status of perception. The traditional reading takes perception to be
the pure sensation: it is free from conceptualization; it is the given; it is the real. A revisionary
reading takes perception to be the structured experience: it is not free from conceptualization;
it is the result of the construction; it is not the given. The two readings disagree on whether
Buddhist Logic is a foundationalism or a coherentism, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s knowledge is reconstruction, not a given.


Second dispute: the status of the exclusion. The traditional reading takes the exclusion
to be the meaning of the word: it is the determination of the particular by the negation of what it
is not. A revisionary reading takes the exclusion to be the process of the cognition: it is the way
the mind grasps the particular; it is not the meaning of the word. The two readings disagree on
whether Buddhist Logic is a semantic theory or a cognitive theory, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not an exclusion.


Third dispute: the status of the particular. The traditional reading takes the particular
to be the real: it is the unique thing; it is the given; it is the object of perception. A revisionary
reading takes the particular to be the limit of the concept: it is not a thing; it is the point at
which the conceptualization fails. The two readings disagree on whether Buddhist Logic is a
realism or a conceptualism, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because
the framework’s identity is a structural condition, not a limit of the concept.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Buddhist Logic is a foundationalism, the
framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a foundationalist
epistemology. If Buddhist Logic is a coherentism, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural
realism and a coherentist epistemology. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to
the Pramān.asamuccaya, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a
way that is compatible with either reading.


65.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Buddhist Logic. The framework shares four structural features with the Buddhist
   Logic position.

       1. The rejection of the real universal. Buddhist Logic holds that the universal is not real;
          it is the exclusion; it is the construction. The framework holds that identity is not a
          universal; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition.
          Both reject the real universal; both hold that the universal is a construction.

       2. The reality of the particular. Buddhist Logic holds that the particular is real; it is the
          unique thing; it is the object of perception. The framework holds that the identity is
          real; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the particular. Both hold that
          the particular is real, and that the particular is the foundation of the knowledge.
732                                                                    Chapter 65. Buddhist Logic


       3. The structure of inference. Buddhist Logic holds that the inference has a structure:
          the reason, the conclusion, and the invariable connection between the two. The
          framework holds that the reconstruction has a structure: the manifestations, the
          identity, and the structural relation between the two. Both hold that there is a
          structure, and that the structure is the condition of knowledge.

       4. The critique of the realist theories. Buddhist Logic holds that the realist theories of
          universals are mistaken; the universal is not real; it is the exclusion. The framework
          holds that the realist theories of identity are mistaken; the identity is not a substance;
          it is the invariance. Both critique the realist theories; both hold that the reality is
          not the universal.




65.6      Points of Divergence


  Points of Divergence

  With Buddhist Logic. The framework diverges from the Buddhist Logic position in
  four respects.

       1. The status of perception. Buddhist Logic holds that perception is the pure sensation;
          it is free from conceptualization; it is the given. The framework holds that perception
          is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is not the given. The
          framework’s perception is structural, not given.

       2. The status of the universal. Buddhist Logic holds that the universal is the exclusion;
          it is the construction; it is not real. The framework holds that the identity is the
          invariance; it is the structure; it is real. The framework’s identity is real, not an
          exclusion.

       3. The status of the particular. Buddhist Logic holds that the particular is the unique
          thing; it is the given; it is the object of perception. The framework holds that
          the identity is the particular; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the
          structural condition. The framework’s identity is structural, not given.

       4. The status of the two means. Buddhist Logic holds that there are two means of
          knowledge: perception and inference. The framework holds that there is one means:
          the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is not perception or
          inference. The framework’s knowledge is structural, not two means.
65.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                733


65.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Buddhist Logic’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not a particular; it is a pattern. The particular is the unique thing; it is
   the given; it is the object of perception. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a
   pattern is not a particular. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of
   particulars.
   Buddhist Logic’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms;
   the realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the levels of the exclusion; they are the levels of the construction. The
   framework’s realms are not levels of the exclusion; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of exclusion.
   Buddhist Logic’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruc-
   tion; it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the perception of the
   particular; it is the inference of the universal; it is the two means. The framework’s
   knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the perception or the inference. The framework’s
   epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the two means.



65.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that a pattern is not a particular,
   and it agrees that the particular is real. But the framework denies that its identity is only
   a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in
   the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
   framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is
   one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The
   distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the
   framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the exclusion. The framework’s realms are ontological levels;
   they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   exclusion. The distinction is between a level of the exclusion (a cognitive level) and a level
   of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the two means. The
734                                                                 Chapter 65. Buddhist Logic


   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a means (a source)
   and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



65.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Buddhist Logic’s cost. If Buddhist Logic accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up
the claim that there are two means of knowledge. It must accept that there is one means: the
reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations. The cost is the loss of the two means: the
perception and the inference are no longer the only means; the reconstruction is the means. It
must also give up the claim that the universal is the exclusion; it must accept that the identity
is the invariance; the identity is real, not an exclusion.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Buddhist Logic’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the perception, of the inference, of the exclusion—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not a perception, and the framework leaves the perception to a
separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Buddhist Logic’s perception
and inference are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Buddhist Logic must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern;
it is a structural condition that the perception and the inference presuppose as their condition.
The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals,
they are complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


65.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Buddhist
   Logic’s term “the particular.” If one substitutes “the particular” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the particular is the unique thing,
   and it is not manifested, because it is the given. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   the particular is multiple. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
65.11. Open Questions                                                                            735


   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Buddhist Logic’s term “the
   exclusion.” If one substitutes “the exclusion” for “expression” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the exclusion
   is the determination of the particular by the negation of what it is not. The framework’s
   expression is structural; the exclusion is conceptual. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Buddhist Logic’s term
   “the two means of knowledge.” If one substitutes “the two means of knowledge” for
   “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the two means are the perception and the
   inference. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the two means are epistemological.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Buddhist Logic is
   resemblance: both reject the real universal, and they differ on whether the rejection
   leaves a structure or an exclusion. Both hold that the particular is real, and they differ
   on whether the particular is the given or the structural condition. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Buddhist
   Logic would be refuted by showing that Buddhist Logic’s particular cannot be formulated
   without the framework’s distinction between structure and given—by showing, that is,
   that Buddhist Logic already distinguishes the structural condition from the given, and
   that the framework’s distinction is a development of Buddhist Logic’s own.



65.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Buddhist Logic’s particular, or
is it a departure from Buddhist Logic? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Buddhist Logic’s particular is already a
structural condition, not a given, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Pramān.asamuccaya and the Pramān.avārttika
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the two means, the three kinds of logical reason,
the exclusion, the particular and the universal, and the critique of the realist theories, and it
has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a particular and a universal—a person, a tradition, a
work of art. Is the thing the particular that is given, or the universal that is excluded? Is the
truth the perception that is direct, or the inference that is conceptual? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between Buddhist Logic’s particular and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Jainism. It states the doctrine of the many-sidedness of reality
(anekāntavāda), the theory of the seven-fold predication (saptabhaṅgı̄), the doctrine of the non-
absolutism (syādvāda), the theory of the karma, and the path of liberation; it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Jainism; and it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the many and of the perspectives is the nearest
Indian analogue to Jainism’s. The present chapter has stated the Buddhist Logic answer to the
problem of knowledge; the next chapter states the Jainism answer, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
Chapter 66

Jainism


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Jainism, one of the oldest living philosophical traditions
of India, founded by Mahāvı̄ra (c. 599–527 BCE), known in the tradition as the Jina (the
Conqueror) and the twenty-fourth Tı̄rthaṅkara. It states the Jain doctrine of the many-sidedness
of reality (anekāntavāda), the theory of the seven-fold predication (saptabhaṅgı̄), the doctrine
of non-absolutism (syādvāda), the doctrine of the categories (tattva), the theory of karma as
material particles, the doctrine of the soul (jı̄va) and non-soul (ajı̄va), and the path of liberation,
with reference to the Tattvārtha-sūtra of Umāsvāti, the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, the Sūtrakr.tāṅga-sūtra,
and the Pravacanasāra of Kundakunda; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of Jainism; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of the many and of the perspectives is the nearest Indian analogue to Jainism’s; it presents the
objections that Jainism would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “many-sidedness,” “non-absolutism,” “the seven-fold predication,” “the soul,”
“the non-soul,” or “the path of liberation,” these are Jainism’s terms, and their sense is fixed by
the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


66.1      A Scene
Consider a group of blind people who are touching an elephant. One touches the trunk and
says: the elephant is like a snake. Another touches the ear and says: the elephant is like a fan.
Another touches the leg and says: the elephant is like a pillar. Another touches the side and
says: the elephant is like a wall. Each of them has a partial knowledge of the elephant; each
of them has a true knowledge of the elephant; each of them is wrong about the elephant. The
trunk is not the elephant; the ear is not the elephant; the leg is not the elephant; the side is not
the elephant. And yet the elephant is all of these, and none of these is the elephant.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the elephant is, or how the blind
people know it, but what the truth is. The truth is not the trunk; the truth is not the ear; the
truth is not the leg; the truth is not the side. The truth is the whole elephant; the truth is the
many-sidedness of the elephant; the truth is the anekāntavāda. The truth is not one-sided; the
truth is many-sided. The one who says that the elephant is only the trunk is wrong; the one who
says that the elephant is only the ear is wrong; the one who says that the elephant is all of these
is right, but only if he adds: “from this point of view.” The truth is always qualified by a point
of view; the truth is always syāt (in some sense).
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the elephant is, or what
the truth is, but what the reality is. The reality is not one; the reality is not many; the reality is

                                                    737
738                                                                           Chapter 66. Jainism


both one and many. The reality is the many-sidedness; the reality is the anekānta. The reality is
the unity of the many perspectives; the reality is the harmony of the many truths. The reality
is not the absolutism of the one; the reality is not the nihilism of the many; the reality is the
non-absolutism of the many-sidedness. This is the teaching of Mahāvı̄ra; this is the teaching of
Jainism.
      The scene is the Jain image, in the Tattvārtha-sūtra and in the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, of the
structure of reality. The blind people are the partial perspectives; the elephant is the many-sided
reality; the truth is the non-absolutism. The scene poses the question that Jainism was the
first to pose in its full form in the Indian tradition. What is reality? Is it one or many? And
what is truth? Is it absolute or qualified? The present chapter states the Jain answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


66.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the Buddhist Logic position: the two means of knowledge, the
three kinds of logical reason, the doctrine of exclusion, the particular and the universal, and the
critique of the realist theories. Buddhist Logic is the great systematic philosophy of knowledge;
it affirms the two means, the theory of inference, and the doctrine of exclusion. Jainism is the
great systematic philosophy of the many-sidedness; it affirms the non-absolutism, the seven-fold
predication, and the many-sidedness of reality. The present chapter states the Jain position, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Jainism was right. The question is what it held, what it can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts, and the
chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Jainism hold? The chapter states the doctrine of
many-sidedness, the seven-fold predication, the non-absolutism, the categories, the theory of
karma, the doctrine of the soul and non-soul, and the path of liberation, with reference to the
Tattvārtha-sūtra, the Ācārāṅga-sūtra, and the Pravacanasāra.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Jainism converge, and where
do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents
the objections that Jainism would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Jainism?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


66.3       The Position

66.3.1      The Many-Sidedness of Reality (Anekāntavāda)

The Jain doctrine of the many-sidedness of reality is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra of Umāsvāti
and in the Ācārāṅga-sūtra. The doctrine is the foundation of the Jain philosophy; it is the
66.3. The Position                                                                                   739


teaching that reality is many-sided, and that no single proposition can capture it.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the many-sidedness. Reality is many-sided; it has many aspects; it has
many properties. The thing is not one; the thing is not many; the thing is both one and many.
The one-sided theories (the absolutism of the one, the absolutism of the many) are false; the
many-sided theory is true. The reality is the anekānta; it is the many-sidedness.


Second feature: the non-absolutism (syādvāda). The non-absolutism is the doctrine that
every proposition is qualified by a point of view; it is the doctrine that every truth is syāt (in
some sense). The proposition “the thing is” is true syāt; the proposition “the thing is not” is
true syāt; the proposition “the thing is and is not” is true syāt; the proposition “the thing is
neither” is true syāt. The syāt is the qualification; it is the recognition of the point of view.


Third feature: the harmony of the perspectives. The perspectives are not contradictory;
they are complementary. The perspective of the trunk is not the perspective of the ear; the
perspective of the ear is not the perspective of the leg; but the three perspectives are the
perspectives of one elephant. The harmony of the perspectives is the harmony of the truths; it is
the harmony of the many-sidedness.

   From the Tradition

   “The thing is, in some sense; the thing is not, in some sense; the thing is and is not, in some
   sense; the thing is neither, in some sense. The many-sidedness is the nature of reality.”
   (Umāsvāti, Tattvārtha-sūtra 5.31–32, trans. after Tatia)


66.3.2     The Seven-Fold Predication (Saptabhaṅgı̄)

The Jain theory of the seven-fold predication is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra and in the
Pravacanasāra. The theory is the logical expression of the many-sidedness; it is the seven ways
of predicating a thing.
   The theory has three features.


First feature: the seven-fold. The seven-fold predication is the seven ways of predicating a
thing: (1) syāt asti (in some sense, it is); (2) syāt nāsti (in some sense, it is not); (3) syāt asti
nāsti (in some sense, it is and is not); (4) syāt avaktavya (in some sense, it is inexpressible); (5)
syāt asti avaktavya (in some sense, it is and is inexpressible); (6) syāt nāsti avaktavya (in some
sense, it is not and is inexpressible); (7) syāt asti nāsti avaktavya (in some sense, it is, is not,
and is inexpressible). The seven are the seven ways of predicating the many-sided reality.


Second feature: the qualification. The qualification (syāt) is the key to the seven-fold; it is
the recognition of the point of view. Without the qualification, the predication is one-sided; with
the qualification, the predication is many-sided. The syāt is not a doubt; it is not a scepticism;
it is the recognition of the many-sidedness.
740                                                                            Chapter 66. Jainism


Third feature: the inexpressible. The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh predications involve
the inexpressible (avaktavya). The inexpressible is not the unknown; it is the simultaneity of
the is and the is not; it is the coincidence of the opposites; it is the many-sidedness that cannot
be expressed in a single proposition. The inexpressible is the limit of the language; it is the
recognition of the many-sidedness.

66.3.3      The Non-Absolutism (Syādvāda)
The Jain doctrine of non-absolutism is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra and in the Pravacanasāra.
The non-absolutism is the doctrine that every proposition is qualified; it is the doctrine that no
proposition is absolute.
      The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the rejection of absolutism. The absolutism is the doctrine that one
proposition is the whole truth; it is the doctrine that one perspective is the only perspective. The
absolutism is the error; it is the one-sidedness; it is the source of the conflict. The non-absolutism
rejects the absolutism; it affirms the many-sidedness; it affirms the qualification.

Second feature: the rejection of scepticism. The scepticism is the doctrine that no
proposition is true; it is the doctrine that all perspectives are false. The scepticism is the error;
it is the nihilism; it is the source of the despair. The non-absolutism rejects the scepticism; it
affirms the many-sidedness; it affirms the truth of the perspectives.

Third feature: the middle way. The non-absolutism is the middle way between the
absolutism and the scepticism. It is not the absolutism of the one; it is not the scepticism of the
many; it is the many-sidedness of the qualified. The middle way is the teaching of Mahāvı̄ra; it
is the teaching of Jainism.

66.3.4      The Categories (Tattva)
The Jain doctrine of the categories is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra. The categories are the
constituents of reality; they are the levels of the analysis.
      The doctrine has three features.

First feature: the soul (jı̄va). The soul is the conscious entity; it is the knower; it is the
experiencer; it is the agent. The soul is eternal; it is uncreated; it is infinite in number. The soul
is the jı̄va; it is the conscious.

Second feature: the non-soul (ajı̄va). The non-soul is the non-conscious entity; it is the
matter; it is the medium of motion; it is the medium of rest; it is the space; it is the time. The
non-soul is the ajı̄va; it is the non-conscious.

Third feature: the categories. The categories are the soul, the non-soul, the influx (āsrava),
                                      . vara), the shedding (nirjarā), and the liberation (moks.a).

The seven categories are the seven truths; they are the seven levels of the analysis.

66.3.5    The Theory of Karma
The Jain theory of karma is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra. The karma is the material particle; it
is the subtle matter; it is the bondage of the soul.
   The theory has three features.

First feature: the karma as matter. The karma is not a metaphysical entity; it is not a
psychological tendency; it is a material particle. The karma is the subtle matter; it is the particle
that attaches to the soul; it is the particle that binds the soul. The karma is the pudgala; it is
the matter.

Second feature: the influx and the bondage. The influx (āsrava) is the flow of the karma
into the soul; it is the cause of the bondage. The bondage (bandha) is the attachment of the
karma to the soul; it is the cause of the suffering. The influx and the bondage are the two aspects
of the karma; they are the two causes of the suffering.

karma; it is the cause of the liberation. The stoppage and the shedding are the two aspects of
the path; they are the two means to the liberation.


66.3.6    The Path of Liberation
The Jain path of liberation is stated in the Tattvārtha-sūtra. The path is the three jewels: the
right faith, the right knowledge, the right conduct.
   The path has three features.

First feature: the right faith. The right faith (samyag-darśana) is the faith in the categories;
it is the faith in the teachings of the Jina; it is the faith in the path. The right faith is the
foundation; it is the condition of the knowledge.

Second feature: the right knowledge. The right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is the knowledge
of the categories; it is the knowledge of the soul and the non-soul; it is the knowledge of the
karma. The right knowledge is the means; it is the condition of the conduct.

Third feature: the right conduct. The right conduct (samyag-cāritra) is the conduct of

means to the liberation.


66.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Jainism is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.
742                                                                            Chapter 66. Jainism


First dispute: the status of many-sidedness. The traditional reading takes many-sidedness
to be a metaphysical doctrine: reality is many-sided; it has many aspects; it has many properties.
A revisionary reading takes it to be an epistemological doctrine: it is a description of the limits
of knowledge; it is the recognition that no single proposition can capture the reality. The two
readings disagree on whether Jainism is a metaphysics or an epistemology, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a
perspective.


Second dispute: the status of the seven-fold predication. The traditional reading takes
the seven-fold predication to be a logical doctrine: it is the seven ways of predicating a thing; it
is the logic of the many-sidedness. A revisionary reading takes it to be a rhetorical device: it
is a way of avoiding the conflict; it is a way of reconciling the perspectives. The two readings
disagree on whether Jainism is a logician or a rhetorician, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a rhetoric.


Third dispute: the status of the non-absolutism. The traditional reading takes non-
absolutism to be a philosophical doctrine: every proposition is qualified; every truth is syāt.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a scepticism: no proposition is true; every perspective is
false. The two readings disagree on whether Jainism is a philosophy or a scepticism, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s truth is one, not
relative.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Jainism is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of many-sidedness.
If Jainism is a sceptic, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a scepticism.
The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Tattvārtha-sūtra, but it does not rest
its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


66.5        Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Jainism. The framework shares four structural features with the Jain position.

        1. The rejection of the one-sidedness. Jainism holds that the one-sidedness is the
            error; the truth is many-sided; the truth is qualified. The framework holds that
            the one-sidedness is the error; the truth is structural; the truth is the structure of
            the manifestation. Both reject the one-sidedness; both hold that the truth is not
            absolute.

        2. The many perspectives. Jainism holds that there are many perspectives; each is a
            partial truth; each is a qualified truth. The framework holds that there are many
            manifestations; each is a partial appearance; each is a qualified appearance. Both
            hold that there are many perspectives, and that each is partial.
66.6. Points of Divergence                                                                        743


       3. The harmony of the perspectives. Jainism holds that the perspectives are comple-
          mentary; they are the perspectives of one reality. The framework holds that the
          manifestations are the expressions of one identity; they are the appearances of one
          structure. Both hold that the perspectives are complementary, and that they are
          the perspectives of one reality.

                                                                    . sā) is the highest virtue;
       4. The non-violence. Jainism holds that the non-violence (ahim
          it is the respect for all living beings. The framework holds that the structural realism
          is the respect for the structure; it is the recognition of the many-sidedness. Both
          hold that there is a respect, and that the respect is the foundation of the ethics.




66.6      Points of Divergence


   Points of Divergence

   With Jainism. The framework diverges from the Jain position in four respects.

       1. The status of many-sidedness. Jainism holds that reality is many-sided; it has many
          aspects; it has many properties. The framework holds that the identity is one; it is
          the invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition. The framework’s
          identity is one, not many-sided; it is the structure that the manifestations exhibit.

       2. The status of the seven-fold predication. Jainism holds that there are seven ways of
          predicating a thing; the seven-fold is the logic of the many-sidedness. The framework
          holds that there is one way of reconstructing a thing; the reconstruction is the reading
          of the manifestations; it is not seven-fold. The framework’s method is structural,
          not seven-fold.

       3. The status of the non-absolutism. Jainism holds that every proposition is qualified;
          every truth is syāt. The framework holds that the truth is one; it is the structural
          truth; it is not qualified by the point of view. The framework’s truth is one, not
          relative.

       4. The status of the soul. Jainism holds that the soul is eternal; it is uncreated; it is
          infinite in number. The framework holds that the identity is not the soul; it is the
          invariance enacted by one source; it is the structural condition. The framework’s
          identity is not a soul; it is a structure.
744                                                                          Chapter 66. Jainism


66.7    The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Jainism’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  not many-sided; it is one-sided. The reality is many-sided; the reality is the anekānta; the
  reality is the harmony of the perspectives. The framework’s identity is one-sided; it is the
  structure that excludes the many-sidedness. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
  one-sidedness, not of many-sidedness.
  Jainism’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
  levels; they are the levels of the many-sidedness; they are the levels of the perspectives.
  The framework’s realms are not levels of the many-sidedness; they are just levels. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of many-sidedness.
  Jainism’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
  the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the many-sided; it is the seven-fold; it
  is the non-absolutism. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction of the one-sided; it
  is not the many-sided. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of one-sidedness,
  not of many-sidedness.



66.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the reality is many-sided, and
  it agrees that the perspectives are complementary. But the framework denies that the
  identity must be many-sided. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
  source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity
  in its realm. The framework’s identity is not one-sided; it is the structural condition under
  which the many perspectives are the perspectives of one reality. The distinction is between
  a one-sidedness (an exclusion) and an identity (a structural condition); the framework
  holds the second, not the first.
  Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
  levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
  that the realms are levels of the many-sidedness. The framework’s realms are ontological
  levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
  many-sidedness. The distinction is between a level of the many-sidedness (a perspectival
  level) and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second,
  not the first.
  Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
  conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
66.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                    745


   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the many-sided. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a many-sidedness
   (a plurality of perspectives) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.



66.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Jainism’s cost. If Jainism accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the
reality is many-sided. It must accept that the identity is the structural condition, and that the
many-sidedness is the manifestation. The cost is the loss of the many-sidedness: the reality is no
longer many-sided; the identity is the structural condition. It must also give up the claim that
the knowledge is the seven-fold; it must accept that the knowledge is the reconstruction; the
reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Jainism’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the many-sidedness, of the seven-fold, of the non-absolutism—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the many-sidedness, and the framework leaves
the many-sidedness to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Jainism’s many-sidedness
is not a mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
Jainism must accept that the framework’s structure is not a one-sidedness; it is a structural
condition that the many-sidedness presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the
loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is
incomplete without the other.


66.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Jainism’s
   term “the many-sidedness.” If one substitutes “the many-sidedness” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Jainism’s many-sidedness is
   the plurality of the aspects, and it is not manifested, because it is the plurality. The
   framework’s identity is one; Jainism’s many-sidedness is many. The substitution fails, and
746                                                                          Chapter 66. Jainism


   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Jainism’s term “the perspective.”
   If one substitutes “the perspective” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the perspective is
   the point of view. The framework’s expression is structural; the perspective is perspectival.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Jainism’s term “the seven-
   fold predication.” If one substitutes “the seven-fold predication” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a
   reading of the manifestations; the seven-fold predication is the seven ways of predicating
   a thing. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the seven-fold is logical. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Jainism is resemblance:
   both reject the one-sidedness, and they differ on whether the rejection leaves a structure or
   a many-sidedness. Both hold that there are many perspectives, and they differ on whether
   the perspectives are the manifestations or the aspects. Neither relation is equivalence;
   neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Jainism would be
   refuted by showing that Jainism’s many-sidedness cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and many-sidedness—by showing, that is, that
   Jainism already distinguishes the structural condition from the many-sidedness, and that
   the framework’s distinction is a development of Jainism’s own.



66.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Jainism’s many-sidedness, or is
it a departure from Jainism? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument
is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Jainism’s many-sidedness is already a structural
condition, not a plurality, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Tattvārtha-sūtra and the Ācārāṅga-sūtra
do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the many-sidedness, the seven-fold predication,
the non-absolutism, the categories, the theory of karma, the doctrine of the soul and non-soul,
and the path of liberation, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
