A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both one and many—a person, a tradition, a work of art. Is
the thing the one that includes the many, or the many that expresses the one? Is the truth the
non-absolutism that qualifies, or the structure that enacts? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Jainism’s many-sidedness and the framework’s identity?

Part IX is now complete. The dialogues with the four great schools of Buddhist and Jain
philosophy—Nāgārjuna, Yogācāra, Buddhist Logic, and Jainism—have been stated. Part X turns
to Chinese philosophy. The first dialogue is with Confucius and Mencius, on the ethical order
and the human nature; the next with Laozi and Zhuangzi, on the Dao and the naturalness; the
next with Mozi and Han Feizi, on the universal love and the law; the next with Zhu Xi and Wang
Yangming, on the principle and the mind; and the last with Chinese Buddhism, on the Chan and
the Pure Land. The Indian tradition has asked what the self is, and what the absolute is; the
Chinese tradition will ask what the way is, and how the human being is to live.
      Part X

Chinese Philosophy




        748
Chapter 67

Confucius and Mencius


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Confucius (Kongzi, 551–479 BCE) and Mencius (Mengzi,
c. 372–289 BCE), the two foundational figures of the Confucian school of Chinese philosophy. It
states Confucius’s account of ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), yi (rightness), zhi (wisdom),
the junzi (the noble person), the rectification of names (zhengming), and the ethical order of
the family and the state; and it states Mencius’s account of human nature as originally good
(xing shan), the four sprouts (si duan) of virtue, the cultivation of the qi (haoran zhi qi), the
mandate of heaven (tianming), and the right of the people to rebellion against a tyrant; with
reference to the Analects (Lunyu), the Mencius (Mengzi), the Great Learning (Daxue), and the
Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Confucius and Mencius; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of identity and manifestation is the nearest Chinese analogue to the Confucian
account of the person and the order; it presents the objections that Confucius and Mencius would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “humaneness,”
“ritual propriety,” “rightness,” “the noble person,” “human nature,” “the four sprouts,” or “the
mandate of heaven,” these are the Confucian terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by
the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


67.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is standing in a courtyard. Her father is inside; her teacher is inside; her
ruler is inside. She is about to enter. How should she enter? Should she enter first, as the most
important? Should she wait for her father? Should she wait for her teacher? Should she wait for
her ruler? The question is not about the door; it is about the order; it is about the ritual; it is
about the relation. The answer is given by the li: the ritual propriety that orders the relations
between the father and the son, the teacher and the student, the ruler and the subject.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not how she should enter, or what the ritual is,
but what makes the ritual right. The ritual is right because it expresses the ren: the humaneness
that is the care for the other; the humaneness that is the love for the other; the humaneness
that is the respect for the other. The ritual without the humaneness is empty; the humaneness
without the ritual is formless. The two are not separate; they are the two aspects of the one
ethical order.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not how she should enter, or
what makes the ritual right, but what the human being is. The human being is not a solitary
individual; the human being is a relation; the human being is a node in the network of the

                                                749
750                                                          Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


relations; the human being is a father, a son, a teacher, a student, a ruler, a subject. The human
being is the ren: the humaneness; the humaneness that is the relation; the relation that is the
ethical order. The human being is not born good; the human being is born with the four sprouts
of goodness; the four sprouts are the beginnings of the virtues; they are the seeds that the
cultivation brings to fruition. This is the teaching of Confucius and Mencius.
      The scene is the Confucian image, in the Analects and in the Mencius, of the structure of
the ethical order. The courtyard is the ritual; the father is the relation; the humaneness is the
foundation. The scene poses the question that Confucius and Mencius were the first to pose in
its full form in the Chinese tradition. What is the human being? What is the ethical order? And
what is the relation between the two? The present chapter states the Confucian answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.



67.2       The Question

The previous part stated the positions of the Buddhist and Jain philosophy: Nāgārjuna, Yogācāra,
Buddhist Logic, and Jainism. The Buddhist and Jain traditions have asked what the self is, and
what the absolute is. The present part turns to Chinese philosophy, and its first dialogue is with
Confucius and Mencius, the two foundational figures of the Confucian school. The Confucian
tradition has asked what the way is, and how the human being is to live.
      The question is not whether Confucius and Mencius were right. The question is what they
held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The
question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Confucius and Mencius hold? The chapter states the
account of humaneness, ritual propriety, rightness, wisdom, the noble person, the rectification of
names, and the ethical order; and the account of human nature, the four sprouts, the cultivation
of the qi, the mandate of heaven, and the right of rebellion, with reference to the Analects and
the Mencius.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the Confucian tradition
converge, and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and
divergence, and it presents the objections that Confucius and Mencius would raise against the
framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the
Confucian tradition? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as
resemblance, not equivalence.



67.3       The Position
67.3. The Position                                                                                751


67.3.1        Confucius: Humaneness (Ren)
Confucius’s account of humaneness is stated in the Analects, especially in the books IV, VI, and
XII. Humaneness is the central virtue of the Confucian ethics; it is the care for the other; it is
the love for the other; it is the respect for the other.
   The account has three features.

First feature: the humaneness as care. Humaneness is the care for the other; it is the
concern for the well-being of the other; it is the love that is not limited to the self. The humane
person is the one who cares for the other; the humane person is the one who treats the other as
an end; the humane person is the one who does not do to the other what she does not want done
to herself.

Second feature: the humaneness as relation. Humaneness is not a solitary virtue; it is
a relational virtue; it is the virtue that is realized in the relations between the father and the
son, the teacher and the student, the ruler and the subject. The humaneness is the relation; the
relation is the ethical order; the ethical order is the humaneness.

Third feature: the humaneness as the foundation. Humaneness is the foundation of the
other virtues; it is the ground of the ritual propriety, the rightness, and the wisdom. The ritual
without the humaneness is empty; the rightness without the humaneness is harsh; the wisdom
without the humaneness is cunning. The humaneness is the foundation; it is the root; it is the
source.

   From the Tradition

   “The humane person is the one who loves others.” (Confucius, Analects 12.22, trans. after
   Legge)


67.3.2        Confucius: Ritual Propriety (Li)
Confucius’s account of ritual propriety is stated in the Analects, especially in the books III, VIII,
and XII. The ritual propriety is the order of the relations; it is the form of the ethical life; it is
the expression of the humaneness.
   The account has three features.

First feature: the ritual as order. The ritual is the order of the relations; it is the way the
father and the son, the teacher and the student, the ruler and the subject, relate to one another.
The ritual is not an arbitrary convention; it is the form of the ethical life; it is the structure of
the social order.

Second feature: the ritual as expression. The ritual is the expression of the humaneness;
it is the form that the humaneness takes; it is the way the humaneness is realized in the world.
The ritual without the humaneness is empty; the humaneness without the ritual is formless. The
two are not separate; they are the two aspects of the ethical life.
752                                                          Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


Third feature: the ritual as transformation. The ritual is the transformation of the
person; it is the way the person is shaped by the practice; it is the way the person becomes the
noble person. The ritual is not a mere formality; it is the practice that transforms the person; it
is the discipline that cultivates the virtue.


67.3.3      Confucius: Rightness (Yi) and Wisdom (Zhi)
Confucius’s account of rightness and wisdom is stated in the Analects, especially in the books II,
IV, and VI. The rightness is the sense of what is right; it is the judgment of the appropriate; it is
the discernment of the good. The wisdom is the knowledge of the right; it is the understanding
of the appropriate; it is the discernment of the good.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the rightness as judgment. The rightness is the judgment of what is right;
it is the discernment of the appropriate; it is the sense of the fitting. The rightness is not the
rule; it is not the law; it is the judgment that applies the rule to the situation. The rightness is
the virtue of the practical wisdom.


Second feature: the wisdom as knowledge. The wisdom is the knowledge of the right; it
is the understanding of the appropriate; it is the discernment of the good. The wisdom is not the
knowledge of the facts; it is the knowledge of the values; it is the knowledge of the ethical order.


Third feature: the unity of the virtues. The rightness and the wisdom are not separate;
they are the aspects of the one virtue; they are the aspects of the humaneness. The humaneness
is the foundation; the rightness is the judgment; the wisdom is the knowledge; the three are the
one virtue; the one virtue is the ethical life.


67.3.4      Confucius: The Noble Person (Junzi)
Confucius’s account of the noble person is stated in the Analects, especially in the books I, IV,
and XV. The noble person is the ideal of the Confucian ethics; it is the person who has realized
the humaneness; it is the person who has cultivated the virtue.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the noble person as the ideal. The noble person is the ideal of the ethical
life; it is the person who has realized the humaneness; it is the person who has cultivated the
virtue. The noble person is not born; the noble person is made; the noble person is the result
of the cultivation; the cultivation is the practice of the ritual; the practice of the ritual is the
transformation of the person.


Second feature: the noble person as the relation. The noble person is not a solitary
individual; the noble person is a relation; the noble person is the father, the son, the teacher, the
student, the ruler, the subject. The noble person is the one who has realized the humaneness in
the relations; the one who has realized the ethical order.
67.3. The Position                                                                                 753


Third feature: the noble person as the contrast. The noble person is the contrast to the
petty person (xiaoren); the noble person is the one who seeks the rightness; the petty person
is the one who seeks the profit. The noble person is the one who is concerned with the virtue;
the petty person is the one who is concerned with the advantage. The contrast is the contrast
between the ethical life and the life of the self-interest.


67.3.5     Confucius: The Rectification of Names (Zhengming)

Confucius’s account of the rectification of names is stated in the Analects, especially in the book
XIII. The rectification of names is the correction of the names; it is the alignment of the names
with the realities; it is the order of the language and the order of the society.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the name and the reality. The name is not an arbitrary label; it is the
expression of the reality; it is the form of the relation. The name “father” is not a sound; it is
the relation of the father; it is the duty of the father; it is the care of the father. The name is
the reality; the reality is the name.


Second feature: the rectification. The rectification is the alignment of the name with the
reality; it is the correction of the name that has lost its reality; it is the restoration of the order.
The rectification is the task of the ruler; it is the task of the noble person; it is the task of the
ethical life.


Third feature: the order. The rectification is the order of the society; it is the order of the
relations; it is the order of the ethical life. When the names are rectified, the society is ordered;
when the society is ordered, the ethical life is realized. The rectification is the foundation; it is
the condition of the order.


67.3.6     Mencius: Human Nature as Originally Good (Xing Shan)

Mencius’s account of human nature is stated in the Mencius, especially in the books II, III, and
VI. The human nature is originally good; it is not originally evil; it is not originally neutral. The
human nature is the seed of the virtue; it is the sprout of the goodness.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the original goodness. The human nature is originally good; it is the
goodness that is innate; it is the goodness that is natural. The human being is not born evil; the
human being is born with the four sprouts of the virtue; the four sprouts are the beginnings of
the goodness; they are the seeds that the cultivation brings to fruition.


Second feature: the four sprouts. The four sprouts are the sprouts of the four virtues:
the sprout of the compassion (ceyin) is the sprout of the humaneness; the sprout of the shame
(xiuwu) is the sprout of the rightness; the sprout of the deference (cirang) is the sprout of the
754                                                             Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


ritual propriety; the sprout of the discernment (shifei) is the sprout of the wisdom. The four
sprouts are the seeds of the four virtues; they are the beginnings of the ethical life.


Third feature: the cultivation. The cultivation is the development of the four sprouts; it is
the nurturing of the seeds; it is the realization of the goodness. The cultivation is the practice
of the ritual; it is the discipline of the ethical life; it is the transformation of the person. The
cultivation is the path; it is the way; it is the realization of the human nature.

   From the Tradition

   “The human being is originally good; the four sprouts are the beginnings of the goodness.”
   (Mencius, Mencius 6A.6, trans. after Legge)


67.3.7      Mencius: The Cultivation of the Qi (Haoran Zhi Qi)

Mencius’s account of the cultivation of the qi is stated in the Mencius, especially in the book II.
The qi is the vital energy; it is the material force; it is the medium of the ethical life.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the qi. The qi is the vital energy; it is the material force; it is the medium of
the ethical life. The qi is not the body; it is not the mind; it is the energy that connects the
body and the mind; it is the energy that is cultivated by the practice.


Second feature: the flood-like qi (haoran zhi qi). The flood-like qi is the qi that is vast
and flowing; it is the qi that fills the body; it is the qi that is the sign of the ethical life. The
flood-like qi is not born; it is cultivated; it is the result of the accumulation of the rightness; it is
the result of the practice of the virtue.


Third feature: the cultivation. The cultivation is the accumulation of the rightness; it is
the practice of the virtue; it is the development of the qi. The cultivation is not a single act; it is
a long discipline; it is the cultivation of the qi; it is the cultivation of the ethical life.


67.3.8      Mencius: The Mandate of Heaven (Tianming) and the Right of
            Rebellion

Mencius’s account of the mandate of heaven and the right of rebellion is stated in the Mencius,
especially in the books I and V. The mandate of heaven is the will of heaven; it is the order of
the cosmos; it is the foundation of the ethical life. The right of rebellion is the right of the people
to overthrow a tyrant; it is the expression of the mandate of heaven; it is the realization of the
ethical order.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the mandate of heaven. The mandate of heaven is the will of heaven; it is
the order of the cosmos; it is the foundation of the ethical life. The heaven is not the sky; it is
67.4. Internal Disputes                                                                           755


the order; it is the principle; it is the source. The mandate is the order; it is the principle; it is
the source. The mandate is the foundation; it is the condition of the ethical life.

Second feature: the right of rebellion. The right of rebellion is the right of the people
to overthrow a tyrant; it is the expression of the mandate of heaven; it is the realization of the
ethical order. The tyrant is not the king; the tyrant is the one who has lost the mandate; the
tyrant is the one who has violated the ethical order. The rebellion is not the violation of the
mandate; it is the restoration of the mandate.

Third feature: the people. The people are the foundation of the state; they are the source
of the mandate; they are the standard of the ethical life. The people are not the subjects; the
people are the ends; the people are the reason of the state. The people are the foundation; they
are the condition of the ethical life.

   From the Tradition

   “The people are the most important; the state is the next; the ruler is the least important.”
   (Mencius, Mencius 7B.14, trans. after Legge)



67.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Confucius and Mencius is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of human nature. The traditional reading takes Mencius’s
account of human nature to be a metaphysical doctrine: the human nature is originally good;
it is the innate goodness. A revisionary reading takes it to be an ethical doctrine: the human
nature is not a fact; it is a task; it is the goal of the cultivation. The two readings disagree
on whether Confucianism is a metaphysics or an ethics, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s identity is a structural condition, not a human
nature.

Second dispute: the status of the ritual. The traditional reading takes the ritual to be
a social order: it is the form of the relations; it is the structure of the society. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a personal practice: it is the way of the transformation; it is the discipline
of the ethical life. The two readings disagree on whether Confucianism is a social philosophy or
a personal philosophy, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the
framework’s manifestation is real, not a social order.

Third dispute: the status of the mandate of heaven. The traditional reading takes the
mandate to be a cosmic order: it is the will of heaven; it is the order of the cosmos. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a political principle: it is the right of the people; it is the standard of the
ethical life. The two readings disagree on whether Confucianism is a cosmology or a political
philosophy, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, not a cosmology.
756                                                            Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Confucianism is a metaphysics, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of human nature.
If Confucianism is an ethics, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and an ethics
of the ethical order. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Analects, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.




67.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Confucius and Mencius. The framework shares four structural features with the
   Confucian position.

        1. The relationality. Confucius holds that the human being is a relation; the human
           being is a node in the network of the relations; the human being is the father, the
           son, the teacher, the student, the ruler, the subject. The framework holds that the
           identity is a structural condition; it is enacted in the manifestations; it is related
           to the other identities. Both hold that the human being is relational, and that the
           relation is constitutive.

        2. The cultivation. Mencius holds that the cultivation is the development of the four
           sprouts; it is the nurturing of the seeds; it is the realization of the goodness. The
           framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
           the development of the identity; it is the realization of the structure. Both hold that
           there is a cultivation, and that the cultivation is the path.

        3. The ethical order. Confucius holds that the ritual is the order of the relations; it is
           the form of the ethical life; it is the expression of the humaneness. The framework
           holds that the structure is the order of the manifestations; it is the form of the
           identity; it is the expression of the structure. Both hold that there is an order, and
           that the order is the ethical life.

        4. The rectification of names. Confucius holds that the rectification is the alignment of
           the names with the realities; it is the correction of the names; it is the restoration
           of the order. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the alignment of the
           manifestations with the identity; it is the correction of the pseudo-identity; it is the
           restoration of the structure. Both hold that there is a rectification, and that the
           rectification is the condition of the order.
67.6. Points of Divergence                                                                       757


67.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Confucius and Mencius. The framework diverges from the Confucian position
   in four respects.

       1. The status of human nature. Mencius holds that the human nature is originally good;
          it is the innate goodness; it is the seed of the virtue. The framework holds that the
          identity is not a human nature; it is the invariance enacted by one source; it is the
          structural condition. The framework’s identity is not good; it is neither good nor
          evil; it is the structure.

       2. The status of the ritual. Confucius holds that the ritual is the order of the relations;
          it is the form of the ethical life. The framework holds that the structure is the order
          of the manifestations; it is the form of the identity. The framework’s structure is not
          a ritual; it is a structural condition.

       3. The status of the mandate of heaven. Mencius holds that the mandate is the will
          of heaven; it is the order of the cosmos. The framework holds that the structure is
          the order of the manifestations; it is the structure of the realms. The framework’s
          structure is not a mandate; it is a structural condition.

       4. The status of the people. Mencius holds that the people are the foundation of the
          state; they are the standard of the ethical life. The framework holds that the identity
          is the foundation of the manifestation; it is the standard of the reconstruction. The
          framework’s identity is not the people; it is the structure.



67.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Confucius’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not a
   relation; it is a pattern. The human being is a relation; the human being is the father, the
   son, the teacher, the student, the ruler, the subject. The framework’s identity is a pattern,
   and a pattern is not a relation. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not
   of relations.
   Mencius’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
   real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they are
   the levels of the human nature; they are the levels of the four sprouts. The framework’s
   realms are not levels of the human nature; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology
   is an ontology of levels, not of human nature.
   Mencius’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
758                                                          Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


   is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the cultivation; it is the development
   of the four sprouts; it is the realization of the goodness. The framework’s knowledge is a
   reconstruction; it is not the cultivation. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology
   of reconstruction, not of cultivation.



67.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Confucius’s objection. The framework agrees that the human being is a
   relation, and it agrees that the relation is constitutive. But the framework denies that
   its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
   source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity
   in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Mencius’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the human nature. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   human nature. The distinction is between a level of the human nature (an ethical level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to Mencius’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the
   cultivation. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a cultivation (a practice) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second,
   not the first.



67.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Confucius and Mencius’s cost. If Confucius and Mencius accept the framework’s reply,
they must give up the claim that the human being is a relation. They must accept that the
identity is a structural condition, and that the relation is a manifestation of the identity. The
cost is the loss of the relationality: the human being is no longer a relation; the identity is the
structural condition. They must also give up the claim that the human nature is originally good;
they must accept that the identity is neither good nor evil; it is the structure.
67.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     759


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Confucius and Mencius, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension
of reality—the dimension of the relation, of the human nature, of the cultivation—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not a relation, and the framework
leaves the relation to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Confucius’s relation and
Mencius’s human nature are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Confucius and Mencius must accept that the framework’s structure
is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the relation and the human nature presuppose
as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the
two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


67.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Confu-
   cius’s term “the humaneness.” If one substitutes “the humaneness” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the humaneness is the care for
   the other, and it is not manifested, because it is the care. The framework’s identity is
   multiple; the humaneness is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Confucius’s term “the ritual.” If
   one substitutes “the ritual” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the ritual is the order of the
   relations. The framework’s expression is structural; the ritual is social. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Mencius’s term “the
   cultivation.” If one substitutes “the cultivation” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the cultivation is the development of the four sprouts. The framework’s
   reconstruction is structural; the cultivation is ethical. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Confucius and Mencius is
   resemblance: both hold that the human being is relational, and they differ on whether the
   relation is the identity or the manifestation. Both hold that there is a cultivation, and they
   differ on whether the cultivation is the ethical practice or the structural reconstruction.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
760                                                          Chapter 67. Confucius and Mencius


   reading of Confucius and Mencius would be refuted by showing that their relationality
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and relation—
   by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the structural condition from the relation,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of their own.




67.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Confucius’s humaneness or
Mencius’s human nature, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it
is a development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Confucius’s
humaneness is already a structural condition, or that Mencius’s human nature is already a
structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Analects and the Mencius do justice
to the texts? The chapter has used the humaneness, the ritual, the rightness, the wisdom, the
noble person, the rectification of names, the human nature, the four sprouts, the cultivation of
the qi, the mandate of heaven, and the right of rebellion, and it has stated what would refute
its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the
chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a relation and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the relation that is lived, or the structure that is enacted? Is the truth the
humaneness that cares, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you about
the relation between Confucius’s humaneness and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Laozi and Zhuangzi. It states the Dao as the ineffable source, the
doctrine of non-action (wuwei), the naturalness (ziran), the relativity of the distinctions, and
the freedom of the sage; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Laozi and
Zhuangzi; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of the structure and of the naturalness is the nearest Chinese analogue to Laozi and
Zhuangzi. The present chapter has stated the Confucian answer to the problem of the ethical
order; the next chapter states the Daoist answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 68

Laozi and Zhuangzi


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Laozi (c. 6th–4th century BCE), the traditional founder
of Daoism and the reputed author of the Daodejing, and Zhuangzi (c. 369–286 BCE), the greatest
of the Daoist philosophers and the author of the Zhuangzi. It states Laozi’s account of the
Dao as the ineffable source, the doctrine of non-action (wuwei), the naturalness (ziran), the
weakness and the softness, and the return to the root; and it states Zhuangzi’s account of the
relativity of the distinctions, the transformation of things (wuhua), the fasting of the mind
(xinzhai), the free wandering (xiaoyao), and the equality of things (qiwu); with reference to the
Daodejing and the Zhuangzi; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of Laozi
and Zhuangzi; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of the structure and of the naturalness is the nearest Chinese analogue to the Daoist
position; it presents the objections that Laozi and Zhuangzi would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind
of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the Dao,” “non-action,” “naturalness,”
“the free wandering,” “the equality of things,” or “the transformation of things,” these are the
Daoist terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the
framework.


68.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing by a river. The water flows; the river moves; the fish swim.
She asks: what is the river? Is it the water? No, the water is not the river; the water is the
content; the river is the course. Is it the course? No, the course is not the river; the course is the
form; the river is the flow. The river is the flow; it is the movement; it is the transformation.
The river is the Dao; it is the way; it is the flow.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the river is, or how it flows, but
what the sage is. The sage is not the one who acts; the sage is the one who does not act; the
sage is the one who lets the things be; the sage is the one who follows the Dao. The sage does
not interfere; the sage does not impose; the sage does not force. The sage is the one who is
in harmony with the Dao; the one who is in harmony with the naturalness; the one who is in
harmony with the flow. This is the doctrine of non-action (wuwei): the action that is not action;
the action that is the letting-be.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the river is, or what the
sage is, but what the Dao is. The Dao is not a thing; it is not a substance; it is not a being. The
Dao is the source; it is the principle; it is the way. The Dao is ineffable; it cannot be named; it
cannot be spoken; it cannot be conceptualized. The Dao that can be named is not the Dao; the

                                                 762
68.2. The Question                                                                              763


name that can be spoken is not the name. The Dao is the silence; it is the emptiness; it is the
mystery. This is the teaching of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
   The scene is the Daoist image, in the Daodejing and in the Zhuangzi, of the structure of
reality. The river is the flow; the sage is the non-action; the Dao is the ineffable. The scene
poses the question that Laozi and Zhuangzi were the first to pose in its full form in the Chinese
tradition. What is the Dao? What is the sage? And what is the relation between the two? The
present chapter states the Daoist answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.



68.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Confucius and Mencius: the humaneness, the ritual
propriety, the rightness, the wisdom, the noble person, the rectification of names, the human
nature, the four sprouts, the cultivation of the qi, the mandate of heaven, and the right of
rebellion. The Confucian tradition has asked what the way is, and how the human being is to
live. The Daoist tradition has asked what the Dao is, and how the human being is to be in
harmony with it. The present chapter states the Daoist position, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
   The question is not whether Laozi and Zhuangzi were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Laozi and Zhuangzi hold? The chapter states the Dao as
the ineffable source, the non-action, the naturalness, the weakness and the softness, the return to
the root, the relativity of the distinctions, the transformation of things, the fasting of the mind,
the free wandering, and the equality of things, with reference to the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the Daoist tradition converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Laozi and Zhuangzi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the Daoist
tradition? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.



68.3       The Position

68.3.1     Laozi: The Dao as the Ineffable Source

Laozi’s account of the Dao is stated in the Daodejing, especially in the chapters 1, 25, and 42.
The Dao is the ineffable source; it is the principle; it is the way.
   The account has three features.
764                                                              Chapter 68. Laozi and Zhuangzi


First feature: the ineffability. The Dao is ineffable; it cannot be named; it cannot be spoken;
it cannot be conceptualized. The Dao that can be named is not the Dao; the name that can
be spoken is not the name. The Dao is the silence; it is the emptiness; it is the mystery. The
language cannot capture the Dao; the concept cannot grasp the Dao; the mind cannot know the
Dao. The Dao is the limit of the language; it is the limit of the concept; it is the limit of the
mind.


Second feature: the source. The Dao is the source; it is the origin; it is the principle. The
Dao is the mother of the ten thousand things; it is the root of the ten thousand things; it is the
ground of the ten thousand things. The Dao is not a thing; it is the source of the things; it is not
a being; it is the source of the beings. The Dao is the source; it is the principle; it is the way.


Third feature: the way. The Dao is the way; it is the path; it is the method. The Dao is the
way of the nature; it is the way of the things; it is the way of the human being. The Dao is the
way that is not a way; it is the path that is not a path; it is the method that is not a method.
The Dao is the way; it is the naturalness; it is the spontaneity.

   From the Tradition

   “The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao. The name that can be named is
   not the constant name.” (Laozi, Daodejing 1, trans. after Lau)



68.3.2      Laozi: Non-Action (Wuwei)

Laozi’s doctrine of non-action is stated in the Daodejing, especially in the chapters 2, 37, and 48.
The non-action is the action that is not action; it is the letting-be; it is the non-interference.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the non-action. The non-action is not the inaction; it is not the passivity; it
is not the laziness. The non-action is the action that is in harmony with the Dao; it is the action
that does not force; it is the action that does not impose. The non-action is the letting-be; it is
the allowing; it is the non-interference.


Second feature: the harmony. The non-action is the harmony with the Dao; it is the
harmony with the nature; it is the harmony with the flow. The sage who practices the non-action
is in harmony with the Dao; the sage who is in harmony with the Dao is the sage who does not
act; the sage who does not act is the sage who lets the things be.


Third feature: the efficacy. The non-action is the most efficacious action; it is the action
that achieves the most; it is the action that does not fail. The non-action is the action that is
not forced; the action that is not forced is the action that succeeds; the action that succeeds is
the action that is in harmony with the Dao.
68.3. The Position                                                                                  765


68.3.3    Laozi: Naturalness (Ziran)

Laozi’s doctrine of naturalness is stated in the Daodejing, especially in the chapters 25 and 64.
The naturalness is the spontaneity; it is the self-so; it is the nature.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the naturalness. The naturalness is the spontaneity; it is the self-so; it is the
nature. The naturalness is not the artificial; it is not the conventional; it is not the imposed. The
naturalness is the way of the Dao; it is the way of the things; it is the way of the human being.


Second feature: the return. The return is the return to the naturalness; it is the return to
the root; it is the return to the Dao. The return is the goal; it is the path; it is the way. The
return is the recognition that the artificial is the deviation; the naturalness is the norm; the Dao
is the source.


Third feature: the simplicity. The simplicity is the naturalness; it is the absence of the
artificial; it is the absence of the desire; it is the absence of the calculation. The simplicity is the
virtue; it is the power; it is the harmony. The simple person is the one who is in harmony with
the Dao; the one who is in harmony with the naturalness; the one who is in harmony with the
flow.


68.3.4    Laozi: Weakness and Softness

Laozi’s doctrine of weakness and softness is stated in the Daodejing, especially in the chapters
43, 76, and 78. The weakness is the strength; the softness is the hardness; the yielding is the
overcoming.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the weakness. The weakness is the strength; it is the power of the yielding;
it is the power of the soft. The weak overcomes the strong; the soft overcomes the hard; the
yielding overcomes the resisting. The weakness is not the weakness of the impotent; it is the
weakness of the flexible; it is the weakness of the adaptive.


Second feature: the water. The water is the image of the weakness; it is the soft; it is the
yielding. The water is the weakest of the things; it is the strongest of the things; it wears away
the rock; it carves the canyon; it nourishes the life. The water is the Dao; it is the way; it is the
flow.


Third feature: the non-contention. The non-contention is the weakness; it is the absence
of the strife; it is the absence of the competition. The one who does not contend is the one who
is not defeated; the one who does not strive is the one who succeeds; the one who yields is the
one who overcomes.
766                                                              Chapter 68. Laozi and Zhuangzi


68.3.5      Zhuangzi: The Relativity of the Distinctions

Zhuangzi’s account of the relativity of the distinctions is stated in the Zhuangzi, especially in the
chapter “Discussion on Making All Things Equal” (Qiwulun). The distinctions are not absolute;
they are relative; they depend on the perspective.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the relativity. The distinctions are relative; they are not absolute; they
depend on the perspective. The big is not absolutely big; it is big in relation to the small. The
right is not absolutely right; it is right in relation to the wrong. The beautiful is not absolutely
beautiful; it is beautiful in relation to the ugly. The distinctions are the constructions of the
perspective; they are not the realities of the things.


Second feature: the perspective. The perspective is the point of view; it is the standpoint;
it is the frame. The perspective determines the distinction; the distinction determines the
judgment; the judgment determines the value. The change of the perspective is the change of
the distinction; the change of the distinction is the change of the judgment; the change of the
judgment is the change of the value.


Third feature: the equality. The equality is the equality of the things; it is the equality
of the distinctions; it is the equality of the perspectives. The equality is not the identity; it is
not the sameness; it is the recognition that the distinctions are relative; the recognition that the
perspectives are partial; the recognition that the things are equal in their relativity.


68.3.6      Zhuangzi: The Transformation of Things (Wuhua)

Zhuangzi’s account of the transformation of things is stated in the Zhuangzi, especially in the
chapter “The Great and Venerable Teacher” (Dazongshi). The transformation is the change; it
is the becoming; it is the flow.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the transformation. The things are in transformation; they are in change;
they are in becoming. The things are not static; they are not fixed; they are not permanent.
The things are the flow; they are the process; they are the transformation. The life becomes the
death; the death becomes the life; the day becomes the night; the night becomes the day. The
transformation is the reality; it is the way; it is the Dao.


Second feature: the dream. The dream is the image of the transformation; it is the image
of the relativity; it is the image of the uncertainty. Zhuangzi dreams of being a butterfly; he
wakes and does not know whether he is Zhuangzi dreaming of being a butterfly or a butterfly
dreaming of being Zhuangzi. The dream is the reality; the reality is the dream; the two are not
separate; the two are the transformation.
68.3. The Position                                                                               767


Third feature: the acceptance. The acceptance is the acceptance of the transformation;
it is the acceptance of the change; it is the acceptance of the flow. The one who accepts the
transformation is the one who is free; the one who is free is the one who is in harmony with the
Dao; the one who is in harmony with the Dao is the sage.


68.3.7    Zhuangzi: The Fasting of the Mind (Xinzhai) and the Free Wandering
          (Xiaoyao)

Zhuangzi’s account of the fasting of the mind and the free wandering is stated in the Zhuangzi,
especially in the chapters “In the World of Men” (Renjianshi) and “Free and Easy Wandering”
(Xiaoyaoyou). The fasting of the mind is the emptying of the mind; the free wandering is the
freedom of the sage.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the fasting of the mind. The fasting of the mind is the emptying of the
mind; it is the elimination of the prejudices; it is the elimination of the desires. The fasting is
not the fasting of the body; it is the fasting of the mind; it is the emptying of the mind; it is the
opening of the mind. The empty mind is the receptive mind; the receptive mind is the mind that
is in harmony with the Dao.


Second feature: the free wandering. The free wandering is the freedom of the sage; it is
the freedom from the attachments; it is the freedom from the distinctions; it is the freedom from
the perspectives. The free wandering is the wandering without the goal; the wandering without
the purpose; the wandering without the destination. The free wandering is the play; it is the joy;
it is the harmony.


Third feature: the sage. The sage is the one who has fasted the mind; the one who has
achieved the free wandering; the one who is in harmony with the Dao. The sage is not the one
who knows; the sage is the one who does not know; the sage is the one who has forgotten the
knowledge; the sage is the one who has forgotten the distinctions. The sage is the one who is
empty; the one who is free; the one who is in harmony.


68.3.8    Zhuangzi: The Equality of Things (Qiwu)

Zhuangzi’s account of the equality of things is stated in the Zhuangzi, especially in the chapter
“Discussion on Making All Things Equal.” The equality is the equality of the things; it is the
equality of the distinctions; it is the equality of the perspectives.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the equality. The equality is the equality of the things; it is the equality of
the distinctions; it is the equality of the perspectives. The equality is not the identity; it is not
the sameness; it is the recognition that the distinctions are relative; the recognition that the
perspectives are partial; the recognition that the things are equal in their relativity.
768                                                             Chapter 68. Laozi and Zhuangzi


Second feature: the pivot. The pivot is the pivot of the Dao; it is the center; it is the axis.
The pivot is the point from which the distinctions are seen as relative; the point from which the
perspectives are seen as partial; the point from which the things are seen as equal. The pivot is
the wisdom; it is the insight; it is the enlightenment.


Third feature: the harmony. The harmony is the harmony of the things; it is the harmony
of the distinctions; it is the harmony of the perspectives. The harmony is not the absence of
the distinction; it is the recognition that the distinctions are relative; the recognition that the
perspectives are partial; the recognition that the things are equal in their relativity. The harmony
is the Dao; it is the way; it is the flow.



68.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Laozi and Zhuangzi is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Dao. The traditional reading takes the Dao to be a
metaphysical principle: it is the source; it is the principle; it is the way. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a linguistic device: it is the limit of the language; it is the silence; it is not a
principle. The two readings disagree on whether Daoism is a metaphysics or a mysticism, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a
structural realism, not a mysticism.


Second dispute: the status of non-action. The traditional reading takes non-action to
be a practical doctrine: it is the letting-be; it is the non-interference. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a political doctrine: it is the minimal government; it is the non- intervention of
the ruler. The two readings disagree on whether Daoism is a practical philosophy or a political
philosophy, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
manifestation is real, not a political order.


Third dispute: the status of the equality of things. The traditional reading takes the
equality to be a metaphysical doctrine: the things are equal in their relativity. A revisionary
reading takes it to be an epistemological doctrine: the perspectives are partial; the distinctions
are relative. The two readings disagree on whether Daoism is a metaphysics or an epistemology,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is
a structural realism, not an epistemology.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Daoism is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the Dao. If
Daoism is a mysticism, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a mysticism.
The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Daodejing, but it does not rest its
case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.
68.5. Points of Convergence                                                                       769


68.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

  With Laozi and Zhuangzi. The framework shares four structural features with the
   Daoist position.

       1. The rejection of the absolutism. Laozi holds that the Dao is ineffable; the Dao cannot
          be named; the Dao cannot be conceptualized. Zhuangzi holds that the distinctions
          are relative; the perspectives are partial; the things are equal in their relativity. The
          framework holds that the identity is a structural condition; it is not an absolute; it
          is the invariance enacted by one source. Both reject the absolutism; both hold that
          the reality is not the absolute.

       2. The naturalness. Laozi holds that the naturalness is the spontaneity; the naturalness
          is the self-so; the naturalness is the nature. The framework holds that the expression
          is a structural tendency; the expression is the enactment; the expression is the
          manifestation. Both hold that there is a naturalness, and that the naturalness is the
          flow.

       3. The transformation. Zhuangzi holds that the things are in transformation; they are
          in change; they are in becoming. The framework holds that the manifestations are
          in transformation; they are in change; they are in becoming. Both hold that there is
          a transformation, and that the transformation is the reality.

       4. The harmony. Laozi holds that the sage is in harmony with the Dao; the sage is in
          harmony with the nature; the sage is in harmony with the flow. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is
          the harmony with the structure; the reconstruction is the harmony with the identity.
          Both hold that there is a harmony, and that the harmony is the goal.



68.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

  With Laozi and Zhuangzi. The framework diverges from the Daoist position in four
   respects.

       1. The status of the Dao. Laozi holds that the Dao is the ineffable source; the Dao is
          the principle; the Dao is the way. The framework holds that the structure is not the
          Dao; it is the invariance; it is the structural condition. The framework’s structure is
          not ineffable; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of non-action. Laozi holds that the non-action is the letting-be; the non-
          action is the non-interference. The framework holds that the expression is a structural
770                                                               Chapter 68. Laozi and Zhuangzi


          tendency; the expression is the enactment; the expression is the manifestation. The
          framework’s expression is not the non-action; it is the structure.

       3. The status of the equality. Zhuangzi holds that the things are equal in their relativity;
          the distinctions are relative; the perspectives are partial. The framework holds that
          the manifestations are real; the manifestations are the expressions of the identity;
          the manifestations are not equal. The framework’s manifestation is real, not equal.

       4. The status of the sage. Zhuangzi holds that the sage is the one who has fasted the
          mind; the one who has achieved the free wandering; the one who is in harmony with
          the Dao. The framework holds that the sage is the one who has reconstructed the
          identity; the one who has read the manifestations; the one who is in harmony with
          the structure. The framework’s sage is structural, not mystical.



68.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Laozi’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
  its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not the
  Dao; it is a pattern. The Dao is the ineffable; the Dao is the source; the Dao is the way.
  The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the Dao. The framework’s
  ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the Dao.
  Zhuangzi’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
  real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they are
  the levels of the transformation; they are the levels of the flow. The framework’s realms
  are not levels of the transformation; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an
  ontology of levels, not of transformation.
  Zhuangzi’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the equality of things; it is the free
  wandering; it is the harmony. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not
  the equality. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of
  equality.



68.8      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to Laozi’s objection. The framework agrees that the Dao is ineffable, and it
  agrees that the source is the principle. But the framework denies that its identity is only
  a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in
  the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
68.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                    771


   framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is
   one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The
   distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the
   framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Zhuangzi’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the transformation. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of
   the transformation. The distinction is between a level of the transformation (a processual
   level) and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second,
   not the first.
   Reply to Zhuangzi’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that
   the concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be
   the equality. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   an equality (a harmony) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second,
   not the first.



68.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Laozi and Zhuangzi’s cost. If Laozi and Zhuangzi accept the framework’s reply, they must
give up the claim that the Dao is the ineffable. They must accept that the structure is the
condition of the manifestation, and that the structure is not the Dao. The cost is the loss of the
ineffability: the Dao is no longer the ineffable; the structure is the condition. They must also
give up the claim that the non-action is the goal; they must accept that the expression is the
goal; the expression is the enactment of the identity.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Laozi and Zhuangzi, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the Dao, of the non-action, of the transformation—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the Dao, and the framework leaves the Dao to a
separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Laozi’s Dao and Zhuangzi’s
transformation are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Laozi and Zhuangzi must accept that the framework’s structure is not a
pattern; it is a structural condition that the Dao and the transformation presuppose as their
772                                                             Chapter 68. Laozi and Zhuangzi


condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not
rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


68.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Laozi’s
   term “the Dao.” If one substitutes “the Dao” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; the Dao is the ineffable source, and it is not manifested,
   because it is the source. The framework’s identity is multiple; the Dao is one. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Laozi’s term “the non-action.”
   If one substitutes “the non-action” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the non-action is
   the letting-be. The framework’s expression is structural; the non-action is practical. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Zhuangzi’s term “the
   equality of things.” If one substitutes “the equality of things” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a
   reading of the manifestations; the equality is the harmony of the things. The framework’s
   reconstruction is structural; the equality is harmonious. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Laozi and Zhuangzi
   is resemblance: both reject the absolutism, and they differ on whether the rejection
   leaves a structure or the Dao. Both hold that there is a transformation, and they
   differ on whether the transformation is the flow or the expression. Neither relation is
   equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Laozi and
   Zhuangzi would be refuted by showing that their Dao cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and Dao—by showing, that is, that they already
   distinguish the structural condition from the Dao, and that the framework’s distinction is
   a development of their own.



68.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.

First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Laozi’s Dao or Zhuangzi’s
transformation, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Laozi’s Dao is already a structural
condition, or that Zhuangzi’s transformation is already a structural condition, has a question the
chapter leaves open.
68.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 773


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi do justice
to the texts? The chapter has used the Dao, the non-action, the naturalness, the weakness and
the softness, the return to the root, the relativity of the distinctions, the transformation of things,
the fasting of the mind, the free wandering, and the equality of things, and it has stated what
would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a
question the chapter leaves open.
