theirs. The present chapter has stated the Neo-Confucian answer to the problem of the principle;
the next chapter states the Chinese Buddhist answer, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 71

Chinese Buddhism


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Chinese Buddhism, the tradition that arose from the
encounter of Indian Buddhism with Chinese thought and developed into the distinctive schools
of Chan (Zen) and Pure Land. It states the Chan doctrine of the Buddha-nature (foxing), the
sudden enlightenment (dunwu), the no-thought (wunian), the seeing of the nature (jianxing), and
the transmission outside the scriptures (jiaowai biechuan); and it states the Pure Land doctrine
of Amitābha (Amituo), the faith (xin), the vow (yuan), the recitation of the name (nianfo), and
the rebirth in the Pure Land (jingtu); with reference to the Platform Sutra (Liuzu Tanjing), the
Lankāvatāra Sutra, the Sukhavativyuha Sutra, the Guan Wuliangshou Jing, and the Compendium
of the Five Lamps (Wudeng Huiyuan); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of Chinese Buddhism; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of the nature and of the enlightenment is the nearest Chinese Buddhist analogue
to theirs; it presents the objections that Chan and Pure Land would raise against the framework;
it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of
relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “the Buddha-nature,” “sudden enlightenment,”
“no-thought,” “the Pure Land,” “Amitābha,” or “the recitation of the name,” these are the terms
of Chinese Buddhism, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not
by the framework.


71.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is sitting in meditation. She closes her eyes; she watches her breath; she
watches her thoughts. A thought arises: a memory of the past. Another thought arises: a plan
for the future. Another thought arises: a judgment about herself. The thoughts are many; the
mind is restless; the consciousness is scattered. She asks: how can I stop the thoughts? The Chan
master answers: you cannot stop the thoughts; you can only see their nature. The thoughts are
empty; the thoughts are the Buddha-nature; the thoughts are not other than the Buddha-nature.
The stopping of the thoughts is not the goal; the seeing of the nature is the goal.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not how to stop the thoughts, or how to see the
nature, but what the Buddha-nature is. The Buddha-nature is not a thing; it is not a substance;
it is not a property. The Buddha-nature is the nature of the mind; it is the original nature; it is
the pure nature. The Buddha-nature is in all beings; it is the potentiality of the enlightenment;
it is the seed of the Buddhahood. The Buddha-nature is not the mind; it is not the body; it is
the nature; it is the source.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the Buddha-nature is, or
how to see it, but what the enlightenment is. The enlightenment is not the gradual realization; it

                                               801
802                                                               Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


is not the accumulation of the knowledge; it is not the result of the practice. The enlightenment is
the sudden realization; it is the immediate seeing; it is the direct experience. The enlightenment
is not the gradual; it is the sudden; it is the instantaneous. The enlightenment is the seeing of
the nature; it is the recognition of the Buddha-nature; it is the realization of the Buddhahood.
      The scene is the image of Chinese Buddhism, in the Platform Sutra and in the Wudeng
Huiyuan, of the structure of the enlightenment. The thoughts are the mind; the Buddha-nature
is the nature; the enlightenment is the sudden seeing. The scene poses the question that Chinese
Buddhism was the first to pose in its full form in the Chinese tradition. What is the Buddha-
nature? How is the enlightenment achieved? And what is the relation between the sudden and
the gradual? The present chapter states the Chinese Buddhist answer, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.


71.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming: the principle and
the material force, the investigation of things, the extension of knowledge, the sincerity of the
will, the cultivation of the person, the mind as the principle, the unity of knowledge and action,
the extension of the innate knowing, and the critique of Zhu Xi. The Neo-Confucian tradition
has asked what the principle is, and how the principle is to be known. The Chinese Buddhist
tradition has asked what the Buddha-nature is, and how the enlightenment is to be achieved.
The present chapter states the Chinese Buddhist position, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether Chinese Buddhism was right. The question is what it held, what
it can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Chinese Buddhism hold? The chapter states the Chan
doctrine of the Buddha-nature, the sudden enlightenment, the no-thought, the seeing of the
nature, and the transmission outside the scriptures; and the Pure Land doctrine of Amitābha,
the faith, the vow, the recitation of the name, and the rebirth in the Pure Land, with reference to
the Platform Sutra, the Lankāvatāra Sutra, the Sukhavativyuha Sutra, and the Wudeng Huiyuan.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the Chinese Buddhist tradition
converge, and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence,
and it presents the objections that Chan and Pure Land would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the
Chinese Buddhist tradition? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation
as resemblance, not equivalence.


71.3       The Position
71.3. The Position                                                                              803


71.3.1    Chan: The Buddha-Nature (Foxing)

The Chan doctrine of the Buddha-nature is stated in the Platform Sutra and in the Lankāvatāra
Sutra. The Buddha-nature is the nature of the mind; it is the original nature; it is the pure
nature.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the Buddha-nature as the mind. The Buddha-nature is the nature of the
mind; it is the original nature; it is the pure nature. The Buddha-nature is not a thing; it is
not a substance; it is not a property. The Buddha-nature is the mind itself; it is the nature of
the mind; it is the source of the enlightenment. The Buddha-nature is in all beings; it is the
potentiality of the Buddhahood.


Second feature: the Buddha-nature as the pure nature. The Buddha-nature is the
pure nature; it is the nature that is not defiled; it is the nature that is not obscured. The
Buddha-nature is the original purity; it is the original clarity; it is the original luminosity. The
defilements are not the nature; they are the adventitious; they are the accidental; they are
the removable. The Buddha-nature is the pure nature; it is the nature that remains when the
defilements are removed.


Third feature: the Buddha-nature as the potentiality. The Buddha-nature is the
potentiality of the Buddhahood; it is the seed of the enlightenment; it is the capacity of the
awakening. The Buddha-nature is not the Buddhahood; it is the potentiality; it is the capacity;
it is the seed. The Buddhahood is the actualization; it is the realization; it is the fruit. The
Buddha-nature is the potentiality; the Buddhahood is the actuality.

   From the Tradition

   “The Buddha-nature is the nature of the mind; it is the original nature; it is the pure
   nature. The Buddha-nature is in all beings; it is the potentiality of the Buddhahood.”
   (Platform Sutra, trans. after Yampolsky)



71.3.2    Chan: The Sudden Enlightenment (Dunwu)

The Chan doctrine of the sudden enlightenment is stated in the Platform Sutra and in the
Wudeng Huiyuan. The sudden enlightenment is the immediate realization; it is the direct seeing;
it is the instantaneous awakening.
   The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the suddenness. The enlightenment is sudden; it is not gradual; it is not
the accumulation of the knowledge; it is not the result of the practice. The enlightenment
is the sudden realization; it is the immediate seeing; it is the instantaneous awakening. The
enlightenment is not the gradual; it is the sudden; it is the instantaneous.
804                                                               Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


Second feature: the directness. The enlightenment is direct; it is not mediated; it is not
conceptual; it is not the inference. The enlightenment is the direct seeing; it is the immediate
experience; it is the intuitive realization. The enlightenment is not the concept; it is not the
inference; it is the direct.


Third feature: the seeing of the nature. The seeing of the nature (jianxing) is the
recognition of the Buddha-nature; it is the realization of the original nature; it is the awakening
to the Buddhahood. The seeing is not the knowledge; it is not the concept; it is the experience.
The seeing is the enlightenment; the enlightenment is the seeing; the two are the same.


71.3.3      Chan: The No-Thought (Wunian)

The Chan doctrine of the no-thought is stated in the Platform Sutra. The no-thought is the
absence of the thought; it is the stillness of the mind; it is the purity of the consciousness.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the no-thought. The no-thought (wunian) is the absence of the thought;
it is the stillness of the mind; it is the purity of the consciousness. The no-thought is not the
suppression of the thought; it is not the elimination of the thought; it is the freedom from the
thought. The no-thought is the thought without the attachment; it is the thought without the
clinging; it is the thought without the defilement.


Second feature: the thought. The thought is not the enemy; it is not the obstacle; it is not
the defilement. The thought is the function of the nature; it is the activity of the mind; it is
the expression of the Buddha-nature. The thought is not the problem; the attachment is the
problem; the clinging is the problem; the defilement is the problem.


Third feature: the freedom. The freedom is the freedom from the attachment; it is the
freedom from the clinging; it is the freedom from the defilement. The freedom is not the absence
of the thought; it is the presence of the thought without the attachment. The freedom is the
no-thought; the no-thought is the freedom.


71.3.4      Chan: The Transmission Outside the Scriptures (Jiaowai Biechuan)

The Chan doctrine of the transmission outside the scriptures is stated in the Wudeng Huiyuan
and in the Platform Sutra. The transmission is the direct transmission; it is the mind-to-mind
transmission; it is the transmission outside the scriptures.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the transmission. The transmission is the direct transmission; it is the
mind-to-mind transmission; it is the transmission outside the scriptures. The transmission is not
the verbal; it is not the scriptural; it is not the conceptual. The transmission is the direct; it is
the immediate; it is the intuitive.
71.3. The Position                                                                               805


Second feature: the outside the scriptures. The outside the scriptures (jiaowai) is the
outside the verbal; it is the outside the conceptual; it is the outside the scriptural. The outside
the scriptures is not the rejection of the scriptures; it is the recognition that the scriptures are
the finger; they are not the moon. The scriptures are the means; they are not the end; they are
the finger; they are not the moon.


Third feature: the separate transmission. The separate transmission (biechuan) is the
separate transmission; it is the transmission that is not the scriptural; it is the transmission that
is the mind-to-mind. The separate transmission is the transmission of the Buddha-nature; it is
the transmission of the enlightenment; it is the transmission of the awakening.


71.3.5    Pure Land: Amitābha (Amituo)

The Pure Land doctrine of Amitābha is stated in the Sukhavativyuha Sutra and in the Guan
Wuliangshou Jing. Amitābha is the Buddha of the Infinite Light; he is the Buddha of the Infinite
Life; he is the Buddha of the Pure Land.
    The doctrine has three features.


First feature: Amitābha. Amitābha is the Buddha of the Infinite Light; he is the Buddha of
the Infinite Life; he is the Buddha of the Pure Land. Amitābha is not the historical Buddha; he
is the celestial Buddha; he is the Buddha of the faith. Amitābha is the savior; he is the refuge;
he is the hope.


Second feature: the Pure Land. The Pure Land is the land of the bliss; it is the land of
the purity; it is the land of the enlightenment. The Pure Land is not the paradise; it is not the
heaven; it is the land of the Buddha. The Pure Land is the land of the practice; it is the land of
the realization; it is the land of the Buddhahood.


Third feature: the vow. The vow (yuan) is the vow of Amitābha; it is the vow to save all
beings; it is the vow to bring all beings to the Pure Land. The vow is the foundation; it is the
condition; it is the cause. The vow is the grace; it is the power; it is the salvation.


71.3.6    Pure Land: The Faith (Xin) and the Recitation of the Name (Nianfo)

The Pure Land doctrine of the faith and the recitation of the name is stated in the Sukhavativyuha
Sutra and in the Guan Wuliangshou Jing. The faith is the trust in Amitābha; the recitation is
the calling of the name.
    The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the faith. The faith (xin) is the trust in Amitābha; it is the reliance on the
vow; it is the confidence in the salvation. The faith is not the knowledge; it is not the concept; it
is not the inference. The faith is the trust; it is the reliance; it is the confidence.
806                                                                 Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


Second feature: the recitation. The recitation (nianfo) is the calling of the name; it is the
repetition of the name; it is the invocation of the Buddha. The recitation is not the meditation;
it is not the study; it is not the philosophy. The recitation is the practice; it is the devotion; it is
the faith.


Third feature: the rebirth. The rebirth (jingtu) is the rebirth in the Pure Land; it is the
entry into the land of the Buddha; it is the attainment of the Buddhahood. The rebirth is not
the death; it is not the annihilation; it is not the extinction. The rebirth is the transformation; it
is the realization; it is the salvation.



71.4         Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Chinese Buddhism is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Buddha-nature. The traditional reading takes the
Buddha-nature to be a metaphysical reality: it is the nature of the mind; it is the original
nature; it is the pure nature. A revisionary reading takes it to be a soteriological concept: it
is the potentiality of the enlightenment; it is the capacity of the awakening. The two readings
disagree on whether Chan is a metaphysics or a soteriology, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a soteriology.


Second dispute: the status of the sudden enlightenment. The traditional reading takes
the sudden enlightenment to be a real event: it is the immediate realization; it is the direct
seeing; it is the instantaneous awakening. A revisionary reading takes it to be a rhetorical device:
it is a way of speaking about the enlightenment; it is not a real event; it is a metaphor. The two
readings disagree on whether Chan is a realism or a rhetoric, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a metaphor.


Third dispute: the relation between Chan and Pure Land. The traditional reading
takes Chan and Pure Land to be rivals: Chan is the path of the self-power; Pure Land is the path
of the other-power; the two are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary:
Chan provides the wisdom; Pure Land provides the faith; the two are the two sides of the one.
The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a rival nor a complement.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Chan is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the Buddha-
nature. If Pure Land is a devotionalism, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism
and a devotionalism. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Platform Sutra,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.
71.5. Points of Convergence                                                                         807


71.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Chan. The framework shares three structural features with the Chan position.

       1. The nature. Chan holds that the Buddha-nature is the nature of the mind; it is the
          original nature; it is the pure nature. The framework holds that the identity is the
          invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. Both hold that there is a nature,
          and that the nature is the original.

       2. The seeing. Chan holds that the enlightenment is the seeing of the nature; it is the
          recognition of the Buddha-nature; it is the realization of the Buddhahood. The
          framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
          the recognition of the identity; it is the realization of the structure. Both hold that
          there is a seeing, and that the seeing is the realization.

       3. The no-thought. Chan holds that the no-thought is the absence of the thought; it is
          the stillness of the mind; it is the purity of the consciousness. The framework holds
          that the structure is the stillness of the manifestation; it is the purity of the identity;
          it is the condition of the expression. Both hold that there is a stillness, and that the
          stillness is the freedom.

   With Pure Land. The framework shares three structural features with the Pure Land
   position.

       1. The faith. Pure Land holds that the faith is the trust in Amitābha; it is the reliance
          on the vow; it is the confidence in the salvation. The framework holds that the
          reconstruction is the trust in the structure; it is the reliance on the identity; it is the
          confidence in the manifestation. Both hold that there is a faith, and that the faith
          is the trust.

       2. The vow. Pure Land holds that the vow is the vow of Amitābha; it is the vow to
          save all beings; it is the vow to bring all beings to the Pure Land. The framework
          holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is the condition of
          the expression; it is the condition of the salvation. Both hold that there is a vow,
          and that the vow is the condition.

       3. The rebirth. Pure Land holds that the rebirth is the rebirth in the Pure Land; it
          is the entry into the land of the Buddha; it is the attainment of the Buddhahood.
         The framework holds that the reconstruction is the rebirth in the structure; it is the
          entry into the identity; it is the attainment of the manifestation. Both hold that
          there is a rebirth, and that the rebirth is the goal.
808                                                                Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


71.6      Points of Divergence


  Points of Divergence

  With Chan. The framework diverges from the Chan position in three respects.

       1. The status of the Buddha-nature. Chan holds that the Buddha-nature is the nature
         of the mind; it is the original nature; it is the pure nature. The framework holds that
         the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. The framework’s
         identity is not the Buddha-nature; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of the sudden enlightenment. Chan holds that the enlightenment is the
         sudden realization; it is the immediate seeing; it is the instantaneous awakening. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is the gradual reading; it is the mediated
         understanding; it is the progressive realization. The framework’s reconstruction is
         not the sudden enlightenment; it is the gradual reading.

       3. The status of the no-thought. Chan holds that the no-thought is the absence of the
         thought; it is the stillness of the mind; it is the purity of the consciousness. The
         framework holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is the
         invariance; it is the expression. The framework’s structure is not the no-thought; it
         is the condition of the thought.

  With Pure Land. The framework diverges from the Pure Land position in three respects.

       1. The status of Amitābha. Pure Land holds that Amitābha is the Buddha of the
         Infinite Light; he is the Buddha of the Pure Land; he is the savior. The framework
         holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. The
         framework’s identity is not the Buddha; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of the faith. Pure Land holds that the faith is the trust in Amitābha; it
         is the reliance on the vow; it is the confidence in the salvation. The framework holds
         that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the understanding
         of the identity; it is the realization of the structure. The framework’s reconstruction
         is not the faith; it is the reading.

       3. The status of the rebirth. Pure Land holds that the rebirth is the rebirth in the
         Pure Land; it is the entry into the land of the Buddha; it is the attainment of the
         Buddhahood. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the realization of the
         identity; it is the attainment of the structure; it is the expression of the manifestation.
         The framework’s reconstruction is not the rebirth; it is the realization.
71.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  809


71.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Chan’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
   its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not the
   Buddha-nature; it is a pattern. The Buddha-nature is the nature of the mind; the Buddha-
   nature is the original nature; the Buddha-nature is the pure nature. The framework’s
   identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the Buddha-nature. The framework’s ontology
   is an ontology of patterns, not of the Buddha-nature.
   Pure Land’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
   are the levels of the Pure Land; they are the levels of the Buddhahood. The framework’s
   realms are not levels of the Pure Land; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is
   an ontology of levels, not of the Pure Land.
   Pure Land’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the faith; it is the recitation of the
   name; it is the rebirth in the Pure Land. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction;
   it is not the faith. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction,
   not of the faith.


71.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Chan’s objection. The framework agrees that the Buddha-nature is the
   original nature, and it agrees that the Buddha-nature is the pure nature. But the framework
   denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
   by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of
   the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural
   condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what
   the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an
   enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Pure Land’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not
   just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the Pure Land. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   Pure Land. The distinction is between a level of the Pure Land (a devotional level) and a
   level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Pure Land’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the faith.
   The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it
810                                                               Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


   is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a faith (a trust)
   and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.




71.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Chan’s cost. If Chan accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the Buddha-
nature is the nature of the mind. It must accept that the identity is the structure, and that the
Buddha-nature is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of the Buddha-nature:
the Buddha-nature is no longer the nature of the mind; the structure is the condition. It must
also give up the claim that the enlightenment is the sudden realization; it must accept that the
reconstruction is the gradual reading; the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.



Pure Land’s cost. If Pure Land accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that
Amitābha is the Buddha of the Infinite Light. It must accept that the identity is the structure,
and that Amitābha is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of Amitābha: Amitābha
is no longer the Buddha; the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that
the faith is the trust in Amitābha; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the
manifestations; the reconstruction is the reading.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Chan and Pure Land, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the Buddha-nature, of the sudden enlightenment, of the faith—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the Buddha-nature, and the
framework leaves the Buddha-nature to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Chan’s Buddha-nature
and Pure Land’s faith are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Chan and Pure Land must accept that the framework’s structure is
not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the Buddha-nature and the faith presuppose as
their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three
are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.
71.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                    811


71.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Chan). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Chan’s term “the Buddha-nature.” If one substitutes “the Buddha-nature” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the Buddha-nature is
   the nature of the mind, and it is not manifested, because it is the nature. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; the Buddha-nature is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Chan’s term “the sudden
   enlightenment.” If one substitutes “the sudden enlightenment” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is
   a reading of the manifestations; the sudden enlightenment is the immediate realization.
   The framework’s reconstruction is gradual; the sudden enlightenment is sudden. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Pure Land). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for Pure Land’s term “Amitābha.” If one substitutes “Amitābha” for “identity” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invari-
   ance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; Amitābha is the Buddha of the
   Infinite Light, and it is not manifested, because it is the Buddha. The framework’s identity
   is multiple; Amitābha is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Pure Land’s term “the
   faith.” If one substitutes “the faith” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   the faith is the trust in Amitābha. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the faith
   is devotional. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Chan is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a nature, and they differ on whether the nature is the Buddha-nature
   or the structure. The relation between the framework and Pure Land is resemblance: both
   hold that there is a faith, and they differ on whether the faith is the trust in Amitābha or
   the reconstruction of the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Chinese Buddhism would be refuted
   by showing that the Buddha-nature and the faith cannot be formulated without the
   framework’s distinction between structure and nature, or between structure and faith—by
   showing, that is, that Chinese Buddhism already distinguishes the structural condition
   from the nature and the faith, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of
   its own.
812                                                             Chapter 71. Chinese Buddhism


71.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Chan’s Buddha-nature or Pure
Land’s faith, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Chan’s Buddha-nature is already a
structural condition, or that Pure Land’s faith is already a structural condition, has a question
the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Platform Sutra, the Lankāvatāra Sutra,
and the Sukhavativyuha Sutra do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the Buddha-nature,
the sudden enlightenment, the no-thought, the seeing of the nature, the transmission outside the
scriptures, the Amitābha, the faith, the vow, the recitation of the name, and the rebirth in the
Pure Land, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts
support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a nature and a faith—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the nature that is seen, or the faith that trusts? Is the truth the sudden
enlightenment that awakens, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell
you about the relation between Chan’s Buddha-nature, Pure Land’s faith, and the framework’s
identity?

Part X is now complete. The dialogues with the five great schools of Chinese philosophy—
Confucius and Mencius, Laozi and Zhuangzi, Mozi and Han Feizi, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming,
and Chinese Buddhism—have been stated. Part XI turns to Japanese philosophy. The first
dialogue is with Shinto, on the kami and the purity; the next with Dōgen and Shinran, on the
Buddha-nature and the faith; and the last with the Kyoto School, on the nothingness and the
world. The Chinese tradition has asked what the way is, and how the human being is to live; the
Japanese tradition will ask what the kami is, and what the nothingness is.
      Part XI

Japanese Philosophy




        814
Chapter 72

Shinto


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Shinto (the Way of the Kami), the indigenous religious
and philosophical tradition of Japan. It states the Shinto account of the kami (the divine beings),
the purity (kiyome) and the pollution (kegare), the Musubi (the generative power), the three
imperial regalia (sanshu no jingi), the relation between the kami and the human being, and
the Shinto view of the world as a sacred order; with reference to the Kojiki (Record of Ancient
Matters), the Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), the Engishiki (Procedures of the Engi Era),
and the Norito (Shinto Prayers); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of
Shinto; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of
the sacred and of the manifestation is the nearest Japanese analogue to Shinto; it presents the
objections that Shinto would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute
the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “kami,” “purity,” “pollution,” “Musubi,” or “the sacred,” these are Shinto’s terms, and
their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


72.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing before a waterfall. The water falls from the cliff; it crashes on
the rocks; it flows into the river. She stands under the waterfall; the cold water pours over her;
her body is cleansed; her mind is stilled; her spirit is purified. She is not praying to the waterfall;
she is not worshipping the water; she is entering the presence of the kami. The waterfall is not
the kami; the waterfall is the place where the kami is present; the waterfall is the sacred space;
the waterfall is the manifestation of the kami.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the waterfall is, or how it purifies,
but what the kami is. The kami is not a god; it is not a spirit; it is not a person. The kami
is the divine being; it is the sacred presence; it is the power of the nature. The kami is in the
mountain, in the river, in the tree, in the rock, in the ancestor, in the emperor. The kami is not
the thing; it is the presence in the thing; it is the power in the thing; it is the sacred in the thing.
The kami is the Musubi; it is the generative power; it is the power of the life; it is the power of
the creation.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the waterfall is, or what
the kami is, but what the purity is. The purity is not the cleanliness; it is not the hygiene; it is
not the physical purity. The purity is the spiritual purity; it is the purity of the heart; it is the
purity of the relation to the kami. The purity is the condition of the presence; it is the condition
of the communion; it is the condition of the blessing. The purity is the kiyome; the pollution is
the kegare; the two are the two conditions of the relation to the kami.

                                                 815
816                                                                             Chapter 72. Shinto


      The scene is the Shinto image, in the Kojiki and in the Norito, of the structure of the sacred.
The waterfall is the sacred space; the kami is the sacred presence; the purity is the condition of
the communion. The scene poses the question that Shinto was the first to pose in its full form
in the Japanese tradition. What is the kami? What is the sacred? And what is the relation
between the human being and the kami? The present chapter states the Shinto answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.


72.2        The Question
The previous part stated the positions of Chinese philosophy: Confucius and Mencius, Laozi
and Zhuangzi, Mozi and Han Feizi, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, and Chinese Buddhism. The
Chinese tradition has asked what the way is, and how the human being is to live. The present
part turns to Japanese philosophy, and its first dialogue is with Shinto, the indigenous tradition
of Japan. The Shinto tradition has asked what the kami is, and what the sacred is.
      The question is not whether Shinto was right. The question is what it held, what it can say
to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts, and the
chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Shinto hold? The chapter states the kami, the purity
and the pollution, the Musubi, the three imperial regalia, the relation between the kami and the
human being, and the sacred order of the world, with reference to the Kojiki, the Nihon Shoki,
the Engishiki, and the Norito.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Shinto converge, and where do
they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it presents the
objections that Shinto would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Shinto?
The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not equivalence.


72.3        The Position

72.3.1      The Kami

The Shinto account of the kami is stated in the Kojiki and in the Nihon Shoki. The kami is the
divine being; it is the sacred presence; it is the power of the nature.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the kami as the divine being. The kami is the divine being; it is the sacred
presence; it is the power of the nature. The kami is not a god; it is not a spirit; it is not a person.
The kami is the presence in the thing; it is the power in the thing; it is the sacred in the thing.
The kami is in the mountain, in the river, in the tree, in the rock, in the ancestor, in the emperor.
72.3. The Position                                                                               817


Second feature: the kami as the many. The kami is not one; the kami is many. There
are the kami of the heaven; there are the kami of the earth; there are the kami of the ancestors;
there are the kami of the emperors. The many kami are not the many gods; they are the many
presences; they are the many powers; they are the many manifestations. The many kami are the
many aspects of the one sacred; they are the many faces of the one power.


Third feature: the kami as the relation. The kami is not the distant; it is not the
transcendent; it is not the otherworldly. The kami is the near; it is the immanent; it is the
present. The kami is in the world; it is in the nature; it is in the human being. The relation
between the human being and the kami is the relation of the presence; it is the relation of the
communion; it is the relation of the blessing.

   From the Tradition

   “The kami are the many presences of the sacred; they are the many powers of the nature;
   they are the many faces of the one power.” (Kojiki, trans. after Philippi)



72.3.2    The Purity (Kiyome) and the Pollution (Kegare)

The Shinto account of purity and pollution is stated in the Engishiki and in the Norito. The
purity is the spiritual purity; the pollution is the spiritual pollution.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the purity. The purity (kiyome) is the spiritual purity; it is the purity of the
heart; it is the purity of the relation to the kami. The purity is the condition of the presence;
it is the condition of the communion; it is the condition of the blessing. The purity is not the
cleanliness; it is not the hygiene; it is not the physical purity.


Second feature: the pollution. The pollution (kegare) is the spiritual pollution; it is the
impurity of the heart; it is the impurity of the relation to the kami. The pollution is the obstacle
to the presence; it is the obstacle to the communion; it is the obstacle to the blessing. The
pollution is not the dirt; it is not the filth; it is not the physical pollution.


Third feature: the purification. The purification (harai) is the removal of the pollution; it
is the restoration of the purity; it is the renewal of the relation to the kami. The purification is
the ritual; it is the washing; it is the cleansing. The purification is the condition of the presence;
it is the condition of the communion; it is the condition of the blessing.


72.3.3    The Musubi

The Shinto account of Musubi is stated in the Kojiki and in the Nihon Shoki. The Musubi is the
generative power; it is the power of the life; it is the power of the creation.
   The account has three features.
818                                                                              Chapter 72. Shinto


First feature: the generative power. The Musubi is the generative power; it is the power
of the life; it is the power of the creation. The Musubi is the power that produces the world; it is
the power that produces the beings; it is the power that produces the life. The Musubi is the
source of the world; it is the source of the beings; it is the source of the life.


Second feature: the two aspects. The Musubi has two aspects: the Takamimusubi (the high
august generative power) and the Kamimusubi (the divine generative power). The two aspects
are the two powers; they are the two principles; they are the two sources. The Takamimusubi is
the power of the heaven; the Kamimusubi is the power of the earth; the two are the two aspects
of the one Musubi.


Third feature: the harmony. The Musubi is the harmony; it is the harmony of the heaven
and the earth; it is the harmony of the kami and the human being; it is the harmony of the
nature and the culture. The harmony is the order; it is the sacred order; it is the order of the
world.


72.3.4      The Three Imperial Regalia (Sanshu no Jingi)
The Shinto account of the three imperial regalia is stated in the Kojiki and in the Nihon Shoki.
The three regalia are the mirror, the sword, and the jewel; they are the symbols of the imperial
authority; they are the symbols of the sacred.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the mirror. The mirror (yata no kagami) is the symbol of the wisdom; it is
the symbol of the truth; it is the symbol of the sacred. The mirror reflects the image; it reflects
the truth; it reflects the sacred. The mirror is the symbol of the Amaterasu (the sun goddess); it
is the symbol of the imperial ancestor.


Second feature: the sword. The sword (kusanagi no tsurugi) is the symbol of the power; it
is the symbol of the valor; it is the symbol of the sacred. The sword cuts the evil; it cuts the
pollution; it cuts the obstacle. The sword is the symbol of the Susanoo (the storm god); it is the
symbol of the imperial power.


Third feature: the jewel. The jewel (yasakani no magatama) is the symbol of the benevolence;
it is the symbol of the compassion; it is the symbol of the sacred. The jewel is the gift; it is the
offering; it is the blessing. The jewel is the symbol of the imperial benevolence; it is the symbol
of the imperial grace.


72.3.5      The Relation Between the Kami and the Human Being
The Shinto account of the relation between the kami and the human being is stated in the Kojiki
and in the Norito. The relation is the relation of the presence; it is the relation of the communion;
it is the relation of the blessing.
      The account has three features.
72.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             819


First feature: the presence. The kami is present in the world; it is present in the nature; it
is present in the human being. The presence is not the distant; it is not the transcendent; it is
not the otherworldly. The presence is the near; it is the immanent; it is the present. The human
being is in the presence of the kami; the human being is in the communion with the kami; the
human being is in the blessing of the kami.


Second feature: the communion. The communion is the relation; it is the relation of the
presence; it is the relation of the blessing. The communion is the ritual; it is the festival; it is the
offering. The communion is the condition of the blessing; it is the condition of the harmony; it is
the condition of the sacred order.


Third feature: the blessing. The blessing is the gift; it is the grace; it is the power. The
blessing is the gift of the kami; it is the grace of the kami; it is the power of the kami. The
blessing is the condition of the life; it is the condition of the prosperity; it is the condition of the
harmony.


72.3.6     The Sacred Order of the World

The Shinto account of the sacred order of the world is stated in the Kojiki and in the Nihon
Shoki. The world is the sacred order; it is the order of the kami; it is the order of the nature.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the sacred order. The world is the sacred order; it is the order of the kami;
it is the order of the nature. The world is not the chaos; it is not the disorder; it is not the
arbitrary. The world is the order; it is the harmony; it is the sacred.


Second feature: the harmony. The harmony is the harmony of the heaven and the earth;
it is the harmony of the kami and the human being; it is the harmony of the nature and the
culture. The harmony is the order; it is the sacred order; it is the order of the world.


Third feature: the human being. The human being is the part of the sacred order; it is
the part of the harmony; it is the part of the world. The human being is not the master; it is not
the conqueror; it is not the exploiter. The human being is the participant; it is the caretaker; it
is the part of the sacred order.


72.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Shinto is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the kami. The traditional reading takes the kami to be a
divine being: it is the sacred presence; it is the power of the nature. A revisionary reading
takes it to be a symbol: it is a way of speaking about the sacred; it is not a divine being. The
two readings disagree on whether Shinto is a polytheism or a symbolism, and the disagreement
820                                                                               Chapter 72. Shinto


matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a symbolism.

Second dispute: the status of purity. The traditional reading takes purity to be a spiritual
reality: it is the purity of the heart; it is the purity of the relation to the kami. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a social convention: it is a way of maintaining the order; it is not a spiritual
reality. The two readings disagree on whether Shinto is a spiritualism or a conventionalism, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is
real, not a convention.

Third dispute: the status of the sacred order. The traditional reading takes the sacred
order to be a cosmic reality: it is the order of the kami; it is the order of the nature. A revisionary
reading takes it to be a political ideology: it is a way of justifying the imperial power; it is not
a cosmic reality. The two readings disagree on whether Shinto is a cosmology or a political
ideology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, not an ideology.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Shinto is a polytheism, the framework’s dialogue
with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a polytheism. If Shinto is a symbolism,
the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a symbolism. The framework holds
that the first reading is closer to the Kojiki, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states
the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


72.5        Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Shinto. The framework shares four structural features with the Shinto position.

        1. The presence. Shinto holds that the kami is present in the world; it is present in
           the nature; it is present in the human being. The framework holds that the identity
           is present in the manifestation; it is present in the appearance; it is present in the
           expression. Both hold that there is a presence, and that the presence is the relation.

        2. The purity. Shinto holds that the purity is the spiritual purity; it is the purity of
           the heart; it is the purity of the relation to the kami. The framework holds that the
           reconstruction is the structural purity; it is the purity of the reading; it is the purity
           of the relation to the identity. Both hold that there is a purity, and that the purity
           is the condition.

        3. The Musubi. Shinto holds that the Musubi is the generative power; it is the power
           of the life; it is the power of the creation. The framework holds that the expression
           is the generative tendency; it is the tendency of the identity; it is the tendency of
           the manifestation. Both hold that there is a generation, and that the generation is
           the power.
72.6. Points of Divergence                                                                      821


       4. The sacred order. Shinto holds that the world is the sacred order; it is the order of
         the kami; it is the order of the nature. The framework holds that the world is the
         structural order; it is the order of the realms; it is the order of the manifestation.
         Both hold that there is an order, and that the order is the sacred.



72.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Shinto. The framework diverges from the Shinto position in four respects.

       1. The status of the kami. Shinto holds that the kami is the divine being; it is the
         sacred presence; it is the power of the nature. The framework holds that the identity
         is the structural condition; it is the invariance; it is the condition. The framework’s
         identity is not the kami; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of purity. Shinto holds that the purity is the spiritual purity; it is the
         purity of the heart; it is the purity of the relation to the kami. The framework holds
         that the reconstruction is the structural purity; it is the purity of the reading; it is
         the purity of the relation to the identity. The framework’s purity is not the spiritual
         purity; it is the structural purity.

       3. The status of the Musubi. Shinto holds that the Musubi is the generative power; it
         is the power of the life; it is the power of the creation. The framework holds that
         the expression is the generative tendency; it is the tendency of the identity; it is the
         tendency of the manifestation. The framework’s expression is not the Musubi; it is
         the structural tendency.

       4. The status of the sacred order. Shinto holds that the world is the sacred order; it
         is the order of the kami; it is the order of the nature. The framework holds that
         the world is the structural order; it is the order of the realms; it is the order of the
         manifestation. The framework’s order is not the sacred order; it is the structural
         order.



72.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Shinto’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not the kami; it is a pattern. The kami is the divine being; the kami is the sacred presence;
   the kami is the power of the nature. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern
   is not the kami. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the kami.
822                                                                            Chapter 72. Shinto


   Shinto’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
   are the levels of the sacred; they are the levels of the kami. The framework’s realms are
   not levels of the sacred; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
   levels, not of the sacred.
   Shinto’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
   the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the communion; it is the presence; it
   is the blessing. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the communion.
   The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the communion.



72.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the kami is the sacred presence,
   and it agrees that the kami is the power of the nature. But the framework denies that
   its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
   source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity
   in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the sacred. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they
   are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the sacred. The
   distinction is between a level of the sacred (a religious level) and a level of manifestation
   (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not
   capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the communion. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a communion (a
   presence) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



72.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Shinto’s cost. If Shinto accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the kami
is the divine being. It must accept that the identity is the structural condition, and that the
kami is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of the kami: the kami is no longer
72.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     823


the divine being; the identity is the structural condition. It must also give up the claim that the
purity is the spiritual purity; it must accept that the reconstruction is the structural purity; the
reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Shinto’s objections, it must give up the
claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the kami, of the sacred, of the communion—that its ontology does not capture.
The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s identity is the
enactment of a structure, but not the kami, and the framework leaves the kami to a separate
inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Shinto’s kami is not a
mistake; it is a dimension of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture. Shinto
must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the
kami presupposes as its condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


72.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Shinto’s
   term “the kami.” If one substitutes “the kami” for “identity” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; the kami is the divine being, and it is not manifested,
   because it is the divine. The framework’s identity is multiple; the kami is multiple. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “expression” is not substitutable for Shinto’s term “the Musubi.”
   If one substitutes “the Musubi” for “expression” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s expression is a structural tendency; the Musubi is
   the generative power. The framework’s expression is structural; the Musubi is generative.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Shinto’s term “the com-
   munion.” If one substitutes “the communion” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the communion is the presence of the kami. The framework’s reconstruc-
   tion is structural; the communion is religious. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Shinto is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a presence, and they differ on whether the presence is the kami
824                                                                          Chapter 72. Shinto


   or the identity. Both hold that there is an order, and they differ on whether the order is
   the sacred or the structural. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither
   is identity. The framework’s reading of Shinto would be refuted by showing that the
   kami cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and
   presence—by showing, that is, that Shinto already distinguishes the structural condition
   from the presence, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of Shinto’s own.




72.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Shinto’s kami, or is it a departure
from Shinto? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not conclusive.
A reader who holds that Shinto’s kami is already a structural condition, not a divine being, has
a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Kojiki, the Nihon Shoki, the Engishiki,
and the Norito do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the kami, the purity, the pollution,
the Musubi, the three imperial regalia, the relation between the kami and the human being, and
the sacred order of the world, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.
