A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a presence and a structure—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the presence that is sacred, or the structure that persists? Is the truth the
kami that is present, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you about
the relation between Shinto’s kami and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Dōgen and Shinran. It states Dōgen’s doctrine of the Buddha-nature,
the practice of zazen, the being-time (uji), and the shikantaza; and Shinran’s doctrine of the tariki
(the other-power), the nembutsu, and the akunin shōki (the evil person as the object of salvation),
with reference to the Shōbōgenzō and the Tannishō. It identifies the internal disputes within the
interpretation of the two thinkers; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the
framework, whose account of the Buddha-nature and of the faith is the nearest Japanese Buddhist
analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated the Shinto answer to the problem of the sacred;
the next chapter states the answer of Dōgen and Shinran, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 73

Dōgen and Shinran


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Eihei Dōgen (1200–1253 CE) and Shinran (1173–1262
CE), the two greatest figures of Kamakura-period Japanese Buddhism and the founders of the
Sōtō Zen and Jōdo Shinshū (True Pure Land) schools respectively. It states Dōgen’s doctrine of
the Buddha-nature (busshō), the practice of zazen as the realization of enlightenment (shushō-
ittō), the being-time (uji), the shikantaza (just sitting), and thegenjōkōan (the actualization
of the koan); and it states Shinran’s doctrine of the other-power (tariki), the nembutsu as the
expression of gratitude, the akunin shōki (the evil person as the primary object of salvation),
and the shinjin (the true entrusting mind); with reference to the Shōbōgenzō, the Eihei Kōroku,
the Tannishō, the Kyōgyōshinshō, and the Yuishinshō; it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of the two thinkers; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of the Buddha-nature and of the faith is the nearest Japanese
Buddhist analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that Dōgen and Shinran would raise
against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “Buddha-nature,”
“zazen,” “being-time,” “other-power,” “nembutsu,” or “shinjin,” these are the terms of the two
thinkers, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the
framework.


73.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is sitting in zazen. She sits on a cushion; she crosses her legs; she
straightens her back; she places her hands in the mudra; she opens her eyes; she breathes. She
does not try to stop the thoughts; she does not try to attain the enlightenment; she does not
try to become a Buddha. She just sits. The sitting is not the means to the enlightenment; the
sitting is the enlightenment. The practice is not the path to the realization; the practice is the
realization. This is Dōgen’s teaching: the practice and the enlightenment are one (shushō-ittō).
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the sitting is, or how it realizes the
enlightenment, but what the Buddha-nature is. The Buddha-nature is not a potentiality; it is
not a seed; it is not a capacity. The Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality; it is the whole of
the practice; it is the whole of the sitting. The Buddha-nature is not something that the person
has; it is what the person is. The Buddha-nature is the being-time (uji): the time is the being;
the being is the time; the two are not separate; they are the same. This is Dōgen’s teaching: the
being-time is the Buddha-nature.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the sitting is, or what the
Buddha-nature is, but what the salvation is. Shinran answers: the salvation is not the self-power

                                                826
73.2. The Question                                                                               827


(jiriki); it is not the effort; it is not the practice. The salvation is the other-power (tariki); it
is the power of Amitābha; it is the vow of Amitābha. The salvation is not the achievement;
it is the gift; it is the grace. The person who realizes that she is evil (akunin) is the person
who is saved; the person who realizes that she cannot save herself is the person who is saved by
the other-power. This is Shinran’s teaching: the evil person is the object of the salvation; the
other-power is the only power.
    The scene is the image of the two thinkers, in the Shōbōgenzō and in the Tannishō, of the
structure of the enlightenment and the salvation. The sitting is the practice; the Buddha-nature
is the being-time; the other-power is the grace. The scene poses the question that Dōgen and
Shinran were the first to pose in its full form in the Japanese Buddhist tradition. What is the
enlightenment? Is it the practice or the gift? And what is the salvation? Is it the self-power or
the other-power? The present chapter states the two answers, and the framework’s dialogue with
them.


73.2      The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Shinto: the kami, the purity and the pollution, the
Musubi, the three imperial regalia, the relation between the kami and the human being, and the
sacred order of the world. The Shinto tradition has asked what the kami is, and what the sacred
is. The Buddhist tradition of Dōgen and Shinran has asked what the enlightenment is, and what
the salvation is. The present chapter states the two positions, and the framework’s dialogue with
them.
    The question is not whether Dōgen and Shinran were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Dōgen and Shinran hold? The chapter states Dōgen’s
Buddha-nature, the shushō-ittō, the being-time, the shikantaza, and the genjōkōan; and it states
Shinran’s other-power, the nembutsu, the akunin shōki, and the shinjin, with reference to the
Shōbōgenzō, the Eihei Kōroku, the Tannishō, and the Kyōgyōshinshō.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Dōgen and Shinran would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
thinkers? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


73.3      The Position
828                                                                  Chapter 73. Dōgen and Shinran


73.3.1      Dōgen: The Buddha-Nature (Busshō)

Dōgen’s account of the Buddha-nature is stated in the Shōbōgenzō, especially in the fascicle
“Busshō” (The Buddha-Nature). The Buddha-nature is not a potentiality; it is not a seed; it is
not a capacity. The Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality; it is the whole of the practice; it
is the whole of the sitting.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the Buddha-nature as the whole. The Buddha-nature is the whole of the
reality; it is the whole of the practice; it is the whole of the sitting. The Buddha-nature is not
something that the person has; it is what the person is. The Buddha-nature is not a part; it is
the whole; it is not the potential; it is the actual; it is not the future; it is the present.


Second feature: the Buddha-nature as the impermanence. The Buddha-nature is the
impermanence; it is the change; it is the flow. The Buddha-nature is not the permanent; it is not
the static; it is not the unchanging. The Buddha-nature is the impermanence; the impermanence
is the Buddha-nature; the two are not separate; they are the same. The Buddha-nature is the
being-time (uji): the time is the being; the being is the time.


Third feature: the Buddha-nature as the practice. The Buddha-nature is the practice;
it is the sitting; it is the zazen. The Buddha-nature is not the theory; it is not the concept; it is
not the doctrine. The Buddha-nature is the practice; the practice is the Buddha-nature; the two
are not separate; they are the same. The practice and the enlightenment are one (shushō-ittō).

   From the Tradition

   “The Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality; it is the whole of the practice; it is the
   whole of the sitting. The Buddha-nature is not something that the person has; it is what
   the person is.” (Dōgen, Shōbōgenzō, “Busshō,” trans. after Tanahashi)


73.3.2      Dōgen: The Practice of Zazen and the Shushō-Ittō

Dōgen’s account of the practice of zazen and the shushō-ittō is stated in the Shōbōgenzō, especially
in the fascicles “Bendōwa” (Negotiating the Way) and “Zazenki” (The Principles of Zazen). The
practice and the enlightenment are one; they are not two; they are the same.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the zazen. The zazen is the sitting; it is the practice; it is the realization. The
zazen is not the means to the enlightenment; the zazen is the enlightenment. The zazen is not
the preparation; it is not the step; it is not the stage. The zazen is the whole; it is the complete;
it is the perfect.


Second feature: the shushō-ittō. The shushō-ittō is the unity of the practice and the
enlightenment; it is the identity of the two; it is the oneness of the two. The practice is not the
73.3. The Position                                                                                     829


path to the enlightenment; the practice is the enlightenment. The enlightenment is not the result
of the practice; the enlightenment is the practice. The two are not separate; they are the same.


Third feature: the shikantaza. The shikantaza is the just sitting; it is the sitting without
the goal; it is the sitting without the object. The shikantaza is not the meditation on the object;
it is not the contemplation of the truth; it is not the visualization of the image. The shikantaza
is the sitting; it is the just sitting; it is the whole sitting.


73.3.3     Dōgen: The Being-Time (Uji)

Dōgen’s account of the being-time is stated in the Shōbōgenzō, especially in the fascicle “Uji”
(Being-Time). The being-time is the time; it is the being; it is the two in one.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the being-time. The being-time (uji) is the time; it is the being; it is the two
in one. The being is not in the time; the being is the time. The time is not the container of the
being; the time is the being. The being and the time are not separate; they are the same. The
being-time is the reality; it is the whole; it is the present.


Second feature: the present. The present is the being-time; it is the whole; it is the complete.
The present is not the point; it is not the moment; it is not the instant. The present is the
whole of the time; it is the whole of the being; it is the whole of the reality. The present is the
being-time; the being-time is the present.


Third feature: the practice. The practice is the being-time; it is the sitting; it is the zazen.
The practice is not the means to the future; the practice is the present. The practice is not
the preparation for the enlightenment; the practice is the enlightenment. The practice is the
being-time; the being-time is the practice.


73.3.4     Dōgen: The Genjōkōan

Dōgen’s account of the genjōkōan is stated in the Shōbōgenzō, especially in the fascicle “Genjōkōan”
(The Actualization of the Koan). The genjōkōan is the actualization of the koan; it is the
realization of the truth; it is the present of the reality.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the genjō. The genjō is the actualization; it is the realization; it is the present.
The genjō is not the theory; it is not the concept; it is not the doctrine. The genjō is the
actualization; it is the realization; it is the present.


Second feature: the kōan. The kōan is the truth; it is the reality; it is the whole. The kōan
is not the puzzle; it is not the riddle; it is not the problem. The kōan is the truth; it is the
reality; it is the whole. The kōan is the Buddha-nature; the Buddha-nature is the kōan.
830                                                               Chapter 73. Dōgen and Shinran


Third feature: the actualization. The actualization is the realization of the kōan; it is the
present of the reality; it is the whole of the practice. The actualization is not the understanding;
it is not the explanation; it is not the interpretation. The actualization is the realization; it is
the present; it is the whole.


73.3.5       Shinran: The Other-Power (Tariki)

Shinran’s account of the other-power is stated in the Tannishō and in the Kyōgyōshinshō. The
other-power is the power of Amitābha; it is the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the other-power. The other-power (tariki) is the power of Amitābha; it is
the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha. The other-power is not the self-power (jiriki);
it is not the effort; it is not the practice. The other-power is the gift; it is the grace; it is the
salvation.


Second feature: the self-power. The self-power (jiriki) is the effort; it is the practice; it is
the achievement. The self-power is not the salvation; it is not the enlightenment; it is not the
liberation. The self-power is the illusion; it is the pride; it is the bondage. The self-power is the
obstacle; the other-power is the salvation.


Third feature: the faith. The faith (shinjin) is the entrusting; it is the trust; it is the reliance
on the other-power. The faith is not the self-power; it is not the effort; it is not the practice. The
faith is the gift; it is the grace; it is the salvation. The faith is the other-power; the other-power
is the faith.

   From the Tradition

   “The other-power is the power of Amitābha; it is the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace of
   Amitābha. The other-power is not the self-power; it is not the effort; it is not the practice.”
   (Shinran, Tannishō, trans. after Hirota)



73.3.6       Shinran: The Nembutsu and the Akunin Shōki

Shinran’s account of the nembutsu and the akunin shōki is stated in the Tannishō and in the
Kyōgyōshinshō. The nembutsu is the recitation of the name; the akunin shōki is the evil person
as the object of the salvation.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the nembutsu. The nembutsu is the recitation of the name; it is the calling of
the name of Amitābha; it is the expression of the gratitude. The nembutsu is not the practice; it
is not the effort; it is not the achievement. The nembutsu is the expression of the faith; it is the
gratitude; it is the joy.
73.4. Internal Disputes                                                                             831


Second feature: the akunin shōki. The akunin shōki is the evil person as the object of the
salvation; it is the doctrine that the evil person is the primary object of the salvation. The evil
person is not the obstacle; the evil person is the object. The evil person is the one who is saved;
the good person is the one who is not saved. The evil person is the object of the compassion; the
good person is the object of the pride.


Third feature: the salvation. The salvation is the gift; it is the grace; it is the other-power.
The salvation is not the achievement; it is not the practice; it is not the effort. The salvation is
the gift of Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha; it is the other-power. The salvation is the
faith; the faith is the salvation.


73.3.7       Shinran: The Shinjin (The True Entrusting Mind)

Shinran’s account of the shinjin is stated in the Tannishō and in the Kyōgyōshinshō. The shinjin
is the true entrusting mind; it is the trust; it is the reliance on the other-power.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the shinjin. The shinjin is the true entrusting mind; it is the trust; it is the
reliance on the other-power. The shinjin is not the self-power; it is not the effort; it is not the
practice. The shinjin is the gift; it is the grace; it is the salvation.


Second feature: the gift. The shinjin is the gift; it is the grace; it is the other-power. The
shinjin is not the achievement; it is not the practice; it is not the effort. The shinjin is the gift of
Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha; it is the other-power.


Third feature: the salvation. The salvation is the shinjin; it is the trust; it is the reliance.
The salvation is not the future; it is not the after-death; it is not the other-world. The salvation
is the present; it is the now; it is the shinjin. The salvation is the shinjin; the shinjin is the
salvation.



73.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Dōgen and Shinran is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Buddha-nature. The traditional reading takes the
Buddha-nature to be a metaphysical reality: it is the whole of the reality; it is the whole of
the practice; it is the whole of the sitting. A revisionary reading takes it to be a soteriological
concept: it is the potentiality of the enlightenment; it is the capacity of the awakening. The
two readings disagree on whether Dōgen is a metaphysics or a soteriology, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a soteriology.
832                                                                Chapter 73. Dōgen and Shinran


Second dispute: the status of the other-power. The traditional reading takes the other-
power to be a real power: it is the power of Amitābha; it is the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace
of Amitābha. A revisionary reading takes it to be a psychological attitude: it is the trust; it
is the reliance; it is the faith. The two readings disagree on whether Shinran is a theism or a
psychology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, not a psychology.

Third dispute: the relation between Dōgen and Shinran. The traditional reading takes
Dōgen and Shinran to be rivals: Dōgen is the path of the self-power; Shinran is the path of
the other-power; the two are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary:
Dōgen provides the practice; Shinran provides the faith; the two are the two sides of the one.
The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a rival nor a complement.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Dōgen is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the Buddha-
nature. If Shinran is a theist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a theism
of the other-power. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Shōbōgenzō, but
it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.


73.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Dōgen. The framework shares three structural features with Dōgen’s position.

        1. The Buddha-nature. Dōgen holds that the Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality;
           it is the whole of the practice; it is the whole of the sitting. The framework holds
           that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. Both hold
           that there is a nature, and that the nature is the whole.

        2. The practice. Dōgen holds that the practice is the enlightenment; the practice is the
           realization; the practice is the whole. The framework holds that the reconstruction
           is the realization; the reconstruction is the reading; the reconstruction is the whole.
           Both hold that there is a practice, and that the practice is the realization.

        3. The being-time. Dōgen holds that the being-time is the time; it is the being; it is
           the two in one. The framework holds that the manifestation is the time; it is the
           identity; it is the two in one. Both hold that there is a being-time, and that the
           being-time is the present.

   With Shinran. The framework shares three structural features with Shinran’s position.

        1. The other-power. Shinran holds that the other-power is the power of Amitābha; it is
73.6. Points of Divergence                                                                       833


          the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha. The framework holds that the
          structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is the condition of the expression;
          it is the condition of the salvation. Both hold that there is an other-power, and that
          the other-power is the grace.

       2. The faith. Shinran holds that the faith is the entrusting; it is the trust; it is the
          reliance on the other-power. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the
          trust in the structure; it is the reliance on the identity; it is the confidence in the
          manifestation. Both hold that there is a faith, and that the faith is the trust.

       3. The evil person. Shinran holds that the evil person is the object of the salvation; the
          evil person is the one who is saved; the good person is the one who is not saved. The
          framework holds that the partial manifestation is the object of the reconstruction;
          the partial manifestation is the one that is read; the complete manifestation is the
          one that is not read. Both hold that there is an object, and that the object is the
          partial.



73.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Dōgen. The framework diverges from Dōgen’s position in three respects.

       1. The status of the Buddha-nature. Dōgen holds that the Buddha-nature is the whole
          of the reality; it is the whole of the practice; it is the whole of the sitting. The
          framework holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the
          condition. The framework’s identity is not the Buddha-nature; it is the condition of
          the manifestation.

       2. The status of the practice. Dōgen holds that the practice is the enlightenment; the
          practice is the realization; the practice is the whole. The framework holds that the
          reconstruction is the reading; the reconstruction is the realization; the reconstruction
          is the whole. The framework’s reconstruction is not the practice; it is the reading.

       3. The status of the being-time. Dōgen holds that the being-time is the time; it is the
          being; it is the two in one. The framework holds that the manifestation is the time;
          it is the identity; it is the two in one. The framework’s manifestation is not the
          being-time; it is the appearance.

   With Shinran. The framework diverges from Shinran’s position in three respects.

       1. The status of the other-power. Shinran holds that the other-power is the power of
         Amitābha; it is the vow of Amitābha; it is the grace of Amitābha. The framework
          holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is the condition of
834                                                                  Chapter 73. Dōgen and Shinran


          the expression; it is the condition of the salvation. The framework’s structure is not
          the other-power; it is the condition.

       2. The status of the faith. Shinran holds that the faith is the entrusting; it is the trust; it
          is the reliance on the other-power. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the
          reading; it is the understanding; it is the realization. The framework’s reconstruction
          is not the faith; it is the reading.

       3. The status of the evil person. Shinran holds that the evil person is the object of the
          salvation; the evil person is the one who is saved. The framework holds that the
          partial manifestation is the object of the reconstruction; the partial manifestation is
          the one that is read. The framework’s partial manifestation is not the evil person; it
          is the partial.



73.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Dōgen’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
  that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
  the Buddha-nature; it is a pattern. The Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality; the
  Buddha-nature is the whole of the practice; the Buddha-nature is the whole of the sitting.
  The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the Buddha-nature. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the Buddha-nature.
  Shinran’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
  real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they are
  the levels of the other-power; they are the levels of the grace. The framework’s realms
  are not levels of the other-power; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an
  ontology of levels, not of the other-power.
  Shinran’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it
  is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the faith; it is the shinjin; it is
  the entrusting. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the faith. The
  framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the faith.



73.8      The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to Dōgen’s objection. The framework agrees that the Buddha-nature is the
  whole of the reality, and it agrees that the Buddha-nature is the whole of the practice. But
  the framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the
  invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment
73.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                      835


   is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the
   structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition
   is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction)
   and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Shinran’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the other-power. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   other-power. The distinction is between a level of the other-power (a soteriological level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to Shinran’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the faith.
   The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it
   is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a faith (a trust)
   and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



73.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Dōgen’s cost. If Dōgen accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
Buddha-nature is the whole of the reality. He must accept that the identity is the structural
condition, and that the Buddha-nature is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss
of the Buddha-nature: the Buddha-nature is no longer the whole; the identity is the structural
condition. He must also give up the claim that the practice is the enlightenment; he must accept
that the reconstruction is the reading; the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.

Shinran’s cost. If Shinran accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
other-power is the power of Amitābha. He must accept that the structure is the condition, and
that the other-power is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the other-power:
the other-power is no longer the grace; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the
claim that the faith is the shinjin; he must accept that the reconstruction is the reading; the
reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Dōgen and Shinran, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension
of reality—the dimension of the Buddha-nature, of the practice, of the other-power—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the Buddha-nature, and the
framework leaves the Buddha-nature to a separate inquiry.
836                                                              Chapter 73. Dōgen and Shinran


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Dōgen’s Buddha-nature
and Shinran’s other-power are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s
structure does not capture. Dōgen and Shinran must accept that the framework’s structure is not
a pattern; it is a structural condition that the Buddha-nature and the other-power presuppose as
their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three
are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.



73.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Dōgen). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Dōgen’s term “the Buddha-nature.” If one substitutes “the Buddha-nature” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the Buddha-nature is
   the whole of the reality, and it is not manifested, because it is the whole. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; the Buddha-nature is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Dōgen’s term “the practice.”
   If one substitutes “the practice” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   the practice is the sitting. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the practice is
   practical. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Shinran). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Shinran’s term “the other-power.” If one substitutes “the other-power” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the other-power is the
   power of Amitābha, and it is not manifested, because it is the power. The framework’s
   identity is multiple; the other-power is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Shinran’s term “the faith.”
   If one substitutes “the faith” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the
   faith is the trust. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the faith is devotional.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Dōgen is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a nature, and they differ on whether the nature is the Buddha-
   nature or the structure. The relation between the framework and Shinran is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a faith, and they differ on whether the faith is the other-power
   or the reconstruction. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is
   identity. The framework’s reading of Dōgen and Shinran would be refuted by showing
73.11. Open Questions                                                                       837


   that their positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between
   structure and nature, or between structure and faith—by showing, that is, that they
   already distinguish the structural condition from the nature and the faith, and that the
   framework’s distinction is a development of their own.




73.11      Open Questions


The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Dōgen’s Buddha-nature or
Shinran’s other-power, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a
development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Dōgen’s Buddha-
nature is already a structural condition, or that Shinran’s other-power is already a structural
condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Shōbōgenzō, the Eihei Kōroku, the
Tannishō, and the Kyōgyōshinshō do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the Buddha-
nature, the shushō-ittō, the being-time, the shikantaza, the genjōkōan, the other-power, the
nembutsu, the akunin shōki, and the shinjin, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A
reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves
open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a practice and a faith—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the practice that realizes, or the faith that trusts? Is the truth the sitting
that is the enlightenment, or the other-power that is the grace? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between Dōgen’s Buddha-nature, Shinran’s other-power, and the framework’s
identity?

The next chapter turns to the Kyoto School. It states the philosophy of Nishida Kitarō, the logic of
the place (basho), the absolute nothingness (zettaimu), the self-identity of absolute contradiction,
and the world of historical reality; and it states the philosophy of Tanabe Hajime, the logic of the
species, the metanoetics, and the philosophy of repentance; with reference to the An Inquiry into
the Good, the Intuition and Reflection in Self-Consciousness, the Philosophy of the Kyoto School,
and the Philosophy as Metanoetics. It identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of the Kyoto School; and it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework,
whose account of nothingness and of the world is the nearest Japanese analogue to theirs. The
present chapter has stated the answer of Dōgen and Shinran to the problem of the enlightenment
and the salvation; the next chapter states the answer of the Kyoto School, and the framework’s
dialogue with it.
Chapter 74

The Kyoto School


Scope. This chapter closes Part XI, the dialogues with Japanese philosophy, and it closes it with
the Kyoto School, the most important philosophical movement of modern Japan, founded by
Nishida Kitarō (1870–1945 CE) and developed by Tanabe Hajime (1885–1962 CE), Nishitani Keiji
(1900–1990 CE), and others. It states Nishida’s philosophy of pure experience (junsui keiken),
the logic of the place (basho no ronri), the absolute nothingness (zettai mu), the self-identity
of absolute contradiction (zettai mujunteki jiko dōitsu), and the world of historical reality; and
it states Tanabe’s logic of the species (shu no ronri), the philosophy of metanoetics (zangedō),
and the philosophy of repentance; with reference to Nishida’s An Inquiry into the Good (Zen no
Kenkyū), Intuition and Reflection in Self-Consciousness (Jikakuteki Shōsatsu ni okeru Chokkan
to Hansei), and The Fundamental Problems of Philosophy (Tetsugaku no Konpon Mondai);
and Tanabe’s Philosophy as Metanoetics (Zangedō to shite no Tetsugaku) and The Logic of
the Species (Shu no Ronri); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the
Kyoto School; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of nothingness and of the world is the nearest Japanese analogue to the Kyoto School; it
presents the objections that the Kyoto School would raise against the framework; it presents the
framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it
states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “pure experience,” “the place,” “absolute nothingness,” “the
self-identity of absolute contradiction,” “the species,” or “metanoetics,” these are the Kyoto
School’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the
framework.


74.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a flower. She sees the color, the shape, the petals. But she
does not see the flower as an object; she does not see the flower as a thing separate from herself.
She sees the flower and herself as one; the seeing is the seen; the subject is the object; the two
are not separate. The experience is not the experience of the subject about the object; it is the
pure experience (junsui keiken); it is the experience before the division of the subject and the
object; it is the experience before the conceptualization.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the pure experience is, or how it is
achieved, but what the place is. The place (basho) is not the physical place; it is not the space;
it is not the location. The place is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground. The place is the
place where the subject and the object appear; it is the place where the knowledge is possible; it
is the place where the experience is realized. The place is the absolute nothingness (zettai mu);
it is the nothingness that is the ground of the being; it is the nothingness that is the source of

                                                839
840                                                                  Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


the experience.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the pure experience is,
or what the place is, but what the world is. The world is not the collection of the things; it is not
the sum of the objects; it is not the totality of the beings. The world is the historical reality; it is
the world of the action; it is the world of the creation. The world is the self-identity of absolute
contradiction (zettai mujunteki jiko dōitsu); it is the identity that contains the contradiction;
it is the unity that contains the opposition. The world is the place where the subject and the
object are one; it is the place where the action and the knowledge are one; it is the place where
the being and the nothingness are one.
      The scene is the image of the Kyoto School, in the Inquiry into the Good and in the Metanoetics,
of the structure of reality. The flower is the pure experience; the place is the absolute nothingness;
the world is the historical reality. The scene poses the question that the Kyoto School was the
first to pose in its full form in the Japanese tradition. What is the experience? What is the
place? And what is the world? The present chapter states the Kyoto School’s answer, and the
framework’s dialogue with it.



74.2        The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Dōgen and Shinran: the Buddha-nature, the practice
of zazen, the being-time, the shikantaza, the other-power, the nembutsu, the akunin shōki, and
the shinjin. The Japanese Buddhist tradition has asked what the enlightenment is, and what the
salvation is. The Kyoto School has asked what the experience is, and what the world is. The
present chapter states the Kyoto School’s position, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether the Kyoto School was right. The question is what it held, what
it can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did the Kyoto School hold? The chapter states Nishida’s
pure experience, the logic of the place, the absolute nothingness, the self-identity of absolute
contradiction, and the world of historical reality; and it states Tanabe’s logic of the species, the
metanoetics, and the philosophy of repentance, with reference to the Inquiry into the Good, the
Intuition and Reflection in Self-Consciousness, the Fundamental Problems of Philosophy, the
Philosophy as Metanoetics, and the Logic of the Species.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the Kyoto School converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the Kyoto School would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the Kyoto
School? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance, not
equivalence.
74.3. The Position                                                                                841


74.3      The Position

74.3.1       Nishida: The Pure Experience (Junsui Keiken)

Nishida’s account of pure experience is stated in the Inquiry into the Good (Zen no Kenkyū,
1911). The pure experience is the experience before the division of the subject and the object; it
is the experience before the conceptualization; it is the immediate experience.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the pure experience. The pure experience (junsui keiken) is the experience
before the division of the subject and the object; it is the experience before the conceptualization;
it is the immediate experience. The pure experience is not the experience of the subject about
the object; it is the experience that is prior to the subject and the object; it is the experience
that is the unity of the two.


Second feature: the unity. The unity is the unity of the subject and the object; it is the
unity of the experience and the experienced; it is the unity of the knower and the known. The
unity is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the unity that contains the difference; it is
the unity that contains the opposition. The unity is the pure experience; the pure experience is
the unity.


Third feature: the immediacy. The immediacy is the immediacy of the experience; it is
the immediacy of the unity; it is the immediacy of the pure experience. The immediacy is not
the mediation; it is not the reflection; it is not the concept. The immediacy is the direct; it is
the immediate; it is the pure. The immediacy is the pure experience; the pure experience is the
immediacy.

   From the Tradition

   “The pure experience is the experience before the division of the subject and the object; it
   is the experience before the conceptualization; it is the immediate experience.” (Nishida,
   An Inquiry into the Good, trans. after Abe-Dilworth)


74.3.2       Nishida: The Logic of the Place (Basho no Ronri)

Nishida’s account of the logic of the place is stated in the Intuition and Reflection in Self-
Consciousness and in the Fundamental Problems of Philosophy. The logic of the place is the
logic of the field; it is the logic of the horizon; it is the logic of the ground.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the place. The place (basho) is not the physical place; it is not the space; it is
not the location. The place is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground. The place is the place
where the subject and the object appear; it is the place where the knowledge is possible; it is the
place where the experience is realized.
842                                                                 Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


Second feature: the logic. The logic is the logic of the place; it is the logic of the field; it is
the logic of the horizon. The logic is not the logic of the subject; it is not the logic of the object;
it is the logic of the place where the subject and the object are. The logic is the logic of the
unity; the logic of the unity is the logic of the place.


Third feature: the absolute nothingness. The absolute nothingness (zettai mu) is the
place; it is the field; it is the horizon. The absolute nothingness is not the relative nothingness; it
is not the absence of the being; it is not the negation of the being. The absolute nothingness is
the ground of the being; it is the source of the being; it is the place where the being appears.
The absolute nothingness is the place; the place is the absolute nothingness.


74.3.3      Nishida: The Absolute Nothingness (Zettai Mu)

Nishida’s account of the absolute nothingness is stated in the Fundamental Problems of Philosophy
and in the Logic of the Place. The absolute nothingness is the ground of the being; it is the
source of the being; it is the place where the being appears.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the absolute nothingness. The absolute nothingness (zettai mu) is the
ground of the being; it is the source of the being; it is the place where the being appears. The
absolute nothingness is not the relative nothingness; it is not the absence of the being; it is not
the negation of the being. The absolute nothingness is the ground; it is the source; it is the place.


Second feature: the ground. The ground is the ground of the being; it is the source of the
being; it is the place where the being appears. The ground is not the being; it is not the thing; it
is not the object. The ground is the nothingness; it is the absolute nothingness; it is the place.


Third feature: the appearance. The appearance is the appearance of the being; it is the
appearance in the place; it is the appearance in the absolute nothingness. The appearance is not
the being; it is not the thing; it is not the object. The appearance is the manifestation; it is the
manifestation in the place; it is the manifestation in the absolute nothingness.


74.3.4      Nishida: The Self-Identity of Absolute Contradiction (Zettai Mujun-
            teki Jiko Dōitsu)

Nishida’s account of the self-identity of absolute contradiction is stated in the Fundamental
Problems of Philosophy and in the Logic of the Place. The self-identity of absolute contradiction
is the identity that contains the contradiction; it is the unity that contains the opposition.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the self-identity. The self-identity (jiko dōitsu) is the identity; it is the unity;
it is the oneness. The self-identity is not the sameness; it is not the identity of the same; it is the
identity that contains the difference; it is the identity that contains the opposition.
74.3. The Position                                                                                   843


Second feature: the absolute contradiction. The absolute contradiction (zettai mujun)
is the contradiction; it is the opposition; it is the difference. The absolute contradiction is not
the relative contradiction; it is not the contradiction of the same; it is the contradiction that is
absolute; it is the contradiction that is the ground of the identity.


Third feature: the self-identity of absolute contradiction. The self-identity of absolute
contradiction (zettai mujunteki jiko dōitsu) is the identity that contains the contradiction; it
is the unity that contains the opposition; it is the oneness that contains the difference. The
self-identity of absolute contradiction is the world; it is the historical reality; it is the place where
the subject and the object are one.


74.3.5     Nishida: The World of Historical Reality
Nishida’s account of the world of historical reality is stated in the Fundamental Problems of
Philosophy and in the Logic of the Place. The world of historical reality is the world of the action;
it is the world of the creation; it is the world of the history.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the world. The world is not the collection of the things; it is not the sum
of the objects; it is not the totality of the beings. The world is the historical reality; it is the
world of the action; it is the world of the creation. The world is the self-identity of absolute
contradiction; it is the identity that contains the contradiction; it is the unity that contains the
opposition.


Second feature: the action. The action is the action of the world; it is the action of the
history; it is the action of the creation. The action is not the action of the subject; it is not
the action of the object; it is the action of the world. The action is the self-identity of absolute
contradiction; it is the identity that contains the contradiction.


Third feature: the history. The history is the history of the world; it is the history of the
action; it is the history of the creation. The history is not the history of the subject; it is not the
history of the object; it is the history of the world. The history is the self-identity of absolute
contradiction; it is the identity that contains the contradiction.


74.3.6     Tanabe: The Logic of the Species (Shu no Ronri)
Tanabe’s account of the logic of the species is stated in the Logic of the Species (Shu no Ronri,
1947). The logic of the species is the logic of the mediation; it is the logic of the concrete; it is
the logic of the historical.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the species. The species (shu) is the mediation; it is the concrete; it is the
historical. The species is not the individual; it is not the universal; it is the mediation between
the individual and the universal. The species is the nation; it is the culture; it is the history.
844                                                                  Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


Second feature: the logic. The logic is the logic of the species; it is the logic of the mediation;
it is the logic of the concrete. The logic is not the logic of the universal; it is not the logic of the
individual; it is the logic of the species. The logic is the logic of the mediation; the logic of the
mediation is the logic of the species.


Third feature: the absolute nothingness. The absolute nothingness is the ground of the
species; it is the source of the species; it is the place where the species appears. The absolute
nothingness is not the relative nothingness; it is not the absence of the being; it is not the
negation of the being. The absolute nothingness is the ground; it is the source; it is the place.


74.3.7      Tanabe: The Philosophy of Metanoetics (Zangedō)

Tanabe’s account of the philosophy of metanoetics is stated in the Philosophy as Metanoetics
(Zangedō to shite no Tetsugaku, 1946). The philosophy of metanoetics is the philosophy of the
repentance; it is the philosophy of the conversion; it is the philosophy of the transformation.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the metanoetics. The metanoetics (zangedō) is the philosophy of the repen-
tance; it is the philosophy of the conversion; it is the philosophy of the transformation. The
metanoetics is not the philosophy of the reason; it is not the philosophy of the logic; it is the
philosophy of the repentance. The metanoetics is the philosophy that recognizes the limits of the
reason; it is the philosophy that recognizes the failure of the reason; it is the philosophy that
recognizes the need for the transformation.


Second feature: the repentance. The repentance (zange) is the repentance of the reason;
it is the conversion of the reason; it is the transformation of the reason. The repentance is not
the regret; it is not the sorrow; it is not the remorse. The repentance is the conversion; it is the
transformation; it is the metanoia. The repentance is the metanoetics; the metanoetics is the
repentance.


Third feature: the other-power. The other-power (tariki) is the power of the absolute; it is
the power of the nothingness; it is the power of the grace. The other-power is not the self-power;
it is not the effort; it is not the reason. The other-power is the grace; it is the gift; it is the
salvation. The other-power is the metanoetics; the metanoetics is the other-power.


74.3.8      Tanabe: The Philosophy of Repentance

Tanabe’s account of the philosophy of repentance is a development of his philosophy of metanoetics.
The philosophy of repentance is the philosophy of the conversion; it is the philosophy of the
transformation; it is the philosophy of the salvation.
      The account has three features.
74.4. Internal Disputes                                                                            845


First feature: the repentance. The repentance (zange) is the repentance of the reason; it is
the conversion of the reason; it is the transformation of the reason. The repentance is not the
regret; it is not the sorrow; it is not the remorse. The repentance is the conversion; it is the
transformation; it is the metanoia.

Second feature: the conversion. The conversion is the conversion of the reason; it is the
conversion of the philosophy; it is the conversion of the thinker. The conversion is not the change
of the mind; it is not the change of the opinion; it is not the change of the belief. The conversion
is the transformation; it is the metanoia; it is the repentance.

Third feature: the salvation. The salvation is the salvation of the reason; it is the salvation
of the philosophy; it is the salvation of the thinker. The salvation is not the achievement; it is
not the effort; it is not the reason. The salvation is the gift; it is the grace; it is the other-power.
The salvation is the repentance; the repentance is the salvation.


74.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of the Kyoto School is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the absolute nothingness. The traditional reading takes
the absolute nothingness to be a metaphysical reality: it is the ground of the being; it is the
source of the being. A revisionary reading takes it to be a soteriological concept: it is the place
of the conversion; it is the place of the repentance. The two readings disagree on whether the
Kyoto School is a metaphysics or a soteriology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a soteriology.

Second dispute: the status of the self-identity of absolute contradiction. The tradi-
tional reading takes the self-identity to be a logical principle: it is the identity that contains the
contradiction; it is the unity that contains the opposition. A revisionary reading takes it to be a
historical reality: it is the world of the action; it is the world of the creation. The two readings
disagree on whether the Kyoto School is a logic or a history, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a logic.

Third dispute: the relation between Nishida and Tanabe. The traditional reading takes
Nishida and Tanabe to be rivals: Nishida is the philosopher of the place; Tanabe is the philosopher
of the species; the two are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary:
Nishida provides the place; Tanabe provides the mediation; the two are the two sides of the one.
The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a rival nor a complement.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the Kyoto School is a metaphysician, the
framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of
nothingness. If the Kyoto School is a soteriology, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural
846                                                                 Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


realism and a soteriology. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Inquiry
into the Good, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


74.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the Kyoto School. The framework shares four structural features with the Kyoto
   School’s position.

       1. The pure experience. Nishida holds that the pure experience is the experience
          before the division of the subject and the object; it is the experience before the
          conceptualization. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of
          the manifestations; it is the reading before the division of the identity and the
          appearance. Both hold that there is an experience, and that the experience is the
          unity.

       2. The place. Nishida holds that the place is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground.
          The framework holds that the context is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground.
          Both hold that there is a place, and that the place is the condition.

       3. The absolute nothingness. Nishida holds that the absolute nothingness is the ground
          of the being; it is the source of the being. The framework holds that the structure is
          the ground of the manifestation; it is the source of the manifestation. Both hold
          that there is a ground, and that the ground is the nothingness.

       4. The self-identity of absolute contradiction. Nishida holds that the self-identity of
          absolute contradiction is the identity that contains the contradiction; it is the unity
          that contains the opposition. The framework holds that the structure is the identity
          that contains the contradiction; it is the unity that contains the opposition. Both
          hold that there is an identity, and that the identity contains the contradiction.



74.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With the Kyoto School. The framework diverges from the Kyoto School’s position in
   four respects.

       1. The status of the absolute nothingness. Nishida holds that the absolute nothingness is
          the ground of the being; it is the source of the being. The framework holds that the
          structure is the ground of the manifestation; it is the condition of the manifestation.
          The framework’s structure is not the nothingness; it is the condition.
74.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                  847


       2. The status of the place. Nishida holds that the place is the field; it is the horizon; it
          is the ground. The framework holds that the context is the field; it is the horizon; it
          is the ground. The framework’s context is not the place; it is the condition.

       3. The status of the pure experience. Nishida holds that the pure experience is the
          experience before the division of the subject and the object; it is the experience
          before the conceptualization. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the
          reading of the manifestations; it is the reading after the division of the identity and
          the appearance. The framework’s reconstruction is not the pure experience; it is the
          structural reading.

       4. The status of the metanoetics. Tanabe holds that the metanoetics is the philosophy
          of the repentance; it is the philosophy of the conversion. The framework holds that
          the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading without
          the repentance. The framework’s reconstruction is not the metanoetics; it is the
          structural reading.




74.7      The Tradition’s Objections


   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Nishida’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
   the absolute nothingness; it is a pattern. The absolute nothingness is the ground of the
   being; the absolute nothingness is the source of the being. The framework’s identity is a
   pattern, and a pattern is not the absolute nothingness. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of patterns, not of the absolute nothingness.
   Tanabe’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
   real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they are
   the levels of the species; they are the levels of the mediation. The framework’s realms are
   not levels of the species; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
   levels, not of the species.
   Tanabe’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
   the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the metanoetics; it is the repentance; it
   is the conversion. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the metanoetics.
   The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the metanoetics.
848                                                                 Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


74.8        The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Nishida’s objection. The framework agrees that the absolute nothingness
   is the ground of the being, and it agrees that the absolute nothingness is the source of
   the being. But the framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and
   the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a
   pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment
   of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern
   (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second,
   not the first.
   Reply to Tanabe’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not
   just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the species. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   species. The distinction is between a level of the species (a historical level) and a level of
   manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Tanabe’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not
   merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts
   do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the metanoetics.
   The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations;
   it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a metanoetics
   (a repentance) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the
   first.



74.9        The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Nishida’s cost. If Nishida accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that
the absolute nothingness is the ground of the being. He must accept that the structure is the
condition, and that the absolute nothingness is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the
loss of the absolute nothingness: the absolute nothingness is no longer the ground; the structure
is the condition. He must also give up the claim that the pure experience is the immediate
experience; he must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.


Tanabe’s cost. If Tanabe accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
species is the mediation. He must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the species
is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the species: the species is no longer the
mediation; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the claim that the metanoetics
74.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     849


is the philosophy of the repentance; he must accept that the reconstruction is the reading; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Nishida and Tanabe, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the absolute nothingness, of the species, of the metanoetics—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the absolute nothingness, and
the framework leaves the absolute nothingness to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Nishida’s absolute
nothingness and Tanabe’s species are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the
framework’s structure does not capture. Nishida and Tanabe must accept that the framework’s
structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the absolute nothingness and the
species presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.


74.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Nishida). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Nishida’s term “the absolute nothingness.” If one substitutes “the absolute nothingness”
   for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the
   absolute nothingness is the ground of the being, and it is not manifested, because it is the
   nothingness. The framework’s identity is multiple; the absolute nothingness is one. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Nishida’s term “the
   pure experience.” If one substitutes “the pure experience” for “reconstruction” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading
   of the manifestations; the pure experience is the immediate experience. The framework’s
   reconstruction is mediated; the pure experience is immediate. The substitution fails, and
   the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Tanabe). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Tanabe’s term “the species.” If one substitutes “the species” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the species is the mediation, and it
   is not manifested, because it is the mediation. The framework’s identity is multiple; the
   species is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
850                                                              Chapter 74. The Kyoto School


   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Tanabe’s term “the meta-
   noetics.” If one substitutes “the metanoetics” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the metanoetics is the philosophy of the repentance. The framework’s
   reconstruction is structural; the metanoetics is repentant. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Nishida is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a ground, and they differ on whether the ground is the absolute
   nothingness or the structure. The relation between the framework and Tanabe is resem-
   blance: both hold that there is a mediation, and they differ on whether the mediation is
   the species or the structure. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither
   is identity. The framework’s reading of the Kyoto School would be refuted by showing that
   its positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure
   and ground, or between structure and mediation—by showing, that is, that the Kyoto
   School already distinguishes the structural condition from the ground and the mediation,
   and that the framework’s distinction is a development of its own.




74.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Nishida’s absolute nothingness or
Tanabe’s species, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Nishida’s absolute nothingness is
already a structural condition, or that Tanabe’s species is already a structural condition, has a
question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Inquiry into the Good, the Intuition
and Reflection in Self-Consciousness, the Fundamental Problems of Philosophy, the Philosophy
as Metanoetics, and the Logic of the Species do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the
pure experience, the logic of the place, the absolute nothingness, the self-identity of absolute
contradiction, the world of historical reality, the logic of the species, the metanoetics, and the
philosophy of repentance, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a ground and a mediation—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the ground that is the nothingness, or the mediation that is the species? Is
the truth the pure experience that is immediate, or the reconstruction that reads? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between Nishida’s absolute nothingness, Tanabe’s species,
and the framework’s identity?

Part XI is now complete. The dialogues with the three great figures of Japanese philosophy—
Shinto, Dōgen and Shinran, and the Kyoto School—have been stated. Part XII turns to Jewish
philosophy. The first dialogue is with Philo and Saadia, on the Logos and the reason; the next
with Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi, on the matter and the nation; the next with Maimonides,
on the Guide of the Perplexed; and the last with Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas, on the dialogue
and the other. The Japanese tradition has asked what the kami is, and what the nothingness is;
the Jewish tradition will ask what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is before
God.
