Philo and Saadia


Scope. This chapter opens Part XII, the dialogues with Jewish philosophy, and it opens it with
Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE) and Saadia Gaon (882–942 CE), the two foundational
figures of Jewish philosophical thought. It states Philo’s account of the Logos as the intermediary
between God and the world, the allegorical method of reading Scripture, the doctrine of the
divine powers (dynameis), the theory of creation, and the ascent of the soul; and it states Saadia’s
account of the unity of God, the creation of the world, the rationality of the commandments
(ta’amei ha-mitzvot), the freedom of the will, and the harmony of reason and revelation, with
reference to Philo’s De Opificio Mundi (On the Creation of the World), the Legum Allegoriae
(Allegorical Interpretation), and the De Vita Contemplativa (On the Contemplative Life); and
Saadia’s Emunot ve-Deot (The Book of Beliefs and Opinions), the Tafsir (the Arabic translation
of the Bible), and the Sefer ha-Galui (The Book of the Exile); it identifies the internal disputes
within the interpretation of the two thinkers; it states the points of convergence and divergence
with the framework, whose account of the Logos and of the unity of God is the nearest Jewish
analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that Philo and Saadia would raise against the
framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the
kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative,
ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “Logos,” “the powers,” “creation,” “the
unity of God,” “the commandments,” or “the harmony of reason and revelation,” these are the
terms of the two thinkers, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.


75.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is reading the opening of Genesis. She reads: “In the beginning God
created the heavens and the earth.” She asks: what does this mean? Is the creation a literal
event in time? Is it a process? Is it a metaphor? Philo reads the verse and says: the creation is
not a literal event; it is the creation of the intelligible world, the world of the Forms, which is
the pattern of the sensible world. The Logos is the instrument of the creation; the Logos is the
intermediary between God and the world; the Logos is the pattern of the cosmos.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the creation is, or how it is described,
but what the unity of God is. Saadia reads the verse and says: God is one; God is not many; God
is not composite; God is not a body; God is not a plurality. The unity of God is the foundation of
the faith; the unity of God is the foundation of the philosophy; the unity of God is the foundation
of the law. The unity of God is the truth; the plurality is the error; the unity is the salvation.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the creation is, or what
the unity of God is, but what the relation between reason and revelation is. Philo says: the

                                                853
854                                                                 Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


reason and the revelation are not enemies; the reason is the handmaid of the revelation; the
revelation is the truth; the reason is the interpretation. Saadia says: the reason and the revelation
are not enemies; the reason is the foundation of the revelation; the revelation is the confirmation
of the reason; the two are the two sources of the truth; the two are the two witnesses of the one
truth.
      The scene is the image of the two thinkers, in the De Opificio Mundi and in the Emunot
ve-Deot, of the structure of the faith and the reason. The creation is the work of the Logos; the
unity of God is the foundation of the faith; the reason and the revelation are the two sources.
The scene poses the question that Philo and Saadia were the first to pose in its full form in
the Jewish tradition. What is the Logos? What is the unity of God? And what is the relation
between reason and revelation? The present chapter states the two answers, and the framework’s
dialogue with them.


75.2       The Question

The previous part stated the positions of Japanese philosophy: Shinto, Dōgen and Shinran, and
the Kyoto School. The Japanese tradition has asked what the kami is, and what the nothingness
is. The present part turns to Jewish philosophy, and its first dialogue is with Philo and Saadia,
the two foundational figures of the Jewish philosophical tradition. The Jewish tradition has
asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is before God. The present
chapter states the two positions, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
      The question is not whether Philo and Saadia were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Philo and Saadia hold? The chapter states Philo’s
Logos, the allegorical method, the divine powers, the creation, and the ascent of the soul; and it
states Saadia’s unity of God, the creation, the rationality of the commandments, the freedom of
the will, and the harmony of reason and revelation, with reference to the De Opificio Mundi, the
Legum Allegoriae, the Emunot ve-Deot, and the Tafsir.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Philo and Saadia would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
thinkers? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


75.3       The Position
75.3. The Position                                                                              855


75.3.1    Philo: The Logos

Philo’s account of the Logos is stated in the De Opificio Mundi and in the Legum Allegoriae.
The Logos is the intermediary between God and the world; it is the instrument of the creation;
it is the pattern of the cosmos.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the Logos as the intermediary. The Logos is the intermediary between
God and the world; it is the mediator; it is the bridge. The Logos is not God; it is not the world;
it is between the two; it is the connection. The Logos is the first-born of God; it is the image of
God; it is the son of God.


Second feature: the Logos as the instrument. The Logos is the instrument of the creation;
it is the tool; it is the means. The Logos is not the creator; it is not the creation; it is the
instrument of the creation. The Logos is the pattern of the cosmos; it is the intelligible world; it
is the world of the Forms.


Third feature: the Logos as the pattern. The Logos is the pattern of the cosmos; it is the
intelligible world; it is the world of the Forms. The Logos is not the sensible world; it is not the
material world; it is the pattern of the sensible world. The Logos is the archetype; the sensible
world is the copy; the two are related as the pattern and the image.

   From the Tradition

   “The Logos is the intermediary between God and the world; it is the instrument of the
   creation; it is the pattern of the cosmos.” (Philo, De Opificio Mundi 24, trans. after Yonge)



75.3.2    Philo: The Allegorical Method

Philo’s account of the allegorical method is stated in the Legum Allegoriae and in the De Vita
Contemplativa. The allegorical method is the reading of the Scripture; it is the interpretation of
the text; it is the discovery of the hidden meaning.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the literal meaning. The literal meaning is the surface meaning; it is the
meaning of the words; it is the meaning of the story. The literal meaning is not the whole
meaning; it is not the deepest meaning; it is not the spiritual meaning. The literal meaning is
the body; the spiritual meaning is the soul.


Second feature: the allegorical meaning. The allegorical meaning is the hidden meaning;
it is the meaning of the symbol; it is the meaning of the allegory. The allegorical meaning is
not the literal meaning; it is not the surface meaning; it is the deep meaning. The allegorical
meaning is the soul; the literal meaning is the body.
856                                                                  Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


Third feature: the spiritual meaning. The spiritual meaning is the highest meaning; it
is the meaning of the spirit; it is the meaning of the faith. The spiritual meaning is not the
allegorical meaning; it is not the literal meaning; it is the meaning that the Spirit reveals. The
spiritual meaning is the truth; the literal meaning is the shadow; the allegorical meaning is the
image.


75.3.3      Philo: The Divine Powers (Dynameis)
Philo’s account of the divine powers is stated in the De Opificio Mundi and in the Legum
Allegoriae. The divine powers are the powers of God; they are the aspects of God; they are the
manifestations of God.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the powers. The powers (dynameis) are the powers of God; they are the
aspects of God; they are the manifestations of God. The powers are not God; they are not the
world; they are the powers of God; they are the aspects of God. The powers are the goodness,
the power, the wisdom; they are the attributes of God; they are the names of God.


Second feature: the Logos as the sum. The Logos is the sum of the powers; it is the
unity of the powers; it is the totality of the powers. The Logos is not the powers; it is not the
attributes; it is the unity of the powers; it is the totality of the attributes. The Logos is the one;
the powers are the many; the Logos is the one in the many; the one is the Logos; the many are
the powers.


Third feature: the manifestation. The manifestation is the appearance of the powers; it is
the appearance of the Logos; it is the appearance of God. The manifestation is not the powers;
it is not the Logos; it is not God; it is the appearance of the powers; it is the appearance of the
Logos; it is the appearance of God.


75.3.4      Philo: The Creation
Philo’s account of the creation is stated in the De Opificio Mundi. The creation is the work of
the Logos; it is the production of the cosmos; it is the formation of the world.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the intelligible world. The intelligible world is the world of the Forms; it is
the world of the Logos; it is the pattern of the cosmos. The intelligible world is not the sensible
world; it is not the material world; it is the pattern of the sensible world. The intelligible world
is the creation of the Logos; it is the first creation; it is the archetype.


Second feature: the sensible world. The sensible world is the world of the senses; it is
the world of the matter; it is the copy of the intelligible world. The sensible world is not the
intelligible world; it is not the world of the Forms; it is the copy of the intelligible world. The
sensible world is the creation of the Logos; it is the second creation; it is the image.
75.3. The Position                                                                                 857


Third feature: the creation. The creation is the work of the Logos; it is the production of
the cosmos; it is the formation of the world. The creation is not the creation from nothing; it is
not the creation from the matter; it is the formation of the matter; it is the ordering of the chaos.
The creation is the work of the Logos; the Logos is the instrument; the God is the creator.


75.3.5    Philo: The Ascent of the Soul

Philo’s account of the ascent of the soul is stated in the Legum Allegoriae and in the De Vita
Contemplativa. The ascent of the soul is the return to God; it is the liberation from the body; it
is the union with the Logos.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the soul. The soul is the image of God; it is the breath of God; it is the spark
of the divine. The soul is not the body; it is not the matter; it is the spirit; it is the life. The
soul is the prisoner of the body; it is the exile in the world; it is the stranger in the material.


Second feature: the ascent. The ascent is the return to God; it is the liberation from the
body; it is the union with the Logos. The ascent is not the physical ascent; it is not the spatial
ascent; it is the spiritual ascent. The ascent is the purification; it is the illumination; it is the
union.


Third feature: the union. The union is the union with God; it is the union with the Logos;
it is the union with the divine. The union is not the identity; it is not the absorption; it is the
communion; it is the presence. The union is the goal; it is the end; it is the salvation.


75.3.6    Saadia: The Unity of God

Saadia’s account of the unity of God is stated in the Emunot ve-Deot (The Book of Beliefs and
Opinions, 933). The unity of God is the foundation of the faith; it is the foundation of the
philosophy; it is the foundation of the law.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the unity. The unity of God is the oneness of God; it is the simplicity of
God; it is the uniqueness of God. The unity is not the numerical unity; it is not the unity of the
species; it is the absolute unity; it is the unity that excludes all multiplicity; it is the unity that
excludes all composition.


Second feature: the attributes. The attributes of God are not distinct from the essence;
they are not added to the essence; they are not the creatures. The attributes are the essence; the
essence is the attributes; the distinction is only in our way of speaking. The attributes are the
names of God; they are the descriptions of God; they are the manifestations of God.
858                                                                Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


Third feature: the creation. The creation is the work of God; it is the production of the
world; it is the formation of the cosmos. The creation is not the creation from the matter; it is
the creation from nothing; it is the production of the being. The creation is the proof of the
unity; the unity is the ground of the creation; the two are the two aspects of the faith.

   From the Tradition

   “The unity of God is the foundation of the faith; it is the foundation of the philosophy; it
   is the foundation of the law.” (Saadia, Emunot ve-Deot I.1, trans. after Rosenblatt)



75.3.7       Saadia: The Creation of the World

Saadia’s account of the creation of the world is stated in the Emunot ve-Deot. The creation is
the work of God; it is the production of the world; it is the formation of the cosmos.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the creation from nothing. The creation is the creation from nothing; it is
the production of the being; it is the formation of the cosmos. The creation is not the creation
from the matter; it is not the formation of the chaos; it is the creation from nothing. The creation
is the proof of the omnipotence; the omnipotence is the ground of the creation; the two are the
two aspects of the faith.


Second feature: the time. The time is the creation of God; it is the production of the time;
it is the formation of the duration. The time is not the eternal; it is not the uncreated; it is the
created. The time is the measure of the creation; the creation is the beginning of the time; the
two are the two aspects of the world.


Third feature: the order. The order is the order of the world; it is the order of the creation;
it is the order of the cosmos. The order is not the chaos; it is not the disorder; it is the order.
The order is the proof of the wisdom; the wisdom is the ground of the order; the two are the two
aspects of the creation.


75.3.8       Saadia: The Rationality of the Commandments (Ta’amei ha-Mitzvot)

Saadia’s account of the rationality of the commandments is stated in the Emunot ve-Deot. The
commandments are the laws of God; they are the rules of the life; they are the paths of the
salvation.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the rationality. The commandments are rational; they are not arbitrary; they
are not irrational. The commandments have reasons; they have purposes; they have meanings.
The commandments are the means to the ends; they are the rules of the life; they are the paths
of the salvation.
75.3. The Position                                                                                859


Second feature: the categories. The commandments are divided into two categories: the
rational commandments and the revealed commandments. The rational commandments are the
commandments that the reason can discover; they are the commandments that the reason can
justify; they are the commandments that the reason can understand. The revealed commandments
are the commandments that the reason cannot discover; they are the commandments that the
reason cannot justify; they are the commandments that the reason can only accept.


Third feature: the purpose. The purpose of the commandments is the perfection of the
soul; it is the purification of the heart; it is the salvation of the person. The commandments are
not the end; they are the means; they are the paths; they are the ways. The commandments are
the means to the perfection; the perfection is the end; the end is the salvation.


75.3.9      Saadia: The Freedom of the Will
Saadia’s account of the freedom of the will is stated in the Emunot ve-Deot. The freedom of
the will is the capacity of the human being; it is the power of the choice; it is the ground of the
responsibility.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the freedom. The freedom is the capacity of the human being; it is the power
of the choice; it is the ground of the responsibility. The freedom is not the absence of the causes;
it is not the absence of the determination; it is the power of the choice; it is the capacity of the
decision.


Second feature: the choice. The choice is the act of the will; it is the decision of the person;
it is the selection of the path. The choice is not the arbitrary; it is not the random; it is the act
of the will; it is the decision of the person. The choice is the ground of the responsibility; the
responsibility is the consequence of the choice.


Third feature: the responsibility. The responsibility is the consequence of the freedom; it
is the result of the choice; it is the ground of the reward and the punishment. The responsibility
is not the burden; it is not the weight; it is the dignity; it is the honor. The responsibility is the
consequence of the freedom; the freedom is the ground of the responsibility.


75.3.10      Saadia: The Harmony of Reason and Revelation
Saadia’s account of the harmony of reason and revelation is stated in the Emunot ve-Deot. The
reason and the revelation are not enemies; they are the two sources of the truth; they are the
two witnesses of the one truth.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the reason. The reason is the source of the truth; it is the witness of the truth;
it is the foundation of the knowledge. The reason is not the enemy of the revelation; it is not the
rival of the revelation; it is the handmaid of the revelation; it is the foundation of the revelation.
860                                                                  Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


Second feature: the revelation. The revelation is the source of the truth; it is the witness of
the truth; it is the confirmation of the reason. The revelation is not the enemy of the reason; it is
not the rival of the reason; it is the confirmation of the reason; it is the completion of the reason.


Third feature: the harmony. The harmony is the harmony of the reason and the revelation;
it is the harmony of the two sources; it is the harmony of the two witnesses. The harmony is not
the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the harmony; it is the agreement. The harmony is the
truth; the truth is the harmony; the two are the two aspects of the one truth.



75.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Philo and Saadia is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the Logos. The traditional reading takes the Logos to be a
metaphysical reality: it is the intermediary between God and the world; it is the instrument of
the creation. A revisionary reading takes it to be a literary device: it is a way of speaking about
the relation between God and the world; it is not a reality. The two readings disagree on whether
Philo is a metaphysician or a literary theorist, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s
dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a literary device.


Second dispute: the status of the unity of God. The traditional reading takes the unity
of God to be a metaphysical reality: it is the oneness of God; it is the simplicity of God. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a theological concept: it is the confession of the faith; it is the
foundation of the law. The two readings disagree on whether Saadia is a metaphysician or a
theologian, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
manifestation is real, not a confession.


Third dispute: the relation between reason and revelation. The traditional reading
takes the harmony of reason and revelation to be a philosophical principle: the two are the two
sources of the truth; the two are the two witnesses of the one truth. A revisionary reading takes
it to be a theological claim: the revelation is the foundation; the reason is the handmaid. The
two readings disagree on whether Saadia is a philosopher or a theologian, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a theology.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Philo is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the Logos. If
Saadia is a theologian, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a theology of
the unity. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the De Opificio Mundi, but it
does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with
either reading.

75.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Philo. The framework shares three structural features with Philo’s position.

       1. The Logos. Philo holds that the Logos is the intermediary between God and the
         world; it is the instrument of the creation; it is the pattern of the cosmos. The
         framework holds that the structure is the intermediary between the identity and
         the manifestation; it is the condition of the expression; it is the pattern of the
         manifestation. Both hold that there is an intermediary, and that the intermediary is
         the Logos.

       2. The creation. Philo holds that the creation is the work of the Logos; it is the
         production of the cosmos; it is the formation of the world. The framework holds that
         the expression is the work of the identity; it is the production of the manifestation;
         it is the formation of the appearance. Both hold that there is a creation, and that
         the creation is the expression.

       3. The ascent. Philo holds that the ascent is the return to God; it is the liberation
         from the body; it is the union with the Logos. The framework holds that the
         reconstruction is the return to the identity; it is the liberation from the appearance;
         it is the union with the structure. Both hold that there is an ascent, and that the
         ascent is the return.

   With Saadia. The framework shares three structural features with Saadia’s position.

       1. The unity of God. Saadia holds that the unity of God is the oneness of God; it is
         the simplicity of God; it is the uniqueness of God. The framework holds that the
         identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. Both hold that there
         is a unity, and that the unity is the foundation.

       2. The creation. Saadia holds that the creation is the work of God; it is the production
         of the world; it is the formation of the cosmos. The framework holds that the
         expression is the work of the identity; it is the production of the manifestation; it is
         the formation of the appearance. Both hold that there is a creation, and that the
         creation is the expression.

       3. The harmony. Saadia holds that the reason and the revelation are not enemies; they
         are the two sources of the truth; they are the two witnesses of the one truth. The
         framework holds that the reason and the manifestation are not enemies; they are
         the two sources of the knowledge; they are the two witnesses of the one structure.
         Both hold that there is a harmony, and that the harmony is the truth.

75.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Philo. The framework diverges from Philo’s position in three respects.

       1. The status of the Logos. Philo holds that the Logos is the intermediary between God
          and the world; it is the instrument of the creation; it is the pattern of the cosmos.
         The framework holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is
          the invariance; it is the structural condition. The framework’s structure is not the
          Logos; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of the creation. Philo holds that the creation is the work of the Logos; it
          is the production of the cosmos; it is the formation of the world. The framework
          holds that the expression is the work of the identity; it is the production of the
          manifestation; it is the formation of the appearance. The framework’s expression is
          not the creation; it is the structural expression.

       3. The status of the ascent. Philo holds that the ascent is the return to God; it is
          the liberation from the body; it is the union with the Logos. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the return to the identity; it is the liberation from the
          appearance; it is the union with the structure. The framework’s reconstruction is
          not the ascent; it is the structural reading.

  With Saadia. The framework diverges from Saadia’s position in three respects.

       1. The status of the unity of God. Saadia holds that the unity of God is the oneness
          of God; it is the simplicity of God; it is the uniqueness of God. The framework
          holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the condition. The
          framework’s identity is not the unity of God; it is the structural condition.

       2. The status of the creation. Saadia holds that the creation is the work of God; it
          is the production of the world; it is the formation of the cosmos. The framework
          holds that the expression is the work of the identity; it is the production of the
          manifestation; it is the formation of the appearance. The framework’s expression is
          not the creation; it is the structural expression.

       3. The status of the harmony. Saadia holds that the reason and the revelation are not
          enemies; they are the two sources of the truth; they are the two witnesses of the one
          truth. The framework holds that the reason and the manifestation are not enemies;
          they are the two sources of the knowledge; they are the two witnesses of the one
          structure. The framework’s harmony is not the harmony of reason and revelation; it
          is the harmony of reason and manifestation.

75.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Philo’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and that
   its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not the
   Logos; it is a pattern. The Logos is the intermediary between God and the world; the Logos
   is the instrument of the creation; the Logos is the pattern of the cosmos. The framework’s
   identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the Logos. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of patterns, not of the Logos.
   Saadia’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms are
   real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they are
   the levels of the unity of God; they are the levels of the creation. The framework’s realms
   are not levels of the unity of God; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of levels, not of the unity of God.
   Saadia’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is
   the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the harmony of reason and revelation;
   it is the two sources of the truth; it is the two witnesses of the one truth. The framework’s
   knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the harmony. The framework’s epistemology is an
   epistemology of reconstruction, not of the harmony.



75.8      The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Philo’s objection. The framework agrees that the Logos is the intermediary
   between God and the world, and it agrees that the Logos is the instrument of the creation.
   But the framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the
   enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a
   pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment
   of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern
  (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second,
   not the first.
   Reply to Saadia’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the unity of God. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   unity of God. The distinction is between a level of the unity of God (a theological level)
   and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.
   Reply to Saadia’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not
864                                                               Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


   merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts
   do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the harmony of
   reason and revelation. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading
   of the manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is
   between a harmony (an agreement) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds
   the second, not the first.



75.9       The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Philo’s cost. If Philo accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
Logos is the intermediary between God and the world. He must accept that the structure is the
condition, and that the Logos is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the
Logos: the Logos is no longer the intermediary; the structure is the condition. He must also give
up the claim that the ascent is the return to God; he must accept that the reconstruction is the
reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.


Saadia’s cost. If Saadia accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
unity of God is the oneness of God. He must accept that the identity is the structure, and that
the unity of God is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss of the unity of God:
the unity is no longer the foundation; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the
claim that the harmony of reason and revelation is the two sources of the truth; he must accept
that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural
reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Philo and Saadia, it must
give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of
reality—the dimension of the Logos, of the unity of God, of the harmony—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the Logos, and the framework leaves the Logos
to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Philo’s Logos and Saadia’s
unity of God are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Philo and Saadia must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern;
it is a structural condition that the Logos and the unity of God presuppose as their condition.
The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals,
they are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.
75.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                     865


75.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Philo). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for
   Philo’s term “the Logos.” If one substitutes “the Logos” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the Logos is the intermediary between God and
   the world, and it is not manifested, because it is the intermediary. The framework’s identity
   is multiple; the Logos is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Philo’s term “the ascent.”
   If one substitutes “the ascent” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the
   ascent is the return to God. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the ascent is
   spiritual. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Saadia). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Saadia’s term “the unity of God.” If one substitutes “the unity of God” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the unity of God is the
   oneness of God, and it is not manifested, because it is the unity. The framework’s identity
   is multiple; the unity of God is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Saadia’s term “the harmony.”
   If one substitutes “the harmony” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   the harmony is the agreement of reason and revelation. The framework’s reconstruction
   is structural; the harmony is theological. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Philo is resemblance:
   both hold that there is an intermediary, and they differ on whether the intermediary is the
   Logos or the structure. The relation between the framework and Saadia is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a unity, and they differ on whether the unity is the unity of God or
   the structure. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The
   framework’s reading of Philo and Saadia would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and Logos,
   or between structure and unity—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the
   structural condition from the Logos and the unity, and that the framework’s distinction is
   a development of their own.



75.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.
866                                                               Chapter 75. Philo and Saadia


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Philo’s Logos or Saadia’s unity
of God, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but
the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Philo’s Logos is already a structural
condition, or that Saadia’s unity of God is already a structural condition, has a question the
chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the De Opificio Mundi, the Legum Allegoriae,
the De Vita Contemplativa, the Emunot ve-Deot, and the Tafsir do justice to the texts? The
chapter has used the Logos, the allegorical method, the divine powers, the creation, the ascent of
the soul, the unity of God, the rationality of the commandments, the freedom of the will, and
the harmony of reason and revelation, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader
who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

Chapter 76

Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058 CE), known in the
Latin West as Avicebron, and Yehuda Halevi (c. 1075–1141 CE), the two great figures of the
Jewish philosophical and poetic tradition in Muslim Spain. It states Ibn Gabirol’s doctrine of
the universal matter and the universal form, the doctrine of the divine will, the theory of the
emanation, and the doctrine of the hierarchy of being; and it states Yehuda Halevi’s doctrine of
the chosen people, the land of Israel, the critique of philosophy, the defense of the tradition, and
the doctrine of the divine encounter, with reference to Ibn Gabirol’s Fons Vitae (The Fountain
of Life, Meqor Hayyim) and the Keter Malkhut (The Royal Crown); and Yehuda Halevi’s Kuzari
(The Book of the Khazar, Sefer ha-Kuzari) and the Divan (the collection of his poems); it
identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the two thinkers; it states the points
of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of matter and of the nation is
the nearest Jewish analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda
Halevi would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each
side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s
reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of
“universal matter,” “universal form,” “the divine will,” “emanation,” “the chosen people,” “the
land of Israel,” or “the divine encounter,” these are the terms of the two thinkers, and their sense
is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


76.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is looking at a stone. She sees the shape, the color, the weight. She asks:
what is the stone made of? The stone is made of matter and form; the matter is the stuff; the
form is the shape. But what is the matter of the stone? The matter of the stone is the earth; the
matter of the earth is the elements; the matter of the elements is the prime matter; the prime
matter is the universal matter. The universal matter is the substrate of all things; it is the stuff
of the cosmos; it is the ground of the material world. And what is the form of the stone? The
form of the stone is the shape; the form of the shape is the quality; the form of the quality is the
essence; the essence is the universal form. The universal form is the pattern of all things; it is
the structure of the cosmos; it is the ground of the intelligible world.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the stone is, or what the matter and
the form are, but what the will is. Ibn Gabirol answers: the will is the power of God; it is the
intermediary between God and the world; it is the source of the matter and the form. The will is
not God; it is not the world; it is the power of God; it is the intermediary. The will is the creator
of the matter and the form; it is the source of the emanation; it is the ground of the hierarchy.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the stone is, or what

                                                868
76.2. The Question                                                                                 869


the will is, but what the people is. Yehuda Halevi answers: the people is not the collection of the
individuals; it is not the sum of the citizens; it is not the totality of the nation. The people is the
chosen people; it is the people of Israel; it is the people of the covenant. The people is not the
biological; it is not the sociological; it is the spiritual; it is the chosen. The people is the people
of the land; the land is the land of Israel; the land is the holy land; the land is the gift of God.
   The scene is the image of the two thinkers, in the Fons Vitae and in the Kuzari, of the
structure of the matter and the nation. The stone is the matter and the form; the will is the
source of the emanation; the people is the chosen people. The scene poses the question that Ibn
Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi were the first to pose in its full form in the Jewish tradition. What
is the matter? What is the form? And what is the people? The present chapter states the two
answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.



76.2      The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Philo and Saadia: the Logos, the allegorical method,
the divine powers, the creation, the ascent of the soul, the unity of God, the creation of the
world, the rationality of the commandments, the freedom of the will, and the harmony of reason
and revelation. The Jewish tradition has asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the
human being is before God. The present chapter states the two positions of Ibn Gabirol and
Yehuda Halevi, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
   The question is not whether Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi were right. The question is what
they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The
question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi hold? The chapter
states Ibn Gabirol’s universal matter and universal form, the divine will, the emanation, and the
hierarchy of being; and it states Yehuda Halevi’s chosen people, the land of Israel, the critique of
philosophy, the defense of the tradition, and the divine encounter, with reference to the Fons
Vitae, the Keter Malkhut, the Kuzari, and the Divan.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
thinkers? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.



76.3      The Position
870                                                  Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


76.3.1      Ibn Gabirol: The Universal Matter and the Universal Form

Ibn Gabirol’s account of the universal matter and the universal form is stated in the Fons Vitae
(The Fountain of Life). The universal matter is the substrate of all things; the universal form is
the pattern of all things; the two are the two principles of the cosmos.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the universal matter. The universal matter is the substrate of all things; it
is the stuff of the cosmos; it is the ground of the material world. The universal matter is not
the particular matter; it is not the matter of the stone; it is not the matter of the earth; it is
the matter of all things; it is the prime matter. The universal matter is the one; the particular
matters are the many; the one is the universal matter; the many are the particular matters.


Second feature: the universal form. The universal form is the pattern of all things; it is
the structure of the cosmos; it is the ground of the intelligible world. The universal form is not
the particular form; it is not the form of the stone; it is not the form of the earth; it is the form
of all things; it is the prime form. The universal form is the one; the particular forms are the
many; the one is the universal form; the many are the particular forms.


Third feature: the composition. The composition is the composition of the matter and the
form; it is the union of the two principles; it is the structure of the cosmos. The composition is
not the matter; it is not the form; it is the union of the two; it is the structure of the thing. The
composition is the reality; the matter and the form are the principles; the composition is the
cosmos.

   From the Tradition

   “The universal matter is the substrate of all things; the universal form is the pattern of all
   things; the two are the two principles of the cosmos.” (Ibn Gabirol, Fons Vitae I.1, trans.
   after Wedeck)



76.3.2      Ibn Gabirol: The Divine Will

Ibn Gabirol’s account of the divine will is stated in the Fons Vitae. The divine will is the power
of God; it is the intermediary between God and the world; it is the source of the matter and the
form.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the will as the power. The will is the power of God; it is the intermediary
between God and the world; it is the source of the matter and the form. The will is not God; it
is not the world; it is the power of God; it is the intermediary. The will is the creator of the
matter and the form; it is the source of the emanation; it is the ground of the hierarchy.
76.3. The Position                                                                                  871


Second feature: the will as the intermediary. The will is the intermediary between God
and the world; it is the mediator; it is the bridge. The will is not God; it is not the world; it is
between the two; it is the connection. The will is the first emanation; it is the first creation; it is
the first manifestation.


Third feature: the will as the source. The will is the source of the matter and the form; it
is the source of the emanation; it is the source of the hierarchy. The will is not the matter; it is
not the form; it is the source of the two; it is the source of the cosmos. The will is the ground; it
is the source; it is the intermediary.


76.3.3       Ibn Gabirol: The Emanation

Ibn Gabirol’s account of the emanation is stated in the Fons Vitae. The emanation is the
production of the cosmos; it is the procession of the many from the one; it is the descent of the
being from the source.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the emanation. The emanation is the production of the cosmos; it is the
procession of the many from the one; it is the descent of the being from the source. The emanation
is not the creation from nothing; it is not the creation from the matter; it is the procession of
the many from the one; it is the descent of the being from the source.


Second feature: the hierarchy. The hierarchy is the order of the emanation; it is the order
of the cosmos; it is the order of the being. The hierarchy is not the chaos; it is not the disorder;
it is the order. The hierarchy is the emanation; the emanation is the hierarchy; the two are the
two aspects of the cosmos.


Third feature: the return. The return is the return to the source; it is the ascent of the
many to the one; it is the ascent of the being to the source. The return is not the emanation; it
is not the descent; it is the ascent; it is the return. The return is the goal; it is the end; it is the
salvation.


76.3.4       Ibn Gabirol: The Hierarchy of Being

Ibn Gabirol’s account of the hierarchy of being is stated in the Fons Vitae and in the Keter
Malkhut. The hierarchy is the order of the being; it is the order of the cosmos; it is the order of
the emanation.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the levels. The hierarchy has levels; it has gradations; it has stages. The
levels are: the divine will, the universal matter and form, the intellect, the soul, the nature, the
body. The hierarchy is the order of the being; it is the order of the cosmos; it is the order of the
emanation.
872                                                   Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


Second feature: the correspondence. The hierarchy is the correspondence between the
macrocosm and the microcosm; it is the correspondence between the cosmos and the human
being; it is the correspondence between the divine and the human. The correspondence is the
key to the Fons Vitae; it is the key to the hierarchy; it is the key to the cosmos.


Third feature: the unity. The unity is the unity of the hierarchy; it is the unity of the
cosmos; it is the unity of the being. The unity is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the
unity that contains the difference; it is the unity that contains the opposition. The unity is the
hierarchy; the hierarchy is the unity; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.


76.3.5      Yehuda Halevi: The Chosen People

Yehuda Halevi’s account of the chosen people is stated in the Kuzari (The Book of the Khazar).
The chosen people is the people of Israel; it is the people of the covenant; it is the people of the
divine election.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the election. The election is the election of the people of Israel; it is the choice
of God; it is the gift of the covenant. The election is not the merit; it is not the achievement; it
is the grace; it is the gift. The election is the foundation of the people; it is the ground of the
nation; it is the source of the history.


Second feature: the people. The people is the people of Israel; it is the people of the
covenant; it is the people of the divine election. The people is not the collection of the individuals;
it is not the sum of the citizens; it is not the totality of the nation. The people is the spiritual; it
is the chosen; it is the holy.


Third feature: the history. The history is the history of the people; it is the history of the
election; it is the history of the covenant. The history is not the history of the individual; it is
not the history of the citizen; it is the history of the people. The history is the history of the
election; the election is the ground of the history; the two are the two aspects of the people.

   From the Tradition

   “The people of Israel is the chosen people; it is the people of the covenant; it is the people
   of the divine election.” (Yehuda Halevi, Kuzari I.95, trans. after Hirschfeld)



76.3.6      Yehuda Halevi: The Land of Israel

Yehuda Halevi’s account of the land of Israel is stated in the Kuzari and in the Divan. The land
of Israel is the holy land; it is the land of the covenant; it is the land of the divine presence.
      The account has three features.
76.3. The Position                                                                                   873


First feature: the land. The land is the land of Israel; it is the holy land; it is the land of
the covenant. The land is not the territory; it is not the geography; it is not the soil. The land is
the holy; it is the chosen; it is the gift. The land is the gift of God; it is the inheritance of the
people; it is the home of the nation.


Second feature: the presence. The presence is the presence of God; it is the presence in
the land; it is the presence in the temple. The presence is not the absence; it is not the distant;
it is not the transcendent. The presence is the near; it is the immanent; it is the present. The
presence is the presence in the land; the land is the place of the presence; the two are the two
aspects of the holy.


Third feature: the return. The return is the return to the land; it is the return to the
presence; it is the return to the covenant. The return is not the physical; it is not the geographical;
it is the spiritual; it is the holy. The return is the goal; it is the end; it is the salvation. The
return is the return to the land; the land is the goal; the goal is the return.


76.3.7     Yehuda Halevi: The Critique of Philosophy
Yehuda Halevi’s critique of philosophy is stated in the Kuzari. The critique is the rejection of
the philosophical foundation; it is the affirmation of the traditional foundation.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the critique of the reason. The reason is not the foundation of the truth; it
is not the source of the knowledge; it is not the ground of the faith. The reason is the human; it
is the limited; it is the fallible. The reason is not the divine; it is not the infallible; it is not the
absolute. The reason is the handmaid; the revelation is the master; the reason is the servant; the
revelation is the lord.


Second feature: the critique of the philosophy. The philosophy is not the foundation of
the truth; it is not the source of the knowledge; it is not the ground of the faith. The philosophy
is the human; it is the limited; it is the fallible. The philosophy is not the divine; it is not the
infallible; it is not the absolute. The philosophy is the speculation; the revelation is the truth;
the philosophy is the opinion; the revelation is the certainty.


Third feature: the affirmation of the tradition. The tradition is the foundation of the
truth; it is the source of the knowledge; it is the ground of the faith. The tradition is the divine;
it is the infallible; it is the absolute. The tradition is the revelation; the revelation is the truth;
the tradition is the certainty; the certainty is the faith.


76.3.8     Yehuda Halevi: The Defense of the Tradition
Yehuda Halevi’s defense of the tradition is stated in the Kuzari. The defense is the affirmation of
the tradition; it is the justification of the faith; it is the defense of the people.
   The defense has three features.
874                                                    Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


First feature: the tradition. The tradition is the foundation of the faith; it is the source of
the knowledge; it is the ground of the people. The tradition is the revelation; the revelation is
the truth; the tradition is the certainty; the certainty is the faith. The tradition is the chain of
the generations; it is the transmission of the truth; it is the heritage of the people.


Second feature: the faith. The faith is the trust in God; it is the reliance on the tradition;
it is the confidence in the revelation. The faith is not the reason; it is not the philosophy; it is
not the speculation. The faith is the trust; it is the reliance; it is the confidence. The faith is the
foundation; it is the source; it is the ground.


Third feature: the people. The people is the people of Israel; it is the people of the covenant;
it is the people of the divine election. The people is not the collection of the individuals; it is not
the sum of the citizens; it is not the totality of the nation. The people is the spiritual; it is the
chosen; it is the holy. The people is the foundation; it is the source; it is the ground.


76.3.9      Yehuda Halevi: The Divine Encounter

Yehuda Halevi’s account of the divine encounter is stated in the Kuzari and in the Divan. The
encounter is the meeting with God; it is the presence of God; it is the revelation of God.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the encounter. The encounter is the meeting with God; it is the presence of
God; it is the revelation of God. The encounter is not the reason; it is not the philosophy; it is
not the speculation. The encounter is the experience; it is the presence; it is the revelation. The
encounter is the foundation; it is the source; it is the ground.


Second feature: the presence. The presence is the presence of God; it is the presence in
the land; it is the presence in the temple. The presence is not the absence; it is not the distant;
it is not the transcendent. The presence is the near; it is the immanent; it is the present. The
presence is the encounter; the encounter is the presence; the two are the two aspects of the divine.


Third feature: the revelation. The revelation is the revelation of God; it is the revelation
in the land; it is the revelation in the temple. The revelation is not the reason; it is not the
philosophy; it is not the speculation. The revelation is the truth; it is the certainty; it is the faith.
The revelation is the encounter; the encounter is the revelation; the two are the two aspects of
the divine.



76.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi is disputed, and the disputes matter for
the dialogue.
76.5. Points of Convergence                                                                        875


First dispute: the status of the universal matter. The traditional reading takes the
universal matter to be a metaphysical reality: it is the substrate of all things; it is the stuff of
the cosmos. A revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophical concept: it is a way of speaking
about the material world; it is not a reality. The two readings disagree on whether Ibn Gabirol
is a metaphysician or a philosopher, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a concept.

Second dispute: the status of the chosen people. The traditional reading takes the
chosen people to be a theological reality: it is the people of Israel; it is the people of the covenant;
it is the people of the divine election. A revisionary reading takes it to be a historical concept:
it is the people of the history; it is the people of the tradition; it is not a theological reality.
The two readings disagree on whether Yehuda Halevi is a theologian or a historian, and the
disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is
real, not a concept.

Third dispute: the relation between Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi. The traditional
reading takes the two to be rivals: Ibn Gabirol is the philosopher; Yehuda Halevi is the theologian;
the two are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary: Ibn Gabirol provides
the metaphysics; Yehuda Halevi provides the theology; the two are the two sides of the one.
The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
neither a rival nor a complement.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Ibn Gabirol is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of matter. If
Yehuda Halevi is a theologian, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
theology of the people. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Fons Vitae,
but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible
with either reading.


76.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Ibn Gabirol. The framework shares three structural features with Ibn Gabirol’s
   position.

       1. The universal matter. Ibn Gabirol holds that the universal matter is the substrate
         of all things; it is the stuff of the cosmos; it is the ground of the material world. The
         framework holds that the manifestation is the appearance of the identity; it is the
         expression of the structure; it is the ground of the material world. Both hold that
         there is a substrate, and that the substrate is the matter.

       2. The universal form. Ibn Gabirol holds that the universal form is the pattern of all
         things; it is the structure of the cosmos; it is the ground of the intelligible world.
876                                                   Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


         The framework holds that the structure is the invariance; it is the condition; it is
          the ground of the intelligible world. Both hold that there is a pattern, and that the
          pattern is the form.

       3. The divine will. Ibn Gabirol holds that the divine will is the power of God; it is
          the intermediary between God and the world; it is the source of the matter and the
          form. The framework holds that the structure is the condition of the manifestation;
          it is the intermediary between the identity and the manifestation; it is the source of
          the expression. Both hold that there is an intermediary, and that the intermediary
          is the will.

  With Yehuda Halevi. The framework shares three structural features with Yehuda
  Halevi’s position.

       1. The chosen people. Yehuda Halevi holds that the chosen people is the people of
          Israel; it is the people of the covenant; it is the people of the divine election. The
          framework holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the
          condition. Both hold that there is a people, and that the people is the chosen.

       2. The land of Israel. Yehuda Halevi holds that the land of Israel is the holy land; it is
          the land of the covenant; it is the land of the divine presence. The framework holds
          that the context is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground. Both hold that there
          is a land, and that the land is the holy.

       3. The divine encounter. Yehuda Halevi holds that the encounter is the meeting with
          God; it is the presence of God; it is the revelation of God. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the presence of the
          identity to the subject; it is the realization of the structure. Both hold that there is
          an encounter, and that the encounter is the presence.



76.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Ibn Gabirol. The framework diverges from Ibn Gabirol’s position in three respects.

       1. The status of the universal matter. Ibn Gabirol holds that the universal matter is the
          substrate of all things; it is the stuff of the cosmos; it is the ground of the material
         world. The framework holds that the manifestation is the appearance of the identity;
          it is the expression of the structure; it is the ground of the material world. The
          framework’s manifestation is not the universal matter; it is the appearance of the
          identity.

       2. The status of the universal form. Ibn Gabirol holds that the universal form is
          the pattern of all things; it is the structure of the cosmos; it is the ground of the
76.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                                    877


         intelligible world. The framework holds that the structure is the invariance; it is the
         condition; it is the ground of the intelligible world. The framework’s structure is not
         the universal form; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       3. The status of the divine will. Ibn Gabirol holds that the divine will is the power
         of God; it is the intermediary between God and the world; it is the source of the
         matter and the form. The framework holds that the structure is the condition of the
         manifestation; it is the intermediary between the identity and the manifestation; it
         is the source of the expression. The framework’s structure is not the divine will; it is
         the condition of the manifestation.

   With Yehuda Halevi. The framework diverges from Yehuda Halevi’s position in three
   respects.

       1. The status of the chosen people. Yehuda Halevi holds that the chosen people is the
         people of Israel; it is the people of the covenant; it is the people of the divine election.
         The framework holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the
         condition. The framework’s identity is not the chosen people; it is the structural
         condition.

       2. The status of the land of Israel. Yehuda Halevi holds that the land of Israel is the
         holy land; it is the land of the covenant; it is the land of the divine presence. The
         framework holds that the context is the field; it is the horizon; it is the ground. The
         framework’s context is not the land of Israel; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       3. The status of the divine encounter. Yehuda Halevi holds that the encounter is the
         meeting with God; it is the presence of God; it is the revelation of God. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
         the presence of the identity to the subject; it is the realization of the structure. The
         framework’s reconstruction is not the divine encounter; it is the structural reading.




76.7      The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Ibn Gabirol’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
   the universal matter; it is a pattern. The universal matter is the substrate of all things;
   the universal matter is the stuff of the cosmos; the universal matter is the ground of the
   material world. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the universal
   matter. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the universal matter.
   Yehuda Halevi’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
   realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
878                                                Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


   levels; they are the levels of the chosen people; they are the levels of the land of Israel.
   The framework’s realms are not levels of the chosen people; they are just levels. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the chosen people.
   Yehuda Halevi’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is recon-
   struction; it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the divine encounter;
   it is the meeting with God; it is the revelation of God. The framework’s knowledge is
   a reconstruction; it is not the divine encounter. The framework’s epistemology is an
   epistemology of reconstruction, not of the divine encounter.




76.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Ibn Gabirol’s objection. The framework agrees that the universal matter
   is the substrate of all things, and it agrees that the universal matter is the stuff of the
   cosmos. But the framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and
   the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a
   pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment
   of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern
   (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second,
   not the first.
   Reply to Yehuda Halevi’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms
   are not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the
   framework denies that the realms are levels of the chosen people. The framework’s realms
   are ontological levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of
   possibility of the chosen people. The distinction is between a level of the chosen people (a
   theological level) and a level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds
   the second, not the first.
   Reply to Yehuda Halevi’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowl-
   edge is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that
   the concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the
   divine encounter. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of
   the manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is
   between a divine encounter (a meeting) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework
   holds the second, not the first.




76.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.
76.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                    879


Ibn Gabirol’s cost. If Ibn Gabirol accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the universal matter is the substrate of all things. He must accept that the structure is
the condition, and that the universal matter is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the
loss of the universal matter: the universal matter is no longer the substrate; the structure is
the condition. He must also give up the claim that the divine will is the intermediary; he must
accept that the structure is the intermediary; the structure is the condition.


Yehuda Halevi’s cost. If Yehuda Halevi accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the
claim that the chosen people is the people of Israel. He must accept that the identity is the
structure, and that the chosen people is a manifestation of the identity. The cost is the loss
of the chosen people: the chosen people is no longer the people of Israel; the structure is the
condition. He must also give up the claim that the divine encounter is the meeting with God; he
must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is
the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda
Halevi, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a
dimension of reality—the dimension of the universal matter, of the chosen people, of the divine
encounter—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the
structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the universal
matter, and the framework leaves the universal matter to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Ibn Gabirol’s universal
matter and Yehuda Halevi’s chosen people are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real
that the framework’s structure does not capture. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi must accept
that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the universal
matter and the chosen people presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss
of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is
incomplete without the others.


76.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Ibn Gabirol). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for Ibn Gabirol’s term “the universal matter.” If one substitutes “the universal
   matter” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the frame-
   work’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm;
   the universal matter is the substrate of all things, and it is not manifested, because it
   is the matter. The framework’s identity is multiple; the universal matter is one. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
880                                                  Chapter 76. Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi


   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Ibn Gabirol’s term “the
   divine will.” If one substitutes “the divine will” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the divine will is the power of God. The framework’s reconstruction is
   structural; the divine will is divine. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance,
   not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Yehuda Halevi). The framework’s term “identity” is not
   substitutable for Yehuda Halevi’s term “the chosen people.” If one substitutes “the
   chosen people” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the
   framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a
   realm; the chosen people is the people of Israel, and it is not manifested, because it is the
   people. The framework’s identity is multiple; the chosen people is one. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Yehuda Halevi’s term
  “the divine encounter.” If one substitutes “the divine encounter” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is
   a reading of the manifestations; the divine encounter is the meeting with God. The
   framework’s reconstruction is structural; the divine encounter is divine. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Ibn Gabirol is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a substrate, and they differ on whether the substrate is the
   universal matter or the structure. The relation between the framework and Yehuda Halevi
   is resemblance: both hold that there is a people, and they differ on whether the people is
   the chosen people or the structure. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi would be
   refuted by showing that their positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and matter, or between structure and people—by showing,
   that is, that they already distinguish the structural condition from the matter and the
   people, and that the framework’s distinction is a development of their own.



76.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Ibn Gabirol’s universal matter
or Yehuda Halevi’s chosen people, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that
it is a development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Ibn Gabirol’s
universal matter is already a structural condition, or that Yehuda Halevi’s chosen people is
already a structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
76.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               881


that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Fons Vitae, the Keter Malkhut, the
Kuzari, and the Divan do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the universal matter, the
universal form, the divine will, the emanation, the hierarchy of being, the chosen people, the
land of Israel, the critique of philosophy, the defense of the tradition, and the divine encounter,
and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a
different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a matter and a people—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the matter that subsists, or the people that is chosen? Is the truth the encounter
that meets, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Ibn Gabirol’s universal matter, Yehuda Halevi’s chosen people, and the framework’s
identity?

framework, whose account of the negative theology and of the law is the nearest Jewish analogue
