framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 77

Maimonides


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with Moses Maimonides (1138–1204 CE), known in the
Jewish tradition as the Rambam and in the Latin West as Maimonides, the greatest of the
medieval Jewish philosophers. It states Maimonides’s negative theology, the doctrine of the divine
attributes, the theory of prophecy, the account of the law (ta’amei ha-mitzvot), the harmony of
reason and revelation, the critique of the Kalam, and the doctrine of the divine providence; with
reference to the Guide of the Perplexed (Moreh Nevukhim), the Mishneh Torah, the Treatise on
the Art of Logic (Ma’amar ha-Higgayon), and the Commentary on the Mishnah; it identifies the
internal disputes within the interpretation of Maimonides; it states the points of convergence
and divergence with the framework, whose account of the negative theology and of the law is
the nearest Jewish analogue to Maimonides; it presents the objections that Maimonides would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading.
It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “negative
theology,” “the divine attributes,” “prophecy,” “the law,” “providence,” or “the harmony of
reason and revelation,” these are Maimonides’s terms, and their sense is fixed by the texts and
by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


77.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is trying to describe God. She says: God is wise; God is powerful; God is
good; God is living. But then she stops and asks: what have I said? Have I described God? Or
have I described my own ideas? The words “wise,” “powerful,” “good,” “living” are the words of
the human being; they are the words of the creature; they are the words of the finite. How can
the finite words describe the infinite God? Maimonides answers: they cannot. The words do not
describe God; they describe the human being’s relation to God; they describe the effects of God
in the world. The attributes are not the essence of God; they are the actions of God; they are
the negations of the imperfections.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the attributes are, or how they
describe God, but what the knowledge of God is. The knowledge of God is not the knowledge of
the essence; it is not the knowledge of the what; it is not the knowledge of the definition. The
knowledge of God is the knowledge of the negation; it is the knowledge of what God is not; it is
the knowledge of the limits of the language. The knowledge of God is the negative theology; it is
the via negativa; it is the silence.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the attributes are, or
what the knowledge of God is, but what the law is. The law is not the arbitrary command; it is
not the irrational decree; it is not the imposition of the will. The law is the rational; it is the

                                               883
884                                                                       Chapter 77. Maimonides


purposeful; it is the good. The law is the means to the perfection of the soul; it is the means to
the knowledge of God; it is the means to the love of God. The law is the harmony of the reason
and the revelation; it is the unity of the philosophy and the faith; it is the truth of the two.
      The scene is the image of Maimonides, in the Guide of the Perplexed, of the structure of the
knowledge and the law. The attributes are the negations; the knowledge is the negative theology;
the law is the rational. The scene poses the question that Maimonides was the first to pose in its
full form in the Jewish tradition. What is the knowledge of God? What is the law? And what is
the relation between reason and revelation? The present chapter states Maimonides’s answer,
and the framework’s dialogue with it.


77.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the position of Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi: the universal matter
and the universal form, the divine will, the emanation, the hierarchy of being, the chosen people,
the land of Israel, the critique of philosophy, the defense of the tradition, and the divine encounter.
The Jewish tradition has asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is
before God. The present chapter states Maimonides’s position, and the framework’s dialogue
with it.
      The question is not whether Maimonides was right. The question is what he held, what he
can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to him. The question has three parts,
and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did Maimonides hold? The chapter states the negative
theology, the divine attributes, the theory of prophecy, the account of the law, the harmony of
reason and revelation, the critique of the Kalam, and the doctrine of the divine providence, with
reference to the Guide of the Perplexed, the Mishneh Torah, the Treatise on the Art of Logic,
and the Commentary on the Mishnah.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and Maimonides converge, and
where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Maimonides would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and Mai-
monides? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


77.3       The Position

77.3.1      Maimonides: The Negative Theology

Maimonides’s account of the negative theology is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially
in Part I, chapters 50–60. The negative theology is the knowledge of God by negation; it is the
knowledge of what God is not; it is the knowledge of the limits of the language.
77.3. The Position                                                                                885


   The account has three features.


First feature: the negation. The negation is the negation of the imperfections; it is the
negation of the finite; it is the negation of the human. The negation is not the affirmation; it is
not the description; it is not the definition. The negation is the removal; it is the purification; it
is the ascent. The negation is the negative theology; the negative theology is the negation.


Second feature: the attributes. The attributes are not the essence of God; they are not the
properties of God; they are not the descriptions of God. The attributes are the actions of God;
they are the effects of God in the world; they are the relations between God and the world. The
attributes are the negations; the negations are the attributes; the two are the two aspects of the
knowledge.


Third feature: the silence. The silence is the end of the knowledge; it is the limit of the
language; it is the rest of the thought. The silence is not the ignorance; it is not the skepticism;
it is not the despair. The silence is the recognition of the limits; it is the recognition of the
transcendence; it is the recognition of the mystery. The silence is the negative theology; the
negative theology is the silence.

   From the Tradition

   “The knowledge of God is the knowledge of the negation; it is the knowledge of what
   God is not; it is the knowledge of the limits of the language.” (Maimonides, Guide of the
   Perplexed I.58, trans. after Pines)



77.3.2    Maimonides: The Divine Attributes

Maimonides’s account of the divine attributes is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially in
Part I, chapters 50–60. The divine attributes are the attributes of God; they are the descriptions
of God; they are the names of God.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the attributes of action. The attributes of action are the actions of God;
they are the effects of God in the world; they are the relations between God and the world. The
attributes of action are not the essence of God; they are not the properties of God; they are not
the descriptions of God. The attributes of action are the actions; the actions are the attributes;
the two are the two aspects of the knowledge.


Second feature: the attributes of negation. The attributes of negation are the negations
of the imperfections; they are the negations of the finite; they are the negations of the human.
The attributes of negation are not the affirmation; they are not the description; they are not the
definition. The attributes of negation are the negations; the negations are the attributes; the two
are the two aspects of the knowledge.
886                                                                        Chapter 77. Maimonides


Third feature: the attributes of essence. The attributes of essence are the essence of God;
they are the properties of God; they are the descriptions of God. The attributes of essence are
not the actions of God; they are not the effects of God; they are not the relations between God
and the world. The attributes of essence are the essence; the essence is the attributes; the two
are the two aspects of the knowledge.


77.3.3      Maimonides: The Theory of Prophecy
Maimonides’s theory of prophecy is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially in Part II,
chapters 32–48. The prophecy is the revelation of God; it is the communication of the truth; it
is the guidance of the people.
      The theory has three features.


First feature: the prophecy. The prophecy is the revelation of God; it is the communication
of the truth; it is the guidance of the people. The prophecy is not the magic; it is not the
divination; it is not the superstition. The prophecy is the natural; it is the rational; it is the
philosophical. The prophecy is the highest form of the knowledge; it is the highest form of the
perfection; it is the highest form of the human.


Second feature: the prophet. The prophet is the one who receives the prophecy; he is the
one who communicates the truth; he is the one who guides the people. The prophet is not the
magician; he is not the diviner; he is not the superstitious. The prophet is the philosopher; he
is the sage; he is the perfect. The prophet is the one who has attained the highest form of the
knowledge; the one who has attained the highest form of the perfection; the one who has attained
the highest form of the human.


Third feature: the imagination. The imagination is the faculty of the images; it is the
faculty of the symbols; it is the faculty of the prophecy. The imagination is not the reason;
it is not the intellect; it is not the thought. The imagination is the faculty that receives the
prophecy; it is the faculty that communicates the truth; it is the faculty that guides the people.
The imagination is the prophecy; the prophecy is the imagination; the two are the two aspects of
the revelation.


77.3.4      Maimonides: The Account of the Law (Ta’amei ha-Mitzvot)
Maimonides’s account of the law is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially in Part III,
chapters 26–49, and in the Mishneh Torah. The law is the command of God; it is the rule of the
life; it is the path of the salvation.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the rationality. The law is rational; it is not arbitrary; it is not irrational.
The law has reasons; it has purposes; it has meanings. The law is the means to the ends; it is
the rule of the life; it is the path of the salvation. The law is the rational; the rational is the law;
the two are the two aspects of the truth.
77.3. The Position                                                                               887


Second feature: the purposes. The purposes of the law are the perfection of the soul; they
are the knowledge of God; they are the love of God. The law is not the end; it is the means; it is
the path; it is the way. The law is the means to the perfection; the perfection is the end; the end
is the love.


Third feature: the categories. The law is divided into two categories: the rational command-
ments and the revealed commandments. The rational commandments are the commandments
that the reason can discover; they are the commandments that the reason can justify; they
are the commandments that the reason can understand. The revealed commandments are the
commandments that the reason cannot discover; they are the commandments that the reason
cannot justify; they are the commandments that the reason can only accept.


77.3.5     Maimonides: The Harmony of Reason and Revelation

Maimonides’s account of the harmony of reason and revelation is stated in the Guide of the
Perplexed. The reason and the revelation are not enemies; they are the two sources of the truth;
they are the two witnesses of the one truth.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the reason. The reason is the source of the truth; it is the witness of the truth;
it is the foundation of the knowledge. The reason is not the enemy of the revelation; it is not the
rival of the revelation; it is the handmaid of the revelation; it is the foundation of the revelation.


Second feature: the revelation. The revelation is the source of the truth; it is the witness of
the truth; it is the confirmation of the reason. The revelation is not the enemy of the reason; it is
not the rival of the reason; it is the confirmation of the reason; it is the completion of the reason.


Third feature: the harmony. The harmony is the harmony of the reason and the revelation;
it is the harmony of the two sources; it is the harmony of the two witnesses. The harmony is not
the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the harmony; it is the agreement. The harmony is the
truth; the truth is the harmony; the two are the two aspects of the one truth.


77.3.6     Maimonides: The Critique of the Kalam

Maimonides’s critique of the Kalam is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially in Part
I, chapters 71–76. The Kalam is the Islamic theology; it is the dialectical theology; it is the
speculative theology.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the critique of the method. The method of the Kalam is the dialectical;
it is the speculative; it is the uncertain. The method is not the demonstrative; it is not the
philosophical; it is not the certain. The method is the opinion; it is not the truth; it is not the
knowledge. The method is the Kalam; the Kalam is the method.
888                                                                     Chapter 77. Maimonides


Second feature: the critique of the premises. The premises of the Kalam are the assump-
tions; they are the conjectures; they are the opinions. The premises are not the demonstrations;
they are not the proofs; they are not the certainties. The premises are the Kalam; the Kalam is
the premises.


Third feature: the critique of the conclusions. The conclusions of the Kalam are the
results; they are the consequences; they are the inferences. The conclusions are not the truths;
they are not the certainties; they are not the knowledge. The conclusions are the Kalam; the
Kalam is the conclusions.


77.3.7      Maimonides: The Doctrine of the Divine Providence

Maimonides’s doctrine of the divine providence is stated in the Guide of the Perplexed, especially
in Part III, chapters 8–24, 51. The providence is the care of God; it is the governance of the
world; it is the guidance of the human.
      The doctrine has three features.


First feature: the providence. The providence is the care of God; it is the governance of the
world; it is the guidance of the human. The providence is not the fate; it is not the determinism;
it is not the necessity. The providence is the care; it is the governance; it is the guidance. The
providence is the divine; the divine is the providence; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Second feature: the human. The human is the object of the providence; he is the recipient
of the care; he is the subject of the guidance. The human is not the animal; he is not the plant;
he is not the mineral. The human is the rational; he is the free; he is the responsible. The human
is the object of the providence; the providence is the care of the human; the two are the two
aspects of the truth.


Third feature: the knowledge. The knowledge is the condition of the providence; it is the
ground of the care; it is the source of the guidance. The knowledge is not the ignorance; it is not
the error; it is not the sin. The knowledge is the truth; it is the certainty; it is the faith. The
knowledge is the condition of the providence; the providence is the result of the knowledge; the
two are the two aspects of the truth.


77.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Maimonides is disputed, and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the negative theology. The traditional reading takes the
negative theology to be a metaphysical doctrine: it is the knowledge of God by negation; it is the
knowledge of what God is not. A revisionary reading takes it to be a linguistic doctrine: it is the
recognition of the limits of the language; it is the silence about God. The two readings disagree
on whether Maimonides is a metaphysician or a linguistic philosopher, and the disagreement
77.5. Points of Convergence                                                                      889


matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a linguistic doctrine.


Second dispute: the status of the law. The traditional reading takes the law to be a
theological doctrine: it is the command of God; it is the rule of the life; it is the path of the
salvation. A revisionary reading takes it to be a political doctrine: it is the order of the society;
it is the governance of the people; it is the guidance of the nation. The two readings disagree on
whether Maimonides is a theologian or a political philosopher, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a political order.


Third dispute: the relation between reason and revelation. The traditional reading
takes the harmony of reason and revelation to be a philosophical principle: the two are the two
sources of the truth; the two are the two witnesses of the one truth. A revisionary reading takes
it to be a political principle: the reason is the foundation; the revelation is the confirmation; the
two are the two aspects of the order. The two readings disagree on whether Maimonides is a
philosopher or a political thinker, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a political order.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Maimonides is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the negative
theology. If Maimonides is a political philosopher, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural
realism and a political philosophy. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the
Guide of the Perplexed, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a
way that is compatible with either reading.


77.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Maimonides. The framework shares four structural features with Maimonides’s
   position.

       1. The negative theology. Maimonides holds that the knowledge of God is the knowledge
         of the negation; it is the knowledge of what God is not; it is the knowledge of the
         limits of the language. The framework holds that the knowledge of the identity is the
         knowledge of the structure; it is the knowledge of the invariant; it is the knowledge
         of the limits of the reconstruction. Both hold that there is a negative moment, and
         that the negative moment is the condition of the knowledge.

       2. The divine attributes. Maimonides holds that the attributes are not the essence
         of God; they are the actions of God; they are the negations of the imperfections.
         The framework holds that the manifestations are not the identity; they are the
         appearances of the identity; they are the expressions of the structure. Both hold
         that the attributes are not the essence, and that the attributes are the relations.
890                                                                     Chapter 77. Maimonides


       3. The law. Maimonides holds that the law is rational; it is the means to the perfection
         of the soul; it is the means to the knowledge of God. The framework holds that the
         structure is rational; it is the condition of the manifestation; it is the condition of
         the expression. Both hold that there is a rationality, and that the rationality is the
         law.

       4. The harmony. Maimonides holds that the reason and the revelation are not enemies;
         they are the two sources of the truth; they are the two witnesses of the one truth.
         The framework holds that the reason and the manifestation are not enemies; they
         are the two sources of the knowledge; they are the two witnesses of the one structure.
         Both hold that there is a harmony, and that the harmony is the truth.



77.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With Maimonides. The framework diverges from Maimonides’s position in four respects.

       1. The status of the negative theology. Maimonides holds that the negative theology
         is the knowledge of God by negation; it is the knowledge of what God is not. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is the knowledge of the identity by the
         reading; it is the knowledge of the structure. The framework’s reconstruction is not
         the negative theology; it is the structural reading.

       2. The status of the divine attributes. Maimonides holds that the attributes are not
         the essence of God; they are the actions of God; they are the negations of the
         imperfections. The framework holds that the manifestations are not the identity;
         they are the appearances of the identity; they are the expressions of the structure.
         The framework’s manifestations are not the attributes; they are the appearances.

       3. The status of the law. Maimonides holds that the law is rational; it is the means to
         the perfection of the soul; it is the means to the knowledge of God. The framework
         holds that the structure is rational; it is the condition of the manifestation; it is
         the condition of the expression. The framework’s structure is not the law; it is the
         condition.

       4. The status of the harmony. Maimonides holds that the reason and the revelation
         are not enemies; they are the two sources of the truth; they are the two witnesses
         of the one truth. The framework holds that the reason and the manifestation are
         not enemies; they are the two sources of the knowledge; they are the two witnesses
         of the one structure. The framework’s harmony is not the harmony of reason and
         revelation; it is the harmony of reason and manifestation.
77.7. The Tradition’s Objections                                                               891


77.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Maimonides’s first objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
   invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
   invariance is not the negative theology; it is a pattern. The negative theology is the
   knowledge of God by negation; the negative theology is the knowledge of what God is not.
   The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the negative theology. The
   framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the negative theology.
   Maimonides’s second objection. The framework says that there are seven realms;
   the realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just
   levels; they are the levels of the law; they are the levels of the reason and the revelation.
   The framework’s realms are not levels of the law; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the law.
   Maimonides’s third objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the harmony of reason and
   revelation; it is the two sources of the truth; it is the two witnesses of the one truth.
   The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the harmony. The framework’s
   epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the harmony.



77.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the negative theology is the
   knowledge of God by negation, and it agrees that the negative theology is the knowledge
   of what God is not. But the framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The
   framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s
   sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s
   identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is one thing,
   and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is
   between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s
   identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the law. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they
   are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the law. The
   distinction is between a level of the law (a legal level) and a level of manifestation (an
   ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not
892                                                                       Chapter 77. Maimonides


   capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the harmony of reason
   and revelation. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a harmony (an agreement) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.



77.9      The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

Maimonides’s cost. If Maimonides accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the negative theology is the knowledge of God by negation. He must accept that the
structure is the condition, and that the negative theology is a manifestation of the structure.
The cost is the loss of the negative theology: the negative theology is no longer the knowledge of
God; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the claim that the law is the command
of God; he must accept that the structure is the condition; the structure is the condition of the
manifestation.

The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts Maimonides’s objections, it must give up
the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension of reality—the
dimension of the negative theology, of the law, of the harmony—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the negative theology, and the framework leaves
the negative theology to a separate inquiry.

The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Maimonides’s negative
theology and law are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Maimonides must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is
a structural condition that the negative theology and the law presuppose as their condition. The
cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are
complements, and each is incomplete without the other.


77.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for Mai-
   monides’s term “the negative theology.” If one substitutes “the negative theology” for
   “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the negative
   theology is the knowledge of God by negation, and it is not manifested, because it is
77.11. Open Questions                                                                        893


   the negation. The framework’s identity is multiple; the negative theology is one. The
   substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Maimonides’s term “the
   law.” If one substitutes “the law” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the
   law is the command of God. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the law is legal.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Maimonides’s term “the
   harmony.” If one substitutes “the harmony” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the harmony is the agreement of reason and revelation. The framework’s
   reconstruction is structural; the harmony is theological. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Maimonides is resem-
   blance: both hold that there is a negative moment, and they differ on whether the negative
   moment is the negative theology or the structural reading. Both hold that there is a
   harmony, and they differ on whether the harmony is the harmony of reason and revelation
   or the harmony of reason and manifestation. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is
   agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading of Maimonides would be refuted
   by showing that the negative theology cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and negation—by showing, that is, that Maimonides al-
   ready distinguishes the structural condition from the negation, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of Maimonides’s own.



77.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Maimonides’s negative theology,
or is it a departure from Maimonides? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Maimonides’s negative theology is already
a structural condition, not a negation, has a question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Guide of the Perplexed, the Mishneh
Torah, the Treatise on the Art of Logic, and the Commentary on the Mishnah do justice to the
texts? The chapter has used the negative theology, the divine attributes, the theory of prophecy,
the account of the law, the harmony of reason and revelation, the critique of the Kalam, and the
894                                                                       Chapter 77. Maimonides


doctrine of the divine providence, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who
holds that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a negation and a law—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the negation that purifies, or the law that commands? Is the truth the harmony
that reconciles, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between Maimonides’s negative theology and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas. It states Buber’s philosophy of
dialogue, the I-Thou and the I-It, the eternal Thou, and the Hasidic teaching; and Rosenzweig’s
philosophy of the star, the revelation and the redemption, and the speech-thinking; and Levinas’s
ethics of the other, the face, the infinite, and the responsibility, with reference to Buber’s I
and Thou (Ich und Du), Rosenzweig’s The Star of Redemption (Der Stern der Erlösung), and
Levinas’s Totality and Infinity (Totalité et Infini) and Otherwise than Being (Autrement qu’être).
It identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the three thinkers; and it states the
points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the dialogue and of
the other is the nearest Jewish analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated Maimonides’s
answer to the problem of the knowledge of God; the next chapter states the answer of Buber,
Rosenzweig, and Levinas, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 78

Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


Scope. This chapter closes Part XII, the dialogues with Jewish philosophy, and it closes it
with three of the greatest Jewish thinkers of the twentieth century: Martin Buber (1878–1965
CE), Franz Rosenzweig (1886–1929 CE), and Emmanuel Levinas (1906–1995 CE). It states
Buber’s philosophy of dialogue, the I-Thou and the I-It, the eternal Thou, and the Hasidic
teaching; Rosenzweig’s philosophy of the star, the revelation and the redemption, and the
speech-thinking; and Levinas’s ethics of the other, the face, the infinite, and the responsibility,
with reference to Buber’s I and Thou (Ich und Du), Rosenzweig’s The Star of Redemption (Der
Stern der Erlösung), and Levinas’s Totality and Infinity (Totalité et Infini) and Otherwise than
Being (Autrement qu’être); it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the
three thinkers; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose
account of the dialogue and of the other is the nearest Jewish analogue to theirs; it presents the
objections that Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas would raise against the framework; it presents
the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation;
and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or
evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “dialogue,” “I-Thou,” “I-It,” “the eternal Thou,”
“the star,” “revelation,” “redemption,” “the face,” “the infinite,” or “responsibility,” these are the
terms of the three thinkers, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.



78.1      A Scene

Consider a person who is looking at a tree. She sees the trunk, the branches, the leaves. But she
does not see the tree as an object; she does not see the tree as a thing separate from herself. She
sees the tree as a Thou; she sees the tree as a presence; she sees the tree as a relation. The tree
is not the It; the tree is not the object; the tree is not the thing. The tree is the Thou; the tree
is the presence; the tree is the relation. This is Buber’s teaching: the I-Thou is the relation of
the presence; the I-It is the relation of the object; the two are the two modes of the relation.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the tree is, or how it is seen, but
what the revelation is. Rosenzweig answers: the revelation is the love of God; it is the presence
of God; it is the address of God. The revelation is not the past; it is not the history; it is not the
doctrine. The revelation is the present; it is the address; it is the love. The revelation is the star;
the star is the revelation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.
    Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the tree is, or what the
revelation is, but what the other is. Levinas answers: the other is not the object; it is not the
thing; it is not the It. The other is the face; the face is the presence; the presence is the infinite.

                                                 895
896                                                  Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


The other is the responsibility; the responsibility is the ethics; the ethics is the first philosophy.
The other is the face; the face is the infinite; the infinite is the responsibility.
      The scene is the image of the three thinkers, in the I and Thou, the Star of Redemption,
and the Totality and Infinity, of the structure of the dialogue and of the other. The tree is the
I-Thou; the revelation is the love; the other is the face. The scene poses the question that Buber,
Rosenzweig, and Levinas were the first to pose in its full form in the Jewish tradition. What is
the dialogue? What is the revelation? And what is the other? The present chapter states the
three answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.


78.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the position of Maimonides: the negative theology, the divine
attributes, the theory of prophecy, the account of the law, the harmony of reason and revelation,
the critique of the Kalam, and the doctrine of the divine providence. The Jewish tradition has
asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is before God. The present
chapter states the three positions of Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas, and the framework’s
dialogue with them.
      The question is not whether Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas were right. The question is
what they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them.
The question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas hold? The chapter
states Buber’s I-Thou and I-It, the eternal Thou, and the Hasidic teaching; Rosenzweig’s star,
the revelation and the redemption, and the speech-thinking; and Levinas’s face, the infinite, and
the responsibility, with reference to the I and Thou, the Star of Redemption, the Totality and
Infinity, and the Otherwise than Being.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the three thinkers converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the three
thinkers? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


78.3       The Position

78.3.1      Buber: The I-Thou and the I-It

Buber’s account of the I-Thou and the I-It is stated in the I and Thou (Ich und Du, 1923). The
I-Thou is the relation of the presence; the I-It is the relation of the object; the two are the two
modes of the relation.
      The account has three features.
78.3. The Position                                                                                897


First feature: the I-Thou. The I-Thou is the relation of the presence; it is the relation of
the dialogue; it is the relation of the encounter. The I-Thou is not the relation of the object; it is
not the relation of the thing; it is not the relation of the It. The I-Thou is the relation of the
whole being; it is the relation of the whole person; it is the relation of the whole presence. The
I-Thou is the relation; the relation is the I-Thou; the two are the two aspects of the dialogue.


Second feature: the I-It. The I-It is the relation of the object; it is the relation of the thing;
it is the relation of the It. The I-It is not the relation of the presence; it is not the relation of
the dialogue; it is not the relation of the encounter. The I-It is the relation of the partial being;
it is the relation of the partial person; it is the relation of the partial presence. The I-It is the
relation; the relation is the I-It; the two are the two aspects of the object.


Third feature: the two modes. The two modes are the two modes of the relation; they are
the two modes of the dialogue; they are the two modes of the presence. The two modes are not
the two things; they are not the two substances; they are not the two beings. The two modes are
the two relations; the relations are the two modes; the two are the two aspects of the dialogue.

   From the Tradition

   “The I-Thou is the relation of the presence; the I-It is the relation of the object; the two
   are the two modes of the relation.” (Buber, I and Thou, trans. after Kaufmann)



78.3.2    Buber: The Eternal Thou

Buber’s account of the eternal Thou is stated in the I and Thou. The eternal Thou is the Thou
of God; it is the presence of God; it is the address of God.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the eternal Thou. The eternal Thou is the Thou of God; it is the presence
of God; it is the address of God. The eternal Thou is not the It; it is not the object; it is not the
thing. The eternal Thou is the Thou; it is the presence; it is the address. The eternal Thou is
the relation; the relation is the eternal Thou; the two are the two aspects of the dialogue.


Second feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the I and the Thou; it is the
relation of the human and the divine; it is the relation of the finite and the infinite. The relation
is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the dialogue; it is the encounter. The relation is
the eternal Thou; the eternal Thou is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the dialogue.


Third feature: the presence. The presence is the presence of God; it is the presence in
the dialogue; it is the presence in the encounter. The presence is not the absence; it is not the
distant; it is not the transcendent. The presence is the near; it is the immanent; it is the present.
The presence is the eternal Thou; the eternal Thou is the presence; the two are the two aspects
of the dialogue.
898                                                  Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


78.3.3      Buber: The Hasidic Teaching

Buber’s account of the Hasidic teaching is stated in his collections of Hasidic tales and in his The
Legend of the Baal-Shem. The Hasidic teaching is the teaching of the presence; it is the teaching
of the joy; it is the teaching of the community.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the presence. The presence is the presence of God; it is the presence in the
world; it is the presence in the life. The presence is not the absence; it is not the distant; it is not
the transcendent. The presence is the near; it is the immanent; it is the present. The presence is
the Hasidic teaching; the Hasidic teaching is the presence; the two are the two aspects of the
dialogue.


Second feature: the joy. The joy is the joy of the presence; it is the joy of the life; it is the
joy of the service. The joy is not the sorrow; it is not the suffering; it is not the pain. The joy is
the presence; it is the life; it is the service. The joy is the Hasidic teaching; the Hasidic teaching
is the joy; the two are the two aspects of the dialogue.


Third feature: the community. The community is the community of the presence; it is the
community of the joy; it is the community of the service. The community is not the individual;
it is not the solitary; it is not the isolated. The community is the presence; it is the joy; it is the
service. The community is the Hasidic teaching; the Hasidic teaching is the community; the two
are the two aspects of the dialogue.


78.3.4      Rosenzweig: The Star of Redemption

Rosenzweig’s account of the star of redemption is stated in the Star of Redemption (Der Stern
der Erlösung, 1921). The star is the symbol of the truth; it is the symbol of the relation; it is the
symbol of the redemption.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the star. The star is the symbol of the truth; it is the symbol of the relation;
it is the symbol of the redemption. The star is not the concept; it is not the system; it is not the
doctrine. The star is the image; it is the symbol; it is the truth. The star is the redemption; the
redemption is the star; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Second feature: the three elements. The three elements are the God, the world, and the
human; they are the three poles of the relation; they are the three points of the star. The three
elements are not the three substances; they are not the three beings; they are not the three
things. The three elements are the three relations; the relations are the three elements; the three
are the three aspects of the truth.
78.3. The Position                                                                                899


Third feature: the redemption. The redemption is the redemption of the world; it is the
redemption of the human; it is the redemption of the truth. The redemption is not the past; it
is not the history; it is not the doctrine. The redemption is the future; it is the hope; it is the
promise. The redemption is the star; the star is the redemption; the two are the two aspects of
the truth.


78.3.5       Rosenzweig: The Revelation and the Redemption

Rosenzweig’s account of the revelation and the redemption is stated in the Star of Redemption.
The revelation is the love of God; it is the presence of God; it is the address of God. The
redemption is the redemption of the world; it is the redemption of the human; it is the redemption
of the truth.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the revelation. The revelation is the love of God; it is the presence of God; it
is the address of God. The revelation is not the past; it is not the history; it is not the doctrine.
The revelation is the present; it is the address; it is the love. The revelation is the star; the star
is the revelation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Second feature: the redemption. The redemption is the redemption of the world; it is the
redemption of the human; it is the redemption of the truth. The redemption is not the past; it
is not the history; it is not the doctrine. The redemption is the future; it is the hope; it is the
promise. The redemption is the star; the star is the redemption; the two are the two aspects of
the truth.


Third feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the revelation and the redemption;
it is the relation of the love and the hope; it is the relation of the present and the future. The
relation is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the relation; it is the dialogue. The
relation is the star; the star is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


78.3.6       Rosenzweig: The Speech-Thinking

Rosenzweig’s account of the speech-thinking is stated in the Star of Redemption and in his essay
“The New Thinking” (Das neue Denken). The speech-thinking is the thinking of the dialogue; it
is the thinking of the speech; it is the thinking of the relation.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the speech. The speech is the speech of the dialogue; it is the speech of the
relation; it is the speech of the presence. The speech is not the concept; it is not the system; it is
not the doctrine. The speech is the dialogue; it is the relation; it is the presence. The speech is
the speech-thinking; the speech-thinking is the speech; the two are the two aspects of the truth.
900                                                   Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


Second feature: the thinking. The thinking is the thinking of the dialogue; it is the thinking
of the relation; it is the thinking of the presence. The thinking is not the concept; it is not the
system; it is not the doctrine. The thinking is the dialogue; it is the relation; it is the presence.
The thinking is the speech-thinking; the speech-thinking is the thinking; the two are the two
aspects of the truth.

Third feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the speech and the thinking; it
is the relation of the dialogue and the presence; it is the relation of the human and the divine.
The relation is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the relation; it is the dialogue. The
relation is the speech-thinking; the speech-thinking is the relation; the two are the two aspects of
the truth.


78.3.7       Levinas: The Face
Levinas’s account of the face is stated in the Totality and Infinity (Totalité et Infini, 1961) and
in the Otherwise than Being (Autrement qu’être, 1974). The face is the presence of the other; it
is the epiphany of the other; it is the infinite.
      The account has three features.

First feature: the face. The face is the presence of the other; it is the epiphany of the other;
it is the infinite. The face is not the object; it is not the thing; it is not the It. The face is the
other; it is the presence; it is the infinite. The face is the responsibility; the responsibility is the
face; the two are the two aspects of the ethics.

Second feature: the infinite. The infinite is the infinite of the other; it is the infinite of the
presence; it is the infinite of the face. The infinite is not the finite; it is not the limited; it is
not the bounded. The infinite is the other; it is the presence; it is the face. The infinite is the
responsibility; the responsibility is the infinite; the two are the two aspects of the ethics.

Third feature: the responsibility. The responsibility is the responsibility for the other; it
is the responsibility of the I; it is the responsibility of the ethics. The responsibility is not the
freedom; it is not the choice; it is not the option. The responsibility is the obligation; it is the
command; it is the ethics. The responsibility is the face; the face is the responsibility; the two
are the two aspects of the ethics.

78.3.8       Levinas: The Infinite
Levinas’s account of the infinite is stated in the Totality and Infinity. The infinite is the infinite
of the other; it is the infinite of the presence; it is the infinite of the face.
      The account has three features.

First feature: the infinite. The infinite is the infinite of the other; it is the infinite of the
presence; it is the infinite of the face. The infinite is not the finite; it is not the limited; it is
not the bounded. The infinite is the other; it is the presence; it is the face. The infinite is the
responsibility; the responsibility is the infinite; the two are the two aspects of the ethics.


Second feature: the totality. The totality is the totality of the same; it is the totality of the

78.3.9     Levinas: The Responsibility

Levinas’s account of the responsibility is stated in the Totality and Infinity and in the Otherwise
than Being. The responsibility is the responsibility for the other; it is the responsibility of the I;
it is the responsibility of the ethics.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the responsibility. The responsibility is the responsibility for the other; it
is the responsibility of the I; it is the responsibility of the ethics. The responsibility is not the
freedom; it is not the choice; it is not the option. The responsibility is the obligation; it is the
command; it is the ethics. The responsibility is the face; the face is the responsibility; the two
are the two aspects of the ethics.


Second feature: the other. The other is the other; it is the presence; it is the face. The
other is not the same; it is not the concept; it is not the system. The other is the infinite; it is
the presence; it is the face. The other is the responsibility; the responsibility is the other; the
two are the two aspects of the ethics.


Third feature: the ethics. The ethics is the ethics of the other; it is the ethics of the presence;
it is the ethics of the face. The ethics is not the ontology; it is not the metaphysics; it is not the
philosophy. The ethics is the first philosophy; it is the ground; it is the source. The ethics is the
responsibility; the responsibility is the ethics; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


78.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas is disputed, and the disputes matter for
the dialogue.
902                                                  Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


First dispute: the status of the I-Thou. The traditional reading takes the I-Thou to be
a metaphysical reality: it is the relation of the presence; it is the relation of the dialogue. A
revisionary reading takes it to be a psychological attitude: it is a way of experiencing the other; it
is not a reality. The two readings disagree on whether Buber is a metaphysician or a psychologist,
and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is
a structural realism, not a psychology.


Second dispute: the status of the star. The traditional reading takes the star to be a
symbol: it is the symbol of the truth; it is the symbol of the relation. A revisionary reading takes
it to be a concept: it is a way of organizing the thought; it is not a symbol. The two readings
disagree on whether Rosenzweig is a symbolist or a conceptualist, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a concept.


Third dispute: the status of the face. The traditional reading takes the face to be a
metaphysical reality: it is the presence of the other; it is the infinite. A revisionary reading takes
it to be a metaphor: it is a way of speaking about the other; it is not a reality. The two readings
disagree on whether Levinas is a metaphysician or a metaphorist, and the disagreement matters
for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a
metaphor.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Buber is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with him is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the dialogue.
If Levinas is a metaphorist, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
metaphorism. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the I and Thou, but it does
not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either
reading.


78.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Buber. The framework shares three structural features with Buber’s position.

        1. The dialogue. Buber holds that the dialogue is the relation of the presence; it is
           the relation of the encounter; it is the relation of the I-Thou. The framework holds
           that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the
           presence; it is the reading of the structure. Both hold that there is a dialogue, and
           that the dialogue is the relation.

        2. The I-Thou. Buber holds that the I-Thou is the relation of the whole being; it is the
           relation of the whole person; it is the relation of the whole presence. The framework
           holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the whole structure; it is the reading
           of the whole identity; it is the reading of the whole manifestation. Both hold that
           there is a relation, and that the relation is the whole.
78.5. Points of Convergence                                                                       903


     3. The eternal Thou. Buber holds that the eternal Thou is the Thou of God; it is the
        presence of God; it is the address of God. The framework holds that the identity is
        the structure; it is the condition; it is the ground. Both hold that there is a presence,
        and that the presence is the eternal.

   With Rosenzweig. The framework shares three structural features with Rosenzweig’s
   position.

     1. The star. Rosenzweig holds that the star is the symbol of the truth; it is the symbol
        of the relation; it is the symbol of the redemption. The framework holds that the
        structure is the pattern of the truth; it is the pattern of the relation; it is the pattern
        of the manifestation. Both hold that there is a pattern, and that the pattern is the
        truth.

     2. The revelation. Rosenzweig holds that the revelation is the love of God; it is
        the presence of God; it is the address of God. The framework holds that the
        reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the presence;
        it is the reading of the structure. Both hold that there is a revelation, and that the
        revelation is the love.

     3. The redemption. Rosenzweig holds that the redemption is the redemption of the
        world; it is the redemption of the human; it is the redemption of the truth. The
        framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
        the reading of the world; it is the reading of the truth. Both hold that there is a
        redemption, and that the redemption is the truth.

   With Levinas. The framework shares three structural features with Levinas’s position.

     1. The face. Levinas holds that the face is the presence of the other; it is the epiphany
        of the other; it is the infinite. The framework holds that the manifestation is the
        appearance of the identity; it is the expression of the structure; it is the presence of
        the identity. Both hold that there is a face, and that the face is the presence.

     2. The infinite. Levinas holds that the infinite is the infinite of the other; it is the
        infinite of the presence; it is the infinite of the face. The framework holds that the
        structure is the condition of the manifestation; it is the condition of the presence;
        it is the condition of the identity. Both hold that there is an infinite, and that the
        infinite is the presence.

     3. The responsibility. Levinas holds that the responsibility is the responsibility for the
        other; it is the responsibility of the I; it is the responsibility of the ethics. The
        framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
        the reading of the other; it is the reading of the structure. Both hold that there is a
        responsibility, and that the responsibility is the ethics.

          manifestation is the appearance of the identity; it is the expression of the structure;

78.7      The Tradition’s Objections


   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Buber’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance, and
   that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is not
   the I-Thou; it is a pattern. The I-Thou is the relation of the presence; the I-Thou is the
   relation of the dialogue; the I-Thou is the relation of the encounter. The framework’s
   identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the I-Thou. The framework’s ontology is an
   ontology of patterns, not of the dialogue.
   Rosenzweig’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
   they are the levels of the star; they are the levels of the revelation and the redemption.
   The framework’s realms are not levels of the star; they are just levels. The framework’s
   ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the star.
   Levinas’s objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction; it is the
   reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the responsibility; it is the ethics; it is
   the face. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the responsibility. The
   framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the ethics.
906                                                 Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


78.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Buber’s objection. The framework agrees that the I-Thou is the relation
   of the presence, and it agrees that the I-Thou is the relation of the dialogue. But the
   framework denies that its identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment
   is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the
   structural condition under which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition
   is what the framework calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction)
   and an enactment (a concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Rosenzweig’s objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the star. The framework’s realms are ontological levels; they
   are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the star. The
   distinction is between a level of the star (a symbolic level) and a level of manifestation
   (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Levinas’s objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not
   capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the responsibility. The
   framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations; it is
   the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a responsibility (an
   ethics) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not the first.



78.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Buber’s cost. If Buber accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
I-Thou is the relation of the presence. He must accept that the structure is the condition, and
that the I-Thou is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the I-Thou: the I-Thou
is no longer the relation; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the claim that
the eternal Thou is the Thou of God; he must accept that the structure is the condition; the
structure is the condition of the manifestation.


Rosenzweig’s cost. If Rosenzweig accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the star is the symbol of the truth. He must accept that the structure is the condition,
and that the star is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the star: the star
is no longer the symbol; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the claim that
the revelation is the love of God; he must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the
manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.
78.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      907


Levinas’s cost. If Levinas accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim that the
face is the presence of the other. He must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the
face is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the face: the face is no longer the
presence; the structure is the condition. He must also give up the claim that the responsibility
is the ethics; he must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Buber, Rosenzweig, and
Levinas, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there
is a dimension of reality—the dimension of the dialogue, of the star, of the face— that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the
framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the dialogue, and the framework
leaves the dialogue to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must
accept that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Buber’s I-Thou,
Rosenzweig’s star, and Levinas’s face are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the
framework’s structure does not capture. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas must accept that the
framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the dialogue and the
face presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the four are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.


78.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Buber). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Buber’s term “the I-Thou.” If one substitutes “the I-Thou” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the I-Thou is the relation of the
   presence, and it is not manifested, because it is the relation. The framework’s identity is
   multiple; the I-Thou is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Buber’s term “the eternal
   Thou.” If one substitutes “the eternal Thou” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the eternal Thou is the Thou of God. The framework’s reconstruction
   is structural; the eternal Thou is divine. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Rosenzweig). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for Rosenzweig’s term “the star.” If one substitutes “the star” for “identity” in the
908                                                Chapter 78. Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas


   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the star is the symbol of the truth,
   and it is not manifested, because it is the symbol. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   the star is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Rosenzweig’s term “the
   redemption.” If one substitutes “the redemption” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the redemption is the redemption of the world. The framework’s recon-
   struction is structural; the redemption is theological. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Levinas). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for Levinas’s term “the face.” If one substitutes “the face” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by
   one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the face is the presence of the other, and it is
   not manifested, because it is the face. The framework’s identity is multiple; the face is
   one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Levinas’s term “the respon-
   sibility.” If one substitutes “the responsibility” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the responsibility is the ethics of the other. The framework’s reconstruc-
   tion is structural; the responsibility is ethical. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Buber is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a dialogue, and they differ on whether the dialogue is the I-Thou or
   the structure. The relation between the framework and Rosenzweig is resemblance: both
   hold that there is a star, and they differ on whether the star is the symbol or the structure.
   The relation between the framework and Levinas is resemblance: both hold that there
   is a face, and they differ on whether the face is the presence or the structure. Neither
   relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s reading
   of Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and dialogue,
   or between structure and face—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the
   structural condition from the dialogue and the face, and that the framework’s distinction
   is a development of their own.



78.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of Buber’s I-Thou, Rosenzweig’s
star, or Levinas’s face, or is it a departure from all three? The chapter has argued that it is a
development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that Buber’s I-Thou is
78.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                            909


already a structural condition, or that Rosenzweig’s star is already a structural condition, or
that Levinas’s face is already a structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the I and Thou, the Star of Redemption,
the Totality and Infinity, and the Otherwise than Being do justice to the texts? The chapter has
used the I-Thou and the I-It, the eternal Thou, the Hasidic teaching, the star, the revelation
and the redemption, the speech-thinking, the face, the infinite, and the responsibility, and it
has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different
reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a dialogue and a face—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the dialogue that encounters, or the face that commands? Is the truth the star
that symbolizes, or the structure that enacts? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between Buber’s I-Thou, Rosenzweig’s star, Levinas’s face, and the framework’s identity?
Part XII is now complete. The dialogues with the four great figures of Jewish philosophy—
Philo and Saadia, Ibn Gabirol and Yehuda Halevi, Maimonides, and Buber, Rosenzweig, and

Levinas—have been stated. Part XIII turns to African and Latin American philosophy. The first
dialogue is with Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub, on the Maat and the reason; the next with
contemporary African philosophy, on the Ubuntu and the community; and the last with Aztec,
Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy, on the cosmology and the liberation. The
Jewish tradition has asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is before
God; the African and Latin American traditions will ask what the community is, and what the
liberation is.
