Chapter 79

Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


Scope. This chapter opens Part XIII, the dialogues with African and Latin American philosophy,
and it opens it with two traditions that are rarely brought together in the same conversation:
the wisdom tradition of ancient Egypt, as it is preserved in the instruction texts (sebayt) of the
Middle and New Kingdoms, and the philosophy of Zara Yaqub (1599–1692 CE), the Ethiopian
philosopher whose Hatata (The Inquiry) is the first systematic philosophical work of sub-Saharan
Africa. It states the Egyptian account of maat (truth, order, and justice), the wisdom of the
instruction texts, the doctrine of the heart and the tongue, and the judgment of the dead; and it
states Zara Yaqub’s account of the creator (Igziabher), the reason of the heart, the critique of the
religions of the time, and the ethics of the love of the neighbor, with reference to the Instructions
of Ptahhotep, the Instructions of Amenemope, the Teachings of Merikare, the Book of the Dead,
and Zara Yaqub’s Hatata; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the two
traditions; it states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account
of order and of the heart is the nearest African analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that
the two traditions would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states
what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the
framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter
speaks of “maat,” “the heart,” “the tongue,” “the creator,” “the reason of the heart,” or “the
love of the neighbor,” these are the terms of the two traditions, and their sense is fixed by the
texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


79.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing before the scales of judgment. On one pan of the scales is the
heart of the deceased; on the other pan is the feather of maat. The heart is weighed against the
truth; the heart is weighed against the order; the heart is weighed against the justice. If the
heart is lighter than the feather, the deceased is justified; if the heart is heavier, the deceased
is condemned. The heart is not the body; it is the seat of the memory; it is the seat of the
conscience; it is the seat of the deeds. The heart is the witness; the heart is the record; the heart
is the truth.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the heart is, or how it is weighed,
but what maat is. Maat is the truth; it is the order; it is the justice. Maat is not the arbitrary; it
is not the convention; it is not the power. Maat is the order of the cosmos; it is the order of the
society; it is the order of the heart. Maat is the goddess; Maat is the principle; Maat is the way.
The pharaoh is the guardian of maat; the sage is the teacher of maat; the just is the servant of
maat.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the heart is, or what

                                                 912
79.2. The Question                                                                                913


maat is, but what the creator is. Zara Yaqub answers: the creator is the one who created the
world; the creator is the one who created the human; the creator is the one who created the
reason. The creator is not the many gods; the creator is not the idols; the creator is not the
creatures. The creator is the one; the creator is the source; the creator is the truth. The creator
has given the reason to the human; the reason is the gift of the creator; the reason is the light of
the creator; the reason is the way to the creator.
   The scene is the image of the two traditions, in the Book of the Dead and in the Hatata, of
the structure of the order and the heart. The heart is the witness; maat is the order; the creator
is the source. The scene poses the question that the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub were the
first to pose in its full form in the African tradition. What is the order? What is the heart? And
what is the creator? The present chapter states the two answers, and the framework’s dialogue
with them.


79.2      The Question
The previous part stated the positions of Jewish philosophy: Philo and Saadia, Ibn Gabirol and
Yehuda Halevi, Maimonides, and Buber, Rosenzweig, and Levinas. The Jewish tradition has
asked what the God of the covenant is, and what the human being is before God. The present
part turns to African and Latin American philosophy, and its first dialogue is with the Egyptian
wisdom and Zara Yaqub. The African tradition has asked what the community is, and what the
liberation is. The present chapter states the two positions, and the framework’s dialogue with
them.
   The question is not whether the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub were right. The question
is what they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to
them. The question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.

First part: the positions. What did the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub hold? The
chapter states the Egyptian account of maat, the wisdom of the instruction texts, the doctrine of
the heart and the tongue, and the judgment of the dead; and it states Zara Yaqub’s account of
the creator, the reason of the heart, the critique of the religions, and the ethics of the love of the
neighbor, with reference to the Instructions of Ptahhotep, the Instructions of Amenemope, the
Teachings of Merikare, the Book of the Dead, and the Hatata.

Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two traditions converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two traditions would raise against the framework.

Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
traditions? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


79.3      The Position
914                                               Chapter 79. Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


79.3.1      Egyptian Wisdom: Maat

The Egyptian account of maat is stated in the Book of the Dead, in the Instructions of Ptahhotep,
and in the Instructions of Amenemope. Maat is the truth; it is the order; it is the justice.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the truth. Maat is the truth; it is the reality; it is the actual. Maat is not the
falsehood; it is not the illusion; it is not the appearance. Maat is the truth of the cosmos; it is
the truth of the society; it is the truth of the heart. The sage speaks the truth; the just acts the
truth; the blessed is the truth.


Second feature: the order. Maat is the order; it is the cosmos; it is the society. Maat is not
the chaos; it is not the disorder; it is not the confusion. Maat is the order of the cosmos; it is
the order of the society; it is the order of the heart. The pharaoh maintains the order; the sage
teaches the order; the just preserves the order.


Third feature: the justice. Maat is the justice; it is the right; it is the good. Maat is not the
injustice; it is not the wrong; it is not the evil. Maat is the justice of the cosmos; it is the justice
of the society; it is the justice of the heart. The judge renders the justice; the sage teaches the
justice; the just practices the justice.

   From the Tradition

   “Maat is the truth; it is the order; it is the justice. The sage speaks the truth; the just acts
   the justice; the blessed is the order.” (Instructions of Ptahhotep, trans. after Lichtheim)



79.3.2      Egyptian Wisdom: The Heart and the Tongue

The Egyptian account of the heart and the tongue is stated in the Instructions of Ptahhotep and
in the Book of the Dead. The heart is the seat of the memory; it is the seat of the conscience; it
is the seat of the deeds. The tongue is the instrument of the speech; it is the instrument of the
truth; it is the instrument of the justice.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the heart. The heart is the seat of the memory; it is the seat of the conscience;
it is the seat of the deeds. The heart is not the body; it is not the flesh; it is not the organ. The
heart is the witness; the heart is the record; the heart is the truth. The heart is weighed against
the feather of maat; the heart is tested by the truth; the heart is judged by the justice.


Second feature: the tongue. The tongue is the instrument of the speech; it is the instrument
of the truth; it is the instrument of the justice. The tongue is not the body; it is not the flesh; it
is not the organ. The tongue is the expression; the tongue is the communication; the tongue is
the truth. The sage controls the tongue; the just speaks the truth; the blessed speaks the justice.
79.3. The Position                                                                                 915


Third feature: the unity. The unity is the unity of the heart and the tongue; it is the unity
of the thought and the speech; it is the unity of the truth and the justice. The unity is not the
identity; it is not the sameness; it is the harmony; it is the agreement. The unity is the truth;
the truth is the unity; the two are the two aspects of maat.


79.3.3     Egyptian Wisdom: The Judgment of the Dead

The Egyptian account of the judgment of the dead is stated in the Book of the Dead. The
judgment is the weighing of the heart; it is the test of the truth; it is the reward of the justice.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the scales. The scales are the scales of maat; they are the scales of the truth;
they are the scales of the justice. The scales are not the arbitrary; they are not the convention;
they are not the power. The scales are the truth; the truth is the scales; the two are the two
aspects of maat.


Second feature: the feather. The feather is the feather of maat; it is the feather of the
truth; it is the feather of the justice. The feather is not the arbitrary; it is not the convention; it
is not the power. The feather is the truth; the truth is the feather; the two are the two aspects
of maat.


Third feature: the judgment. The judgment is the judgment of the heart; it is the judgment
of the truth; it is the judgment of the justice. The judgment is not the arbitrary; it is not the
convention; it is not the power. The judgment is the truth; the truth is the judgment; the two
are the two aspects of maat.


79.3.4     Zara Yaqub: The Creator

Zara Yaqub’s account of the creator is stated in the Hatata (The Inquiry, 1667). The creator is
the one who created the world; the creator is the one who created the human; the creator is the
one who created the reason.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the creator. The creator is the one who created the world; the creator is the
one who created the human; the creator is the one who created the reason. The creator is not
the many gods; the creator is not the idols; the creator is not the creatures. The creator is the
one; the creator is the source; the creator is the truth. The creator is the Igziabher; the Igziabher
is the creator; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Second feature: the creation. The creation is the work of the creator; it is the production
of the world; it is the formation of the human. The creation is not the emanation; it is not the
necessity; it is not the accident. The creation is the act of the creator; the act is the creation;
the two are the two aspects of the truth.
916                                              Chapter 79. Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


Third feature: the reason. The reason is the gift of the creator; it is the light of the creator;
it is the way to the creator. The reason is not the enemy of the creator; it is not the rival of the
creator; it is the gift of the creator; it is the light of the creator. The reason is the way; the way
is the reason; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

   From the Tradition

   “The creator is the one who created the world; the creator is the one who created the
   human; the creator is the one who created the reason.” (Zara Yaqub, Hatata, trans. after
   Sumner)


79.3.5      Zara Yaqub: The Reason of the Heart
Zara Yaqub’s account of the reason of the heart is stated in the Hatata. The reason of the heart
is the reason that is in the heart; it is the reason that is in the human; it is the reason that is in
the creation.
      The account has three features.

First feature: the reason. The reason is the gift of the creator; it is the light of the creator;
it is the way to the creator. The reason is not the enemy of the creator; it is not the rival of the
creator; it is the gift of the creator; it is the light of the creator. The reason is the way; the way
is the reason; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Second feature: the heart. The heart is the seat of the reason; it is the seat of the conscience;
it is the seat of the deeds. The heart is not the body; it is not the flesh; it is not the organ. The
heart is the witness; the heart is the record; the heart is the truth. The heart is the seat of the
reason; the reason is the light of the heart; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Third feature: the reason of the heart. The reason of the heart is the reason that is in the
heart; it is the reason that is in the human; it is the reason that is in the creation. The reason of
the heart is not the reason of the head; it is not the reason of the school; it is not the reason of
the book. The reason of the heart is the reason of the creator; the reason of the creator is the
reason of the heart; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


79.3.6      Zara Yaqub: The Critique of the Religions
Zara Yaqub’s critique of the religions is stated in the Hatata. The critique is the rejection of the
religions of the time; it is the affirmation of the reason; it is the defense of the truth.
      The critique has three features.

First feature: the critique of the religions. The religions of the time are the religions of
the many gods; they are the religions of the idols; they are the religions of the creatures. The
religions of the time are not the religion of the creator; they are not the religion of the truth;
they are not the religion of the reason. The religions of the time are the error; the error is the
religions; the two are the two aspects of the falsehood.
79.4. Internal Disputes                                                                                917


Second feature: the affirmation of the reason. The reason is the gift of the creator; it is
the light of the creator; it is the way to the creator. The reason is not the enemy of the creator;
it is not the rival of the creator; it is the gift of the creator; it is the light of the creator. The
reason is the way; the way is the reason; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Third feature: the defense of the truth. The truth is the truth of the creator; it is the
truth of the reason; it is the truth of the heart. The truth is not the falsehood; it is not the
error; it is not the illusion. The truth is the creator; the creator is the truth; the two are the two
aspects of the truth. The defense of the truth is the defense of the creator; the defense of the
creator is the defense of the truth.


79.3.7     Zara Yaqub: The Ethics of the Love of the Neighbor

Zara Yaqub’s ethics of the love of the neighbor is stated in the Hatata. The ethics is the ethics
of the love; it is the ethics of the neighbor; it is the ethics of the creator.
   The ethics has three features.


First feature: the love. The love is the love of the neighbor; it is the love of the other; it is
the love of the creator. The love is not the hatred; it is not the envy; it is not the jealousy. The
love is the truth; the truth is the love; the two are the two aspects of the ethics.


Second feature: the neighbor. The neighbor is the other; it is the human; it is the creature.
The neighbor is not the enemy; it is not the stranger; it is not the alien. The neighbor is the
other; the other is the neighbor; the two are the two aspects of the ethics.


Third feature: the ethics. The ethics is the ethics of the love; it is the ethics of the neighbor;
it is the ethics of the creator. The ethics is not the law; it is not the command; it is not the rule.
The ethics is the love; the love is the ethics; the two are the two aspects of the truth.



79.4      Internal Disputes

The interpretation of the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub is disputed, and the disputes matter
for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of maat. The traditional reading takes maat to be a metaphysical
reality: it is the truth; it is the order; it is the justice. A revisionary reading takes it to be a social
convention: it is a way of maintaining the order; it is not a reality. The two readings disagree
on whether the Egyptian wisdom is a metaphysics or a conventionalism, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism,
not a convention.
918                                                Chapter 79. Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


Second dispute: the status of the creator. The traditional reading takes the creator to be
a metaphysical reality: it is the one who created the world; it is the one who created the human;
it is the one who created the reason. A revisionary reading takes it to be a philosophical concept:
it is a way of speaking about the ground of the world; it is not a reality. The two readings disagree
on whether Zara Yaqub is a metaphysician or a philosopher, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a concept.


Third dispute: the relation between the two. The traditional reading takes the two to be
rivals: the Egyptian wisdom is the wisdom of the many gods; Zara Yaqub is the philosopher of
the one creator; the two are opposed. A revisionary reading takes them to be complementary:
the Egyptian wisdom provides the order; Zara Yaqub provides the reason; the two are the two
sides of the one. The two readings disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a
structural realism, neither a rival nor a complement.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the Egyptian wisdom is a metaphysician, the
framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of
maat. If Zara Yaqub is a philosopher, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism
and a philosophy of the reason. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Book
of the Dead, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.



79.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the Egyptian wisdom. The framework shares three structural features with the
   Egyptian position.

        1. The order. The Egyptian wisdom holds that maat is the order; it is the cosmos; it is
           the society. The framework holds that the structure is the order; it is the cosmos;
           it is the manifestation. Both hold that there is an order, and that the order is the
           truth.

        2. The heart. The Egyptian wisdom holds that the heart is the seat of the memory; it is
           the seat of the conscience; it is the seat of the deeds. The framework holds that the
           identity is the seat of the structure; it is the seat of the invariance; it is the seat of
           the manifestation. Both hold that there is a heart, and that the heart is the witness.

        3. The judgment. The Egyptian wisdom holds that the judgment is the weighing of the
           heart; it is the test of the truth; it is the reward of the justice. The framework holds
           that the reconstruction is the weighing of the manifestations; it is the test of the
           structure; it is the reward of the identity. Both hold that there is a judgment, and
           that the judgment is the truth.
79.6. Points of Divergence                                                                         919


   With Zara Yaqub. The framework shares three structural features with Zara Yaqub’s
   position.

       1. The creator. Zara Yaqub holds that the creator is the one who created the world;
          the creator is the one who created the human; the creator is the one who created the
          reason. The framework holds that the identity is the one; the identity is the source;
          the identity is the structure. Both hold that there is a creator, and that the creator
          is the source.

       2. The reason. Zara Yaqub holds that the reason is the gift of the creator; it is the
          light of the creator; it is the way to the creator. The framework holds that the
          reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the light of the identity; it
          is the way to the structure. Both hold that there is a reason, and that the reason is
          the light.

       3. The love. Zara Yaqub holds that the love is the love of the neighbor; it is the love of
          the other; it is the love of the creator. The framework holds that the reconstruction
          is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it is the reading
          of the structure. Both hold that there is a love, and that the love is the truth.



79.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With the Egyptian wisdom. The framework diverges from the Egyptian position in
   three respects.

       1. The status of maat. The Egyptian wisdom holds that maat is the truth; it is the
          order; it is the justice. The framework holds that the structure is the invariance; it
          is the condition; it is the ground. The framework’s structure is not maat; it is the
          condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of the heart. The Egyptian wisdom holds that the heart is the seat of the
          memory; it is the seat of the conscience; it is the seat of the deeds. The framework
          holds that the identity is the seat of the structure; it is the seat of the invariance; it
          is the seat of the manifestation. The framework’s identity is not the heart; it is the
          structural condition.

       3. The status of the judgment. The Egyptian wisdom holds that the judgment is the
         weighing of the heart; it is the test of the truth; it is the reward of the justice.
         The framework holds that the reconstruction is the weighing of the manifestations;
          it is the test of the structure; it is the reward of the identity. The framework’s
          reconstruction is not the judgment; it is the structural reading.

   With Zara Yaqub. The framework diverges from Zara Yaqub’s position in three respects.
920                                               Chapter 79. Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


       1. The status of the creator. Zara Yaqub holds that the creator is the one who created
          the world; the creator is the one who created the human; the creator is the one who
          created the reason. The framework holds that the identity is the one; the identity is
          the source; the identity is the structure. The framework’s identity is not the creator;
          it is the structural condition.

       2. The status of the reason. Zara Yaqub holds that the reason is the gift of the creator;
          it is the light of the creator; it is the way to the creator. The framework holds that
          the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the light of the identity;
          it is the way to the structure. The framework’s reconstruction is not the reason; it
          is the structural reading.

       3. The status of the love. Zara Yaqub holds that the love is the love of the neighbor; it

          reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it
          is the reading of the structure. The framework’s reconstruction is not the love; it is
          the structural reading.




79.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  The Egyptian wisdom’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
  invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
  invariance is not maat; it is a pattern. Maat is the truth; maat is the order; maat is the
  justice. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not maat. The framework’s
  ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of maat.
  Zara Yaqub’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
  are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
  are the levels of the creator; they are the levels of the reason. The framework’s realms are
  not levels of the creator; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
  levels, not of the creator.
  Zara Yaqub’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
  it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the reason of the heart; it is
  the light of the creator; it is the way to the creator. The framework’s knowledge is a
  reconstruction; it is not the reason of the heart. The framework’s epistemology is an
  epistemology of reconstruction, not of the reason.
79.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      921


79.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the Egyptian wisdom’s objection. The framework agrees that maat is the
   truth, and it agrees that maat is the order. But the framework denies that its identity
   is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
   *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its
   realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Zara Yaqub’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
   not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the creator. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   creator. The distinction is between a level of the creator (a theological level) and a level
   of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Zara Yaqub’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the reason
   of the heart. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a reason of the heart (a light) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.



79.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

The Egyptian wisdom’s cost. If the Egyptian wisdom accepts the framework’s reply, it
must give up the claim that maat is the truth. It must accept that the structure is the condition,
and that maat is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of maat: maat is no longer
the truth; the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that the heart is the seat
of the memory; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.

Zara Yaqub’s cost. If Zara Yaqub accepts the framework’s reply, he must give up the claim
that the creator is the one who created the world. He must accept that the structure is the
condition, and that the creator is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the
creator: the creator is no longer the source; the structure is the condition. He must also give up
the claim that the reason is the gift of the creator; he must accept that the reconstruction is the
reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.
922                                             Chapter 79. Egyptian Wisdom and Zara Yaqub


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the Egyptian wisdom
and Zara Yaqub, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that
there is a dimension of reality—the dimension of maat, of the creator, of the reason—that its
ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the
framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not maat, and the framework leaves
maat to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the Egyptian wisdom’s
maat and Zara Yaqub’s creator are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the
framework’s structure does not capture. The Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub must accept
that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that maat and the
creator presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the
opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
others.


79.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Egyptian wisdom). The framework’s term “identity” is not
   substitutable for the Egyptian term “maat.” If one substitutes “maat” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; maat is the truth, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the truth. The framework’s identity is multiple; maat is one.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Egyptian term “the
   judgment.” If one substitutes “the judgment” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the judgment is the weighing of the heart. The framework’s reconstruction
   is structural; the judgment is eschatological. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Zara Yaqub). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for Zara Yaqub’s term “the creator.” If one substitutes “the creator” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the creator is the
   one who created the world, and it is not manifested, because it is the creator. The
   framework’s identity is multiple; the creator is one. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for Zara Yaqub’s term “the
   reason of the heart.” If one substitutes “the reason of the heart” for “reconstruction” in
   the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is
79.11. Open Questions                                                                             923


   a reading of the manifestations; the reason of the heart is the light of the creator. The
   framework’s reconstruction is structural; the reason of the heart is divine. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the Egyptian wisdom is
   resemblance: both hold that there is an order, and they differ on whether the order is maat
   or the structure. The relation between the framework and Zara Yaqub is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a creator, and they differ on whether the creator is the source or
   the structure. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity.
   The framework’s reading of the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub would be refuted by
   showing that their positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction
   between structure and maat, or between structure and the creator—by showing, that is,
   that they already distinguish the structural condition from maat and the creator, and that
   the framework’s distinction is a development of their own.




79.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.




First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Egyptian maat or Zara
Yaqub’s creator, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the Egyptian maat is already
a structural condition, or that Zara Yaqub’s creator is already a structural condition, has a
question the chapter leaves open.




Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.




Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Instructions of Ptahhotep, the Instruc-
tions of Amenemope, the Teachings of Merikare, the Book of the Dead, and the Hatata do justice
to the texts? The chapter has used maat, the heart and the tongue, the judgment of the dead,
the creator, the reason of the heart, the critique of the religions, and the ethics of the love of the
neighbor, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts
support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both an order and a reason—a person, a tradition, a work of
art. Is the thing the order that judges, or the reason that illuminates? Is the truth the heart
that is weighed, or the creator that is the source? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between the Egyptian maat, Zara Yaqub’s creator, and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to contemporary African philosophy. It states the debate between the

philosophy of the sage, the hermeneutics of the culture, and the critique of the colonial reason,
with reference to the works of Placide Tempels, Alexis Kagame, John Mbiti, Kwame Gyekye,

wisdom and Zara Yaqub to the problem of the order and the reason; the next chapter states the
answer of the contemporary African philosophy, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 80

Contemporary African Philosophy


Scope. This chapter is the dialogue with contemporary African philosophy, the tradition of
philosophical reflection that emerged in Africa in the twentieth century, in the wake of the colonial
encounter and the struggle for independence. It states the debate between the ethnophilosophy
(ethnophilosophie) of Placide Tempels, Alexis Kagame, and John Mbiti, and the professional
philosophy of Kwasi Wiredu, Paulin Hountondji, and Peter Bodunrin; it states the doctrine of
ubuntu (the community), the philosophy of the sage, the hermeneutics of the culture, and the
critique of the colonial reason; it states the account of the person as a communal being, the ethics
of solidarity, the theory of the African logos, and the project of the conceptual decolonization,
with reference to Tempels’s La philosophie bantoue (Bantu Philosophy), Kagame’s La philosophie
bantu-rwandaise de l’être (The Bantu-Rwandan Philosophy of Being), Mbiti’s African Religions
and Philosophy, Wiredu’s Philosophy and an African Culture, Hountondji’s African Philosophy:
Myth and Reality, Gyekye’s An Essay on African Philosophical Thought, and the Report on the
Teaching of Philosophy in Africa (UNESCO, 1980); it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of contemporary African philosophy; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the community and of the reason is the nearest
African analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that contemporary African philosophy would
raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “ethnophilosophy,”
“professional philosophy,” “ubuntu,” “the sage,” “communal being,” “solidarity,” or “conceptual
decolonization,” these are the terms of the contemporary African philosophers, and their sense is
fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


80.1     A Scene
Consider a person who is sitting in a village. She sees the elders gathered; she sees the children
playing; she sees the neighbors helping one another. She asks: what is the person? The person is
not the isolated individual; the person is not the solitary ego; the person is not the independent
substance. The person is the community; the person is the relation; the person is the ubuntu.
The person is a person through the other persons; the person is a person through the community;
the person is a person through the ubuntu.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the person is, or how the community
is formed, but what the philosophy is. Tempels answers: the philosophy is the wisdom of the
ancestors; it is the wisdom of the tradition; it is the wisdom of the sages. The philosophy is
not the individual speculation; it is not the personal opinion; it is not the private thought. The
philosophy is the collective wisdom; the collective wisdom is the philosophy; the two are the two

                                                925
926                                               Chapter 80. Contemporary African Philosophy


aspects of the tradition.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the person is, or what
the philosophy is, but what the reason is. Wiredu answers: the reason is the universal; it is the
critical; it is the free. The reason is not the ethnic; it is not the traditional; it is not the local.
The reason is the human; it is the critical; it is the free. The philosophy is the critical reflection;
the critical reflection is the philosophy; the two are the two aspects of the reason. The reason is
the same in all cultures; the philosophy is the same in all cultures; the two are the two aspects of
the truth.
      The scene is the image of the contemporary African philosophy, in the La philosophie bantoue
and in the Philosophy and an African Culture, of the structure of the community and the reason.
The village is the community; the wisdom is the philosophy; the reason is the universal. The
scene poses the question that the contemporary African philosophy was the first to pose in its
full form in the African tradition. What is the person? What is the philosophy? And what is
the reason? The present chapter states the answer of the contemporary African philosophy, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.


80.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the position of the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub: maat, the
heart and the tongue, the judgment of the dead, the creator, the reason of the heart, the critique
of the religions, and the ethics of the love of the neighbor. The African tradition has asked what
the community is, and what the liberation is. The present chapter states the position of the
contemporary African philosophy, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether the contemporary African philosophy was right. The question
is what it held, what it can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to it. The
question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the position. What did the contemporary African philosophy hold? The chapter
states the debate between the ethnophilosophy and the professional philosophy, the doctrine of
ubuntu, the philosophy of the sage, the hermeneutics of the culture, the critique of the colonial
reason, the account of the person as a communal being, the ethics of solidarity, the theory of the
African logos, and the project of the conceptual decolonization, with reference to the works of
Tempels, Kagame, Mbiti, Wiredu, Hountondji, Gyekye, and the UNESCO report of 1980.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the contemporary African
philosophy converge, and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence
and divergence, and it presents the objections that the contemporary African philosophy would
raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the
contemporary African philosophy? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the
relation as resemblance, not equivalence.

80.3      The Position

80.3.1       The Ethnophilosophy and the Professional Philosophy
The debate between the ethnophilosophy and the professional philosophy is stated in Tempels’s
La philosophie bantoue (1945), Kagame’s La philosophie bantu-rwandaise de l’être (1956), Mbiti’s
African Religions and Philosophy (1969), Wiredu’s Philosophy and an African Culture (1980),
and Hountondji’s African Philosophy: Myth and Reality (1976). The debate is the foundation of
the contemporary African philosophy; it is the discussion of what the African philosophy is.
   The debate has three features.

First feature: the ethnophilosophy. The ethnophilosophy is the philosophy of the tradition;
it is the philosophy of the ancestors; it is the philosophy of the sages. The ethnophilosophy is
not the individual speculation; it is not the personal opinion; it is not the private thought. The
ethnophilosophy is the collective wisdom; the collective wisdom is the philosophy; the two are
the two aspects of the tradition. Tempels holds that the Bantu have a philosophy; Kagame holds
that the Bantu have a logic; Mbiti holds that the African have a religion and a philosophy.

Second feature: the professional philosophy. The professional philosophy is the philosophy
of the individual; it is the philosophy of the critical; it is the philosophy of the free. The professional
philosophy is not the collective wisdom; it is not the tradition; it is not the sage. The professional
philosophy is the critical reflection; the critical reflection is the philosophy; the two are the two
aspects of the reason. Wiredu holds that the philosophy is the critical reflection; Hountondji
holds that the philosophy is the critical discourse; Bodunrin holds that the philosophy is the
universal.

Third feature: the debate. The debate is the debate between the two; it is the debate
between the tradition and the critical; it is the debate between the collective and the individual.
The debate is not the opposition; it is not the war; it is not the enmity. The debate is the
dialogue; the dialogue is the debate; the two are the two aspects of the philosophy. The debate
is the foundation of the contemporary African philosophy; the contemporary African philosophy
is the debate; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

   From the Tradition

   “The African philosophy is the debate between the ethnophilosophy and the professional
   philosophy; it is the dialogue between the tradition and the critical.” (Hountondji, African
   Philosophy: Myth and Reality, trans. after Singer)


80.3.2       The Doctrine of Ubuntu
The doctrine of ubuntu is stated in the African tradition, and in the contemporary African
philosophy. Ubuntu is the community; it is the relation; it is the person. Ubuntu is the word of
the Nguni languages of southern Africa; it is the word of the philosophy of the person.
   The doctrine has three features.
928                                              Chapter 80. Contemporary African Philosophy


First feature: ubuntu as the community. Ubuntu is the community; it is the relation; it is
the person. Ubuntu is not the individual; it is not the solitary; it is not the independent. Ubuntu
is the community; the community is ubuntu; the two are the two aspects of the person. The
person is a person through the other persons; the person is a person through the community; the
person is a person through ubuntu.


Second feature: ubuntu as the relation. Ubuntu is the relation; it is the connection; it is
the bond. Ubuntu is not the isolation; it is not the separation; it is not the estrangement. Ubuntu
is the relation; the relation is ubuntu; the two are the two aspects of the person. The person is
a person through the relation; the person is a person through the connection; the person is a
person through the bond.


Third feature: ubuntu as the person. Ubuntu is the person; it is the human; it is the
being. Ubuntu is not the animal; it is not the thing; it is not the object. Ubuntu is the person;
the person is ubuntu; the two are the two aspects of the human. The person is a person through
the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the person; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


80.3.3      The Philosophy of the Sage
The philosophy of the sage is stated in the ethnophilosophy, and in the contemporary African
philosophy. The sage is the elder; he is the wisdom; he is the tradition.
      The philosophy has three features.


First feature: the sage. The sage is the elder; he is the wisdom; he is the tradition. The
sage is not the individual; he is not the solitary; he is not the independent. The sage is the
community; he is the relation; he is the ubuntu. The sage is the representative of the tradition;
he is the voice of the ancestors; he is the teacher of the wisdom.


Second feature: the wisdom. The wisdom is the wisdom of the ancestors; it is the wisdom
of the tradition; it is the wisdom of the community. The wisdom is not the individual speculation;
it is not the personal opinion; it is not the private thought. The wisdom is the collective wisdom;
the collective wisdom is the philosophy; the two are the two aspects of the tradition. The wisdom
is the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the wisdom; the two are the two aspects of the person.


Third feature: the tradition. The tradition is the tradition of the ancestors; it is the
tradition of the community; it is the tradition of the wisdom. The tradition is not the past; it
is not the history; it is not the memory. The tradition is the present; it is the living; it is the
actual. The tradition is the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the tradition; the two are the two aspects of
the person.


80.3.4      The Hermeneutics of the Culture
The hermeneutics of the culture is stated in the contemporary African philosophy, especially in
Gyekye’s An Essay on African Philosophical Thought (1987) and in Wiredu’s Cultural Universals
80.3. The Position                                                                               929


and Particulars (1996). The hermeneutics is the interpretation; it is the reading; it is the
understanding.
   The hermeneutics has three features.


First feature: the interpretation. The interpretation is the reading of the culture; it is
the understanding of the tradition; it is the analysis of the wisdom. The interpretation is not
the description; it is not the repetition; it is not the transcription. The interpretation is the
understanding; the understanding is the interpretation; the two are the two aspects of the
philosophy.


Second feature: the culture. The culture is the culture of the community; it is the culture
of the tradition; it is the culture of the wisdom. The culture is not the nature; it is not the
biology; it is not the race. The culture is the human; it is the social; it is the historical. The
culture is the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the culture; the two are the two aspects of the person.


Third feature: the philosophy. The philosophy is the philosophy of the culture; it is
the philosophy of the tradition; it is the philosophy of the wisdom. The philosophy is not the

is the understanding of the culture; the understanding of the culture is the philosophy; the two

80.3.5    The Critique of the Colonial Reason

The critique of the colonial reason is stated in the contemporary African philosophy, especially
in Hountondji’s The Struggle for Meaning (1987) and in Mbembe’s Critique of Black Reason
(2013). The critique is the rejection of the colonial reason; it is the affirmation of the African
reason; it is the project of the conceptual decolonization.
   The critique has three features.


First feature: the colonial reason. The colonial reason is the reason of the colonizer; it
is the reason of the oppressor; it is the reason of the conqueror. The colonial reason is not the
universal; it is not the human; it is not the truth. The colonial reason is the particular; it is the
European; it is the Western. The colonial reason is the error; the error is the colonial reason; the
two are the two aspects of the falsehood.


Second feature: the African reason. The African reason is the reason of the African; it
is the reason of the colonized; it is the reason of the oppressed. The African reason is not the
particular; it is not the ethnic; it is not the local. The African reason is the universal; it is the
human; it is the truth. The African reason is the truth; the truth is the African reason; the two
are the two aspects of the reason.

Third feature: the conceptual decolonization. The conceptual decolonization is the
project of the liberation; it is the project of the critique; it is the project of the reconstruction.
The conceptual decolonization is not the rejection of the reason; it is not the rejection of the
philosophy; it is not the rejection of the truth. The conceptual decolonization is the liberation of
the reason; the liberation of the reason is the conceptual decolonization; the two are the two
aspects of the truth. The conceptual decolonization is the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the conceptual
decolonization; the two are the two aspects of the person.


80.3.6      The Account of the Person as a Communal Being
The account of the person as a communal being is stated in the contemporary African philosophy,

      The account has three features.


First feature: the communal being. The communal being is the being of the community;

Second feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the community; it is the relation

Third feature: the ubuntu. The ubuntu is the community; it is the relation; it is the person.

80.3.7      The Ethics of Solidarity

      The ethics has three features.


First feature: the solidarity. The solidarity is the solidarity of the community; it is the
solidarity of the relation; it is the solidarity of the ubuntu. The solidarity is not the individualism;

Second feature: the community. The community is the community of the persons; it is

80.3.8     The Theory of the African Logos

The theory of the African logos is stated in the contemporary African philosophy, especially in
Kagame’s La philosophie bantu-rwandaise de l’être and in Tempels’s La philosophie bantoue. The
logos is the reason; it is the word; it is the order.
    The theory has three features.

not the chaos; it is not the disorder; it is not the confusion. The logos is the reason; the reason is

Second feature: the word. The word is the word of the ancestors; it is the word of the

it is not the private. The word is the collective; it is the traditional; it is the communal. The
word is the logos; the logos is the word; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Third feature: the order. The order is the order of the community; it is the order of the

the confusion. The order is the reason; the reason is the order; the two are the two aspects of

80.3.9      The Project of the Conceptual Decolonization
The project of the conceptual decolonization is stated in Wiredu’s Conceptual Decolonization
(1995) and in Hountondji’s The Struggle for Meaning. The project is the liberation of the reason;
it is the critique of the colonial reason; it is the reconstruction of the African philosophy.
      The project has three features.

First feature: the decolonization. The decolonization is the liberation of the reason; it
is the critique of the colonial reason; it is the reconstruction of the African philosophy. The
decolonization is not the rejection of the reason; it is not the rejection of the philosophy; it is not
the rejection of the truth. The decolonization is the liberation; the liberation is the decolonization;
the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Second feature: the conceptual. The conceptual is the conceptual; it is the reason; it is the
philosophy. The conceptual is not the empirical; it is not the practical; it is not the political.
The conceptual is the reason; the reason is the conceptual; the two are the two aspects of the
truth. The conceptual is the logos; the logos is the conceptual; the two are the two aspects of
the reason.

Third feature: the project. The project is the project of the liberation; it is the project of
the critique; it is the project of the reconstruction. The project is not the rejection; it is not the
destruction; it is not the negation. The project is the liberation; the liberation is the project; the
two are the two aspects of the truth. The project is the ubuntu; the ubuntu is the project; the
two are the two aspects of the person.


80.4       Internal Disputes
The interpretation of the contemporary African philosophy is disputed, and the disputes matter
for the dialogue.

First dispute: the status of the ethnophilosophy. The traditional reading takes the
ethnophilosophy to be a philosophy: it is the philosophy of the tradition; it is the philosophy of the
ancestors; it is the philosophy of the sages. A revisionary reading takes it to be an anthropology:
it is the description of the culture; it is not a philosophy. The two readings disagree on whether
the ethnophilosophy is a philosophy or an anthropology, and the disagreement matters for
the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not an
anthropology.

Second dispute: the status of ubuntu. The traditional reading takes ubuntu to be a
metaphysical reality: it is the community; it is the relation; it is the person. A revisionary
reading takes it to be an ethical concept: it is the solidarity; it is the ethics; it is not a reality.
The two readings disagree on whether ubuntu is a metaphysics or an ethics, and the disagreement
matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not a
concept.
80.5. Points of Convergence                                                                     933


Third dispute: the relation between the ethnophilosophy and the professional
philosophy. The traditional reading takes the two to be rivals: the ethnophilosophy is the
tradition; the professional philosophy is the critical; the two are opposed. A revisionary reading
takes them to be complementary: the ethnophilosophy provides the content; the professional
philosophy provides the method; the two are the two sides of the one. The two readings
disagree on whether the two are rivals or complements, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, neither a rival
nor a complement.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the ethnophilosophy is a philosophy, the
framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a philosophy of the
tradition. If the professional philosophy is the only philosophy, the dialogue is a dialogue between
a structural realism and a critical philosophy. The framework holds that the first reading is
closer to the La philosophie bantoue, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the
dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.



80.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the contemporary African philosophy. The framework shares four structural
   features with the contemporary African philosophy.

       1. The community. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the community is
         the foundation; it is the relation; it is the ubuntu. The framework holds that the
         structure is the condition; it is the invariance; it is the ground. Both hold that there
         is a community, and that the community is the foundation.

       2. The person. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the person is the
         communal being; he is the relation; he is the ubuntu. The framework holds that the
         identity is the structural condition; it is the invariance; it is the enactment. Both
         hold that there is a person, and that the person is relational.

       3. The ethics. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the ethics is the ethics
         of the community; it is the ethics of the relation; it is the ethics of the ubuntu. The
         framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is
         the reading of the other; it is the reading of the structure. Both hold that there is
         an ethics, and that the ethics is the solidarity.

       4. The decolonization. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the decol-
         onization is the liberation of the reason; it is the critique of the colonial reason;
         it is the reconstruction of the African philosophy. The framework holds that the
         reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the structure;
         it is the liberation of the identity. Both hold that there is a decolonization, and that
         the decolonization is the liberation.
934                                              Chapter 80. Contemporary African Philosophy


80.6      Points of Divergence

  Points of Divergence

  With the contemporary African philosophy. The framework diverges from the
  contemporary African philosophy in four respects.

       1. The status of the community. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the
         community is the foundation; it is the relation; it is the ubuntu. The framework
         holds that the structure is the condition; it is the invariance; it is the ground. The
         framework’s structure is not the community; it is the condition.

       2. The status of the person. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the person
         is the communal being; he is the relation; he is the ubuntu. The framework holds
         that the identity is the structural condition; it is the invariance; it is the enactment.
         The framework’s identity is not the communal being; it is the structural condition.

       3. The status of the ethics. The contemporary African philosophy holds that the ethics
         is the ethics of the community; it is the ethics of the relation; it is the ethics of
         the ubuntu. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading of the
         manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it is the reading of the structure. The
         framework’s reconstruction is not the ethics; it is the structural reading.

       4. The status of the decolonization. The contemporary African philosophy holds that
         the decolonization is the liberation of the reason; it is the critique of the colonial
         reason; it is the reconstruction of the African philosophy. The framework holds
         that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the
         structure; it is the liberation of the identity. The framework’s reconstruction is not
         the decolonization; it is the structural reading.



80.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  The contemporary African philosophy’s first objection. The framework says that
  identity is a structural invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction.
  But a structural invariance is not the ubuntu; it is a pattern. The ubuntu is the community;
  the ubuntu is the relation; the ubuntu is the person. The framework’s identity is a pattern,
  and a pattern is not the ubuntu. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not
  of the ubuntu.
  The contemporary African philosophy’s second objection. The framework says
  that there are seven realms; the realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation.
  But the realms are not just levels; they are the levels of the community; they are the
  levels of the ubuntu. The framework’s realms are not levels of the community; they are
80.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      935


   just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels, not of the community.
   The contemporary African philosophy’s third objection. The framework says that
   knowledge is reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the
   wisdom of the ancestors; it is the wisdom of the tradition; it is the wisdom of the sages.
   The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the wisdom of the ancestors. The
   framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the wisdom.



80.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the first objection. The framework agrees that the ubuntu is the community,
   and it agrees that the ubuntu is the relation. But the framework denies that its identity
   is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a
   *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its
   realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the second objection. The framework agrees that the realms are not just
   levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework denies
   that the realms are levels of the community. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   community. The distinction is between a level of the community (a social level) and a
   level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the third objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge is not merely
   conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the concepts do
   not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the wisdom of the
   ancestors. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a wisdom (a tradition) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second,
   not the first.



80.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


The contemporary African philosophy’s cost. If the contemporary African philosophy
accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the ubuntu is the community.
It must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the ubuntu is a manifestation of
the structure. The cost is the loss of the ubuntu: the ubuntu is no longer the community; the
structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that the wisdom of the ancestors is
936                                              Chapter 80. Contemporary African Philosophy


the knowledge; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the contemporary African
philosophy, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is
a dimension of reality—the dimension of the ubuntu, of the community, of the wisdom of the
ancestors—that its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the
structural account: the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the ubuntu,
and the framework leaves the ubuntu to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the contemporary African
philosophy’s ubuntu and wisdom are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the
framework’s structure does not capture. The contemporary African philosophy must accept that
the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that the ubuntu and the
wisdom presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of
the opposition: the two are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without the
other.


80.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test. The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable for the
   contemporary African philosophy’s term “the ubuntu.” If one substitutes “the ubuntu”
   for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   identity is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the
   ubuntu is the community, and it is not manifested, because it is the community. The
   framework’s identity is multiple; the ubuntu is one. The substitution fails, and the relation
   is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the contemporary African
   philosophy’s term “the wisdom of the ancestors.” If one substitutes “the wisdom of the
   ancestors” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the statements change:
   the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the wisdom of the
   ancestors is the tradition of the community. The framework’s reconstruction is structural;
   the wisdom of the ancestors is traditional. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the contemporary African
   philosophy’s term “the decolonization.” If one substitutes “the decolonization” for “re-
   construction” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s
   reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; the decolonization is the liberation of
   the reason. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the decolonization is political.
80.11. Open Questions                                                                          937


   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the contemporary
   African philosophy is resemblance: both hold that there is a community, and they differ
   on whether the community is the ubuntu or the structure. Both hold that there is a
   decolonization, and they differ on whether the decolonization is the liberation of the reason
   or the liberation of the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement;
   neither is identity. The framework’s reading of the contemporary African philosophy would
   be refuted by showing that its positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s
   distinction between structure and ubuntu, or between structure and wisdom—by showing,
   that is, that the contemporary African philosophy already distinguishes the structural
   condition from the ubuntu and the wisdom, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of its own.




80.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.



First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the contemporary African
philosophy’s ubuntu or its wisdom, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it
is a development, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the contemporary
African philosophy’s ubuntu is already a structural condition, or that its wisdom is already a
structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.



Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.



Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the La philosophie bantoue, the La philosophie
bantu-rwandaise de l’être, the African Religions and Philosophy, the Philosophy and an African
Culture, the African Philosophy: Myth and Reality, the An Essay on African Philosophical Thought,
and the UNESCO report do justice to the texts? The chapter has used the ethnophilosophy,
the professional philosophy, the ubuntu, the sage, the hermeneutics of the culture, the critique
of the colonial reason, the communal being, the ethics of solidarity, the African logos, and the
conceptual decolonization, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a community and a reason—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the community that constitutes, or the reason that criticizes? Is the truth
the ubuntu that relates, or the decolonization that liberates? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between the contemporary African philosophy’s ubuntu and the framework’s
identity?

The next chapter turns to Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy. It states
the Aztec cosmology and the doctrine of the teotl, the Inca cosmology and the doctrine of the
pachamama, the philosophy of the liberation, the dependency theory, the theology of the liberation,
and the decolonial turn, with reference to the Florentine Codex, the Popol Vuh, the Comentarios
Reales of the Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, and the works of Enrique Dussel, Gustavo Gutiérrez,
Aníbal Quijano, and Walter Mignolo. It identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation
of the Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy; and it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the cosmos and of the liberation
is the nearest Latin American analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated the answer of
the contemporary African philosophy to the problem of the community and the reason; the next
chapter states the answer of the Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy, and
the framework’s dialogue with it.

Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


Scope. This chapter closes Part XIII, the dialogues with African and Latin American philosophy,
and it closes it with three traditions that are rarely brought together in the same conversation:
the cosmology of the Aztec (Mexica) tradition, as it is preserved in the Florentine Codex and
in the Popol Vuh of the Quiché Maya; the cosmology of the Inca tradition, as it is preserved
in the Comentarios Reales of the Inca Garcilaso de la Vega and in the Huarochirí Manuscript;
and the philosophy of liberation and the decolonial turn of contemporary Latin America, as it
is developed by Enrique Dussel, Gustavo Gutiérrez, Aníbal Quijano, and Walter Mignolo. It
states the Aztec account of teotl (the sacred power), the doctrine of the ollin (the movement),
the account of the tonalli and the teyolia (the two souls), and the ethics of the neltiliztli (the
rootedness); and it states the Inca account of the pachamama (the mother earth), the apus
(the mountain spirits), the hanan and hurin (the two halves), and the ethics of the ayni (the
reciprocity); and it states the philosophy of liberation, the dependency theory, the theology of
liberation, and the decolonial turn, with reference to the Florentine Codex, the Popol Vuh, the
Comentarios Reales, the Huarochirí Manuscript, and the works of Dussel, Gutiérrez, Quijano,
and Mignolo; it identifies the internal disputes within the interpretation of the three traditions; it
states the points of convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the cosmos
and of the liberation is the nearest Latin American analogue to theirs; it presents the objections
that the three traditions would raise against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it
states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would
refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the
chapter speaks of “teotl,” “ollin,” “tonalli,” “teyolia,” “neltiliztli,” “pachamama,” “apus,” “ayni,”
“liberation,” “dependency,” or “decoloniality,” these are the terms of the three traditions, and
their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


81.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing on a mountain. Below her is the valley; above her is the sky;
around her is the world. She asks: what is the world? The world is not the collection of the
things; it is not the sum of the objects; it is not the totality of the beings. The world is the
sacred; it is the teotl; it is the pachamama. The world is the living; it is the moving; it is the
sacred. The mountain is the apu; the earth is the pachamama; the sky is the teotl. The world is
the sacred; the sacred is the world; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the world is, or how it is sacred, but
what the human is. The human is not the master; he is not the conqueror; he is not the exploiter.
The human is the caretaker; he is the participant; he is the part of the cosmos. The human is the
tonalli; he is the teyolia; he is the two souls. The human is the neltiliztli; he is the rootedness;

                                                 939
940                                Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


he is the truth. The human is the ayni; he is the reciprocity; he is the relation. The human is
the part of the cosmos; the cosmos is the whole; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the world is, or what
the human is, but what the liberation is. Dussel answers: the liberation is the liberation of the
poor; it is the liberation of the oppressed; it is the liberation of the other. The liberation is not
the development; it is not the modernization; it is not the progress. The liberation is the critique
of the colonial reason; it is the affirmation of the other; it is the ethics of the liberation. The
liberation is the teotl; the teotl is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.
      The scene is the image of the three traditions, in the Florentine Codex, the Comentarios
Reales, and the Philosophy of Liberation, of the structure of the cosmos and the liberation. The
mountain is the apu; the earth is the pachamama; the human is the tonalli; the liberation is the
teotl. The scene poses the question that the three traditions were the first to pose in its full form
in the Latin American tradition. What is the cosmos? What is the human? And what is the
liberation? The present chapter states the three answers, and the framework’s dialogue with
them.


81.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the position of the contemporary African philosophy: the ethnophi-
losophy and the professional philosophy, the ubuntu, the sage, the hermeneutics of the culture,
the critique of the colonial reason, the communal being, the ethics of solidarity, the African
logos, and the conceptual decolonization. The African tradition has asked what the community
is, and what the liberation is. The present chapter states the position of the Aztec, Inca, and
contemporary Latin American philosophy, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
      The question is not whether the three traditions were right. The question is what they held,
what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The question
has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did the three traditions hold? The chapter states the Aztec
teotl, the ollin, the tonalli and the teyolia, and the neltiliztli; the Inca pachamama, the apus, the
hanan and hurin, and the ayni; and the philosophy of liberation, the dependency theory, the
theology of liberation, and the decolonial turn, with reference to the Florentine Codex, the Popol
Vuh, the Comentarios Reales, the Huarochirí Manuscript, and the works of Dussel, Gutiérrez,
Quijano, and Mignolo.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the three traditions converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the three traditions would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the three
traditions? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.
