81.3      The Position

81.3.1     Aztec: Teotl and Ollin

The Aztec account of teotl and ollin is stated in the Florentine Codex and in the Popol Vuh
of the Quiché Maya. Teotl is the sacred power; it is the divine; it is the cosmos. Ollin is the
movement; it is the change; it is the life.
    The account has three features.


First feature: teotl. Teotl is the sacred power; it is the divine; it is the cosmos. Teotl is not
the many gods; it is not the idols; it is not the creatures. Teotl is the one; it is the source; it
is the truth. Teotl is the sacred; the sacred is teotl; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.
Teotl is the power; it is the energy; it is the life. Teotl is the ollin; the ollin is teotl; the two are
the two aspects of the sacred.


Second feature: ollin. Ollin is the movement; it is the change; it is the life. Ollin is not the
static; it is not the fixed; it is not the permanent. Ollin is the movement; it is the change; it is
the life. Ollin is the cosmos; the cosmos is ollin; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. Ollin
is the teotl; the teotl is ollin; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.


Third feature: the cosmos. The cosmos is the cosmos; it is the world; it is the sacred. The
cosmos is not the collection; it is not the sum; it is not the totality. The cosmos is the sacred; it
is the living; it is the moving. The cosmos is the teotl; the teotl is the cosmos; the two are the
two aspects of the sacred. The cosmos is the ollin; the ollin is the cosmos; the two are the two
aspects of the movement.

   From the Tradition

   “Teotl is the sacred power; it is the divine; it is the cosmos. Ollin is the movement; it is
   the change; it is the life.” (Florentine Codex, trans. after Dibble-Anderson)



81.3.2     Aztec: The Tonalli and the Teyolia

The Aztec account of the tonalli and the teyolia is stated in the Florentine Codex. The tonalli is
the first soul; it is the heat; it is the fate. The teyolia is the second soul; it is the heart; it is the
memory.
    The account has three features.


First feature: the tonalli. The tonalli is the first soul; it is the heat; it is the fate. The
tonalli is not the body; it is not the flesh; it is not the organ. The tonalli is the heat; it is the
fate; it is the soul. The tonalli is in the head; it is in the blood; it is in the breath. The tonalli is
the first soul; the first soul is the tonalli; the two are the two aspects of the person.
942                                 Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


Second feature: the teyolia. The teyolia is the second soul; it is the heart; it is the memory.
The teyolia is not the body; it is not the flesh; it is not the organ. The teyolia is the heart; it
is the memory; it is the soul. The teyolia is in the heart; it is in the breast; it is in the chest.
The teyolia is the second soul; the second soul is the teyolia; the two are the two aspects of the
person.


Third feature: the two souls. The two souls are the two souls; they are the two principles;
they are the two aspects. The two souls are not the body; they are not the flesh; they are not
the organs. The two souls are the tonalli and the teyolia; the tonalli and the teyolia are the two
souls; the two are the two aspects of the person. The two souls are the person; the person is the
two souls; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


81.3.3      Aztec: The Neltiliztli

The Aztec account of the neltiliztli is stated in the Florentine Codex and in the Popol Vuh. The
neltiliztli is the rootedness; it is the truth; it is the foundation.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the neltiliztli. The neltiliztli is the rootedness; it is the truth; it is the
foundation. The neltiliztli is not the arbitrary; it is not the convention; it is not the power. The
neltiliztli is the truth; the truth is the neltiliztli; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The
neltiliztli is the rootedness; it is the foundation; it is the ground. The neltiliztli is the teotl; the
teotl is the neltiliztli; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.


Second feature: the truth. The truth is the truth; it is the reality; it is the actual. The
truth is not the falsehood; it is not the illusion; it is not the appearance. The truth is the teotl;
the teotl is the truth; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The truth is the neltiliztli; the
neltiliztli is the truth; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos.


Third feature: the foundation. The foundation is the foundation; it is the ground; it is the
source. The foundation is not the arbitrary; it is not the convention; it is not the power. The
foundation is the teotl; the teotl is the foundation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The
foundation is the neltiliztli; the neltiliztli is the foundation; the two are the two aspects of the
cosmos.


81.3.4      Inca: The Pachamama and the Apus

The Inca account of the pachamama and the apus is stated in the Comentarios Reales of the Inca
Garcilaso de la Vega and in the Huarochirí Manuscript. The pachamama is the mother earth; it
is the cosmos; it is the sacred. The apus are the mountain spirits; they are the guardians; they
are the powers.
      The account has three features.
81.3. The Position                                                                               943


First feature: the pachamama. The pachamama is the mother earth; it is the cosmos; it
is the sacred. The pachamama is not the soil; it is not the ground; it is not the matter. The
pachamama is the mother; it is the source; it is the life. The pachamama is the sacred; the sacred
is the pachamama; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos. The pachamama is the teotl; the
teotl is the pachamama; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Second feature: the apus. The apus are the mountain spirits; they are the guardians; they
are the powers. The apus are not the mountains; they are not the rocks; they are not the stones.
The apus are the spirits; they are the guardians; they are the powers. The apus are in the
mountains; they are in the heights; they are in the peaks. The apus are the spirits; the spirits
are the apus; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the cosmos. The cosmos is the cosmos; it is the world; it is the sacred. The
cosmos is not the collection; it is not the sum; it is not the totality. The cosmos is the sacred; it
is the living; it is the moving. The cosmos is the pachamama; the pachamama is the cosmos; the
two are the two aspects of the sacred. The cosmos is the apus; the apus are the cosmos; the two
are the two aspects of the sacred.


81.3.5    Inca: The Hanan and Hurin

The Inca account of the hanan and hurin is stated in the Comentarios Reales and in the
Huarochirí Manuscript. The hanan is the upper half; it is the high; it is the masculine. The
hurin is the lower half; it is the low; it is the feminine.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the hanan. The hanan is the upper half; it is the high; it is the masculine.
The hanan is not the lower; it is not the low; it is not the feminine. The hanan is the high; it is
the masculine; it is the upper. The hanan is the half; the half is the hanan; the two are the two
aspects of the cosmos. The hanan is the teotl; the teotl is the hanan; the two are the two aspects
of the sacred.


Second feature: the hurin. The hurin is the lower half; it is the low; it is the feminine. The
hurin is not the upper; it is not the high; it is not the masculine. The hurin is the low; it is the
feminine; it is the lower. The hurin is the half; the half is the hurin; the two are the two aspects
of the cosmos. The hurin is the pachamama; the pachamama is the hurin; the two are the two
aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the two halves. The two halves are the two halves; they are the two principles;
they are the two aspects. The two halves are not the one; they are not the same; they are not
the identity. The two halves are the hanan and the hurin; the hanan and the hurin are the
two halves; the two are the two aspects of the cosmos. The two halves are the complement; the
complement is the two halves; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.

81.3.6      Inca: The Ayni

81.3.7      Contemporary Latin America: The Philosophy of Liberation
The philosophy of liberation is stated in Dussel’s Philosophy of Liberation (1977) and in his
Ethics of Liberation (1998). The philosophy of liberation is the philosophy of the poor; it is the
philosophy of the oppressed; it is the philosophy of the other.
      The philosophy has three features.

First feature: the liberation. The liberation is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation
of the oppressed; it is the liberation of the other. The liberation is not the development; it is not
the modernization; it is not the progress. The liberation is the critique of the colonial reason; it
is the affirmation of the other; it is the ethics of the liberation. The liberation is the teotl; the
teotl is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Second feature: the poor. The poor is the poor; he is the oppressed; he is the other. The
poor is not the rich; he is not the oppressor; he is not the same. The poor is the other; the other
is the poor; the two are the two aspects of the liberation. The poor is the teotl; the teotl is the
poor; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Third feature: the other. The other is the other; he is the poor; he is the oppressed. The
other is not the same; he is not the rich; he is not the oppressor. The other is the other; the
other is the poor; the two are the two aspects of the liberation. The other is the teotl; the teotl
is the other; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

   “The liberation is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation of the oppressed; it is the

81.3.8       Contemporary Latin America: The Dependency Theory
The dependency theory is stated in the works of Raúl Prebisch, Theotônio dos Santos, and Andre
Gunder Frank. The dependency theory is the theory of the dependency; it is the theory of the
periphery; it is the theory of the exploitation.
   The theory has three features.

First feature: the dependency. The dependency is the dependency of the periphery on the
center; it is the dependency of the poor on the rich; it is the dependency of the oppressed on the
oppressor. The dependency is not the development; it is not the modernization; it is not the
progress. The dependency is the exploitation; it is the domination; it is the oppression. The
dependency is the teotl; the teotl is the dependency; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Second feature: the periphery. The periphery is the periphery; it is the poor; it is the
oppressed. The periphery is not the center; it is not the rich; it is not the oppressor. The
periphery is the other; the other is the periphery; the two are the two aspects of the liberation.
The periphery is the teotl; the teotl is the periphery; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Third feature: the center. The center is the center; it is the rich; it is the oppressor. The
center is not the periphery; it is not the poor; it is not the oppressed. The center is the same;
the same is the center; the two are the two aspects of the domination. The center is the teotl;
the teotl is the center; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

81.3.9       Contemporary Latin America: The Theology of Liberation
The theology of liberation is stated in Gutiérrez’s A Theology of Liberation (1971). The theology
of liberation is the theology of the poor; it is the theology of the oppressed; it is the theology of
the other.
   The theology has three features.

First feature: the liberation. The liberation is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation
of the oppressed; it is the liberation of the other. The liberation is not the development; it is not
the modernization; it is not the progress. The liberation is the critique of the colonial reason; it
is the affirmation of the other; it is the ethics of the liberation. The liberation is the teotl; the
teotl is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.

Second feature: the poor. The poor is the poor; he is the oppressed; he is the other. The
poor is not the rich; he is not the oppressor; he is not the same. The poor is the other; the other
is the poor; the two are the two aspects of the liberation. The poor is the teotl; the teotl is the
poor; the two are the two aspects of the truth.
946                                  Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


Third feature: the God. The God is the God of the poor; he is the God of the oppressed; he
is the God of the other. The God is not the God of the rich; he is not the God of the oppressor;
he is not the God of the same. The God is the other; the other is the God; the two are the two
aspects of the liberation. The God is the teotl; the teotl is the God; the two are the two aspects
of the truth.


81.3.10      Contemporary Latin America: The Decolonial Turn

The decolonial turn is stated in Quijano’s “Coloniality of Power, Eurocentrism, and Latin
America” (2000) and in Mignolo’s The Darker Side of Western Modernity (2011). The decolonial
turn is the critique of the coloniality; it is the affirmation of the decolonial; it is the project of
the liberation.
      The turn has three features.


First feature: the coloniality. The coloniality is the coloniality of power; it is the coloniality
of knowledge; it is the coloniality of being. The coloniality is not the colonialism; it is not the
past; it is not the history. The coloniality is the present; it is the actual; it is the living. The
coloniality is the teotl; the teotl is the coloniality; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


Second feature: the decolonial. The decolonial is the decolonial; it is the critique; it is the
liberation. The decolonial is not the colonial; it is not the domination; it is not the oppression.
The decolonial is the other; the other is the decolonial; the two are the two aspects of the
liberation. The decolonial is the teotl; the teotl is the decolonial; the two are the two aspects of
the truth.


Third feature: the liberation. The liberation is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation
of the oppressed; it is the liberation of the other. The liberation is not the development; it is not
the modernization; it is not the progress. The liberation is the critique of the colonial reason; it
is the affirmation of the other; it is the ethics of the liberation. The liberation is the teotl; the
teotl is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the truth.


81.4       Internal Disputes

The interpretation of the Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy is disputed,
and the disputes matter for the dialogue.


First dispute: the status of teotl. The traditional reading takes teotl to be a metaphysical
reality: it is the sacred power; it is the divine; it is the cosmos. A revisionary reading takes it
to be a cultural concept: it is a way of speaking about the sacred; it is not a reality. The two
readings disagree on whether the Aztec tradition is a metaphysics or a cultural studies, and
the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a
structural realism, not a cultural studies.
81.5. Points of Convergence                                                                       947


Second dispute: the status of pachamama. The traditional reading takes pachamama to
be a metaphysical reality: it is the mother earth; it is the cosmos; it is the sacred. A revisionary
reading takes it to be an ecological concept: it is a way of speaking about the environment; it is
not a reality. The two readings disagree on whether the Inca tradition is a metaphysics or an
ecology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
manifestation is real, not a concept.

Third dispute: the status of the liberation. The traditional reading takes the liberation
to be a political reality: it is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation of the oppressed; it
is the liberation of the other. A revisionary reading takes it to be a theological concept: it is
the liberation of the God; it is the liberation of the faith; it is not a political reality. The two
readings disagree on whether the contemporary Latin American philosophy is a politics or a
theology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, neither a politics nor a theology.
   The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If the Aztec tradition is a metaphysics, the
framework’s dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of
teotl. If the contemporary Latin American philosophy is a politics, the dialogue is a dialogue
between a structural realism and a politics of liberation. The framework holds that the first
reading is closer to the Florentine Codex, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states
the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


81.5      Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With the Aztec tradition. The framework shares three structural features with the
   Aztec position.

       1. The sacred. The Aztec tradition holds that teotl is the sacred power; it is the divine;
          it is the cosmos. The framework holds that the structure is the invariance; it is the
          condition; it is the ground. Both hold that there is a sacred, and that the sacred is
          the cosmos.

       2. The movement. The Aztec tradition holds that ollin is the movement; it is the change;
          it is the life. The framework holds that the expression is the structural tendency; it
          is the change; it is the manifestation. Both hold that there is a movement, and that
          the movement is the life.

       3. The rootedness. The Aztec tradition holds that neltiliztli is the rootedness; it is the
          truth; it is the foundation. The framework holds that the structure is the ground; it
          is the truth; it is the condition. Both hold that there is a rootedness, and that the
          rootedness is the truth.

   With the Inca tradition. The framework shares three structural features with the Inca
   position.
948                               Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


      1. The mother earth. The Inca tradition holds that pachamama is the mother earth; it
        is the cosmos; it is the sacred. The framework holds that the structure is the ground;
        it is the condition; it is the source. Both hold that there is a mother earth, and that
        the mother earth is the sacred.

      2. The mountain spirits. The Inca tradition holds that the apus are the mountain
        spirits; they are the guardians; they are the powers. The framework holds that the
        manifestations are the appearances of the identity; they are the expressions of the
        structure; they are the presences. Both hold that there are mountain spirits, and
        that the mountain spirits are the powers.

      3. The reciprocity. The Inca tradition holds that the ayni is the reciprocity; it is the
        exchange; it is the relation. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the
        reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it is the reading of
        the structure. Both hold that there is a reciprocity, and that the reciprocity is the
        relation.

  With the contemporary Latin American philosophy. The framework shares three
  structural features with the contemporary Latin American position.

      1. The liberation. The contemporary Latin American philosophy holds that the lib-
        eration is the liberation of the poor; it is the liberation of the oppressed; it is the
        liberation of the other. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading
        of the manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it is the reading of the structure.
        Both hold that there is a liberation, and that the liberation is the truth.

      2. The dependency. The contemporary Latin American philosophy holds that the
        dependency is the dependency of the periphery on the center; it is the dependency
        of the poor on the rich; it is the dependency of the oppressed on the oppressor. The
        framework holds that the manifestation is the appearance of the identity; it is the
        expression of the structure; it is the presence of the identity. Both hold that there is
        a dependency, and that the dependency is the exploitation.

      3. The decolonial. The contemporary Latin American philosophy holds that the de-
        colonial is the critique of the coloniality; it is the affirmation of the other; it is the
        project of the liberation. The framework holds that the reconstruction is the reading
        of the manifestations; it is the reading of the other; it is the reading of the structure.
        Both hold that there is a decolonial, and that the decolonial is the liberation.

81.7      The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  The Aztec tradition’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural
  invariance, and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural
  invariance is not teotl; it is a pattern. Teotl is the sacred power; it is the divine; it is the
  cosmos. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not teotl. The framework’s
  ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of teotl.
  The Inca tradition’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the
  realms are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels;
  they are the levels of the pachamama; they are the levels of the apus. The framework’s
  realms are not levels of the pachamama; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is
  an ontology of levels, not of the pachamama.
  The contemporary Latin American philosophy’s objection. The framework says
  that knowledge is reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge
  is the liberation; it is the critique of the colonial reason; it is the ethics of the other.
  The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the liberation. The framework’s
  epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the liberation.
81.8. The Framework’s Reply                                                                      951


81.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to the Aztec tradition’s objection. The framework agrees that teotl is the
   sacred power, and it agrees that teotl is the cosmos. But the framework denies that its
   identity is only a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one
   source—a *this*, in the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity
   in its realm. The framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under
   which a thing is one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework
   calls *act*. The distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a
   concrete act); the framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to the Inca tradition’s objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
   not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the pachamama. The framework’s realms are ontological
   levels; they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the
   pachamama. The distinction is between a level of the pachamama (a sacred level) and a
   level of manifestation (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to the contemporary Latin American philosophy’s objection. The frame-
   work agrees that the knowledge is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a
   dimension of knowledge that the concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that
   the knowledge must be the liberation. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject.
   The distinction is between a liberation (a critique) and a reconstruction (a reading); the
   framework holds the second, not the first.



81.9     The Cost of Each Side
The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.

The Aztec tradition’s cost. If the Aztec tradition accepts the framework’s reply, it must give
up the claim that teotl is the sacred power. It must accept that the structure is the condition,
and that teotl is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of teotl: teotl is no longer
the sacred power; the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that neltiliztli is
the rootedness; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the
reconstruction is the structural reading.

The Inca tradition’s cost. If the Inca tradition accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up
the claim that pachamama is the mother earth. It must accept that the structure is the condition,
and that pachamama is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of pachamama:
pachamama is no longer the mother earth; the structure is the condition. It must also give up
the claim that the ayni is the reciprocity; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading
of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.
952                                Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


The contemporary Latin American philosophy’s cost. If the contemporary Latin Ameri-
can philosophy accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim that the liberation is the
liberation of the poor. It must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the liberation
is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the liberation: the liberation is no
longer the liberation of the poor; the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim
that the decolonial is the critique of the coloniality; it must accept that the reconstruction is the
reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of the three traditions, it
must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a dimension
of reality—the dimension of teotl, of pachamama, of the liberation—that its ontology does not
capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not teotl, and the framework leaves teotl to a separate
inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that the Aztec tradition’s teotl,
the Inca tradition’s pachamama, and the contemporary Latin American philosophy’s liberation
are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure does not capture.
The three traditions must accept that the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural
condition that teotl, pachamama, and the liberation presuppose as their condition. The cost
of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the four are not rivals, they are
complements, and each is incomplete without the others.


81.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Aztec). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for the Aztec term “teotl.” If one substitutes “teotl” for “identity” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted
   by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; teotl is the sacred power, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the sacred. The framework’s identity is multiple; teotl is one.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Aztec term “neltiliztli.”
   If one substitutes “neltiliztli” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   neltiliztli is the rootedness. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; neltiliztli is
   sacred. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Inca). The framework’s term “identity” is not substitutable
   for the Inca term “pachamama.” If one substitutes “pachamama” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
81.11. Open Questions                                                                           953


   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; pachamama is the mother earth,
   and it is not manifested, because it is the sacred. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   pachamama is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Inca term “ayni.” If
   one substitutes “ayni” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements, the statements
   change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations; ayni is the
   reciprocity. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; ayni is social. The substitution
   fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (contemporary Latin America). The framework’s term
  “identity” is not substitutable for the contemporary Latin American term “the liberation.”
   If one substitutes “the liberation” for “identity” in the framework’s statements, the
   statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source,
   and it is manifested in a realm; the liberation is the liberation of the poor, and it is
   not manifested, because it is the liberation. The framework’s identity is multiple; the
   liberation is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the contemporary Latin
   American term “the decolonial.” If one substitutes “the decolonial” for “reconstruction”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction
   is a reading of the manifestations; the decolonial is the critique of the coloniality. The
   framework’s reconstruction is structural; the decolonial is political. The substitution fails,
   and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and the Aztec tradition
   is resemblance: both hold that there is a sacred, and they differ on whether the sacred
   is teotl or the structure. The relation between the framework and the Inca tradition is
   resemblance: both hold that there is a mother earth, and they differ on whether the
   mother earth is pachamama or the structure. The relation between the framework and
   the contemporary Latin American philosophy is resemblance: both hold that there is a
   liberation, and they differ on whether the liberation is the liberation of the poor or the
   reconstruction of the identity. Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither
   is identity. The framework’s reading of the three traditions would be refuted by showing
   that their positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between
   structure and teotl, or between structure and pachamama, or between structure and the
   liberation—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the structural condition
   from teotl, pachamama, and the liberation, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of their own.



81.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Aztec teotl, the Inca
pachamama, or the contemporary Latin American liberation, or is it a departure from all
954                                Chapter 81. Aztec, Inca, and Contemporary Latin American


three? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the argument is not conclusive. A
reader who holds that the Aztec teotl is already a structural condition, or that the Inca pachamama
is already a structural condition, or that the contemporary Latin American liberation is already
a structural condition, has a question the chapter leaves open.

Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.

Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Florentine Codex, the Popol Vuh, the
Comentarios Reales, the Huarochirí Manuscript, and the works of Dussel, Gutiérrez, Quijano,
and Mignolo do justice to the texts? The chapter has used teotl, ollin, the tonalli and the
teyolia, the neltiliztli, pachamama, the apus, the hanan and hurin, the ayni, the liberation, the
dependency, the theology of liberation, and the decolonial turn, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a cosmos and a liberation—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the cosmos that is sacred, or the liberation that is political? Is the truth the
81.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                             955


teotl that is the sacred, or the reconstruction that reads? What does your answer tell you about
the relation between the Aztec teotl, the Inca pachamama, the contemporary Latin American
liberation, and the framework’s identity?

Part XIII is now complete. The dialogues with the three great traditions of African and Latin
American philosophy—the Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub, the contemporary African philosophy,
and the Aztec, Inca, and contemporary Latin American philosophy—have been stated. Part XIV
turns to other traditions. The first dialogue is with Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism, on the
dualism and the cosmic struggle; and the last with Gnosticism and Hermeticism, on the gnosis
and the cosmos. The African and Latin American traditions have asked what the community is,
and what the liberation is; the other traditions will ask what the dualism is, and what the gnosis
is.

Other Traditions

Chapter 82

Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism


Scope. This chapter opens Part XIV, the dialogues with the other traditions, and it opens it
with two dualist traditions of ancient Iran: Zoroastrianism, the religion founded by Zarathustra
(c. 1500–1000 BCE), known in the tradition as the prophet of the one God, Ahura Mazda; and
Manichaeism, the religion founded by Mani (216–274 CE), known in the tradition as the prophet
of the two principles. It states the Zoroastrian account of Ahura Mazda and the Amesha Spentas
(the holy immortals), the cosmic dualism of asha (truth and order) and druj (falsehood and
disorder), the doctrine of the two spirits (spenta mainyu and angra mainyu), the freedom of the
human will, and the eschatology of the renovation (frashokereti); and it states the Manichaean
account of the two principles (the Father of Greatness and the King of Darkness), the cosmic
struggle, the doctrine of the three times (past, present, future), the doctrine of the light and the
darkness, the elect and the hearers, and the eschatology of the separation; with reference to the
Gathas of Zarathustra, the Avesta, the Bundahishn, and the Denkard; and the Cologne Mani
Codex, the Kephalaia, the Shabuhragan, and the Psalms of the Bema; it identifies the internal
disputes within the interpretation of the two traditions; it states the points of convergence and
divergence with the framework, whose account of the dualism and of the cosmic struggle is the
nearest Iranian analogue to theirs; it presents the objections that the two traditions would raise
against the framework; it presents the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the
other; it states the kind of relation; and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It
makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “dualism,” “the
two principles,” “the two spirits,” “the cosmic struggle,” “light and darkness,” “renovation,” or
“separation,” these are the terms of the two traditions, and their sense is fixed by the texts and
by the interpretive tradition, not by the framework.


82.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is standing in a field. She sees the wheat growing; she sees the weeds
growing; she sees the two together. She asks: why is there both wheat and weed? If the world
were created by the good, why is there evil? If the world were created by the evil, why is there
good? The two are mixed; the two are together; the two are intertwined. Zoroaster answers:
there are two spirits; the one is the holy; the other is the evil. The holy spirit creates the life; the
evil spirit creates the death. The two are at war; the two are in struggle; the two are in conflict.
The human is free; the human can choose; the human can side with the holy or with the evil.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the wheat and the weed are, or why
they are mixed, but what the light and the darkness are. Mani answers: the light is the good; the
darkness is the evil. The light is the Father of Greatness; the darkness is the King of Darkness.
The two are the two principles; the two are the two substances; the two are the two roots. The

                                                  957
958                                               Chapter 82. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism


two are not the same; the two are not the one; the two are the two. The two are at war; the
two are in struggle; the two are in conflict. The light is mixed with the darkness; the light is
imprisoned in the darkness; the light is to be liberated from the darkness.
      Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the wheat and the weed
are, or what the light and the darkness are, but what the cosmos is. The cosmos is the field of
the struggle; it is the arena of the conflict; it is the place of the war. The cosmos is not the
peace; it is not the harmony; it is not the rest. The cosmos is the struggle; the struggle is the
cosmos; the two are the two aspects of the war. The cosmos is the mixture; the mixture is the
cosmos; the two are the two aspects of the struggle. The cosmos is the light and the darkness;
the light and the darkness are the cosmos; the two are the two aspects of the war.
      The scene is the image of the two traditions, in the Gathas and in the Kephalaia, of the
structure of the dualism and the cosmic struggle. The wheat and the weed are the two spirits;
the light and the darkness are the two principles; the cosmos is the struggle. The scene poses
the question that Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism were the first to pose in its full form in the
Iranian tradition. What is the dualism? What is the struggle? And what is the cosmos? The
present chapter states the two answers, and the framework’s dialogue with them.



82.2       The Question

The previous part stated the positions of African and Latin American philosophy: the Egyptian
wisdom and Zara Yaqub, the contemporary African philosophy, and the Aztec, Inca, and
contemporary Latin American philosophy. The African and Latin American traditions have
asked what the community is, and what the liberation is. The present part turns to the other
traditions, and its first dialogue is with Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism. The Iranian tradition
has asked what the dualism is, and what the cosmic struggle is. The present chapter states the
two positions, and the framework’s dialogue with them.
      The question is not whether Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism were right. The question is
what they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them.
The question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism hold? The chapter
states the Zoroastrian Ahura Mazda and the Amesha Spentas, the cosmic dualism of asha and
druj, the two spirits, the freedom of the will, and the eschatology of the renovation; and it states
the Manichaean two principles, the cosmic struggle, the three times, the light and the darkness,
the elect and the hearers, and the eschatology of the separation, with reference to the Gathas, the
Avesta, the Bundahishn, the Denkard, the Cologne Mani Codex, the Kephalaia, the Shabuhragan,
and the Psalms of the Bema.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two traditions converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two traditions would raise against the framework.
82.3. The Position                                                                                  959


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
traditions? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.


82.3      The Position

82.3.1     Zoroastrianism: Ahura Mazda and the Amesha Spentas
The Zoroastrian account of Ahura Mazda and the Amesha Spentas is stated in the Gathas of
Zarathustra and in the Avesta. Ahura Mazda is the one God; he is the wise lord; he is the creator.
The Amesha Spentas are the holy immortals; they are the aspects of God; they are the powers
of God.
   The account has three features.

First feature: Ahura Mazda. Ahura Mazda is the one God; he is the wise lord; he is the
creator. Ahura Mazda is not the many gods; he is not the idols; he is not the creatures. Ahura
Mazda is the one; he is the source; he is the truth. Ahura Mazda is the good; the good is Ahura
Mazda; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. Ahura Mazda is the light; the light is Ahura
Mazda; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.

Second feature: the Amesha Spentas. The Amesha Spentas are the holy immortals; they
are the aspects of God; they are the powers of God. The Amesha Spentas are not the many gods;
they are not the idols; they are not the creatures. The Amesha Spentas are the aspects; they
are the powers; they are the manifestations. The Amesha Spentas are the Vohu Manah (the
good mind), the Asha Vahishta (the best truth), the Khshathra Vairya (the desirable dominion),
the Spenta Armaiti (the holy devotion), the Haurvatat (the wholeness), and the Ameretat (the
immortality). The Amesha Spentas are the powers; the powers are the Amesha Spentas; the two
are the two aspects of the sacred.

Third feature: the creation. The creation is the work of Ahura Mazda; it is the production
of the world; it is the formation of the cosmos. The creation is not the emanation; it is not the
necessity; it is not the accident. The creation is the act of Ahura Mazda; the act is the creation;
the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The creation is the good; the good is the creation; the
two are the two aspects of the sacred.

   From the Tradition

82.3.4    Zoroastrianism: The Freedom of the Will

The Zoroastrian account of the freedom of the will is stated in the Gathas and in the Avesta. The
freedom of the will is the capacity of the human; it is the power of the choice; it is the ground of
the responsibility.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the freedom. The freedom is the capacity of the human; it is the power of
the choice; it is the ground of the responsibility. The freedom is not the absence of the causes; it
is not the absence of the determination; it is the power of the choice; it is the capacity of the

Second feature: the choice. The choice is the act of the will; it is the decision of the person;

act of the will; it is the decision of the person. The choice is the ground of the responsibility;
the responsibility is the consequence of the choice. The choice is the human; the human is the
choice; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The choice is the good; the good is the choice;
the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the responsibility. The responsibility is the consequence of the freedom; it
is the result of the choice; it is the ground of the reward and the punishment. The responsibility
is not the burden; it is not the weight; it is the dignity; it is the honor. The responsibility is the

82.4      Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism is disputed, and the disputes matter for
the dialogue.
966                                                 Chapter 82. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism


First dispute: the status of the dualism. The traditional reading takes the dualism to
be a metaphysical reality: it is the two principles; it is the two substances; it is the two roots.
A revisionary reading takes it to be a symbolic expression: it is a way of speaking about the
good and the evil; it is not a reality. The two readings disagree on whether the two traditions
are a metaphysics or a symbolism, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue,
because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a symbolism.

Second dispute: the status of the two spirits. The traditional reading takes the two
spirits to be real entities: the spenta mainyu is the holy spirit; the angra mainyu is the evil
spirit. A revisionary reading takes them to be aspects of the one God: the spenta mainyu is
the creative aspect; the angra mainyu is the destructive aspect. The two readings disagree
on whether Zoroastrianism is a dualism or a monism, and the disagreement matters for the
framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s manifestation is real, not an aspect.

Third dispute: the status of the cosmic struggle. The traditional reading takes the
cosmic struggle to be a real event: it is the war of the light and the darkness; it is the conflict of
the two principles. A revisionary reading takes it to be a myth: it is a way of speaking about the
human condition; it is not a real event. The two readings disagree on whether Manichaeism is a
cosmology or a mythology, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because
the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a mythology.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Zoroastrianism is a dualism, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a dualism. If Manichaeism is
a cosmology, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a cosmology. The
framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Gathas, but it does not rest its case on
this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is compatible with either reading.


82.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Zoroastrianism. The framework shares three structural features with the Zoroas-
   trian position.

        1. The dualism. Zoroastrianism holds that there is a dualism of asha and druj; it is the
           dualism of the truth and the falsehood; it is the dualism of the order and the disorder.
           The framework holds that there is a dualism of the identity and the manifestation; it
           is the dualism of the structure and the appearance; it is the dualism of the invariance
           and the expression. Both hold that there is a dualism, and that the dualism is the
           cosmos.

        2. The struggle. Zoroastrianism holds that there is a struggle of the two spirits; it is
           the war of the good and the evil; it is the conflict of the light and the darkness. The
           framework holds that there is a struggle of the identity and the manifestation; it is
           the tension of the structure and the appearance; it is the conflict of the invariance
82.6. Points of Divergence                                                                        967


         and the expression. Both hold that there is a struggle, and that the struggle is the
         cosmos.

       3. The renovation. Zoroastrianism holds that there is a renovation of the world; it is
         the restoration of the cosmos; it is the victory of the good. The framework holds
         that there is a reconstruction of the identity; it is the restoration of the structure; it
         is the victory of the invariance. Both hold that there is a renovation, and that the
         renovation is the sacred.

   With Manichaeism. The framework shares three structural features with the Manichaean
   position.

       1. The two principles. Manichaeism holds that there are two principles: the Father
         of Greatness and the King of Darkness; they are the light and the darkness; they
         are the good and the evil. The framework holds that there are two principles: the
         identity and the manifestation; they are the structure and the appearance; they are
         the invariance and the expression. Both hold that there are two principles, and that
         the two principles are the cosmos.

       2. The mixture. Manichaeism holds that there is a mixture of the light and the darkness;
         it is the mixture of the two principles; it is the mixture of the two substances. The
         framework holds that there is a mixture of the identity and the manifestation; it is
         the mixture of the structure and the appearance; it is the mixture of the invariance
         and the expression. Both hold that there is a mixture, and that the mixture is the
         cosmos.

       3. The separation. Manichaeism holds that there is a separation of the light and the
         darkness; it is the separation of the two principles; it is the separation of the two
         substances. The framework holds that there is a separation of the identity and the
         manifestation; it is the separation of the structure and the appearance; it is the
         separation of the invariance and the expression. Both hold that there is a separation,
         and that the separation is the sacred.

82.7     The Tradition’s Objections

   The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

   Zoroastrianism’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
   and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
   not asha; it is a pattern. Asha is the truth; asha is the order; asha is the cosmos. The
   framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not asha. The framework’s ontology is
   an ontology of patterns, not of asha.
   Manichaeism’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
   are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
   are the levels of the light; they are the levels of the darkness. The framework’s realms are
   not levels of the light; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of
   levels, not of the light.
   Manichaeism’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
   it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the separation; it is the liberation
   of the light; it is the victory of the good. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it
   is not the separation. The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction,
   not of the separation.



82.8     The Framework’s Reply

   The Framework’s Reply

   Reply to Zoroastrianism’s objection. The framework agrees that asha is the truth,
   and it agrees that asha is the order. But the framework denies that its identity is only a
   pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in
   the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
   framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is
   one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The
   distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the
   framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
   Reply to Manichaeism’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
   not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
   denies that the realms are levels of the light. The framework’s realms are ontological levels;
   they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the light.
   The distinction is between a level of the light (a cosmic level) and a level of manifestation
  (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
   Reply to Manichaeism’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
   is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
   concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the
   separation. The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the
970                                               Chapter 82. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism


   manifestations; it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between
   a separation (a liberation) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the
   second, not the first.



82.9     The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.


Zoroastrianism’s cost. If Zoroastrianism accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the
claim that asha is the truth. It must accept that the structure is the condition, and that asha is
a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of asha: asha is no longer the truth; the
structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that the two spirits are the two spirits;
it must accept that the identity and the manifestation are the two conditions; the two conditions
are the structure and the appearance.


Manichaeism’s cost. If Manichaeism accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the
claim that the two principles are the two substances. It must accept that the identity and the
manifestation are the two conditions, and that the two conditions are the structure and the
appearance. The cost is the loss of the two substances: the two substances are no longer the two
principles; the structure and the appearance are the two conditions. It must also give up the
claim that the separation is the liberation; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading
of the manifestations; the reconstruction is the structural reading.


The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Zoroastrianism and
Manichaeism, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there
is a dimension of reality—the dimension of asha, of the two principles, of the separation—that
its ontology does not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account:
the framework’s identity is the enactment of a structure, but not asha, and the framework leaves
asha to a separate inquiry.


The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Zoroastrianism’s asha
and Manichaeism’s two principles are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the
framework’s structure does not capture. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism must accept that
the framework’s structure is not a pattern; it is a structural condition that asha and the two
principles presuppose as their condition. The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of
the opposition: the three are not rivals, they are complements, and each is incomplete without
the others.
82.10. The Kind of Relation                                                                      971


82.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Zoroastrianism). The framework’s term “identity” is not
   substitutable for the Zoroastrian term “asha.” If one substitutes “asha” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; asha is the truth, and it
   is not manifested, because it is the truth. The framework’s identity is multiple; asha is
   one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Zoroastrian term “the
   renovation.” If one substitutes “the renovation” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the renovation is the restoration of the cosmos. The framework’s recon-
   struction is structural; the renovation is eschatological. The substitution fails, and the
   relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The substitution test (Manichaeism). The framework’s term “identity” is not
   substitutable for the Manichaean term “the light.” If one substitutes “the light” for
  “identity” in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity
   is the invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the light is the
   good, and it is not manifested, because it is the light. The framework’s identity is multiple;
   the light is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Manichaean term “the
   separation.” If one substitutes “the separation” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s
   statements, the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the
   manifestations; the separation is the liberation of the light. The framework’s reconstruc-
   tion is structural; the separation is cosmic. The substitution fails, and the relation is
   resemblance, not equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Zoroastrianism is
   resemblance: both hold that there is a dualism, and they differ on whether the dualism is
   asha and druj or the identity and the manifestation. The relation between the framework
   and Manichaeism is resemblance: both hold that there is a mixture, and they differ on
   whether the mixture is the light and the darkness or the identity and the manifestation.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism would be refuted by showing that their
   positions cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure
   and asha, or between structure and the light—by showing, that is, that they already
   distinguish the structural condition from asha and the light, and that the framework’s
   distinction is a development of their own.



82.11      Open Questions
The dialogue leaves three questions open.
972                                               Chapter 82. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Zoroastrian asha or the
Manichaean light, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development,
but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the Zoroastrian asha is already
a structural condition, or that the Manichaean light is already a structural condition, has a
question the chapter leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Gathas, the Avesta, the Bundahishn,
the Denkard, the Cologne Mani Codex, the Kephalaia, the Shabuhragan, and the Psalms of the
Bema do justice to the texts? The chapter has used Ahura Mazda and the Amesha Spentas, the
cosmic dualism of asha and druj, the two spirits, the freedom of the will, the eschatology of the
renovation, the two principles, the cosmic struggle, the three times, the light and the darkness,
the elect and the hearers, and the eschatology of the separation, and it has stated what would
refute its reading. A reader who holds that the texts support a different reading has a question
the chapter leaves open.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that is both a dualism and a struggle—a person, a tradition, a work
of art. Is the thing the dualism of the truth and the falsehood, or the struggle of the light and
the darkness? Is the truth the renovation that restores, or the reconstruction that reads? What
does your answer tell you about the relation between the Zoroastrian asha, the Manichaean light,
and the framework’s identity?

The next chapter turns to Gnosticism and Hermeticism. It states the Gnostic myth of the fall of
the divine spark, the doctrine of the demiurge, the knowledge (gnosis) as the means of salvation,
the elect and the pneumatic; and the Hermetic doctrine of the All and the Nous, the Corpus
Hermeticum, the Asclepius, and the Poimandres; with reference to the Nag Hammadi library, the
Apocryphon of John, the Gospel of Truth, the Corpus Hermeticum, and the Asclepius. It identifies
the internal disputes within the interpretation of the two traditions; and it states the points of
convergence and divergence with the framework, whose account of the gnosis and the cosmos is
the nearest analogue to theirs. The present chapter has stated the answer of Zoroastrianism and
Manichaeism to the problem of the dualism and the struggle; the next chapter states the answer
of Gnosticism and Hermeticism, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
Chapter 83

Gnosticism and Hermeticism


Scope. This chapter closes Part XIV, the dialogues with the other traditions, and it closes it with
two esoteric traditions of late antiquity: Gnosticism, the diverse movement of the first centuries
CE that taught salvation through knowledge (gnosis), and Hermeticism, the tradition of the
Corpus Hermeticum that taught the unity of the cosmos and the ascent of the soul. It states
the Gnostic myth of the divine spark and its fall, the doctrine of the demiurge and the archons,
the knowledge (gnosis) as the means of salvation, the distinction between the pneumatic, the
psychic, and the hylic, and the eschatology of the return of the spark; and it states the Hermetic
doctrine of the All and the Nous, the Poimandres and the ascent of the soul, the doctrine of the
macrocosm and the microcosm, and the path of the rebirth (palingenesia); with reference to the
Nag Hammadi library, the Apocryphon of John, the Gospel of Truth, the Gospel of Philip, the
Corpus Hermeticum, the Asclepius, and the Poimandres; it identifies the internal disputes within
the interpretation of the two traditions; it states the points of convergence and divergence with
the framework, whose account of the gnosis and of the cosmos is the nearest analogue to theirs;
it presents the objections that the two traditions would raise against the framework; it presents
the framework’s reply; it states what each side costs the other; it states the kind of relation;
and it states what would refute the framework’s reading. It makes no normative, ethical, or
evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “gnosis,” “the divine spark,” “the demiurge,” “the
archons,” “the pneumatic,” “the All,” “the Nous,” “the ascent,” or “the rebirth,” these are the
terms of the two traditions, and their sense is fixed by the texts and by the interpretive tradition,
not by the framework.


83.1      A Scene
Consider a person who is sitting in a dark room. She is asleep; she is dreaming; she does not
know that she is dreaming. She dreams that she is awake; she dreams that the room is the world;
she dreams that the darkness is the light. Then she hears a voice; the voice calls her; the voice
awakens her. She opens her eyes; she sees the light; she sees the room; she sees the world. She
knows that she was dreaming; she knows that the darkness was the sleep; she knows that the
light is the waking. The knowledge is the awakening; the awakening is the gnosis; the gnosis is
the salvation.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose she asks not what the dream is, or how she awakens,
but what the spark is. The spark is the divine; it is the light; it is the life. The spark is in her; it
is in the human; it is in the world. The spark is not the body; it is not the mind; it is not the
ego. The spark is the divine; the divine is the spark; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
The spark has fallen; it has fallen into the body; it has fallen into the world; it has fallen into
the darkness. The fall is the imprisonment; the imprisonment is the fall; the two are the two

                                                  974
83.2. The Question                                                                               975


aspects of the suffering. The return is the liberation; the liberation is the return; the two are the
two aspects of the salvation.
   Now consider a third case, hardest of all. Suppose she asks not what the dream is, or what
the spark is, but what the cosmos is. Hermes answers: the cosmos is the All; it is the whole; it is
the one. The cosmos is not the many; it is not the parts; it is not the fragments. The cosmos is
the whole; the whole is the cosmos; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The cosmos is
the Nous; the Nous is the cosmos; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The cosmos is the
macrocosm; the human is the microcosm; the two are the two aspects of the one.
   The scene is the image of the two traditions, in the Apocryphon of John and in the Poimandres,
of the structure of the gnosis and the cosmos. The dream is the ignorance; the spark is the
divine; the cosmos is the All. The scene poses the question that Gnosticism and Hermeticism
were the first to pose in its full form in the late antique tradition. What is the gnosis? What
is the spark? And what is the cosmos? The present chapter states the two answers, and the
framework’s dialogue with them.



83.2     The Question

The previous chapter stated the position of Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism: Ahura Mazda and
the Amesha Spentas, the cosmic dualism of asha and druj, the two spirits, the freedom of the
will, the eschatology of the renovation, the two principles, the cosmic struggle, the three times,
the light and the darkness, the elect and the hearers, and the eschatology of the separation. The
Iranian tradition has asked what the dualism is, and what the cosmic struggle is. The present
chapter states the position of Gnosticism and Hermeticism, and the framework’s dialogue with it.
   The question is not whether Gnosticism and Hermeticism were right. The question is what
they held, what they can say to the framework, and what the framework can say to them. The
question has three parts, and the chapter treats them in turn.


First part: the positions. What did Gnosticism and Hermeticism hold? The chapter states
the Gnostic myth of the divine spark and its fall, the demiurge and the archons, the gnosis,
the three classes, and the eschatology of the return; and it states the Hermetic doctrine of the
All and the Nous, the Poimandres and the ascent, the macrocosm and the microcosm, and the
rebirth, with reference to the Nag Hammadi library, the Apocryphon of John, the Gospel of
Truth, the Gospel of Philip, the Corpus Hermeticum, the Asclepius, and the Poimandres.


Second part: the comparison. Where do the framework and the two traditions converge,
and where do they diverge? The chapter states the points of convergence and divergence, and it
presents the objections that the two traditions would raise against the framework.


Third part: the relation. What is the kind of relation between the framework and the two
traditions? The chapter applies the substitution test, and it states the relation as resemblance,
not equivalence.
