83.3       The Position

83.3.1      Gnosticism: The Divine Spark and Its Fall
The Gnostic account of the divine spark and its fall is stated in the Apocryphon of John and in
the Gospel of Truth. The spark is the divine; it is the light; it is the life. The spark is in the
human; it is in the world; it is in the darkness.
      The account has three features.

First feature: the spark. The spark is the divine; it is the light; it is the life. The spark
is not the body; it is not the mind; it is not the ego. The spark is the divine; the divine is the
spark; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The spark is in the human; it is in the world; it
is in the darkness. The spark is the light; the light is the spark; the two are the two aspects of
the sacred.

Second feature: the fall. The fall is the fall of the spark; it is the fall into the body; it is
the fall into the world; it is the fall into the darkness. The fall is not the creation; it is not the
nature; it is not the necessity. The fall is the imprisonment; the imprisonment is the fall; the two
are the two aspects of the suffering. The fall is the forgetfulness; the forgetfulness is the fall; the
two are the two aspects of the ignorance.

Third feature: the imprisonment. The imprisonment is the imprisonment of the spark; it
is the imprisonment in the body; it is the imprisonment in the world; it is the imprisonment in
the darkness. The imprisonment is not the rest; it is not the peace; it is not the harmony. The
imprisonment is the suffering; the suffering is the imprisonment; the two are the two aspects of
the fall. The imprisonment is the ignorance; the ignorance is the imprisonment; the two are the
two aspects of the darkness.

   From the Tradition

   “The spark is the divine; it is the light; it is the life. The spark has fallen; it has fallen into
   the body; it has fallen into the world; it has fallen into the darkness.” (Apocryphon of
   John, trans. after Robinson)


83.3.2      Gnosticism: The Demiurge and the Archons
The Gnostic account of the demiurge and the archons is stated in the Apocryphon of John and
in the Gospel of Philip. The demiurge is the creator of the world; he is the ignorant; he is the
arrogant. The archons are the rulers of the world; they are the powers; they are the servants of
the demiurge.
      The account has three features.

First feature: the demiurge. The demiurge is the creator of the world; he is the ignorant;
he is the arrogant. The demiurge is not the true God; he is not the good; he is not the light.
The demiurge is the false god; the false god is the demiurge; the two are the two aspects of the
83.3. The Position                                                                                977


ignorance. The demiurge is the creator; the creator is the demiurge; the two are the two aspects
of the error. The demiurge is the Yaldabaoth; the Yaldabaoth is the demiurge; the two are the
two aspects of the error.


Second feature: the archons. The archons are the rulers of the world; they are the powers;
they are the servants of the demiurge. The archons are not the true powers; they are not the
good; they are not the light. The archons are the false powers; the false powers are the archons;
the two are the two aspects of the ignorance. The archons are the rulers; the rulers are the
archons; the two are the two aspects of the error. The archons are the servants; the servants are
the archons; the two are the two aspects of the error.


Third feature: the world. The world is the world; it is the creation; it is the prison. The
world is not the good; it is not the light; it is not the sacred. The world is the prison; the prison
is the world; the two are the two aspects of the fall. The world is the darkness; the darkness is
the world; the two are the two aspects of the ignorance. The world is the error; the error is the
world; the two are the two aspects of the demiurge.


83.3.3    Gnosticism: The Knowledge (Gnosis)

The Gnostic account of the knowledge is stated in the Gospel of Truth and in the Gospel of
Philip. The knowledge (gnosis) is the knowledge of the divine; it is the knowledge of the spark;
it is the knowledge of the self.
   The account has three features.


First feature: the knowledge. The knowledge (gnosis) is the knowledge of the divine; it is
the knowledge of the spark; it is the knowledge of the self. The knowledge is not the reason; it is
not the philosophy; it is not the speculation. The knowledge is the revelation; the revelation is
the knowledge; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The knowledge is the awakening; the
awakening is the knowledge; the two are the two aspects of the salvation.


Second feature: the self. The self is the self; it is the spark; it is the divine. The self is not
the body; it is not the mind; it is not the ego. The self is the spark; the spark is the self; the two
are the two aspects of the sacred. The self is the knowledge; the knowledge is the self; the two
are the two aspects of the salvation. The self is the divine; the divine is the self; the two are the
two aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the salvation. The salvation is the salvation of the spark; it is the liberation
from the body; it is the liberation from the world; it is the liberation from the darkness. The
salvation is not the development; it is not the progress; it is not the evolution. The salvation is
the knowledge; the knowledge is the salvation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The
salvation is the return; the return is the salvation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
978                                                     Chapter 83. Gnosticism and Hermeticism


83.3.4      Gnosticism: The Three Classes

The Gnostic account of the three classes is stated in the Apocryphon of John and in the Gospel
of Philip. The three classes are the pneumatic; they are the spiritual; they are the elect. The
psychic; they are the soulish; they are the intermediate. The hylic; they are the material; they
are the lost.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the pneumatic. The pneumatic is the spiritual; he is the elect; he is the one
who has the gnosis. The pneumatic is not the psychic; he is not the hylic; he is not the lost. The
pneumatic is the spiritual; the spiritual is the pneumatic; the two are the two aspects of the
sacred. The pneumatic is the spark; the spark is the pneumatic; the two are the two aspects of
the sacred.


Second feature: the psychic. The psychic is the soulish; he is the intermediate; he is the
one who has the faith. The psychic is not the pneumatic; he is not the hylic; he is not the lost.
The psychic is the soulish; the soulish is the psychic; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
The psychic is the intermediate; the intermediate is the psychic; the two are the two aspects of
the sacred.


Third feature: the hylic. The hylic is the material; he is the lost; he is the one who has the
ignorance. The hylic is not the pneumatic; he is not the psychic; he is not the saved. The hylic
is the material; the material is the hylic; the two are the two aspects of the darkness. The hylic
is the lost; the lost is the hylic; the two are the two aspects of the darkness.


83.3.5      Gnosticism: The Eschatology of the Return

The Gnostic account of the eschatology of the return is stated in the Gospel of Truth and in the
Gospel of Philip. The return is the return of the spark; it is the return to the divine; it is the
return to the light.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the return. The return is the return of the spark; it is the return to the
divine; it is the return to the light. The return is not the development; it is not the progress; it
is not the evolution. The return is the liberation; the liberation is the return; the two are the
two aspects of the sacred. The return is the salvation; the salvation is the return; the two are
the two aspects of the sacred.


Second feature: the liberation. The liberation is the liberation of the spark; it is the
liberation from the body; it is the liberation from the world; it is the liberation from the darkness.
The liberation is not the imprisonment; it is not the fall; it is not the ignorance. The liberation is
the return; the return is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The liberation
is the knowledge; the knowledge is the liberation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
83.3. The Position                                                                                  979


Third feature: the divine. The divine is the divine; it is the light; it is the life. The divine
is not the demiurge; it is not the archons; it is not the world. The divine is the true God; the
true God is the divine; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The divine is the spark; the
spark is the divine; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


83.3.6     Hermeticism: The All and the Nous
The Hermetic account of the All and the Nous is stated in the Corpus Hermeticum and in the
Poimandres. The All is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one. The Nous is the mind; it is the
intellect; it is the divine.
    The account has three features.

First feature: the All. The All is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one. The All is not
the many; it is not the parts; it is not the fragments. The All is the whole; the whole is the All;
the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The All is the cosmos; the cosmos is the All; the two
are the two aspects of the sacred.

Second feature: the Nous. The Nous is the mind; it is the intellect; it is the divine. The
Nous is not the body; it is not the sense; it is not the passion. The Nous is the mind; the mind
is the Nous; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The Nous is the divine; the divine is the
Nous; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.

Third feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the All and the Nous; it is the
relation of the cosmos and the mind; it is the relation of the whole and the divine. The relation
is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the relation; it is the dialogue. The relation is the
All; the All is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The relation is the Nous;
the Nous is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.

   From the Tradition

   “The All is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one. The Nous is the mind; it is the
   intellect; it is the divine.” (Corpus Hermeticum I.1, trans. after Copenhaver)


83.3.7     Hermeticism: The Poimandres and the Ascent
The Hermetic account of the Poimandres and the ascent is stated in the Poimandres and in the
Corpus Hermeticum. The Poimandres is the shepherd; it is the guide; it is the Nous. The ascent
is the ascent of the soul; it is the return to the divine; it is the union with the Nous.
    The account has three features.

First feature: the Poimandres. The Poimandres is the shepherd; it is the guide; it is
the Nous. The Poimandres is not the man; it is not the teacher; it is not the master. The
Poimandres is the Nous; the Nous is the Poimandres; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.
The Poimandres is the guide; the guide is the Poimandres; the two are the two aspects of the
sacred.
980                                                      Chapter 83. Gnosticism and Hermeticism


Second feature: the ascent. The ascent is the ascent of the soul; it is the return to the
divine; it is the union with the Nous. The ascent is not the descent; it is not the fall; it is not
the imprisonment. The ascent is the liberation; the liberation is the ascent; the two are the two
aspects of the sacred. The ascent is the return; the return is the ascent; the two are the two
aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the union. The union is the union with the Nous; it is the union with the
divine; it is the union with the whole. The union is not the identity; it is not the absorption; it
is not the annihilation. The union is the knowledge; the knowledge is the union; the two are the
two aspects of the sacred. The union is the sacred; the sacred is the union; the two are the two
aspects of the sacred.


83.3.8      Hermeticism: The Macrocosm and the Microcosm

The Hermetic account of the macrocosm and the microcosm is stated in the Corpus Hermeticum
and in the Asclepius. The macrocosm is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one. The microcosm
is the human; it is the part; it is the image.
      The account has three features.


First feature: the macrocosm. The macrocosm is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one.
The macrocosm is not the many; it is not the parts; it is not the fragments. The macrocosm is the
whole; the whole is the macrocosm; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The macrocosm is
the cosmos; the cosmos is the macrocosm; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Second feature: the microcosm. The microcosm is the human; it is the part; it is the image.
The microcosm is not the whole; it is not the one; it is not the cosmos. The microcosm is the
human; the human is the microcosm; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The microcosm
is the image; the image is the microcosm; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Third feature: the relation. The relation is the relation of the macrocosm and the microcosm;
it is the relation of the cosmos and the human; it is the relation of the whole and the part. The
relation is not the identity; it is not the sameness; it is the relation; it is the image. The relation
is the macrocosm; the macrocosm is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The
relation is the microcosm; the microcosm is the relation; the two are the two aspects of the
sacred.


83.3.9      Hermeticism: The Rebirth (Palingenesia)

The Hermetic account of the rebirth is stated in the Corpus Hermeticum and in the Poimandres.
The rebirth (palingenesia) is the rebirth of the soul; it is the transformation; it is the salvation.
      The account has three features.
83.4. Internal Disputes                                                                          981


First feature: the rebirth. The rebirth (palingenesia) is the rebirth of the soul; it is the
transformation; it is the salvation. The rebirth is not the death; it is not the destruction; it is
not the annihilation. The rebirth is the renewal; the renewal is the rebirth; the two are the two
aspects of the sacred. The rebirth is the transformation; the transformation is the rebirth; the
two are the two aspects of the sacred.


Second feature: the transformation. The transformation is the transformation of the soul;
it is the transformation of the human; it is the transformation of the life. The transformation
is not the destruction; it is not the annihilation; it is not the end. The transformation is the
renewal; the renewal is the transformation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred. The
transformation is the rebirth; the rebirth is the transformation; the two are the two aspects of
the sacred.


Third feature: the salvation. The salvation is the salvation of the soul; it is the salvation of
the human; it is the salvation of the life. The salvation is not the death; it is not the destruction;
it is not the annihilation. The salvation is the rebirth; the rebirth is the salvation; the two are
the two aspects of the sacred. The salvation is the transformation; the transformation is the
salvation; the two are the two aspects of the sacred.


83.4        Internal Disputes
The interpretation of Gnosticism and Hermeticism is disputed, and the disputes matter for the
dialogue.


First dispute: the status of the demiurge. The traditional reading takes the demiurge
to be a real entity: he is the creator of the world; he is the ignorant; he is the arrogant. A
revisionary reading takes him to be a symbol: he is a way of speaking about the ignorance; he
is not a real entity. The two readings disagree on whether Gnosticism is a metaphysics or a
symbolism, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s
structure is a structural realism, not a symbolism.


Second dispute: the status of the gnosis. The traditional reading takes the gnosis to be
a real knowledge: it is the knowledge of the divine; it is the knowledge of the spark; it is the
knowledge of the self. A revisionary reading takes it to be an experience: it is the experience
of the awakening; it is not a knowledge. The two readings disagree on whether Gnosticism is a
knowledge or an experience, and the disagreement matters for the framework’s dialogue, because
the framework’s manifestation is real, not an experience.


Third dispute: the status of the All. The traditional reading takes the All to be a
metaphysical reality: it is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one. A revisionary reading takes
it to be a concept: it is a way of speaking about the whole; it is not a reality. The two readings
disagree on whether Hermeticism is a metaphysics or a philosophy, and the disagreement matters
982                                                       Chapter 83. Gnosticism and Hermeticism


for the framework’s dialogue, because the framework’s structure is a structural realism, not a
concept.
      The three disputes matter for the dialogue. If Gnosticism is a metaphysician, the framework’s
dialogue with it is a dialogue between a structural realism and a metaphysics of the spark.
If Hermeticism is a philosophy, the dialogue is a dialogue between a structural realism and a
philosophy of the All. The framework holds that the first reading is closer to the Apocryphon
of John, but it does not rest its case on this reading; it states the dialogue in a way that is
compatible with either reading.


83.5       Points of Convergence

   Points of Convergence

   With Gnosticism. The framework shares three structural features with the Gnostic
   position.

        1. The spark. Gnosticism holds that the spark is the divine; it is the light; it is the life.
           The framework holds that the identity is the invariance; it is the structure; it is the
           condition. Both hold that there is a spark, and that the spark is the divine.

        2. The fall. Gnosticism holds that the spark has fallen; it has fallen into the body;
           it has fallen into the world; it has fallen into the darkness. The framework holds
           that the manifestation is the appearance of the identity; it is the expression of the
           structure; it is the presence of the identity. Both hold that there is a fall, and that
           the fall is the imprisonment.

        3. The return. Gnosticism holds that the return is the return of the spark; it is the
           return to the divine; it is the return to the light. The framework holds that the
           reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the presence;
           it is the reading of the structure. Both hold that there is a return, and that the
           return is the salvation.

   With Hermeticism. The framework shares three structural features with the Hermetic
   position.

        1. The All. Hermeticism holds that the All is the cosmos; it is the whole; it is the one.
           The framework holds that the structure is the whole; it is the one; it is the condition.
           Both hold that there is an All, and that the All is the cosmos.

        2. The Nous. Hermeticism holds that the Nous is the mind; it is the intellect; it is the
           divine. The framework holds that the identity is the structure; it is the invariance;
           it is the condition. Both hold that there is a Nous, and that the Nous is the divine.

        3. The rebirth. Hermeticism holds that the rebirth is the rebirth of the soul; it is the
           transformation; it is the salvation. The framework holds that the reconstruction
83.6. Points of Divergence                                                                        983


          is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the structure; it is the
          realization of the identity. Both hold that there is a rebirth, and that the rebirth is
          the salvation.



83.6      Points of Divergence

   Points of Divergence

   With Gnosticism. The framework diverges from the Gnostic position in three respects.

       1. The status of the spark. Gnosticism holds that the spark is the divine; it is the
          light; it is the life. The framework holds that the identity is the structure; it is
          the condition; it is the ground. The framework’s identity is not the spark; it is the
          structural condition of the manifestation.

       2. The status of the demiurge. Gnosticism holds that the demiurge is the creator of the
         world; he is the ignorant; he is the arrogant. The framework holds that the structure
          is the condition of the manifestation; it is the invariance; it is the ground. The
          framework’s structure is not the demiurge; it is the condition of the manifestation.

       3. The status of the return. Gnosticism holds that the return is the return of the spark;
          it is the return to the divine; it is the return to the light. The framework holds
          that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the
          structure; it is the realization of the identity. The framework’s reconstruction is not
          the return; it is the structural reading.

   With Hermeticism. The framework diverges from the Hermetic position in three
   respects.

       1. The status of the All. Hermeticism holds that the All is the cosmos; it is the whole;
          it is the one. The framework holds that the structure is the whole; it is the one; it is
          the condition. The framework’s structure is not the All; it is the condition of the
          manifestation.

       2. The status of the Nous. Hermeticism holds that the Nous is the mind; it is the
          intellect; it is the divine. The framework holds that the identity is the structure; it
          is the invariance; it is the condition. The framework’s identity is not the Nous; it is
          the structural condition.

       3. The status of the rebirth. Hermeticism holds that the rebirth is the rebirth of the
          soul; it is the transformation; it is the salvation. The framework holds that the
          reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; it is the reading of the structure;
          it is the realization of the identity. The framework’s reconstruction is not the rebirth;
          it is the structural reading.

83.7    The Tradition’s Objections

  The Tradition’s Objections to the Framework

  Gnosticism’s objection. The framework says that identity is a structural invariance,
  and that its manifestations are known by reconstruction. But a structural invariance is
  not the spark; it is a pattern. The spark is the divine; the spark is the light; the spark
  is the life. The framework’s identity is a pattern, and a pattern is not the spark. The
  framework’s ontology is an ontology of patterns, not of the spark.
  Hermeticism’s objection. The framework says that there are seven realms; the realms
  are real; they are the structure of manifestation. But the realms are not just levels; they
  are the levels of the All; they are the levels of the Nous. The framework’s realms are not
  levels of the All; they are just levels. The framework’s ontology is an ontology of levels,
  not of the All.
  Hermeticism’s second objection. The framework says that knowledge is reconstruction;
  it is the reading of the manifestations. But knowledge is the rebirth; it is the transformation;
  it is the salvation. The framework’s knowledge is a reconstruction; it is not the rebirth.
  The framework’s epistemology is an epistemology of reconstruction, not of the rebirth.



83.8    The Framework’s Reply

  The Framework’s Reply

  Reply to Gnosticism’s objection. The framework agrees that the spark is the divine,
  and it agrees that the spark is the light. But the framework denies that its identity is only
  a pattern. The framework’s identity is the invariance enacted by one source—a *this*, in
  the framework’s sense—and the enactment is the *act* of the identity in its realm. The
  framework’s identity is not a pattern; it is the structural condition under which a thing is
  one thing, and the enactment of that condition is what the framework calls *act*. The
  distinction is between a pattern (an abstraction) and an enactment (a concrete act); the
  framework’s identity is the second, not the first.
  Reply to Hermeticism’s first objection. The framework agrees that the realms are
  not just levels, and it agrees that they are levels of the manifestation. But the framework
  denies that the realms are levels of the All. The framework’s realms are ontological levels;
  they are the levels of the manifestation; they are the conditions of possibility of the All.
  The distinction is between a level of the All (a cosmic level) and a level of manifestation
  (an ontological level); the framework holds the second, not the first.
  Reply to Hermeticism’s second objection. The framework agrees that the knowledge
  is not merely conceptual, and it agrees that there is a dimension of knowledge that the
  concepts do not capture. But the framework denies that the knowledge must be the rebirth.
  The framework’s knowledge is the reconstruction; it is the reading of the manifestations;
  it is the presence of the identity to the subject. The distinction is between a rebirth (a
83.9. The Cost of Each Side                                                                     985


   transformation) and a reconstruction (a reading); the framework holds the second, not
   the first.




83.9      The Cost of Each Side

The dialogue has a cost for each side, and the cost must be stated.



Gnosticism’s cost. If Gnosticism accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim
that the spark is the divine. It must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the
spark is a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the spark: the spark is no longer
the divine; the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that the return is the
return of the spark; it must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations;
the reconstruction is the structural reading.



Hermeticism’s cost. If Hermeticism accepts the framework’s reply, it must give up the claim
that the All is the cosmos. It must accept that the structure is the condition, and that the All is
a manifestation of the structure. The cost is the loss of the All: the All is no longer the cosmos;
the structure is the condition. It must also give up the claim that the rebirth is the salvation; it
must accept that the reconstruction is the reading of the manifestations; the reconstruction is
the structural reading.



The framework’s cost. If the framework accepts the objections of Gnosticism and Hermeti-
cism, it must give up the claim that its ontology is complete. It must accept that there is a
dimension of reality—the dimension of the spark, of the All, of the rebirth—that its ontology does
not capture. The cost is the loss of the completeness of the structural account: the framework’s
identity is the enactment of a structure, but not the spark, and the framework leaves the spark
to a separate inquiry.



The cost of the dialogue. If the dialogue is to be a genuine dialogue, each side must accept
that the other has something to say. The framework must accept that Gnosticism’s spark and
Hermeticism’s All are not mistakes; they are dimensions of the real that the framework’s structure
does not capture. Gnosticism and Hermeticism must accept that the framework’s structure is not
a pattern; it is a structural condition that the spark and the All presuppose as their condition.
The cost of the dialogue is the loss of the simplicity of the opposition: the three are not rivals,
they are complements, and each is incomplete without the others.
986                                                    Chapter 83. Gnosticism and Hermeticism


83.10      The Kind of Relation

   The Kind of Relation (Resemblance, Not Equivalence)

   The substitution test (Gnosticism). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for the Gnostic term “the spark.” If one substitutes “the spark” for “identity”
   in the framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the
   invariance enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the spark is the divine,
   and it is not manifested, because it is the spark. The framework’s identity is multiple; the
   spark is one. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Gnostic term “the
   return.” If one substitutes “the return” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   the return is the return of the spark. The framework’s reconstruction is structural; the
   return is eschatological. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The substitution test (Hermeticism). The framework’s term “identity” is not substi-
   tutable for the Hermetic term “the All.” If one substitutes “the All” for “identity” in the
   framework’s statements, the statements change: the framework’s identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source, and it is manifested in a realm; the All is the cosmos, and it is not
   manifested, because it is the cosmos. The framework’s identity is multiple; the All is one.
   The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not equivalence.
   The framework’s term “reconstruction” is not substitutable for the Hermetic term “the
   rebirth.” If one substitutes “the rebirth” for “reconstruction” in the framework’s statements,
   the statements change: the framework’s reconstruction is a reading of the manifestations;
   the rebirth is the transformation of the soul. The framework’s reconstruction is structural;
   the rebirth is spiritual. The substitution fails, and the relation is resemblance, not
   equivalence.
   The kind of relation. The relation between the framework and Gnosticism is resemblance:
   both hold that there is a spark, and they differ on whether the spark is the divine or the
   structure. The relation between the framework and Hermeticism is resemblance: both
   hold that there is an All, and they differ on whether the All is the cosmos or the structure.
   Neither relation is equivalence; neither is agreement; neither is identity. The framework’s
   reading of Gnosticism and Hermeticism would be refuted by showing that their positions
   cannot be formulated without the framework’s distinction between structure and the spark,
   or between structure and the All—by showing, that is, that they already distinguish the
   structural condition from the spark and the All, and that the framework’s distinction is a
   development of their own.




83.11      Open Questions

The dialogue leaves three questions open.
83.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                             987


First question. Is the framework’s identity a development of the Gnostic spark or the Hermetic
All, or is it a departure from both? The chapter has argued that it is a development, but the
argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds that the Gnostic spark is already a structural
condition, or that the Hermetic All is already a structural condition, has a question the chapter
leaves open.


Second question. Can the framework’s expression be stated without the notion of enactment?
The chapter has argued that it cannot, but the argument is not conclusive. A reader who holds
that expression can be stated without an enactment has a question the chapter leaves open.


Third question. Does the framework’s reading of the Apocryphon of John, the Gospel of
Truth, the Gospel of Philip, the Corpus Hermeticum, the Asclepius, and the Poimandres do
justice to the texts? The chapter has used the spark, the demiurge, the archons, the gnosis, the
three classes, the return, the All, the Nous, the Poimandres, the ascent, the macrocosm and the
microcosm, and the rebirth, and it has stated what would refute its reading. A reader who holds
that the texts support a different reading has a question the chapter leaves open.

      The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.



Scope

This chapter states the traditions that the volume mentions in passing, but does not treat in a
full dialogue. It does not offer a comparison of structures, as the dialogues of Parts II–XIV do; it
offers a map of what the volume does not cover, and a statement of why it does not cover it.
It makes no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of a tradition’s
name, it uses the name as a historical and structural label; its sense is fixed by the tradition and
by the interpretive literature, not by the framework.



The Principle of Selection

The volume’s method (Part I) requires that a dialogue satisfy ten criteria of depth: it must
state the tradition’s position with reference to primary texts, identify its internal disputes, state
the points of convergence and divergence, present the tradition’s strongest objections to the
framework, present the framework’s reply, state what each side costs the other, state the kind of
relation, state what would refute the framework’s reading, and state the questions the dialogue
leaves open. A dialogue that satisfies the ten is a full dialogue; a dialogue that fails any of them
is incomplete.
    The selection of traditions for full dialogue has been governed by two considerations.
    First, the framework’s central concepts must have developed in the tradition with sufficient
depth to sustain a dialogue on the ten criteria. The traditions of Parts II–XIV were selected
because they developed the concepts of identity, manifestation, light, mediation, unity and
multiplicity, or the structure of the real with a precision that allowed the ten criteria to be
satisfied.
    Second, the tradition must stand in a relation to the framework that the dialogue could
state with precision. A tradition that developed a concept in a vocabulary entirely alien to
the framework, or that made no claim that the framework could address, would not sustain a
dialogue on the ten criteria.
    These two considerations exclude many traditions, and the exclusions are not judgments of
the traditions’ worth. They are statements of what the volume’s method can and cannot do.
A tradition that is not treated in a full dialogue is not thereby judged inferior; it is a tradition
whose dialogue with the framework the volume has not been able to undertake.

                                                990
                                                                                                991


The Traditions Not Treated
The following traditions are mentioned in passing, and the reader is directed to the primary
texts and to the secondary literature for each. The list is not exhaustive; it names the traditions
whose absence from the volume’s dialogues a reader is most likely to notice.


The Indigenous Philosophies of North America and Oceania

The philosophical traditions of the indigenous peoples of North America and Oceania are among
the oldest living traditions of the world, and they have developed accounts of the relation between
the human being, the land, and the sacred that are of the first philosophical importance. The
framework’s account of the relation between identity, manifestation, and realm (Parts III–IV of
the main book) would have much to learn from these traditions, and a dialogue with them would
be a substantial contribution.
   The volume does not undertake this dialogue, and the reason is stated openly: the volume’s
author does not have the acquaintance with the primary texts and the interpretive literature that
the ten criteria of depth require. A dialogue that summarized these traditions from secondary
sources, without engagement with what the traditions themselves say, would fail the first criterion
of depth (Definition 3.1), and the volume does not offer such a dialogue.
   The reader who wishes to undertake this dialogue is invited to do so; the volume’s method
(Part I) states the criteria that the dialogue would have to satisfy.


The Lesser-Known Schools of the Traditions Covered

The traditions of Parts II–XIV are treated through representative figures and schools, and
each tradition contains schools and thinkers that the dialogues do not treat. The Neoplatonic
commentaries on Aristotle, the Byzantine theological tradition, the Syriac philosophical tradition,
the lesser-known schools of Indian epistemology, the later Confucian and Neo-Confucian thinkers
after Wang Yangming, and the contemporary thinkers of each tradition who are not yet part of
a recognized school—all of these are mentioned in passing, and a full treatment would require a
dialogue of its own.
   The volume’s dialogues state the tradition’s position through the figures and schools that have
shaped its central concepts; they do not claim to be histories of the traditions. The reader who
seeks a fuller history of a tradition is directed to the secondary literature cited in the footnotes.


The Contemporary Philosophers Not Yet Part of a Recognized Tradition

The framework’s dialogues with the contemporary West (Part V) treat the thinkers whose work
has shaped the philosophical landscape: Husserl, Heidegger, Whitehead, Wittgenstein, Quine and
Davidson, Kripke and Lewis, Derrida and Deleuze. The contemporary philosophical landscape
contains many other thinkers whose work is of the first importance, and whose relation to the
framework would be worth stating.
   The volume does not treat them, and the reason is the same as before: a dialogue on the ten
criteria would require an acquaintance with the thinker’s work that the volume does not have,
992                                                Chapter 84. Traditions Mentioned in Passing


and a summary from secondary sources would fail the first criterion. The reader who wishes to
undertake the dialogue is invited to do so.


The African and Latin American Traditions Beyond Those Treated
The volume’s dialogues with African and Latin American philosophy (Part XIII) treat the
Egyptian wisdom and Zara Yaqub, the contemporary African philosophy, and the Aztec, Inca,
and contemporary Latin American philosophy. The traditions of Africa and Latin America are
many, and the volume’s treatment is a selection, not a survey.
      The traditions of the African diaspora, the indigenous philosophies of the Amazon and the
Andes that are not treated in Part XIII, and the contemporary Latin American thinkers whose
work is not part of the liberation and decolonial traditions—all of these are mentioned in passing,
and a full treatment would require a dialogue of its own.


The Kind of Relation Between the Volume and the Traditions
Not Treated
The relation between the volume and the traditions not treated is not one of the four relations
stated in Chapter 2 (identity, equivalence, agreement, resemblance). It is a different relation: the
relation of a comparative inquiry to the traditions it does not compare.
      The relation has three features.
      First, the volume does not state a claim about the traditions not treated. It does not say
that they are correct, incorrect, equivalent to the framework, or resembling it. It says that they
are traditions whose dialogue with the framework has not been undertaken, and it marks the
absence as an open question, not as a verdict.
      Second, the volume does not use the traditions not treated as a ground of justification for
the framework. The framework’s principles are justified by the arguments of the main book, not
by the traditions it compares itself with, and this holds for the traditions it does not compare
itself with as well. The absence of a dialogue with a tradition is not a premise in any argument
of the volume.
      Third, the volume invites the reader to undertake the dialogues it has not undertaken. The
method of Part I states the criteria that the dialogue would have to satisfy; the primary texts and
the secondary literature state the tradition’s position; the dialogue itself would be a contribution
to the inquiry that the volume makes possible.


The Open Questions of the Chapter
The chapter leaves three questions open.
      First question. What is the criterion by which a tradition should be selected for a full
dialogue? The chapter states the two considerations that governed the volume’s selection, but it
does not claim that these are the only considerations. A reader who proposes a different criterion,
or who shows that the volume’s selection fails its own criterion, has a question the chapter leaves
open.
                                                                                                993


   Second question. Can a tradition be treated in a full dialogue without the author’s acquain-
tance with its primary texts? The chapter holds that it cannot, and it states the first criterion of
depth as the reason. A reader who holds that a dialogue can be adequate without primary-text
acquaintance, or who shows that the volume’s own dialogues fall short of the criterion, has a
question the chapter leaves open.
   Third question. What is the relation between the traditions not treated and the framework?
The chapter states that the relation is not one of the four relations of Chapter 2, but it does not
state what the relation is. A reader who proposes a fifth relation, or who shows that the relation
is one of the four after all, has a question the chapter leaves open.


What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not provide a complete list of the traditions not treated. It names the
traditions whose absence a reader is most likely to notice, and it states the principle of selection.
A complete list would be a different undertaking, and it would not serve the chapter’s purpose.
   Second, the chapter does not offer a comparison of the traditions not treated with the
framework. It states the absence of the comparison, and it marks the absence as an open question.
A comparison would be a dialogue, and a dialogue would have to satisfy the ten criteria of depth.
   Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the volume’s selection is adequate.
It states the two considerations that governed the selection, and it invites the reader to assess
the selection by the criteria the chapter states. The assessment is the reader’s task, not the
chapter’s.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a tradition you know that the volume does not treat. What would a dialogue between
the framework and that tradition look like? Which of the ten criteria of depth would the dialogue
satisfy most easily, and which would it satisfy with the greatest difficulty? What does your
answer tell you about the limits of the volume’s method?
   The next chapter turns to the open questions of dialogue. It states the questions that the
volume’s dialogues raise but do not settle, and it marks the horizon that the volume leaves open.
Bibliography


This bibliography lists, for each dialogue, the principal texts on which the dialogue draws. Entries
are keyed by the code [Dn-m], where n is the number of the chapter and m the number of the
source within it. Each entry gives the author, the title, and the date of composition or first
publication; editions and translations are to be cited in the notes of the chapter in which a
passage is quoted. The entries are principal texts, not an exhaustive literature, and the secondary
literature on each tradition is to be added chapter by chapter as the dialogues are revised.

alphabetical order, with the dates that the dialogue uses and the chapter in which the thinker
or tradition is treated. Where a date is traditional or approximate, it is marked as such. The
glossary identifies; it does not summarize, and the reader who wishes to know what a thinker
held is directed to the chapter.

Index of Concepts


The index lists the framework’s concepts and, for each, the dialogues in which the concept
receives sustained discussion. A dialogue is listed under a concept when the chapter names the
concept in its statement of the nearest analogue, or when the concept recurs in the chapter often
enough to be a topic of the dialogue and not a passing term. The thresholds are stated in the
notes to the index; a concept that is named only in passing is not listed. The reader who wishes
to follow a concept through the volume should begin with the dialogues listed here.

Chapter 38, Chapter 41, Chapter 43, Chapter 71, Chapter 79, Chapter 82, Chapter 83

Chapter 36, Chapter 44, Chapter 47, Chapter 50, Chapter 56, Chapter 57, Chapter 60, Chapter 63,
Chapter 67, Chapter 74, Chapter 78, Chapter 82

Chapter 57, Chapter 58, Chapter 60, Chapter 63, Chapter 64, Chapter 67, Chapter 72, Chapter 78,
Chapter 81

ter 43, Chapter 48, Chapter 74

Unity and multiplicity. Chapter 4, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 19, Chapter 20, Chapter 23,
Chapter 36, Chapter 37, Chapter 38, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 52,
Chapter 55, Chapter 61, Chapter 66, Chapter 70, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 76, Chapter 80

Chapter 67, Chapter 69, Chapter 72, Chapter 78, Chapter 79, Chapter 80

Viability. Chapter 31, Chapter 69

Time. Chapter 5, Chapter 10, Chapter 22, Chapter 26, Chapter 27, Chapter 29, Chapter 30,

Notes to the index. The thresholds are, by the number of occurrences in the chapter: light,
ten; mediation, five; unity and multiplicity, ten; time, five; death, four; self-awareness, three;
viability, two; identity, manifestation, and relation and order, forty, since these terms occur in
every dialogue and are listed only where they are the concept at issue or are unusually frequent.
